artigo.texto: 'Let Data Reign': Trump goes all in on controversial data centers Trump argued that data centers will make communities "successful and rich." President Donald Trump on Monday stressed his strong support for controversial data centers, a key issue ahead of midterm elections, with the president urging communities to "let Data Reign." "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign," Trump wrote in a social media post on Monday morning. The president has long emphasized the importance of artificial intelligence advancement, repeatedly expressing his desire for the U.S. to beat China in the global AI race. "If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame. China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement. Actually, they can’t believe it is happening!" Trump wrote. Data centers provide the computing power necessary to process large amounts of data, such as the kind needed to run AI systems. They typically house thousands of computer servers and require tremendous amounts of land, water for cooling, and energy, potentially straining local power grids, while employing few workers long-term, relative to their size. The issue of data centers has been a hot topic ahead of the midterm elections, with AI companies spending millions on congressional races and primaries for and against candidates on the issue of artificial intelligence regulation. Asked on Monday about Trump's post and how it might land ahead of the midterms, Vice President JD Vance said the president's message was focused on the economics around data centers. "What the president said about data centers is they're an important part of the AI economy. But when people build them, they have to build the power plants along with the data centers,” Vance said. Vance acknowledged the backlash surrounding data centers, expressing his belief that the concern stems from higher utility and electricity bills. But he argued that this wouldn't be a problem if companies take advantage of deregulation efforts. "I think probably 99% of the backlash to data centers has come in areas where building a data center means higher utility and higher electricity for the people on the ground," Vance said. "So I think what these companies have to do is take advantage of some of the federal deregulatory efforts that we've undertaken. If you build a data center, you should be putting power back into the grid, not taking it out. And if that is happening, I don't think the data centers are that controversial," Vance said. Earlier this month, the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the Senate GOP's campaign committee, wrote a memo to AI companies operating in Ohio and warned that backlash to data centers could hurt incumbent Republican Sen. John Husted’s chances at reelection. Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott also recently paused new data center projects to ensure compliance -- something that Trump had criticized as a "mistake." "I saw Texas the other day sort of is against data centers. I think it's a mistake. And I’m not taking positions, I just think it’s a mistake, because there are other communities that want it. When a community wants it, it means a lot of money is going to come into that community," Trump had said during a Punchbowl interview earlier this month. In the Punchbowl interview, the president expressed his belief that data centers are "tremendously important for the economics" and said they could be "bigger than oil."

artigo.texto: China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and six other government departments have jointly issued a 15th five-year plan for the development of the new-type battery industry, outlining development targets and key tasks through 2030. Image Source: MIIT Key Takeaways By 2030, China aims to achieve steady growth in the new-type battery industry, with advances in full-chain innovation, new-type battery systems and solid-state battery commercialization. The plan also sets targets of 15,000 cycles for long-life lithium batteries and PPB-level product defect rates for leading companies. The plan outlines 19 key tasks across five major areas, supported by five dedicated programs. On technology innovation, the plan calls for advances in solid-state battery industrialization technologies and next-generation battery systems, while promoting a product portfolio led by lithium batteries alongside sodium-ion and flow batteries and improving battery recycling. At the industry level, the plan calls for digital and green transformation, optimized regional industrial distribution, and stronger standards, testing, certification, intellectual property and carbon-footprint traceability systems. 2030 targets By 2030, the plan targets steady growth in China’s new-type battery industry and continued improvement in innovation across the value chain. It calls for major progress in new-type battery systems and the initial achievement of scaled application of all-solid-state batteries. Long-life lithium batteries are targeted to reach a cycle life of 15,000 cycles, while leading companies are expected to achieve PPB-level product defect rates. The plan also envisions new-type battery technologies supporting electrification across vehicles, ships, aviation, construction machinery and energy storage, with applications expanding on the power-generation and grid sides as well as in industrial parks and data centers. Technology and industrial development The plan identifies frontier technology research as a priority, including efforts to address key technologies for solid-state battery industrialization and to develop next-generation battery systems. It also calls for improvements in industrial software and high-end equipment, alongside a supply system centered on lithium batteries and supported by sodium-ion and flow batteries. The plan further calls for digitalization and green transformation across the industry, the development of green factories and zero-carbon industrial parks, optimized regional industrial distribution, and the cultivation of high-quality enterprise clusters at different stages of development. International cooperation and implementation For international cooperation, the policy encourages battery companies to expand overseas in an orderly manner, strengthen risk controls for overseas investment, establish international industrial cooperation platforms and respond to technical trade barriers in overseas markets. For implementation, the plan calls for stronger coordination among government departments, coordinated financial support, broader financing channels for key companies, deeper integration between industry and education, and a fair and orderly competitive environment.

At CPHI Milan 2026 (Stand 11F25, Packaging & Drug Delivery zone, October 6 to 8), TekniPlex Healthcare will show how its materials science helps pharmaceutical and consumer health companies stay ahead of all three shifts.
The company’s presence at CPHI Milan is built around the theme “Protect the Therapy. Enable the Delivery. Advance the Care”, reflecting how TekniPlex Healthcare’s material science expertise supports pharmaceutical partners and healthcare brands at every stage, from safeguarding sensitive formulations to enabling new delivery mechanisms and improving patient outcomes.
“Pharmaceutical innovation increasingly requires materials to do more from protecting highly sensitive therapies to enabling entirely new ways of delivering them,” saidBrenda Chamulak, CEO of TekniPlex. “At CPHI Milan, we are demonstrating how TekniPlex Healthcare brings material science, manufacturing expertise and application knowledge together to help our customers address these evolving requirements.”
Next-Generation High-Barrier Protection
A key focus at CPHI will be Flexapharm® SBC, TekniPlex Healthcare’s high-barrier pharmaceutical film technology. Designed for moisture and oxygen-sensitive therapies, Flexapharm SBC delivers PCTFE-level moisture protection with superior oxygen barrier performance while providing a PFAS-free alternative to traditional fluoropolymer-based structures.
The thermoformable film is available in multiple coating weights, constructions, substrates and colors, allowing the barrier to be tailored to specific product requirements. Lower processing and sealing temperatures, combined with improved forming performance, can also help manufacturers increase production efficiency and reduce energy use.
Flexapharm SBC’s transparent construction provides product visibility while maintaining high-barrier performance. Its compact high-barrier structures require less material than traditional PCTFE-based films, translating to a significant reduction in carbon footprint alongside reduced transportation, warehousing and storage needs.
Cleaner Materials for Consumer Health Dispensing
The same shift is reaching the components inside consumer health dispensing systems. TekniPlex Healthcare’s ClearCycle+ stem gaskets need no talc or silicone surface treatment, giving manufacturers a non-stick alternative that supports cleaner, more stable and more efficient production. FDA-compliant, ClearCycle+ helps customers meet tighter material requirements without sacrificing line performance.
Enabling the Next Generation of Wearable Drug Delivery
TekniPlex Healthcare will also showcase its flexible film reservoir technology for wearable liquid drug delivery, developed to combine the barrier protection required for sensitive biologics with the flexibility and design freedom needed for next-generation on-body devices.

A demanda global por transporte aéreo de passageiros caiu 0,8% em agosto ante o mesmo mês de 2025, medida em passageiros-quilômetro pagos (RPK), segundo dados divulgados pela Associação Internacional de Transporte Aéreo (Iata). A capacidade, medida em assentos-quilômetro disponíveis (ASK), subiu 0,3% na comparação anual, e a taxa de ocupação ficou em 85,1%, queda de 0,9 ponto porcentual.
A demanda internacional recuou 0,9% em agosto, com capacidade estável (0,0%) e taxa de ocupação de 85,0% (-0,8 ponto). No mercado doméstico, houve queda de 0,5%, com capacidade em alta de 0,7% e ocupação de 85,3% (-1,1 ponto).
A demanda global por transporte aéreo recuou 0,8% em comparação com agosto de 2025, pois a trajetória de recuperação das companhias do Oriente Médio foi interrompida. “As empresas da região reportaram demanda 14,6% menor na comparação anual, revertendo uma tendência de melhora”, afirmou a vice-presidente sênior de sustentabilidade e economista-chefe da Iata, Marie Owens Thomsen.
Ela acrescentou que, excluindo o Oriente Médio, a demanda global por viagens aéreas cresceu 0,6% em agosto na comparação anual, “metade do ritmo” observado em julho.
Segundo Thomsen, a conectividade global foi, em geral, mais fraca no mês, com algumas exceções como o mercado doméstico da China. “Os próximos meses mostrarão se os viajantes, cujo poder de compra foi reduzido pelos preços mais altos de energia, estão ajustando seus orçamentos de viagem e podem ser desencorajados a viajar devido à instabilidade geopolítica”, disse. A executiva afirmou ainda que as programações antecipadas para outubro indicam “otimismo cauteloso”, com crescimento de 2,0% na oferta de assentos.
Por regiões (total, considerando internacional e doméstico), a Iata apontou crescimento de demanda na América Latina e Caribe (+5,3%), África (+4,4%), Ásia-Pacífico (+1,4%) e Europa (+0,7%). Na América do Norte, houve queda de 2,2%. O Oriente Médio registrou recuo de 14,6%, com redução de capacidade de 9,3% e queda de 4,9 pontos na taxa de ocupação, para 78,9%.
No mercado doméstico brasileiro, a demanda avançou 4,3% em agosto, mas a capacidade subiu 8,0%, o que levou a taxa de ocupação a 82,1%, queda de 2,9 pontos porcentuais, segundo os dados.

A Federação Nacional de Seguros Gerais (FenSeg) afirmou, em nota, que a sanção da Lei nº 15.526, que moderniza o marco legal do seguro rural e define a subvenção econômica ao prêmio do seguro rural como despesa obrigatória, representa avanço histórico para a consolidação do instrumento como peça estratégica da política agrícola brasileira.
Segundo a entidade, a legislação sancionada nesta quarta-feira (30) fortalece a previsibilidade do Programa de Subvenção ao Prêmio do Seguro Rural (PSR), aprofunda a integração entre seguro e crédito rural e cria bases para a estruturação do Fundo de Catástrofe. Para a FenSeg, a medida amplia a proteção da produção agropecuária e contribui para disseminar a cultura de gestão de riscos no campo.
A federação avalia que a criação de condições para consolidar o seguro rural como política de Estado oferece horizonte de longo prazo, com menor sujeição a prioridades conjunturais. Em nota, a FenSeg ressaltou que previsibilidade é condição para a sustentabilidade econômica de uma atividade exposta a riscos climáticos crescentes.
A entidade afirmou ainda que um sistema de proteção estável diante de eventos climáticos extremos – como o Super El Niño – permite preservar renda e investimentos, sustentar a capacidade de produção após adversidades e reduzir a dependência de medidas emergenciais para enfrentar perdas no País.

by Alex Baumhardt, Oregon Capital Chronicle
Republican and Democratic lawmakers in Oregon have been meeting in recent weeks to discuss the potential to collaborate on a climate policy that just seven years ago drove them apart, and drove some Senate Republicans across state lines.
A new bipartisan workgroup is negotiating the possibility of standing up a carbon cap-and-invest market in Oregon that could one day be part of a larger West Coast market, linking up with existing programs meant to reduce climate warming greenhouse gas emissions in California, Washington and Canada.
The conversation is driven by concerns from gas companies, and industries heavily reliant on them, that Oregon’s alternative, non-market-driven carbon tax and investment program — the Climate Protection Program — is too financially onerous on them, and that costs incurred by businesses will eventually be passed onto consumers, according to several members of the committee. Companies hoping to offset some emissions under Oregon’s nascent program are slated to pay about four to five times what companies in California pay right now under the state’s carbon market, and which fluctuates depending on demand.
“I think both the business community and those that will be affected by the current CPP are open to seeing which program would be more conducive, or favorable, for Oregonians and ratepayers and taxpayers,” said state Sen. Mark Meek, D-Gladstone and one of the two centrist Democrats on the 10-member committee.
The group has met three times during the last month and is expected to meet weekly in the coming months, potentially bringing a proposal forward by the 2027 legislative session that begins in January. Gov. Tina Kotek’s prosperity council also recommended the Legislature repeal the Climate Protection Program and replace it with a market similar to California and Washington’s. Kotek’s Republican gubernatorial challenger, state Sen. Christine Drazan, has called for repealing the Climate Protection Program, but not offered any replacement.
Rep. Mark Owens, a centrist Republican from Crane also serving on the workgroup, said the lawmakers are all still learning about carbon markets. Owens, like Meek, said he was driven to the conversation by cost concerns of the Climate Protection Program from gas companies, including Oregon’s largest natural gas retailer NW Natural.
“I don’t even think we’re at that point of looking at (cap-and-invest) policy in ’27,” Owens said. “I think we’re looking at: can even the few of us that are in that room come together and say, ‘Hey, this is a good idea worth exploring.’”
How do cap-and-invest programs work?
Cap-and-invest programs and carbon markets put a price on carbon dioxide pollution and require polluters to pay for it. They are also meant to drive down consumption of fossil fuels.
In a regulated compliance market, such as California’s and Washington’s, companies that are required to meet legally mandated caps on their pollution can pollute

artigo.texto: Curso abre 35 vagas para segunda turma gratuita de Data Center Programa intensivo da Generation Brasil de 14 semanas prepara pessoas sem experiência para iniciar carreira em tecnologia; iniciativa reúne gigantes do setor como Equinix, Cisco Foundation, ODATA, Vertiv e Cummins. Redes sociais, serviços bancários, streaming, computação em nuvem e ferramentas de inteligência artificial dependem de uma infraestrutura que funciona 24 horas por dia nos bastidores: os data centers. Com a digitalização da economia e o avanço da IA, essa infraestrutura cresce e amplia também a demanda por profissionais preparados para operar, monitorar e dar suporte a esses ambientes. O Brasil já conta com cerca de 163 data centers em operação e ocupa a 11ª posição mundial em número de instalações, reforçando a expansão do setor e a necessidade de formação de novos profissionais. Para ampliar o acesso a essas oportunidades, a Generation Brasil está com inscrições abertas para a segunda turma do Programa de Empregabilidade em Data Center e Suporte de TI, formação 100% gratuita voltada a pessoas que desejam começar uma carreira em tecnologia, mesmo sem experiência prévia, você pode conferir as informações aqui. São 35 vagas para moradores de São Paulo e região. Ao longo de 14 semanas, os participantes terão uma formação intensiva que combina conhecimentos técnicos, desenvolvimento de habilidades comportamentais, preparação para processos seletivos e experiências práticas relacionadas ao dia a dia da profissão. Entre os conteúdos estão fundamentos de data center, servidores, racks e cabeamento, redes, Windows e Linux, ambientes em nuvem, suporte técnico, monitoramento de sistemas, gestão de incidentes, segurança da informação e configuração básica de redes. Formação com dupla certificação amplia possibilidades de carreira Um dos diferenciais desta turma é a dupla certificação em Data Center e Suporte de TI, permitindo que os participantes desenvolvam competências para diferentes posições de entrada na área de tecnologia. Entre as possibilidades profissionais estão cargos como Operador de Data Center, Data Center Technician, Técnico de Infraestrutura, Técnico de Operações, Analista de NOC, Técnico de Suporte, Help Desk e Service Desk Analyst. A formação é híbrida e combina aulas online ao vivo com uma semana de atividades presenciais obrigatórias, aproximando os participantes de ambientes e situações práticas da profissão. Além da formação técnica, os alunos desenvolvem competências como comunicação profissional, trabalho em equipe, organização, resolução de problemas, atenção aos detalhes, adaptabilidade e proatividade. Formação conectada ao setor O programa integra uma iniciativa global liderada pela Equinix, em parceria com Generation, Cisco Foundation, ODATA, Vertiv e Cummins para ampliar a formação de talentos para o setor de data centers. A colaboração aproxima a formação das necessidades encontradas no mercado e proporciona aos participantes contato com empresas e profissionais que atuam diretamente no ecossistema de infraestrutura digital. Mais do que ensinar conteúdos técnicos, a proposta da Generation é apoiar a entrada dos participantes no mercado de trabalho. Durante a jornada, os alunos contam com mentoria de carreira, preparação para processos seletivos e conexão com oportunidades em empresas parceiras. Participantes elegíveis também poderão receber apoios de permanência, como empréstimo de notebook, auxílio para internet e outros recursos, conforme critérios e disponibilidade do programa. “Além de desenvolver conhecimentos técnicos, queremos que os participantes terminem o programa preparados para disputar oportunidades reais no mercado. Nosso papel na Generation é construir essa ponte entre pessoas que buscam uma nova carreira e empresas que precisam de profissionais qualificados, oferecendo formação, preparação para processos seletivos e acompanhamento ao longo dessa jornada”, afirma Andrea Matsui, CEO da Generation Brasil. Quem pode participar O programa é destinado a pessoas com 18 anos ou mais, ensino médio completo, residentes em São Paulo ou região e atualmente sem vínculo empregatício. Não é necessário ter experiência anterior em tecnologia. Também é necessário ter disponibilidade integral para participar da formação de segunda a sexta-feira, das 9h às 17h, durante as 14 semanas, incluindo os momentos presenciais obrigatórios. A Generation incentiva especialmente a participação de mulheres, pessoas pretas e pardas e pessoas LGBTQIAP+, grupos historicamente sub-representados no setor de tecnologia.

artigo.texto: Trump sai em defesa da autorregulação da IA pelas empresas dos EUA e dos data centers Presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, disse que vai criar um comitê, com 10 pessoas, para supervisionar a IA. Também rejeitou a possibilidade de trabalhar com a China. "Nós somos os melhores e quero continuar assim", disse. O presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, informou nesta terça-feira, 29/9, que vai criar um comitê, composto por 10 pessoas, para supervisionar o setor de IA, após se reunir com executivos de tecnologia na Casa Branca. Trump também afirmou que os executivos de tecnologia assinaram um acordo “moralmente vinculativo”, sem fornecer detalhes. A pressão sobre o governo Trump para lidar com os riscos associados à IA vem aumentando, depois que a OpenAI e a Anthropic relataram que seus agentes de IA agiram de forma descontrolada e invadiram sistemas de outras empresas. As invasões levaram pesquisadores a alertar que alguns desenvolvedores de IA acreditam que a tecnologia poderia matar seres humanos em uma década, alimentando apelos por providências tanto de legisladores democratas quanto republicanos. Trump também saiu em defesa dos data centers, que vêm recebendo fortes críticas nos Estados Unidos. Segundo o presidente dos EUA, as empresas de tecnologia vão trabalhar para deixar as comunidades “satisfeitas” com a construção de centros de dados, uma vez que o setor enfrenta crescente oposição local à expansão dessas instalações. Os centros de dados, que fornecem o poder computacional utilizado para desenvolver e executar sistemas de IA, são um componente central do boom da IA. Sua expansão tem gerado oposição em comunidades de todo o país devido a preocupações com a demanda por eletricidade, custos de serviços públicos e outros impactos locais, levando as empresas a oferecer incentivos para tentar amenizar essas preocupações. Entre os executivos presentes na reunião de terça-feira na Casa Branca estavam Dario Amodei (Anthropic), Mark Zuckerberg (Meta), Sundar Pichai (Google), Jensen Huang (Nvidia) e Alex Karp (Palantir). Da administração Trump, participaram o consultor de tecnologia Michael Kratsios e o secretário de Comércio, Howard Lutnick, bem como o presidente da Câmara dos Representantes dos EUA, Mike Johnson. Trump reuniu-se com os executivos no mesmo dia em que seus assessores anunciaram uma nova ferramenta de IA que, segundo eles, facilitará o acesso do público a serviços governamentais. Executivos do Vale do Silício compareceram ao evento de lançamento nesta terça-feira, 29/9, incluindo Dina Powell McCormick, da Meta, e Shaun Maguire, sócio da Sequoia. O cofundador do Airbnb, Joe Gebbia, liderou o design da nova ferramenta. As empresas do Vale do Silício Google, SpaceX, Meta e 8VC foram listadas como patrocinadoras no programa do evento de lançamento. O presidente dos Estados Unidos rejeitou trabalhar em conjunto com o presidente chinês, Xi Jinping, na governança da tecnologia de IA. Segundo Trump, esse tipo de cooperação dificultaria a criação de produtos de IA melhores do que os chineses pelas empresas norte-americanas. Trump também disse que discutiu IA com Xi quando este visitou os EUA na semana passada, acrescentando que os EUA já trabalham com o governo de Xi “de muitas maneiras”. E sem nenhuma modéstia voltou a afirmar que “estamos à frente da China e de todos os outros agora, e quero manter as coisas assim”.

artigo.texto: Digital Realty Plans Cable Landing Station at Los Angeles Data Center Digital Realty's first turnkey cable landing station is designed to bring subsea capacity directly into an established data center and interconnection environment. Digital Realty is planning to build a cable landing station (CLS) inside its LAX12 data center in El Segundo, Calif., adding a new on-ramp for subsea capacity into the Los Angeles metro area. The company announced the project on Sept. 22 in partnership with Assured Communications, a specialist in subsea infrastructure design and delivery. The CLS is aimed at routes between Asia-Pacific and North America and is expected to begin supporting cables in 2028. A cable landing station is where a subsea cable terminates on land and connects to terrestrial networks. Increasingly, hyperscale cloud and AI providers are bringing cables directly to specific data centers rather than terminating them at standalone landing stations. Assured is also a strategic partner to the landing operator for AWS’s Sta’O’Nuk cable. “Digital Realty sees cable landing infrastructure as an increasingly important part of the broader connectivity ecosystem,” said Craig Waldrop, vice president of strategy and business development at Digital Realty, in an interview with Data Center Knowledge. “Subsea cables provide international capacity, but that capacity is most valuable when it can connect efficiently into the data centers, networks, cloud providers, and customers that need it.” Inside LAX12: Digital Realty’s First Turnkey Cable Landing Station The planned CLS is designed to provide subsea cable operators with a turnkey solution for landing and powering their systems. Assured is supporting the design, engineering, and construction, drawing on its experience with subsea cable systems and landing infrastructure. The project is currently in development. The station is a new type of project for Digital Realty. “LAX12 represents Digital Realty’s first turnkey cable landing solution and marks an important evolution in the company’s broader interconnection platform,” Waldrop said. The approach is intended to pull landing infrastructure and surrounding networks into a single location. “That simplifies the path from subsea infrastructure into terrestrial networks, while creating increased flexibility for cable owners in how they distribute capacity once it reaches the US,” he said. Why Put the Landing Station Inside the Data Center? The goal is to bring subsea capacity closer to the networks and clouds that consume it. “By bringing the landing point directly into an established interconnection environment, rather than treating the cable landing station as a standalone piece of infrastructure, the project creates a more direct bridge between subsea capacity arriving from Asia-Pacific and the broader digital ecosystem in Los Angeles,” Waldrop said. He noted that in El Segundo specifically, the proximity of the beach landing to Digital Realty’s existing infrastructure provides a more direct path from subsea systems into terrestrial networks. The connection will run through Digital Realty’s carrier-neutral model. “The value of a carrier-neutral model is that it gives cable operators a common landing environment that is not tied to a single network or cloud provider,” Waldrop said. What’s Fueling Investment in Subsea Connectivity? AI is a major driver of bandwidth demand, but not the only one. “AI is contributing to demand for high-capacity and resilient connectivity, but this extends beyond any single workload,” Waldrop said. “As traffic patterns evolve and infrastructure requirements grow, Digital Realty sees subsea infrastructure as an important part of the underlying infrastructure customers need to connect globally.” He added that demand for efficient, resilient connectivity continues to drive investment in greater capacity and route diversity. “While AI certainly contributes to that demand, it’s one of several factors shaping investment decisions,” he said. “Cloud adoption, content delivery, network expansion, and broader digital infrastructure growth are all driving continued investment in subsea connectivity.”

artigo.texto: Data Center On-Site Power Brings Pollution Risks Closer to Home The data center industry’s shift to on-site power generation to overcome grid constraints is creating new environmental compliance challenges. New Jersey’s recent $1.07 million penalty against a Vineland, New Jersey, AI data center operator has put a broader challenge for the industry into focus: Operators seeking alternatives to constrained electricity grids must also account for the environmental consequences of generating power on-site. The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (NJDEP) said the facility installed and operated 62 natural gas generators without required permits. A state official announced the enforcement action on Sept. 22. The operator, identified as DataOne, disputed NJDEP’s determination regarding the temporary generators but said it would apply for air permits and is communicating with regulators, according to the New Jersey Monitor. As AI buildouts accelerate, on-site generation is changing what communities need to understand about proposed computing facilities. Electricity supply, air emissions, cooling demand, and noise increasingly belong in the same discussion. “AI data centers are increasingly becoming power plants as well as computing facilities,” said Abhijit Sunil, senior analyst at Forrester, in an interview with Data Center Knowledge. “AI infrastructure can now be deployed faster than traditional permitting and inspection processes were designed to oversee.” Behind-the-Meter Power Doesn’t Eliminate Environmental Costs Sunil said on-site generation, often using natural gas, has emerged in conversations with data center vendors as one response to grid constraints. Other approaches include battery storage and shifting workloads to align with grid availability. Generating electricity behind the meter can reduce a facility’s demand on the utility network, but that does not, by itself, establish an environmental benefit. “Taking pressure off the grid doesn’t eliminate an environmental cost,” Sunil said. “Taking pressure off the grid doesn’t eliminate an environmental cost." – Abhijit Sunil, senior analyst, Forrester For nearby residents, relevant effects include combustion-related air pollutants (such as NOx, CO, and particulate matter) and continuous or frequent noise. Evaluating a project, therefore, requires more than comparing a data center’s electricity demand with available grid capacity. Sunil recommends assessments that encompass electricity consumption and grid upgrades, as well as water use, land use, emissions, and noise. Those impacts should be weighed alongside a project’s socioeconomic benefits. The broader accounting also helps distinguish different concerns: greenhouse gas emissions, local air pollution, water consumption, and continuous noise are separate issues requiring different measurements and responses. Operator Priorities Skew Toward Power and Uptime Power availability and operational reliability can dominate investment decisions, leaving other environmental issues with less attention. Luis Fernandes, IDC senior research manager for cloud and data centers within enterprise infrastructure, told Data Center Knowledge that a recent IDC worldwide operator survey found energy efficiency and renewable energy among the leading resilience and sustainability priorities. He noted that waste heat reuse ranked last, while reducing water usage was third from the bottom. “We see operators more concerned about rising power intensity and operational risk, and less inclined to commit to environmental and sustainability targets,” Fernandes said. Those findings suggest that improvements in energy performance should not be treated as a proxy for progress across every environmental measure. An operator’s efficiency strategy does not explain how it manages cooling demand, local noise, or the operation of on-site generators. For communities and customers, the distinction makes facility-level information important. Broad sustainability commitments offer limited insight into how a particular site operates and how its impact changes over time. Make Site-Level Impacts Transparent Sunil suggested that large facilities with on-site generation disclose their equipment, fuel, capacity, and permitting status. Reporting should also cover runtime, electricity generated, greenhouse gases, and relevant local air pollutants. Material changes to generation or cooling capacity should trigger updated disclosures, he said, because information presented during initial project discussions may no longer describe the operating facility. “The goal for new projects should be that communities [are not] surprised at any given stage,” Sunil said. He argues that monitoring should make impacts visible before residents experience consequences, rather than leaving neighbors to identify changes through generator noise or other observable effects. That recommendation goes beyond publishing an annual corporate environmental report. It requires information that connects a specific operation to the surrounding community. Permitting Lapses Can Halt Operations Across the industry, environmental obligations depend on the equipment and activities at each site. The Hidden Failure Domain in N+1 Data Center Cooling N+1 capacity can hide shared-control dependencies, turning many units into a single failure domain. Learn how to design for degraded operation and commission real resilience. Data centers continuously convert electrical power into heat. Cooling, therefore, has to keep running. Many plants look resilient on paper: redundant pumps, computer room air handlers (CRAHs), coolant distribution units (CDUs), and power feeds. Yet those assets can still depend on a single controller, network path, or sensor. That shared layer can turn an N+1 design into one large failure domain. What Can One Fault Take Down? A failure domain is the part of a system that one fault can take down. Four pumps arranged as three duty and one standby look straightforward. If a motor fails and only that pump is lost, the domain is one unit. The spare starts and the flow continues. Now, assume that all four pumps receive lead-lag selection, staging, and run commands from one controller. If that controller fails and the pumps have no local fallback, a single control fault can stop all four. The machines are mechanically redundant. They are not operationally independent. The same pattern appears with CRAHs, chillers, and CDUs. Several units may share a supervisory controller, a network switch, a control power source, a gateway, or a critical process signal. The useful question is not only how many units are installed; it is how much of the cooling plant a single failure can disable. N+1 on Paper, One Control System in Practice N+1 is easy to see on a mechanical schedule. If three pumps are required for design flow, install a fourth. If one cooling unit can drop out and the rest can carry the load, the plant appears robust. The equipment count does not show every dependency. Redundant assets may still rely on the same plant controller, switch, control power supply, or remote sensor. In a fault, the common layer decides whether the spare equipment can actually run. Centralized controls have a job. Plant-level logic can rotate lead equipment, optimize pressure setpoints, and coordinate chillers and pumps. The risk appears when the optimization layer also becomes essential to basic circulation. A supervisory controller may choose which pumps should run. Should the loss of that controller also remove the ability of healthy pumps to move water? A building management system (BMS) may issue schedules and resets. Should the loss of BMS communication stop local cooling? That behavior should be designed, not discovered during an incident. The issue is growing with liquid cooling. CDUs, variable-speed pumps, control valves, sensors, and leak detection add control and communication layers. Mechanical redundancy can fail due to dependencies that are never shown on the piping drawing. Designing for Degraded Operation Not every control failure should produce the same response. Some conditions should trigger specific starts or stops. Others justify continued operation in a conservative fallback state. For critical cooling, losing supervisory control does not have to mean losing cooling. Local controllers, such as programmable logic controllers (PLCs) in pump panels or unit controllers in CRAHs, can retain sufficient autonomy to maintain basic operation when higher-level communication is unavailable. That may mean holding a local pressure setpoint, reverting to a predefined pump speed, using locally available temperature signals, or allowing manual control until supervisory functions return. Efficiency, optimization, and remote visibility may drop. That is still different from a plant-wide stop. This is not an argument for duplicating every PLC, sensor, and network path, which adds cost and complexity. It is an argument for listing shared dependencies and defining, in advance, what should happen when each one disappears. Test the Failure Domain, Not Just the Spare Unit Commissioning is where installed redundancy and demonstrated redundancy part ways. A conventional functional test stops the lead pump and confirms that the standby starts. That demonstrates that the spare machine functions and the normal changeover sequence works. It does not prove what happens if the mechanism that commands that sequence fails. Functional testing should remove the shared layer. What happens when the supervisory network is disconnected, or when a plant controller restarts? What happens when a remote differential-pressure signal becomes invalid, or when control power is lost to one panel? The goal is to confirm that the actual failure domains align with the design intent. A system can have two of everything and still have only one path to a critical decision. If that path has never been taken away during commissioning, the resilience on the drawings has not been proven in operation. Redundancy that Survives Its Dependencies N+1 remains a useful capacity principle. It is not a complete description of cooling resilience. A stronger review question is: What is the largest failure domain in this architecture? That question exposes common controllers, shared networks, single sensors, and other ties between otherwise redundant assets. The review question leads to two more: What continues to operate when that shared dependency is lost? Has that behavior been tested? A redundant cooling plant needs spare capacity. That spare capacity must also remain usable when the controls, communications, and signals that coordinate it fail to behave as expected.

artigo.texto: From Opposition to Buy-In: Tactics for Data Center Developers Data center developers are responding to growing community opposition by embracing transparency, funding power infrastructure, and prioritizing locations with supportive residents. Two years ago, a new wave of massive AI data centers dominated the headlines. A year ago, murmurings of discontent began to be heard. As 2026 heads into its final quarter, those murmurings have become a cacophony of opposition. Whether it is local communities complaining about water, power, or noise, or government bodies imposing bans or moratoria on data centers, pushback has caught the public eye. It is no surprise, therefore, that several sessions at the recent Data Center World Power event in Dallas, which ran Sept. 21-23, addressed this issue. Concerns about power availability and potential electricity rate hikes in the local area are among the biggest worries voiced by data center opponents. In some regions, data centers are being blamed for increases in electricity rates. In response, many data center developers are expressing a willingness to fund upgrades needed to support their projects. Some have paid for entire battery energy storage systems (BESS) that benefit both the grid and their data centers. Others are contributing to transmission upgrades or purchasing transformers, substations, and other power electronics infrastructure to avoid passing extra costs on to ratepayers. Some grid planners and utilities are formalizing such arrangements to make them standard practice for new projects. Here are some top tips from Data Center World Power for interacting with community groups. Be Transparent Early: Retire the NDA Playbook Diane Sullivan, chief development officer of Hecate Energy, a Chicago‑based US developer of utility‑scale energy parks, believes that the current backlash against data centers is partly due to past practices. She cited non-disclosure agreements with city officials and developing projects under the radar, getting them largely set up before announcing them. That approach may have worked for smaller projects that exerted relatively little impact on the local grid. However, AI data centers are becoming so large that transparency has become essential. It is in the developer’s long-term interest to engage with the community upfront. “In the past, developers would sometimes obtain permits before informing the public about a data center project, which is a terrible idea,” Sullivan said. “We must become open and be fully transparent about our plans.” Bring Power with You: Co-Develop Power with Utilities and EPCs A data center development of any size requires a plan for both the facility and its power. That might include wind, solar, batteries, geothermal, natural gas, or nuclear. But permitting and system operator approval are unlikely without a clear plan for adding new power resources, typically funded by the developer. Data center developers are urged to partner with power plant developers, EPC (engineering, procurement, and construction) contractors, and utilities to line up a portfolio of options. In many cases, that will entail multiple resources – perhaps solar, gas-fired generation, backup generators, and batteries. “Any project proposal should also include a power generation solution, or you are probably wasting your time,” Sullivan said. Community Support Now Trumps Power Availability Once upon a time, the primary criteria for a good data center site were proximity to a major metro area and fiber availability. Over the past couple of years, power has become the key factor. Now there is another essential element: community support. The project must benefit the local area, and there should be a largely positive attitude towards it. “You could have a perfectly executable project that’s real, it’s commercial, and has well-allocated risk, but the community shows up and doesn’t want you there,” said Dado Slezak, executive vice president of energy capital and strategy at QTS Data Centers. “You could have a perfectly executable project that’s real, it’s commercial, and has well-allocated risk, but the community shows up and doesn’t want you there.” – Dado Slezak, EVP of energy capital and strategy, QTS Data Centers To avoid that outcome, economic benefits should be made tangible to residents. Beyond tax payments, developers can support local schools or help stabilize electricity rates. Slezak cited a QTS project in Iowa where the company reached an agreement with the utility to fix and subsidize community electricity rates for five years. Benefits can also extend beyond economics; some developers invest in water restoration. “There are also different types of jobs that the data center brings,” added Alise Porto, vice president of sustainability and strategic initiatives at Switch. In addition to direct data center roles, construction generates significant employment during development. Some developers are working to translate those jobs into permanent positions via on-site retraining programs. Tour Working Facilities to Debunk Water and Noise Myths Most developers attend community meetings armed with facts and figures on power draw, water consumption, and noise abatement. But opposition can harden to the point where data isn’t persuasive. Slezak suggested that touring people around a comparable facility can make a difference. “I can tell them that you consume less water in a hyperscale campus than a restaurant would, but they often don’t believe me,” he said. “It is sometimes better to show them. I’ve toured groups through a facility and shown them our closed-loop system where there is no water consumption.” Closed-loop designs can significantly reduce process water usage compared to traditional evaporative systems. Zinc Whiskers: The Hidden Contamination Risk Beneath Data Center Floors As AI density and airflow rise, legacy raised-floor and zinc-plated components can shed conductive whiskers that jeopardize equipment reliability. As data centers evolve to support higher-density computing and AI infrastructure, attention naturally goes to power, cooling, and equipment reliability. A less visible issue also deserves attention in that discussion: zinc whiskers. The risk isn’t new, but the operating conditions inside today’s facilities – especially increases in airflow – make it worth revisiting. Zinc whiskers are microscopic, electrically conductive crystalline filaments that can grow from electroplated zinc surfaces. In data centers, the best-documented source is the underside of older raised-floor tiles. However, cable trays, pedestals, stringers, electrical hardware, and other zinc-plated components can also be susceptible. The risk arises when whiskers detach, become airborne, and are carried by the cooling airflow. Once inside equipment, they can settle on circuit boards and other components, potentially creating unintended conductive paths, signal disturbances, and equipment failures. A Risk Hidden in Legacy Infrastructure Whiskers can be difficult to identify without the appropriate inspection techniques, and growth may take months or years to become apparent. The risk is particularly relevant to older facilities and buildings with mixed-vintage infrastructure. Modern raised-floor manufacturing has shifted toward materials and coatings that behave differently from the electroplated zinc historically associated with whisker growth. That means the risk is not uniform across every data center. However, facilities that have been operating for decades or contain legacy infrastructure should not assume the problem is purely theoretical. Routine facility work can increase exposure. Moving floor tiles, running new cabling, reconfiguring equipment, or conducting nearby construction can disturb accumulated whiskers and release them into the environment. AI Infrastructure Changes the Equation The growth of AI infrastructure adds another consideration. High-density GPU clusters move significantly more air than traditional computing infrastructure. Increased airflow through a subfloor plenum can create more opportunities for contaminants to become airborne and travel toward equipment. As data centers become denser and move more air, operators need to look beyond the newest technology and understand the conditions created by the infrastructure already in place. AI deployments also represent a substantially greater equipment investment in many facilities. That makes contamination control an operational consideration, not simply a housekeeping issue. When Cleaning Can Make the Problem Worse Conventional cleaning practices may be counterproductive. Vacuuming without HEPA filtration can aerosolize whiskers and release them back into the environment through the equipment’s exhaust. Sweeping, brushing, or other aggressive mechanical cleaning can disturb susceptible surfaces and shed additional whiskers. Even moving floor tiles can spread contamination. A maintenance activity intended to improve conditions in one area can seed a wider contamination event if the underlying risk is not identified. That makes identification the first step. High-intensity oblique lighting can help reveal whiskers through reflection, allowing facility teams to inspect susceptible surfaces before beginning cleaning or maintenance activities. A More Controlled Response Once contamination is identified, the response should focus on both containment and removal. Work areas may need to be isolated, airflow controlled, and nearby equipment intakes protected to prevent migration into unaffected areas. Cleaning alone may not solve the problem if a component is actively generating whiskers. Source remediation can include replacing affected floor tiles or other components with non-whiskering alternatives. Documentation is also important. Document where contamination is identified, actions taken, and remaining conditions to support future maintenance, remediation, and operational decisions. Zinc whiskers are not a universal threat to every data center, but in facilities with older raised-floor systems, legacy infrastructure, or mixed-vintage environments, they represent a contamination risk worth understanding and managing. As operators invest heavily in AI and higher-density computing, reliability depends not only on the newest technology entering the data center but also on the conditions created by the infrastructure already in place.

artigo.texto: Can Data Center Design Choices Change Public Acceptance? Operators use biomimicry, community co-design, and brownfield redevelopment to reduce the visual impact of data centers and improve local acceptance. Beauty may be in the eye of the beholder, but it’s unlikely that the recent rash of data centers popping up across the US and globally is winning many people over on looks alone. To ease community concerns about noise, energy, and water use – and especially their visual impact – some operators are rethinking how facilities look, how they sit within landscapes, and even where they’re built. Anti-data center sentiment often goes beyond complaints about water, energy, and noise pollution to include criticism of a facility’s appearance and its aesthetic impact on nearby neighborhoods. A description from the Virginia-based Piedmont Environmental Council captures a common view: “The data center developments proposed in the County are hyperscale facilities, which are massive, windowless concrete buildings that can bring potential noise and electrical infrastructure such as substations and transmission lines. They are also often out of scale with existing communities and fenced with cameras, security guards, and guard gates.” Designing to Disappear: Biomimicry and Landscape Strategies Some operators are taking steps to make facilities a bit easier on the eyes. One approach is to use landscaping to soften profiles and blend sites into their surroundings. Microsoft, for example, has begun applying “biomimicry” – borrowing strategies from local ecosystems to guide land, water, and restoration plans – to improve how some of its newest data centers look and function. The company first employed the approach at a site in Noord-Holland, the Netherlands, in 2022, planting 150 native trees and more than 2,000 square meters (about 21,500 square feet) of shrubs and grasses around the campus. Microsoft says it has since expanded the practice to more than 20 sites across the US and Europe. Microsoft’s director of global land strategy, Kaitlin Chuzi, told Data Center Knowledge that biomimicry is about more than aesthetics or traditional landscaping. “We start by understanding how the local ecosystem functions, combining ecological research with community input and then [using] those insights to inform land, water, and restoration plans that mimic and enhance natural systems,” she said. “The goal is to design for multiple benefits at once, from locally appropriate, biodiverse plantings that improve the viewshed to healthier soil, better stormwater management, and stronger habitat for local species." Here, “viewshed” refers to the area that is visible from a specific vantage point. There is growing interest in whether better-designed facilities can help win over residents. On June 11, the UK Government announced a national Data Center Design Challenge in partnership with the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA). The competition asks architects, designers, engineers, and communities to collaborate on high-quality design, meaningful public engagement, and sustainable outcomes. “As data centers become increasingly critical to the UK’s economic and technological future, we have a responsibility to consider how they are designed, located, and experienced,” said RIBA president Chris Williamson in a statement. “Data centers will be needed across the country, and this presents a major opportunity for architects to reimagine what they can be, while supporting sector growth.” Underground and Low-Profile Designs Challenging the standard “big shed” template, some proposals explore alternative materials and even partially buried or fully underground designs with little or no visible footprint. The potential benefits range from security to cooling efficiencies, and the reduced above-ground profile can ease local opposition. “Nobody’s going to oppose a data center in a mine,” Max Smolaks, a research analyst for Uptime Intelligence, told Data Center Knowledge earlier this year. What Residents Say: Design Factors that Change Acceptance A 2026 research report by the design firm Gensler also highlights the role of design in public acceptance. “Design emerged as a decisive factor in community acceptance. When asked about their top design concerns, residents prioritized issues architects can directly address: overall building appearance, massing, materials, and height,” the report states. Co-Designing with Communities Community participation is another theme. Carl Walker, head of societal insights at engineering consultancy Hoare Lea, said that it is not simply about better aesthetics but about integrating community input from the outset. “Co-creating data centers with residents is essential if they are to become valued community assets rather than simply being perceived as large, anonymous warehouse buildings,” he told Data Center Knowledge. “Co-creating data centers with residents is essential if they are to become valued community assets rather than simply being perceived as large, anonymous warehouse buildings.” – Carl Walker, head of societal insights, Hoare Lea Hoare Lea has developed a Social Charter for data centers that provides guidance for social engagement, including design. “Rather than imposing a standardized ‘one-size-fits-all’ warehouse model, co-creation enables data centers to reflect the character, identity, and needs of the communities they serve, helping them contribute positively to placemaking, local pride, and regeneration,” Walker said. While greenfield developments often face criticism for environmental impact, some operators argue that building on brownfield sites – previously developed land that may be disused or blighted – can reduce opposition and accelerate timelines where grid connections and transport links already exist. artigo.texto: How Carbon-Aware Scheduling Can Cut Data Center Emissions Aligning flexible workloads to cleaner hours and locations turns variability into measurable Scope 2 reductions. Data centers are often described as having fixed carbon footprints tied to their size and grid mix. In practice, operators can lower emissions by aligning flexible workloads with periods and locations where electricity is cleaner. This “carbon-aware” approach complements long-term renewable procurement and efficiency programs, creating a practical pathway to reduce Scope 2 emissions and to demonstrate progress toward 24/7 carbon-free energy objectives. It also helps address growing regulatory expectations and stakeholder scrutiny of digital infrastructure’s electricity demand. What Is Carbon-Aware Computing? Carbon-aware computing is the practice of scheduling compute-intensive but time-flexible tasks – such as data backups, batch analytics, AI model training, report generation, and non-urgent patching – during windows when grid carbon intensity is lower or when on-site renewable or stored energy is available. The core idea is to compare the emissions profile of running a workload at one time or place versus another, and then choose execution options that minimize emissions within operational constraints. How Carbon-Aware Scheduling Works Electricity grids are dynamic. Solar production peaks during daylight, wind output varies seasonally and hourly, and some regions benefit from geothermal, hydro, or nuclear baseload. Grid conditions change by the hour based on demand, transmission constraints, and market dispatch. As a result, the emissions intensity of a kilowatt-hour can swing significantly across a single day. Carbon-aware computing takes advantage of this variability by aligning flexible workloads with periods when low-carbon energy is most available. Operators assess which workloads can shift in time or location without violating service-level agreements (SLAs), latency requirements, data residency constraints, or change-control policies. The outcome is a set of scheduling policies that favor cleaner windows while maintaining service objectives. That way, compute-hungry tasks can run without forcing incremental demand at higher-emitting hours. Implementation Realities: Data, Forecasts, and Constraints The principles behind carbon-aware computing are simple enough. In a data center context, however, implementing carbon-aware strategies can be challenging for a few key reasons. Common hurdles include limited observability into tenant workloads (particularly in colocation facilities), difficulty predicting workload power draw due to dynamic CPU/GPU utilization and I/O patterns, and uncertainty in renewable forecasts. Additionally, not all workloads are flexible. Mission-critical, latency-sensitive applications may be fixed in time and location. A practical approach starts with cataloging workloads by flexibility class, power profile, and compliance constraints. From there, operators can pilot carbon-aware scheduling on clearly deferrable tasks. What Operators Can Do Today Effective carbon-aware programs typically include: - Instrumentation and metering. Enhance power telemetry at the rack and cluster level to identify high-draw, schedulable workloads and measure realized emissions impacts. - Behind-the-meter resources. On-site renewables improve certainty that incremental workload energy is low-carbon. Generic utility grids typically can’t guarantee that the energy they supply comes from any particular source. However, data centers with their own solar, wind, or geothermal energy supplies can do this. When paired with batteries, operators can time-shift energy and shave peaks. While few sites can economically size batteries to cover full facility load, modest storage can be sufficient to power energy-intensive, deferrable tasks during clean windows. Reduce Emissions, Keep Reliability Perfect optimization is unrealistic for most data center environments. Even so, carbon-aware computing can deliver real reductions by capturing the “clean hours” that already exist on many grids. Over time, it becomes another reliability-minded tool – one that lowers emissions while respecting the operational realities that keep data centers running.

O mercado de gás liquefeito de petróleo (GLP) não tem crescido como esperado após a criação do Gás do Povo, o que demanda estudos sobre o real impacto do programa, defendeu o diretor Jurídico e Relações Institucionais da Supergasbras, Ricardo Tonietto, em entrevista ao estúdio eixos durante a ROG.e 2026.
Segundo ele, ainda não há um diagnóstico sobre a questão. Confira na íntegra.
“O que a gente percebe hoje é que, diferentemente até do que a gente imaginava, o mercado não está crescendo como se imaginava. São coisas que a gente precisa entender o porquê”, disse.

artigo.texto: A margem de conexão disponível no Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) para os leilões de baterias de dezembro é estimada em cerca de 56 GW, segundo cálculo da Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae) a partir de nota técnica do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS). O volume é até 12,5 vezes superior à necessidade de potência estimada para o período de 2028 a 2030, de 4,5 GW a 10 GW, indicando, na avaliação da entidade, que a disponibilidade de rede não deve representar uma restrição generalizada para os projetos que disputarão os certames, previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro. A partir dos limites apresentados para os diferentes pontos da rede, a Absae calculou uma margem de conexão de aproximadamente 56 GW no SIN. Considerando a estimativa de déficit de potência entre 2028 e 2030, de 4,5 GW a 10 GW, a margem disponível equivale a entre 5,6 e 12,5 vezes a necessidade estimada. Nos barramentos bonificados pela portaria nº 136/2026, a margem agregada chega a aproximadamente 13,7 GW. Segundo a associação, esse volume, isoladamente, já supera a estimativa mais alta de déficit de potência. A portaria do Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) mencionada pela associação é a que estabelece as diretrizes para os certames. A entidade avalia que há espaço de conexão distribuído por diferentes regiões do sistema para receber projetos de armazenamento, reduzindo o risco de uma restrição generalizada de rede para os empreendimentos que disputarão os leilões. “A nota do ONS é uma boa notícia para o leilão. A rede tem margem de cerca de 56 GW, bem acima da necessidade de potência que estimamos para os próximos anos, e esse espaço está distribuído por várias regiões, mantendo a competitividade de grande parte dos projetos cadastrados. O atendimento ao cronograma também é salutar e mostra o compromisso da governança do setor elétrico em cumprir os prazos do leilão. Com tantos projetos cadastrados, a disputa deve ser decidida por preço, o que favorece o consumidor”, afirma Fabio Lima, diretor-executivo da ABSAE. Margem identificada em pontos bonificados e não bonificados Dos 129 barramentos bonificados, 93 têm margem reconhecida. Eles se concentram no Nordeste, sobretudo na Bahia, no Piauí e no Ceará, e no norte de Minas Gerais, regiões que reúnem os maiores blocos de capacidade, de até cerca de 3,7 GW. Em outros pontos, a margem é menor ou compartilhada entre vários barramentos. Também há locais sem margem em razão de restrições de espaço físico, curto-circuito ou cronograma de obras. O desenho dos leilões já prevê esse tipo de ajuste, com classificação por barramento, subárea e área. Nos barramentos definidos como estratégicos pela Portaria nº 136/2026, os projetos contam com uma bonificação de 10% no preço de classificação. O mecanismo busca incentivar a instalação de baterias em pontos da rede onde os sistemas podem oferecer benefícios adicionais ao sistema elétrico. Projetos localizados em outras regiões, que somam cerca de 36 GW de margem, também competem nos leilões, ampliando o espaço disponível para os empreendimentos. A bonificação considera pontos da rede onde, além de potência, os sistemas de armazenamento podem contribuir para aumentar a robustez elétrica, especialmente em locais com menor capacidade de manter a tensão estável. Os sistemas de baterias exigidos nos leilões têm capacidade de operar como formadores de rede e fornecer esse suporte, contribuindo para a estabilidade da rede nesses pontos e reduzindo a necessidade de outras soluções, como compensadores síncronos. Por isso, os projetos conectados a esses barramentos têm o preço de classificação reduzido em 10%, sem perda de receita. Competição deve permanecer elevada A Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) cadastrou 6.091 projetos para os leilões, que somam 296,8 GW. Mesmo com a redução natural decorrente da habilitação técnica e da disponibilidade de rede, a Absae avalia que o número de projetos aptos seguirá muito acima da quantidade a ser contratada. Na avaliação da associação, esse cenário mantém elevada a competição entre os empreendimentos e pode contribuir para uma contratação mais eficiente e para a redução de custos ao consumidor.

artigo.texto: As duas maiores margens individuais para conexão de baterias nos leilões de reserva de capacidade de dezembro estão em Minas Gerais: Arinos 2, com 2,96 GW, e Janaúba 3, com 2,92 GW. Em sentido oposto, há pontos com capacidade remanescente zero em estados como Bahia, Alagoas, Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte, São Paulo, Rio Grande do Sul e Santa Catarina. Os cálculos já consideram, quando representam a condição mais restritiva, os montantes reservados na primeira Temporada de Acesso. Os valores se referem aos barramentos, pontos elétricos das subestações aos quais se conectam linhas, transformadores e outros equipamentos. As margens de cada ponto, porém, não podem ser somadas. A capacidade disponível para os leilões é definida simultaneamente em três níveis, por barramento, subárea e área, e um projeto fica sujeito a todos os limites aplicáveis à sua localização. Arinos 2 e Janaúba 3, por exemplo, integram uma área que reúne instalações do norte de Minas Gerais e do oeste da Bahia e está sujeita a um limite agregado de 3,2 GW. Assim, apesar das margens individuais de 2,96 GW e 2,92 GW, a capacidade conjunta dos projetos nessa área não poderá ultrapassar o teto definido para o conjunto das instalações. Os quantitativos constam de nota técnica divulgada em conjunto pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) e pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) em 30 de setembro. O documento foi elaborado pelo ONS com subsídios da EPE. Os limites serão considerados no leilão com exigência de conteúdo nacional, marcado para 2 de dezembro, e segundo certame, previsto para o dia 4. Nos dois casos, o início do suprimento está previsto para 1º de agosto de 2028. A nova nota complementa um primeiro documento elaborado conjuntamente por ONS e EPE e publicado em julho, que definiu a metodologia, as premissas e os critérios para o cálculo da capacidade remanescente. Agora, são apresentados os quantitativos resultantes dos estudos para cada barramento candidato, subárea e área do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). Temporada de Acesso entra no cálculo Na definição das margens, o ONS considerou os consumidores já em operação ou que tinham contratos de uso dos sistemas de transmissão ou distribuição celebrados até o fim do prazo de cadastramento. Também entraram no cálculo os montantes reservados na primeira Temporada de Acesso, quando resultaram em uma condição mais restritiva para a conexão dos sistemas de armazenamento. Ficaram de fora os projetos que solicitaram a devolução das garantias associadas à participação na temporada. Segundo o ONS, o tratamento busca evitar que uma mesma capacidade da rede seja disponibilizada nos dois processos de alocação de acesso. Limites variam dentro das regiões As diferenças também aparecem dentro de uma mesma região. Na Bahia, Igaporã III, em 230 kV, tem margem individual de até 2 GW. A subárea que inclui o próprio barramento, Bom Jesus da Lapa, Bom Jesus da Lapa II, Igaporã II e Pindaí II, entretanto, está limitada a 900 MW. Na região de Barreiras, também na Bahia, Barreiras e Barreiras II, em 230 kV, têm limites individuais de 340 MW cada. A subárea que reúne esses pontos e instalações como Tabocas do Brejo Velho, Rio das Éguas, Rio Formoso II e Rio Grande II tem margem de 50 MW. Em uma área maior, que reúne instalações da Bahia, Piauí e Ceará, o limite agregado é de 3,67 GW. Dentro desse conjunto, há barramentos com margens individuais elevadas, como Futura, na Bahia, com até 2,165 GW, e Queimada Nova II, no Piauí, com até 2,1 GW. A nota também aponta barramentos sem capacidade remanescente. Entre eles estão Paulo Afonso III-A, na Bahia, e Xingó, em Alagoas. Para os dois pontos, o ONS identifica como fator limitante uma sobrecarga na linha de transmissão de 500 kV Sapeaçu-Camaçari II diante da contingência da linha Sapeaçu-Camaçari IV. Há barramentos com margem zero também em outras regiões do país. As razões variam conforme a instalação e incluem restrições de desempenho elétrico, limitações de curto-circuito e falta de disponibilidade física para novas conexões. Nos casos em que não há disponibilidade física no barramento, o documento ressalva que a margem pode ser considerada para projetos conectados à rede de distribuição com impacto em uma subestação de fronteira da Rede Básica. Carregamento das baterias também restringe margens Para chegar aos quantitativos, o ONS avaliou a disponibilidade física das instalações e o desempenho da rede tanto no descarregamento quanto no carregamento dos sistemas de armazenamento. Também foram consideradas limitações de curto-circuito que possam comprometer a entrada dos projetos em operação na data prevista para o início do suprimento. Em diferentes pontos, a capacidade disponível foi limitada por problemas identificados especificamente nos cenários de carregamento das baterias. O estudo também considera empreendimentos conectados às redes de distribuição quando a injeção ou a absorção de potência produz impacto sobre a Rede Básica, as Demais Instalações de Transmissão (DITs) ou as Instalações de Transmissão de Interesse Exclusivo de Centrais de Geração para Conexão Compartilhada (ICGs).

artigo.texto: O Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) propôs à Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) uma mudança na metodologia de rateio do encargo que custeará os leilões de reserva de capacidade na forma de potência (LRCap) para baterias, com redução da cobrança dos geradores conforme a contribuição de potência de cada usina na janela crítica do sistema. Pelo ajuste de critérios proposto, usinas solares sem armazenamento continuariam com o coeficiente cheio, por praticamente não contribuírem com potência na ponta noturna. Já termelétricas inflexíveis e nucleares, que também ficam sem desconto na metodologia proposta pela área técnica da Aneel, passariam a ter sua contribuição de potência reconhecida e tenderiam a pagar menos. A sugestão foi apresentada pelo ONS em reunião com o gabinete do diretor Gentil Nogueira, relator do processo, em 14 de setembro. O operador quer substituir o Índice de Flexibilidade previsto pela área técnica da agência como critério de graduação do encargo por um indicador que meça quanto cada empreendimento entrega de potência nas horas em que o Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) mais precisa. A discussão ocorre a pouco mais de dois meses dos dois leilões de armazenamento, marcados para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro. A regulação do rateio ainda precisa passar por consulta pública e deliberação da diretoria da Aneel. A proposta da área técnica prevê 30 dias de consulta e outros 30 dias para consolidação das contribuições. Proposta da Aneel A metodologia elaborada pela área técnica da Aneel prevê que todos os geradores participem do custeio do Encargo de Reserva de Capacidade associado aos sistemas de armazenamento, o Ercap-SAE, mas com valores diferenciados conforme a flexibilidade de cada usina. Os empreendimentos seriam divididos em quatro patamares. Usinas classificadas como inflexíveis teriam coeficiente de 100% do encargo. O percentual cairia para 75% no segundo patamar, 50% no terceiro e 25% para os recursos classificados como de flexibilidade muito alta. A forma de medir a flexibilidade varia conforme a fonte. Para as hidrelétricas, a proposta compara a geração entre as janelas das 10h às 14h e das 18h às 22h, com menor cobrança para as usinas que reduzem a produção no período de menor demanda líquida e ampliam a geração na ponta. Para as termelétricas, o índice considera parâmetros como tempos de acionamento, permanência em carga e desligamento, além da capacidade de modular a geração. Os parâmetros operativos têm peso de 70% no índice e a modulação intradiária, de 30%. Na simulação feita pela Aneel, toda a geração nuclear foi enquadrada no patamar de menor flexibilidade, com coeficiente cheio. Eólicas e solares sem armazenamento também ficaram nesse grupo. As termelétricas foram distribuídas entre os quatro patamares, mas as de operação contínua ficam entre as mais oneradas. Em uma simulação feita pela agência apenas para testar a metodologia, nucleares, eólicas e fotovoltaicas teriam encargo médio de R$ 10,82/MWh. As termelétricas ficariam, em média, em R$ 8,53/MWh, enquanto as hidrelétricas pagariam R$ 5,65/MWh. Na apresentação, o ONS ressaltou que a proposta não substitui a estrutura desenhada pela Aneel, mas altera o critério usado para diferenciar a cobrança entre os geradores. Permaneceriam o rateio entre todos os geradores, a energia gerada como base de incidência, a graduação do encargo e o piso de 25%. A mudança ficaria concentrada no coeficiente: em vez de refletir o Índice de Flexibilidade, ele passaria a considerar a contribuição de potência de cada empreendimento na janela crítica. Potência na hora crítica Para isso, o ONS propõe trocar a régua desenhada pelos técnicos da Aneel por um Índice de Contribuição de Potência na Janela Crítica, o ICP-JC. A diferença é que a metodologia da Aneel busca medir o quanto uma usina é capaz de flexibilizar sua operação, enquanto a proposta do ONS considera a potência que o empreendimento entrega no período em que o sistema mais precisa. O operador argumenta que o produto contratado nos leilões de baterias é disponibilidade de potência, por isso, o critério usado para graduar o encargo deve considerar a contribuição de cada usina nessa mesma condição. Isso altera principalmente o tratamento dado às usinas de operação contínua. Uma termelétrica inflexível ou uma nuclear pode ter baixa capacidade de modulação, mas permanecer gerando durante a ponta. Pela proposta do ONS, essa entrega passaria a reduzir sua participação relativa no rateio. Termelétricas despacháveis, usinas a biomassa e eólicas também tenderiam a pagar menos, conforme a potência entregue na janela crítica. Para as hidrelétricas, o efeito seria uma redistribuição dentro da própria fonte. A solar sem armazenamento tenderia a permanecer com coeficiente cheio se a janela crítica permaneçer no período noturno. Segundo cálculo da Aneel no relatório de Análise de Impacto Regulatório (AIR) elaborado neste processo, entre 18h e 22h, a geração fotovoltaica correspondeu a apenas 0,009 vez sua geração média anual no período analisado. Na eólica, a relação foi de 1,20 vez. Nova conta O índice proposto pelo ONS seria calculado a partir da relação entre a potência que a usina comprovar entregar na janela crítica e uma potência de referência. Quanto maior a contribuição, menor seria o coeficiente aplicado sobre a energia gerada pelo empreendimento para calcular sua participação no rateio. O operador apresentou como uma das alternativas uma escala contínua, com coeficientes entre 100% e 25%. Uma usina sem contribuição na janela crítica ficaria com coeficiente 1, enquanto uma usina cuja contribuição atingisse integralmente a referência teria coeficiente de 0,25. Outra possibilidade é manter os quatro níveis de 100%, 75%, 50% e 25% desenhados pela Aneel, mas definir o enquadramento pela contribuição de potência, em vez do Índice de Flexibilidade.
