artigo.texto: A província de Chubut busca impulsionar novas ferramentas de financiamento sustentável para melhorar sua competitividade com o desenvolvimento de mercado de carbono. O governador Ignacio “Nacho” Torres apresentou esses objetivos durante o encerramento de “Carbono Chubut: valorizando os serviços ecossistêmicos da Patagônia“, um evento que reuniu referências públicas, científicas, acadêmicas e produtivas. Um encontro com foco na captura de carbono O encontro analisou estratégias para reduzir emissões, valorizar os serviços ecossistêmicos e gerar instrumentos econômicos vinculados à captura de carbono. A agenda incluiu desde a restauração do bosque nativo e a prevenção de incêndios, até a energia solar e eólica, o hidrogênio verde, os biocombustíveis e a pecuária regenerativa. Torres afirmou que a política ambiental pode ser articulada com uma estratégia de desenvolvimento econômico. “Este Congresso é importantíssimo. Temos uma premissa inegociável: enfrentar a mudança climática não é um obstáculo ao desenvolvimento. Temos uma província com uma diversidade impressionante: floresta, estepe, cordilheira e mar. E essa diversidade temos que cuidar”, afirmou o governador. Os créditos de carbono como ferramenta de financiamento Um dos principais eixos do encontro foi o potencial dos créditos de carbono como ferramenta de financiamento. O objetivo é que os projetos capazes de capturar carbono ou reduzir emissões possam gerar recursos para sustentar iniciativas ambientais e produtivas. “A prevenção de incêndios é um tema central para nós. Ao mesmo tempo, estamos trabalhando na restauração para reimplantar nosso bosque nativo. Vai levar tempo, mas tem que ser uma política de Estado a longo prazo. E os créditos de carbono são fundamentais para financiar esses projetos”, destacou Torres. O governador também focou na captura de carbono nos solos e seu possível impacto econômico. “É muito importante trabalhar na captação de carbono em nosso solo. É uma oportunidade enorme e temos que fomentá-la para sermos mais competitivos”, afirmou. Chubut já conta com sete parques fotovoltaicos A estratégia provincial contempla, além disso, o crescimento das energias renováveis. Torres indicou que Chubut conta atualmente com mais de sete parques fotovoltaicos. Também destacou os incentivos fiscais destinados ao setor, juntamente com a possibilidade de que famílias, empresas e cooperativas produzam energia renovável e comercializem seus excedentes. “Descarbonizar é medir, reduzir emissões e ganhar eficiência”, afirmou o mandatário, ao vincular a transição energética com a necessidade de acompanhar atividades eletrointensivas e uma demanda crescente de eletricidade. Um marco normativo para o mercado de carbono provincial Outro dos objetivos é avançar para um marco normativo provincial para o mercado de carbono. O vice-governador Gustavo Menna destacou que o debate desenvolvido durante o encontro poderia contribuir para impulsionar uma legislação específica na Legislatura. De fato, o próprio edifício legislativo já incorporou 260 painéis solares. Segundo foi exposto durante o evento, este sistema permite reduzir mais de 23% o consumo de energia proveniente da rede. Além disso, evita a emissão de cerca de 118 toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente por ano. Um plano alinhado com as metas climáticas de 2030 O secretário de Meio Ambiente e Controle do Desenvolvimento Sustentável, Juan José Rivera, explicou que a iniciativa faz parte do Plano de Resposta à Mudança Climática provincial. O trabalho visa identificar estratégias de descarbonização para diferentes atividades e avançar na monetização dos serviços ecossistêmicos. Chubut também conta com normativa específica sobre emissões de metano e trabalha com o horizonte das metas estabelecidas para 2030. Restauração de florestas, biochar e pecuária sustentável O evento também abordou projetos de restauração da Floresta Andina, florestamento e reflorestamento, e o uso de biochar para capturar carbono e melhorar os solos. Também foram discutidas alternativas de manejo sustentável para a estepe, os pastos e a pecuária ovina. Além disso, foram analisadas as possibilidades do hidrogênio verde, dos biocombustíveis avançados, da energia eólica e solar, juntamente com ferramentas para medir e verificar a redução de emissões. O desafio colocado pela província é converter essas capacidades ambientais e energéticas em projetos que possam acessar financiamento e atrair capital. Torres afirmou que o objetivo é contar com regras que permitam a Chubut “ser competitivo e ponta de lança em um tema que hoje demanda o mundo”.

artigo.texto: Pesquisa inÃ©dita mapeia projetos e programas do mercado de carbono no Brasil e em Minas Levantamento sistematiza 118 projetos voluntÃ¡rios e 30 iniciativas jurisdicionais e reÃºne dados sobre impactos e lacunas no mercado de carbono brasileiroÂ compartilhe Um levantamento inédito sobre projetos voluntários e programas jurisdicionais de Redução de Emissões por Desmatamento e Degradação Florestal (REDD+) no Brasil já identificou e sistematizou 118 projetos voluntários de REDD+ no Brasil, a maior parte concentrada na região amazônica. Quanto às iniciativas jurisdicionais, foram identificadas pelo menos 30 leis, decretos, editais, e programas nos nove estados da Amazônia Legal e em Mato Grosso do Sul. Veja o resultado na plataforma Territórios em Disputa: REDD+ e Conflitos no Brasil. Fique por dentro das notÃcias que importam para vocÃª! O estudo e a plataforma foram desenvolvidos por pesquisadores da Fundação Rosa Luxemburgo e do Programa de Pós-Graduação de Ciências Sociais em Desenvolvimento, Agricultura e Sociedade (CPDA), da Universidade Federal Rural do Rio de Janeiro (UFRRJ) em parceria com o Coletivo de Pesquisa Desigualdade Ambiental, Economia e Política. A pesquisa visa reunir e organizar dados sobre os projetos e políticas, além de informações sobre comunidades atingidas e conflitos ambientais associados a essas iniciativas. No caso dos programas jurisdicionais, o estudo concentrou-se inicialmente nos estados da Amazônia Legal e no Mato Grosso do Sul, considerando o avanço dessas políticas nesses territórios. O levantamento reúne dados sobre localização, área, status, atores envolvidos, comunidades atingidas e comercialização de créditos pelos projetos, além de denúncias públicas, relatos comunitários e documentos sobre conflitos socioambientais associados às iniciativas de REDD+ e ao avanço do mercado de carbono no país. A pesquisa também identificou lacunas de transparência que dificultam saber quem financia determinadas iniciativas, quem administra os recursos e de que forma as comunidades participam das decisões. O objetivo do mapeamento é dar visibilidade não só aos projetos e políticas em andamento, mas às a disputas territoriais, violações de direitos e outras formas de violência registradas em áreas onde esses projetos estão em operação. A partir da análise de diferentes fontes, os pesquisadores buscaram compreender também como as iniciativas de REDD+ se relacionam com processos de financeirização da natureza, controle territorial e mudanças nas formas de uso da floresta. Nesta primeira etapa, o estudo concentra-se principalmente na Amazônia, região que reúne a maior parte dos projetos de REDD+ em operação no Brasil. A expectativa é ampliar gradualmente o escopo do levantamento para outras regiões do país à medida que novos estudos forem realizados. Segundo Elisangela Soldatelli Paim, coordenadora do Programa Latino-Americano de Clima e Energia da Fundação Rosa Luxemburgo, a pesquisa surgiu diante da dificuldade de acessar informações detalhadas sobre projetos e políticas de REDD+, frequentemente dispersas entre diferentes fontes e apresentadas em linguagem técnica. “A pesquisa reuniu informações que estavam dispersas em diferentes documentos, relatórios e registros públicos. Ao tornar esses dados mais acessíveis, esperamos fortalecer o debate público sobre os impactos dessas iniciativas nos territórios e contribuir para a defesa dos direitos das populações afetadas”, afirma. Nos últimos anos, denúncias públicas, reportagens e estudos passaram a relacionar parte dos projetos brasileiros de mercado de carbono a situações de assédio, falta de informação adequada e restrições ao uso tradicional dos territórios. As iniciativas envolvidas comercializam créditos de carbono gerados por uma redução do desmatamento que, em muitos casos, é questionada e estão localizados em territórios de povos indígenas, comunidades tradicionais, camponeses e outras populações rurais. Para Elisangela, esses registros levantam uma questão central sobre o funcionamento do mercado de compensação de emissões: até que ponto as empresas podem compensar suas emissões por meio de projetos associados a conflitos sobre direitos territoriais ou a restrições ao uso tradicional dos territórios?. Valores e compradores Entre novembro de 2025 e março de 2026, os pesquisadores analisaram registros de organizações internacionais e das principais certificadoras que operam os padrões do mercado voluntário de créditos de carbono no Brasil, Verra e Cercarbono, para identificar projetos brasileiros voltados à redução do desmatamento. Os registros consultados informam volumes de créditos comercializados e seus beneficiários, mas não tornam públicos os valores efetivamente pagos nas transações. Essa ausência de informações impede identificar com precisão quanto dos recursos movimentados pelo mercado chega aos projetos, aos intermediários e às comunidades envolvidas. Para dimensionar o mercado, o levantamento adotou como referência uma estimativa média de R$ 35 por crédito de carbono. O valor, no entanto, não permite determinar quanto foi efetivamente pago em cada operação nem como os recursos foram distribuídos entre os diferentes agentes envolvidos. Plataforma de consulta Os resultados do levantamento passam a ser disponibilizados na plataforma Territórios em Disputa: REDD+ e Conflitos no Brasil, criada para reunir e tornar acessíveis informações sobre projetos de REDD+, agentes envolvidos, territórios impactados e registros de conflitos socioambientais associados a essas iniciativas. O portal reúne dados sobre a localização dos projetos e sobre empresas, certificadoras, governos, organizações e outros atores envolvidos, além de informações relacionadas aos territórios e às comunidades afetadas. A proposta é funcionar como uma fonte pública de consulta para pesquisadores, jornalistas, organizações da sociedade civil, gestores públicos e comunidades interessadas no tema. artigo.texto: TAMPA, Fla. (WFTS) — Tampa Electric is moving to build a financial firewall between future data centers and existing customers, filing a proposal with state regulators that would require large energy users to cover the full cost of the power infrastructure needed to serve them. The proposal, submitted this week to the Florida Public Service Commission, comes as utilities across the country race to prepare for explosive growth in data centers, the facilities that power artificial intelligence, cloud computing and other digital services. Watch full report from Jada Williams Under the plan, any new customer with an expected peak demand of 50 megawatts or more, enough electricity to power tens of thousands of homes, would be classified as a "large load customer" and face a new set of rules designed to prevent costs from being shifted onto existing ratepayers. "Tampa Electric's responsibility is very clear. We must protect our existing customers while we're planning responsibly for the future," Tampa Electric spokesperson Cherie Jacobs said. What TECO is proposing The utility's filing stems from a new Florida law that requires electric companies to establish tariffs for large-load customers, including large-scale data centers. According to the filing, customers meeting the 50-megawatt threshold would be required to pay for: - New power generation needed to serve their facilities - Transmission upgrades - Energy storage projects - Distribution and infrastructure improvements - Certain fuel transportation costs - Additional grid-related expenses associated with their operations The filing specifically states the tariffs are designed to "reasonably ensure that each large load customer bears its own full cost of service and that such cost is not shifted to the company's general body of ratepayers." That language directly addresses one of the biggest concerns surrounding data centers nationwide: whether residential customers could eventually pay for utility upgrades needed to support massive power-demand projects. Long-term commitments required The proposal also requires companies to make long-term commitments before connecting to TECO's system. Under the filing, large-load customers would be required to sign contracts lasting at least 20 years. Customers that terminate service early could face financial penalties tied to remaining infrastructure costs. The filing also requires three years' notice before ending service and includes additional fees if companies fail to provide sufficient notice. "Incoming large load customers have to foot the bill for that," Jacobs said. "Our existing customers come first." Companies may have to provide millions in financial security One lesser-known element of the filing involves financial guarantees. For some large-load customers, TECO could require security deposits, letters of credit or other financial assurances valued at up to $2 million per megawatt of contracted demand, depending on the customer's financial profile. The requirement is intended to protect existing customers if a project is canceled or fails to meet contractual obligations. Initial capacity capped at 1 gigawatt The filing also limits the first customer class, known as LLCS-1, to a combined total of 1 gigawatt of large-load demand. After that threshold is reached, future projects would move into a second customer class with project-specific cost calculations. For perspective, one gigawatt of power demand is roughly equivalent to the electricity consumption of hundreds of thousands of homes, according to the proposal. To prepare for that possibility, TECO's filing anticipates investments including: - 600 megawatts of energy storage - 600 megawatts of new generating capacity tied to modernization plans at Big Bend Power Station - New transmission facilities needed to support future large-load growth New restrictions on foreign-owned entities The proposal includes another provision likely to draw attention. Under requirements included in the filing and tied to state law, TECO would be prohibited from providing service under the new tariffs to certain "foreign entities." The filing references entities controlled by governments identified in Florida law as foreign countries of concern and requires customers to submit ownership affidavits verifying compliance. No large-scale data center currently proposed in Hillsborough Despite growing concern among residents and local elected officials, there is currently no major data center proposal under review in Hillsborough County. Still, county commissioners have begun discussing potential regulations for future projects, including restrictions on using county drinking water supplies for cooling and a possible moratorium on AI-focused data centers in unincorporated areas while land-use policies are developed. County leaders say those conversations are aimed at preparing now rather than reacting later. What's next? TECO filed the proposal with the Florida Public Service Commission on Sept. 30. The commission must approve the plan before it can take effect. The utility says the review process could take several months and potentially stretch into early next year. For now, the proposal offers a glimpse of how Florida utilities are preparing for a future in which energy-hungry data centers may become increasingly common and where regulators, utilities and local governments are trying to answer the same question: who should pay for the infrastructure needed to support them? artigo.texto: Greenwood County’s newly formed ad hoc data center committee began its work Wednesday by selecting its leadership and choosing water and sewer as the first issue it will examine. The seven-member committee unanimously selected Steve Coleman as chairman during its first meeting at the Greenwood County Library. Dave Schofield was selected as vice chairman. Coleman was appointed by District 6 Councilman Robbie Templeton, and Schofield was appointed by Councilman Dayne Pruitt of District 5. Dr. Adam Eichelberger was not present for the meeting. The committee was created after months of debate over whether data centers should be permitted in Greenwood County and, if so, what parameters there should be. County Council Chairman Theo Lane sat with committee members until Coleman was elected as the committee chairperson, then Lane moved into the audience. Lane encouraged members to approach the subject one issue at a time. “The purpose of this group is to make a recommendation to the Planning Commission and the County Council as to whether data centers are appropriate to be placed within Greenwood County, and if so, what regulations and safeguards should be in place,” Lane said. Lane said the committee will likely examine subjects such as water and sewer use, power demand, noise, buffers and other concerns raised during public hearings earlier this year. County staff will help identify experts to speak at meetings and information requested by the committee for each topic. Topics for studyThe committee was presented with a list of issues that emerged repeatedly during months of public discussion over data centers. The proposed topics include buffers and setbacks, power, water and sewer, noise, height and visual impacts, air quality, lighting, medical impacts, heat generation, wildlife impacts, environmental impacts and economic impacts. The list is intended as a starting point rather than a fixed agenda. Committee members can add, remove or combine subjects as their work progresses. Members were also provided two versions of the data center zoning amendment County Council considered earlier this year: the original proposal and the version the council ultimately approved after amending it. The original proposal would have established data centers as a conditional use in the county’s I-1 light industrial, I-2 heavy industrial and RDD rural development districts, subject to a series of regulations. Council ultimately took a different approach and amended the original proposal. The approved version states that data centers are to be excluded and denied in the I-1, I-2 and RDD zoning districts. Chappell told members the prior amendments give the committee a framework rather than requiring it to start from scratch. The committee could ultimately recommend leaving the prohibition in place or recommend changes that would allow some form of data center development under new regulations, or allow no data centers at all. Committee members also discussed visiting an operating data center as part of their research. Betty Boles asked whether members would have an opportunity to tour a facility. Chappell said arrangements would need to be worked out between the committee chairman and County Council, but said he believed there was an understanding that members would likely need to visit a data center at some point. For its first substantive meeting, the committee agreed to begin with water and sewer. County staff said that topic would be one of the easier areas for arranging speakers quickly, with officials from Greenwood Commissioners of Public Works, Greenwood Metropolitan District or other utility providers potentially invited to address the committee. Committee structureThe committee consists of seven voting members, one appointed by each County Council member. Council member Cathy Miller and Planning Commission Chairman John Lake will serve as non-voting liaisons between the committee and their respective bodies. Lane told the Index-Journal before Wednesday’s meeting that although additional seats had previously been discussed, the final committee would remain limited to the seven district appointees. Lane said adding representatives from other organizations, such as business or community groups, risked “muddying the water,” while council’s formal action had established the seven district positions. After being elected chairman, Coleman said he is entering the process without a predetermined position on data centers. He added that he was not a “data center aficionado” and viewed his lack of direct experience as an opportunity to approach the issue with a clean slate. “My leadership style has always been: we’re open-minded, respectful of others and others’ opinions, and making fact-based critical decisions that are the best for our community,” Coleman said. Public process Much of Wednesday’s organizational meeting focused on how the committee will conduct its business. Chappell reminded members that the committee is a public body subject to South Carolina’s Freedom of Information Act. “You are a public body, so you’re going to be subject to the same rules as Planning Commission, County Council, any other city council, any other public body,” Chappell said. Meetings must be publicly announced, and members cannot meet privately as a quorum to discuss committee business. That includes group phone calls or other communications involving enough members to constitute a meeting. County staff will prepare agendas and minutes, and meetings will be livestreamed, recorded and posted to the county’s website. The committee also agreed generally to allow public comment related to the topic being discussed at each meeting. artigo.texto: Mercedes-Benz and ProLogium have entered a joint testing agreement that will give the auto maker priority access to ProLogium‘s latest Gen4 battery cells, and which builds on a near-decade-long partnership between the companies focused on developing next-generation battery technologies for mobility. Under the agreement, ProLogium’s Gen4 battery technology will undergo electrical, thermal and safety testing at Mercedes-Benz facilities and specialist external testing institutes. The results will be used to assess the technology’s suitability for potential integration into future vehicles. ProLogium’s Gen4 battery platform is designed around five core attributes: safety, performance, energy density, scalable manufacturing and cost competitiveness. Its safety architecture combines a non-flammable inorganic electrolyte, ceramic separator technology and ProLogium’s proprietary active safety mechanism. The platform is also designed to support fast charging, high power output and performance at low temperatures. Vincent Yang, founder and CEO of ProLogium, said, “Over nearly a decade, our collaboration with Mercedes-Benz has evolved from early cell development and validation to testing our latest Gen4 technology for future vehicle applications. For next-generation batteries, true value comes from turning years of innovation into scalable manufacturing and commercially viable products. With Mercedes-Benz’s early investment and support for our European expansion, together with the strong support of the French government and the European Union, we are advancing toward large-scale production in Europe and building a manufacturing footprint to serve global markets.” “At Mercedes-Benz, we are committed to shaping the future of electric mobility through technological leadership and innovation. Our long-standing partnership with ProLogium is a strong example of how we bring the best expertise together to advance next-generation battery technologies,” said added Jörg Burzer, member of the board of management, Mercedes‑Benz Group, chief technology officer, development and procurement. “By combining ProLogium’s pioneering solid-state battery approach with Mercedes-Benz’s deep battery development, testing and integration capabilities, we are taking the next step in exploring advanced battery technologies for future electric vehicles.” Since 2016, the partnership between the two companies has progressed from early hybrid solid-state Gen3 development and joint testing to potential future vehicle platform planning. Mercedes-Benz has also become a long-term global automotive partner and strategic investor in ProLogium, extending the relationship beyond product validation. The collaboration has included validation of multiple lithium-ceramic battery formats, including pouch cells and ProLogium’s next-generation prismatic cells, as well as its Bi-Polar technology. ProLogium’s Taoke Gigafactory in Taiwan has completed GWh-scale manufacturing validation and supports C-sample production, Demo Car programs and future commercial production. ProLogium’s planned Dunkirk Gigafactory, with a future capacity of up to 44GWh, is expected to establish localized European manufacturing and supply-chain capacity, replicating the proven production model developed in Taiwan. Once the first phase of this factory is completed, ProLogium will be able to provide commercial cells to European customers at a scale large enough to support electric vehicle platforms on the continent. artigo.texto: Previsão para as Ações da Bloom Energy: BE dispara quase 11%, a demanda por energia de data centers de IA pode continuar impulsionando as ações? Em 29 de setembro (ET), as ações da Bloom Energy saltaram 10,8%, a US$ 291,25, impulsionadas pela alta demanda de data centers de IA por geração local de energia e parcerias estratégicas, como com a Oracle e a Brookfield. A receita do segundo trimestre disparou 165,5% ano a ano, atingindo US$ 1,065 bilhão, e a empresa elevou suas projeções para 2026. Apesar da forte expansão e do valuation elevado (P/S de 23,3x), os riscos incluem a execução de projetos, aprovações regulatórias e volatilidade técnica, com zona de resistência crítica entre US$ 302 e US$ 305. TradingKey - Em 29 de setembro (ET), a Bloom Energy (BE) fechou em alta de 10,8%, cotada a US$ 291,25, atingindo uma máxima intradiária de US$ 302,25, com o volume de negociação alcançando aproximadamente 23,69 milhões de ações, significativamente acima das médias recentes. Na sessão anterior, a BE havia recuado 8,95%, indicando um aumento acentuado na volatilidade do preço das ações em patamares elevados. [Fonte: TradingView] De acordo com informações divulgadas pela cidade de Fremont, a Bloom Energy adquiriu uma instalação local de aproximadamente 158.000 pés quadrados para expandir suas operações e prevê criar centenas de empregos em manufatura avançada. A finalidade específica, a capacidade adicional e o cronograma de produção ainda não foram anunciados. O analista David Arcaro, do Morgan Stanley, acredita que a expansão reflete a forte demanda contínua pelos produtos da empresa. O Jefferies manteve sua recomendação de "manutenção" (Hold) e elevou o preço-alvo de US$ 229 para US$ 264, valor que continua abaixo do último preço de fechamento da BE. Escassez de Energia em Data Centers de IA Impulsiona Demanda por Geração Local de Energia O consumo de energia por clusters de servidores de IA continua a subir, enquanto os ciclos de construção para conexão à rede elétrica e infraestrutura de transmissão permanecem longos, levando alguns data centers a adotarem soluções de geração de energia no próprio local. As células de combustível de óxido sólido da Bloom Energy podem gerar eletricidade nas instalações dos clientes, reduzindo a dependência de capacidade adicional da rede elétrica, embora os projetos ainda precisem garantir o fornecimento de combustível e obter as licenças necessárias. O contrato-máster de prestação de serviços assinado entre a Oracle e a Bloom Energy cobre até 2,8 GW em sistemas de células de combustível, dos quais 1,2 GW já foi contratado e teve sua implantação iniciada, com a capacidade remanescente dependendo de aquisições subsequentes e do progresso dos projetos. A Bloom Energy e a Brookfield também ampliaram sua estrutura de financiamento para projetos de infraestrutura de IA de US$ 5 bilhões para US$ 25 bilhões, com o capital específico a ser liberado à medida que os projetos avançarem. A Bloom Energy declarou que seu segmento de infraestrutura de IA atendeu a quase 24 clientes, representando aproximadamente 250 MW de capacidade. A administração da empresa também destacou que grandes hyperscalers dos EUA, além de mais de uma dúzia de provedores de nuvem para IA, laboratórios de IA e operadores de data centers, validaram e aprovaram suas soluções de suprimento de energia. Receita cresce 166% à medida que entrega de projetos se torna fundamental A receita da Bloom Energy no segundo trimestre atingiu US$ 1,065 bilhão, uma alta de 165,5% na comparação anual; a margem bruta GAAP subiu de 26,7% para 33,4%, e o fluxo de caixa operacional foi de US$ 226,4 milhões. A empresa elevou sua projeção de receita para 2026 para a faixa de US$ 3,9 bilhões a US$ 4,2 bilhões, com o ponto médio representando um crescimento anual de aproximadamente 100%; a projeção para o LPA não GAAP foi fixada entre US$ 2,55 e US$ 2,85. Com base em um valor de mercado de aproximadamente US$ 94,2 bilhões em 29 de setembro e no ponto médio da projeção de receita de US$ 4,05 bilhões, o índice preço/vendas (P/S) nos últimos 12 meses da BE é de aproximadamente 23,3x. O valuation atual exige que a empresa mantenha um crescimento relativamente rápido e conclua a expansão de capacidade e as entregas de projetos em grande escala conforme o planejado. As principais áreas de atenção daqui para frente incluem o uso pretendido e o cronograma de comissionamento da nova instalação em Fremont, se a capacidade restante de 1,6 GW sob o acordo com a Oracle pode ser convertida em compras firmes e as variações na margem bruta. Além disso, gasodutos de gás natural, licenças de qualidade do ar e o avanço da construção de projetos como o Project Jupiter também podem impactar a implantação de equipamentos e o cronograma de reconhecimento de receita. Calculados a partir da mínima intradiária de US$ 197,50 em 1º de setembro até a máxima intradiária de aproximadamente US$ 302,30 em 29 de setembro, os níveis de retratação de Fibonacci de 0,236, 0,382, 0,500 e 0,618 são de aproximadamente US$ 279,87, US$ 262,27, US$ 249,90 e US$ 237,53, respectivamente. [Fonte: TradingView] Em caso de alta, a faixa de US$ 302 a US$ 305 é atualmente a principal zona de resistência. Se a BE fechar acima de US$ 305 com forte volume, o próximo nível a ser observado é de US$ 330 a US$ 331, correspondente ao nível de extensão de Fibonacci de 1,272; após um novo rompimento, a atenção pode se voltar para o nível de extensão de 1,618 em torno de US$ 367. artigo.texto: Construction companies are now facing the second wave of inflation. By Wolf Richter for WOLF STREET. The amount spent on the construction of data centers spiked by another 7.5% in August from July, and by 73% year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $85 billion, according to construction data from the Census Bureau today. Since the beginning of 2021, the annual rate of construction spending on data centers has spiked by 823%. These amounts only reflect the construction costs of the buildings, the improvements around the buildings, and the equipment integrated into the buildings, such as HVAC systems. But that’s the cheap part of a data center. Not included here is the expensive part: equipping the completed data center buildings with servers and racks, with electronic and optical equipment to connect the servers to the internet, and with the electrical equipment that supplies the servers with prodigious amounts of power, including in many cases onsite diesel or gas-turbine power generators. Though nothing that needs to be funded can grow on an exponential curve for long, the AI data center construction mania is continuing along a near-exponential curve for now, despite increasing efforts on the ground by people, municipalities, and state governments – including in Texas! – to slow it down or block it. Data centers, their demand on power, their effect on electricity prices, and related issues have entered midterm election rhetoric. Building the data centers and purchasing the equipment has sent shockwaves of demand through big parts of the industrial economy: WHOOSH, Go Orders at US Manufacturers of “Core Capital Goods,” Fueled by the AI Infrastructure Boom: Attracting the skilled labor to build the data centers and install the equipment and get it up and running has sent shockwaves of demand through the labor market, with reports of labor shortages emanating from other projects, as specialists get pulled away by data center projects’ whatever-it-takes approach to spending, including on salaries for highly skilled labor. Construction of power plants and distribution infrastructure has also taken off, though planning and permitting takes years before construction can even start. Construction spending in the power sector rose by 0.8% in August from July and by 8.5% year-over-year to an annual rate of $186 billion. Since the beginning of 2021, the spending rate has increased by 58%. Power plant construction spending includes the costs of the power generation equipment, unlike data center construction costs that do not include the servers and related equipment, which are the most expensive part of a data center. Factory construction spending growth – “growth,” not actual spending – has taken a backseat to the mania of data centers; “actual spending” on factory construction ($168 billion annual rate) is still nearly double the spending on data centers ($85 billion annual rate). Spending on factory construction at an annual rate of $168 billion in August was unchanged from July, and down by 19.8% year-over-year. But it was still 126% higher than what it had averaged over the six-year period 2015-2020. The costs of the production equipment inside the factory – such as industrial robots and systems that produce semiconductors – are not included in these figures here, though they can dwarf the costs of the building. Once the factories are built and equipped and production starts, their real contribution to the economy and employment begins and continues for decades. Building a factory is not a one-time shot but a long-term contribution to US production. It’s not the construction spending per se that matters but the future production that will come from these factories. Construction companies face the second wave of inflation. The Producer Price Index (PPI) for construction materials – steel mill products, concrete, lumber, gypsum, etc. – spiked by 10.1% year-over-year in August. And since the beginning of 2025, when this second wave of inflation started, this PPI has spiked by 15.8%. The PPI for nonresidential construction services spiked by 9.4% year-over-year and by 11.8% since the beginning of 2025. artigo.texto: A infraestrutura computacional voltada ao processamento de algoritmos avançados e serviços de nuvem consolidou-se como um dos principais vetores de consumo de energia do planeta. De acordo com o relatório internacional intitulado “IA encontra a rede elétrica: moldando o cenário energético dos data centers”, divulgado pela Capgemini, a aceleração das atividades de data centers tem colocado pressão inédita sobre os sistemas de transmissão e distribuição de eletricidade. O levantamento indica que mais de 60% dos executivos do setor elétrico contam com ferramentas de inteligência artificial para destravar saltos expressivos de produtividade operacional e eficiência na gestão de fluxos de potência. A pesquisa da multinacional de consultoria e tecnologia entrevistou 612 diretores e executivos seniores do setor de energia elétrica envolvidos no atendimento a instalações de missão crítica, além de 175 lideranças proprietárias e operadoras de centros de processamento de dados e cerca de 20 especialistas industriais globais. O estudo abrangeu 21 nações distribuídas por América do Norte, Europa, Ásia-Pacífico e América Latina, incluindo o Brasil. A análise central apresentada pela organização pontua que o descompasso entre a velocidade de implantação de servidores de alta densidade e a expansão física da infraestrutura de transmissão exige uma reestruturação imediata dos modelos operacionais de utilidades públicas. Descompasso operacional e o panorama da infraestrutura elétrica Historicamente, a expansão das redes elétricas mundiais baseou-se em ciclos previsíveis de planejamento de longo prazo, com cronogramas de amortização de ativos que costumam variar entre 15 e 30 anos. Por outro lado, a evolução dos clusters de computação intensiva voltados ao treinamento de grandes modelos de linguagem opera em ciclos tecnológicos bienais ou trienais. As empresas responsáveis pelo fornecimento energético sustentam que essa discrepância temporal cria gargalos no atendimento a novos pontos de conexão, gerando filas de espera para interligação de novos complexos industriais de tecnologia em polos consolidados. No recorte da América Latina, e especificamente no mercado brasileiro, as alegações do estudo refletem tensões próprias do arranjo regional. Embora o parque gerador nacional exiba predominância de fontes renováveis — como hidrelétricas, parques eólicos e complexos solares —, as limitações nas linhas de transmissão interestaduais e a volatilidade climática exigem respostas rápidas de despacho. O documento da Capgemini argumenta que a corrida das empresas de tecnologia (hyperscalers) por contratos de fornecimento firme de energia verde intensificou a necessidade de soluções computacionais que monitorem o balanço entre oferta e demanda em tempo real, mitigando riscos de instabilidade sistêmica. Em termos setoriais, concessionárias enfrentam custos crescentes de modernização de subestações antigas e desafios regulatórios relacionados à integração de fontes distribuídas. A consultoria alega que, enquanto o consumo bruto de eletricidade impulsionado por cargas computacionais continuará em alta pelos próximos três a cinco anos, o setor de utilidades públicas opera com taxas de adoção de tecnologias digitais abaixo do potencial necessário para suportar essa carga sem perdas substanciais de receita ou interrupções de fornecimento. Os agentes autônomos diferenciam-se de algoritmos convencionais de aprendizado por possuírem capacidade de percepção contextual, tomada de decisão algorítmica e execução de manobras de chaveamento sem dependência contínua de intervenção humana em centros de controle operacional (CCO). Conforme sustenta a organização responsável pelo diagnóstico, o plano de mais de metade dos operadores (58%) em ativar agentes nos próximos 24 meses visa conter custos operacionais associados à manutenção preventiva e aumentar a velocidade de restauração do sistema diante de eventos climáticos severos ou oscilações imprevistas de carga provocadas por data centers. Aplicações técnicas da automação algorítmica e impactos corporativos A introdução sistemática de soluções analíticas no segmento de utilidades tem o potencial de remodelar a produtividade corporativa em múltiplos elos da cadeia de valor. artigo.texto: TOOELE, Utah — The Utah National Guard armory here is a private, first-class of a building. Formally called a readiness center, it’s where Utah’s citizen soldiers can train and prepare to deploy. Maintenance costs are piling up at the one-story, two-tone building. The guard would like to replace it. Taxes – state and federal – have traditionally paid for National Guard building projects. Utah is looking at another source of funding: a controversial data center in Box Elder County, north of the Great Salt Lake. It’s not a welcome plan at the Fraternal Order of Eagles lodge next door to the Tooele armory. On a recent afternoon, data center skepticism was being served alongside longneck bottles of beer. From a stool at the lodge, Doug Rogers, who served 10 years in the U.S. Air Force and reserves as an aircraft mechanic, said he has “mixed emotions” about data centers and is “not really in favor of AI because you never know what to believe anymore.” FOX 13 reviewed hundreds of pages of documents and hours of audio from public meetings to learn about the military connections with Stratos, the data center project proposed in Box Elder County by investor and “Shark Tank” star Kevin O’Leary. A plan would take taxes generated by Stratos to fund construction projects for the Utah National Guard. But Stratos backers are also hoping the U.S. military or defense contractors join big AI companies in becoming customers at the data center. “Utah is in the perfect location with the right educated workforce,” the Canadian O’Leary told FOX 13 in June, “with the right fiber and technology and the right defense, and people that have the DNA to support the military.” ALL THAT IT CAN BE Stratos is being developed on land leased and under the control of a state agency called the Military Installation Development Authority. Known as MIDA, it’s the agency that would collect taxes from Stratos to help fund those National Guard projects. Clearfield Mayor Mark Shepherd serves on MIDA’s governing board. In an interview with FOX 13, Shepherd said the first time he heard the Stratos pitch, he thought it was a good project with “phenomenal benefit to the military.” “There is income generated from Stratos that will help the National Guard,” Shepherd said. Not that Shepherd, who says he does not have a security clearance, knows all the National Guard projects that MIDA will help construct. “A lot of that'll be classified,” Shepherd said. “As those are made known to us, we can share those.” Besides replacing the armory in Tooele, public documents reveal a few projects MIDA could develop for the National Guard: - A new hangar for helicopters the Utah National Guard wants to station in Cedar City. - The Utah National Guard’s main base, Camp Williams, would like a new physical fitness center and other training facilities. - The guard would like to replace its nearly 50-year-old headquarters along Interstate 15 in Draper. In all, MIDA lists 27 Utah National Guard properties where it could build or renovate. Without money from Stratos, Shepherd said, the projects would either have to compete with other states for money from the Pentagon or be paid for with taxes paid by everyday Utahns. The Utah National Guard has “got to be paid for somewhere,” Shepherd said. Representatives of the Utah National Guard declined to go on camera with FOX 13 but in emails emphasized the project list is fluid. Also, it could be years before Stratos generates any money for MIDA to share. A MILITARY ASSET The Utah Legislature created MIDA in 2007, though its origins can be traced to the 1990s. The Department of Defense was closing bases. Utah’s Hill Air Force Base was considered for an honorable discharge, or – as politicians saw it – a crash landing the state’s economy wouldn’t walk away from. While Hill escaped the cuts, Utah legislators decided to bolster the base’s economic defenses. They created MIDA to promote partnerships with the U.S. military, hoping to make Hill too important to close. MIDA has developed Falcon Hill, a business park adjacent to the Air Force base. It’s also developed an addition to Deer Valley ski resort that caters to military personnel and veterans. Stratos has created far more controversy than previous MIDA projects, inciting protests at public meetings. State Sen. Brady Brammer, R-Highland, plans to file a bill that could require MIDA developments to have more direct ties to the military. “You've got a whole lot bigger development that's on private land,” Brammer said of Stratos, “not military land, and it's not next to a military base. “And so, has that gone beyond what MIDA should do? And I think most people feel like maybe it has.” Brammer clarified that he is not seeking to stop Stratos. Back at the Eagles lodge next to the armory in Tooele, Rogers said if the choice was between building Stratos and funding the National Guard by raising his taxes, he’d pay the higher taxes. “I think that would be the ticket,” Rogers said, “because I don't know what this data center is going to do.”

artigo.texto: [News] China Unveils 15th Five-Year Battery Plan, Targets Initial Large-Scale All-Solid-State Battery Deployment by 2030 China is setting out its next-stage roadmap for emerging battery technologies, with solid-state and sodium-ion batteries among the key areas targeted for further development. According to Xinhua News, China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and six other government departments released the 15th Five-Year Plan for the Development of the New Battery Industry on September 28. TechNews adds that the plan also calls for expanding the use of new battery technologies in areas including energy storage and data centers. By 2030, the plan targets breakthroughs in advanced electrode materials, novel electrolytes, and high-end auxiliary materials, alongside major progress in next-generation battery technologies. It also aims to achieve initial large-scale application of all-solid-state batteries, extend the cycle life of long-life lithium batteries to 15,000 cycles, and reduce product defect rates among leading companies to the parts-per-billion (PPB) level. TechNews adds that the plan seeks to expand new battery applications beyond the EV market. It calls for greater integration of new batteries with clean energy and energy-consuming equipment, extending their use to ships, aviation, intelligent robots, and construction machinery. For energy storage, targeted applications include power generation, power grids, industrial parks, and data centers, expanding the role of new batteries in next-generation power systems. Beyond the 2030 targets, Xinhua notes that the plan outlines 19 key tasks across five areas. These include developing intelligent production lines for key battery manufacturing processes, advancing new battery structures such as flexible and internally series-connected designs, improving battery lifecycle data management, accelerating industry standards, and strengthening intellectual property and trade-secret protections. The new roadmap comes as all-solid-state battery development continues to advance globally. According to TrendForce, the global all-solid-state battery (ASSB) industry is moving from laboratory development toward engineering validation and pilot production in 2026. Some leading companies have advanced to Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs) 5–6, with Toyota, Honda, Nissan, and Samsung SDI slightly ahead in small-scale pilot production. Meanwhile, Chinese companies including CATL, BYD, and FAW are advancing their own pilot lines toward TRL 4–5. China Accelerates ASSB Pilot Production and Vehicle Validation China is seeing progress in ASSB pilot production and product validation. According to China Energy News, several domestic companies are advancing pilot lines in 2026. BYD’s first sulfide-based ASSB pilot line in Shenzhen entered operation in February with planned capacity of 2 GWh, while GAC’s ASSB pilot line has also begun operations and is expected to conduct small-scale vehicle testing in 2026. Gotion High-tech, meanwhile, has completed its first ASSB experimental line with designed capacity of 0.2 GWh. Vehicle validation is also moving forward. National Business Daily notes that BYD plans to begin demonstration deployment of ASSBs in vehicles around 2027 before moving toward large-scale adoption after 2030. Changan aims to begin vehicle validation in 2026 and gradually move toward mass production in 2027, while Chery plans targeted vehicle deployment in 2026 and batch vehicle validation in 2027. artigo.texto: Demanda de data centers assegura aumento da capacidade das termelétricas A estrutura dos afamados data centers exige fornecimento contínuo, estável e de confiabilidade superior a 99%, por isso, essas usinas vêm ganhando destaque Atualizado Projeções do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) apontam salto importante na capacidade instalada das termelétricas, que funcionam como uma espécie de “seguro” para suprir a demanda de energia em horários de pico, ou quando fontes intermitentes geram menos. A estimativa para os próximos anos é passar dos atuais 39.483 MW para 45.982 MW em 2030. O otimismo do setor vem não apenas do recente Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade (LRCAP 2026), que contratou 18.977 MW — entre novas termelétricas, as já existentes e ampliação de hidrelétricas —, mas também da antecipação de contratos que previam adicionar 1.678,4 MW ao Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) no início de setembro. Para 2027, o setor projeta nova expansão por meio de leilões de capacidade, segundo a Associação Brasileira de Geradoras Termelétricas (Abraget). Também impulsiona o setor a demanda de energia por data centers, que exigem fornecimento contínuo, estável e de confiabilidade superior a 99%. Por isso, termelétricas — especialmente as movidas a gás natural e biomassa — vêm ganhando destaque na segurança energética de infraestruturas críticas e do sistema elétrico nacional. Xisto Vieira Filho, presidente da Abraget, explica que o risco de déficit de oferta no setor elétrico para os próximos anos pode superar o limite de 5% estabelecido pelo Conselho Nacional de Política Energética (CNPE) em cenários de forte estresse hidrológico, períodos severos de seca ou alta demanda. “Essa projeção reforça a necessidade de novas termelétricas para garantir a segurança de suprimento”, diz. Estimulados por esse cenário, operadores vêm ampliando seus investimentos. A Mercurio Partners, por exemplo, está desembolsando R$ 1,4 bilhão na construção de cinco usinas termelétricas a gás natural em Alagoas (Pilar I, II, III, IV e V). Essas unidades, que venderam 241,63 MW no LRCAP 2026, serão implantadas em duas fases. A primeira, de 145,72 MW, para atendimento ao SIN a partir de outubro de 2028. Os outros 95,91 MW para atendimento a partir de agosto de 2029. “Os contratos têm prazo de 15 anos e vão gerar cerca de mil empregos diretos durante a construção”, informa Alexandre Americano, CEO da Mercurio Partners. Ele explica que o complexo de Pilar será composto de usinas 100% flexíveis, que, por sua modularidade tecnológica, poderão ser despachadas (acionadas) a qualquer momento pelo ONS. A Mercurio Partners também venceu a renovação do contrato da UTE Paulínia Verde (SP). Conectada à rede da Comgás, a usina de 23,4 MW retomou as operações em agosto. A Origem Energia investirá R$ 2 bilhões na construção de sete usinas termelétricas, também em Alagoas, onde já possui uma operação integrada de soluções energéticas baseadas no gás natural. Os projetos somam 372 MW de capacidade instalada. Pilar Nova (187 MW) e Pilar (135 MW) têm entrada em operação comercial prevista para outubro de 2028, enquanto as outras cinco usinas Manguaba, com 10 MW cada uma, estão previstas para agosto de 2029. “O diferencial importante desses projetos é sua configuração modular. As usinas serão constituídas por motores de 10 MW, cuja configuração permite ajustar a geração em diferentes patamares, adequando a potência entregue à demanda do ONS”, diz Carolina Szczerbacki, diretora de geração de energia da empresa. Segundo a executiva, esses projetos materializam a estratégia de integração gás-energia da empresa, agregando valor ao gás de produção própria e oferecendo ao sistema geração flexível e confiável. “A companhia tem apetite para ampliar sua capacidade termelétrica e pretende avaliar a participação nos próximos leilões de reserva de capacidade.” A Eneva, também vencedora no LRCAP, com 5,06 GW de capacidade contratada, deve investir R$ 18,2 bilhões em empreendimentos com início de operação previsto para 2028 até 2031. Os novos projetos — usinas termelétricas movidas a gás natural — estão concentrados em Sergipe, Ceará e região Sudeste do país. “Trata-se de empreendimentos estruturantes, integrados à infraestrutura de gás natural e localizados em regiões onde a Eneva já tem experiência operacional e presença consolidada”, diz Christiano Vieira, diretor-executivo de regulação do sistema elétrico da companhia. Segundo ele, a expansão inclui o Hub Sergipe (vencedor no produto 2028), com três novas usinas associadas a um terminal de GNL já operacional; o Hub Ceará (vencedor no produto 2030), que reúne duas usinas integradas a um novo terminal de GNL no porto de Pecém; e o Hub Sudeste (vencedor no produto 2031), formado por quatro usinas que utilizarão gás natural proveniente de uma nova infraestrutura de GNL . Sobre curtailment decorrente do excesso de geração, que impacta geradoras de energia solar e eólica, Vieira Filho, da Abraget, explica que as termelétricas estão muito menos expostas a esse tipo de restrição. Ainda assim, algumas térmicas podem ser impactadas, dependendo de sua localização elétrica. Americano, da Mercurio Partners, diz que fontes despacháveis não costumam sofrer curtailment, já que são ligadas exatamente para suprir a carga que renováveis não conseguem suprir.

artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich- During the 7th China Liaoning International Investment and Trade Fair, BYD Battery signed strategic cooperation agreements with the Yingkou municipal government, and separately with the Liaoyang government and Xiamen Xiangyu Group. The partnerships target zero-carbon demonstration projects, new-energy supply chain synergy, and logistics electrification. To electrify port-area transport, they will scale up pure-electric heavy trucks for short-haul container drayage and steel-plant transfers, backed by integrated solar-storage-charging stations. On the zero-carbon front, the plan calls for integrated source-grid-load-storage systems and carbon-emission monitoring platforms. The partners will also push battery recycling to build a green circular industrial system for the port area. Next up, Yingkou will map out application scenarios across ports, steel mills, and industrial parks, teaming up with BYD Battery to draft an annual construction schedule. That same day, BYD Battery, the Liaoyang government, and Xiamen Xiangyu Group signed a three-way strategic framework agreement. Drawing on Xiangyu's aluminum supply chain, the trio will expand ties in battery structural parts, body components, and new-material supply — while jointly exploring integrated "new-energy heavy truck plus solar-storage-charging" solutions. To keep the collaboration on track, they will establish a mechanism for annual high-level talks, dedicated task forces, and information sharing.

artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no EXCLUSIVO CNBC: Demanda por infraestrutura de IA cresce apesar de juros e regras para data centers, diz CEO da CoreWeave Publicado 30/09/2026 • 20:36 | Atualizado há 8 horas KEY POINTS As regulamentações sobre data centers não reduziram a demanda por infraestrutura de inteligência artificial, segundo Mike Intrator, CEO da CoreWeave. Em entrevista exclusiva à CNBC, o executivo afirmou que as novas regras podem alterar a localização dos projetos, mas não devem diminuir a necessidade de infraestrutura para IA. Intrator participou nesta terça-feira (30) da reunião de executivos de grandes empresas de tecnologia com o presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump. Na entrevista, ele também falou sobre a entrada em produção do primeiro cliente mundial na arquitetura Vera Rubin, da Nvidia. “Esse é um momento incrível para poder lançar a tecnologia mais recente. Trouxemos nosso primeiro cliente. É o primeiro cliente do mundo a entrar em produção na arquitetura Vera Rubin”. A Cognition é o primeiro cliente da plataforma. A empresa, disse Intrator, poderá utilizar a nova tecnologia para ampliar suas operações à medida que a arquitetura seja incorporada à infraestrutura de nuvem. “Nós vamos poder usar essa tecnologia para realmente impulsionar sua empresa. E eu acho que vocês verão isso à medida que a tecnologia se prolifera pela nuvem, à medida que trazemos mais clientes para a nossa infraestrutura”. A arquitetura Vera Rubin combina unidades de processamento gráfico (GPU) e a CPU da Nvidia em um mesmo sistema. Para Intrator, a integração dos dois componentes permite ampliar o desempenho da infraestrutura utilizada pelas empresas para aplicações de inteligência artificial. “A maneira como funciona é que a Vera Rubin é uma tecnologia interessante porque ela reúne a GPU, como todos sabem, e também a CPU da Nvidia”, afirmou. O CEO da CoreWeave explicou que a companhia trabalha com um grande volume de CPUs fora dos servidores Vera Rubin que entrega, mas destacou a integração entre os dois componentes dentro de um único servidor. “A integração dessas duas peças de hardware em um único servidor é incrivelmente poderosa e realmente vai impulsionar, gerar ganhos incríveis em termos dos investimentos que as empresas estão fazendo, já que essas duas estão tão bem sincronizadas dentro do único servidor”. Questionado sobre as regras que diferentes estados norte-americanos vêm discutindo para a construção de data centers, Intrator afirmou que a CoreWeave não registrou queda nos pedidos. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC “Não houve absolutamente nenhuma redução nos pedidos”. As regulamentações podem mudar onde a infraestrutura será instalada, mas não alterariam a demanda por capacidade computacional necessária para o desenvolvimento de aplicações de IA. Intrator afirmou que a procura continua elevada porque empresas seguem investindo na construção de infraestrutura e buscando retorno sobre esses ativos. “O mercado está procurando por mais infraestrutura porque há empresas que estão construindo e extraindo o valor da construção dessa infraestrutura. É só uma questão de onde você a coloca, nada mais”, afirmou. O executivo também comentou o impacto das taxas de juros sobre os investimentos em infraestrutura de IA. Segundo ele, a alta dos juros aumenta o custo dos projetos, mas esse efeito precisa ser analisado em conjunto com a evolução das margens do negócio. “As taxas estão subindo, o que está tornando as coisas mais caras”. Para o CEO da CoreWeave, porém, a rentabilidade da infraestrutura colocada em operação vem crescendo em ritmo superior ao aumento dos juros. “O que é importante tirar desta discussão é que as margens que estamos obtendo estão crescendo mais rápido do que as taxas de juros estão subindo”, afirmou. Na avaliação do executivo, a análise dos custos financeiros isoladamente não representa todo o cenário econômico da infraestrutura voltada à inteligência artificial. “Você não pode olhar para as taxas no vácuo. artigo.texto: MARANA, Ariz. (KGUN) — The Marana Planning Commission voted unanimously Wednesday evening on proposed regulations for data centers in the town, focusing on noise near neighborhoods and decommissioning requirements for any data centers built within town limits, however some residents don't think it's enough. The regulations are designed to support existing rules in Marana's Land Development Code. After the planning commission approved them, the proposed regulations were sent to the Marana Town Council for consideration. Data centers have been a growing topic in Marana, with the rezoning for one data center already approved near Luckett Road and an application for a second project submitted to the Marana Town Council. Not everyone was pleased with the outcome... "I didn't even know that this was happening until the public notice went out," Marana Councilmember-Elect Jackie McGuire said. MacGuire said the council did not share all documents related to the regulations during their public meeting and expressed frustration over a lack of community involvement in drafting the ordinance. "It's extremely disappointing to see them do this without a lot of visibility into who is involved in writing the ordinance...when they have so many outspoken people who've wanted to be a part of this process," McGuire said. "Why are they still not engaging those people?" McGuire also raised concerns about whether the council fully understands the broader impacts data centers could have on Marana. "There are so many other issues associated with data centers that I think over the last several months have become extremely clear all over national news," McGuire said. "They just don't go far enough and don't address enough of the potential negative impacts." The planning commission acknowledged public concerns, with Marana Planning Commissioner David Bowen addressing issues raised by residents. "People had valid concerns and had valid concerns, with water and electricity being among them," Bowen said. "However, we have taken all those things and built them into current regulations, and it's a fluid and evolving part of our town code." Some residents remained unconvinced. Resident Sue Ritz pushed back on the commission's approach. "You guys don't have the tools that you need. You think you can do this on your own; you cannot," Ritz said. The proposed regulations will now go before the Marana Town Council for consideration. — JJ McKinney joined KGUN 9 in July of 2025 as a multimedia journalist. He graduated from Colorado State University in May of 2025 with a degree in journalism and media communications and a minor in law. With a background in investigative reporting and documentary filmmaking, JJ is dedicated to giving a platform to the voices of his community. artigo.texto: EBRD considers senior financing for 1.95GW solar, 3.9GWh battery storage project in Egypt By Staff Writer UK-based European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) is considering senior financing to fund the development and operation of a solar with storage base load power project in Egypt. The Energy Valley project comprises a 1.95-gigawatt (GW) solar photovoltaic project integrated with 3,935 megawatt-hours (MWh) of battery energy storage systems (BESS) and associated transmission infrastructure, according to project information posted on EBRD’s website. The hybrid development is designed to provide at least 100MWac of 24-hour solar-based baseload power. The financing would comprise A and B loans to Energy Valley SAE, a special purpose vehicle (SPV) owned by Scatec and potentially other co-sponsors. The website didn’t disclose the amounts but said the financing is currently classified as ‘In Exploratory, Pending Final Review.’ The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), African Development Bank (AfDB), European Investment Bank (EIB) and Italy's Cassa Depositi e Prestiti (CDP) are identified as co-lenders. The project is also expected to benefit from first-loss risk cover under the European Fund for Sustainable Development Plus (EFSD+) Hi-Bar guarantee programme. Electricity generated by the project will be sold to the Egyptian Electricity Transmission Company (EETC) under a 25-year power purchase agreement (PPA). Four project locations The development will comprise infrastructure across four locations in Egypt. - The main hybrid facility in East Minya will comprise the entire 1.95GW solar PV capacity and a 1.5GWh BESS. - At Al Sarirya, the project will include a 500/220/22kV substation and a 2.5km, 500kV overhead transmission line. - A separate facility at Abu Qir in Alexandria will comprise a 1.435GWh BESS and a 33/220kV substation. - At Nagaa Hammadi in Qena, Scatec plans a 1GWh BESS, a 33/220kV substation and an overhead transmission line. The project information identifies JA Solar, Tongwei and DMEGC as solar PV suppliers, while Sungrow has been selected as the BESS supplier. The project is one of the first hybrid renewable projects with integrated BESS and the first of its kind designed to produce a 24/7 solar baseload of at least 100MWac in Egypt, according to EBRD. (Writing by SA Kader; Editing by Anoop Menon) (anoop.menon@lseg.com ) Subscribe to our Projects' PULSE newsletter that brings you trustworthy news, updates and insights on project activities, developments, and partnerships across sectors in the Middle East and Africa.

artigo.texto: Remuneração das baterias por múltiplos serviços é o Santo Graal do mercado Foi, justamente, um modelo bem-sucedido de remuneração que levou os Estados americanos do Texas e da Califórnia a expandirem o armazenamento de energia em baterias Atualizado Depois de um crescimento acelerado nos últimos três anos, a capacidade instalada de armazenamento de energia em baterias nos Estados Unidos deverá atingir o patamar recorde de 106 GW até o fim de 2028, de acordo com projeções divulgadas pela Administração de Informação de Energia (EIA) norte-americana. Nos próximos dois anos e meio serão acrescidos 54 GW aos atuais 52 GW de capacidade de armazenamento em baterias. É um mercado dominado por fabricantes de tecnologia de ponta, integradores de sistemas e gigantes industriais, que investem pesado. A Tesla, por exemplo, está finalizando a construção de sua megafábrica de baterias em Sparks, Nevada, com capacidade inicial de 10 GW, com investimentos de US$ 3,6 bilhões. Outra gigante do setor, a LG Energy Solution está expandindo sua rede de produção de baterias para sistemas de armazenamento de energia no Michigan e no Arizona. “As políticas de precificação de energia têm criado condições favoráveis para o armazenamento de energia em baterias em alguns Estados norte-americanos, casos da Califórnia e do Texas — e isso é um diferencial muito grande em relação ao mercado brasileiro”, destaca Rafael Ferreira, presidente do conselho consultivo da Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae). Camila Ramos, diretora-executiva da Clean Energy Latin America (Cela), concorda: “O aprendizado mais valioso que a experiência norte-americana pode trazer para o Brasil não está no tamanho, na capacidade do sistema, mas no desenho de mercado”. Ela diz que na Califórnia o armazenamento em grande escala surgiu como resposta às altas abruptas de demanda e quedas rápidas da geração de energia ao longo do dia. Já no Texas, a bateria é remunerada por múltiplos serviços ao mesmo tempo. Ou seja, a bateria é remunerada por tudo o que oferece: flexibilidade, segurança e resposta rápida. “Quando o Brasil destravar a remuneração de serviços ancilares e permitir que a bateria monetize seus vários usos ao mesmo tempo, o mercado brasileiro deixará de crescer por necessidade e passará a crescer por retorno”, diz Ramos.

artigo.texto: By Vivian Emoni The University of Nigeria, Nsukka (UNN) says robust approval criteria are essential to protecting Nigeria’s interests in the carbon market. The Vice-Chancellor of the UNN, Prof. Simon Ortuanya, made the call at a stakeholders` workshop on draft review and validation of Nigeria’s Host Country Approval (HCA) criteria for carbon market operations, on Tuesday in Abuja. The workshop was organised by National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), and the Resource and Environmental Policy Research Centre (REPRC-EfD Nigeria). Ortuanya also called for clear, practical and transparent criteria for approving carbon market projects, while emphasising the need for evidence-based and transparent HCA criteria to strengthen Nigeria’s carbon market framework. He commended the NCCC and the Resource and Environmental Policy Research Centre (REPRC-EfD Nigeria) for convening the workshop. He said the collaboration demonstrated the importance of partnerships between government and research institutions in developing evidence-based policies. The vice chancellor, who was represented by Prof. Nnaemeka Chukwuone, Director, REPRC-EfD Nigeria, also appreciated the Partnership for Economic Policy (PEP) and Hewlett for supporting the project financially. He said the global carbon market offered opportunities to mobilise climate finance, reduce greenhouse gas emissions and accelerate the transition to a low-carbon economy. He said that such opportunities are particularly important for Nigeria as it pursued economic growth, industrial development and energy access and poverty reduction. “A well-governed carbon market could help mobilise resources needed to achieve those objectives while addressing the challenges of climate change. “the Federal Government has taken steps to institutionalise carbon market governance through the approval of the carbon market framework. “The next critical step is to support the framework with clear, practical and transparent HCA criteria for carbon market projects. “The criteria will guide project eligibility, screening and assessment, while clarifying institutional responsibilities and approval procedures,” he said. Ortuanya noted that the criteria would cover measurement, reporting and verification, environmental and social safeguards, and alignment with Nigeria’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC). He said they would also address registry and transparency arrangements as well as carbon accounting, adding that the criteria must protect Nigeria’s interests. He said the proposed HCA criteria were developed from research, noting that effective public policies should be informed by credible evidence and stakeholder engagement. He said the workshop would allow participants to examine the proposed criteria from regulatory, institutional, investment, environmental, social and implementation perspectives. The vice-chancellor urged participants to identify gaps, clarify institutional responsibilities and propose practical solutions to strengthen the approval and authorisation procedures. He expressed confidence that the technical sessions, stakeholder discussions and plenary deliberations would generate recommendations for refining and finalising the HCA criteria. The Director General of the NCCC, Dr Omotenioye Majekodunmi, said that carbon markets could mobilise climate finance, unlock private investment, support green industrialisation and create jobs if underpinned by clear goals and transparency. Majekodunmi said the Climate Change Act 2021 provided the legal foundation for coordinated climate action, while the Nigerian Carbon Market Framework guided participation in carbon markets. She said the criteria must protect Nigeria’s national interests while providing certainty for credible investors and project developers, ensuring genuine mitigation outcomes and sustainable development. Majekodunmi said that the carbon projects must respect host communities, promote social inclusion and align with national climate priorities while protecting Nigeria’s ability to achieve its NDC. The director said the criteria should prevent double-counting, strengthen confidence in Nigeria’s carbon market and ensure communities received transparent, fair and enforceable benefits from carbon finance. She said the workshop would test whether the criteria were practical, legally sound and technically robust, urging participants to make frank and constructive contributions before declaring the workshop open. Prof. Adekola Adenikinju, Partnership for Economic Policy (PEP) Scientific Adviser, commended the NCCC and the REPRC-EfD Nigeria for convening stakeholders to strengthen Nigeria’s carbon market framework. Adenikinju said the global carbon market offered opportunities to mobilise climate finance, reduce greenhouse gas emissions and accelerate Nigeria’s transition to a low-carbon economy. He said the proposed criteria would guide project eligibility, institutional responsibilities, measurement, reporting and verification, environmental safeguards, NDC alignment, registry, transparency and carbon accounting. artigo.texto: Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) face relatively limited exposure to the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), but incoming carbon pricing schemes could help producers further cut costs and increase the region’s exports to Europe. CBAM is the tool implemented by the EU to prevent carbon leakage of some products covered by its emissions trading system (ETS) by putting a cost on emissions embedded in their imports. The mechanism entered its definitive regime on Jan. 1, 2026, with importers required to surrender certificates from 2027 for covered goods of iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, electricity, and hydrogen. On the face of it, economies in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) seem unlikely to be hit hard by the increased costs faced by EU importers of these products. Additionally, where a carbon price is effectively paid on covered emissions in the third country, the corresponding amount can be deducted from the CBAM liability, reducing the incremental cost for exporters to the EU. This creates a potential opportunity for LAC as governments introduce carbon pricing systems. The emissions trading systems under construction in Brazil, Colombia, and the Dominican Republic are particularly relevant for reducing producers’ carbon payments and exposure in several sectors. Other countries like Trinidad & Tobago and Venezuela have greater challenges ahead. OVERALL PICTURE EU importers get 2% of total CBAM products from Brazil, which ranks 14th globally. It is the only LAC country that ranks in the top 20 globally. China tops the list, with nearly 17% of all CBAM-covered imports coming from the Asian state, while Turkiye and the UK make up the top three. The World Bank collated data to examine CBAM exposure, focusing on three key variables, which allows for a closer look at how different countries and sectors may be affected by the system once certificates are surrendered from Jan. 1, 2027. The three variables used are: - Carbon payment per dollar of production or imports: This is calculated by multiplying a country’s carbon emission intensity in a given sector by the EU carbon price. t indicates the implied CBAM cost for each dollar of imported goods. - Share of a country’s exports in a given sector destined for the EU market: This shows how dependent a country is on EU imports in that sector. - Trade Exposure Index (TEI): This combines the first two variables to provide a comprehensive indicator of exposure, where greater values represent higher CBAM exposure for a given sector. Based on the data, the Americas are not at significant trade and economic risk compared to countries like Egypt, Uzbekistan, India, or Ukraine. However, Brazil, Venezuela, and Trinidad & Tobago are likely to face the greatest challenges once CBAM is fully operational. IRON AND STEEL Looking only at the overall CBAM export levels lends a skewed perspective, given that, for instance, there is no electricity exported from LAC to the EU. But looking at iron and steel exports, for example, shows that there may be some significant impacts for producers in certain countries in the region. Iron and steel is one of the sectors that face the most considerable CBAM exposure, with Brazil the most affected country in LAC. Colombia follows with a TEI of 0.75%, sending 12% of its exports to the EU with a 9% carbon payment per dollar, while Venezuela is close behind, with a TEI of 0.7%, 15% of exports to the EU, and an 8% carbon cost. Countries like Trinidad & Tobago, Argentina, Mexico, and Peru show more limited exposure due to lower trade volumes or more favourable emissions profiles, though they remain at a disadvantage. A number of LAC countries have carbon costs lower than the EU average of 3%, which suggests that they may be able to gain a competitive advantage against local producers. The Dominican Republic has both a high share of exports to the EU – nearly 30% – alongside having the lowest carbon cost intensity of LAC countries, at 0.4% per dollar imported. ALUMINIUM, FERTILISERS, AND CEMENT For fertilisers, Trinidad & Tobago is the most exposed in the region, with a carbon cost intensity of nearly 110%, which outstrips the EU average of around 50%, according to analysis by price reporting agency OPIS. The World Bank figures show that fertiliser exports to the EU make up over 20% of the country’s sectoral exports and 20% of its domestic output, resulting in a high TEI of 11.6%. Turning to the aluminium sector, the World Bank figures suggest Venezuela will be the most exposed, with 35% of its aluminum exports going to the EU, and its carbon cost at around 3.5% per dollar, leaving it with a TEI of 0.85%. Brazil will again be at a disadvantage, mainly due to its high carbon payment of 8% – which is around eight times the EU average. The World Bank figures suggest that LAC cement exporters could become more competitive in the European market as the carbon intensity of their production processes puts them in a favourable position. Brazil is the most competitive in the region, with a carbon cost intensity of 32% and a high export share of cement to the EU at about 45%. Colombia’s carbon cost intensity (46%) is slightly lower, still remaining below the EU sector average of 48%. CARBON PRICING LEVER Brazil and Colombia are the countries in LAC that could benefit the most from rolling out their respective cap-and-trade ETS. The two countries have some of the highest exposure indexes at an aggregate level, but also for iron and steel, fertilisers, and aluminium. Hence, introducing domestic carbon pricing could reduce their CBAM liabilities by allowing carbon prices paid domestically to be deducted from the cost faced by EU importers. Over time, the schemes could also incentivise producers to cut their emissions intensity, further reducing their CBAM exposure and potentially improving their competitiveness in the EU market.
