artigo.texto: Colombia’s newly appointed environment minister on Tuesday announced the revocation of a decree issued by the previous administration that introduced stringent rules for the country’s carbon markets, while signalling plans to remove a cap on the amount of credits allowed to offset the national carbon tax. “Today, I am revoking [ministerial] Decree 0973 … for legal reasons,” Fabio Arjona, head of the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development (MADS), said during a panel at the Medellin Climate Week. Decree 0973/26 was issued on the last day of the previous administration, led by former President Gustavo Petro, an open critic of the voluntary carbon market (VCM). Citing social and environmental safeguards, the decree introduced stricter requirements for projects seeking to participate in the VCM, including several evaluation stages through the national RENARE registry – which is not fully operational – and crediting periods. It also established responsibilities for buyers of carbon certificates. Since the draft decree was opened for public consultation in June, several market participants voiced concerns over the rules, warning that they could seriously affect the continuity of the market. Some observers said the decree was too broad and that implementing several of its provisions would be difficult, while others described it as excessively restrictive and, in some cases, contradictory. Read more: FEATURE: Too detailed, too vague – Colombian observers pan VCM regs, for different reasons “From a technical standpoint, it was horrific. It was a depth charge placed under the possibility of a carbon market,” Arjona said in Medellin. Legal experts also told Carbon Pulse that the decree contained several potential procedural flaws, including the lack of prior consultation with all ethnic communities that could be affected by regulation of this scope, given the importance of REDD+ projects to Colombia’s domestic carbon market. The ministry also said in a Tuesday statement that the Ministry of Finance and Public Credit and other relevant authorities with competencies did not provide a concept before the decree was published. Even before taking office, Arjona told local media his intention to revoke the decree. At the time of publication, the resolution revoking the decree had not yet been published on the MADS website. However, a source from MADS confirmed to Carbon Pulse that the revocation was already signed and is in publication process. According to a press release, the ministry will “correct the procedure and construct a new regulatory framework”. “We will build the new framework openly, through genuine public consultation and dialogue with the private sector, developers, and buyers. The rules are written with those who operate in the market, not behind their backs,” the minister said. REMOVING THE OFFSETTING CAP Arjona also gave an initial indication that he intends to remove the 50% cap introduced by the Petro administration in 2022 on the carbon tax’s non-causation (Spanish: no causacion) mechanism, which allows liable entities to avoid paying the levy by purchasing domestic carbon credits. “I am also announcing that, for the [National] Development Plan, I am proposing to restore 100% of the non-causation of the carbon tax,” he said in Medellin. In addition to revoking Decree 0973, the minister had also expressed an interest in removing the offsetting cap before taking office, with the aim of restoring demand for local certificates and reviving a market that has been under pressure. While revoking a ministerial regulation falls within the ministry’s powers, several market participants had previously said that restoring the non-causation mechanism to 100% would be more complicated, as the current cap was established through a law – the 2022 tax reform – and amid the government’s tight fiscal position. Minister Arjona will also propose the change in Congress, according to the press release. Proposing the change in Congress and for inclusion in the 2026-30 National Development Plan, the government’s overarching public policy framework which undergoes consultation with several ministries and civil society, would therefore represent a step in that direction. FIRST OFFICIAL SIGNAL Arjona’s comments in Medellin mark the first official signal from MADS on carbon markets under far-right President Abelardo De La Espriella. Officials also recently announced renewed talks with Singapore to revive the Article 6 memorandum of understanding between the two states. De La Espriella’s environmental policy is based on his ‘ABC Agenda: Water, Biodiversity, and Communities’, which takes a more supportive approach to carbon markets than the previous administration. Carbon Pulse learned that, during the presidential election campaign, market advocates presented proposals to the main candidates aimed at reviving demand. Their suggestions were particularly well received by De La Espriella’s team, and several were ultimately included in the ABC Agenda. artigo.texto: Gotion High-Tech teams up with Volkswagen to pour 3.2 billion euros into building a battery factory, securing its entry ticket to the European market, yet the tight carbon footprint shackle has only just been put in place. Gotion High-Tech's joint venture factory in Europe with PowerCo brings opportunities as well as challenges including compliance requirements. Energy Foresight learned that on September 28, Gotion High-Tech and PowerCo, the battery subsidiary of Volkswagen, signed an agreement with a total investment of 3.222 billion euros, under which the two parties will set up three joint ventures in Valencia, Spain, Sulany, Slovakia, and Kenitra, Morocco. The day after the news was released, Gotion High-Tech hit the 10% price limit 8 minutes after the market opened, with pending orders exceeding 890,000 lots. What is worth noting about this matter is not the figures themselves. The global installed capacity of power batteries reaches nearly 1000GWh a year, and the planned production capacity of 37GWh is far from an unprecedented huge investment. What really deserves attention is the structure of this transaction: Gotion will contribute approximately 1.598 billion euros, while PowerCo will contribute approximately 1.624 billion euros, making the contributions of both parties almost equal. In terms of equity arrangement, for the 29.1GWh project in Valencia, PowerCo holds 51% of the shares to take the controlling stake, and Gotion holds 49%; for the 8.4GWh project in Sulany and the 100,000-ton cathode material project in Morocco, Gotion holds 51% of the shares and takes the controlling stake. This is not an ordinary overseas factory construction investment. It is a transaction concerning the access right to the European market. Volkswagen has delivered far more than just a factory The Valencia plant is not a project built from scratch by Gotion. The plant was previously led and promoted by PowerCo. The Spanish government has allocated more than 260 million euros in subsidies to the plant through the PERTEVEC program, of which 152 million euros are cash subsidies that the Valencia joint venture has obtained before this investment. Instead of directly acquiring the plant, Gotion enters the project by capital increase to PowerCoSpain, and participates in subsequent construction and operation. However, the construction progress of the plant has been repeatedly delayed. After years of independent development by PowerCo, the mass production of cells has never been realized. This situation is exactly the same as that of Northvolt. The once highly promising "top battery enterprise" in Europe declared bankruptcy after burning 15 billion U.S. dollars of investment, and the plan for the Heide plant in Germany was once stranded, before it was taken over and promoted by the U.S. company Lyten. According to data from the IEA, Chinese enterprises including CATL, BYD, and CALB control about 80% of the global battery production capacity. European automakers have calculated an account: the comprehensive production cost of large-scale mass-produced power batteries is about 30% higher than that in China, the electricity price is 3 to 5 times that of China, and the hourly wage of workers is 5 times that of China. Volkswagen's choice is very pragmatic. Rather than continuing to burn money in a project that cannot be operated smoothly, it is better to hand over the factory to the party that can make it run properly. The conditions for Gotion to take over are also clear: in exchange for a 49% equity stake, it obtains an existing base that has received government subsidies and is located in the core of Spain's automotive industry cluster. Spain is an important production base of the Volkswagen Group in Europe, and the geographical location of the Valencia plant determines that it serves Volkswagen's vehicle production lines in Southern Europe rather than Gotion's own business. The arrangements for Slovakia and Morocco are the opposite. Gotion holds a 51% controlling stake in these two projects, keeping the key link of cell manufacturing in its own hands, and at the same time using the 100,000-ton lithium iron phosphate cathode material production capacity in Morocco to provide upstream supply for European battery bases. The trade facilitation conditions between Morocco and the European Union itself serve as a buffer to avoid tariff barriers. The EU's carbon footprint rule is a hurdle that Gotion has not yet crossed However, obtaining the factory and equity does not mean getting the passport to enter the European market. The EU's mandatory carbon footprint declaration for energy storage batteries has come into effect on February 18, 2026, and the Digital Battery Passport will be implemented on February 18, 2027. What is more tricky is the design of the accounting rules: only two models, "national average power consumption mix" and "directly connected power", are retained for carbon footprint calculation, and the green certificates commonly purchased by Chinese enterprises are not recognized. This means that even if Gotion uses green power to produce cathode materials in Morocco, the carbon footprint data will still fail to meet the requirements if the power source is not recognized by the EU accounting system. Since August this year, the EU Customs has changed its regulation on the carbon footprint declaration of imported batteries from "pass after declaration" to mandatory random inspection. Several batches of battery products exported from China to the Port of Rotterdam have been detained because their green power certificates do not meet the requirements. Gotion's layout of cathode materials in Morocco and cell manufacturing in Spain and Slovakia follows the correct direction of localized production. However, from the compliance of raw material source codes and power mix factors to mineral due diligence and recycled material proportion, every item requires rebuilding the data system of the supply chain. artigo.texto: Li wants to learn from Xiaomi to "raise fish", while CATL aims to become the "Huawei" in the battery industry. Li Xiang has finally responded to the "de-CATL" narrative. On September 28, Li Xiang released a public statement addressing external disputes over Li Auto's self-developed batteries. From his perspective, regarding automakers' in-house battery R&D as an attempt to replace CATL is essentially a zero-sum game mindset. Li Auto's drive for in-house battery R&D is not aimed at kicking CATL out of the supply chain, and the truth is even the opposite. Li Xiang specifically thanked CATL and called the company Li Auto's "comrade-in-arms". From the 5C ultra-fast charging battery of Li ONE to MEGA, many originally quite aggressive indicators were first defined by Li Auto for product requirements, then jointly developed with CATL, and finally landed with the support of CATL's engineering and manufacturing capabilities. This statement sounds very sincere, but while denying the "de-CATL" trend, Li Xiang also mentioned three things to explain why Li Auto must continue to adhere to in-house battery R&D: to proactively meet unmet user demands, fully integrate batteries into the entire vehicle system, and open up data across the full life cycle of batteries. In other words, Li Auto can continue to purchase batteries from CATL and is willing to continue cooperating with CATL, but one thing is changing: the capabilities that used to be largely controlled by battery manufacturers will be taken back by Li Auto. It aims to master product definition, system integration and data, and leave the manufacturing work to CATL, Sunwoda or more suppliers. This is no longer a simple matter of "whether to get rid of CATL", but an attempt to turn the power battery industry chain into a white box and turn all battery manufacturers into its own "workers". On the other side, CATL is obviously not satisfied with only being a manufacturer that produces batteries for others. One party wants to white-box the supply chain, while the other wants to become a system-level platform in the battery industry. What Li Auto and CATL are really competing for may never be orders for several batteries, but who will define the batteries of next-generation vehicles. Li Xiang starts to "tame" battery manufacturers Li Xiang's goal may not be to fully develop a battery better than CATL's on his own, but to turn the battery from a "black box" in the hands of suppliers into a "white box" that Li Auto can define, disassemble, and replace suppliers for. Once this goal is achieved, Li Auto's control over the battery industry chain will undergo fundamental changes. After all, as long as the power battery is always a "black box" provided by suppliers, what automakers can truly master will be very limited. What material system the battery needs, how the cell should be designed, what level the fast charging should reach, how to balance service life and safety, and even when the next-generation product will be iterated, all these are largely determined by battery manufacturers. For ordinary automakers, this may not be a problem, but for a company like Li Auto that sells hundreds of thousands of vehicles a year and wants to make smart cars a highly integrated product, this means that one of its most important components with the highest cost proportion is not fully under its own control. What Li Xiang wants to do now is to take back this part of the capability. Judging from this public statement, what Li Auto wants to master in the future is user demands, product definition, vehicle system integration and data across the full battery life cycle, while the actual large-scale manufacturing can still be handed over to CATL, or introduced to other battery enterprises. Li Auto does not necessarily need to become a battery manufacturer itself, but hopes to decide why the battery is designed in this way, what indicators it needs to meet, and how the next-generation product will be upgraded. As for who will produce it in the end, it can be left to the supply chain for full competition. This white-box OEM model is actually not new. In the past decade, one of the most mature companies that played this model well in China's technology industry is Xiaomi. From the very beginning, Xiaomi has not tried to bring the entire industrial chain into its own company. Screens can be purchased, cameras can be purchased, storage can be purchased, structural parts can be purchased, and assembly can be handed over to foundries. What is truly in Xiaomi's hands is product definition. The selling price of a hardware device, what materials to use, what hardware to configure, what screen to choose, how to design the system, and what kind of consumers to target, all these must be decided by Xiaomi itself. The remaining links that can be handed over to the supply chain are handed over to the supply chain as much as possible. Even for the same component, Xiaomi will not only bind one supplier, but introduce as many enterprises as possible to compete. The result of this approach is that suppliers are increasingly like callable modules. Whoever has mature technology will be used, whoever has lower price will get more share, and whoever cannot keep up with the requirements of next-generation products can be replaced by new suppliers. As the industrial chain becomes more mature and standardized, Xiaomi's control over the supply chain has become increasingly strong. By 2025, this model has supported a large-scale hardware ecosystem. The best proof is that the gross profit margin of the mobile phone business, which is restricted by many black-box components such as Qualcomm's products, is only 10.9%, while the gross profit margin of IoT and life consumer products that control the white-box supply chain is as high as 23.1%. artigo.texto: AI data center boom fuels US battery storage demand, opens new avenue for LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI, SK On South Korean battery makers could find fresh opportunities in the US energy storage market as Seoul's decision to invest in a multibillion-dollar gas-fired power complex in Texas underscores growing demand for reliable electricity to power artificial intelligence data centers. On Wednesday (US time), US President Donald Trump announced plans for South Korea to invest $200 billion in US projects under Seoul’s broader $350 billion strategic investment package agreed as part of a trade deal with Washington last year. Among the projects announced is a $22.3 billion combined-cycle gas-fired power complex in Encinal, Texas, designed to supply electricity to nearby AI data centers. Korean firms are expected to seek contracts related to equipment supply, engineering, construction and long-term maintenance for the Texas project, according to industry officials. While no Korean battery maker has yet been confirmed as an ESS supplier for the project, the development highlights a growing opportunity emerging around AI data center power infrastructures. Powering the AI boom The Texas project highlights the pressing need for dependable power to support energy-hungry AI infrastructure. Amid this demand, battery energy storage systems are increasingly being deployed alongside conventional generation to stabilize power supply and manage fluctuations in energy demand. AI data centers run huge clusters of graphics processing units, which can experience rapid changes in power consumption. Even brief interruptions in electricity supply can disrupt operations, creating demand for power systems that can respond almost instantly. ESS can help tackle those fluctuations by storing electricity when demand is lower and releasing it when consumption spikes, complementing gas-fired generation and easing pressure on the power grid. Paring conventional power generation with battery storage is already gaining traction in the US. At SpaceXAI's Colossus data center in Memphis, Tennessee, Tesla’s Megapack ESS is being installed alongside gas turbines powering the complex. “Installing gas-fired power generation alongside ESS near data centers is becoming almost commonplace," said Jung Won-seok, an analyst at iM Securities, adding that such configurations are likely to become an important part of data center power infrastructures. The Texas project comes as the US energy storage industry is targeting 1 terawatt-hour of installed storage capacity by the end of 2032. This trend is opening a major new growth engine for Korean battery suppliers looking to diversify beyond electric vehicle batteries. According to a report released this month by the US Energy Storage Coalition, reaching the target would require average annual growth of about 25 percent, increasing installed power capacity by more than 300 percent and energy storage capacity by over 500 percent from current levels. Korean battery makers race to capture US storage boom Against that backdrop, South Korea’s three major battery makers, LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI and SK On are stepping up their push into the North American ESS market, in part by converting existing EV battery production lines for ESS and expanding local production. Their strategies are increasingly built around lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, batteries, which offer cost and thermal stability advantages, making them more suited for large-scale ESS applications. LG Energy Solution recently began production at its facility in Lansing, Michigan, expanding its ESS production to five sites across the US and Canada. The company aims to secure more than 50 gigawatt-hours of annual LFP battery production capacity for ESS in North America by the end of this year. The company has also secured more than 3 trillion won in new ESS orders during the first half, including projects on AI data centers. LG Energy Solution's battery energy storage system recently qualified for Nvidia's DSX Ready program, which identifies power, cooling and other infrastructure products that meet requirements for NVidia-based AI factories. LG Energy Solution was the only Korean battery maker among the initial BESS suppliers in the program. Samsung SDI is also expanding its capacity for energy storage in the US. The company has been converting part of the production lines at StarPlus Energy, its joint venture in Indiana with Stellantis, for ESS, and plans to mass produce LFP batteries there beginning in the fourth quarter. The company has recently taken full ownership of a separate Indiana battery plant it previously jointly held with General Motors, with plans to add an ESS line there as well. SK On, meanwhile, is converting part of its existing EV battery production lines in Georgia to manufacture LFP batteries for ESS applications. In August, the company signed a five-year agreement with US energy storage firm NeoVolta Power to supply 9 gigawatt-hours of LFP battery cells from 2027 to 2031. SK On also plans a separate agreement for an additional 9 gigawatt-hours of cells this year. To meet its expansion plans, SK On has signed LFP cathode material supply agreements with Korean battery material suppliers, including Posco Future M and L&F, strengthening its supply chain for US-based production. For Korea’s battery industry, the US energy storage boom offers a chance to diversify revenue amid slowing EV battery demand, while making use of plants already built in North America. sahn@heraldcorp.com

artigo.texto: By changing which minerals remain in anthracite before activation, researchers created carbons with markedly different pore structures, adsorption behavior, and electrochemical characteristics. Paper: Residual minerals tune coal-derived porous carbon for adsorption and energy storage. AI-generated abstract conceptual image created using ChatGPT/OpenAI A recent study, published as an Article in Press by Scientific Reports, examines how residual mineral species are associated with changes in the structure and performance of porous carbon derived from Taixi anthracite. The study compares hydrochloric acid (HCl), sodium hydroxide (NaOH), and combined NaOH–HCl deashing treatments before KOH activation. The findings support a role for residual mineral species during carbon formation and show how precursor treatment can change the resulting porous carbon for methylene blue adsorption and supercapacitor applications. Understanding the role of residual minerals Porous carbon supports applications ranging from water treatment and gas adsorption to electrochemical energy storage. Its high surface area, tunable pore structure, and chemical stability make it attractive for these applications, but the required structural characteristics vary with the intended use. Micropores provide abundant sites for ion storage, while larger pores help molecular and ion transport. Coal is an attractive precursor for large-scale porous-carbon production because of its abundance, low cost, and established industrial supply chain. Coal also contains naturally occurring mineral matter, which is commonly removed before activation to reduce ash content and improve carbon purity. Mineral matter may play a more active role in carbon formation than its classification as an impurity. Residual calcium, iron, and magnesium species can influence gasification and local reactions during activation, while aluminosilicate phases may affect pore development through templating or by restricting access to parts of the carbon matrix. The study examines whether the type and amount of residual minerals influence the properties of coal-derived porous carbon. Engineering porous carbon through selective deashing The researchers selected Taixi anthracite as the carbon precursor and prepared four precursor states. They kept one portion of the coal untreated and designated it TX. They treated the other portions with HCl, NaOH, or sequential NaOH–HCl treatment, producing TX-S, TX-J, and TX-JS, respectively. The researchers then activated all four precursors with KOH at a precursor-to-KOH mass ratio of 1:4, yielding TX-PC, TX-S-PC, TX-J-PC, and TX-JS-PC. The “-PC” suffix denotes the activated porous carbon product derived from each precursor. The chemical treatments resulted in markedly different ash contents. Untreated TX contained 3.06% ash. The paper's main text gives an ash content of 2.06% for HCl-treated TX-S. NaOH treatment reduced it to 1.93%, and the combined treatment further decreased it to 0.31%. X-ray fluorescence analysis identified silicon as the dominant mineral element in the original coal, followed by aluminum, iron, calcium, and magnesium. The two individual treatments altered the residual mineral composition in distinct ways. HCl removed more than 90% of most metallic elements but retained higher levels of aluminum- and silicon-related species, whereas NaOH removed aluminum and silicon while retaining more calcium, iron, and magnesium. The researchers then characterized the resulting carbons using nitrogen adsorption, X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, scanning electron microscopy, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and Boehm titration. Thermogravimetric analysis provided information on thermal behavior, while methylene blue adsorption experiments assessed adsorption capacity and temperature dependence. Residual mineral profiles are associated with pore structure and application performance All four carbons developed highly porous structures dominated by micropores, with specific surface areas ranging from 2451 to 3101 m²/g and total pore volumes from about 1.3 to 1.76 cm³/g. Changing the precursor deashing treatment produced clear differences in pore distribution. TX-S-PC, derived from the HCl-treated precursor, achieved the highest surface area of 3101 m²/g and the largest pore volume of 1.76 cm³/g. The NaOH-derived TX-J-PC had the highest micropore surface area fraction, at 72.1%. The researchers propose that residual minerals may help explain these differences during KOH activation. Calcium-, iron-, and magnesium-containing species may alter local carbon reactivity, while mineral-derived phases could act as local templates for pore formation. The authors did not directly establish the mineral transformations or reaction pathways during activation. Boehm titration measured 2.695 - 3.074 mmol/g of oxygen-containing groups, while FTIR showed that the main types of surface groups were similar across the four carbons. These structural and chemical differences translated into contrasting application outcomes. Methylene blue adsorption increased rapidly during the first 30 minutes and reached equilibrium after 60 minutes. The HCl-derived TX-S-PC achieved the highest equilibrium capacity at 1140.94 mg/g, while TX-PC reached equilibrium more rapidly. TX-JS-PC delivered 1108.78 mg/g and maintained comparatively consistent adsorption across the tested temperatures. Adsorption fell as temperature rose from 30 to 50 °C; the authors described the process as exothermic and predominantly physical. Electrochemical testing showed trade-offs between charge-storage capacity, ion transport, rate performance, and cycling stability. The NaOH-derived TX-J-PC provided the highest capacitance, 179.64 F/g at 0.1 A/g, while TX-PC supported faster charge and ion transport. artigo.texto: On September 29, Rakusou Mirai announced the "PackGo Cube" mobile battery, featuring a semi-solid state battery, and the "Ostand Q3 Leather Tone Nature Series" smartphone case, which incorporates natural textures, both under its TORRAS brand. The PackGo Cube is priced at 14,990 yen, and the Ostand Q3 Leather Tone Nature Series at 8,480 yen. These products are proposed as smartphone peripherals that balance everyday portability with stylish design. The PackGo Cube is a 10,000mAh mobile battery equipped with an integrated carabiner and a 75cm auto-retracting USB-C cable. When using a single port, it supports up to 45W output, making it suitable for charging not only smartphones but also tablets and laptops. In addition to its compact design, weighing approximately 249g, the use of a semi-solid state battery, ATL cells, and graphene ensures peace of mind during portability and helps suppress heat generation. The Ostand Q3 Leather Tone Nature Series is a stand case that features the feel of organic silicone material and a delicate texture reminiscent of natural objects. It comes in calm color tones, such as a green inspired by moss gardens and a yellow evoking wind or rock surfaces. A 360-degree rotating spring-loaded stand is built into the back. This design supports video viewing and video calls in both portrait and landscape orientations, enhancing ease of daily use. The PackGo Cube is scheduled for sequential release starting in October, while the Ostand Q3 Leather Tone Nature Series is available on the official online store. TORRAS, with its motto "be here now," is developing small appliances and accessories that enhance the smartphone experience. These two new products, while highlighting their functionality, stand out for their emphasis on textures that make users want to carry them every day.

artigo.texto: My weekend with the tech bros began at Pascal’s Rager, a house party in Washington, DC, cohosted by Micah Bock, who works at the Department of Homeland Security, and Madison Campbell, a flame-throwing, rage-baiting tech influencer with more than 62,000 followers on X. The conversations that night were off the record, but I can tell you there were 500 cigarettes, a tray of Zyns, and a guest list filled with Trump officials and bleach-blonde women in Chanel-esque jackets with impossibly short miniskirts. I can also tell you that MAGA-associated folks are using suspiciously Trumpian accents and slurs I swore were dead and gone. Next up, on Saturday night, I went to a pro-data-center party whose flyer had gone viral the prior week after one of the organizers, Pirate Wires writer Jonas Du, posted about it on X. “In light of the bipartisan psychosis over AI data centers,” the Partiful read, “it’s about time that the people who haven’t lost their minds get together and celebrate the glory of American compute.” It was catnip to MAGA-aligned, Andreessen Horowitz–backed edgelords. After all, wasn’t it silly that, all across the country, congressmen and governors who used to welcome data centers in their state are succumbing to the techno-phobic wokes? According to Data Center Watch, $64 billion of data center projects have already been blocked or delayed. And why? Sure, there’s the holy triptych of problems: 5,000-gallon fuel spills, brown sink water, skyrocketing electricity bills. But also, to hear the party organizers tell it, tech companies have failed to make people understand the benefits, like how one county in Virginia has raked in $1.1 billion in tax revenue from data centers alone. Despite mounting protests from residents, it’s now considered the “data center capital of the world.” One organizer, Casey Given, CEO of libertarian nonprofit Young Voices, said that he wanted to party to counter the “crazy apocalyptic” anti-AI folks, and “shift the Overton window in a more techno-optimist direction.” Enter Data After Dark, tech bros’ attempt at making data centers sexy. With the permission of the organizers, I invited Taylor Frazier McCollum, a newly inspired anti-data-center activist from Prince George’s County, Maryland, to be my date. Last year, when she found out that a hyperscale data center was going to be built one mile from her grandparents’ home, she started researching and learned of a community near Memphis that faced significant air pollution after Elon Musk’s xAI (now called SpaceXAI) built natural gas turbines to power its data center nearby. (Vanity Fair has reached out to SpaceXAI for comment.) She started a petition, which reached over 25,000 signatures, to fight data center construction in her own county and has since quit her job as a cosmetologist to spend more time organizing across the country. I meet up with Frazier McCollum at a bar, and she arrives wearing a T-shirt that reads, “If my mouth doesn’t say it, my face will.” When we enter PubKey, also known as the Bitcoin bar cofounded by crypto enthusiast Thomas Pacchia, we quickly realize that everyone is dressed much better than us, the men in crisp suits with baseball caps that say “Let Data Reign” and the women in slinky silk dresses and kitten heels. We walk past a DJ and a large screen playing an endless loop of Tony Stark, Ana de Armas as the platonic ideal of an AI girlfriend in Blade Runner 2049, and stylized shots of blinking servers. On the dance floor, it’s a ratio of six men to one woman. We duck into a side room—a macho “whiskey bar” with leather couches and a large American flag—and strike up a conversation with Neeraja Deshpande, a conservative writer who tells us she’s concerned by what she sees as the prevailing national sentiment that “growth and human flourishing are at odds with each other.” “It’s not just an imaginary thing that’s happening,” Frazier McCollum responds. She cites studies that show Maryland could face rolling blackouts due to data center energy consumption; she’s watched data centers crop up in the counties around her, and she’s afraid that, if she doesn’t fight these projects, her community won’t have air conditioning, her schools won’t have constant electricity. “But I think that’s a zero-sum vision of energy in general,” Deshpande says. In her eyes, many of the concerns raised by anti-data-center activists are either overblown or solvable, and she points to nuclear reactors as a solution that would address energy issues without increasing emissions. “I would oppose nuclear as well,” Frazier McCollum retorts. Her and Deshpande are arguing on different grounds: Frazier McCollum cares about her immediate access to clean water, pollutant-free air, and affordable electricity, while Deshpande speaks in decades, forgiving the follies of today if they pave the way for future abundance. The conversation is respectful, but it’s clear to me that there is a chasm between their points of view that won’t be bridged today. At 10 p.m. it’s time for speeches, which amount to little more than rally cries. One speaker who runs a pro-AI political firm blames the “Chinese” for convincing us that AI is an energy-guzzling, bill-raising monster. Another speaker, Manhattan Institute fellow Daniel Di Martino, derides the “crazy” and “Luddite” arguments against data centers, before reassuring the crowd that “the good guy with a gun beats the bad guy with a gun.” Frazier McCollum raises her eyebrows as if to say, “Would that make me the bad guy with the gun here?” Then a protester, a young man in a suit, bursts onto the stage and yells something about water usage. I can’t hear him because everyone is already talking over the speeches anyway. But once the crowd registers it’s a protester, they join together in a feral chant: “USA! USA! artigo.texto: Trina Storage, the energy storage business of Trinasolar, has announced the successful commissioning of its first battery energy storage project in Portugal, delivered in partnership with independent power producer (IPP) Prosolia Energy. The 15 MW / 60 MWh Albispark battery energy storage system, located in Castelo Branco, is integrated with an existing 34.4 MWp solar plant, making it one of the largest battery energy storage systems currently in operation in Portugal. The project represents an important milestone for both companies. For Prosolia Energy, Albispark is its first international utility-scale battery storage hybridization project, while for Trina Storage it marks the company's first commissioned battery storage installation in Portugal, supporting the country's transition towards a more flexible, renewable-based electricity system. Under the project, Trina Storage supplied an integrated utility-scale battery energy storage solution, including Elementa battery cabinets, power conversion systems (PCS), medium-voltage skids, power plant controller (PPC) and commissioning services, delivering a complete solution designed to maximize renewable energy utilization while supporting grid flexibility. Supporting Portugal's Next Phase of Renewable Integration As Portugal continues to increase renewable generation, battery energy storage is becoming essential for improving grid stability, increasing renewable utilization and providing greater operational flexibility. The Albispark project demonstrates how hybrid solar-plus-storage systems can enable renewable energy to be stored and dispatched when demand is highest, helping maximize the value of renewable generation while strengthening grid resilience. "The successful commissioning of Albispark represents an important milestone for Trina Storage in Portugal," said Gabriele Buccini, Head of Trina Storage Europe at Trinasolar. "As our first operational battery storage project in the country, it demonstrates our ability to deliver integrated utility-scale storage solutions that support Europe's evolving energy landscape. We are proud to partner with Prosolia Energy on this landmark project and look forward to supporting many more storage deployments across Portugal in the coming years." Pedro Pereira da Silva, Country Manager of Prosolia Energy in Portugal, said: "Albispark is an important milestone for Prosolia Energy and demonstrates the value that battery storage brings to the energy transition. Together with Trina Storage, we have delivered a project that improves grid flexibility and reinforces the foundations for future hybrid renewable projects in Portugal." Building a Long-Term Presence in Portugal The commissioning of Albispark marks the beginning of Trina Storage's expansion in Portugal. In addition to this project, the company is currently supporting several battery energy storage projects across the Portuguese market, reflecting growing demand for utility-scale storage as the country accelerates renewable energy deployment and grid modernization. The project also forms part of Portugal's Recovery and Resilience Plan (PRR), supporting the country's efforts to increase grid flexibility and accelerate renewable energy integration.

artigo.texto: Executivos das maiores produtoras de etanol do Brasil e de outros países se reuniram esta semana em São Paulo para discutir os desafios e as oportunidades do setor para seguir crescendo. Um dos painéis do evento, considerado o mais tradicional do setor na América Latina, o Teco Novonesis, teve como tema “Futuro do etanol: eficiência, carbono e mercado”. Era a hora de compartilhar boas notícias - e outras nem tanto. A melhor delas é a de que vêm por aí muitas oportunidades no mercado externo, como o uso do etanol no transporte marítimo, na produção de combustível para aviação e na geração de créditos de carbono. A parte difícil é saber que, por enquanto, com a multiplicação de investimentos na produção, o mercado brasileiro enfrenta um cenário de “sobreoferta” de etanol. “O que está acontecendo é um franco sucesso do etanol de milho como modelo de negócio e isso vem atraindo capital de uma série de investidores para botar de pé o etanol de milho”, afirmou Daniel Lopes, vice-presidente de Novos Negócios e Sustentabilidade da FS, em entrevista ao AgFeed, logo após sua apresentação no painel. Ele lembra que quando a empresa iniciou o negócio no Brasil, em 2017, o etanol de milho era 1% do mercado. “Hoje já está em 30% e a gente vê isso chegando a 40% ou mais em 2 ou 3 anos. São investidores buscando uma atratividade de investimento, retorno sobre o capital, mas isso também está gerando uma sobreoferta de etanol”, ponderou. As políticas governamentais, como o aumento na mistura de etanol na gasolina este ano, têm ajudado o setor, porém os especialistas reunidos no evento concordam que é necessário mais que isso, para disseminar o uso do biocombustível em outros estados e também avançar nas exportações. Apesar dos desafios, Lopes abriu sua participação no Teco falando de um “mercado endereçável” para o etanol, globalmente, de “um trilhão de litros”. Hoje a produção mundial está em cerca de 110 bilhões de litros. “Hoje são 100 bilhões de litros. A gente tem um potencial de mais 400 bilhões de litros no aéreo, mais 400 bilhões no marítimo, e só aí já estamos em 900”, detalhou ele, na conversa com o AgFeed, sobre a previsão trilionária. O patamar mencionado leva em conta ainda a transição de veículos e máquinas que funcionam a diesel e tendem a cada vez mais serem adaptados para o etanol. “Temos no diesel, só no Brasil, 17 bilhões (de litros), mas um potencial ainda maior quando a gente começa a falar de outros mercados para acessar o diesel, como no caso de maquinário agrícola, de aviação agrícola, de colheitadeira, de plantio de milho e de soja, e o mercado elétrico também”, afirmou. No mesmo painel, a gerente global de marketing da Novonesis, Kim Bertz, também trouxe uma mensagem de otimismo para o grupo de empresários. Mostrou que o etanol acrescentou US$ 50 bilhões à economia americana, evoluindo muito nas últimas décadas, apoiado por políticas de incentivo. Ela ressaltou que também nos EUA o foco agora é seguir trabalhando as questões relacionadas à menor pegada de carbono e ao desenvolvimento de novos mercados, como o combustível marítimo. “50% do negócio é otimista. E aí, a gente se pergunta, o que mudou? O que aconteceu? A gente vê que não foi o milho, o milho continua sendo um pilar sólido. A gente vê que não é a valorização dos coprodutos, dos produtos de biorefinarias”. Marcos Duda Schmitiz, gerente de desenvolvimento de negócios da Novonesis no Brasil, foi moderador do painel. Segundo ele, a tradicional pesquisa feita junto aos participantes do evento mostrou que 93% do público segue otimista em relação aos negócios. “A gente vê que a relação de confiança da indústria em relação à oferta e demanda de etanol é que está pressionada, por isso buscamos trazer aqui alguns temas como o aprendizado do mercado americano, onde a indústria é bem mais madura”, disse. A visão é que as tecnologias mais avançadas para aumentar o rendimento e a eficiência das plantas passa a ser ainda mais importante em cenários desafiadores. O mercado de baixo carbono Os empresários e executivos da indústria do etanol confiam que, ao longo do tempo, o biocombustível será compensando financeiramente pela importância para a descarbonização do planeta. As oportunidades não estão apenas no potencial de crescimento de uso do produto, reduzindo emissões no setor de transportes. A própria FS foi chamada ao evento para dar detalhes do seu projeto pioneiro de captura e estocagem de carbono no solo, o chamado BECCS (Bioenergy with Carbon Capture and Storage, na sigla em inglês). O foco da empresa é ter o “primeiro etanol carbono negativo do mundo”, já que o CO2 gerado no processo de fermentação do milho para produzir o biocombustível, será comprimido, desidratado e depois injetado a cerca de 1.200 metros de profundidade no subsolo, na unidade de Lucas do Rio Verde (MT). “Nosso projeto de BECCS está 99% pronto, todas as instalações de compressão, de injeção concluídas. A gente está trabalhando muito próximo agora, tanto com a ANP, quanto com a SEMA (Secretaria Estadual do Meio Ambiente) de Mato Grosso, para ter a liberação de todas as licenças desse projeto, que está pronto para operar”, contou Lopes, na conversa com o AgFeed. Segundo ele, por ser um projeto inédito no País, o processo de autorização, para os reguladores, também é mais desafiador. Estão faltando a licença de operação (LO), concedida pelo órgão estadual, e a autorização de operação (AO), a ser feita pela Agência Nacional de Petróleo (ANP). O investimento da FS no projeto deve totalizar R$ 560 milhões. Já foram aportados cerca de R$ 450 milhões. “Ainda faltam uns R$ 100 milhões a desembolsar, mas que já está contratado, então já estamos com bastante conforto que esse vai ser o capex do projeto”. artigo.texto: The US energy storage system (ESS) market is growing faster than previously expected. The market had been widely expected to slow amid reduced tax incentives and supply-chain uncertainty last year. But rapidly rising power demand from artificial intelligence (AI) data centers and improving battery supply conditions in the US are lifting the market outlook. Wood Mackenzie said in its recently published US Energy Storage Market Monitor that annual ESS installations in the US are expected to rise more than 50% from current levels on a megawatt (MW) basis over the next five years. The consultancy raised its forecast for cumulative installations through 2031 to 207 gigawatts (GW)/715 gigawatt-hours (GWh). A year ago, the market was expected to slow. In a report published in September last year, Wood Mackenzie forecast a four-year correction in the US ESS market beginning in 2026. It projected cumulative installations of 87.8 GW/281.2 GWh by 2029. Utility-scale ESS installations were expected to fall 10% in 2027 from the previous year. In reality, installations have not declined this year. US ESS installations rose 5% in the first half from a year earlier. Full-year installations are also expected to remain at a similar level to last year. The second quarter saw a record in terms of storage capacity. The US installed 5.4 GW/18.9 GWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS) in the second quarter. The increase in storage capacity reflects longer ESS durations. The average duration of ESS installations in the US rose to 3.5 hours in the second quarter from 2.8 hours a year earlier. This means more systems are capable of storing more electricity and supplying it for longer periods at the same power output. The key factor behind the stronger market outlook is AI data centers. As data centers expand rapidly, securing sufficient power on time is becoming a bigger challenge. Building new power plants and transmission networks can take considerable time, while ESS can be installed relatively quickly to respond to rising electricity demand. Wood Mackenzie expects the utility-scale ESS market to grow at an average annual rate of 8% over the next five years, driven by data-center power demand. The consultancy expects more than 130 GW/534 GWh of new utility-scale ESS capacity to be installed from 2026 through 2031. Alison Finney, a researcher at Wood Mackenzie, said, “The expansion of data-center construction is strengthening the outlook across every segment of the US ESS market.” She added that utility-scale ESS could quickly provide the power needed by data centers as hyperscalers face difficulties connecting to the power grid. Slower electric-vehicle demand is also benefiting the US ESS market. As demand for EV batteries falls below expectations, excess production capacity is emerging at local battery plants, prompting battery makers to convert existing EV production lines to ESS applications. LG Energy Solution plans to increase its annual North American production capacity for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries for ESS to more than 50 GWh by the end of this year. Its cumulative ESS order backlog has surpassed 140 GWh. Samsung SDI plans to use three of the four production lines at StarPlus Energy (SPE), its joint venture plant with Stellantis, to make LFP batteries for ESS. It also plans to expand production sites to include Synergy Cells, which is being converted into a standalone plant, to increase its US production capacity for LFP batteries for ESS. SK On is using its Georgia plant, SK Battery America (SKBA), to produce LFP batteries for ESS. In August, it signed a supply agreement with US-based NeoVolta Power for 9 GWh from 2027 through 2031 and is pursuing an additional 9 GWh of cooperation. With Samsung SDI and SK On following LG Energy Solution in converting EV production lines to ESS applications, all three Korean battery makers are expected to produce LFP batteries for ESS in North America from the fourth quarter of this year. Their combined US production capacity for LFP batteries for ESS is expected to exceed 100 GWh annually from 2028.

Please enter the email address you use for your account so we can send you a link to reset your password: The bill would let states and utilities discriminate against data centers and crypto miners, requiring them to pay higher rates to cover the full cost of any system upgrades. Call it the data center double tap. A wonky set of provisions in the Senate’s bipartisan permitting deal would rewrite federal electricity law to allow states and utilities to discriminate against artificial intelligence data centers and crypto miners for the first time. The proposal would force AI data centers to pay for any new transmission infrastructure required to serve them — while still paying full freight to use the rest of the power grid. It could even let states require the facilities to subsidize other customers’ power rates. Senator Martin Heinrich, the ranking Democrat on the Senate energy committee, mentioned the provisions during a press event announcing the deal on Wednesday, but they have so far attracted less attention than the bill’s other measures. If enacted, the bill will “mean that we actually require big load centers — whether that’s a factory or a data center — to not pass those costs on to the American consumer by statute, not suggestion,” he said. The bill arguably goes further than that summary. It creates new carve-outs in federal law that disadvantage data centers and crypto miners specifically, allowing states to discriminate against them as compared to other large-scale customers. It also protects electricity customers from the future risk of data centers failing to pay their bills. The proposal comes at an auspicious time. Utilities are already gearing up to spend tens of billions of dollars building new transmission lines and power infrastructure to meet energy demand from AI data centers. The law would seek to ensure that tech companies and data center developers bear the cost of those upgrades. Since the data center boom got underway, just about everyone involved — tech companies, utilities, environmentalists, and even President Trump — has agreed on one thing: Normal Americans should not pay for data centers’ burden on the power system. These expenses can be significant, especially for the transmission system. Because a single computing facility can guzzle gigawatts of energy at once, compressing a city’s worth of power demand into just a few acres, it often requires the construction of specialized new infrastructure, or it risks causing blackouts and brownouts for nearby customers. In 2024, utility customers in the country’s largest power market paid $4.3 billion for transmission upgrades to supply data centers, according to a Union of Concerned Scientists report. Trump enshrined guarantees against these payments in his Ratepayer Protection Pledge in March. That document vowed that data center companies must pay for all of the electricity used to run their facilities, any new power plants required to generate that electricity, and any “new power delivery infrastructure upgrades.” There’s just one issue: Under federal law, the last part of that pledge is nearly impossible. Since the early 1990s, federal law has prohibited utilities from charging customers for both the cost of using specific transmission infrastructure and the cost of using the rest of the power grid. The origins of that ban go back to a 1992 case where a power plant in one utility’s service area wanted to sell electricity to a neighboring utility. The local utility wanted to charge it the “normal” cost of using its power grid, plus a special fee to cover the cost of crowding its own customers off the necessary transmission lines. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission ruled that was illegal. Instead, it said, utilities could make a customer pay for the “incremental” cost of using specific transmission lines, such as those built to service their facility. Or they could charge for the “embedded” costs of the existing power grid. Utilities could not charge customers for both “incremental and embedded” costs, it said; instead, utilities had to choose the higher of the two. FERC formalized the policy in 1994. Electricity law has changed significantly since then, and those FERC rules don’t apply to power plants, Ari Peskoe, the director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School, told me. But the ban still applies to electricity customers — even very big ones, like data centers. Peskoe wrote a Utility Dive article in April credited with first identifying the clash between the FERC rules, the data center boom, and the White House’s pledge. artigo.texto: A Vertiv, empresa global em infraestrutura digital crítica, anunciou hoje sua participação no Data Center World Brasil 2026, evento que reunirá líderes, especialistas e empresas para discutir os principais avanços em Data Centers e infraestrutura digital, de 6 a 8 de outubro, no São Paulo Expo, em São Paulo, Brasil. Durante o evento, os participantes discutirão como a adoção da Inteligência Artificial (IA), a expansão das redes e dos Data Centers, o crescimento da computação em Nuvem e a Transformação Digital de forma mais ampla estão moldando as prioridades de infraestrutura em toda a América Latina. A agenda incluirá temas relacionados à energia, gerenciamento térmico, conectividade, continuidade operacional e requisitos de infraestrutura para ambientes de maior densidade. A Vertiv estará presente com um estande onde clientes, parceiros e profissionais do setor poderão se reunir com especialistas da empresa para trocar perspectivas e explorar oportunidades relacionadas a novas implementações, expansões e modernização da infraestrutura. A participação da Vertiv também incluirá sessões de networking de negócios com os principais stakeholders do setor. “A rápida adoção da IA, da Computação em Nuvem e o aumento da demanda por processamento estão levando as empresas a tomar decisões de infraestrutura que afetam sua capacidade de escalar, adotar novas tecnologias e manter a continuidade operacional. Isso significa avaliar como projetar e operar uma infraestrutura crítica capaz de responder às crescentes demandas por energia, gerenciamento térmico e disponibilidade”, afirmou Alex Sasaki, vice-presidente de Vendas da Vertiv para a América Latina. “O Brasil conta com diversos fatores de crescimento que impulsionam o mercado de Data Centers à medida que a digitalização avança em toda a América Latina. O Data Center World Brasil 2026 representa uma oportunidade para trocar perspectivas com os principais tomadores de decisão do setor e discutir as possibilidades que poderão moldar a próxima etapa de desenvolvimento da região.” Serviço Vertiv.com

artigo.texto: A produção tropicalizada de baterias garantirá a segurança da matriz energética brasileira De olho no potencial do país, fabricantes traçam planos de longo prazo para suprir o mercado de armazenamento de energia Atualizado Mercado ainda incipiente no país, as soluções de armazenamento de energia em baterias, essenciais para garantir flexibilidade e segurança às redes elétricas, ganham um novo impulso com a queda no custo das baterias de íon-lítio no mercado internacional, com a maior facilidade de negociação nos contratos de energia e com a perspectiva de avanços no ambiente regulatório — inclusive com o esperado Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade destinado a sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, agendado para dezembro. As ações dos fabricantes de tecnologia no mercado brasileiro focam estratégias de longo prazo, visando consolidar uma produção tropicalizada, como avalia Alexandre Baldy, vice-presidente sênior da multinacional chinesa BYD no Brasil, que anunciou em fevereiro deste ano um investimento de R$ 500 milhões para a fabricação de Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias — em inglês, Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) — no país. “Estamos falando de uma decisão de longo prazo”, define. “É um movimento baseado na confiança que temos no potencial desse mercado e na importância que o armazenamento terá para o futuro da matriz energética brasileira”, diz. Segundo Baldy, a estratégia visa desenvolver capacidade industrial local e, ao mesmo tempo, criar condições para que uma cadeia brasileira de fornecedores cresça junto com esse mercado. “Esse processo de nacionalização também permitirá atender aos requisitos previstos pelo Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) e pelo Ministério de Minas e Energia para o Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade, ampliando o acesso dos investidores a linhas de financiamento do banco, tanto para projetos ligados ao leilão quanto para outras aplicações”, afirma. No leilão, há dois segmentos: armazenamento nacional, com exigência de, no mínimo, 15% de componentes locais, e geral, sem requisitos de nacionalização. A Contemporary Amperey Technology Co., Limited (CATL), outro superfabricante chinês de tecnologia, pretende fornecer para os dois. Para participar do leilão nacional, a CATL anunciou uma parceria estratégica com o Grupo Moura, um dos principais fabricantes de baterias do país, sediado no município de Belo Jardim (PE). “Para maximizar nosso impacto, estamos nos preparando ativamente, em conjunto com parceiros nacionais, para fornecer equipamentos credenciados, implementando plataformas avançadas de armazenamento com capacidade nativa de frid-forming [seguidores de redes]”, explica Ray See, vice-presidente de negócios para as Américas da CATL. Ele diz que, além de fornecer equipamentos, a parceria com o Grupo Moura visa integrar os sistemas de baterias localmente com um fabricante nacional e cumprir as regras de nacionalização previstas pelo governo federal. Para suprir o leilão de armazenamento geral, a CATL vai importar os equipamentos. Nos últimos anos, as vendas acumuladas de soluções BESS no Brasil somaram somente 1,9 GWh, dos quais 730 MWh foram comercializados em 2025, especialmente nos setores comercial e industrial. Nesse ano, os financiamentos registrados em BESS atingiram R$ 126 milhões. É um volume maior que o registrado em 2024 (R$ 117 milhões), mas que não reflete a real expansão da tecnologia no país, aponta levantamento do Clean Energy Latin America (Cela), uma boutique de investimentos do setor de energia renovável da região. “A expectativa é que os primeiros leilões dedicados exclusivamente ao armazenamento, previstos para 2026, marquem uma nova fase de escala para o segmento, com impacto direto nos volumes de financiamento”, confia Camila Ramos, diretora-executiva do Cela. “Podemos ter até um crescimento explosivo dos sistemas de armazenamento por baterias no Brasil nos próximos oito anos”, acredita Markus Vlasits, presidente da Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae). “A corrida das empresas estrangeiras e brasileiras por esse mercado deve movimentar mais de R$ 80 bilhões em investimentos até 2034”, diz. Só o leilão previsto para este ano deve destravar R$ 10 bilhões em projetos, estima Vlasits. Segundo ele, esse aumento dos negócios no setor de armazenamento de energia em baterias é movido pela redução de quase 70% no custo das baterias de lítio nos últimos três anos e a necessidade crescente de flexibilidade no sistema elétrico do país para gerenciar as diversas fontes de energias renováveis, como a solar e eólica. “Teremos muitos projetos dos fabricantes voltados para atender o setor comercial e industrial, além de projetos de descarbonização na região amazônica”, destaca. A WEG avalia que o potencial de negócios não se restringe apenas a grandes projetos. “Acreditamos muito também nas aplicações de médio porte, principalmente soluções BESS junto à carga e combinado com geração distribuída”, diz Manfred Peter Johann, vice-presidente de automação e sistemas da WEG. “A bateria pode ajudar a superar gargalos de fornecimento de energia e limitações da rede, garantir backup e maior confiabilidade para o consumidor e permitir arbitragem de energia entre diferentes horários.” No início deste ano, a WEG anunciou a construção de uma nova fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) em Itajaí (SC), com financiamento de R$ 280 milhões do programa BNDES Mais Inovação. A nova unidade ampliará capacidade produtiva para até 2 GWh ao ano e deverá entrar em operação no segundo semestre de 2027, informa Johann. “Praticamente todo o sistema pode ser industrializado no país”, indica. “O principal componente que ainda depende de importação é a célula da bateria, cuja fabricação exige uma escala muito maior para se tornar economicamente competitiva.” Praticamente dominado por fabricantes de tecnologia de ponta e gigantes industriais, o mercado de BESS movimenta t

artigo.texto: A regional gaúcha da Associação Brasileira da Indústria Elétrica e Eletrônica Regional (Abinee-RS) realizou mais uma edição de sua reunião-almoço nesta terça-feira, em Porto Alegre, abordando as oportunidades a partir da instalação de projetos de data center no Rio Grande do Sul, além de empreendimentos ligados à tecnologia, como o cabo submarino Malbec, cuja chegada ocorre no município de Balneário Pinhal, no litoral Norte. Representantes do segmento industrial e do governo do estado, apresentando números do setor, estiveram presentes no evento. O CEO da Parks, Fabio Cierro, comentou a respeito do andamento do projeto de um data center de R$ 500 milhões no Distrito Industrial de Cachoeirinha, na região Metropolitana. Para o diretor regional e vice-presidente da Abinee, Régis Haubert, as oportunidades tecnológicas têm relação com o momento de transformação digital e inteligência artificial, e o RS pode se beneficiar com isto. “Basicamente, temos aqui no estado um fornecimento e uma capacidade de energia muito boas. Também não nos preocupa a questão da formação técnica, porque temos qualificação e formação profissional muito boa, tanto nos cursos de graduação, quanto nos tecnólogos. O que precisamos é, cada vez mais, agregar a produção local de equipamentos, para que possamos atrair a demanda de nosso próprio mercado”, disse Haubert. Questionado a respeito dos desafios climáticos, o diretor da Abinee disse que eventos naturais como o El Niño são cíclicos. “Precisamos nos adequar às condições e mitigar para evitar problemas”, salientou ele. O vice-prefeito de Balneário Pinhal, Jorge Fonseca, comentou brevemente sobre os bastidores que levaram à construção e implantação da estrutura da V.tal, e que fará a comunicação de dados de milhões de usuários dos serviços da Meta, como WhatsApp, Facebook, Threads e Instagram, aumentando a conectividade e confiabilidade da Internet. Este é o primeiro cabo internacional a atingir diretamente o território gaúcho. “Após esta surpresa inicial, acredito que estamos fazendo a lição de casa, que é entender um pouco de processos, se apropriar de situações e fazer com que Balneário Pinhal não seja apenas um local de passagem do cabo. Já visitamos estruturas semelhantes em Montevidéu a convite da Antel (companhia estatal de telecomunicações do Uruguai) e tivemos bons diálogos com o governo do estado. Temos áreas já com licenciamentos ambientais disponíveis e estamos em uma aproximação com a CEEE Equatorial para analisar a qualidade da energia. São fatores muito significativos para nossas pretensões”, salientou Fonseca.

artigo.texto: From Isaac Anumihe, Abuja As the world seeks to transit towards climate finance and support greenhouse gas emission reductions as well as accelerate transition to a low-carbon economy, Federal Government has approved the carbon market framework objectives. Speaking at the National Stakeholder Review and Validation Workshop on the draft host country approval criteria for Nigeria’s carbon market operations, in Abuja, Vice Chancellor, University of Nigeria, Nsukka (UNN), Professor Simon Uchenna Ortuanya, said that the approval represented an important step towards establishing a structured system for carbon market operations in the country. Ortuanya, who was represented by the Director of Resource and Environmental Policy Research Centre, UNN, (REPRC-EfD), Dr Nnaemeka Chukwuone, stated that it’s against this background that the next official task is to ensure that the framework is supported by clear, practical and transparent host country approval criteria. “These criteria will provide guidance on the eligibility, screening and assessment of carbon market projects. They will also clarify institutional responsibilities, approval procedures, measurement, reporting and verification requirements, environmental and social safeguards; alignment with Nigeria’s Nationally -Determined Contribution (NNDC) registry and transparency arrangements, and carbon accounting” he said The criteria, the VC explained, should be sufficiently robust to protect Nigeria’s interests while remaining practical, predictable and responsive to the realities of implementation. “I am glad that the development of the proposed host country approval criteria was guided by sound research” he said. Before she declared the workshop open, the Director General, National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), Dr Omotenioye Majekodunmi, said that having approved the carbon market framework, the task before stakeholders is therefore clear — to establish post-country approval criteria that protect Nigeria’s national interests while providing the certainty that credible investors and project developers need. According to her, at the heart of the process is a simple principle that Nigeria must participate in carbon markets on terms that are credible, transparent, equitable and beneficial to the people. “Carbon projects must deliver genuine mitigation outcomes. They must contribute to sustainable development, respect host communities, and promote social inclusion and align with national climate and development priorities” she said. In his remarks, PEP’s Scientific Adviser, Professor Adeola Adenikinju, maintained that the global carbon market presents important opportunities for countries seeking to mobilise climate finance, support greenhouse gas emission reduction and removal, and accelerate the transition to a low-carbon economy. For Nigeria, he noted, these opportunities are particularly significant as it has become imperative for Nigeria to pursue economic growth, industrial development, and energy access and poverty reduction while responding to the challenges of climate change. In his opinion, a well-governed carbon market can help mobilise the resources required to support poverty reduction and grow economy.ENDS

artigo.texto: Gotion has begun delivering its Gotion Grid 5MWh energy storage systems to the Nefertiti and Horus projects in Egypt, an infrastructure that will become one of the largest independent energy storage facilities on the African continent, the deployment began on September 28 with the simultaneous departure of 50 heavy-duty trucks from Gotion’s facilities in Jinzhai and Nantong, China. The trucks are transporting units developed by the company for large-scale electrical storage applications, designed to improve the stability of power grids and facilitate the integration of renewable energy. Gotion promotes energy storage systems for Egypt’s grid The Nefertiti and Horus projects represent Egypt’s first standalone, large-capacity energy storage facilities, the infrastructure will be developed by AMEA Power, built by China Energy Engineering Group, and equipped with Gotion’s technological solutions. The integration of these systems will strengthen the stability of the Egyptian electricity grid through more efficient management of energy generation and consumption. Furthermore, it will facilitate greater integration of renewable sources such as solar and wind power, reducing the variability associated with these resources, the project aligns with Egypt’s energy transition goals for 2030, which seek to increase the share of clean sources within its electricity mix and strengthen the security of the national energy supply. Storage technology designed for extreme conditions Gotion Grid systems were developed to operate in environments with high temperatures, sandstorms and exposure to salt fog, common conditions in various regions of Egypt. The technology incorporates solutions aimed at ensuring operational safety, electrical stability and availability during extended operating cycles. The equipment offers millisecond response capability, allowing for compensation of rapid variations in electricity demand and improving network operation with greater participation of renewable generation. These features will allow for the optimization of the use of solar energy produced in Benban and provide flexibility to the electrical system to manage peak demand associated with the Zafarana wind farm. Gotion accelerates the delivery of large-scale energy storage The company completed the first shipment three months after the agreement was signed, a process that required coordination between the manufacturing, international transport and implementation stages of the project in Egypt. The start of the delivery represents a significant step forward for the development of energy storage infrastructure in the continent, where these technologies play a fundamental role in integrating larger volumes of renewable energy and improving the reliability of electricity grids. According to AMEA Power, this collaboration expands opportunities for energy cooperation between China, the Middle East, and Africa, as Gotion continues to expand its energy storage solutions beyond the Asian market. artigo.texto: A startup whose founder has vowed to "make nuclear great again" is planning to place hundreds of reactors on federal land in Utah, according to documents reviewed by NPR. Valar Atomics is planning what it calls "Project Beehive" on over 9,000 acres of land held under the Bureau of Land Management near Price, Utah. The facility would include data centers and some 456 small nuclear reactors, along with a facility to produce nuclear fuel and others for storing nuclear waste, according to a proposal from the company to federal regulators. In aggregate, the reactors would produce around 9.6 gigawatts of power for the data centers and even more thermal heat for other industrial applications. Currently, the entire state of Utah produces only around 4 gigawatts of electricity on average (though its peak capacity in summer can reach around 10 gigawatts). The project's timeline calls for nonnuclear construction to begin as soon as the end of this year, with the first reactors coming online sometime in 2028. Valar has also sought the use of around 650 acres of state land as part of the same project, according to state records. The Salt Lake Tribune first reported on the project's use of state land last week, but not the much larger proposed use of federal lands. The project has raised alarm among local activists, who are already facing a slew of data center proposals in the state. "It's concerning to see that the Trump administration, with the support of the state of Utah, is pushing this forward on significant acreage of public lands," said Neal Clark, wildlands director at the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, a Utah-based nonprofit that seeks to protect public lands. "The coalition of people who are concerned about these things completely transcends political lines," added Lexi Tuddenham, the executive director of the Healthy Environment Alliance of Utah, which has tracked nuclear-related industries in the state. Tuddenham said that at the moment her primary goal is to raise awareness. "The biggest thing we can do right now is to let people know about it." In a written statement, the Bureau of Land Management's Utah office confirmed it had received an application from the company. "We are currently reviewing the application for completeness," it told NPR in an email. As the application moves through the required National Environmental Policy Act process, "we will make sure the public has meaningful opportunities to provide input," it added. Valar did not immediately respond to NPR's request for comment. In an interview with NPR in July, Valar CEO Isaiah Taylor said his company was committed to safety and community engagement. "We're doing it responsibly and accountably to this community," he said of a smaller test reactor that the company was operating in a neighboring county. Small reactors, big plan Project Beehive reveals the scale of the ambitions held by a new generation of companies planning a comeback for nuclear power. The companies are backed by the Trump administration, which has enacted a slew of regulatory reforms over the past year and a half to make their "small modular reactors" easier to test and build. Valar has been both closely involved with those reforms and a beneficiary of them. Taylor was in the room when President Trump signed a series of executive orders last year designed to accelerate the development of nuclear power, and his company was accepted into the Department of Energy's Reactor Pilot Program in August 2025. This past February, the U.S. military flew Valar's test reactor from California to Utah aboard a C-17 transport aircraft. The reactor, known as Ward 250, received rapid approval this year after the Department of Energy conducted a quiet overhaul of its internal safety and security regulations for nuclear reactors. It achieved criticality by reaching a self-sustaining nuclear reaction in June, in a tentlike structure in the Utah desert about 30 miles from the site of Project Beehive. At a press event on July 1, the company marked another milestone when it used Ward 250 to produce electricity. Taylor powered up the test reactor and used a simple thermoelectric system to run a single Nvidia microchip. "Ladies and gentlemen, Valar Atomics just became the first startup in history to make nuclear electricity right here," he told the crowd. The scale of Project Beehive vastly outstrips that July demonstration. Since the turn of the century, the U.S. has switched on just three new nuclear power plants, producing a total of around 3.4 gigawatts of electricity. Those reactors are far larger than the small modular reactors that Valar plans to use, and each costs many billions of dollars to build. Valar and other companies are hoping to upend the nuclear business model because small reactors can be mass-produced and placed in series, like a set of nuclear batteries. Valar's 25-megawatt electric units could be installed one at a time, allowing Project Beehive to be built in phases over a number of years. That in turn would reduce the cost and allow the site to enter operation relatively quickly. According to a document reviewed by NPR, the full site could be completed by 2032. Tuddenham said she thinks the use of federal lands for such a project is unprecedented. "In this case, I think it's bigger than the local community," she said. "If we have facilities like this on public land for waste storage, for massive nuclear development, for data centers, that's going to have tremendous implications for how public lands are used." NPR's Shannon Bond contributed to this report. Contact Geoff Brumfiel on Signal at gbrumfiel.13 Copyright 2026 NPR Loading...
