artigo.texto: Sistemas de armazenamento de energia podem gerar até R$ 6 bilhões por ano em benefícios ao sistema elétrico brasileiro, segundo estudo da ABSAE (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia) em parceria com a consultoria Volt Robotics. A estimativa considera a utilização de baterias para atender parte da necessidade adicional de potência prevista para 2028 no SIN (Sistema Interligado Nacional), calculada entre 4,5 GW e 6,5 GW, além dos efeitos econômicos de sua contratação no LRCAP (Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade) Os números incorporam ganhos potenciais com redução de encargos, arbitragem de energia, menor acionamento de usinas térmicas e aproveitamento de energia que atualmente é perdida por vertimentos e cortes de geração renovável. A premissa adotada é que a necessidade de potência deve ser definida antes da escolha da tecnologia. O aumento do consumo eleva a demanda nos horários de maior utilização e exige recursos capazes de entregar capacidade firme justamente nesses períodos. A partir daí, térmicas, hidrelétricas, baterias e outras tecnologias elegíveis podem ser comparadas segundo sua capacidade de atender à necessidade e o custo associado à operação. Os cenários considerados pelo estudo combinam diferentes trajetórias de crescimento da carga, postergação da entrada de usinas termelétricas contratadas no LRCAP de 2026 e maior expansão solar. Na hipótese mais abrangente, a necessidade adicional chega a 6,5 GW. O estudo utiliza 6 GW de baterias com cinco horas de duração como cenário intermediário para simular os efeitos do armazenamento sobre a operação do sistema. Baterias respondem à ponta A principal característica destacada é a capacidade de o BESS concentrar sua atuação nas horas em que o sistema efetivamente precisa de potência. Enquanto determinados recursos de geração precisam permanecer ligados durante períodos muito mais longos para atender a uma necessidade de apenas algumas horas, as baterias podem absorver energia em momentos de menor carga e devolvê-la durante a rampa de demanda e o período de ponta. O estudo chama atenção para os custos associados à baixa flexibilidade de parte do parque térmico. Em uma das simulações, uma termelétrica com tempo mínimo de permanência de 72 horas precisaria permanecer acionada para atender a uma necessidade concentrada em apenas dois dias, fazendo com que 89% do custo associado à operação fosse remunerado pelo armazenamento no cenário analisado. A avaliação também mostra que parcela relevante do parque térmico possui tempos de partida superiores à duração de algumas necessidades críticas. Para 2030, o estudo distribui a capacidade analisada em três faixas.Em 6% com tempo de partida inferior a quatro horas, 49% entre quatro e 12 horas e 45% acima de 12 horas. A conclusão apresentada é que a duração e a frequência da necessidade são fatores importantes para determinar a aderência das baterias. Preços e encargos Além de fornecer potência, o BESS poderia produzir efeitos sobre diferentes componentes do custo de operação. Uma das simulações aponta redução de aproximadamente 11% na variabilidade intradiária do PLD nos quatro submercados, com quedas estimadas entre 10% e 13% no desvio-padrão intradiário. Para o estudo, preços mais estáveis reduzem riscos associados à contratação de energia. Outro mecanismo analisado é a arbitragem. As baterias podem ser carregadas em períodos de preços menores e descarregadas quando o preço está mais elevado. Considerando os preços observados entre 2024 e agosto de 2026 e a simulação realizada pela Volt Robotics, o ganho acumulado de arbitragem chega a R$ 1,3 bilhão, equivalente a uma média de R$ 487 milhões por ano. Esse resultado é tratado no estudo como uma receita capaz de abater parte do custo da capacidade contratada. O armazenamento também aparece associado à redução de encargos. O levantamento aponta que os consumidores pagaram R$ 4,7 bilhões em encargos entre 2024 e julho de 2026, dos quais R$ 3,6 bilhões, ou 76%, correspondem a parcelas relacionadas a constrained-on, unit commitment e serviços ancilares que poderiam ser reduzidas pela atuação do BESS nas premissas utilizadas. Em uma estimativa considerada conservadora, a atuação das baterias evitaria cerca de R$ 629 milhões por ano em encargos, acumulando R$ 1,7 bilhão entre 2024 e agosto de 2026 quando aplicadas as premissas da simulação. O cálculo não incorpora integralmente alguns benefícios considerados de atuação parcial, como deslocamento hidráulico e serviços ancilares. Energia desperdiçada Um dos efeitos destacados pelo estudo está relacionado ao aproveitamento de energia que atualmente pode ser perdida por vertimento turbinável e curtailment de fontes renováveis. A estimativa indica que até 88% da energia utilizada para recarregar o BESS poderia vir dessas duas fontes, dependendo do ano e das condições do sistema. Em 2025, por exemplo, a análise estima que 86% da energia necessária para a recarga poderia ter origem em energia que seria desperdiçada. Em janeiro a agosto de 2026, essa proporção sobe para 88%. A lógica seria priorizar primeiro o aproveitamento do vertimento turbinável e, em seguida, da geração renovável que seria cortada. Esse aproveitamento teria reflexos financeiros. O estudo estima R$ 2,7 bilhões em benefícios entre 2024 e agosto de 2026, considerando o aproveitamento de vertimento turbinável, curtailment e, em determinado cenário, geração hidrelétrica adicional. Desse total, R$ 2,264 bilhões corresponderiam a benefícios para as hidrelétricas e R$ 417 milhões ao aproveitamento de energia renovável que seria cortada. Menor dependência de térmicas O armazenamento também modifica a necessidade de acionamento de usinas termelétricas. A simulação aponta deslocamento de 11.045 GWh por ano de geração térmica, considerando constrained-on, geração na ordem de mérito e unit commitment. Aplicado um fator médio de emissão de 543 kg de CO₂ por MWh, o resultado estimado chega a 5,99 milhões de toneladas de CO₂ evitada

artigo.texto: Sauk Rapids Reaches Agreement On NextEra Battery Facility, Accepts Limited Local Control SAUK RAPIDS (WJON News) -- The Sauk Rapids City Council has reluctantly approved a development agreement for a proposed battery storage facility. Monday night, the council voted 3-2 in favor of the agreement worked out between city staff and Mayhew Lake Energy Storage LLC, a NextEra Energy Resources company. All five council members are opposed to the project's location, but three members decided any agreement is better than no agreement at all. Under Minnesota law, the authority for the project rests solely with the Public Utilities Commission, and the city has limited authority over the project. Mayor Jason Ellering says the proposed battery energy storage facility would sit on prime land for city growth. It's smack dab in the middle of a significant development corridor for the city as we continue to grow. What the next 30 years look like for the city, I think that it is important to take that into consideration. What the property is going to look like, it'll be there indefinitely. The city council previously approved two objection letters to the PUC outlining the city's concerns with the proposed location. With the approval of the development agreement, the city will rescind the letter to the PUC citing its opposition to the project. Sauk Rapids City Attorney Adam Ripple says the agreement is an attempt to make lemonade out of lemons and to mitigate the impact on the city if the project moves forward. artigo.texto: Should Americans provide subsidies through the tax code for Meta’s creation of AI data centers and compensation paid to its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg? If you think the answer is yes, then you might believe that the Trump administration is doing an excellent job enforcing tax laws and that the two major pieces of tax legislation he and Congressional Republicans have enacted have left the revenue code in really good shape. On the other hand, if you think Meta should not be subsidized (through the tax code or in any other way) for building AI data centers and for compensating Mark Zuckerberg, then you should believe something is seriously wrong with our tax laws and how they are enforced. Earlier this year, ITEP described how Meta paid just 3.5 percent of its profits in federal corporate income taxes in 2025 – and why its effective tax rate for the year may turn out to be even lower than that. Today the New York Times explains part of how the company pulled that off, reporting that Meta is claiming the research tax credit — a tax break enacted decades ago to encourage innovation and experimentation — to pay for the equipment it uses in data centers to power its AI activities. The research credit is a tax subsidy that is supposed to encourage companies to conduct research and experiment to find answers, innovations, new processes, or approaches that are not already known. It is not supposed to simply subsidize whatever equipment a tech company needs to do its business. As the Times mentions, this is not Meta’s first R&D credit-abusing rodeo: the company is already embroiled in a longstanding dispute with the IRS over its claim that more than $4 billion in compensation paid to Mark Zuckerberg should count as eligible research expenses because he allegedly invented new features on Facebook. When most people hear the term “research”, they might think of people in lab coats trying to cure cancer or engineers searching for a way to make a more powerful engine. We do not think of Mark Zuckerberg figuring out how to use our personal data to help other companies tempt us to buy something when we are looking at Facebook to catch up on some relative or friend who we are too lazy to call. The research credit has long been used to subsidize things that normal people would not call “research.” Years ago, Congress had a chance to reform the credit before they made it a permanent part of the tax code and lawmakers passed up that opportunity. More recently, a study found that the research credit seems to subsidize many companies for doing things they would do anyway and encourages many to just recharacterize activities as research in order to obtain this tax break. When you give research credits to a company that is sitting on $43 billion of cash and cash equivalents, as Meta was at the beginning of 2025, it seems especially clear that the company involved already has the means to spend whatever it wants on whatever it wants and won’t be swayed by tax incentives into changing its plans. It is not surprising that a profit-seeking company will seek to lower its tax bill in whatever ways Congress and the IRS allow. What’s unusual about Meta is its willingness to identify the limits of what the law allows and then blow right past them. The company openly admits that over $2.6 billion of the tax breaks it claimed last year alone are “uncertain,” meaning they believe that tax authorities would likely disallow them if they were scrutinized. The budgetary stakes for the U.S. are potentially huge: the Times’ new revelations suggest that one of the most profitable corporations in American history is attempting to use the biggest capital-spending boom in the history of the world to reduce its already-low tax rates even more. In theory, it is up to the IRS and the Treasury Department to make it clear that equipment used in data centers is not “research.” Given that we have more than two more years of federal agencies serving under President Trump, the one American who fervently supports building more AI data centers, the only hope is that the next Congress begins to ask questions about Meta’s outlandish tax maneuvers.

artigo.texto: Round Up: commissioners back two school grant bids, set data center moratorium hearing Davidson County commissioners voted this week to support grant applications for new high school buildings in both Lexington and Thomasville, and agreed to schedule an Oct. 26 public hearing on a temporary moratorium on data centers, in a meeting that ran more than three hours and included heated public comment. Lexington High School The board's longest discussion centered on Lexington City Schools' application to the state's Needs-Based Public School Capital Fund for a new Lexington Senior High School. The application is due Oct. 2. Lexington City Schools Superintendent Dr. Ron Anthony told commissioners the school, described by speakers as 73 years old and the oldest school building in the county, has water intrusion, aging systems, structural settlement, and accessibility and life-safety deficiencies. He presented three options: limited repairs at $15.5 million, a $58 million renovation, or new construction that would use a county match of about $41 million to unlock roughly $62 million in state funding. Anthony said the school has the third-highest performance data in Davidson County and is rated a B school, arguing that students are succeeding despite the building. The district says Lexington Senior High earned its first B under the state's school performance grades in the latest results, with a graduation rate of 91.7%. Anthony did not specify which schools the county comparison covers, and the claim could not be independently verified. Outside rankings are less favorable: U.S. News ranks the school 410th among 604 ranked high schools in North Carolina, and the nonprofit GreatSchools gives it a 3 out of 10 rating. Anthony also noted that the school's auditorium serves as a community emergency shelter. Lexington City Board of Education Chair Angela Mcduffie told commissioners that renovation "band-aids" are no longer responsible. A commissioner who is a former teacher cited leaking ceilings, buckling floors and barriers under the Americans with Disabilities Act. Commissioners spent considerable time on how to pay for the local share. Commissioners discussed a worst-case scenario for a $104 million project, in which the county would need to borrow about $15 million after applying lottery funds, existing capital money and a possible $10 million transfer from dredging funds. They noted that upcoming debt relief from the Oak Grove project could help support that borrowing. One commissioner put the county's requested contribution at $41,255,567. The county attorney, Adam Jones, cautioned that approving the application "as written" effectively certifies that the county has the required local funding available, which could commit it to the full project cost and roughly $42 million in local money. Project architect Miki Keller said the state's main focus is the match tied to the $62 million grant, about $15.5 million in local funds, and that the firm would reduce scope if costs change. Anthony said he would work with the architect within 48 hours to propose cuts, and he was willing to negotiate on a reduced estimate of about $90 million to $95 million. Commissioners clarified that the vote authorizes applying for the grant rather than approving construction, and they voted to approve the application. Thomasville High School Commissioners then approved Thomasville City Schools' application in about six minutes. Rodney Shotwell said the building scope of the revised proposal is intact but planned athletic upgrades and some renovations were cut. The plan requests $15.5 million in local funds to complete a $77.5 million new school. Shotwell also described severe problems at a closed career-technical building and the need for a $1.2 million infrastructure project. Commissioners said that if neither district wins a grant, they would revert to existing allocations and revisit renovation funding for Thomasville High and other schools. Data center moratorium The board voted 4-2 to schedule an Oct. 26 public hearing on a temporary moratorium on data centers. The vote did not adopt the moratorium itself, Jones stressed. A four-month moratorium was discussed. Supporters said a pause would give time to study impacts, gather citizen input, and let planning staffer Lee Crook finish a zoning text amendment for data centers. One commissioner said the county has no specific data center regulations and argued a pause would also give state and federal officials a chance to explain policies they have promoted without answering local questions. Another commissioner said a moratorium would allow time to design plans in which large data center investments could fund schools and reduce property taxes for long-term residents and seniors. Shell said commissioners already have authority to scrutinize applications and worried a moratorium could delay an acceptable project midstream, "handcuffing" future boards. One commissioner initially described the moratorium as sending an anti-business signal before saying the commissioner supported it as a pause. Planning and Zoning Director Lee Crook said regulatory work can continue during a moratorium and that private land sales to data centers cannot be blocked but would be subject to any adopted regulations. Jones warned that adopting a moratorium and a new ordinance simultaneously would undermine the moratorium's purpose. Jones and Hiller said the county cannot offer targeted tax relief without state legislation, though Cabarrus County uses economic development incentives to fund such programs. During the discussion, Shell told a member of the audience to "shut up" after a tense exchange, and other officials called for decorum. Shell later apologized. artigo.texto: vivo has officially announced the global launch of the vivo X Fold6, its latest flagship foldable smartphone after the China launch back in June. Aimed at mobile professionals, the new device integrates expanded productivity software, a high-capacity battery system, upgraded imaging hardware developed with ZEISS, and a slimmed-down chassis. Multitasking Software and AI Features The X Fold6 launches with OriginOS 7 Fold, supported by the Origin Smooth Engine for sustained multitasking performance. Central to the software experience is the Multi-Task Workbench, which includes: - Origin Workbench: A workspace configuration featuring one primary window alongside four auxiliary windows to keep core tasks centered while monitoring secondary activities. - Multi-Split Screen: Supports up to four freely resizable side-by-side windows. - AI Cross-App Drag: Allows direct dragging and dropping of content between active applications. The operating system also incorporates several built-in AI productivity utilities. AI Meeting Assistant provides in-person transcription and structured summaries via AI Recorder, alongside real-time subtitles through AI Captions. AI File Manager handles scattered content with automated naming, summaries, topic categorization, and a column-based view. Reading workflows are supplemented by AI Reader Mode, which reformats PDFs into an eBook format. For external displays, vivo Office Kit enables a Desktop Mode when hooked up to a compatible monitor or television. The device also integrates Jovi, an AI agent capable of scheduling tasks and running cross-device workflows across smartphones and PCs via voice commands. System protection is handled by vivo’s Security Shield, which monitors app permissions, network security, and potential installation risks. Hardware, Battery, and Form Factor The X Fold6 is powered by the MediaTek Dimensity 9500 Super Edition platform, customized in partnership with vivo alongside an Ultra-Efficient Concurrent Engine to manage power and graphical loads. The phone is powered by a 6,900 mAh BlueVolt Battery utilizing fifth-generation silicon anode technology to fit the large capacity into a narrow frame. The power cell also incorporates third-generation semi-solid-state battery technology, designed to sustain discharge efficiency in temperatures down to –20°C. Charging options include 80W wired FlashCharge, 40W wireless FlashCharge, and wireless reverse charging. The physical construction features an Ultra-Reliable Lightweight Hinge, 2.5D flat metal framing, and vivo’s Minimal Ring camera module. The phone is offered in two variants: - Prism Black: 4.4 mm thick unfolded, weighing 228 grams. - Horizon Blue: 4.8 mm thick unfolded, weighing 235 grams. The device carries IPX8 and IPX9 water resistance ratings alongside an IP5X dust resistance rating. Network performance is managed by a 1+4 Communication Chipset, supported by an integrated Data Store feature that allows users to purchase local cellular data plans across 129 countries and regions directly from the device. Dual Displays and Camera System Visuals are delivered via the ZEISS Master Color Display setup on both panels: - Inner Display: An 8.02-inch panel using Samsung M14 luminescent material. - Cover Display: A 6.51-inch panel using BOE Q11 luminescent material. Both screens feature 8T-LTPO backplanes supporting a 1–120 Hz adaptive refresh rate, a minimum brightness level of 1 nit, and a local peak brightness of up to 5,000 nits. For photography and videography, the device uses the vivo ZEISS Co-engineered Imaging System powered by the dedicated vivo Imaging Chip V3+: - Main Camera: A 200 MP sensor (Samsung HPB Large Sensor) featuring ZEISS T* coating and optical image stabilization (OIS). - Telephoto Camera: A ZEISS APO telephoto unit utilizing a Sony LYTIA 602 sensor with vivo’s VCS technology, a 3x periscope design, telephoto macro capabilities, and up to 100x ZEISS HyperZoom. Software features for the camera array include Motion Portrait 2.0 for subject tracking, Stage Mode with an AI True Clarity Engine supporting 4K 60 fps Dolby Vision video, Night Flash Portrait, and dedicated multi-focal length portrait capture. The folding form factor also supports Split-Screen Preview, an external teleprompter display, an interactive cover screen for children and pets, and a Left-Screen Preview mode that places previous captures alongside the live viewfinder. vivo X Fold6 specifications - 8.02-inch (2504 x 2312 pixels) 2K+ AMOLED LTPO display with 1-120Hz refresh rate, HDR 10+, up to 5000 nits brightness, UTG Glass, Dolby Vision - 6.51-inch (2528×1120 pixels) FHD+ AMOLED LTPO display with 1-120Hz refresh rate, up to 5000 nits brightness, Dolby Vision - Octa-Core Dimensity 9500 Super Edition 3nm processor with Arm Mali-G1 Ultra MC12 GPU - 12GB LPDDR5X RAM with 512GB UFS 4.1 storage - OriginOS 7 based on Android 17 - Dual SIM - 200MP camera with 1/1.4″ Samsung HPB sensor, f/1.68 aperture, OIS, Zeiss T* coating, 50MP ultra-wide camera with f/2.05 aperture, 15mm focal length, 50MP 3x periscope telephoto camera with 1/1.95″ Sony LYT602 sensor, f/2.57 aperture, ZEISS optics - 20MP front camera on the inside and outside with f/2.4 aperture - Side-mounted fingerprint sensor - USB Type-C Audio, Stereo speakers - Dimensions: 157.16×145.66×4.4mm (expanded)/ 74.26×9.4mm (Closed); Weight: 228g (Black), 235g (Blue) - Dust and Waterproof (IP58, IP59, IPX8, IPX9 ratings) - 5G SA/NSA, Dual 4G VoLTE, Wi-Fi 7 802.11 ax (2.4GHz and 5GHz), Bluetooth 5.4 LE, GPS (L1 + L5 Dual band), BeiDou, GLONASS, Galileo, QZSS, NavIC, NFC, USB Type-C - 6900mAh (typical) battery with 80W fast charging, 40W wireless charging, reverse wireless charging Even though the phone has been launched globally, the company has still not announced the pricing or availability and said that it will be announced depending on the local launch.

artigo.texto: Satélites de baixa órbita (LEO) e geoestacionários (GEO) podem desempenhar funções complementares em futuras arquiteturas de data centers no espaço, segundo executivos das operadoras Astranis e da Eutelsat. A avaliação foi apresentada nesta quinta-feira, 1º, durante o Congresso Latino-Americano de Satélites, no Rio de Janeiro. Head de vendas para as Américas da Astranis, Omar Trujillo disse que essa evolução deve ocorrer de forma gradual, começando pelo processamento dos dados gerados por satélites de observação antes de sua transmissão à Terra. Nesse cenário, Trujillo vê espaço para uma arquitetura multiórbita. Satélites LEO poderiam processar informações e utilizar equipamentos GEO para retransmitir os dados, reduzindo a necessidade de enviar todo o conteúdo bruto diretamente ao solo. "Agora, um data center em satélite GEO seria algo de mais longo prazo", ponderou. Processamento embarcado Diretor de vendas para conectividade da Eutelsat do Brasil, Eloi Stivalletti também avalia que a capacidade computacional embarcada tende a aumentar. "A indústria vai agregar funcionalidades de processamento e capacidades de armazenamento maiores no GEO", afirmou. Ele avaliou que, em uma arquitetura multiórbita, os dados poderiam ser tratados no espaço e apenas as informações necessárias seriam posteriormente enviadas ao usuário. A companhia, inclusive, já prevê processamento a bordo na nova geração de satélites da OneWeb, com gerenciamento dinâmico de capacidade e cobertura. "Não que isso vá, de maneira alguma, substituir os data centers terrestres", afirmou o executivo da Eutelsat. "Mas vão ser um complemento bastante importante", completou. SpaceX A discussão em torno da viabilidade técnica de um projeto como esse ganhou projeção após, em janeiro, a SpaceX (dona da Starlink) entrar com um pedido de autorização à Comissão Federal de Comunicações dos Estados Unidos (FCC) para lançar e operar um novo sistema não geoestacionário de até 1 milhão de satélites voltados a data centers orbitais. No mês seguinte, a FCC aceitou analisar o pedido. O projeto da empresa ligou um alerta no mercado. Amazon, por exemplo, acusou a empresa de Elon Musk de "reservar órbitas" com plano de 1 milhão de satélites. A empresa, inclusive, pediu ao órgão americano que rejeite a solicitação da SpaceX.

artigo.texto: Early-stage plans to build a hyperscale data center in Bow, N.H. have drawn opposition from residents and intensified debate among state politicians over how to handle the costs of artificial intelligence. Over 100 people gathered outside of a selectboard meeting in Bow, N.H., on Sept. 22 to rally against the plans to build an artificial intelligence data center at Merrimack Station, a former coal plant, according to Kendra Ford, an organizer of the protest with the climate justice campaign No Coal No Gas. In May, a separate application for the approval to construct a data center in Nottingham, N.H., was withdrawn due to backlash. State senate president Sharon Carson, R-Londonderry, and Gov. Kelly Ayotte announced in the past month that Republicans would pursue moratoriums on data center construction. On Aug. 20, during a meeting at the Rotary Club of Portsmouth, Ayotte said New Hampshire is “not the appropriate location” for a data center. The position marks a sharp turn from her position in August 2025, when she signed off on a bill deregulating energy providers who do not use the public power grid, allowing them to develop energy projects without New Hampshire Public Utilities oversight. “It does not make sense at all to site a data center in New Hampshire,” she said at the meeting. “We don’t have the energy for it.” Ayotte’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment on a timeline for the moratorium. In a Sept. 17 press release, Carson wrote that state Senate Republicans “agree with Gov. Ayotte” on banning data center construction. “Senate Republicans will pursue legislation to protect New Hampshire taxpayers from shouldering the costly demands of data center development and ensure our communities are not left to pay the price,” the press release read. Carson did not provide a timeline for legislative action in the press release. Seven Republican senators and representatives did not respond to multiple requests for comment; two declined to comment. Another two were absent for scheduled interviews and declined to follow up at a later date. Residents first raised concerns about a large-scale data center in Bow after New Hampshire consumer advocate Don Kreis posted on X on Aug. 31 that during a meeting with Eversource — New England’s largest energy delivery company — one of the company’s officials mentioned conversations with a developer about a potential 200-megawatt data center in Bow. New Hampshire currently has no hyperscale data centers. Instead, the state has 24 small operational data centers that total 14.5-megawatts in power, according to the U.S. Data Center Map. Hyperscale data centers can “stress” local power grids, according to Thayer School of Engineering professor Anthony Rizzo. “If you’re not building more power plants … then you’re going to be siphoning power that would go elsewhere, and that can cause problems,” he said. “Part of the problem with building data centers is then also building power plants to power them.” In April, Granite Shore Power, which owns Merrimack Station, filed a request with the U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to begin preliminary studies with Eversource on the possibility of connecting to the power grid to construct a hyperscale, 350-megawatt project. Bow Selectboard chair Kip McDaniel said at the board’s Sept. 29 meeting that Bow has not since communicated with Granite Shore Power on the subject, or received a project application. Bow resident Kevin McManus, who attended the Sept. 22 protest and said he lives less than a mile from Merrimack Station, said he is “concerned” about a center causing noise pollution, consuming utilities and harming the riverfront. “Assuming they [the town] taxed them for the full value of this thing, it would be a huge decrease in our tax bills,” he said. “But I don’t care.” No Coal No Gas, which is run by climate justice and renewable energy movement 350 New Hampshire, coordinated the Sept. 22 rally to demonstrate to local officials that “the people don’t want it,” Ford explained in an interview with The Dartmouth. “We will make sure that there are several people from Bow and folks from other towns at every planning board and zoning board meeting for the foreseeable future until we hear that there is not going to be a data center,” she said. She added that the residents are concerned about a potential data center’s noise pollution and damage to the nearby river. An Eversource spokesperson wrote in a statement to The Dartmouth that the company is “obligated” to answer proposals from developers and evaluate whether projects would be able to connect to their grid. “We have no role in determining whether potential projects are allowed to interconnect to our system if developers are willing to incur specific associated costs — including for studies, assessments and necessary infrastructure upgrades — and if those projects receive required local, state and federal approvals in the future,” they wrote. Some economics and energy experts said the costs of the project would depend heavily on how it is structured. Kreis said in an interview with The Dartmouth that data center development “could be a win-win” financially for “all electric customers in the state” by lowering rates. “I think it is at least theoretically possible to design rates and terms of service that would make data centers a net benefit to all of the state’s electric customers,” he said. “If we put a data center online and require it to curtail its use of electricity from the grid at certain peak hours, and basically manage consumption, that could reduce costs for everybody, because the data center would pay a big share of the utility’s [Eversource] fixed costs.” Thayer School of Engineering associate professor Junbo Zhao, who researches energy grids, said data centers “could” provide economic growth opportunities for the state. “This will be billions of dollars of investment to the local community,” he said. “Good for the state, good f

artigo.texto: Com capacidade produtiva de 4 GWh por ano, a nova fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias da WEG, em construção em Itajaí (SC), receberá investimento total estimado de R$ 330 milhões, segundo ampliação do projeto anunciada pela companhia na última semana. De acordo com a empresa, o início das operações está previsto para o segundo semestre de 2027. A expansão faz parte da estratégia da WEG de acompanhar o crescimento do mercado de armazenamento de energia no Brasil, em um momento de preparação para o primeiro Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade de Armazenamento, previsto para dezembro de 2026. Com a atualização, o projeto passa a incorporar maior nível de automação e ganhos de eficiência industrial, que, segundo a companhia, permitirão ampliar a capacidade produtiva da unidade. A WEG aponta o avanço das fontes renováveis e a necessidade de maior flexibilidade e segurança para o sistema elétrico como fatores que vêm impulsionando a demanda por soluções de armazenamento no país. “O mercado de armazenamento de energia vive um momento de forte expansão, impulsionado pelo crescimento das fontes renováveis e pela necessidade crescente de maior flexibilidade e segurança para o sistema elétrico”, afirmou Manfred Peter Johann, vice-presidente de Automação e Sistemas da WEG. “A ampliação deste projeto demonstra a capacidade da WEG de adaptar rapidamente seus investimentos para atender às necessidades do mercado e apoiar o desenvolvimento sustentável do setor energético brasileiro”, concluiu Johann. Todo o conteúdo do Canal Solar é resguardado pela lei de direitos autorais, e fica expressamente proibida a reprodução parcial ou total deste site em qualquer meio. Caso tenha interesse em colaborar ou reutilizar parte do nosso material, solicitamos que entre em contato através do e-mail: redacao@canalsolar.com.br.

artigo.texto: A brief stop-work order was issued and then retracted for construction on the DC BLOX Thunderbird data center on Sept. 11 and 12. The order was issued after a nearby resident reported heavy machinery and work starting on the site without a posted permit. After an inspection, work was allowed to continue on the site under a drainage permit, which is required to be visibly posted on the site. While the construction continues, there are still concerns from some community members about the presence of private security and local police near the site. Frustrations have continued to rise after a lack of communication from DC BLOX. Megan Lapa is a member of Eastside Community Action (ECA), which has been organizing against the data center since it was proposed in July. “It’s the audacity of it,” Lapa said. “They want to come here and build this project, but they’re not telling us anything beyond what they’re required to. They’re not listening to our concerns or what we’re saying.” ECA has filed a petition for judicial review of the variance of use the Metropolitan Development Commission approved for development of the site. The petition says that the request did not adequately meet the requirements for a variance of use of a site zoned Industrial 3. “[The] goal is to get this [land] in the hands of the community,” Lapa said. “Whether that’s for a different industrial development or whatever it may be, we want to be able to have some [community input].” While the ECA has expressed its dislike of the project, some Butler students are experiencing the same issue in their own communities. Sophia McKinley, a sophomore philosophy and political science double major, is from Kokomo, Ind., a community an hour north of campus, which has also shown strong opposition to its own data center project. “Being at [Butler], so much of our curriculum is community-based,” McKinley said. “[Data centers] are an issue we’re seeing affect students in their hometown; we should carry that over [to] caring about it here.” McKinley sees the issue as an opportunity for students to get more involved in the local community. “This is the time you’re going to be most available to care, have the resources to [get involved] and be around people your age that care about similar things,” McKinley said. “If you’re seeing so many of your peers passionate about this, maybe it’s time to think about why that is.” While communities remain wary of data centers in their area, some involved are supportive of the initiatives, particularly the potential industrial and monetary benefits. Michael-Paul Hart is the city-county councilor for District 20, where the site is located. District 20 is also where Google withdrew a rezoning request for a data center last year after community disagreement and an expected no-vote from the City-County Council. “[Thunderbird Commerce Center] is a site that has power already,” Hart said. “It is surrounded by other industrial-type uses. If you were going to pick a site, [this] is a good site given its history of being a brownfield [and] being a manufacturing area.” Hart says that the development will provide benefits to District 20, allowing for further investment into the community as a result of potential tax abatements, commonly referred to as tax breaks, and community impact payments. “[The data center buildings] will be the smallest [ones] over there, but they will pay seven to 10 times more because of [the] equipment inside it, even under tax abatement,” Hart said. “In this case, the charity and community impact is between [$7 million] and $8 million. Without a tax abatement, I can’t get those checks.” While a vote for tax abatements for the DC BLOX site has not been scheduled, abatements were recently approved for the Sabey Decatur Township data center project and a vote on abatements for the Metrobloks site is scheduled for Oct. 21. DC BLOX could not be reached for comment at the time of publication.

artigo.texto: A Intel lançou a versão 26.3.5 (2026Q3) do seu Media Driver para Linux, adicionando suporte oficial à Crescent Island, sua próxima GPU voltada para acelerar cargas de trabalho em Data Centers. No novo driver, a placa é listada sob o código CRI, ao lado de outras plataformas da empresa como Panther Lake, Nova Lake e Battlemage. - ElmorLabs apresenta novo medidor de energia com recursos inéditos para placas de vídeo - Novo projeto homebrew leva streaming de jogos de PC a portátil clássico da Nintendo A implementação marca um passo fundamental no suporte de software de código aberto, ativando os motores dedicados à decodificação, codificação e processamento de vídeo do componente. Embora a empresa ainda não tenha publicado a tabela com os codecs e formatos suportados, a atualização sinaliza o avanço no desenvolvimento da infraestrutura para clientes corporativos. ESPECIFICAÇÕES E ARQUITETURA: Xe3P, não Xe3LP Diferente de relatórios anteriores que apontavam o uso da arquitetura Xe3LP, a Intel confirmou oficialmente que a Crescent Island é baseada na arquitetura Xe3P. Projetada principalmente para tarefas de inferência em Inteligência Artificial (IA), a placa combina capacidade computacional robusta com recursos dedicados de mídia: - Núcleos/Motores: 32 núcleos Xe e 256 motores XMX. - Memória: Capacidade expandida de até 480 GB de LPDDR5X (originalmente anunciada com 160 GB). - Consumo e Design: Formato PCIe resfriado a ar com consumo de 350W. ATUALIZAÇÕES NO ECOSSISTEMA LINUX Em paralelo ao driver de mídia, foi lançado o VPL GPU Runtime 26.3.5, que adiciona o suporte ao acelerador e organiza a família Wildcat Lake dentro do ecossistema Panther Lake no runtime. O pacote também inclui ajustes na estrutura de referência RAB para o codec HEVC, visando otimizar a qualidade das transmissões.

artigo.texto: Do you think Donald Trump is a secret R.E.M. fan? Trump was, wittingly or not, channeling “Shiny Happy People” when selling the virtues of data centers alongside some of Big Tech’s biggest names this week. They were gathered together to discuss how to win the global AI race without killing everyone. A noble mission. “This is a group that loves local communities,” Trump said, as the tech leaders around him stared like reluctant teenagers visiting an elderly relative, showing little enthusiasm for their supposed love of communities. These billionaire nerds are going to “work with local communities” on data centers to make them “very, very happy,” Trump said. How? By pumping them with enough money to buy off their concerns about these resource-devouring behemoths. Put another way, the tech brolionaires are going to throw their love around, take it into your town, and then put it in the ground as foundations for a data center. But don't worry, where the flowers used to grow, gold and silver will shine instead. And the local people will all be shiny happy people holding hands. No time to cry, happy, happy. You get the tedious drift. If you didn’t understand why a lot of R.E.M. fans kept it secret before, perhaps it’s a little clearer now. Trump reached into his own political lexicon for what to brand this inducement for reluctant residents: “you could call it a dividend because a dividend sounds right.” Ah yes, Trump’s solve-all “dividend,” currently going through a midterms test run. The trouble is, aren’t data centers just too unpopular for this form of legal-but-unsubtle bribery to work? In Congress, data centers are the AI issue scrambling the two main parties. Among voters, opposition crosses party lines, and the facilities have become attack-ad material before November’s midterms. The polling is grim reading for the likes of Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Pew found that 60 percent of Americans would be uncomfortable with a new data center nearby, including 54 percent of Republicans. Yet research on paying communities to accept other unwanted projects suggests Trump’s instinct is pretty sound. Money can buy goodwill, with caveats. The $10K Data Center Dividend In Hazle Township, Pennsylvania, NorthPoint Development has promised every eligible household $10,000 if it builds its Project Hazelnut campus, as part of a $165 million package that also pledges $7 million a year to the township for 15 years. That’s some dividend, but the offer hasn’t quieted the opposition to the data center at the heart of it all. Many local residents still oppose the data center, and city officials have previously rejected the development. “Ten-thousand dollars doesn’t match how much it’s going to tank my property value,” Jeff Fasnacht, a retired teacher who lives nearby, told The Wall Street Journal. Still, throwing money at your opponents isn’t futile in these fights. In a recent Boston experiment, doubling a developer’s offer from $1,500 to $3,000 per person raised support for nearby housing by 2.6 percentage points—modest, but meaningful when proposals averaged 49 percent support. Across Michigan wind-farm townships, surveyed landowners paid at least $1,000 a year were more supportive of additional turbines than those paid less or nothing. In Pennsylvania, a 2016 study linked more fracking “impact fee” revenue to greater support for a hypothetical gas project. Among residents already aware of fracking, the link was stronger when money went to municipalities rather than counties. Hazle Hits All the Tripwires The same literature helps explain what’s happening in Hazle. Among 520 Michigan landowners surveyed twice after a wind project opened, views diverged mainly on whether people judged the planning process fair, and only secondarily on whether they had a financial stake. A national survey of 1,705 wind-farm neighbors found compensation’s effect lost statistical significance once they accounted for broader attitudes. The authors called it “not a panacea.” In Boston, money stopped mattering once proposals included affordable housing, which the researchers argue triggers symbolic reasoning. And a classic Swiss study found that offering compensation roughly halved acceptance of a nuclear waste site. A civic duty became a transaction. Hazle’s offer trips nearly every wire. It came in June, seven months after township supervisors denied the project’s land-development plan and after a county judge turned down the developer’s appeal. It pays out only once the first building earns a certificate of occupancy. The fight has become symbolic, giving it coherence and a marker of local identity. At a township meeting in June, opponents wore “Project Hazlenot” T-shirts. What Trump’s Dividend Tells Us Trump’s own dividend is instructive. At the Republican National Convention in Dallas on September 9, he promised $5,000 to every adult citizen if, and only if, Republicans keep Congress. It is a temptingly juicy offer. More registered voters favor the idea than oppose it, 48 percent to 40 percent in an Economist/YouGov poll. But here’s the rub for Trump: 57 percent think he won’t deliver. His dividend has a credibility problem. The data center dividend has the opposite one. In Hazle, the worry isn’t that the developer won’t deliver. It’s that it will. The check arrives stapled to the building nobody really wants, even if anyone is tempted by the moolah. Alaskan Minerals Alaska shows a lucrative model. It has paid residents an annual dividend since 1982, paid for after the first year by earnings on a fund built with the state’s mineral royalties, communities rewarded for the resources around them. Nobody has to approve a project to receive it. The money arrives every year, a share of what the ground has already yielded. Interfering with it, a paper from the libertarian Cato Institute notes, risks political suicide. The same paper also argues, however, that AI’s proceeds don’t fit Alaska’s logic bec

artigo.texto: Gotion High-tech and Volkswagen to Invest €3.2 Billion in Battery Production Across Three European Sites Chinese power battery maker Gotion High-tech (002074.SZ) and PowerCo, the battery platform under Volkswagen, have finalized a European joint venture plan with a total investment of €3.222 billion (approximately $3.7 billion). According to an announcement released on September 28, the two parties will establish joint ventures in Valencia, Spain; Surany, Slovakia; and Kenitra, Morocco, to build cell manufacturing and LFP cathode material production capacity. The day after the announcement, Gotion High-tech's shares hit the daily limit-up just eight minutes after market open, with more than 890,000 lots locked in buy orders. This represents a structural upgrade in how Chinese battery companies expand overseas. Gotion High-tech is no longer merely a cell supplier to Volkswagen, but is now co-owning European local production capacity with the world's second-largest automaker at a nearly equal capital contribution ratio. Gotion's total contribution is approximately €1.598 billion, while PowerCo's is approximately €1.624 billion—nearly identical in scale. The equity arrangements across the three joint ventures reveal a clear strategic division of labor. The Valencia project, the largest in investment scale, plans an annual capacity of 29.1 GWh of lithium batteries with a total investment of approximately €2.262 billion, with PowerCo holding a 51% controlling stake and Gotion holding 49%. Gotion's subsidiary has also secured a €1.094 billion engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contract for the project. The Surany, Slovakia project plans 8.4 GWh of cell capacity with a total investment of approximately €480 million, with Gotion holding a 51% controlling stake. The Kenitra, Morocco project plans an annual output of 100,000 tonnes of LFP cathode material, also with a total investment of approximately €480 million, with Gotion holding a 51% controlling stake. All three projects are expected to have construction periods of no more than five years. The Compliance Logic Behind the Equity Structure The arrangement of Volkswagen holding the controlling stake in the Spanish plant is no accident. In May 2025, the European Commission issued a legislative proposal for the Industrial Accelerator Act, which imposes restrictive foreign investment clauses on four major industries including batteries and electric vehicles, with conditions such as foreign ownership not exceeding 49%, mandatory technology transfer, and a local employee ratio of no less than 50%. PowerCo's 51% stake in the Valencia plant neatly sidesteps the foreign ownership cap. The deeper compliance pressure comes from the EU Battery Regulation. Carbon footprint declarations for energy storage batteries became mandatory on February 18, 2026, and the digital battery passport will take effect on February 18, 2027. The accounting rules only recognize two models—"national average electricity consumption mix" and "directly connected electricity"—while the green certificates commonly purchased by Chinese companies are not accepted. Since August this year, EU customs has shifted from a "declare-and-pass" approach to mandatory random inspections of carbon footprint declarations for imported batteries, and several batches of Chinese battery products exported to the Port of Rotterdam have already been detained for non-compliant green power certificates. Against this backdrop, moving production lines to the Atlantic side—manufacturing directly in Europe or in countries with trade facilitation arrangements with the EU—has become the most direct path to reducing compliance costs. Morocco has existing trade arrangements with the EU and signed a Belt and Road cooperation plan with China in 2023, while its labor costs are significantly lower than Western Europe. Locating the cathode material base there effectively brings upstream costs into the European supply chain radius. Volkswagen's Predicament and Gotion's Opportunity Volkswagen is going through the pains of transformation. In 2025, group sales revenue was €321.91 billion, down 0.8%, but operating profit was only €8.87 billion—a 53% plunge and the worst result since 2016—with the operating margin falling from 5.9% to 2.8%. In March this year, Volkswagen signaled plans to cut approximately 50,000 jobs in Germany by 2030; on September 3, the supervisory board unanimously approved the 2030 future plan: cutting 100,000 jobs globally, about 15% of its 650,000-strong workforce, halving its vehicle lineup, and placing four German plants on the closure list. PowerCo was originally meant to carry Volkswagen's ambition for an entire battery supply chain, but after the European EV boom cooled, its expansion pace slowed steadily: the fourth plant site selection was shelved in November 2023, the introduction of external investors was postponed in 2024, and only one of two planned production lines in Salzgitter was ultimately built. The retreat of Europe's battery industry extends beyond this. Northvolt, once seen as the hope of the entire continent, declared bankruptcy after burning through $15 billion in investment; ACC, the joint venture of Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz, and TotalEnergies, also pressed pause on two gigafactories. European automakers have done the math: the comprehensive production cost of mass-produced power batteries is about 30% higher than in China, electricity prices are three to five times higher, and worker hourly wages are five times higher. Volkswagen's choice has therefore become pragmatic—rather than continuing to pour money into projects that cannot get off the ground, it is better to hand the factory to someone who can make it work. artigo.texto: Why It Matters The House overwhelmingly passed bipartisan legislation to prevent households and small businesses from bearing electricity infrastructure costs created by large data centers. The H.R. 9340 Ratepayer Protection Act would amend the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act of 1978 to establish a federal standard specifying who pays for electricity-system upgrades required by very large new users, particularly data centers. State utility regulators and nonregulated utilities would be required to consider adopting the standard. Under the standard, rates for covered large-load customers would be designed to recover the full incremental cost of generation, transmission, or distribution upgrades necessary to serve those customers, including costs incurred if a customer terminates its service agreement or otherwise stops purchasing electricity. Utilities would also require financial assurances or contributions to cover the cost of necessary upgrades before making them. A large-load customer is a nonresidential electricity consumer that operates information technology infrastructure and related systems for data storage and computational applications and services, with an aggregate peak demand of at least 100 megawatts at a single site or campus. In practical terms, the approach is intended to prevent residential and other ratepayers from subsidizing infrastructure built primarily to serve very large data-center loads. The consumer question is whether households and smaller commercial customers should bear the costs of capacity added primarily to meet that new demand. The Big Picture Rep. Gabe Evans (R-CO) introduced the bill on June 18, with Rep. Kathy Castor (D-FL) as its original cosponsor, and referred it to the House Energy and Commerce Committee. The Energy Subcommittee forwarded the bill to the full committee by voice vote on June 24. The full committee later ordered the bill reported as a substitute by a unanimous 52-0 vote. It was formally reported as H. Rept. 119-814 on Sept. 10 and placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 713. The House considered the legislation under suspension of the rules and passed amended bill 417-3 on Sept. 16. The Senate received the measure the following day and, after two readings, placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 684 on Sept. 24. The legislation comes amid rapid growth in electricity demand driven by data centers, artificial intelligence and cloud computing. The House committee report cited estimates that data centers account for roughly 4% to 5% of U.S. electricity consumption and noted that electricity demand has begun to rise after years of relatively flat consumption. The legislation does not itself require state utility regulators to adopt the proposed ratemaking standard. Instead, under the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act, regulators and nonregulated utilities would generally have to begin considering the standard within one year and complete that consideration and make a determination within two years. States that have already implemented or considered the standard or a comparable policy could qualify for an exception from those requirements. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that the bill would not affect the federal budget. CBO classified the requirement for state regulatory commissions to consider the standard as an intergovernmental mandate and estimated that the resulting administrative costs would be small. The central policy tension is how to protect existing ratepayers from infrastructure costs associated with large new data centers while preserving state authority over retail electricity rates and supporting continued investment in data-center and artificial intelligence infrastructure. Partisan Perspectives Supporters, including the House Energy and Commerce Committee, argue that the bill protects consumers from data-center-driven rate increases while maintaining U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence and technology. The bill attracted overwhelming bipartisan support. Evans, a Republican, introduced it with Castor, a Democrat, and the Energy and Commerce Committee advanced it 52-0 before the House approved it 417-3. Supporters argue that large data centers should bear the incremental costs of generation, transmission and distribution infrastructure needed specifically to serve their electricity demand rather than shifting those costs to existing customers. The American Public Power Association has said it shares the goal of protecting existing customers from costs associated with serving data centers but opposes creating a new federal Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act mandate requiring utilities to consider the standard. The organization has argued that many public power utilities already have rates or policies addressing data centers and other large loads. The Bottom Line The Ratepayer Protection Act matters because it seeks to establish a nationwide process for allocating electricity infrastructure costs associated with extremely large data-center loads. Rather than directly imposing a national retail electricity rate, the legislation would require state regulators and nonregulated utilities to consider a federal standard under which covered data centers would bear the full, incremental cost of the generation, transmission and distribution upgrades necessary to serve them, backed by financial assurances or upfront contributions. H.R. 9340 has passed the House and is now on the Senate Legislative Calendar as Calendar No. 684. It would still need Senate approval and the president's signature to become law. artigo.texto: Not Cars. Not Energy Storage. Tesla's Robotics and Robotaxi Ambitions Are the Real Reason the Stock Is Priced Like a Tech Company. Key Points - Tesla shares are priced shockingly high, even by technology stock standards. - Given the potential profit centers the company is currently developing, however, this premium valuation makes sense. - It could take far longer than most investors might expect for the business to justify the stock's current valuation. Most investors understand that you typically have to pay a premium price to buy good growth stocks. But shares of electric vehicle (EV) maker Tesla(NASDAQ: TSLA) are taking the premise to an extreme. The stock's currently priced at 200 times this year's projected earnings of $1.75 per share, and over 160 times next year's expected earnings of $2.16 per share. That's expensive by any standard, including in the technology sector. The valuation (sort of) makes sense, though, when you understand what Tesla is in the process of becoming. Soon, it will no longer be an EV company that also makes and markets solar panels and energy-storage batteries. Instead, the plan is for it to be a robotics and robotaxi outfit that also manufactures electric vehicles. Investors are pricing the stock based on this hoped-for future rather than what the business is doing in the present. Here's what they need to know. Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Comparing and contrasting Although the company is winding down its solar roof tile business, it still makes and markets its own solar panels, as well as the energy storage equipment that makes these panels practical power sources. Moreover, EVs remain Tesla's biggest business -- accounting for $20.5 billion of its $28.2 billion in Q2 revenue -- and Tesla is still the second-biggest name in the global EV market, right behind China's BYD. Moreover, last quarter's year-over-year top-line growth of 26% suggests the company still has a little bit of magic left. Its stock's price, however, has left the organization's fiscal results in the rear-view mirror. Shares aren't expensive simply because Tesla is struggling to turn its revenues into profits, to be clear. The stock's also expensive by revenue standards, trading at 13 times trailing-12-month sales versus the S&P 500's trailing price-to-sales ratio of 3.7. For further comparison, the S&P 500 is currently trading at a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of 23.5 and a forward P/E of just under 20. Based on these numbers, Tesla trades at valuations between 4 and 10 times those of the average publicly traded company. It's not like we've never seen something like this before, though. Sometimes, a company eventually grows into such steep valuations. Think Amazon, for example. The market's pricing in growth that hasn't even started yet Getting straight to the point, investors are pricing in a large amount of the future growth they expect from Tesla, as opposed to pricing the stock based on the business's current results. And there are two key components to this highly anticipated future. One of them is robotaxis. Tesla's robotaxi ride-hailing venture, which at this early stage still relies largely on its Model Y vehicles, is up and running in a handful of markets. Its purpose-built Cybercab, however, represents the next generation of this venture's tech. Although the company has only rolled out a small fleet of Cybercabs in one market so far-- Austin, Texas -- it's reportedly planning to launch Cybercab-supported robotaxi services in a dozen states before the end of this year. Although the development of these autonomous taxis has been agonizingly slow, once they're ready for wider-spread commercialization, the deployment is apt to happen fast. This will plug Tesla into a robotaxi market that Goldman Sachs expects to grow from nearly nothing now to $415 billion globally by 2035, with $48 billion of that being generated within the United States alone. The other factor pumping up Tesla stock's premium valuation is arguably even more exciting. That's Tesla's entry into the AI-enabled humanoid robotics space. CEO Elon Musk suggested early this year that the company would be commercially selling its humanoid Optimus robots at scale by the end of 2027, and he hasn't said anything since to suggest that the timeline will have to be pushed back. The commercial debut of these robots could be game-changing for the company -- not to mention the world -- in light of Musk's assessment that "Optimus will be not just Tesla's biggest product ever, but probably the biggest product ever." Although that remains to be seen, Barclays believes the market for humanoid work robots will grow to $200 billion annually by 2035. While even Musk concedes his company is facing stiff robotics competition from China, just capturing a healthy fraction of this potential business could be a boon for Tesla and its shareholders. Advertisement The growth Tesla needs from robots and robotaxis So how much optimism about the robotics and robotaxi businesses are investors pricing in here? It's difficult to say for sure. But we can come up with a rough idea. As it stands right now, Tesla is on pace to do on the order of $106 billion worth of EV, solar panel, and battery-storage business this year, en route to a top line of over $120 billion next year. How much more revenue would the company need to generate with robotaxis and Optimus to make its current $1.4 trillion market cap make sense? Even allowing for the type of premium valuation that many technology stocks achieve, Tesla would need a top line on the order of $300 billion to $400 billion for its current stock price to reflect a valuation in line with its peers. artigo.texto: Amprius Technologies will convert an American electric vehicle battery line into a drone cell factory with a Department of War grant of up to $75 million, the Fremont, California company announced on Monday, September 28. The line is run by an unnamed South Korean battery maker and is supposed to turn out 12 million silicon-anode cells a year for Group 1 through 3 drones starting in early 2028. The conversion costs about $100 million, with Amprius and its partner covering the rest in kind. CEO Tom Stepien went on CNBC the same morning and called it a $75 million grant. The company’s own announcement says a majority of that award is unfunded. Most Of The $75 Million Still Needs Congress To Appropriate It Amprius’s announcement says a majority of the award remains unfunded and subject to future appropriations. Payments also depend on the government accepting specified milestones, which the company says it may not hit on time or at all. The money comes through the Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment program. Amprius signed the deal, a fixed-price Other Transaction Agreement called Project acCELLerate, on September 23, its 8-K filing shows. The government has obligated about $22 million so far, from fiscal 2025 research and development funds, for a base period that runs to September 22, 2028. That is less than a third of the headline number. The size of the bet is in Stepien’s own numbers. He told CNBC that the 12 million cells represent about $150 million in incremental annual revenue. In August, Amprius raised its full 2026 revenue guidance to at least $140 million. One converted line, fully funded and fully sold, would more than double the company. Amprius Walked Away From Its Own Colorado Factory Before Choosing A Retrofit Amprius announced in March 2023 that it would spend $190 million turning a 774,155-square-foot building in Brighton, Colorado, into a battery factory, and the Department of Energy later selected it for a $50 million grant toward the project. Amprius cancelled the plant in June 2025. Earlier this year the company paid $20 million to end its Brighton lease, Manufacturing Dive reported from a securities filing. On CNBC, Stepien sold the new plan as the opposite of Brighton: “We’re not pouring concrete, we’re not putting steel up.” After Brighton, it reads as a lesson learned. Amprius now builds through partners. One of its South Korean contract manufacturers has delivered cells since September 2025, and Nanotech Energy in Northern California is its U.S. partner for cylindrical cells. The new line adds pouch cells. A separate Defense Innovation Unit contract for NDAA-compliant drone batteries now totals $18.1 million. Stepien told CNBC that the anode, cathode, separator and electrolyte all have to come from outside a foreign entity of concern in about 15 months. Stepien Says China Still Makes Cheaper Cells That Customers Want Stepien told CNBC that Amprius still has cells made in China. He said the company is happy with their cost and production, and so are many customers. He expects a balance, with buyers chasing the best technology often buying Chinese and contract-bound buyers needing cells made elsewhere. That second group is growing because the Pentagon wrote it into the rules. Prepared Senate testimony from the Drone Dominance Program in March said Phase II would ban systems using batteries or motors from covered countries. On the August earnings call, Stepien said about half of the 19 drone makers invited to the Fort Carson demonstration use Amprius cells. The program opened its $450 million Phase 3 this week. The dependency is older than the program. A former senior defense official named batteries among the top three Chinese parts in Blue UAS aircraft, as DroneXL laid out in its NDAA-compliant drones guide. In October 2024, Beijing ordered Dongguan Poweramp, Skydio’s sole battery supplier, to cut the company off, and Skydio rationed batteries shipped with its drones. On air, Stepien called the cells twice as energy dense as anything else out there. The announcement is narrower: up to twice the energy density of conventional graphite-anode cells. DroneXL’s Take Batteries are the right place for this money. When Beijing cut off Skydio’s battery supplier in 2024, America’s largest drone maker had to ration packs, and no American-made airframe fixed that. A domestic cell line closes that gap. It won’t close the price gap, and Stepien said as much on national TV when he praised his Chinese cells’ cost. My read is that the Korean-run American line sells first to buyers whose contracts leave no choice, while the police departments and delivery operators Stepien pitched on CNBC keep buying on price. That is how fair competition should work. I’d rather see the Pentagon pay for a factory than ban a supplier. The weak point is the money. A mostly unfunded grant is a promise that depends on Congress, and the early-2028 date only holds if those appropriations arrive. Sources: Amprius Technologies, CNBC, Manufacturing Dive, Amprius 8-K, Amprius Q1 2026 results (SEC), Nasdaq. DroneXL uses automated tools to support research and source retrieval. artigo.texto: Redata elétricas: Safra aponta lucro para o setor O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva aprovou, neste mês, o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center, conhecido como Redata. A medida envolve incentivos fiscais para centros de processamento de dados no Brasil. Com isso, o setor elétrico pode se tornar um dos principais beneficiados, segundo análise do banco Safra. Incentivo fiscal impulsiona demanda por energia O Redata cria condições tributárias favoráveis para a instalação e operação de data centers no país. Esses empreendimentos são grandes consumidores de eletricidade, o que tende a elevar a demanda por energia. O Safra destaca que a demanda de eletricidade dos data centers deve crescer 15% ao ano até 2030, conforme dado da Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA). Esse crescimento representa uma oportunidade relevante para as companhias do setor elétrico. Projeções indicam expansão significativa da capacidade O Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia (PDE 2035), elaborado pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), projeta que o Brasil pode alcançar 20 GW de capacidade instalada de data centers até 2035. O Safra avalia que esse número pode ser ainda maior com a implementação do Redata. A expansão da infraestrutura digital, portanto, deve pressionar positivamente o consumo de energia no médio e longo prazo. Experiência americana serve de referência O Safra utiliza a experiência dos Estados Unidos como referência para estimar os impactos no Brasil. Os analistas enxergam um potencial para um aumento de 2,7% na demanda, caso a participação dos data centers passe de 5% para 8% da demanda total de energia. Esse cenário, se concretizado, traria ganhos expressivos para o setor elétrico nacional. Distribuidoras podem ser as primeiras beneficiadas Com o aumento do consumo, as distribuidoras de energia tendem a registrar maior volume de vendas. O Safra cita que esse cenário beneficiaria distribuidoras como ENEL, CPFL (CPFE3), Light (LIGT3), Equatorial (EQTL3) e Energisa (ENGI3). Essas empresas atuam em regiões estratégicas e podem capturar a demanda adicional dos novos data centers. Alta de preços e pagamentos por capacidade Além do volume, os preços da energia também podem ser impactados. O banco cita a alta de preços de energia em regiões dos EUA, que aumentaram aproximadamente 30% entre 2020 e 2025, tanto por uma maior demanda dos data centers quanto possivelmente por condições climáticas e custos de combustíveis. Nesse contexto, maiores pagamentos por capacidade podem beneficiar Axia (AXIA3) e Copel (CPLE3), segundo os analistas. Oportunidade para o interior paulista Para empresários e comerciantes da região noroeste paulista, o avanço dos data centers pode gerar efeitos indiretos na economia local. A expansão da infraestrutura digital demanda serviços de construção, manutenção e fornecimento de equipamentos, o que pode aquecer o comércio e a indústria regional. Além disso, a maior estabilidade energética e o crescimento econômico decorrente podem favorecer o ambiente de negócios em cidades como Araçatuba, Birigui e Penápolis. O Redata ainda não teve todos os seus detalhes regulamentados, mas a expectativa é de que os incentivos entrem em vigor em breve. As empresas do setor elétrico já monitoram o tema de perto, pois a demanda adicional pode representar um novo ciclo de investimentos. A fonte não detalhou os prazos exatos para a implementação das regras. Perguntas Frequentes O que é o Redata e como ele pode impactar as empresas de energia elétrica? O Redata é o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center, aprovado pelo presidente Lula, que oferece incentivos fiscais para centros de processamento de dados no Brasil. Segundo o Safra, essa medida pode aumentar a demanda de eletricidade dos data centers, beneficiando companhias do setor elétrico. Quais distribuidoras de energia podem se beneficiar com o crescimento dos data centers no Brasil? De acordo com o Safra, distribuidoras como ENEL, CPFL (CPFE3), Light (LIGT3), Equatorial (EQTL3) e Energisa (ENGI3) podem ser beneficiadas caso a participação dos data centers na demanda total de energia aumente de 5% para 8%, gerando um acréscimo de 2,7% na demanda. Por que o Safra acredita que Axia e Copel podem lucrar com o Redata? O Safra observa que nos EUA os preços de energia subiram cerca de 30% entre 2020 e 2025 devido à maior demanda de data centers, e projeta que maiores pagamentos por capacidade no Brasil podem beneficiar Axia (AXIA3) e Copel (CPLE3).

Continue reading CATL’s Chinese battery factory in Debrecen (eastern Hungary) is increasing its workforce. Following the launch of trial operations for battery cell production—which followed the ongoing production of modules—the workforce will be increased from the current 2,800 to 3,300 by the end of the year, announced the Debrecen plant’s chief operating officer at a press event showcasing the facility on Thursday. Qin Liang added that the third production line has already been launched in the module manufacturing operation, which began in 2024; since then, more than 500,000 modules have been produced, powering approximately 10,000 vehicles across Europe. Module production has generated 100 billion forints in revenue for the company to date, on which taxes were paid in Hungary, the manager noted. The Debrecen plant is designed to meet the needs of European automakers, producing nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, the director said, adding that the Debrecen plant ensures long-term stability, jobs, and new business opportunities for the region. Qin Liang noted that the cell factory received its operating permit in August, fulfilled all conditions specified in the permits, and began trial production of battery cells on the first two production lines on September 22. After making a few technical adjustments, the company will begin cell production on the other two lines as well. During the trial run, CATL’s experts will continuously monitor the equipment, the quality and safety of the products, and full compliance with regulatory requirements. The new cell factory has a maximum annual capacity of 40 GWh, all of which has already been fully booked by customers, they explained. The first phase of the project has now been completed with an investment of approximately 900 billion forints (2.44 billion euros/1 euro = 368 forints), and once full capacity is reached, 4,000 people will be employed at the plant. In response to a query from MTI, however, they confirmed that the entire project is planned in three phases; the total investment of 3,000 billion forints will create jobs for 9,000 people, and the annual capacity will be 100 GWh. They added that they are open to negotiations with the government regarding the project, noting that they had an agreement for 129 billion forints in state subsidies to implement the first phase. Shen Feng, CATL’s managing director responsible for European operations, said at the press conference that cell production began in Germany in 2022. Chinese workers initially accounted for 40 percent of the workforce, compared with 60 percent for German workers, but today 90 percent of the workforce is German. In Debrecen, Chinese and local workers currently each account for 50 percent of the workforce; according to their plans, the proportion of Hungarian workers will reach 90 percent by 2030. Qin Liang added that they will launch a supplier campaign in October to increase the involvement of local businesses in production. He noted that they currently have more than 300 local suppliers, 80 percent of whom are from Debrecen and the surrounding region. The plant manager also addressed the Debrecen plant’s water consumption, which is a particularly sensitive issue in Debrecen. He noted that they have developed water-saving technology—specifically, a cooling tower—that drastically reduces the plant’s water requirements. As an example of water conservation, he mentioned that in Debrecen, finished cells are cleaned with a laser rather than with water before delivery. Thanks to the adiabatic cooling towers introduced in 2025, the plant can operate with 30 percent lower water consumption than originally planned and is capable of using graywater (treated water). They added that the plant is already capable of receiving graywater, but the local water utility is not yet able to supply it. The company will continuously provide the authorities with information on the plant’s water and energy consumption as well as its emissions, while monitoring data will be published every two months so that the public can also access it.
