artigo.texto: Mercedes-Benz has secured priority access to ProLogium’s latest Gen4 solid-state battery cells, expanding a partnership that could help bring higher-energy, safer, and more efficient batteries to future electric vehicles. The companies signed a joint testing agreement on September 24, 2026. Mercedes-Benz will test ProLogium’s Gen4 cells for electrical, thermal, and safety performance at its own facilities and at specialist testing centers. One point is important: the official announcement describes “priority access,” not exclusive rights. The agreement gives Mercedes-Benz early access to test the technology, but it does not say that Mercedes has exclusive global rights to the cells. The deal builds on nearly 10 years of cooperation between the two companies. Mercedes-Benz invested in ProLogium in 2022 and joined its board as part of efforts to develop next-generation battery technology. Jörg Burzer, Mercedes‑Benz Group AG, Chief Technology Officer, said: “At Mercedes-Benz, we are committed to shaping the future of electric mobility through technological leadership and innovation. Our long-standing partnership with ProLogium is a strong example of how we bring the best expertise together to advance next-generation battery technologies. By combining ProLogium’s pioneering solid-state battery approach with Mercedes-Benz’s deep battery development, testing, and integration capabilities, we are taking the next step in exploring advanced battery technologies for future electric vehicles.” More Energy, Less Weight: Gen4’s Big Battery Pitch Solid-state batteries replace the liquid electrolyte used in conventional lithium-ion cells with a solid material. The technology can allow manufacturers to use higher-capacity materials while reducing some fire and safety risks linked to liquid electrolytes. ProLogium’s Gen4 lithium ceramic battery uses a fully inorganic electrolyte and ceramic separator. The company says its anode-less version can reach 430–470 Wh/kg and 1,000–1,100 Wh/L at the cell level. These specifications come from the company. They show cell-level performance, not the energy density of a full vehicle battery pack. ProLogium states that Gen4 combines high energy density with fast charging. It also performs well in low temperatures and has better safety features. Its active safety system is intended to help prevent thermal runaway. The potential benefit for EVs is significant. Higher energy density means a battery can store more energy without adding as much weight. That could support longer driving range or allow automakers to use smaller battery packs for the same range. Mercedes Has Already Put Solid-State to the Road Test Mercedes-Benz has been testing solid-state batteries on public roads since 2025. In September 2025, the company reported that a modified EQS test vehicle traveled 1,205 kilometers on a single charge from Stuttgart to Malmö. The vehicle arrived with about 137 kilometers of remaining range. That vehicle used lithium-metal solid-state cells supplied by Factorial Energy, not ProLogium. Mercedes-Benz announced that the new battery boosts usable energy by 25%. It also maintains a weight and size similar to the standard EQS battery. The demonstration showed the potential of solid-state technology, but it was a test vehicle rather than a mass-produced model. The new ProLogium agreement gives Mercedes another route to develop the technology and compare different solid-state battery approaches. The EV Battery Market Is Getting Bigger—Fast The timing is important because global demand for EV batteries is growing rapidly. The International Energy Agency estimates that EV battery deployment hit 1.2 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2025. This is nearly a 30% increase from 2024 and over seven times the level in 2020. EV batteries accounted for more than 70% of total battery deployment during the year. Global electric-car sales also exceeded 20 million units in 2025, up about 20% year over year. One in every four new cars sold worldwide was electric. That is creating strong demand for batteries that can deliver better range, faster charging, and improved safety without sharply increasing vehicle cost. But solid-state technology is entering a market already dominated by conventional lithium-ion batteries. The global battery industry remains heavily concentrated. The IEA says global lithium-ion battery manufacturing capacity exceeded 4 TWh at the end of 2025, up about 30% from 2024. China accounted for more than 80% of global manufacturing capacity and more than 80% of battery-cell production. Chinese battery makers also supplied almost 75% of global EV battery deployment in 2025. This creates a major challenge for European automakers seeking more control over their battery supply chains. Solid-state batteries could offer both a technology advantage and a chance to diversify supply. ProLogium is building its first overseas gigafactory in Dunkirk, France, giving Europe another potential source of advanced battery cells. ProLogium Is Moving Toward Mass Production ProLogium has already moved beyond the laboratory stage. The company began mass production of its Gen3.5 lithium ceramic battery in Taiwan in September 2026. A third-party TÜV test confirmed a 381 Wh/kg gravimetric energy density and 903 Wh/L volumetric energy density for its 185.4-Ah large-format cell. ProLogium says its Taiwan gigafactory had shipped more than 800,000 cells by 2026. It is now preparing to bring Gen4 production to Europe. The Dunkirk factory broke ground in February 2026. ProLogium’s current plan calls for 0.8 GWh of Gen4 production in 2028, with capacity rising to 4 GWh by 2030 and 12 GWh by 2032. The company has also reserved land that could allow the site to expand to as much as 48 GWh in the future. This planned expansion will be important if automakers want solid-state cells at meaningful scale. Europe Wants More Local Battery Production The European link is important for Mercedes-Benz. artigo.texto: With one foot in the Capitol and the other already on the campaign trail, the Senate is poised to consider a bill Wednesday that sounds, at least, like it would shield consumers from rising utility costs tied to data centers. The truth is far more complex — and a lot less consequential. Politically, Republicans are betting that the Ratepayer Protection Act will show voters they care about addressing the cost of living. Crucially, the legislation also would help one of the GOP’s own — Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio — who’s facing a tough re-election fight and has become a prime target for political attacks over data centers. Husted and the GOP claim that the legislation would protect consumers from paying more for electricity as a result of data centers. But, in practice, the legislation is little more than a recommendation. The measure would require state utility regulators to consider adopting new federal standards to ensure data center companies foot their own bill within two years. Because the legislation accomplishes about as much as a press release, Democrats appear poised to oppose it — or, at least, block it from advancing on an expedited timeline before the midterm elections. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., called the bill a “fraud, plain and simple.” Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., likened it to a “political act.” Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., said that “it’s clearly designed to help them in campaigns” and not “actually solve any problems, because it does nothing.” And Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., told MS NOW that it’s a “a political ploy to enable Husted to go home and boast about getting a bill done when it’s really a fraud on consumers.” While the bill received overwhelming bipartisan support in the House, passing earlier this month in a 417-3 vote, Senate Democrats are instead labeling it a “bait-and-switch.” And some Republicans acknowledge that the bill does more politically than it does practically. “Would I like to do more? Yeah,” Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said. “But on the other hand, is it better than nothing? Yeah.” Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., agreed that the bill doesn’t accomplish much, noting that most utilities are “managed through local and state decision making.” But he also agreed that it “probably would help” Husted in his re-election efforts. Ohio’s Senate seat — one of a growing number that Republicans are rushing to shore up ahead of November — could be instrumental in determining control of the Senate next year. Husted, who has routinely trailed in the polls in his bid for a full six-year term, has faced an onslaught of ads in Ohio — including from his Democratic rival, former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown — casting him as the “face of data centers” that are contributing to higher energy bills. On Tuesday, Husted called his data center legislation “the only bill that has a chance to get to the president’s desk before we get to the election.” Asked why the bill does not make the regulations mandatory, Husted answered that it was because “the states run the grids, and so you have to work with the states to do that.” If Democrats block the bill during a procedural vote on Wednesday, Husted and other Republicans appear eager to cast Democrats as obstructionists. Husted told reporters that it’s up to Democrats “to determine whether or not they want to play politics or they want to solve affordability issues for the American people.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said that voting against the bill “makes it pretty hard for Democrats” to attack Husted over data centers and the cost of living. “It’s a chance to actually make law. It’s not just making a point,” Thune said Tuesday.

artigo.texto: Scaling India’s BESS Electronics for Energy Transition ⚡ Quick Read - What happened: India’s energy storage requirement is projected to surge from 82 GWh in 2026-27 to 411.4 GWh by 2031-32, with BESS accounting for 236.22 GWh. - Why it matters: EPCs and developers must look beyond battery cells to the electronics layer—BMS, power conversion, and thermal controls—to ensure system reliability and grid performance. - Watch: The evolution of domestic manufacturing standards for BMS and power electronics as the industry shifts toward larger, multi-hour grid-scale storage. Background and Context As India accelerates its renewable energy transition, the focus on energy storage has intensified. According to the Central Electricity Authority’s (CEA) National Electricity Plan, the nation’s total energy-storage requirement is projected to rise from approximately 82 GWh in 2026-27 to a massive 411.4 GWh by 2031-32. Within this framework, Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are expected to contribute 236.22 GWh. To support this trajectory, the government has introduced viability-gap funding mechanisms, incentivizing developers to integrate storage with renewable projects. Key Details While procurement trends show a shift toward larger, multi-hour grid-scale applications, the industry must pivot its focus toward the electronics layer. A modern BESS is a complex integration of cells, battery-management systems (BMS), power-conversion equipment, sensors, and thermal-management systems. The BMS, in particular, is critical; as systems move toward higher voltages and longer durations, the BMS architecture must manage complex parameters including voltage monitoring, cell balancing, and fault detection. The localization conversation in India is expanding beyond simple battery-pack assembly. There is a growing need to domesticate printed circuit board assemblies, control boards, communication modules, and power-management systems. This shift is not merely for import substitution but is essential to customize systems for India’s unique operating conditions, such as extreme temperatures and grid fluctuations. What This Means for EPCs and Developers For EPC contractors and developers, reliability is the new benchmark for project success. As BESS installations scale, an electronics failure can compromise system availability and grid performance. Consequently, manufacturing and procurement processes must prioritize inspection, functional testing, and traceability. The ability to track the production history and test results of critical electronic assemblies is becoming a vital component of the broader reliability architecture required for long-term project viability. What Happens Next India’s standards ecosystem is currently evolving to match this market growth. New regulatory frameworks covering electrical energy-storage systems and safety requirements are expected to create greater consistency in system design and performance. As the nation continues to integrate massive amounts of variable renewable energy, the development of a robust domestic electronics supply chain will be the cornerstone of India’s energy security. This transition reflects the broader maturity of the India renewable energy sector as it moves from pilot projects to a sophisticated, grid-integrated ecosystem.

artigo.texto: UERC Approves Tariffs for 76 MW/190 MWh BESS Projects ⚡ Quick Read - What happened: The UERC has formally approved the competitive bidding tariffs for four BESS projects in Uttarakhand, totaling 76 MW capacity and 190 MWh of storage. - Why it matters: This regulatory approval provides the necessary financial certainty for developers to proceed with large-scale storage integration in the Himalayan state’s grid. - Watch: The project commissioning timeline, with operations scheduled to commence by October 1, 2026. Background and Context The integration of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) is becoming a critical component of India’s energy transition, particularly in regions with significant hydro and solar potential. The Uttarakhand Electricity Regulatory Commission (UERC) has taken a decisive step in this direction by approving the tariffs for four strategic battery energy storage projects. This move is part of a broader push to stabilize the state’s grid and manage peak demand effectively. Key Details The approved projects represent a total capacity of 76 MW with an energy storage capacity of 190 MWh. These facilities are strategically located at Khatima, Dhakrani, Pathri, and Tiloth. The tariffs were determined through a transparent competitive bidding process, ensuring cost-effectiveness for the state’s distribution infrastructure. The projects are slated to be fully operational by October 1, 2026, marking a significant milestone for the state’s renewable energy roadmap. What This Means for EPCs and Developers For EPC contractors and renewable energy developers, this approval signals a maturing market for storage solutions in India. The formal adoption of tariffs by the UERC mitigates regulatory risk, which is often a primary concern for project financiers. Developers involved in these sites can now proceed with procurement and construction activities with the assurance of a stable revenue stream. Furthermore, the selection of these specific locations suggests a focus on strengthening regional grid resilience, offering potential opportunities for local infrastructure development and grid-balancing services. What Happens Next With the regulatory hurdles cleared, the focus will now shift to the execution phase. Developers are expected to finalize their supply chain arrangements for battery modules and balance-of-system (BOS) components. As India continues to scale its renewable energy sector, these 76 MW/190 MWh projects serve as a blueprint for how state regulators can facilitate the deployment of storage to manage the intermittency of renewable sources. The successful commissioning of these sites by October 2026 will be closely monitored by stakeholders across the Indian power sector as a benchmark for future BESS tenders.

artigo.texto: What does Louisiana’s AI Data Center Boom Mean for the State? Meta is expanding its Richland Parish artificial intelligence (AI) data center to a planned 5 gigawatts of computing capacity, while questions involving new power generation, utility regulation, water use, environmental permitting, tax incentives and public disclosure have all made headlines. Tulane Law’s Haley Gentry, Assistant Director of the Institute for Water Resources Law & Policy, looks at what these centers mean for communities and the state. Gentry is an environmental lawyer who focuses on water resource management and public decision-making processes. - AI data centers are arriving in Louisiana on a scale we haven’t seen before. What makes Louisiana attractive for these projects, and what does a facility of this size actually mean for the state’s economy, energy, water and other infrastructure? Through recent legislative measures and statewide economic incentives, Louisiana’s government has signaled that data centers are a priority sector for economic growth. There are multiple major proposed data center projects in Louisiana – Meta’s Hyperion facility in Richland Parish, multiple Amazon Web Services data center campuses in the Shreveport/Bossier City area, Anthropic in West Feliciana Parish, and a recently announced large data center project in Rapides Parish. Many factors contribute to the current economic development trends across the state. For one, Louisiana has promoted large tracts of industrial and agricultural land across the state already zoned for development. In 2024, Louisiana lawmakers passed generous sales and use tax exemptions related to data center equipment. Entergy’s interest in expanding its power generation capacity in connection with data centers played a crucial role in early negotiations with Meta. Most recently, utility regulators are using an expedited process to review utility applications for new generation to serve large load customers. Louisiana is likely considered an ideal region because of its access to energy infrastructure and transit corridors, like the Mississippi River. Plus, there is a historical abundance of water resources, making Louisiana attractive from a development standpoint, as water shortages are constraining economic activity, especially in Western states. However, there is much more to the water question, which we can get to in a moment. AI data centers pose risks to the grid due to the amount of power they require. They also can create localized water issues. It is difficult to encompass the wide range of potential impacts (primarily related to water usage, but also from a water quality perspective) because the type of cooling system employed, energy source, surface versus groundwater sourcing, and whether facilities rely on municipal water services, or are using on-site private water wells, can alter the inquiry. Even more, it is critical to acknowledge tradeoffs in various types of cooling technologies. Evaporative cooling is the most water-intensive type of cooling process and poses the biggest risk to local water supplies. Air cooling uses a minimal amount of water but much more energy. So, if coal, gas, or nuclear generation is used to power a hyperscale data center, water is still being consumed, just in a different location. Some data centers are tapping into municipal water services. While it certainly would be easier to get a sense of water usage if going through a public entity, this raises a set of related concerns. First, the physical infrastructure needed to deliver larger volumes of water (and the effluent water that would be treated after it’s used for cooling) strains aging drinking water infrastructure. Moreover, there is something to be said about using pretreated municipal potable water for cooling rather than domestic use. - What are the biggest legal and regulatory issues surrounding the development of AI data centers — and where does authority lie among federal, state, and local governments? There are many critical questions about the regulation of artificial intelligence technology itself and what role governments should play in the actual oversight and use of the large language models as they are integrated into all facets of society and what protections workers/creators will have into the future. Yet in terms of governance, a key legal issue is the widespread use of nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) between officials and developers. In Louisiana, even elected officials, members of the cabinet, and the governor himself signed NDAs with Meta. That means that there has been little public input or comprehensive review across agencies or between jurisdictions. There is not much by way of federal regulatory oversight for data centers. Most of the land-use and water resource decisions fall primarily to state agencies, and various federal review processes that come into play for components of data centers (pipelines and transmission lines through waters and wetlands) have been expedited in response to several of President Trump’s executive orders. A key legal issue is the protection and management of water resources. Water for public use is the highest priority under both state law and U.S. Supreme Court jurisprudence. However, Louisiana currently does not have the frameworks in place to comprehensively manage water resources and prevent conflicts. For example, a company relying on groundwater can drill wells on their site, register the wells and estimated withdrawal rates with Louisiana’s Department of Conservation & Energy (LDCE), but from then on does not have to monitor, report or restrict usage absent a formal emergency declaration for that region or aquifer. However, LDCE is currently taking steps toward groundwater oversight through an ongoing rulemaking, but more robust authority will likely be needed to ensure local water supplies are not compromised. artigo.texto: - Renewable - 2 min read India needs integrated energy storage policy to build resilience against geopolitical shocks: S&P Global Gauri Jauhar emphasizes the importance of energy resilience for India's future energy security and storage policies. An integrated framework for storage across various energy sources is essential for long-term stability. Speaking exclusively to ANI, Gauri Jauhar, Global Executive Director for Strategic Climate & Clean Energy Initiatives and CERA Week at S&P Global Energy, outlined strategic imperatives for India's energy security and transition roadmap. Addressing the need for strategic buffers, Jauhar emphasized moving beyond siloed approaches. "The one word that comes is energy resilience. That resilience has to be factored in to build buffers and storage of all kinds," Jauhar said. She called for an integrated framework linking electron and molecule storage across crude, LPG, jet fuel, natural gas, battery energy storage systems (BESS), and pumped hydro. On macroeconomic stability, Jauhar highlighted that while crude import dependence remains high, India's refining sector acts as a vital buffer. Refined petroleum product exports generate foreign exchange earnings that cover approximately 25% of the total amount spent on crude oil imports, reinforced by ongoing capacity expansions at refineries in Rajasthan and Numaligarh. To manage supply risks, Indian energy firms continue to expand procurement channels. "Today, India imports crude from 41 different countries," Jauhar explained, adding that options are constantly evaluated to pivot import sources, citing renewed access to Venezuelan crude and shipments from the US. However, she observed longer shipping routes naturally introduce freight cost inflation, which can add to general price pressures and trigger broader monetary policy responses. Regarding clean energy transitions, Jauhar clarified that green hydrogen's impact on domestic oil displacement will be gradual. With nearly 70% of the National Green Hydrogen Mission's initial focus geared toward exports, green hydrogen will act primarily as an export earner to buffer the balance of payments over the medium to long term. Concurrently, India remains a premier destination for energy transition investments alongside the US and China, driven by a record 55 gigawatts of renewable energy capacity added this year alongside policy pushes in nuclear power and battery storage. Finally, regarding end-consumer impacts, Jauhar stated that retail petrol and diesel rates remain shielded through active adjustments in central and state tax structures alongside initiatives like the Ethanol Blending Program. artigo.texto: State Environment Cabinet Secretary James Kenney again called out the developers behind a secretive data center in Grant County for neglecting to engage with the community. “NMED is aware — as you are no doubt also aware — that your proposed data center project has significant community opposition,” Kenney wrote in a Tuesday letter, in apparent reference to community organizing in response to the proposal and a data center moratorium Grant County commissioners will vote on Oct. 22. “My concern is not about Site Layer 1, LLC failing to meet the minimum requirements for regulatory notice; my concern is about Site Layer 1, LLC’s lack of community outreach and engagement in the relevant New Mexico communities.” Residents found out about the data center through a small notice in a legal notice in the Silver City Daily Press, which said the facility could consume about 2.3 million cubic feet of natural gas every hour — enough gas to power 900 homes for a year. Its annual carbon emissions would be equivalent to those of about 282,600 cars. Kenney’s Tuesday message follows a Sept. 18 letter, in which he wrote that after calling, leaving voicemails and emailing, the Environment Department had yet to hear from Granite Renewables, the company behind the data center. The company did not respond to repeated requests for comment from The New Mexican, either, and the developer's only public point of contact is an empty floor of an office tower in midtown Manhattan. Blake Marcus, the project developer, responded Sept. 25, writing “representatives have met virtually with Grant and Hidalgo County officials in the fall of 2025 to discuss this project.” He provided his phone number in the Sept. 25 correspondence, which he had not done before. At a Sept. 24 meeting, Grant County Commissioners said none of them had any contact so far with the data center’s developers. Kenney took issue with this “general reference” to the virtual meeting and asked for further documentation of public engagement. He also wrote developers needed to meet with the Environment Department’s Air Quality Bureau and present a detailed project description prior to submitting a formal application, which should include “transparent calculations.” Don’t eat the mushrooms New Mexico State University sent an email Monday warning those on campus not to consume false parasol mushrooms, which resemble ones you could cook. These mushrooms — which turn green under the caps, identifying them as inedible — are multiplying after recent storms. They won’t kill you, “but when consumed they can ‘teach you a lesson’ as they may cause symptoms that include perspiration, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhea,” Soum Sanogo, a plant pathology professor at NMSU, said in a statement. The Instagram account @affirmationsnmsu, took the message to heart: “I will not eat the toxic mushrooms,” their post reads, with an image of glittering false parasol fungi. artigo.texto: AI data centers: How much are ratepayers on the hook for? Ahead of the midterm elections, Congress is scrambling to show that it understands voter concerns about AI data centers and their potential impact on electricity rates. But answering the question of how much of those costs will be shouldered by residential utility customers is surprisingly difficult to answer. That uncertainty is at the heart of a growing fight on Capitol Hill, as lawmakers advance competing proposals aimed at protecting ratepayers in a debate that often belies the complexity of the underlying economics. On Capitol Hill this week, Republicans have been trying to push through the Ratepayer Protection Act, sponsored by Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted. The bill would have state utilities consider holding "large-load" customers responsible for the increased costs. Husted is in a heated reelection campaign against Democrat Sherrod Brown, who lost his Senate seat in 2024. Brown has made Husted's past support of data centers in Ohio a major campaign issue. The bill easily passed the House in September with strong bipartisan support. Senate Minority Leader Sen. Chuck Schumer opposes the measure, saying its protections for ratepayers are voluntary. Instead, Schumer is promoting the GRID Savings Act, a similar bill authored by New Mexico Democrat Sen. Martin Heinrich, which he says has more teeth. Several other data center and AI-related bills are at various stages in the legislative process. The cost of AI is showing up in customers' bills The question of how much of the energy and grid costs are being borne by ratepayers is a complicated one and has no universal answer, experts tell NPR. They say it varies by utility and state, but that in the end residential electricity customers will pay for a share of the AI buildout. By one estimate, Maryland customers, for example, pay somewhere around $168 to $216 more per year on their electricity bills primarily due to the data center boom. "We're talking tens to hundreds of millions of dollars [of infrastructure] that are being built by these local utilities," says Connor Waldoch, co-founder and chief strategy officer at Grid Status, which focuses on making electricity-market data easier to access and understand. "In many cases, it is just ultimately going to end up in customers' bills." Tracking the impact of data center growth on residential bills isn't easy, however. How much of the increase is passed on to residential customers and when, depends on utilities' power-purchasing contracts, retail rates and regulatory decisions about who pays, according to Lucy Qiu, a professor at the School of Public Policy at the University of Maryland. PJM is a regional transmission organization that coordinates the electricity grid and wholesale power market across 13 states and the District of Columbia. It supplies power to Northern Virginia, home to the largest concentration of data centers in the world. PJM's Independent Market Monitor estimates that data centers have cost their 67 million ratepayers about $29 billion over roughly the past two years. "Everyone pays those costs," says Ari Peskoe, director of the Harvard Electricity Law Initiative. "They're spread across the region to every business and resident that has an electricity meter." How to determine who the grid infrastructure benefits? Data center growth can push up wholesale costs of energy by increasing demand. This determines how much generating capacity utilities and regional grid operators need to secure, Qiu says. There are also costs with building new power lines, substations and other infrastructure to connect data centers to the grid. Determining how much of that exclusively serves data centers — and how much also benefits other customers — is part of the difficulty in determining who gets the bill, she says. "It really depends on the scale of the upgrade and also how utilities are doing the accounting of that different share, whether it's being used solely by the data centers or also being shared by other customers," Qiu says. No "single, clean number" Even so, "a single, clean number" that applies nationwide is just not possible, Harvard's Peskoe says, because "a lot of the data about how much particular data centers are paying is hidden behind non-disclosure agreements." Those NDAs have become a major sore spot on the local level, as residents opposed to new data centers call out local officials for the secrecy that has surrounded many deals. A study last year by the University of Mary Washington found that NDAs had been signed in 80% of Virginia localities where there were existing, approved or proposed data centers. In an email to NPR, Jeremy L. Slayton, a spokesman for Dominion Energy, which serves Loudoun County, Va., home to about 250 data centers, said, "We recover costs for distribution and transmission infrastructure from customers." "These assets are core to the reliable electric service we provide our customers. All costs we recover from customers are reviewed and approved by the Virginia State Corporation Commission," he said, referring to the independent state agency that regulates public utilities. Added costs of building out in a hurry There is still another factor at play, University of Maryland's Qiu says. The data center industry is in a hurry and waiting for new power-generation technologies doesn't seem to be in the cards. As a result, to meet the demand, utility companies will likely need to opt for less efficient power plants and those costs will be passed onto consumers over time, as well. One other consideration is optics, Waldoch of Grid Status says. Big customers like AI data centers pay less per kilowatt hour for power than residential customers do. Think of it as a volume discount. artigo.texto: Gore Street Energy Storage Fund (LSE:GSF) has refinanced its 200 MW / 400 MWh Big Rock battery energy storage project in California through a new approximately $52.4 million debt facility with First Citizens Bank. The new financing comprises a five-year term loan and letter of credit facility and replaces the project's previous $60 million facility. Management said the refinancing reflects Big Rock's move into a more established operational phase and represents progress in reducing portfolio financing costs. The Big Rock facility has a capacity of 200 MW and energy storage capacity of 400 MWh. About Gore Street Energy Storage Fund Gore Street Energy Storage Fund is a specialist investment company focused on grid-scale energy storage assets. The company invests in and operates battery storage facilities designed to provide flexibility and other services to electricity networks. Its portfolio includes the Big Rock project in California, which is held through subsidiary Big Rock ESS Assets LLC.

artigo.texto: Data center company stays silent at public meeting Central City residents question a proposed data center as city leaders work on ordinance CENTRAL CITY, Iowa (KCRG) - Central City residents packed the Falcon Civic Center Wednesday night looking for answers about a proposed data center, but the company behind the project did not speak. The facility would be 18,000 square feet and within city limits near the Linn County Fairgrounds. City leaders emphasize smaller size The city council says the data center would be much smaller than hyperscale facilities being built near the airport in Cedar Rapids. It is about the size of four basketball courts. The proposed data center would sit on about 3 acres, use 4 megawatts of electricity. It would use a closed-loop cooling system with no water needed for cooling. The city says the project would create up to 10 full-time jobs. The developer estimates nearly $986,000 a year in public revenue from taxes and fees. City Council member Dustin Moyer said the council is in the early stages of plans for the data center and is working on drafting an ordinance. “The moment this was brought to our attention it was something at a scale beyond a little shed in a backyard, we said, ‘No, we are putting a moratorium in place, we need time to collect public input,” Moyer said. Residents question company’s silence At the meeting, people said they expected to hear from Charlie White, a representative of the project, but did not. “How come we didn’t hear from him? We are not understanding the attraction to this one company,” one resident said. White did not speak to TV9 on the record, saying he is not authorized to speak to the media and that he is concerned about his safety. Company gives statement Aurum’s CEO JohnPaul Baric provided a statement that reads in part: “It is our desire for the Elk Data Center Project to bring skilled jobs, work for local contractors, and tax revenue to Central City. We’re working to show how smaller data centers can fit into communities through careful planning and cooperation with residents.” Moyer said the council will continue to work on the ordinance, and hearing from the public. Wednesday night was part of that process. Copyright 2026 KCRG. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: The world’s appetite for electricity is climbing at a pace that conventional energy infrastructure simply cannot match. According to a comprehensive review published in Discover Electrochemistry by Ranjeet Singh, Alok Kumar Chaudhari, Ekta Sonker, Pradeep Kumar Rao and Piyush Kumar Sonkar, global energy demand could triple by the end of this century, driven by population growth and rising living standards in developing countries. Because most of today’s energy still comes from fossil fuels, hydropower and nuclear plants, the environmental toll of greenhouse gases, radioactive byproducts and disrupted water ecosystems continues to mount. The authors argue that the missing piece of a clean energy future is not generation but storage: efficient electrical energy storage systems that can buffer the intermittent output of renewables, power electric vehicles and keep portable electronics running. The physics of storing electricity is inherently lossy. Energy is lost during conversion, and more can be lost when stored energy is reconverted back into electricity. Among the competing storage technologies, electrochemical systems have captured the most research attention, spanning solar cells, hydrogen storage materials, rechargeable batteries and electrochemical capacitors. Their performance is described by two fundamental parameters: energy density, the amount of energy stored per unit mass or volume, and power density, the rate at which that energy can be delivered. Batteries store charge through faradaic reactions deep in the bulk of their electrodes, giving them high energy density but modest power. Electrochemical capacitors, by contrast, store charge near the electrode surface, sacrificing energy density for the ability to deliver explosive bursts of power. This is precisely where nanomaterials change the game. When particle dimensions shrink to the nanoscale, the fraction of surface atoms rises dramatically and the distance ions must travel from a particle’s core to its surface collapses. For lithium-ion systems, where the diffusion rate of lithium ions within electrodes dictates charging speed, this is a decisive advantage. Size reduction also alters surface energy, can shrink thermal stability, and triggers quantum confinement effects that widen a semiconductor’s bandgap, allowing optical properties to be tuned simply by changing particle size. Gold offers the most striking illustration: bulk gold is yellow, nanoscale gold turns pink, and at those dimensions it becomes an excellent catalyst. These size-dependent properties give engineers an extra design variable, alongside composition, pressure and temperature, for tailoring storage devices. The review also surveys the synthesis toolbox that makes such precision possible. The sol-gel method slowly converts liquid solutions into solid materials through controlled chemical reactions. Electrospinning draws polymer melts into nanofibers under an electric field, offering fine control over diameter and alignment. Molecular beam epitaxy sprays metal atoms onto substrates in vacuum for single-crystal thin films, while chemical vapor deposition builds up films from the vapor phase and underpins most commercial production of carbon nanotubes and graphene. Mechanical milling grinds bulk materials down with high-energy ball mills, cheap and simple but prone to contamination, and hydrothermal or solvothermal synthesis grows highly crystalline metal oxide nanoparticles and nanowires under elevated pressure and temperature. Every one of these routes demands rigorous characterization, from electron microscopy that images atomic lattices to X-ray diffraction, spectroscopy and zeta potential measurements that pin down crystal structure, chemical state and colloidal stability. Supercapacitors occupy a technological middle ground between batteries and conventional capacitors, and nanomaterials have transformed their electrode design. In electric double-layer capacitors, capacitance follows the relationship C equals epsilon times A divided by d, meaning high capacitance demands large surface area and tiny charge separation. Conventional dielectric capacitors separate charge across a dielectric a few microns thick, but double-layer devices achieve separations near one nanometer, producing vastly greater capacitance. Carbon is the star performer here: activated carbon electrodes reach surface areas up to 3000 square meters per gram, mesoporous carbons up to 1730, while carbon nanotubes, despite lower surface area of 100 to 400 square meters per gram, offer superb conductivity. Graphene’s theoretical 2675 square meters per gram is undermined by sheet agglomeration, but strategies such as curved graphene and carbon nanotube separators have pushed energy densities to 136 watt-hours per kilogram at 80 degrees Celsius. Pseudocapacitors take a different route, storing charge through fast, reversible faradaic redox reactions at the electrode surface. Conducting polymers such as polyaniline, polypyrrole and polythiophene are cheap, easily processed and highly charge-dense. A polyaniline hydrogel gelled and doped with the natural plant compound phytic acid achieved a conductivity of 0.11 siemens per centimeter and a specific capacitance near 480 farads per gram, thanks to shortened pi-pi stacking distances and hierarchical porosity. Hybrid PEDOT/CNT electrodes have demonstrated stable self-discharge across 10,000 galvanostatic cycles by suppressing the redox-shuttle effect that plagues activated carbon systems. Metal oxides push theoretical capacitance even higher, with 1358 farads per gram for ruthenium dioxide and 1370 for manganese dioxide, though poor conductivity limits most oxides. Depositing manganese dioxide on nanoporous gold reached 1145 farads per gram, and MOF-derived cobalt sulfide nanoflowers retained 95 percent of their capacitance after 5000 charge-discharge cycles. artigo.texto: A controversial data center proposal cleared another hurdle this week in Inver Grove Heights after the developer filed a lawsuit against the city. The Inver Grove Heights City Council approved a major site plan Monday that calls for a nearly 55,000-square-foot data center to be constructed at the former Travel Tags site. Monday’s decision comes two weeks after the council voted to amend its yearlong data center moratorium after the developer, Florida-based QLevr, filed a lawsuit against the city challenging the validity of the moratorium. In a letter to the city council, attorneys for Larkin Hoffman, who represent the developer, called the city’s moratorium decision “arbitrary” and “capricious.” The lawsuit, which was filed in Dakota County District Court, could have cost the city at least $20 million. As for the city’s liability insurance, that maxes out at $1 million, meaning any amount over that threshold would have fallen to the city’s taxpayers. With the city voting to amend the moratorium, the developer agreed to dismiss the case. Controversial decision The recent decision to amend the moratorium was not a unanimous one. At the Sept. 14 meeting, several council members expressed frustration about the city’s lack of options given the lawsuit. Council member Mary T’Kach, who cast the sole vote against the amendment, said, “I think our litigating attorneys should be litigating this.” This week, again, council members appeared to struggle to lend their support to the project. When Mayor Brenda Dietrich asked for a motion to approve the site plan, silence followed until she herself made the motion. “Is there a second?” Dietrich asked. Another pregnant pause followed until council member John Murphy spoke up. “Hilarious,” he said. “I’ll second it.” T’Kach, again, was the sole vote against. Site plan QLevr, a real estate company that specializes in data centers, intends to build a new 54,000-square-foot data center on a 13.9-acre property at 5890 Carmen Ave. As proposed, the data center will be a 3-megawatt facility in its initial phase and a 5-megawatt facility at full buildout, which is considered to be smaller than most hyperscale data centers in Minnesota. For context, Meta’s data center campus in Rosemount has a capacity of approximately 308 megawatts. QLver’s site plan also calls for a closed-loop water system for cooling data center equipment and a screened mechanical equipment area. The proposed 23-foot-tall screening wall for the equipment is an acoustic sound wall, which provides noise dampening, according to the site plan. The property, located just west of the South St. Paul Municipal Airport, is zoned as Limited Industrial, which permits data centers, said Kevin Shay, the city’s planning manager. Next steps for QLver include an approved development contract and a building permit from the city. Inver Grove Heights initially approved the interim moratorium on June 26 with the intent of giving the city time to study the potential impacts of data centers. The city’s moratorium is still in place until next June.

artigo.texto: A NorthPoint Development fez uma proposta indecente aos moradores de Hazle Township, uma pequena cidade de 10 mil habitantes no interior da Pensilvânia: US$ 10 mil por residência para aceitar a instalação de um grande data center na cidade. Hazle Township tem 4,5 mil residências, e se todo mundo topar, a conta ficaria em US$ 45 milhões, uma gota de água num projeto de data center, cuja conta total fica na casa dos bilhões de dólares. O problema, sintomático de como está a coisa nos Estados Unidos com o boom dos data centers no momento, é que quase ninguém topou. Segundo reporta o Wall Street Journal, só 100 moradores aceitaram o pagamento. A conta dos moradores é simples: a instalação de um data center pode causar uma desvalorização dos seus imóveis muito maior do que os US$ 10 mil, por conta de problemas como aumento do barulho, das contas de energia e o temor de redução da oferta de água. Nos seus comunicados, a NorthPoint Development até disse que não vai usar água potável para resfriar os equipamentos e diz que o barulho ouvido nos arredores será equivalente a uma máquina de lavar louça, mas não colou. A empresa também patrocinou um festival local e prometeu mais US$ 120 milhões em investimentos ao longo de 15 anos. A oferta de dinheiro foi feita em junho, após a Prefeitura negar a autorização para a construção do data center e ainda impor uma moratória a esse tipo de projeto, por 180 dias. O número de cidades e estados que adotaram moratórias a novos projetos como esses já soma 294, segundo o Bitcoin Policy Institute. Em 2024, eram 6. Os estados de Nova York e Texas anunciaram pausas na aprovação de novos centros de dados. Na Pensilvânia, o governador Josh Shapiro vetou NDAs entre governos locais e empresas, para evitar acordos secretos. Uma pesquisa do Gallup, do começo do ano, apontou que mais americanos (71%) são contra ter centros de dados na vizinhança do que uma usina nuclear (51%). Parte do problema é que as grandes empresas de tecnologia não querem colocar um data center em qualquer lugar. Empresas como a NorthPoint Development correm atrás de grandes extensões de terra com acesso a redes elétricas de alta capacidade e infraestrutura de água. Hazle Township fica numa dessas áreas, a cerca de 400 quilômetros do grande hub de data centers no chamado Data Center Alley da Virgínia, onde fica a famosa região AWS us-east-1 e circulam nada menos de 70% do tráfego de internet do mundo.

artigo.texto: The Tribune and Illinois Answers Project’s recent investigation into tax incentives and assessment reductions for data centers performed a public service by putting real numbers into an important debate. Tax policy should be transparent, and every incentive should be open to scrutiny. But the investigation captures only one side of the ledger. As mayor of a community that has hosted data centers for more than 25 years, I also have seen what those investments produce: Substantial revenue for schools and local governments, private investment in aging industrial areas and family-sustaining union construction jobs. Data centers in Elk Grove Village collectively generated approximately $60 million in property taxes for the 2025 tax year. Over the past year, they also generated $11.1 million in building permit fees, $4.5 million in electric utility tax revenue and more than $1 million in sales tax revenue. Some of those revenues are recurring and some are to construction, but all of them support real public needs. The Tribune calculated that incentives on five Elk Grove Village data center complexes saved their owners about $14.5 million in 2025 and concluded that, without those property tax incentives, the average village homeowner’s property tax bill would have been roughly $33 lower — but that calculation is misleading. The reporting would lead you to believe that Elk Grove Village residents are paying more because data centers are here. In actuality, the projects in question received the Cook County Class 6B property tax incentive, a temporary tax reduction designed to encourage new or substantially rehabilitated industrial development and the reoccupation of abandoned industrial property. Even with the temporary 6B property tax incentive, all of these data centers are generating significantly more property tax revenue than the industrial properties did before they became data centers. The 6B incentive does not erase the additional tax base created by the development; it just temporarily reduces the amount of new property tax revenue collected during the temporary incentive period. And when the incentive expires after 12 years, that additional property tax revenue remains part of the village’s tax base for decades to come. The 6B is a temporary form of tax relief that allows communities such as Elk Grove, located on the Cook County border, to compete with communities in neighboring counties where the taxes are lower. Elk Grove Village is home to the largest industrial park in North America, and we have decades of experience using the tax incentive to attract development, including data centers, that delivers a net benefit to the community. Data centers pay millions of dollars to school districts without adding students to classrooms. They require inspections, infrastructure and public safety planning, much like any other development, but they do not create the daily traffic, school enrollment, or service demands associated with a large residential development, warehouse or office campus. That makes them unusually valuable contributors to the local tax base. Additionally, data centers are recession-proof businesses that will continue to produce revenue during periods of economic downturn. The impact of data centers also reaches beyond property taxes. In 2024, when data center construction projects generated more than $3 million in permit fees, we returned that money directly to residents by sending a $200 Visa gift card to each of approximately 14,000 households. That was only possible because major data center investment generated revenue beyond what was needed to cover the village’s planned expenses during that fiscal year. In fiscal year 2026, Elk Grove Village permitted approximately $1.2 billion in private-sector construction. Data center construction, expansion and interior buildouts were the primary contributors. That investment supports contractors, suppliers, skilled tradespeople and other businesses throughout the region. On average, more than 1,000 people are working on data center construction in Elk Grove Village on a given day, many in high-paying union careers. Illinois should insist that data center developers pay the infrastructure costs they create, protect ratepayers and natural resources, use strong labor standards and deliver measurable community benefits. But we should not mistake accountability for hostility to investment. That is why I welcome the work of the Coalition for Responsible Data Centers, which is bringing together municipal leaders, labor, businesses and community voices to pursue responsible, pro-growth policy. State leaders should listen to communities with real experience, not only abstract projections or worst-case assumptions. In Elk Grove Village, data centers are not theoretical. Neither are the revenue, jobs and investments they generate. Craig B. Johnson is the mayor of Elk Grove Village. Submit a letter, of no more than 400 words, to the editor here or email letters@chicagotribune.com.

artigo.texto: Planejando, a forte demanda dos data centers pode ser atendida com segurança energética Para isso, a rede de transmissão precisa ser expandida para dar conta da alta demanda de energia dos, cada vez mais gigantescos, centros de dados A expansão dos data centers para atender o processamento de grandes volumes de dados e imagens — resultante do crescente uso da computação em nuvem e da inteligência artificial (IA) — acende um sinal de alerta de como os recursos energéticos exigidos por esses empreendimentos serão administrados. Um dos desafios é garantir que a segurança do sistema elétrico não seja comprometida, o que significa que a rede de transmissão também deve se expandir para dar conta da nova demanda de energia dos centros de dados. Há também desafios ambientais, como a demanda por água para resfriar equipamentos, e o ruído produzido por eles — questões que, no exterior, levantam oposição. Mas, por aqui, a visão que prevalece é a de que os data centers são importantes para a soberania digital, além de uma boa oportunidade para atrair investimentos. A matriz elétrica limpa e as fontes renováveis, ou de baixa emissão, são um dos apelos do país e um dos requisitos do Redata, regime de benefícios fiscais recentemente aprovado pelo Senado Federal para incentivar o segmento. “Como a energia elétrica pesa entre 40% e 60% no custo operacional de um data center, ter acesso a fontes de geração renovável com preços competitivos e fornecimento estável faz diferença na viabilidade econômica desses empreendimentos e ajuda a atrair investimentos para o país”, afirma Carlos Fogarolli, sócio-líder para a indústria de tecnologia, mídia e telecomunicações da Deloitte. Mas o ritmo da demanda por data centers tem crescido mais rápido do que a capacidade da rede de transmissão de energia consegue acompanhar, considera Fogarolli. Ele informa que, para reduzir essa distância, a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) estima em R$ 128,6 bilhões o investimento necessário até 2034 para viabilizar 30 mil quilômetros de novas linhas de transmissão e 82 mil megavolt-ampère (MVA) em novas subestações. Um data center leva, em média, de 18 a 24 meses para ser implantado no Brasil, prazo mais curto do que o de uma obra de transmissão de grande porte. “Isso ajuda a explicar por que a entrada em operação de novos data centers antes da conclusão dessas obras é vista como um risco concreto, com reflexo direto na segurança do fornecimento e nos custos de energia da região”, afirma Fogarolli. Na opinião do diretor-presidente da ISA Energia, Rui Chammas, o atual sistema de transmissão do país tem condições de acompanhar o crescimento da demanda energética, desde que haja planejamento e coordenação entre as novas unidades e a expansão da rede elétrica. “Como os data centers preveem expansões futuras de carga, é fundamental que essa demanda seja informada aos agentes envolvidos no planejamento setorial para dimensionar os investimentos necessários na infraestrutura de transmissão.” A Associação Brasileira de Data Centers (ABDC) aponta que o Brasil tem 162 data centers em operação, a maior parte no Sudeste, seguido pelo Sul e pelo Nordeste, região que mais vem atraindo unidades por oferecer energia eólica e solar, terrenos e conexões com os cabos submarinos de comunicação. E há uma forte tendência de expansão. A capacidade de data centers no país deve quadruplicar nos próximos cinco anos, passando de cerca de 1 gigawatt (GW) em 2025 para mais de 4 GW no início da década de 2030, segundo o Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS). “Os números mais recentes já incluem 27 contratos de conexão assinados e 30 solicitações de acesso à Rede Interligada Nacional com parecer favorável, indicando que grande parte dos projetos está avançando em paralelo aos investimentos em infraestrutura de transmissão planejados para os próximos anos”, opina Rodrigo Borges, diretor-executivo da Aurora Energy Research. Parcerias com fornecedores de energia renovável estão entre as estratégias para viabilizar projetos. É o caso da Omnia Data Centers, que está construindo um data center localizado no Complexo Industrial e Portuário do Pecém (CE), com investimentos de R$ 12 bilhões e voltado para um único cliente, a ByteDance, controladora da rede social TikTok. “A disponibilidade de energia renovável foi um dos fatores estratégicos considerados na escolha da localização da unidade, com capacidade de 200 megawatts (MW) e que será abastecida pelos parques eólicos no Ceará e no Piauí a partir de um contrato com a Casa dos Ventos”, afirma Rodrigo Abreu, CEO da Omnia Data Centers. Para se ter uma ideia da magnitude desses projetos, o Estado de Sergipe consome entre 150 MW e 200 MW de energia com carga constante, segundo a EPE. A estratégia da Scala, que conta com 13 data centers em operação e outros sete em desenvolvimento, é contar com infraestrutura elétrica própria, com a construção de três subestações. Além de uma unidade em Tamboré, na Grande São Paulo, que teve investimentos de US$ 10 bilhões e que chegará a 20 data centers quando concluída, vai inaugurar um segundo data center de larga escala (“hyperscale”), chamado de AI City, localizado no Rio Grande do Sul, voltado para IA, e que aproveita a infraestrutura elétrica já existente. “O clima mais ameno da região reduzirá o consumo de energia destinado à refrigeração e vai operar com PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness, ou Eficácia no Uso de Energia) de 1,2, métrica usada para definir a eficiência energética do data center, além de dispensar uso contínuo de água durante a operação”, afirma Fabio Yanaguita, diretor de energia da Scala. artigo.texto: Datacenters impulsionam investimentos no setor elétrico Incentivos do Redata e avanço da IA reforçam o potencial de expansão do setor, com efeitos para distribuidoras e geradoras de energia 3 minutos Publicado em A expansão da infraestrutura digital, impulsionada pela inteligência artificial e pelo Redata, abre uma nova frente de crescimento para as empresas de utilities. A expansão dos datacenters no Brasil pode criar uma nova fonte relevante de demanda para o setor elétrico nos próximos anos. O avanço da inteligência artificial, a necessidade crescente de capacidade computacional e os incentivos fiscais previstos no Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de DataCenters, o Redata, reforçam a atratividade do país para novos investimentos. O Brasil já reúne condições competitivas para receber projetos dessa natureza, com disponibilidade de recursos energéticos, conexões por cabos e escala relevante. A combinação desses fatores pode favorecer a instalação de novas estruturas e ampliar os investimentos em geração, transmissão e distribuição de energia. Inteligência artificial amplia consumo de eletricidade Globalmente, a demanda de eletricidade dos datacenters deve crescer 15% ao ano até 2030, segundo estimativas da Agência Internacional de Energia, a IEA. As projeções seguem em revisão para cima diante da adoção acelerada de modelos de inteligência artificial, que exigem maior capacidade de processamento e servidores mais avançados. Nos Estados Unidos, a maior utilização de servidores voltados a cargas de trabalho de IA contribuiu para que os data centers dobrassem seu consumo de eletricidade. A experiência internacional indica que a infraestrutura digital pode ganhar relevância crescente no planejamento do setor elétrico, sobretudo em regiões que concentram grandes instalações. Brasil pode alcançar 20 GW até 2035 No Brasil, o Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia 2035, elaborado pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética, a EPE, projeta que o país pode alcançar 20 gigawatts de capacidade instalada de datacenters até 2035. Desse total, 5,6 gigawatts poderiam entrar em operação até 2030. Os projetos devem se concentrar principalmente em duas regiões. No Sudeste, os destaques são a Grande São Paulo, Campinas e Rio de Janeiro. No Nordeste, Ceará e Sergipe aparecem como áreas com potencial para receber novos investimentos. Os pedidos de conexão à rede elétrica também sinalizam a dimensão dessa oportunidade. Há 77 projetos relacionados à instalação de datacenters, que somam cerca de 26 gigawatts de capacidade até 2038. O volume equivale a aproximadamente 50% da atual demanda de pico de energia do Brasil. Redata pode estimular novos investimentos O Redata instituiu um regime tributário voltado à instalação e à expansão de datacenters no país. A medida prevê a suspensão de tributos federais incidentes sobre equipamentos elegíveis de tecnologia da informação e comunicação. Após a conclusão dos investimentos e o cumprimento dos requisitos aplicáveis, os tributos suspensos poderão ser convertidos em alíquotas zero. A redução dos custos iniciais dependerá da composição dos equipamentos de cada projeto e das regulamentações que definirão os produtos elegíveis. Ainda assim, o programa pode reduzir parte da desvantagem de custos do Brasil em relação a outros mercados internacionais. Em contrapartida, as empresas participantes deverão atender requisitos de eficiência hídrica e inovação. Entre as exigências, está o investimento de 2% do valor dos equipamentos incentivados em pesquisa e desenvolvimento local. Além disso, os beneficiários deverão atender integralmente sua demanda contratada de eletricidade com fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão, por meio de contratos de fornecimento de energia ou autoprodução. Esse requisito pode favorecer os portfólios diversificados de geração do Brasil, com destaque para ativos hidrelétricos, eólicos e solares. Utilities podem se beneficiar da nova demanda A análise do Safra aponta potencial de alta para o setor de utilities a partir da expansão dos datacenters. Considerando a experiência dos Estados Unidos como referência, a demanda por eletricidade no Brasil poderia crescer 2,7% acima do cenário-base da EPE. A projeção considera uma situação em que os datacenters passam a responder por 8% da demanda total de energia, ante uma participação de 5% no cenário-base. O movimento poderia beneficiar distribuidoras com presença nas regiões que devem concentrar novos projetos, como Enel, CPFL, Light, Equatorial e Energisa. As geradoras também podem capturar oportunidades. Em algumas regiões dos Estados Unidos, onde a demanda dos datacenters avançou de forma mais intensa, os preços de energia subiram cerca de 30% entre 2020 e 2025. Embora fatores como condições climáticas e custos de combustíveis também tenham influenciado esse movimento, maiores pagamentos por capacidade podem beneficiar empresas como Axia e Copel. Impacto deve aparecer a partir de 2029 A construção de datacenters costuma levar entre 18 e 48 meses. Por isso, a maior necessidade de energia dessas instalações deve começar a impactar a demanda elétrica de forma mais relevante a partir de 2029. Até lá, a expansão dependerá da execução dos projetos, da disponibilidade de conexão à rede, da contratação de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão e da regulamentação complementar do Redata. A expansão dos datacenters pode, portanto, representar uma nova etapa para o setor elétrico brasileiro. Além de elevar o consumo de energia, o avanço dessas estruturas tende a reforçar a importância de ativos de geração limpa, infraestrutura de rede e capacidade de atendimento a grandes consumidores. artigo.texto: Quarta-feira, 30 de setembro de 2026 Por Redação O Sul | 29 de setembro de 2026 A instalação de grandes centros de processamento pode representar aumento significativo da demanda local por eletricidade. Foto: Reprodução O crescimento dos data centers e da demanda por infraestrutura para inteligência artificial abriu uma discussão sobre o impacto que o aumento do consumo de energia pode provocar no sistema elétrico brasileiro. A expansão desses centros de processamento exige grandes quantidades de eletricidade e levou o governo e especialistas a discutir como os custos adicionais deverão ser distribuídos entre empresas, consumidores e demais usuários da rede. Os data centers são estruturas utilizadas para armazenar e processar grandes volumes de informações. Com a expansão da inteligência artificial, a necessidade de capacidade computacional aumentou e empresas de tecnologia passaram a buscar locais com disponibilidade de energia, infraestrutura de transmissão e condições para ampliar suas operações. O aumento da demanda ocorre em um momento em que o sistema elétrico brasileiro já enfrenta desafios relacionados ao equilíbrio entre oferta e consumo. O país ampliou significativamente a geração de fontes renováveis, especialmente solar e eólica, mas enfrenta limitações na transmissão e períodos em que parte da energia disponível não consegue ser aproveitada. Em artigo publicado pela CNN Brasil, o ex-presidente da Petrobras e ex-ministro Jean Paul Prates afirmou que é legítimo discutir quem deverá pagar os custos associados à energia necessária para abastecer os novos data centers. Segundo ele, a expansão dessas estruturas pode pressionar os sistemas elétricos e elevar custos em determinadas regiões. A discussão ocorre em meio à expectativa de novos investimentos em infraestrutura digital no País. A instalação de grandes centros de processamento pode representar aumento significativo da demanda local por eletricidade, exigindo reforços em linhas de transmissão, subestações e equipamentos. O impacto sobre as tarifas depende, entre outros fatores, de como esses investimentos serão estruturados e de quem ficará responsável pelos custos de expansão da rede. Uma parte das despesas pode estar associada diretamente aos empreendimentos, enquanto outros investimentos podem integrar a infraestrutura compartilhada do sistema. O tema ganhou importância também porque o Brasil tenta utilizar a disponibilidade de fontes renováveis como um diferencial para atrair investimentos ligados à tecnologia. A oferta de energia de menor intensidade de carbono é apontada como uma das vantagens para empresas que precisam abastecer instalações de grande consumo. Ao mesmo tempo, especialistas têm alertado para o risco de uma expansão sem planejamento integrado. O setor elétrico brasileiro convive com momentos de excesso de geração renovável em determinadas regiões e horários, enquanto enfrenta restrições para transportar essa energia até os locais de consumo. A discussão sobre os data centers se soma, portanto, a um problema mais amplo do setor elétrico. Segundo especialistas, o país precisa ampliar o planejamento da transmissão e da capacidade de armazenamento para lidar com o crescimento da demanda e com a variabilidade das fontes renováveis. Outro ponto envolve o custo da energia para consumidores e empresas. Dados mostram que o preço da eletricidade para o setor produtivo brasileiro, em valores em dólar, acumulou alta de 327,7% entre 2000 e junho de 2026. No mesmo período, a alta foi de 145,3% nos Estados Unidos e de 12,5% na União Europeia.

artigo.texto: Last Tuesday, there was a large turnout at a Bow Selectmen meeting, preceded by a rally with residents from Bow and nearby towns that will be affected by the pollution of air, water and noise from a possible AI data center, particularly one fast-tracked without input from stakeholders. I am a longtime resident of Bow with a background as an environmental science educator and advocate for climate justice. I was one of many who raised major concerns about the environmental and health risks of data centers and requested a moratorium on these data centers until these problems are addressed. I was part of the long struggle to close down the dangerous coal-fired power plant, and had hoped with many others that the site would be used to support affordable renewable energy. I am a co-leader of the Concord Chapter of Climate Hope Affiliates, a faith-based advocacy group for climate justice, and several of our chapters across the country have been successful in advocating for members of Congress to support bipartisan legislation to examine and regulate AI data centers. Data centers consume enormous amounts of energy and water at a financial and environmental cost borne by residents. The United States has more than 3,000 data centers. Of particular concern are “hyperscale” data centers that demand at least 50 MW of power — enough electricity for a small city. Sixty-eight hyperscale facilities operate today, and 267 more are planned. Nationwide, communities are protesting existing and proposed data centers. A local ban might protect one community from data center pollution, but it cannot protect all communities across the country. Two bills before Congress offer a national response. Reps. Rob Menendez (D-NJ) and Greg Casar (D-TX) have introduced the Preventing Rate Inflation in Consumer Energy (PRICE) Act (HR 6983) and the Data Center Transparency Act (HR 6984). The PRICE Act would require large data centers to generate the electricity they consume and transition to 100% clean energy by 2040. The Data Center Transparency Act would require federal agencies to report regularly on data centers’ air pollution, water use, energy consumption and effects on household utility bills. Our representatives in Congress should cosponsor these bills if they have not already done so, or explain what other action they will take to protect our communities and state. Our senators should introduce companion legislation. The PRICE Act applies to data centers with a power demand of at least 50 MW. It provides a timetable for transitioning to clean energy. A data center’s energy would need to be 75% clean by 2035 and 100% clean by 2040. Failure to comply would result in a civil penalty that could be as high as $100,000 per day until the requirement is met. To establish a more comprehensive approach, the Data Center Transparency Act would make the broader environmental and consumer impacts of data centers transparent to the public. It would require the EPA to collect data every three months on impacts related to water, local utilities, greenhouse gas emissions and the cumulative impact of emissions on overburdened communities. It would additionally require the Energy Information Administration to collect data every six months on both a data center’s energy consumption and any impacts on household energy bills. With more and more massive data centers being built, the question is where they will land. Local bans and moratoriums are effective, but we need a unified movement across the United States to protect all of us and the environment. Climate Hope Affiliates is highlighting one particularly egregious data center in Memphis. Local chapters are hosting community discussions and postcard-writing parties in towns and cities across the U.S. Attendees watch a 17-minute video about a predominantly Black community in Memphis that has been struggling to address the pollution from an XAI data center that, at the time of filming, was the world’s largest supercomputer. The video illustrates a familiar pattern of environmental injustice: a powerful corporation adds pollution to an already overburdened, predominantly Black community, while the concerns of residents are discounted and environmental protection laws are blatantly disregarded. A number of solutions are needed, but for starters, no one should have to live near the gas turbines or diesel generators that help power some data centers. The fossil fuels that generate the energy cause air and water pollution which causes a myriad of heart and lung problems as well as problems for the animal life in the water. The low-frequency noise pollution sounds like jet engines 24/7, causing ringing of the ears, tinnitus and stress, which causes heart problems. No one should have those in their backyard. This is why the two bills are currently being championed by Climate Hope Affiliates and Creation Justice Ministries, an ecumenical organization that brings more than 35 different denominations together in common cause for environmental stewardship. The Rev. Dr. Brooks Berndt, who directs Climate Hope Affiliates and serves as the Environmental Justice Minister, explains this broad approach by saying, “Ultimately, the key to bringing about the needed solutions is for members of communities across the country to come together to build a bigger ‘we,’ so that when we say not in ‘our’ backyard, we mean everyone’s backyard.” Several New England Conferences have resolutions about a moratorium on data centers. Please urge all four of our Congresspeople and Senators to support these two important bills. We are taking care of business in our back yard, but the urgent need to address AI data centers is a nationwide issue that demands our action. It’s a matter of money versus morals, greed versus health. Sue Moore, from Bow, is co-Leader of the Concord Climate Hope Affiliates with an MS in Environmental Health Science, a Teacher/Naturalist with Audubon and an environment/climate activist.

artigo.texto: Battery Storage Gains Traction in Maharashtra C&I Sector ⚡ Quick Read - What happened: Commercial and industrial (C&I) consumers in Maharashtra are increasingly adopting battery energy storage systems (BESS) to manage peak demand and mitigate the impact of new restrictions on renewable energy banking. - Why it matters: These storage solutions allow businesses to shift surplus daytime solar generation to evening hours, effectively bypassing time-of-day banking limitations and ensuring grid stability. - Watch: Further regulatory shifts regarding time-of-day (ToD) tariffs and banking policies that could accelerate the commercial viability of service-based storage models. Background and Context The energy landscape in Maharashtra is undergoing a significant shift as commercial and industrial (C&I) consumers seek more robust solutions for peak demand management. With the state introducing proposed restrictions on the use of banked renewable energy across different time-of-day (ToD) periods, businesses are finding it increasingly difficult to rely solely on traditional net-metering or banking arrangements. This regulatory tightening has acted as a catalyst, pushing the adoption of battery energy storage systems (BESS) to the forefront of corporate energy strategies. Key Details The core challenge for many C&I entities in Maharashtra is the mismatch between peak solar generation hours—typically midday—and peak consumption hours, which often extend into the evening. Previously, banking renewable energy allowed these consumers to offset costs effectively. However, the new policy environment aims to limit this flexibility, forcing consumers to find alternative ways to utilize their generated power. BESS technology offers a direct solution by enabling the storage of surplus daytime renewable energy for discharge during high-tariff evening periods. Furthermore, the emergence of service-based storage models is lowering the barrier to entry, allowing businesses to bypass high upfront capital expenditures while transferring performance and maintenance risks to specialized energy service providers. What This Means for EPCs and Developers For EPC contractors and renewable energy developers, this trend signals a pivot toward integrated energy solutions. The market is moving beyond simple solar PV installations toward hybrid projects that incorporate storage components. Developers who can offer ‘energy-as-a-service’ models, where the storage infrastructure is managed and financed by the provider, are likely to see increased demand from industrial clients looking to optimize their power costs without heavy balance-sheet impact. EPCs should prepare for a rise in retrofitting existing solar sites with BESS to ensure compliance and continued operational efficiency for their clients. What Happens Next As Maharashtra continues to refine its renewable energy policies, the integration of storage will become a standard requirement for large-scale C&I projects. The success of these initial BESS deployments will likely influence regulatory frameworks in other Indian states, potentially creating a nationwide template for storage-integrated renewable energy. Within the broader India renewable energy sector, this shift underscores the transition from a focus on pure capacity addition to a focus on grid-responsive, reliable, and dispatchable power, which is essential for the country’s long-term decarbonization goals.
