artigo.texto: Geely has purchased a 30% stake in Nio Power, the battery-swap and charging division of EV manufacturer Nio. Dating back to November 2023, when Nio and Geely entered a battery-swap strategic partnership, the automotive giant’s 30% stake, worth $2.4bn USD, reflects the two Chinese firms’ agreement to cooperate on technology and capital. In March 2024, the tie-up was expanded to charging network connectivity. Geely’s stake means the two parties will jointly develop unified battery-swap technologies and standards. Geely is also developing battery-swappable models, with Nio providing battery-swap services, infrastructure, and network. The partnership is set to accelerate Nio’s Power Swap Station network, which aims to operate 10,000 global battery swap stations by 2030, when annual electricity demand across the network is expected to exceed 10 billion kilowatt-hours. By the end of 2027, Geely plans to build 22,000 charging stations with over 100,000 charging connectors. This includes more than 15,000 charging stations with the brand’s new ‘Smart Charging’ tech. This latest piece of AI-based charging tech offers mega-rapid charging speeds of up to 2,250 kilowatts (2.2 megawatts). Importantly for Geely, it significantly dwarfs arch-rival BYD’s 1.5MW ‘Flash’ charging network. While Geely and BYD seem to be entering a charging-speed arms race, Nio’s battery-swap system offers a third way of EV charging. In early 2026, Nio reported completing over 100 million battery swaps. When a motorist arrives at a Nio Power Swap Station, the vehicle’s sensors and automated driver systems move it into the swap bay. A robotic system underneath removes the old battery and installs a fresh, laser-guided replacement pack. Nio’s diagnostic systems then run an automated health check on the new battery and driver systems before the driver departs the station. The entire swap takes from three to five minutes. Founded in 2014, Shanghai-based Nio believes battery swapping is quicker than refuelling an internal combustion-engined car and using a rapid charger. In the UK, these usually max out at around 150kW at present. Battery swapping is also aimed at eliminating range anxiety by offering drivers the choice of switching between a smaller battery for short journeys and a larger pack for longer distances. However, detractors view Nio’s setup as financially and operationally inefficient, given the 1.5 million yuan (approximately $2.2m) it costs to build a battery swap station, along with the network’s $140m annual maintenance costs. Since Nio introduced its battery swap system in 2018, it has consistently run at a net loss as the company prioritises the network’s long-term scaling and infrastructure roll-out.

artigo.texto: MANITOWOC COUNTY (NBC 26) — Manitowoc County released a drafted ordinance this week outlining requirements for future data centers, including limits on acreage and protections for farmland and water. Watch the full broadcast story here: The ordinance is being created during an 18-month moratorium on data centers, which ends in October 2027. It would limit data centers to 500 acres, with no more than 100 acres converted from agricultural use. County Executive Tyler Martell said preserving farmland is a priority. "Manitowoc is a very rural county, agriculture is very important ... we want to make sure that we are preserving that farmland," Martell said. The ordinance would also require a closed-loop cooling system, which reduces the amount of water used. Manitowoc County Farm Bureau President Brent Sinkula said water protection is the most critical provision. "The water loop is the biggest one. Even if they recycle the water any type of leak or anything in there is going to end up in our service water, the ground water and that is what we are farmers rely on for ourselves, for our live stocks and our families," Sinkula said. Additionally, noise monitoring and air quality plans would be part of the ordinance. "Air and noise pollution, obviously when you have live stock especially out on pasture or outside any air pollution is going to get in there and as for noise .. I know when it comes to poultry if it's over a certain decibel it will affect the animals more," Sinkula said. At public hearings, some residents have called for a permanent ban on data centers. Martell said that is not an option. "We can't just ban a type of development .. we don't get to decide what kind of business applies we just need to make sure we have a consistent set of rules that are fair and reasonable so when a business does desire to build in Manitowoc County, here are the expectations," said Martell. "Landowners have the right to sell their land if they so choose, we have to make sure we are respectful of that as well. When you are piecing multiple parcels of land together that's when the planning and zoning steps in." Martell added that no data center developers have approached the county yet, and the ordinance is meant to be proactive. The draft will now go to the Planning and Zoning Commission for review. Martell expects public hearings before the commission makes a recommendation to the County Board. You can read the full ordinance draft here. artigo.texto: Center point considers rules for possible data center City and county leaders discuss ordinance before any proposal is submitted CENTER POINT, Iowa (KCRG) - Center Point leaders are considering what to do if a data center wants to come to town, even before there is a proposal on the table. The city council teamed up with Center Point’s planning and zoning commission. They met with County Supervisor Brandi Meisheid to review the county’s rules. Using Linn and Johnson counties as models, leaders zeroed in on power grid demands, cooling systems, and requiring utility impact studies. No data center has approached Center Point yet, but the mayor says they want to set the rules before developers come knocking. “I think it’s important to be proactive about having an ordinance so this way when or if we are ever approached by a data center, we have a path forward,” Mayor Traer Morgan said. Public comment raises questions During public comment, people questioned whether the city is prepared for the long-term impact of a data center. Some people thanked the city for getting ahead on a proposed ordinance. The council says after this discussion they now believe they have enough information to draft a data center ordinance. artigo.texto: SECI Floats Tender for Standalone BESS Projects in India ⚡ Quick Read - What happened: The Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) has invited bids for standalone battery energy storage systems (BESS) under the ‘SECI-ESS-IV’ scheme to provide on-demand energy across India. - Why it matters: This tender represents a critical move toward grid stability and peak-load management, offering a significant opportunity for developers to scale storage assets. - Watch: Interested bidders must submit their proposals by the deadline of October 30, 2026. Background and Context The Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) has officially launched a new tender for standalone battery energy storage systems (BESS) across India, categorized as SECI-ESS-IV. This initiative is part of the government’s broader strategy to integrate large-scale storage solutions into the national power grid, ensuring that renewable energy remains reliable even when solar and wind generation are unavailable. By focusing on ‘on-demand’ energy supply, the tender aims to address the intermittency challenges inherent in the country’s rapidly expanding renewable energy portfolio. Key Details The SECI-ESS-IV tender invites developers to submit bids for the supply of energy through standalone BESS infrastructure. This move is designed to facilitate the procurement of storage capacity that can be dispatched during peak demand hours, thereby enhancing grid flexibility. The submission window for this tender is currently open, with the final deadline for bid submissions set for October 30, 2026. While specific capacity figures for this tranche are being finalized, the scale of the tender signals a continued commitment to the national BESS roadmap. What This Means for EPCs and Developers For EPC contractors and renewable energy developers, this tender marks a significant shift toward the commercialization of storage-as-a-service. Developers will need to focus on optimizing the levelized cost of storage (LCOS) and ensuring high round-trip efficiency to remain competitive. EPC firms with expertise in large-scale battery integration and grid-scale power electronics are expected to see increased demand for their services as these projects move toward the execution phase. The ability to manage complex supply chains for battery cells and power conversion systems will be a key differentiator for successful bidders. What Happens Next Following the October 30, 2026, bid submission deadline, SECI will conduct a technical and financial evaluation of the proposals. Successful developers will be awarded the contracts, which will likely include long-term storage off-take agreements. As India continues to target its ambitious 500 GW non-fossil fuel capacity goal by 2030, the deployment of BESS projects like those under SECI-ESS-IV will be fundamental to maintaining grid stability. The success of this tender will likely influence future policy frameworks and the scaling of pumped hydro and battery storage technologies across the Indian renewable energy sector. 📊 Key Data The following table outlines the key parameters of the SECI-ESS-IV standalone BESS tender.

artigo.texto: Senate Democrats on Wednesday defeated a pair of bills that aimed to address data center-related affordability concerns and limit Congress members' ability to profit on the stock market while in office, arguing both were watered-down proposals. The data center bill, dubbed the Ratepayer Protection Act, failed on a vote of 57-43. A second bill, known as the Stop Insider Trading Act, which also includes a controversial voter-identification provision, was defeated on a party-line, 53-47 vote. Each bill needed 60 votes to overcome the Senate filibuster. Republicans will likely use the votes as fodder on the campaign trail this fall, as the GOP seeks to hold narrow majorities in both chambers despite President Donald Trump's falling approval ratings and persistent concerns about affordability. The Senate is due to recess as soon as Wednesday, as lawmakers seeking reelection will return to their home states to campaign ahead of the 2026 midterm election. "EVERY Senate Democrat just joined 94% of House Democrats in voting AGAINST banning congressional stock trading.," House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., posted to X immediately following the vote. The bill, he said, provides "the accountability the American people demand. But every Democrat blocked it from becoming law." The Ratepayer Protection Act, which passed the House on a 417-3 vote earlier this month, would establish a regulatory framework that states could consider adopting to require large artificial intelligence data centers to cover their own energy costs, rather than passing them down to customers. But Democrats have railed against the measure. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., called the proposal a "toothless messaging bill" in a speech in the Senate on Tuesday. "The bill is a fraud. I can sum up the shortcomings of Republicans' data center bill with one word: optional," Schumer said. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who has called for a national moratorium on data centers until developers can demonstrate they will cover the full cost of their construction and operation, called the legislation a "silly piece of nonsense." "Give us something of substance and we'll vote on it," Warren said ahead of the vote. Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, the top Democrat on the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, cited similar concerns when he blocked the bill earlier this month after Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, requested unanimous consent for quick passage. Husted is in a "toss up" race for reelection against former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, according to The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter. Brown has accused his opponent of helping to bring data centers to the state when he was lieutenant governor. Husted and other Republicans could use a messaging win on the data center front, which has evolved in recent months into a potent campaign issue as opponents seek stricter guardrails for developers. Meanwhile, the congressional stock trading bill, passed the House in July on a 232-198 vote, would prohibit sitting members of Congress from buying individual stocks. But it would not force members to divest their existing portfolios, a sticking point for some Democrats who have advocated a more stringent trading ban. Republicans tacked on to the measure a controversial voter identification provision, which Democrats largely oppose. Schumer similarly criticized the stock-trading proposal on Tuesday, calling it a "theatrical farce" and the voter ID provision a "poison pill." And Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said the Republican proposal was a half measure. "It's obviously a sign that they don't take seriously the issue of insider trading. If you wanted to get a stock ban done, you would put a stock ban on the floor," Kaine said on Wednesday. Husted, in a post to X on Tuesday, called both proposals "commonsense, bipartisan bills." "Lowering energy costs, requiring photo ID to vote, and banning stock trading for members of Congress could be bipartisan wins," Husted wrote. "Senate Democrats are the only ones standing in the way of delivering what the American people have asked us to do." — Irit Skulnik contributed to this story.

artigo.texto: On Thursday, Google will attempt to launch a prototype satellite into space to test the feasibility of building AI data centers in the cosmos. The effort is called Project Suncatcher. Google gave the New York Times an exclusive first look at the effort, “set to become the first step toward that goal by a major tech company,” the outlet wrote. University of Virginia professor Peter Beling is in the School of Data Science, where he serves as interim associate dean for research, and is an affiliate of UVA’s National Security Data and Policy Institute. He is an AI and systems engineering expert and has talked previously about the AI race to outer space. Beling talked with UVA Today about Google’s latest venture. Q. What is Google trying to do with Project Suncatcher? A. What they’re trying to do is understand the opportunity for putting data centers in space. Given that we can’t deliver electricity as quickly as the demand for AI is growing, there’s an expanding gap. We need more and more energy. There are also other issues people have discussed many times, like potential environmental impacts from water use or from heat on land temperatures. Q. How could a data center work in orbit? A. It’s much more like there’ll be server racks, more or less floating. They won’t be connected by wires; they’re going to be connected by laser communications. Google is taking its recent generation of AI chips and trying to see whether, in a space environment, they would really be functional. There’s no atmosphere to slow down the particles that are zipping around the solar system, so they’ll be hitting the chips. The question is, will the chips keep functioning in space? Q. What might one of these data centers look like? A. The first Google Suncatcher prototype will be about the size of a refrigerator, according to The New York Times. And then the solar panels unfold. Think of it as a box, not too big, surrounded by these big panels. Q. Why consider space at all? A. There’s plenty of energy in the form of solar if you can get your satellites in the right orbit. In space, what you have to rely on is radiative cooling. You basically have the infrared radiation coming off of a hot object and just sort of going off into space. That’s how the object cools. So you need a big surface area.

artigo.texto: Leilões de armazenamento em baterias são essenciais, mas rateio dos custos gera discussão A definição de como será o rateio dos custos está longe de um consenso e colocou em lados opostos geradoras, grandes consumidores, governo, Congresso e a Aneel Atualizado O primeiro leilão brasileiro de reserva de capacidade destinado a sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS, na sigla em inglês), previsto para ocorrer nos dias 2 e 4 dezembro, vem gerando questionamentos regulatórios que podem levar ao adiamento do certame. A possibilidade de atraso no cronograma permanece no radar do setor em virtude do impasse, ainda sem solução à vista, sobre quem deverá pagar a conta pela disponibilidade do sistema. A legislação atual (Lei nº 15.269/2025) determina que o Encargo de Potência para Reserva de Capacidade (ERCAP) será integralmente arcado pelas geradoras de energia. À Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) caberá a regulamentação de como esse rateio será feito na prática. A definição está longe de um consenso e acabou colocando em lados opostos geradoras, grandes consumidores, governo, Congresso e a Aneel. As empresas de geração, bem como as entidades de classe que as representam, defenderam na última audiência pública, realizada pela Aneel em Brasília no início de setembro, um rateio generalizado desse custo. O argumento é que o leilão de baterias contribuirá para o reequilíbrio de todo o sistema elétrico, que passa atualmente por problemas de excesso na oferta de energia durante horas específicas e por escassez em outras, ocasião em que as termelétricas precisam ser acionadas. Impasses à parte, o fato é que o tempo está correndo contra. A Aneel precisa aprovar a versão definitiva do edital e do contrato até o dia 27 de outubro, tendo prazo limite até o dia 1º de novembro para efetivamente publicar toda a documentação no Diário Oficial. Além da audiência pública, tramita na Câmara projeto de lei de autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim (Cidadania/SP), propondo a divisão dessa conta com todos os agentes do setor, e não apenas com os geradores. O diretor-geral da Aneel, Sandoval Feitosa, acredita que uma possível aprovação às vésperas do leilão trará ainda mais instabilidade, mas Rodrigo Sauaia, presidente-executivo da Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (Absolar), entidade que reúne as geradoras de energia solar, considera a aprovação do PL essencial para sanar a atual insegurança e imprevisibilidade do setor. “Será um aperfeiçoamento do marco legal porque eliminaria um tratamento distinto para soluções que prestam o mesmo serviço ao Sistema Interligado Nacional [SIN]. A regra atual cria uma assimetria regulatória incompatível com o princípio da neutralidade tecnológica, introduzindo insegurança jurídica para o primeiro Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade destinado ao BESS”, diz Sauaia. Já para Diogo Zaverucha, diretor da unidade de armazenamento (BESS) da Brasol, empresa que já tem mais de 4 GW em projetos de armazenamento cadastrados na Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) para o certame, o país alcançou o arcabouço regulatório básico necessário para fazer esse mercado acontecer. Ele é enfático ao afirmar a relevância do leilão como forma de garantir energia firme para blindar o país contra riscos de apagões à noite, além de reduzir os níveis de cortes forçados de geração (curtailment) aplicados pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) nas usinas solares e eólicas do Nordeste. “Estamos muito otimistas com a realização do leilão em dezembro deste ano. Acreditamos que há segurança jurídica e base técnica suficientes para bater o martelo. É inegável, contudo, que existe um nó pendente que precisa ser desatado sobre quem vai pagar a conta dos encargos de reserva de capacidade.” O executivo considera que a nota técnica emitida pela Aneel detalha as diretrizes para a equalização do rateio, e que há chances altas de resolver o impasse nos tribunais ou na própria regulação da agência antes que o primeiro lance seja dado, sem provocar atrasos. A importância do leilão para corrigir gargalos é fato inquestionável para o setor e o edital enfrenta o problema diretamente ao concentrar 71% da potência leiloada na região Nordeste, segundo Celio Eustáquio de Moura, presidente da Associação Brasileira dos Sindicatos e Associações Representantes das Indústrias de Energias (Abrasenergias). Ao instalar as baterias coladas às subestações críticas de transmissão, o sistema ganhará flexibilidade, já que o excedente de energia limpa será integralmente absorvido e guardado de forma localizada. A possibilidade de adiamento, no entanto, preocupa. “Não estamos trabalhando com essa perspectiva, mas ela existe, devido à complexidade jurídica desse rateio”, diz Moura. O advogado Alexandre Leite, sócio da área de energia do escritório Dias Carneiro Advogados, também enxerga essa possibilidade. “Há risco de judicialização do leilão envolvendo geradores, fundos de investimento e outros participantes que se sintam prejudicados pelas regras estabelecidas. O leilão é importante, mas foi estruturado antes de haver uma regulamentação suficientemente madura. A ausência de regras consolidadas durante etapas importantes do processo gerou insegurança e pode alimentar disputas futuras”, conclui Leite, que também é membro da Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae) e do Instituto Brasileiro de Estudos do Direito da Energia (IBDE). Ele observa que o edital do leilão criou restrições classificadas como excessivas por parte do mercado. Por exemplo, o aumento das garantias exigidas, limitações para associação das baterias a determinados projetos já contratados e restrições à troca de controle societário dos empreendimentos. Na sua avaliação, muitas dessas medidas não atacam diretamente os riscos que a Aneel pretende evitar, que são o de garantir a segurança financeira dos contratos e a do fornecimento contínuo de energia. artigo.texto: LG entra na rede da Nvidia para resfriar data centers de IA Empresa passa a integrar a NVIDIA Partner Network como parceira preferencial em energia e resfriamento; unidades de distribuição de fluido serão exibidas em Singapura. A LG Electronics passou a integrar a NVIDIA Partner Network como parceira preferencial em soluções de energia e resfriamento. O anúncio, feito em 28 de setembro, está relacionado ao fornecimento de sistemas de gerenciamento térmico para data centers de inteligência artificial de alta densidade. A unidade de distribuição de fluido de resfriamento (CDU) de 2,6 MW da LG recebeu a qualificação NVIDIA DSX Ready CDU. Segundo a empresa, ela tem a maior capacidade entre as unidades com essa qualificação no marketplace da Nvidia no momento da consulta. Modelos de 600 kW e 1 MW também concluíram a qualificação de infraestrutura da companhia. As CDUs fornecem fluido de resfriamento diretamente a componentes como CPUs e GPUs e podem operar em conjunto com sistemas de resfriamento a ar. Os equipamentos qualificados serão apresentados na Data Centre World Asia 2026, nos dias 29 e 30 de setembro, no Marina Bay Sands, em Singapura. A LG afirma que pretende buscar, até o fim de 2026, a qualificação da Nvidia para uma CDU de 4 MW. James Lee, presidente da LG ES Company, disse que a entrada na rede de parceiros faz parte da estratégia da empresa para atender à expansão da infraestrutura de IA. – Resumen (español) LG Electronics se incorporó a la NVIDIA Partner Network como socio preferente en soluciones de energía y refrigeración. Su unidad de distribución de refrigerante de 2,6 MW recibió la calificación NVIDIA DSX Ready CDU. La empresa presentará sus unidades calificadas en Data Centre World Asia 2026, que se celebrará los días 29 y 30 de septiembre en Singapur. Summary (English) LG Electronics has joined the NVIDIA Partner Network as a preferred partner for power and cooling solutions. Its 2.6 MW coolant distribution unit received NVIDIA DSX Ready CDU qualification. The company will display its qualified units at Data Centre World Asia 2026 in Singapore on September 29 and 30.

artigo.texto: Em 30 de setembro, o vice-ministro da Agricultura e do Meio Ambiente, Le Trong Yen, presidiu uma reunião sobre a situação do trabalho do Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas durante os primeiros nove meses do ano e a implementação das tarefas para os últimos três meses de 2026. Segundo o Sr. Nguyen Tuan Quang, Diretor do Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas, nos primeiros nove meses de 2026, o Departamento prestou consultoria proativa e concluiu muitas tarefas importantes, conforme orientação do Governo Central e da liderança do Ministério. No que diz respeito à institucionalização das principais políticas do Partido, o Departamento liderou o desenvolvimento de um projeto sobre a gestão e utilização de créditos de carbono, que serviu de base para a publicação da Conclusão nº 71-KL/TW, de 17 de julho de 2026, pela Secretaria, sobre a gestão e utilização de créditos de carbono para o desenvolvimento socioeconômico sustentável e a segurança nacional. Simultaneamente, o Departamento colaborou com o Ministério do Meio Ambiente para assessorar na elaboração da Conclusão nº 75-KL/TW, de 28 de julho de 2026, do Comitê Central do Partido, sobre proteção ambiental e resposta proativa às mudanças climáticas na nova era; e para finalizar e submeter à promulgação o Programa de Ação Governamental completo e o Programa de Ação do Ministério para implementar essa conclusão. O Departamento coordenou-se estreitamente com o Departamento do Meio Ambiente para finalizar o projeto de lei que altera e complementa diversos artigos da Lei de Proteção Ambiental, para que o Governo o apresente à Comissão Permanente da Assembleia Nacional. O projeto encontra-se atualmente em fase de revisão técnica para garantir sua apresentação em tempo hábil à Assembleia Nacional, para apreciação e aprovação na sessão de outubro. O progresso na elaboração de documentos políticos e legais, de acordo com o programa de trabalho de 2026, está dentro do cronograma, sem atrasos em nenhum documento. De agora até o final do ano, o Departamento continuará a desenvolver um Decreto e uma Circular em paralelo com o projeto de alteração e complementação de diversos artigos da Lei de Proteção Ambiental, visando garantir a coerência do sistema jurídico. O Sr. Nguyen Tuan Quang, Diretor do Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas, forneceu informações sobre os resultados das tarefas realizadas. Foto: Trung Nguyen. O Departamento recomendou ao Ministério que submeta ao Governo uma Resolução aprovando o Acordo de Implementação do Artigo 6º do Acordo de Paris entre o Governo do Vietname e o Governo de Singapura. Atualmente, o Governo aprovou acordos bilaterais de troca de créditos de carbono com Singapura e o Japão; relativamente à Coreia do Sul e à Suíça , o Departamento está a promover negociações técnicas, prevendo-se a assinatura até ao final do ano. Em relação aos inventários de gases de efeito estufa, o Departamento mantém inventários em nível nacional, organiza sessões de treinamento para orientar empresas no cálculo e na redução de emissões e está implementando um sistema online de relatórios de inventário para reduzir custos e aumentar a transparência dos dados. No âmbito das relações externas, o Departamento está finalizando um plano para preparar uma delegação vietnamita para participar de importantes conferências internacionais sobre o clima ainda este ano. Segundo o diretor Nguyen Tuan Quang, nos últimos três meses de 2026, o Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas concentrará todos os recursos na conclusão do sistema de documentos legais imediatamente após a aprovação da proposta de emenda à Lei de Proteção Ambiental pela Assembleia Nacional; na implementação da Conclusão nº 71-KL/TW e da Conclusão nº 75-KL/TW; na aceleração da reforma dos procedimentos administrativos e na continuidade da coordenação da operação da plataforma de negociação de carbono; na organização da reunião do Comitê Conjunto Vietnã-Japão em outubro; na preparação meticulosa da delegação internacional e na modernização da infraestrutura do Banco de Dados Nacional de Mudanças Climáticas. Olhando para o futuro, até 2030, a unidade definiu como foco continuar a aprimorar o quadro político, pesquisando proativamente e preparando uma proposta para a Lei de Mudanças Climáticas, com um plano para submetê-la à Assembleia Nacional em 2029. Para melhorar a eficácia da coordenação de tarefas, representantes do Departamento de Ciência e Tecnologia enfatizaram a necessidade de padronizar normas técnicas, regulamentos e sistemas de medição, relato e verificação (MRV) em diversas áreas. Simultaneamente, a atualização do banco de dados nacional sobre mudanças climáticas deve seguir os princípios de "precisão, completude, integridade e viabilidade" para apoiar efetivamente o esforço nacional de transformação digital. Representantes do Departamento de Cooperação Internacional compartilharam as pressões práticas enfrentadas durante as negociações do Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris e sugeriram a possibilidade de criar um "banco de propostas de projetos" para compartilhar as experiências do Vietnã em resposta às mudanças climáticas com outros países. Representantes do Departamento de Meio Ambiente também propuseram o fortalecimento da integração de dados de monitoramento e a estreita vinculação das estratégias de desenvolvimento da economia circular e da economia verde ao roteiro para a redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa. O vice-ministro Le Trong Yen solicitou que a liderança e a equipe do Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas se concentrem intensamente em tarefas essenciais. Deve ser dada prioridade à finalização do projeto de lei que altera e complementa certos artigos da Lei de Proteção Ambiental, bem como aos projetos de decretos e circulares que orientam sua implementação. Simultaneamente, a pesquisa e o desenvolvimento da Lei de Mudanças Climáticas devem ser acelerados. O vice-ministro Le Trong Yen fez as considerações finais da reunião. Foto: Khuong Trung. artigo.texto: O mercado de carbono vietnamita precisa de impulso para gerar liquidez. A bolsa de carbono doméstica está operacional há mais de dois meses, mas registrou apenas 7 transações com 1.310 cotas, indicando que o maior desafio atualmente é criar uma demanda real para compra e venda. A bolsa de carbono doméstica foi oficialmente lançada, mas a liquidez permanece baixa, pois a demanda por compra e venda ainda não é suficiente. O desafio atual não é apenas ter uma bolsa, mas criar o incentivo para que as empresas participem efetivamente das negociações. Em 29 de junho de 2026, a bolsa de carbono doméstica iniciou oficialmente suas operações na plataforma da Bolsa de Valores de Hanói (HNX), marcando a transição da fase de preparação para a operação experimental do mercado de carbono doméstico. Na conferência de imprensa regular do Ministério da Agricultura e do Meio Ambiente, realizada em 16 de setembro, o vice-diretor do Departamento de Mudanças Climáticas, Nguyen Tuan Quang, afirmou que, após mais de dois meses de operação, a bolsa registrou 7 transações, totalizando 1.310 cotas negociadas. Entretanto, o Sr. Nguyen Tuan Anh, Vice-Diretor Geral da HNX, afirmou que mais de 510 milhões de toneladas de cotas foram registradas; o sistema nacional de registro conta com 92 organizações participantes, principalmente dos setores siderúrgico, cimenteiro e de energia térmica. Assim, a diferença entre o volume de mercadorias registado e o volume real de negociações indica que existem bolsas e mercadorias disponíveis, mas não em quantidade suficiente para criar liquidez. Segundo o Sr. Nguyen Tuan Anh, a HNX tem como objetivo operar o mercado de forma segura, estável e tranquila, ao mesmo tempo que continua a aprimorar o sistema e a adicionar canais de negociação online para facilitar a formação de uma demanda real. Para determinar o preço e a liquidez, o mercado precisa de adesão por parte das empresas; isso inclui a escassez de quotas e os custos de emissão que as empresas enfrentam. O Dr. Le Xuan Nghia, Diretor do Instituto de Consultoria e Desenvolvimento (CODE) e membro do Conselho Consultivo Nacional de Política Financeira e Monetária, acredita que um preço do carbono em torno de US$ 147 por tonelada poderia impactar significativamente as decisões empresariais. Quando o custo das emissões se tornar muito alto, as empresas terão que ponderar entre a compra de direitos de emissão e o investimento em soluções de redução de emissões. Além das quotas, os créditos de carbono são uma mercadoria importante no mercado. Por regulamentação, os créditos negociáveis devem ter origem a partir de 1 de janeiro de 2021 e enquadrar-se nos mecanismos especificados, incluindo os previstos nos artigos 6.2 e 6.4 do Acordo de Paris e os mecanismos nacionais de créditos de carbono. Você também pode gostar O fornecimento de créditos pode ser gerado a partir de diversas atividades de redução de emissões nas empresas, como tratamento e reciclagem de resíduos, redução das emissões de metano em aterros sanitários ou utilização de subprodutos como matérias-primas, desde que atendam aos requisitos de medição de acordo com as normas. No entanto, a oferta potencial não significa necessariamente que essa oferta seja imediatamente comercializável. Segundo a Sra. Pham Lien Anh, representante da IFC (International Finance Corporation), muitas empresas investiram em economia de energia e redução de emissões, mas não exploraram totalmente o potencial para a geração de créditos de carbono. Enquanto isso, a capacidade de mensurar, relatar, avaliar e verificar os resultados da redução de emissões (MRV) ainda está em fase inicial. Segundo o Sr. Nguyen The Minh, Diretor da Divisão de Banco de Investimento da An Binh Securities Joint Stock Company, a baixa liquidez na fase inicial é previsível para um mercado novo. O número de créditos elegíveis é limitado, a padronização ainda não foi implementada em larga escala e a oferta e a demanda ainda não estão intimamente ligadas. O Sr. Minh argumentou que as empresas atualmente não consideram o mercado de carbono um canal de financiamento importante; a capacidade de consultoria nacional é limitada, enquanto o custo de contratação de especialistas estrangeiros é elevado. Os padrões técnicos para avaliação, certificação e listagem de certificados no mercado precisam ser aprimorados. Segundo o Sr. Minh, um período piloto suficientemente longo e mecanismos de incentivo são necessários para atrair membros e desenvolver uma equipe de consultores nacionais. Outro fator determinante vem do mercado internacional. O Mecanismo de Ajustamento de Carbono nas Fronteiras (CBAM) da União Europeia está a exercer ainda mais pressão sobre as empresas exportadoras com elevadas emissões. Segundo a Sra. Pham Lien Anh, o custo atual da conformidade com o CBAM é de aproximadamente 75 euros por tonelada de CO2 equivalente. Se os mecanismos internacionais permitirem a utilização de uma parte dos créditos de carbono para compensar as obrigações, a procura por créditos de conformidade poderá aumentar ainda mais. A pressão para a adoção de práticas sustentáveis também se estende às indústrias manufatureiras voltadas para a exportação. O setor têxtil é um exemplo. Embora não esteja entre os 110 primeiros estabelecimentos a receber cotas, muitas empresas do setor tiveram que migrar para energias limpas e energia solar fotovoltaica em telhados, conforme exigido por marcas internacionais para manter seus pedidos. Nesse contexto, o mercado de carbono não se resume apenas à conformidade ambiental, mas está se tornando parte da competitividade e da capacidade de participar das cadeias de suprimentos globais. artigo.texto: Palm Springs extends data center moratorium to 2028 The facilities were described as a “stress on local infrastructure and environmental assets with very limited community benefits,” by city staff during Wednesday’s meeting. The Palm Springs City Council on Wednesday extended a moratorium on approving data center applications and permits through Aug. 25, 2028, giving the city time to write zoning rules for the facilities. The council first adopted the moratorium on Aug. 26 as a 45-day interim urgency ordinance set to expire Oct. 10. The extension adds 22 months and 15 days, for a total of two years. State law requires a four-fifths vote to extend an urgency ordinance, and the motion carried. Local reporting and journalism you can count on. Subscribe to The Palm Springs Post The city’s municipal and zoning codes do not define or regulate data centers, and no zoning standards, setback rules, noise standards, utility demand thresholds or environmental mitigation requirements have been adopted for them. Planning Director Chris Hadwin said the concerns behind the moratorium include environmental impacts and heavy demands on land, electricity, water and fossil fuels. He also cited “stress on local infrastructure and environmental assets with very limited community benefits.” The ordinance defines a data center as a structure or site used primarily to store, manage, process and transmit digital data, including server farms, cloud computing and artificial intelligence processing. Equipment that is secondary to another permitted use, such as servers serving a hospital, office or hotel, is excluded. Hadwin said the definition “is mirroring a national standard and what other cities throughout California and the nation are doing in terms of defining data centers.” Hadwin said the extension allows city planners time to integrate rules about data centers into the ongoing zoning code update by “establishing development standards, permitted uses, and locations of where these might make sense in Palm Springs, as well as identifying any specific environmental considerations that need to be taken into account,” Hadwin said. The moratorium is meant to be rescinded when the new code is adopted, possibly in the same vote. Staff also said they will meet with Coachella Valley partners, industry professionals, the tech sector and environmental groups. Councilmember Jeffrey Bernstein said the definition may need revisiting as the industry changes. He cautioned that gaps could let a project slip through. “We know there’s gray area,” he said. Councilmember Grace Garner urged those who spoke up at recent meetings about data centers to take more interest in the city’s zoning code update. “The zoning code in general is a really important document that also impacts the sustainability of our city,” she said, and that it covers all aspects of planning from density and building design to parking. She also encouraged attendance at an upcoming listening session related to heat and shade.

artigo.texto: They always say, “Follow the money.” When we do that, we wind up in some interesting places. In the case of the money we’re about to follow today, well, just hang on. At last week’s meeting of Virginia’s Health Insurance Reform Commission, the State Corporation Commission Bureau of Insurance announced that monthly premiums for the state’s Healthcare Exchange are being reduced. That’s a lot of titles with capital letters to get through, but it’s not every day that rates for anything go down. Keven Patchett, executive director for the Virginia Health Exchange, told the commission that about 200,000 people will benefit from the lower rate. He attributed this to the $150 million that the General Assembly had added to the program’s funding this year. Democratic legislators were quick to point out that they were able to increase this funding because the state’s treasury will be fattened by $600 million in revenue from Virginia’s new tax on the electricity that data centers use. That tax was the compromise between those who wanted to eliminate the sales tax exemption on data centers eight years early and those who felt that would set a bad example by going back on the state’s word that the exemption will run through 2035. Not long after last week’s commission meeting, Senate Democrats sent out a news release: “Virginia Senate Democrats Applaud Newly Announced Virginia Healthcare Exchange Premium Monthly Reductions Funded by Data Center Consumption Tax.” This somewhat stretches the definition of “newly announced” because Cardinal healthcare reporter Emily Schabacker wrote back in July that these premiums would be going down, but let’s move on. The Democrats’ release went on to say: “The Virginia Premium Savings program represents a decisive action by Virginia’s Democratic majority to protect healthcare coverage for working families following Congress’s failure to renew enhanced federal Affordable Care Act premium subsidies that expired on December 31, 2025. The new premiums announced at the HIRC meeting demonstrate the remarkable impact of this historic investment.” It went on to include several charts to show what the release said were “Real Examples: How Virginia’s Data Center Tax Funds Healthcare Affordability.” Here’s one of them: Now, as Paul Harvey used to say, here’s the rest of the story. On the one hand, this action demonstrates how that tax revenue from data centers’ electricity consumption is being used to fund what General Assembly Democrats consider worthy priorities. There’s another way to look at this, though: Virginia is now yoked to data centers as a way to fund healthcare — and other things. The current law taxes data centers at a rate of $0.011 per kilowatt hour on all electricity consumed at each center on a monthly basis. There’s a philosophical question here we won’t get to today: Why are data centers singled out for their electricity use? Yes, they use a lot of power, but so do other things. A Walmart Supercenter might use more power per day than some small data centers. On a square-footage basis, cannabis growhouses — which we’ll soon have — use more electricity than data centers. If we’re now taxing electrons, why are we singling out one industry? Why shouldn’t we treat all electrons equally? If we’re taxing data centers just because they’re unpopular, is that a good precedent? Those will have to be questions for another day. The new law caps this tax at $600 million in revenue, with any excess returned to data center companies. Laws, though, can change and laws that set a particular dollar figure are often susceptible to changes when inflation changes their value. Let’s assume that Virginia’s current number of data centers — the Data Center Map puts their number at 674 but other sites give different figures — is sufficient to generate that $600 million in revenue. This seems a good assumption. Based on that, this particular tax does not create an incentive for Virginia to add more data centers — because they’d just wind up paying electricity taxes in excess of that $600 million cap, so the money would get returned. There are other incentives for Virginia to attract more data centers (primarily local tax revenue) and, of course, some disincentives (power consumption, water consumption, political blowback). However, what happens when a future Virginia legislature decides it wants more than $600 million a year from data centers? Maybe those future legislators cite inflation for devaluing that $600 million. Maybe they cite growing demands that need to be funded. Maybe they cite both. We know both will happen eventually. At what point does Virginia decide that it needs more data centers so it can fund whatever it wants to fund? At whatever point that is, then data centers turn from a nuisance into a necessity. Let’s suppose that the $600 million cap is lifted someday so that the tax brings in whatever amount it can bring in. If that were to happen, then Virginia has a clear incentive to want more data centers because more data centers would mean more power consumption — which would mean more tax revenue to pay for the Healthcare Exchange and other things. Years ago, we saw the lottery sold to Virginia voters as a way to fund schools. (This is often misunderstood. The lottery revenues can never equal the amount schools need, so the lottery doesn’t generate “extra” revenue for schools. It’s just an accounting measure under which the first part of school funding comes from lottery revenue, the rest from the general fund.) We’re currently seeing off-track betting presented to voters in Amherst and Pulaski counties as a way to generate tax revenue that can help reduce pressure on property tax bills. artigo.texto: What leaders are arguing about According to diplomats familiar with the talks, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis intend to reopen the carbon-market dispute during a Tuesday meeting in Prague. Their ask is to put off the 2028 step that would bring heating and road transport fuels into the EU's Emissions Trading System, the add-on commonly referred to as ETS2. Their rationale, per those diplomats: with prices still elevated, expanding the market now would hit the buildings and transport sectors and strain people's purchasing power. Who wants the plan to proceed A group of six countries is pushing back on another delay after the expansion had already slipped by a year. Denmark, the Netherlands, Spain, Finland, Sweden and Luxembourg warned in a document shared with other EU governments, "We are concerned by recent calls for further amendments to and postponement of ETS2." They added, "Going forward, EU businesses and households need political stability and predictability." That split captures the EU's balancing act. The bloc wants to stay on track for net zero by 2050 without undercutting its competitiveness with the US and China or prompting voter blowback over higher costs. Elections next year in France, Italy, Spain and Poland only raise the political temperature. Prices, policy and the market Since the war started, the price of gas in Europe has climbed to over twice its earlier level, and earlier in September it reached the highest point since late 2022. Power has jumped too, with prices up around 77% in France and roughly 60% in Germany. To ease concerns about adding ETS2 on top of that, the European Commission has outlined tools to prevent sharp price moves and soften energy cost worries. EU ministers are expected to sign off on those tweaks on Oct. 9 in Luxembourg. Beyond the ETS2 timing fight, Meloni and Babis also plan to discuss a wider revamp of ETS1, the current carbon market, put forward by the commission in July. They also want to lessen how carbon prices affect electricity by, for a limited period, capping the degree to which emission costs are passed into wholesale power prices. And they favor tighter transparency and oversight, with closer monitoring by the European Commission, the European Securities and Markets Authority and the EU Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators. Established in 2005, the EU's cap-and-trade system sets progressively tighter emission caps for more than 10,000 installations across industries such as steel, cement and chemicals. Across the bloc, carbon charges make up about 11% of the average electricity bill, with a bigger effect where fossil fuels dominate. In Poland, that share can reach as high as 24%. artigo.texto: How unpopular are large data centers in Wisconsin? Very unpopular, as 74% of voters in a new poll said they believe the costs of data centers outweigh their benefits. The poll, released Wednesday by the Marquette University Law School, said opposition to large data centers is up nearly 20 points from the 55% that opposed them a year ago. For data center operators, the news is actually better than it was a month ago in the Marquette poll, when 78% opposed them. Opposition to data centers has grown most sharply among independents and Democrats since last October, with 83% of independents and 90% of Democrats now saying the costs outweigh the benefits, the poll said. Republican opposition increased through July, but has declined by 10 percentage points since then, to 57%, in September. The so-called hyperscale data centers accommodate artificial intelligence, which is also increasingly unpopular. The Marquette poll said two-thirds of voters now believe AI is bad for society. The technology’s growing unfavorability comes as chip maker Nvidia unveiled a new security platform to stop AI agents from hacking and AI executives agreed to self-police their development of the technology. The poll was conducted Sept. 16-23, interviewing 843 Wisconsin registered voters.

artigo.texto: A controversial energy project in Southern California is moving forward after city leaders dramatically changed course. In Chino, the City Council reversed an earlier denial and approved a large battery storage facility that had faced strong local opposition. Here's what to know As the Daily Bulletin reported, the council's vote put the project back on track after the council had rejected the proposal. Batteries store power when it is cheap and plentiful, such as during overnight hours, and send it back to the grid when demand rises. That ability to shift energy is one of the biggest advantages of large-scale battery projects. They can prevent outages, improve grid reliability, and reduce the need to fire up backup power plants during times of peak demand. At the same time, these projects can create concerns about safety, noise, zoning, traffic, and more. More background California has relied heavily on battery storage as it adds renewable electricity to the grid. Solar and wind power are critical for cutting pollution, but because their production varies depending on weather conditions, batteries smooth out the available supply. Still, battery storage has become a flashpoint in some cities. Residents and officials often want information about fire prevention, emergency response plans, maintenance, and how a facility could affect nearby public spaces. What's being done? Across California, developers and public officials are under pressure to pair new battery projects with safety measures and transparent planning. That can include fire suppression systems, monitoring technology, property setbacks from sensitive areas, and coordination with local emergency responders. Cities also play an important role in making sure residents understand what is being proposed before votes take place. Clear public outreach, open hearings, and detailed safety reviews can help communities weigh trade-offs with greater confidence. Where can I learn more? Battery storage is expanding in California and beyond, even as communities continue to debate where and how these projects should be built. • In San Diego, Peregrine Energy Storage started one of the biggest battery projects in the region. • In Idaho, Idaho Power enlisted Prevalon to build the state's largest battery storage system. • Near Las Vegas, the Gemini project brought the largest solar and battery system online. • At Nevada's Reid Gardner site, a former coal plant became a huge grid battery hub. • Utility officials said geothermal power was a massive battery right under communities' feet. artigo.texto: Karbon‑X (OTCQB:KARX) Reports Record Fiscal 2026 Revenue of $55.9 Million as Company Scales Global Carbon Market Operations Revenue increased approximately 1,670% year over year during the Company's first full fiscal year of large-scale carbon credit trading. - Record fiscal 2026 revenue of $55.9 million, up approximately 1,670% year over year - Completed first full fiscal year of large-scale carbon credit trading - Expanded trading and project development operations across Europe, Latin America and North America - Total assets increased 42% to $9.6 million from $6.8 million - Converted $7.0 million of convertible notes and accrued interest into 10.6 million shares of common stock All financial amounts are stated in U.S. dollars unless otherwise noted. CALGARY, AB / ACCESS Newswire / October 1, 2026 / Karbon‑X Corp. KARX ("Karbon‑X" or the "Company"), a vertically integrated climate solutions company operating across global carbon markets, today reported financial and operational results for the fiscal year ended May 31, 2026, reflecting a significant increase in operating scale across its carbon credit trading and project development activities. Karbon‑X generated record fiscal 2026 revenue of $55.9 million, compared with $3.16 million in fiscal 2025, representing an increase of approximately 1,670% year over year. Gross profit was $0.86 million, compared with $0.80 million in the prior year. Fiscal 2026 results reflected a shift in revenue mix toward high-volume, lower-margin trading activity as Karbon‑X completed its first full year of large-scale carbon credit trading. "Fiscal 2026 moved Karbon-X into a new stage of commercial growth," said Chad Clovis, Chief Executive Officer of Karbon-X. "Revenue reached nearly eighteen times the prior-year level as we scaled our trading activity, expanded our project development presence across three continents and built a broader operating platform. As key projects advance beyond their initial investment and development phases and toward measurement, reporting and verification activities, we see an opportunity to build higher-margin revenue streams through future credit issuances. This foundation positions us for the next phase of growth, with a focus on improving our revenue mix, strengthening margins and translating our global capabilities into long-term shareholder value." Watch: CEO Update: Fiscal 2026 in Review Fiscal 2026 Financial Highlights - Record revenue of $55.9 million, compared with $3.16 million in fiscal 2025, representing approximately 1,670% year-over-year growth - Gross profit of $0.86 million, compared with $0.80 million in fiscal 2025 - Total assets increased 42% to $9.6 million at May 31, 2026, compared with $6.8 million at May 31, 2025 - Converted $7.0 million of convertible notes and accrued interest into 10.6 million shares of common stock, including a $3.5 million note issued to Hedera Foundation SEZC and approximately $1.1 million of accrued interest Fiscal 2026 Business Highlights 1. Scaled Carbon Credit Trading Karbon‑X completed its first full year of large-scale carbon credit trading, driving a significant increase in revenue and commercial activity. 2. Expanded Across Three Continents The Company established trading and project development operations across Europe, Latin America and North America, significantly expanding its international reach and participation in global carbon markets. 3. Strengthened Project Development Capabilities On June 27, 2025, Karbon‑X completed an asset acquisition from Allcot AG, adding a diversified portfolio of carbon projects, intellectual property, databases and contractual rights. The acquisition expanded the Company's project development capabilities and international presence across key carbon markets. 4. Broadened Industrial Market Participation Karbon‑X continued to serve customers across mining, forestry, transportation, civil earthworks, and oil and gas services as it expanded its commercial carbon market activities. 5. Expanded Consumer Access Alongside its business-to-business operations, Karbon-X continued to operate its globally available mobile application, providing individuals with subscription-based access to verified climate projects. Depending on the subscription selected, users are allocated verified carbon credits corresponding to approximately 200 to 400 kilograms of CO₂ per month. These allocations are traceable to the underlying projects, with the associated credits retired in aggregated batches in accordance with the Company's retirement process. In fiscal 2027, Karbon-X intends to continue growing its consumer subscription offering as part of its broader strategy to develop recurring, customer-facing revenue alongside its institutional and carbon market operations. 6. Balance Sheet and Debt Conversion Karbon‑X ended fiscal 2026 with total assets of $9.6 million, an increase of 42% from $6.8 million at May 31, 2025. During fiscal 2026, holders converted $7.0 million of convertible notes and accrued interest into 10.6 million shares of common stock, including a $3.5 million convertible note issued to Hedera Foundation SEZC together with approximately $1.1 million of accrued interest, converted in May 2026. Subsequent to fiscal year end and through August 31, 2026, an additional approximately $0.79 million of convertible note principal, accrued interest and related fees was converted to equity, further reducing the Company's outstanding convertible debt obligations. Karbon‑X had 94,885,028 common shares outstanding as of May 31, 2026. Building on Scale in Fiscal 2027 Following a year of significant revenue growth and international expansion, Karbon-X enters fiscal 2027 with a substantially larger operating platform spanning carbon credit trading, project development and customer-facing climate solutions. artigo.texto: A produção tropicalizada de baterias garantirá a segurança da matriz energética brasileira De olho no potencial do país, fabricantes traçam planos de longo prazo para suprir o mercado de armazenamento de energia Atualizado Mercado ainda incipiente no país, as soluções de armazenamento de energia em baterias, essenciais para garantir flexibilidade e segurança às redes elétricas, ganham um novo impulso com a queda no custo das baterias de íon-lítio no mercado internacional, com a maior facilidade de negociação nos contratos de energia e com a perspectiva de avanços no ambiente regulatório — inclusive com o esperado Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade destinado a sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, agendado para dezembro. As ações dos fabricantes de tecnologia no mercado brasileiro focam estratégias de longo prazo, visando consolidar uma produção tropicalizada, como avalia Alexandre Baldy, vice-presidente sênior da multinacional chinesa BYD no Brasil, que anunciou em fevereiro deste ano um investimento de R$ 500 milhões para a fabricação de Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias — em inglês, Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) — no país. “Estamos falando de uma decisão de longo prazo”, define. “É um movimento baseado na confiança que temos no potencial desse mercado e na importância que o armazenamento terá para o futuro da matriz energética brasileira”, diz. Segundo Baldy, a estratégia visa desenvolver capacidade industrial local e, ao mesmo tempo, criar condições para que uma cadeia brasileira de fornecedores cresça junto com esse mercado. “Esse processo de nacionalização também permitirá atender aos requisitos previstos pelo Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) e pelo Ministério de Minas e Energia para o Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade, ampliando o acesso dos investidores a linhas de financiamento do banco, tanto para projetos ligados ao leilão quanto para outras aplicações”, afirma. No leilão, há dois segmentos: armazenamento nacional, com exigência de, no mínimo, 15% de componentes locais, e geral, sem requisitos de nacionalização. A Contemporary Amperey Technology Co., Limited (CATL), outro superfabricante chinês de tecnologia, pretende fornecer para os dois. Para participar do leilão nacional, a CATL anunciou uma parceria estratégica com o Grupo Moura, um dos principais fabricantes de baterias do país, sediado no município de Belo Jardim (PE). “Para maximizar nosso impacto, estamos nos preparando ativamente, em conjunto com parceiros nacionais, para fornecer equipamentos credenciados, implementando plataformas avançadas de armazenamento com capacidade nativa de frid-forming [seguidores de redes]”, explica Ray See, vice-presidente de negócios para as Américas da CATL. Ele diz que, além de fornecer equipamentos, a parceria com o Grupo Moura visa integrar os sistemas de baterias localmente com um fabricante nacional e cumprir as regras de nacionalização previstas pelo governo federal. Para suprir o leilão de armazenamento geral, a CATL vai importar os equipamentos. Nos últimos anos, as vendas acumuladas de soluções BESS no Brasil somaram somente 1,9 GWh, dos quais 730 MWh foram comercializados em 2025, especialmente nos setores comercial e industrial. Nesse ano, os financiamentos registrados em BESS atingiram R$ 126 milhões. É um volume maior que o registrado em 2024 (R$ 117 milhões), mas que não reflete a real expansão da tecnologia no país, aponta levantamento do Clean Energy Latin America (Cela), uma boutique de investimentos do setor de energia renovável da região. “A expectativa é que os primeiros leilões dedicados exclusivamente ao armazenamento, previstos para 2026, marquem uma nova fase de escala para o segmento, com impacto direto nos volumes de financiamento”, confia Camila Ramos, diretora-executiva do Cela. “Podemos ter até um crescimento explosivo dos sistemas de armazenamento por baterias no Brasil nos próximos oito anos”, acredita Markus Vlasits, presidente da Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae). “A corrida das empresas estrangeiras e brasileiras por esse mercado deve movimentar mais de R$ 80 bilhões em investimentos até 2034”, diz. Só o leilão previsto para este ano deve destravar R$ 10 bilhões em projetos, estima Vlasits. Segundo ele, esse aumento dos negócios no setor de armazenamento de energia em baterias é movido pela redução de quase 70% no custo das baterias de lítio nos últimos três anos e a necessidade crescente de flexibilidade no sistema elétrico do país para gerenciar as diversas fontes de energias renováveis, como a solar e eólica. “Teremos muitos projetos dos fabricantes voltados para atender o setor comercial e industrial, além de projetos de descarbonização na região amazônica”, destaca. A WEG avalia que o potencial de negócios não se restringe apenas a grandes projetos. “Acreditamos muito também nas aplicações de médio porte, principalmente soluções BESS junto à carga e combinado com geração distribuída”, diz Manfred Peter Johann, vice-presidente de automação e sistemas da WEG. “A bateria pode ajudar a superar gargalos de fornecimento de energia e limitações da rede, garantir backup e maior confiabilidade para o consumidor e permitir arbitragem de energia entre diferentes horários.” No início deste ano, a WEG anunciou a construção de uma nova fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) em Itajaí (SC), com financiamento de R$ 280 milhões do programa BNDES Mais Inovação. A nova unidade ampliará capacidade produtiva para até 2 GWh ao ano e deverá entrar em operação no segundo semestre de 2027, informa Johann. “Praticamente todo o sistema pode ser industrializado no país”, indica. “O principal componente que ainda depende de importação é a célula da bateria, cuja fabricação exige uma escala muito maior para se tornar economicamente competitiva.” Praticamente dominado por fabricantes de tecnologia de ponta e gigantes industriais, o mercado de BESS movimenta t

artigo.texto: Proven project execution, intelligent software, and engineering expertise combine to deliver safe, reliable energy storage at scale HELSINKI, October 01, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Technology group Wärtsilä and RCT Solutions GmbH today launched Valo, a global battery energy storage system integrator designed to help customers navigate the growing complexity of delivering utility-scale energy storage projects. Energy storage projects are getting bigger, but scale is only part of the challenge. The real complexity lies in delivering systems that can meet evolving grid and market requirements globally, executing flexible, secure, and resilient responses in microseconds. This is where Valo's end-to-end solution stands apart. "Customers should not have to manage a collection of technologies and vendors and hope everything works together as intended," said Dr. Luke Witmer, Chief Technology Officer of Valo. "The performance of an energy storage project depends on how effectively every element of the system is managed altogether. Integration defines outcomes. Valo is built to take accountability for those outcomes by bringing hardware, software, engineering, and long-term services together under one roof." Valo may be new as a company, but it is not new to energy storage. Wärtsilä's Energy Storage business is already a leading global system integrator with utility-scale storage technology, intelligent controls and optimisation software, system integration expertise, and comprehensive lifecycle services developed across some of the world's most demanding power markets. Germany-based RCT Solutions contributes deep engineering expertise, global supply chain capabilities, and international experience designing and establishing large-scale battery and solar manufacturing operations. Together, these position Valo with enhanced operational flexibility and supply chain resilience to accelerate innovation and support customer growth. Valo enters the market with 20+ GWh in over 130 utility-scale energy storage projects worldwide. For existing customers, the new company will provide continuity alongside expanded capability. The technologies and teams they know today remain in place, now supported by broader engineering, supply chain, and manufacturing expertise. "Energy storage has a defining role in building a more reliable and resilient energy future," said Prof. Dr. Peter Fath, Chief Executive Officer of Valo. "Valo has the experience, technology, and people to deliver reliable performance at scale from day one. But our ambition goes further. We will raise the standard for how energy storage systems are designed, delivered, and supported throughout their lifetime."

artigo.texto: O Google programou o lançamento experimental de um satélite equipado com um chip de inteligência artificial para testar processamento computacional em baixa órbita. A iniciativa investiga se parte da infraestrutura hoje concentrada em data centers terrestres pode operar fora do planeta. Receba todas as análises e informações da Geocracia pelo WhatsApp O equipamento integra o Project Suncatcher, foi desenvolvido com a Planet e deverá seguir no veículo Transporter-18, da SpaceX. O teste avaliará se uma unidade de processamento tensorial suporta vibração, pressão, temperatura e radiação próprias do ambiente espacial. A hipótese favorável combina incidência solar mais direta e a possibilidade de processar grandes cargas de dados em constelações. No território, o interesse decorre da pressão exercida por data centers convencionais sobre redes elétricas e sistemas de abastecimento de água. A escala comercial continua incerta. Entre os obstáculos estão a degradação dos componentes, a comunicação por laser entre satélites, a manutenção de equipamentos em órbita e a necessidade de tornar o conjunto tecnicamente eficaz e economicamente competitivo. Já conversou com o território hoje? Experimente a Geocracia.ai O lançamento é um experimento e não significa que servidores orbitais estejam prontos para substituir instalações em solo. artigo.texto: Proposed changes to free carbon allowances could halve the investment generated by the Commission’s planned conditions for industrial support, the EU executive warned. The clash with lawmakers in Brussels exposed a central dispute in the carbon market overhaul: how much relief companies should receive, and what they should deliver in return. “We want to stop being in the business of handing out free lunches,” Rosalinde van der Vlies, the Commission’s director for carbon markets and clean mobility, told Parliament’s environment committee. She supported much of rapporteur Peter Liese’s (EPP/DEU) draft report but challenged changes to investment requirements and intervention in carbon prices. Tight is right. Too tight is broken. — Peter Liese (EPP/DEU), rapporteur of Committee on the Environment, Climate and Food Safety The debate concerns a revision proposed in July to support industrial competitiveness while delivering the EU’s 2040 climate target. The emissions trading system requires covered companies to surrender allowances equivalent to their emissions. Some manufacturers receive allowances free of charge to reduce the risk of production moving to countries with weaker climate rules. More breathing space, but on what terms? Mr Liese’s opening statement, read by fellow European People’s Party MEP Jessica Polfjärd (SWE) in his absence, argued that the carbon market needed to give industry a more realistic path towards cleaner production. “Tight is right. Too tight is broken,” he said in the statement. He supported linking additional free allowances to investment and protecting jobs. But his draft seeks to adjust the Commission’s approach as businesses struggle with energy costs and international competition. He also urged governments to use carbon-market revenues more effectively to finance clean energy. The Commission argued that free allowances had always been intended to give companies time to develop and implement cleaner technologies. Ms Van der Vlies said that, after 14 years and €255 billion in free allocation, too little investment had followed. The Commission wanted to continue and expand support, she said, while ensuring it strengthened European production. Her sharpest objection concerned a proposed exemption from investment conditions covering 40 per cent of installations. That would halve the investment volume compared with the Commission’s proposal, she told MEPs. The figure was the Commission’s assessment of the draft’s impact, rather than an agreed finding of the committee. Companies that moved first fear losing out The disagreement also ran within Mr Liese’s own political group. After presenting his statement, Ms Polfjärd explicitly switched to speaking for herself and criticised the draft. Weakening the carbon market, she argued, could disadvantage companies that had already invested heavily in reducing emissions. “We must reward the frontrunners, not make them regret that they moved first,” she said. Ms Polfjärd also questioned whether the Commission’s proposed Investment Booster would favour new investments over businesses that had already taken the financial risk of building cleaner facilities. Other groups challenged the reform from opposite directions. Czech conservative Alexandr Vondra rejected investment conditions as another regulatory burden and called for free allowances to remain available for longer. Dutch socialist Mohammed Chahim questioned whether either the Commission’s proposal or Mr Liese’s draft would deliver the emissions reductions needed for the EU’s climate target. “It doesn’t add up,” he said. We want to stop being in the business of handing out free lunches. — Rosalinde van der Vlies, Commission’s director for carbon markets and clean mobility Renew Europe’s Emma Wiesner (SWE) argued that weakening emissions trading would prolong exposure to expensive imported fossil fuels. Industry needed certainty and investment, she said, but reducing several elements of the system at once would undermine the incentive to move towards cleaner production. Carbon prices become another dividing line The Commission also opposed proposed changes to the mechanism for dealing with excessive carbon-price fluctuations. Ms Van der Vlies warned against trying to “engineer a carbon price through frequent market intervention”, arguing that this would reduce predictability for investors and make emissions reductions more costly. The committee had already backed keeping a mechanism that removes surplus allowances from the market in September, while proposing a larger reserve buffer to give industry more flexibility. There was more common ground over directing revenues towards the transition. Mr Liese argued that governments had not used the money efficiently enough. Socialist MEP Annalisa Corrado (ITA) similarly warned that revenues needed to support cleaner production rather than disappear into general national budgets. Thursday’s discussion did not settle Parliament’s position. The committee is due to vote on 1 December, with amendments closing on 6 October. The negotiations will now test whether lawmakers can give struggling manufacturers more room without weakening incentives to cut emissions. They must also preserve investment certainty for companies already making the transition.

artigo.texto: American Battery Technology Company receives licence for up to US$100M in black-mass exports Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security authorised sales under specified terms; the company did not name an export buyer or shipment date. On Oct. 1, American Battery Technology Company NASDAQABAT announced it had received a U.S. Commerce licence covering up to US$100 million in recycled black-mass export sales. The approved ceiling exceeds the US$21.7 million of revenue the company reported for its fiscal year ended June 30, 2026, but the licence is not a purchase order. The Oct. 1 announcement names the U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security as the issuer; it identifies no export buyer, contract term or shipment date. The company's GlobeNewswire copy appeared at 6 a.m. EDT on Oct. 1, ahead of the regular Nasdaq session. The previous close could not measure a share reaction to the licence. The Reno, Nevada, company recycles spent batteries and manufacturing scrap at its first commercial plant, which began operating in 2023, according to the Oct. 1 release. It produces copper, aluminum, steel, lithium-rich intermediates and black mass. The black mass contains lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese and graphite for further refining. The company's Sept. 14 results put the first facility's processing design at 20,000 tonnes a year, while reporting US$24.8 million in fiscal 2026 cost of goods sold. Against US$21.7 million in revenue, that left a US$3.1 million GAAP gross loss. The same report showed US$1.7 million in adjusted gross profit after excluding depreciation and stock-based compensation. The company held US$49.5 million in cash and reported no outstanding debt at June 30, according to those results. A licensed export shipment would give investors a dated sale to compare with the US$100 million authorisation, but the Oct. 1 release supplies no shipment schedule. Licence Terms and Export Volumes Remain Undisclosed The company described the permission as a Defense Priorities and Allocation System licence to sell exported recycled black mass under specified terms. Its Oct. 1 release links the decision to recently enacted federal export controls on critical battery materials. It does not disclose the licence's expiry, permitted tonnage, destinations or sale price per tonne. "The ability to continue selling exported recycled black mass critical minerals supports current operations, strengthens the company's market position, and further enhances its ability to capitalize on growing demand for critical minerals across global supply chains," the company said in its Oct. 1 release. Those annual sales include more than black mass: the company also reports revenue from recycled products and byproducts. The Oct. 1 announcement gave no revenue forecast for exports under the licence. The US$100 million is a regulatory sales ceiling, not a projection of black-mass revenue. The Sept. 14 results said the company was developing a second recycling facility designed to handle about 100,000 tonnes of battery material a year. Chief executive Ryan Melsert said in the Oct. 1 release that the facility is supported by US$150 million in competitive U.S. Department of Energy grants. The Oct. 1 announcement does not set a commissioning date for that proposed capacity; the grants are separate from any black-mass export sales. Read more: E3 Lithium says Clearwater engineering advances toward completion in 2027 The first export order or shipment under the licence announced on Oct. 1 is the next test of its commercial value. The company has given no date for either, leaving the announced US$100 million as a ceiling until sales are disclosed.

artigo.texto: While President Trump was holding a press conference at the White House this morning and extolling the AI-related work of Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, SpaceX’s Elon Musk, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and a promo for Wednesday night’s South Park episode dropped. It was less salutary. Here’s the logline for Episode 6 of Season 29: “Butters is unhappy with the data centers that the billionaires are building in our backyards.” The clip opens with an X-Pest exterminator guy ringing the doorbell at Butters’ home. Watch on Deadline “I understand you’ve got some billionaires in your backyard,” he says. “Yeah, there’s more of these stupid billionaires every day!” replies Butters. The first image from the episode (see it above) shows Butters in what appears to be his backyard with the X-Pest exterminator guy, who has strapped on his tank of poison and has his sprayer wand at the ready. The topic of data centers is a hot one across the country and especially in Hollywood, where unions and workers worry about job displacement and writers and directors express concern over what it might do to their art. Among the biggest players in the data center land rush is, of course, Oracle CEO and Paramount-WBD deal financier Larry Ellison. South Park airs on Comedy Central, which is owned by Paramount. As in the past, the show’s creators are seemingly not afraid to bite the hand that feeds them. Mark Ruffalo and others have decried the introduction of “really profoundly scary technology” into Hollywood and how AI might impact media outlets soon to be owned by Ellison and his son David. “Larry is a classic oligarch,” wrote Ruffalo. “They are crushing workers and consolidating the wealth of the world for their own power and concentrated dominance.” Paramount, for its part, responded by accusing Ruffalo of using “antisemitic tropes” in his argument, especially when linking the Ellisons’ studio acquisition to Oracle’s work with the Israeli military.
