artigo.texto: Resumo - Redata foi aprovado neste mês e cria regime tributário para serviços de data center - Safra vê oportunidade para companhias do setor elétrico com o novo regime - Sete elétricas podem se beneficiar do cenário de expansão dos data centers - Distribuidoras como ENEL, CPFL, Light, Equatorial e Energisa entram na lista - Axia e Copel podem ganhar com maiores pagamentos por capacidade - Demanda de eletricidade dos data centers pode crescer 15% ao ano até 2030 A aprovação neste mês do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center, o Redata, colocou o setor elétrico no radar do Safra. Segundo o banco, o novo regime de incentivos fiscais cria uma oportunidade para companhias de energia, à medida que a expansão dos data centers no Brasil deve pressionar a demanda por eletricidade nos próximos anos. Na leitura do Safra, sete empresas do setor podem se beneficiar desse cenário. Entre as distribuidoras aparecem ENEL, CPFL, Light, Equatorial e Energisa. Já no campo das geradoras, os maiores pagamentos por capacidade tenderiam a favorecer Axia e Copel. Data centers pressionam a demanda por energia O apetite dos data centers por eletricidade explica boa parte do otimismo. A demanda de energia desses centros de processamento pode crescer 15% ao ano até 2030, um ritmo que reforça a expectativa de expansão do consumo no país. Segundo o Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia, o PDE 2035, a capacidade instalada de data centers projetada para 2035 no Brasil é de 20 GW. O avanço tende a elevar a fatia dos data centers dentro do consumo total de energia. Num cenário em que essa participação sobe de 5% para 8% da demanda total, o aumento potencial no consumo de energia seria de 2,7%. O ponto de partida considerado é de 5% de participação, com projeção de chegada a 8%. Pressão de preços já aparece nos EUA O efeito da expansão dos data centers sobre os preços de energia já tem referência internacional. Entre 2020 e 2025, regiões dos Estados Unidos registraram alta de cerca de 30% nos preços de energia.

artigo.texto: hug this cuddly toy, and hear the piercing scream of real AI data centers for ‘adopt a data center,’ basura interviewed dozens of people living near data centers across the US. Adopt A Data Center takes the form of a plush data center toy Adopt A Data Center is a satirical project by New York-based creative studio Basura for music artist Big Data. Basura is known for unconventional creative projects including ‘Dirt Shoes.’ The project takes the form of a plush data center toy that plays the high-pitched hum of a real AI data center when hugged, using a familiar object to examine the ways technological progress is presented and experienced. The project explores the emotional packaging of technological advancements, using satire as a way to encourage closer attention to the facts surrounding data centers. Its accompanying ‘Adoption Site’ collects links to research and reporting on their impact, while Basura interviewed dozens of people living near data centers across the US. The sound used in the toy comes from a resident in Virginia. Childhood toy look combines with Big Tech’s visual language Called ‘Bezzy,’ the toy draws on the plush animals sold by organizations such as WWF through initiatives including Adopt-a-Seals and Adopt-A-Pandas. Its design combines the visual language of an 80s childhood toy with that of a corporate mascot. Round eyes, a coy smile, and long, shaggy arms and legs give the data center a softer, more vulnerable appearance. All 20 toys were handmade. The design avoids a new or highly polished look, instead aiming for the familiarity of an object that has always been around. At the same time, details of its appearance are carefully considered, reflecting the engineered visual language associated with Big Tech. ‘Adopt A Data Center examines the stories we are sold, versus the reality communities experience, as one of the greatest revolutions in human history plays out,’ comments Rajeev Basu, artist and founder of Basura. The uneasy relationship between people and technology The project connects the physical presence of data centers with the broader relationship between people and technology. ‘Big Tech encroaches into every area of our lives. We’re rarely totally happy about the benefits, but we’re also powerless. AI data centers are like the physical embodiment of that same feeling,’ explains Alan Wilkis, Big Data. Created for Big Data, whose music explores the relationship between humans and machines, Adopt A Data Center coincides with the upcoming release of the artist’s new album, 4.0. project info: name: Adopt A Data Center designer: Basura | @basuranewyork music artist: Big Data designboom has received this project from our DIY submissions feature, where we welcome our readers to submit their own work for publication. See more project submissions from our readers here.

artigo.texto: Pumped hydropower, flow batteries and industrial heat batteries already have operating projects. Their applications differ, from supplying electricity to delivering steam for industrial processes. For businesses considering energy storage, the choice depends on the service required, the duration of supply and the evidence from installations operating under comparable conditions. Start with the job the storage system must do Power and energy describe different capabilities. Megawatts measure the rate at which a system can deliver power; megawatt-hours measure the quantity of energy stored or delivered. A hypothetical system supplying 10 MW for four hours would deliver 40 MWh. That calculation alone says nothing about its efficiency, cost or usable lifetime. Duration matters too. The US Department of Energy defines long-duration energy storage as systems capable of delivering electricity for at least 10 hours. A technology suited to that task may answer a different need from one designed for short, frequent bursts. Pumped storage provides an established reference point Pumped storage hydropower stores energy by moving water to an upper reservoir. When electricity is required, water flows down through turbines; pumping restores the stored energy for another cycle. The Department of Energy describes pumped storage as a well-established commercial technology. Its commercial history provides a reference point for newer storage technologies. For a proposed project, the practical questions should concern the actual site, construction requirements and operating role. Comparing an established reservoir scheme with a new battery solely by storage capacity would overlook much of what determines whether either is suitable. Flow batteries have operating projects to examine Vanadium flow batteries are another technology with examples beyond laboratory testing. In a 2023 announcement, manufacturer Invinity reported that an 8.4 MWh system at the Chappice Lake solar and storage project in Alberta had begun operating. That is evidence of deployment, although a supplier announcement is not an independent assessment of lifetime performance. The next questions are more demanding: how much energy does the installation deliver, how often is it available, and what maintenance does it require? For buyers, several years of relevant operating data would be more useful than a headline capacity figure alone. Evidence from one installation should also be assessed against the conditions of the proposed next project. Thermal storage serves a different market Some storage systems supply industrial heat rather than returning electricity to the grid. In October 2025, Rondo reported that its 100 MWh industrial heat battery at a California facility was operating automatically each day, using on-site solar electricity to support continuous steam production. The distinction matters: a thermal storage capacity cannot be compared directly with an electrical battery capacity as though both deliver the same product. For an industrial customer, the relevant output may be steam at the temperature, pressure and reliability its process requires. Three different decisions for storage buyers A grid operator looking for electricity after sunset needs to know the required power, the number of hours of supply and how the store will recharge. An industrial site looking for steam needs to specify the heat output its process can accept. These are different purchasing decisions, even when both projects use electricity to charge. Consider a hypothetical requirement to supply 5 MW for 12 hours. That represents 60 MWh delivered over the period. A storage capacity of 60 MWh on a specification sheet would still need checking against the usable output, operating limits and losses stated for that system. The calculation defines the requirement; it does not establish that a particular product meets it. For a steam user, the equivalent starting point is its heat demand and operating schedule. The Rondo example concerns an industrial heat service, while Chappice Lake concerns electricity storage alongside solar generation. Their announced capacities describe projects serving different needs. Compare the evidence, as well as the technology The commercial assessment should use the same system boundary for each option. An equipment price cannot be compared fairly with a price that also covers installation and maintenance. A buyer needs a defined service and a consistent cost breakdown before the alternatives can be ranked. What would demonstrate readiness for wider deployment? A useful assessment begins with the project’s status. Is it announced, under construction, commissioned or operating routinely? It should then examine measured output, the period covered by the results and the conditions under which testing took place. Commercial questions belong alongside technical ones: what does the complete installation cost, who maintains it, and what happens when components need replacing? The answers determine whether a system can meet a customer’s requirements over its working life. Innovation News Network’s wider guide to emerging technologies explores innovations across multiple sectors. For energy storage buyers, the decisive evidence is sustained performance: how reliably a system supplies the electricity or heat their operation needs.

artigo.texto: Residents in Palm Beach County will not have to worry about developers applying for another hyperscale AI data center — at least for a year. The Palm Beach County Commission unanimously approved a one-year moratorium last month on related large-scale proposals to give county officials time to develop stricter regulations that address several areas of concern. The final vote adopting the moratorium was held during the commission’s zoning meeting on Thursday, Sept. 24. It came after county staff received multiple data center applications and this summer’s rejection of the controversial Project Tango near 20-Mile Bend. The moratorium language defines a large-scale data center as one that is a single-location facility with an anticipated monthly peak load of 50 megawatts or more and contains electronic equipment used to store and process digital information. Importantly, it will not apply to applications that have already been submitted. Those who gave public comments supported the moratorium but still wanted a broader definition of what is classified as a data center. “I don’t think data centers, especially large ones, like the ones that you want to build desperately, should be here at all,” Sergei Kelley said. County staff developed the ordinance to follow state statutes that allow local governments to regulate large-load power customers and large-scale data centers by using a 50-megawatt threshold. Going outside of that language could lead to legal challenges through Senate Bill 180, which restricts municipal leaders from changing their land development codes until 2027. At the ordinance’s first reading in August, county commissioners were interested in creating a task force to help create the new regulations on hyperscale data centers. Since then, some commissioners’ stance on establishing this type of advisory committee changed. Staff prepared a resolution that would create an Emerging Issues Technical Advisory Committee, which would primarily assist with making data center regulations but also provide input on any future related issues. Commissioners would each appoint one member, with the entire board appointing two at-large members. Members would need to fit certain criteria based on their knowledge or expertise in a specific area of concern. Those appointed would serve for a three-year term or at the discretion of the commission. County staff estimated that getting the committee up and running could take two to three months. Commissioners were concerned about the timeline of the committee’s operation. Multiple meetings will be necessary, and given the high-interest topics, they will draw a significant amount of public comment. “I fear that we’re adding an extra layer of work, not only for staff, but also for the interested parties in the public, who want to participate in this as well,” Palm Beach County Vice Mayor Marci Woodward said. “That would be my reason not to support doing the advisory committee.” Whitney Carroll, executive director of the Planning, Zoning & Building Department, said that the county is also looking to hire a consultant to assist in the matter. A consultant could give better direction on how to write regulations and provide subject matter expertise, she said. County staff members have already made a request for information to get an estimate of how much hiring an outside agency could cost. So far, they have received offers ranging from $200,000 to $2 million, which would be on top of paying staff to work on the matter as well. “We want to get this done the correct way, and we want to get it done quickly, in the most efficient way that we possibly can,” Carroll said. “A consultant can also engage with the public and do stakeholder outreach.” Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter disputed the need for hiring a consultant, especially after learning about the high price tag. “The whole point of this was community engagement,” Baxter said. “The whole point was to hear from the residents, hear their thoughts and what they want, and put this together… If we have people volunteering to do this for free who are experts, why are we going to spend all this money?” Commissioner Joel Flores recalled that experts during the meeting on Project Tango were hired by developers. He saw the value of investing in a consultant who could give a more objective, informative opinion. He added that delegating this work to staff would be a large workload and cause other applications to get backed up. “This is one of those things I think we have to get it right,” Flores said. “At $200,000, I know it’s nothing to sneeze at, but sometimes you just have to make an investment.” The commissioners rejected the idea of forming a technical advisory committee 4-2, with Commissioner Bobby Powell and Baxter dissenting. They subsequently passed a motion to direct staff to bring a contract for a consultant on the matter for the commission’s consideration that passed 5-1, with Baxter once again dissenting. Commissioner Maria Sachs was absent from the meeting. The large-scale data center moratorium will last until September 2027. In other business, the commissioners voted 6-0 to receive and file the Countywide Transportation Master Plan. County officials executed a contract with consulting firm WSP to develop the plan meant to establish a multi-jurisdictional planning framework for safe, connected transportation and mobility through 2050. In early September, the commissioners requested that staff and WSP return to the board with more detailed descriptions of proposed projects and costs associated with them.

artigo.texto: Quando as florestas não apenas preservam a vegetação, mas também criam valor em carbono. Além de fornecer madeira, conservar o solo e a água e proteger a biodiversidade, as florestas estão se tornando uma parte importante do mercado de carbono. Graças à sua capacidade de absorver e armazenar CO₂, as florestas podem gerar créditos de carbono – um tipo de “ativo verde” que está atraindo cada vez mais atenção nos esforços de redução de emissões do Vietnã. Da conservação florestal a valiosas "toneladas de carbono" Imagine uma floresta como um tipo especial de "fábrica". Uma fábrica típica produz bens, enquanto as árvores absorvem CO₂ do ar, armazenando carbono em seus troncos, galhos, folhas e solo. Se uma floresta for bem protegida, a quantidade de carbono armazenada nela pode ser registrada, medida e convertida em valiosas reduções de emissões no mercado. Este é um dos fundamentos para a criação de créditos de carbono florestal. Em termos simples, um crédito de carbono normalmente representa 1 tonelada de CO₂ equivalente que é reduzida, absorvida e armazenada no âmbito de um programa que cumpre os requisitos de medição, reporte e verificação. Uma vez verificados esses resultados, eles podem ser negociados ou utilizados através de mecanismos apropriados. Isso abre uma nova perspectiva sobre o valor das florestas: a "capacidade de absorção de carbono" de uma floresta deixa de ser apenas um benefício ambiental invisível e passa a ser um valor quantificável. Em 2024, o Vietnã recebeu um pagamento de US$ 51,5 milhões, equivalente a VND 1,35 trilhão, do Fundo de Parceria para o Carbono Florestal (FCPF), por meio do Banco Mundial , referente à redução das emissões florestais. Esse pagamento está vinculado à redução de 10,3 milhões de toneladas de emissões de CO₂ na região Centro-Norte durante o período de 2018-2019. Notavelmente, o programa gerou um total de 16,2 milhões de toneladas de reduções de emissões verificadas durante esse período, superando as 10,3 milhões de toneladas inicialmente acordadas. Você também pode gostar Por trás dessas "toneladas de carbono" estão milhares de pessoas e comunidades envolvidas na proteção das florestas. Segundo o Banco Mundial, o pagamento de US$ 51,5 milhões relacionado ao programa beneficiou mais de 70.000 proprietários florestais e 1.356 comunidades que vivem perto de florestas. Assim, preservar as florestas não se trata apenas de preservar um recurso natural, mas também pode gerar recursos financeiros para aqueles que as protegem. Quando florestas, metano e o mercado de carbono se encaixam em um mesmo cenário. Na Cúpula das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas (COP26), o Vietnã se comprometeu a atingir emissões líquidas zero até 2050, com o objetivo de reduzir as emissões de metano em pelo menos 30% até 2030 em comparação com os níveis de 2020. Para atingir esse objetivo, o Vietnã precisa reduzir simultaneamente as emissões de metano da agricultura , da indústria e do tratamento de resíduos, ao mesmo tempo que aumenta a capacidade de sequestro e armazenamento de carbono nas florestas. As florestas, portanto, desempenham um papel fundamental. Por um lado, a proteção florestal ajuda a limitar a quantidade de CO₂ gerada pelo desmatamento e pela degradação florestal. Por outro lado, a restauração e o desenvolvimento florestal contribuem para o aumento da quantidade de carbono armazenada no ecossistema. É por isso que o setor florestal pode se tornar um dos importantes contribuintes para o mercado de carbono do Vietnã. No entanto, para que uma floresta se torne verdadeiramente uma fonte valiosa de créditos de carbono, ela não pode simplesmente se basear no fato de que "as árvores absorvem CO₂". As emissões de carbono devem ser medidas, monitoradas, relatadas e verificadas de forma confiável. Os resultados da redução de emissões também precisam ser claramente definidos para evitar situações em que a mesma quantidade de redução de emissões seja contabilizada ou reivindicada várias vezes. O Vietnã deu um passo importante com o Decreto 107/2022/ND-CP, que estabelece um arcabouço para a implementação piloto da transferência de resultados de redução de emissões e da gestão financeira de acordos de pagamento por redução de emissões na região Centro-Norte. As autoridades florestais consideram isso um ponto de virada para o Vietnã, que agora inicia a transição para a troca, transferência e comercialização de resultados de redução de emissões, incluindo o carbono florestal. Você também pode gostar A história do centro-norte do Vietnã demonstra claramente que um mercado de carbono não é algo tão improvável. Melhor proteção florestal, restauração de florestas, maior absorção de CO₂... se comprovados por dados confiáveis, todos esses fatores podem contribuir para a criação de novo valor. E esse valor, se distribuído de forma justa, pode retornar aos produtores florestais, proprietários de florestas e comunidades que dependem delas. No futuro, à medida que o mercado de carbono do Vietnã se expandir para mais setores, os créditos florestais poderão se tornar uma das fontes importantes. Mas o mais importante não é apenas a quantidade de créditos vendidos ou o dinheiro arrecadado. Trata-se de transformar os benefícios da conservação florestal em um incentivo econômico suficientemente forte para dar às pessoas mais razões para proteger as florestas. Uma floresta gerida de forma sustentável pode, simultaneamente, conservar água, preservar o solo, manter a biodiversidade, absorver carbono e criar meios de subsistência adicionais. Ao mesmo tempo, o mercado de carbono pode servir de ponte entre esses valores aparentemente intangíveis, permitindo que sejam reconhecidos, mensurados e devolvidos à comunidade como recursos.

artigo.texto: Estudo do Rabobank destaca o potencial do Brasil para se tornar líder no mercado de créditos de carbono. O mercado de créditos de carbono no solo apresenta-se como uma nova oportunidade de financiamento para a agricultura regenerativa no Brasil. O país, com seu vasto potencial agrícola e áreas disponíveis para recuperação, pode remunerar produtores que adotem práticas que aumentem o estoque de carbono no solo. Uma análise do Rabobank enfatiza que o Brasil possui as condições necessárias para se tornar um dos principais mercados de créditos de carbono no solo globalmente. Dados da Embrapa indicam que dos 177 milhões de hectares de pastagens no país, cerca de 28 milhões, ou 15%, estão degradados e têm potencial para serem restaurados com práticas regenerativas. ✨ Essa transição, embora promissora, requer investimentos iniciais, modificações no manejo e um período de adaptação. Entre os benefícios da agricultura regenerativa estão o aumento da matéria orgânica no solo, maiores índices de produtividade, melhor retenção de água e a mitigação de riscos climáticos. O Rabobank ressalta que é necessário expandir os mecanismos de financiamento e remuneração ambiental, como prêmios em cadeias de suprimento sustentáveis e linhas de crédito favoráveis, incluindo créditos de carbono. O mercado já desenvolveu metodologias para medir e monitorar o aumento de carbono armazenado no solo, e os primeiros projetos no Brasil estão avançando nas fases de validação, monitoramento e emissão de créditos. Segundo o estudo de Andrés Padilla, Fernanda Casagrande e Roberto Strumpf, a expansão desse mercado dependerá do avanço desses projetos, da adesão dos produtores, do aumento da demanda, da segurança regulatória e da preservação da integridade ambiental. artigo.texto: No processo de transição energética, mais do que ampliar a produção de fontes limpas, o desafio agora é garantir que a eletricidade esteja disponível exatamente quando o sistema elétrico precisar. Nesse contexto, a publicação da Portaria Normativa do Ministério de Minas e Energia que estabelece as diretrizes do primeiro Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência por meio de sistemas de armazenamento em baterias (LRCAP de 2026 – Armazenamento) representa um dos movimentos mais relevantes dos últimos anos para a modernização do setor. O certame está previsto para acontecer em dezembro. Pela primeira vez, o Brasil cria um mecanismo estruturado para contratar em larga escala capacidade de armazenamento de energia elétrica. O País passa a reconhecer que baterias se tornam parte da infraestrutura estratégica para a segurança energética, ao armazenarem a eletricidade produzida em momentos de maior oferta e a devolverem ao sistema quando a demanda aumenta ou quando há redução na geração das fontes renováveis, especialmente, solar e eólica. É uma reserva inteligente, capaz de responder rapidamente às necessidades operacionais do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). Essa característica torna o armazenamento uma peça indispensável em uma matriz elétrica cada vez mais renovável. Afinal, fontes como o sol e o vento oferecem enormes vantagens ambientais, mas têm uma característica inerente: são variáveis. A geração solar desaparece à noite. A intensidade dos ventos oscila ao longo do dia. Quanto maior a participação dessas fontes na matriz, maior também será a necessidade de mecanismos capazes de equilibrar oferta e demanda em tempo real. É justamente esse equilíbrio que o leilão pretende fortalecer. Os projetos vencedores serão remunerados não pela energia vendida, mas pela disponibilidade de potência. O sistema pagará para que essas baterias estejam prontas para entrar em operação sempre que o Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) determinar sua recarga ou descarga. Trata-se de uma lógica semelhante a de um seguro: espera-se utilizá-lo apenas quando necessário.

artigo.texto: Gerando resumo No Brasil, um maço de cigarros carrega 83% de tributos. Um casaco de pele, 81%. Já as baterias que armazenam energia limpa e garantem a confiabilidade do sistema elétrico pagam 84%. Tributamos como supérfluo, ou como vício, um equipamento que se tornou infraestrutura essencial no mundo inteiro e que, no Brasil, poderia ajudar a reduzir a conta de luz. A distorção ganha urgência às vésperas das eleições. Com eventos climáticos extremos e mais frequentes, decisões sobre o setor elétrico dizem respeito à segurança energética e à competitividade da indústria nacional. O Brasil reúne condições únicas para liderar essa transformação: um dos melhores recursos solares do mundo e uma matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável. A energia solar já é a segunda maior fonte da matriz, fruto de uma década que mobilizou mais de R$ 320 bilhões em investimentos. Mas o sistema não foi projetado para essa velocidade. Cortes de geração renovável, inversões de fluxo nas redes e pressões tarifárias mostram que desperdiçamos energia limpa e barata enquanto o consumidor paga uma conta de luz que sobe acima da inflação. É exatamente esse o problema que as baterias ajudam a resolver. Elas armazenam energia nos momentos de maior geração e a devolvem quando o sistema mais precisa, aumentando a confiabilidade, reduzindo desperdícios e custos sistêmicos e diminuindo a dependência de combustíveis fósseis nos horários de pico. Segundo a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), o armazenamento pode atrair mais de R$ 200 bilhões em investimentos na próxima década. O que trava esse potencial é, em boa medida, a tributação. Corrigi-la não é conceder subsídio: é dar às baterias tratamento isonômico em relação às demais tecnologias do setor elétrico. Enquanto essa distorção persistir, a sociedade seguirá exposta a riscos operacionais e custos desnecessários. O próximo governo também precisará evitar retrocessos. A inclusão recorrente de “jabutis” em projetos de lei para privilegiar combustíveis fósseis aumenta a conta dos consumidores e indica ao mercado uma direção na contramão do mundo. Cada política pública deve ser guiada pela eficiência e pelo interesse coletivo. A transição energética precisa ser política de Estado, com planejamento, estabilidade regulatória e visão de longo prazo. Aos candidatos deste ano, fica uma pergunta: por que o Brasil ainda cobra mais imposto da bateria do que do cigarro? Quem tiver a melhor resposta estará mais preparado para decidir o futuro energético do País.

artigo.texto: A provedora de infraestrutura de dados Aterio informou que o campus de data centers de inteligência artificial planejado pela Oracle Corp. (NYSE:ORCL) em Wisconsin pode sofrer atrasos relacionados à sua conexão com a rede elétrica regional. Os atrasos relatados, no entanto, não foram confirmados pela Oracle até o momento da publicação. A Vantage Data Centers está desenvolvendo o campus “Projeto Lighthouse” de 500 acres para a Oracle em Port Washington, Wisconsin. A construção física está progredindo, com as licenças já obtidas e dois dos quatro edifícios planejados já concluídos, de acordo com o relatório. É necessária conexão à energia elétrica antes do início das operações Aterio afirmou que o campus não poderá iniciar as operações de sua infraestrutura de computação até que a American Transmission Co., a concessionária de transmissão local, construa uma nova linha de energia de alta tensão conectando o local à rede elétrica mais ampla. O projeto de transmissão está atualmente passando por uma análise regulatória mais aprofundada. Segundo Aterio, a Comissão de Serviços Públicos de Wisconsin revogou a aprovação inicial do projeto de transmissão e reiniciou o período de revisão legal depois que os desenvolvedores apresentaram centenas de alterações no escopo do projeto. O cronograma regulatório revisado pode afetar o momento em que a eletricidade estará disponível para o complexo de data centers. A Aterio estima que uma geração de energia significativa poderá chegar no início de 2028 A Oracle tem como meta começar a usar as instalações em Wisconsin no segundo semestre de 2027. No cenário mais provável descrito pela Aterio, o fornecimento significativo de eletricidade não chegaria ao campus antes do início de 2028. A empresa de pesquisa também descreveu um cenário em que a análise regulatória estadual leva um ano inteiro, um prazo que, segundo ela, é padrão para projetos de serviços públicos dessa escala. Nesse cenário, o campus pode não atingir sua capacidade total de geração de energia até abril de 2029. Esses prazos são estimativas da Aterio e não foram confirmados pela Oracle nem pelos órgãos reguladores de Wisconsin. Relatório surge após atualização sobre o projeto do Novo México O relatório sobre Wisconsin surge na sequência de uma atualização relativa ao “Projeto Júpiter”, um campus da Oracle em grande escala localizado no Novo México. A Oracle alertou recentemente que poderia atrasar os pagamentos relacionados ao projeto do Novo México, citando atrasos envolvendo gasodutos e licenças ambientais pendentes. A empresa tem mantido a posição de que o projeto no Novo México permanece dentro do cronograma. Os desenvolvimentos nos dois projetos destacam os requisitos de infraestrutura e regulamentação envolvidos na construção de grandes complexos de centros de dados, incluindo o acesso à eletricidade e outros serviços públicos. Todos os investimentos envolvem riscos, incluindo a potencial perda do principal. O desempenho passado não é indicativo de resultados futuros. artigo.texto: BUFFALO, N.Y. (WBEN).....The Buffalo Common Council has taken the first - and expected step - towards creating a two year moratorium on data center development projects within the city. Next up: A local law, crafted by the city's Corporation Counsel office, that prevents any new data center construction and development while the moratorium is in place. That law is expected to be before the council by early October, with a formal vote to follow. Buffalo is now joined the growing list of municipalities and larger governments that have hot the pause button when it comes to data center development. Mayor Sean Ryan said he supports the council vote. "We need clear safeguards that put Buffalo residents first," Ryan said. New York, this summer, at the urging of Gov. Kathy Hochul put a one-year moratorium on data center developments. The Buffalo data center ordinance will be created by a nine--person task force that includes public and private sector interests. "There is a lot of misinformation on both sides," said Ellicott District Councilwoman and Council Majority Leader Leah Halton-Pope. "Hopefully, the task force cam work its way through all that." The moratorium was crafted by North District Councilman Joseph Golembek Jr., who said he has concerns about projects that may be developed near residential neighborhoods. "It could destroy a neighborhood's quality of life," Golembek said. Data centers are coming under fire - mostly for environmental reasons including noise, heavy drains on power supplies and on water supplies. When Buffalo developed its Green Code development blueprint a decade ago, data centers did not figure into economic landscape. Golembek said he hopes the moratorium will address that development void. "Just like what we did 15 years ago with food truck regulations, we want to address this new form of development," Golembek said. "My sole mission is to protect the interests of the residents of the City of Buffalo." Moratorium is the first step; local law still needed

artigo.texto: Dive Brief: - Facilities seeking backup power will help boost annual installations in the commercial-sector energy storage market 27% in megawatt terms through 2031, according to an estimate by the American Clean Power Association and renewable power data firm Wood MacKenzie. - Data centers facing grid-connection bottlenecks are a big driver of the growth. “Storage can provide needed capacity faster, cheaper and more reliably than gas alone," Allison Feeney, research analyst at Wood Mackenzie, says in a summary of the U.S. Energy Storage Monitor that the firm puts out with ACP, released this week for the third quarter of 2026. - When utility-scale and residential sectors are factored in, annual installations of energy storage are expected to grow more than 50% in megawatt terms through 2031. Utility-scale storage will see 8% average annual growth, and residential storage 9% average annual growth, over the next five years, the report says. Dive Insight: Energy storage encompasses several technologies, but most commercial applications are battery systems, and about 90% of those are lithium-ion, the International Energy Agency says based on 2025 data. Hydroelectric, thermal and compressed air are among the other types of systems. Those are generally utility-scale applications, EIA says. Innovation in the battery space is giving facilities options in addition to lithium-ion. Google, for instance, closed a deal earlier this year with Form Energy and utility Xcel Energy to install 30 GWh of battery storage at one of its data centers in the form of iron-air batteries, which engineers tout for their duration. “By … pioneering long-duration storage … we are helping to build a more resilient system,” Amanda Peterson Corio, Google’s head of data center energy, said when the deal was announced. Form Energy says on its website that its batteries can release energy for up to 100 hours, delivering power “for multiple days at a time.” In the ACP-Wood Mackenzie analysis, improving durations, particularly in utility-scale and residential applications, is one reason the sector saw an increase in megawatt hours even though the number of installations dipped in the second quarter. “Longer duration … systems drove MWh growth,” the report said. The average duration of U.S. energy storage systems increased from 2.8 hours to 3.5 hours, the report said. Changes in public policy priorities are supporting storage growth, too. In addition to states and municipalities requiring data centers and other large load users to bring their own power, which in many cases include a storage component, public entities at local, state and federal levels are pushing virtual power plants. VPPs are programs in which utilities leverage excess capacity in commercial facilities, homes and other sources to support grid power. Storage is a frequent component of VPPs. “Distributed storage's value proposition is broadening beyond customer-centric benefits to include grid services, as the industry seeks to position virtual power plants … as a key enabler of load growth,” the report says. Looking at second-quarter data, the ACP-Wood Mackenzie analysis says 48 MW of energy storage was installed in the commercial property segment. That’s down from the first quarter, which was unusually high, it says, because of a rush in California by facilities and households installing storage before state tax incentives dropped. Although the reduced incentives took effect in 2023, the state’s top court didn’t settle questions about their legality until June, spurring the rush. As a result, while the storage installed in the second quarter is lower than in the first quarter, it’s in line with historic norms, the report says. Utility-scale deployments for the quarter totaled 4.7 GW/17.6 GWh, down 8% year-over-year in MW terms, which the report attributes to market saturation. Residential deployments also declined, falling 15%, to 676 MW, which the report attributes in part to the federal clean energy and energy efficiency tax credits eliminated in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Despite the quarterly drop among the segments, the outlook is bright for the next five years because of the broader trends favoring energy storage, the report says. “With a strong pipeline and continued technology improvements, the outlook for storage remains exceptionally strong,” John Hensley, ACP’s senior vice president of markets and policy analysis, said in a statement.

artigo.texto: The investment was financed through EU-funds available during the previous government.Continue reading SolServices Kft. and Huawei Technologies Hungary are developing one of the region’s largest battery energy storage systems (BESS), with a power capacity of 150 megawatts (MW) and a storage capacity of 300 megawatt-hours (MWh). The companies announced at a press conference in Budapest on Wednesday that construction of the full portfolio is expected to be completed in the first quarter of 2027. Representatives of the companies signed an agreement on Wednesday to implement the energy storage project at Huawei’s annual renewable energy conference, the Digital Power Summit 2026. Róbert Szabó, director of the Digital Power business at Huawei Technologies Hungary, emphasized that commissioning the 150 MW/300 MWh energy storage facility planned for early 2027 will make state-of-the-art smart technology an integral part of Hungary’s energy system. The system will provide the grid with the flexibility that is essential for the continued expansion of renewable energy sources. He added that hybridization is a key strategic priority for both companies: coordinated operation of different generation and storage technologies enables more efficient use of the grid and greater system-wide flexibility. The total cost of implementing the project is approximately €50 million, and the entire investment will be financed on a commercial basis, Gábor Juhász-Farkas, managing director of SolServices Kft., told MTI. Citing data from holadelej.hu, he said that during the summer, on one of the most critical days of the energy crisis, solar generation accounted for 85% of the country’s electricity consumption. At the same time, this has created new challenges: the most important questions now are when energy is generated, when it is used, and how the entire energy system can be made more resilient and flexible. He stressed that hybridization provides the best answer to these challenges. Grid capacity is currently one of the scarcest resources in Hungary’s electricity system, Juhász-Farkas noted. When a solar power plant’s connection point is considered on an annual average, it is utilized only 16% of the time, leaving 84% of the infrastructure unused. As an example of hybridization, he noted that combining solar and wind power with battery energy storage can increase grid utilization to more than 40%. Juhász-Farkas explained that the companies are working together to develop an integrated energy platform in which solar power, energy storage, wind power, and geothermal energy do not operate in isolation, but instead complement and reinforce one another as part of an interconnected system. He said that the project’s commercial financing demonstrates that storage is no longer a technology of the future, but a commercially viable solution that can be built on a market basis.” He said the scale of the cooperation can be illustrated by the fact that a fully charged energy storage system would be capable of compensating for the loss of peak-generation output from an entire unit of the Paks nuclear power plant for more than half an hour. If this storage capacity had entered the market with its surplus supply, it would have had the effect of reducing prices by 40%, he indicated. SolServices operates solar power facilities with a combined capacity of approximately 380 MW across Hungary, making it the country’s third-largest operating investment of this type. Under the new agreement, the company will build energy storage capacity alongside its existing solar parks. The first storage units have already been commissioned in Mezőtúr and Mezőberény, and commercial operation of the full storage portfolio is expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027, he said. Huawei Technologies, the largest Chinese privately owned company, operates in more than 170 countries, and its products and services are used by nearly one-third of the world’s population. All five of Huawei’s business groups—telecommunications, enterprise, cloud, digital power, and consumer—generated more than $120 billion in revenue globally last year. SolServices Kft. is one of Hungary’s leading renewable energy companies. Since 2017, the company has participated in the development of more than 1 gigawatt of large-scale solar power generation capacity. Via MTI, Featured image: Pexels

artigo.texto: East Hampton wants 2 battery plants shut down pending new fire systems East Hampton Town is demanding that the owners of two East-End battery-energy storage plants, including one impacted by forever chemicals, cease operations of LIPA-contracted facilities in East Hampton and Montauk by Friday until new fire suppression systems are in place. The demand follows a meeting between town officials and co-battery owner NextEra earlier this week, and revelations by the state earlier this month that a fire-suppression system was responsible for toxic contamination discovered at one of the sites earlier this year. In a letter to battery owner NextEra on Tuesday, a copy of which was obtained by Newsday, East Hampton Town supervisor Kathee Burke-Gonzalez wrote that the town remains "deeply concerned" about the "pace and scope" of actions being taken by the owners to "protect the health and safety" of town residents and the environment. Suffolk County Executive Ed Romaine and East Hampton Village Mayor Jerry Larsen have previously called for the East Hampton facility on Cove Hollow Road to cease operations, Newsday reported. NextEra spokesman Chris Curtland at the time said NextEra remains "committed to working with local and state officials on the investigation. The project is operating safely." NextEra and East Hampton didn't immediately respond to requests for comment. Newsday reported in May that the plant was the subject of a federal lawsuit by the Suffolk County Water Authority concerning forever chemicals from the East Hampton plant that affected drinking water wells. New York State has since determined that the toxins known as PFPrA were the result of a fire suppression system used during a May 2023 thermal runaway fire at the facility that took 30 hours to get under control. No agency, state or local, or NextEra has released information about the cause of the fire. Earlier this week, the state Department of Environmental Conservation in an email told Newsday it "does not have the authority to regulate the design or operations at the [East Hampton] facility, nor does DEC have the authority to investigate causes of a fire beyond the environmental impacts it may have caused." In her letter to NextEra, Burke-Gonzalez referenced a Sept. 25 meeting she had with battery-plant officials, noting that the company said it could remove all "Novec 1230" fire suppression equipment from both the East Hampton and Montauk battery plants in two weeks, and to take the system’s automatic fire-suppression system offline even sooner. But Burke-Gonzalez said the town would not approve that modification to the fire suppression systems "without a detailed report from a qualified engineer confirming that water alone is sufficient to extinguish any fire at the facility. East Hampton also requested that the company take "immediate" interim remedial measures to ensure the safety of residents around the plant, including excavation and off-site disposal of "all impacted soil," demanding that the soil be removed to a licensed facility outside of East Hampton Town. East Hampton also is demanding that soil and groundwater sampling be done at five-foot intervals around the plant "to determine whether additional remedial measures are necessary," including remediating groundwater. Tests by the state and Suffolk County have shown PFPrA at upward of 10,000 parts per billion, well above a site-specific screening level set by the state Department of Health of 3 parts per billion, Newsday has reported. "In the interim," Burke Gonzalez wrote, "and until Novec 1230 [fire suppression system] has been taken offline under an approved alternative fire-suppression plan and the required remediation at the 3 Cove Hollow Road facility has been completed, the affected facilities should cease operations by Friday, Oct. 2, 2026." The town, she wrote, "does not believe continued operation is appropriate while these unresolved risks remain." Up close with Gilgo killer's court officer ... Deadly North Bellport shooting ... artigo.texto: The backlash against data centers is growing, driven by concerns about their environmental impact, effects on local communities, and demands on public infrastructure. But the backlash is also developing a partisan dimension. Recent polling shows that Democrats are substantially more likely than Republicans to oppose data centers and that support has fallen sharply over the past year, particularly among Democrats. Much of that shift reflects growing concerns about the resources data centers consume. The risk is that legitimate concerns about particular projects become absorbed into a broader partisan narrative in which data centers are treated as inherently harmful. Those concerns deserve serious attention, but Democrats should be wary of allowing opposition to data centers to become an ideological reflex. The campaign against data centers increasingly resembles the opposition that wind and solar projects have faced for years. Large infrastructure projects create real local impacts, but those impacts can often be managed without abandoning investments that serve broader economic and environmental goals. Democrats once made that case in support of clean energy. They should be careful not to abandon it now that the infrastructure in question is data centers. Indeed, many objections to data centers closely resemble objections to clean energy projects. Some residents simply do not want large industrial facilities in their communities, whether that means wind turbines altering the landscape, solar farms replacing open land, or massive data centers appearing in rural areas. Others object to noise, whether from wind turbines or the backup generators and cooling equipment associated with data centers. Similar disputes arise over who bears the costs and who receives the benefits. Private landowners may profit directly by selling or leasing their property, while neighboring residents worry about effects on property values or quality of life. Infrastructure presents another source of tension. Both clean energy projects and data centers require substantial investments in transmission lines, substations, roads, and other supporting infrastructure. Residents understandably worry that public resources or utility customers will ultimately bear costs associated with a private company’s investment, particularly if a developer abandons a project. The concerns about data centers are not frivolous, but neither were the concerns raised about wind and solar development. The appropriate response was not to halt clean energy construction altogether. Policymakers instead sought ways to reduce conflicts and distribute benefits more broadly. Developers and communities experimented with approaches such as agrivoltaics, which allows solar generation and agricultural production to coexist on the same land. The broader lesson is not that every concern about new infrastructure proves unfounded. Some problems are real and require meaningful safeguards, while others reflect uncertainty, exaggerated claims, or resistance to development itself. Policymakers should distinguish among them rather than treating every objection as equally persuasive. The same approach should guide data center development, with practical solutions to genuine concerns about water use, electricity costs, noise, land use, and community impacts. For years, Democrats were among the strongest advocates for deploying clean energy despite local opposition. They correctly recognized that building wind and solar capacity could create jobs, generate local tax revenue, and help build the industries that would underpin the future American economy. That basic judgment remains sound. Clean energy projects are worth pursuing even when individual projects generate controversy and when some of the companies developing them are large, profitable corporations. The same principle should apply to data centers. The United States is in the midst of a major technological transformation driven by artificial intelligence. Data centers are the physical infrastructure supporting that transformation. They also represent a significant source of construction and investment, often in communities seeking new economic opportunities. Data center growth can also support clean energy expansion. Major technology companies have made substantial commitments to reduce the carbon intensity of their operations and are investing in new sources of electricity, including wind, solar, and nuclear power. Microsoft’s agreement to support the restart of the Three Mile Island nuclear plant illustrates the scale of investment that growing demand for computing is helping mobilize. Some communities will reasonably decide that a particular data center proposal is not appropriate for a particular location. Others may demand changes to address concerns about water, electricity, noise, or local infrastructure. Policymakers should take those concerns seriously and ensure that their communities benefit from these infrastructure investments. But blanket moratoriums and reflexive opposition to data center development treat complex and often addressable challenges as reasons to stop building altogether. The United States does not need to choose between technological progress and protecting communities. Policymakers can establish rules that mitigate genuine harms and fairly allocate costs while allowing investment to proceed. Democrats understood that approach when the infrastructure at issue was wind turbines and solar panels. They should apply the same judgment to the infrastructure powering the next generation of the American economy. Image credit: Chad Davis/Flickr

artigo.texto: As the entire tech industry shifts its focus to the development of artificial intelligence, there are almost 3,000 planned or ongoing data center projects across the country. At the same time, numerous tech executives and members of President Donald Trump’s administration continue to champion data centers and AI as the next boon of economic progress. Yet, the discontent seen in communities nationwide has made it clear: Data centers are not working for Americans. While politicians across the political spectrum promise local economic benefits, many data centers receive obscure tax breaks and lackluster environmental regulations that encourage development to the detriment of local communities. Furthermore, these massive facilities often leech off of local public utilities, skyrocketing energy bills for households and weighing down local infrastructure. Apart from these immediate impacts, the construction, cooling and powering of these data centers can devastate local environments and watersheds. This stimulates immense distrust and frustration with pro-data center politicians and has unified bipartisan sentiment against data center construction throughout the country — almost three-quarters of Americans now oppose data center projects in their area. Data centers look to create incredibly large returns for their owners and partners, but those returns are currently happening at the expense of the local communities they reside in. If data centers are going to be significantly involved in our future, the communities they impact need a share in the profits they create. Instead of prolonging the ongoing cycle of deception and discontent, citizens, corporations and governments can work together and leverage data center development to invest in infrastructure, community sustainability and environmental resilience. First, private interests should be responsible for internalizing the external costs of data center construction and operation. Data centers are driving a substantial revitalization of fossil fuel electricity generation to accommodate their immense energy needs. Beyond releasing high carbon emissions, it is estimated that the air pollution from these sources can create annual localized public health costs as high as $20 billion by 2028. They also tap into local water resources for cooling, threatening the integrity of piped water sources. Accordingly, the baseline for a data center to be built must include commitments to fulfill energy needs with strictly clean, renewable sources and investments in environmentally friendly cooling methods. Second, stakeholders also have to resolve the financial issues that data centers create. In many cases, state and local governments create tax breaks and other incentives to encourage developers to build data centers. These incentives are generating hundreds of millions — and in a few cases, billions — of dollars in lost annual revenue for state governments across the country. If data centers are to support the local communities they inhabit, all levels of government across the country must be aligned on holding them accountable for their full share of development costs, operational expenses and taxes. Furthermore, data centers that are integrated into local utilities strain infrastructure through their huge water and energy demands. This rising demand risks rate hikes for nearby households and businesses. To compensate for this, governments must require that data center developers invest in expanding generation capacity to the required level and building efficient water use systems, instead of leaving the costs to consumers. Across the country, most of the communities rallying against data center proposals are demanding moratoriums on data center construction or the blocking of permits. Right now, data centers are built and operated at the expense of the public and should be opposed. In this effort, many communities have been successful: Local opposition led to project cancellations worth $68 billion over April, May and June of this year alone. In a modern data center, every 100 megawatts of capacity generates more than $340 million per year in revenue. For perspective, the data center currently under construction in Saline Township has a capacity of almost 1,383 megawatts. While we must respect the will of local constituencies in demanding moratoriums — like those in Ypsilanti — the value created by these facilities presents an opportunity we should consider. Communities, aligned with local, state and national governments, should force developers and tech companies to redistribute shares of their profits to infrastructure projects or other investments through intentional, intelligent policy decisions. The best way to accomplish this is to mandate extensive and complete investment in sustainable infrastructure from data center developers. This should first include responsible construction practices, like dust suppression and pollutant monitoring to minimize air pollution, hazardous runoff and waste. Next, data centers should invest in a sufficient capacity of clean energy that is situated to the local geography. Alongside this, they must also invest in facilities that are efficient and implement sustainable engineering in order to minimize environmental costs during the following decades of operation. The true list of responsible investments extends far beyond this, but these are some of the most important and neglected across the sector today. While a moratorium can keep a community safe, it is a neutral outcome. If we allow data centers while prioritizing community investment, more jobs will be created and sustained, and more tangible, shared value will be added to local communities. Facilitating investment in sustainability can aid communities in becoming more resilient to climate and environmental crises while also driving the energy transition. artigo.texto: BYD said the flagship sedan will feature “unprecedented disruptive technology” and will reportedly be the first EV to use its solid-state batteries. BYD takes on ultra-luxe brands with Yangwang EV sedan Yangwang is BYD’s highest-end brand with ultra-luxury models ranging from electric hypercars to extreme off-road SUVs. BYD also uses Yangwang to showcase its breakthrough technologies. In the past, Yangwang vehicles have debuted with disruptive new tech, including BYD’s quad-motor e4 platform, second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging, and its Disus Intelligent Body Control System. A new Yangwang model was recently spotted testing in China that, according to local reports, will push the brand further into the elite segment. New images of the vehicle surfaced online, revealing a nearly identical design to the Rolls-Royce Phantom. It will even be BYD’s first vehicle with rear-hinged coach doors. Hu Xiaoqing, Yangwang’s general manager, shared a few images of the flagship sedan on Weibo and confirmed that the car’s name has yet to be finalized. Internally, BYD is calling it “HU” for now. The new model is “the culmination of three years of meticulous development by Yangwang, featuring the brand’s signature design language, and is an ultra-luxury executive sedan.” No other details were revealed, but one image shows the vehicle at BYD’s Flash Charging station, suggesting it can support megawatt fast charging. According to China’s Autohome, Yangwang’s executive-class EV sedan will be BYD’s first EV to use solid-state batteries among other new technologies. Zheng Yu, Yangwang’s executive general manager, confirmed the new model will feature “unprecedented disruptive technology,” but didn’t reveal specifics. The sedan measures about 5.5 meters in length, or about the size of the Mercedes-Benz Maybach S-Class. BYD executive vice president Stella Li confirmed in an exclusive interview with Carwow.es earlier this month that the company is “in the leading position” in solid-state battery tech and its commercialization. Li said that BYD will “prove it” with its first vehicle equipped with solid-state batteries set to debut in 2027. BYD’s battery R&D team is “very strong,” Li said, adding that they are studying the battery chemistry as well as the manufacturing and equipment needed for mass production. FinDreams, BYD’s battery business, aims to begin producing sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries in limited batches in 2027, scaling up to mass production by 2030. Will Yangwang’s ultra-luxe sedan be the first to showcase BYD’s solid-state batteries? If it does, it will likely be offered on higher-priced variants, while standard models could still use BYD’s latest Blade LFP batteries. Top comment by Blake I expect this will have sold state batteries. The huge sales price means they can afford to ‘hand make’ the batteries and have a high failure rate. Solid state batteries will matter more when it comes to the inherent complexities of mass production Outside of that, the flagship model is expected to feature BYD’s quad-motor e4 platform, delivering over 1,000 hp combined. BYD has yet to announce prices or any details, but reports estimate the Yangwang sedan will cost over 2 million yuan, or nearly $300,000. The Yangwang U7, the brand’s current luxury electric sedan, starts at just 658,000 yuan ($98,000). According to Autohome, the new executive-class sedan is expected to make its official debut in October, so we should learn more shortly. Check back soon. We’ll keep you updated. artigo.texto: COEP Technological University and JSW Projects have signed an agreement to establish an indigenous lithium-ion battery technology centre at the university’s research facility in Chikhali, Pune district, in a project estimated to cost ₹800 crore. The centre will be developed in two phases and is planned to include battery prototyping, pilot-scale research and development facilities. According to the report by Loksatta, the project will support the development of lithium-ion battery cell technology within Pune’s academic and engineering ecosystem. The agreement was signed by COEP registrar Dr D. N. Sonawane and JSW Group executive vice-president Naresh Lalwani. COEP vice-chancellor Prof Sunil Bhirud, Dr S. P. Mahajan, dean Prof P. A. Sadgir, Dr Ranjit Date, professor of practice Dr Sarika Kelkar and other university officials attended the signing. JSW senior vice-president Amitabh Singh, associate vice-president Chandrakant Mahalingam and deputy general managers Vijay Chaudhary and Sudeep Sarkar were also present. Bhirud said the centre could help develop an indigenous alternative to imported batteries and contribute to India’s effort to build domestic capability. He said students would receive opportunities to learn advanced battery technology and work on practical applications, while the facility would provide a wider platform for research, innovation and technology development. The project places an engineering university at the centre of a technology area that has implications for electric mobility, energy storage and industrial manufacturing. However, the supplied report does not specify the proposed capacity of the facility, the exact timeline for either phase, the technologies to be developed, or whether the centre will manufacture commercial battery cells. JSW Group chairman Sajjan Jindal said India had spent substantial foreign exchange on crude oil imports over several decades and needed to develop advanced skills and capabilities to manufacture batteries domestically. He described the partnership with COEP, which has a 172-year engineering history, as a collaboration that could create new opportunities across industry, research and education. The agreement marks a new industry-academia initiative for Pune’s research landscape. Its eventual impact will depend on the execution of the two phases, the research infrastructure established at Chikhali, and the translation of laboratory and pilot-scale work into deployable battery technologies. The next milestones will be the detailed implementation of the project and the development of the proposed centre.

artigo.texto: A "mina de ouro" dos créditos de carbono do Vietnã: aguardando um impulso dos fluxos de capital internacional. (NB&CL) Globalmente, os mercados de créditos de carbono estão desempenhando um papel cada vez mais importante na transição para uma economia de baixas emissões, ao mesmo tempo que abrem um canal para a mobilização de capital para projetos verdes. Entretanto, no Vietname, embora a bolsa de carbono esteja em funcionamento há apenas cerca de 3 meses e o volume de negociações ainda seja limitado, considera-se que esta é uma fase fundamental para um mercado de carbono mais sistemático, com um potencial significativo proveniente da oferta interna de créditos e da crescente procura do mercado internacional. Em entrevista a um repórter do jornal "Jornalistas e Opinião Pública", o Sr. Nguyen Vo Truong An, Vice-Diretor Geral da ASEAN Carbon Credit Exchange Joint Stock Company, afirmou que o Vietnã possui grande potencial em termos de fornecimento de créditos de carbono. Segundo ele, nos próximos 1 a 3 anos, juntamente com a conclusão dos mecanismos, padrões e canais de negociação, o mercado poderá entrar em um período de forte desenvolvimento, abrindo mais oportunidades para empresas e fluxos de investimento internacional. O Vietnã possui um vasto potencial para desenvolver seu mercado de carbono. + Como você avalia o atual mercado de créditos de carbono no Vietnã, particularmente seu potencial de desenvolvimento e o progresso alcançado em sua formação? Em primeiro lugar, é preciso afirmar que o Vietnã não carece de potencial para desenvolver um mercado de carbono. O país possui um espaço considerável para a geração de créditos de carbono, desde suas áreas de florestas naturais e plantadas até programas de transformação agrícola com foco em baixas emissões no Delta do Mekong. Além disso, o Vietnã possui um potencial significativo em energias renováveis, tratamento de resíduos, recuperação e utilização de biogás, bem como inúmeros projetos de redução de emissões nos setores de manufatura e indústria. Se explorado e desenvolvido adequadamente, esse potencial poderá se tornar uma importante fonte de créditos de carbono para os mercados nacional e internacional. No entanto, o mercado de créditos de carbono no Vietnã ainda está em fase inicial. Embora a bolsa de carbono tenha iniciado oficialmente suas operações no final de junho de 2026, o mercado ainda está em fase piloto e precisa de mais tempo para expandir a oferta de créditos, estabelecer uma demanda estável de negociação, refinar o mecanismo de precificação e melhorar a liquidez. Contudo, esta é uma fase crucial para o Vietname testar ferramentas e tecnologias de negociação, enquanto continua a aperfeiçoar o quadro legal e os mecanismos operacionais. Os resultados desta fase piloto servirão de base para ajustes, lições aprendidas e para a criação de uma base sólida para o desenvolvimento transparente e eficiente do mercado, atraindo mais empresas para participar no futuro. Após a fase piloto, os resultados obtidos servirão de base para que o Vietnã aprimore ainda mais seus mecanismos operacionais, corrija as deficiências e desenvolva gradualmente um mercado de carbono transparente e eficiente, capaz de conectar as necessidades de compradores e vendedores. Assim, o mercado não só impulsiona projetos de redução de emissões, como também contribui para a concretização da meta de emissões líquidas zero até 2050. A bolsa de carbono do Vietnã foi oficialmente lançada no final de junho de 2026. No entanto, após três meses de operação, o volume de transações bem-sucedidas permanece bastante limitado. Na sua opinião, quais são os motivos para isso? - Na minha opinião, ao avaliar o volume de negociação nos primeiros três meses, é necessário, em primeiro lugar, distinguir claramente entre o mercado de carbono obrigatório e o mercado de carbono voluntário, porque esses dois mercados são formados com objetivos e motivações de negociação diferentes. Um mercado de carbono obrigatório é estabelecido para atingir o objetivo de gerir e aplicar políticas nacionais de redução de emissões. Nesse mecanismo, o Estado identifica as entidades sujeitas à gestão, atribui quotas de emissão e estipula obrigações de cumprimento. As empresas participam dessas transações principalmente para cumprir suas obrigações de emissões, como a compra de cotas adicionais ou o uso de créditos de carbono que podem ser compensados de acordo com os regulamentos. Portanto, a escala e a frequência das transações dependem muito do plano de alocação de cotas, das obrigações de conformidade e do escopo das empresas incluídas no sistema. Você também pode gostar Os mercados voluntários de carbono têm dinâmicas diferentes. Empresas, instituições financeiras ou investidores podem participar com base na necessidade voluntária de reduzir emissões, cumprir compromissos climáticos, desenvolver projetos ou investir em ativos de carbono. Portanto, esse mercado possui uma gama mais ampla de participantes e o potencial para conexões mais diretas com compradores, investidores e fluxos de capital internacionais. Considerando essa diferença, o volume limitado de negociações na bolsa obrigatória na fase inicial é compreensível. Como o número de entidades obrigadas a cumprir as normas, as quotas alocadas e a necessidade de compensação ainda estão em desenvolvimento, a demanda por negociações naturalmente não pode ser alta imediatamente. A longo prazo, os dois mercados se complementam. O mercado obrigatório fornece a base para a implementação de políticas e para as necessidades de conformidade interna, enquanto o mercado voluntário expande o espaço de negociação e mobiliza recursos além do escopo das obrigações obrigatórias. artigo.texto: A public records request regarding a July 27 meeting between one of the main companies behind Project Jupiter and Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham provided virtually no information on its content. The meeting with Oracle occurred as the timeline around an important permitting process for the massive and controversial data center in Santa Teresa was accelerated seemingly out of the blue in late July. The New Mexico Environment Department hearing officer Max Shepherd initially favored a later October date for an air quality permit hearing given its “highly technical” nature, doubling down at a July 27 scheduling conference even after being pushed by the developers to move it up. Officials with Oracle met with the governor that same day. Two days later, Shepherd advanced the hearing to Sept. 14, leading some to speculate there was a connection. “This proceeding is becoming more focused on reaching a result favorable to the governor’s economic development agenda than ensuring a fair process and protecting the due process rights of the parties and the public,” said Mariel Nanasi, executive director and attorney for New Energy Economy, at the time. Leah March, a spokesperson for the governor, wrote in an email Aug. 12 that "the governor routinely takes meetings with companies like Oracle to stay informed, as she did in July for a general update.” “The governor does not interfere in state agencies' regulatory decisions and has made no effort to influence the outcome of Project Jupiter’s air permit application,” March wrote. “Instead, it is her responsibility to ensure that state agencies meet their statutory obligations for a fair, transparent and independent process." The data center's regulatory proceedings have shaped up to be a bitter battle. Shepherd recused himself from the hearing on Aug. 23 and the state Supreme Court placed proceedings for Project Jupiter's air quality permit and water use on pause before allowing them to continue in a Sept. 17 decision. The New Mexican requested on Aug. 13 any notes, agenda, emails or other correspondence regarding the July 27 meeting between the governor and Oracle. On Aug. 18, the Governor’s Office acknowledged the request and said it would respond on or before Aug. 28. On Aug. 28, the request was deemed “excessively burdensome or broad due to the large volume of potentially responsive records and the time required to review those records for redactions or withholding required or permitted by law.” The new deadline was set as Sept. 14, on which day the materials were made available. The Governor’s Office closed the request, marking it as complete. However, the only material included was a photo of an iMessage exchange with the governor’s schedule for the day. The Oracle meeting took up one line. The completed request did not include the governor’s official schedule for the week, which was sent to the The New Mexican Aug. 10 by an environmental advocacy group. In a phone call Tuesday, Donicia Herrera, a records custodian at the Office of the Governor, said that after conducting a full search of records to fulfill the request, that was “all that came up.” Julia Gentin is a reporter for The Las Cruces New Mexican, The Santa Fe New Mexican and Searchlight New Mexico through a partnership with Report for America, a national service program that places journalists into local newsrooms. artigo.texto: Subscribe to The Y’all — a weekly dispatch about the people, places and policies defining Texas, produced by Texas Tribune journalists living in communities across the state. LUBBOCK — A new water tower in Turkey: $3 million. Upgrades for a museum in Stamford: $400,000. A first responders appreciation barbecue in Medina County: $10,000. These are just some of the public investments data center companies have paid for across rural Texas in the past year. According to Texas Tribune analysis, data center companies have donated or invested more than $343 million across the Lone Star state for various community needs, including school programs, infrastructure repairs and emergency services. Much of that money has gone to the very communities that have fought against data center development and are seemingly an effort to win over public support through their bottomless bank accounts. The Texas Tribune reviewed news releases, public meeting agendas and interviewed local officials to understand how data centers are using their money in Texas. Because not every donation is made public, the total — the first of its kind compiled in Texas — is likely an undercount. Google donated millions of dollars to the Haskell area for its hospital, pregnancy center and other causes. Rowan Digital Infrastructure is giving $38 million to Temple for its water infrastructure, along with more money for STEM Centers at schools in nearby small towns. Data centers also created community action grants, which are used for recurring investments in the communities they’re building in. Others, such as Google’s Texas Water Impact Fund, provide funds to restore resources that cause concern for Texans or provide direct lump sum donations to both community and state funds. As data centers move into the state at a rapid pace, Texas communities in mostly rural areas face a fiscal cliff from property tax cuts, inflation and overall economic uncertainty. Over the last year, data center companies have stepped in as a white knight of community investment. “There is no question that these data centers are an opportunity for rural communities that are living in the margin,” said Suzanne Bellsnyder, an editor and publisher of two Panhandle newspapers and a Substack focused on rural issues. “Most infrastructure resources are paid with tax dollars, and there’s not a ton there.” It’s not a new strategy. Major corporations regularly invest in communities and make charitable gifts big and small. Oil and gas companies in West Texas, for example, have donated to fire and police stations and hosted back-to-school backpack drives to weave themselves into communities. Data centers have also capitalized on tax breaks from both state and local governments. A Texas Tribune analysis earlier this year found the state will forgo at least $3 billion in sales tax revenue over the next two years due to the exemption for the state’s booming data center industry. Because of the negative public perception toward data centers, however, they still have some ways to go. In an August poll from The Texas Politics Project, a nonpartisan research hub focused on Texas government and politics, 57% of respondents said they would oppose the construction of a data center in their communities. “I hope their intentions are good, and they’re not just trying to buy these communities off,” Bellsnyder said. Tied into the community It’s been two years since a tornado struck Temple, a city of just over 96,000 people that lies 70 miles north of Austin. The city was devastated. Hundreds of homes and businesses were severely damaged or destroyed. One of the buildings lost was the beloved Sammons Community Center, where senior citizens could come together for bingo, swimming and meals. The price tag for the city’s recovery was high — $7.7 million. Then, Rowan Digital Infrastructure stepped in. The company is developing a $4.2 billion data center campus with six facilities planned in East Temple. Earlier this month, Rowan announced a $38 million investment in Temple’s public infrastructure, including $25 million to the South Temple Water Infrastructure Capital Program and $10 million for an aquifer storage and recovery program. As for the Sammons Community Center, city leaders have proposed a $15 million bond to rebuild it. If voters approve the measure, Rowan has promised to put $3 million to help the project. It’s one of many actions that has made Rowan stand out to Tim Davis, Temple’s mayor, particularly since the company is not making money from the town yet. “To go ahead and invest dollars into the community for a current need is very generous of them,” Davis said. “That tells me they want to work hard to have a positive impact, and they’ve chosen to help the city.” Gaining public support is an important tactic for data center companies coming to Texas, and one that can’t be ignored. Over the last year, communities all over the state have voiced opposition to data centers coming to their areas — their main concerns being rising electric bills, losing water and housing issues. Some cities have prevented developments from moving forward. For example, a project in East Texas was pulled after community backlash and Lubbock leaders passed a 90-day moratorium on large-scale projects following a citizen-led petition. Nathaniel Brown, director of public relations for Rowan, admits that integrating into a community hasn’t been an easy task. Brown said Rowan began hosting neighbor dinners every month for residents to talk with the construction team and ask them questions. The company has also held public hearings, open houses and have Facebook pages dedicated to its project updates. “This development doesn’t happen in a vacuum. It needs to be able to fit into the community’s vision for their area,” Brown said. Google has used a similar strategy.
