artigo.texto: Few rideshares come with a theme, but SpaceX’s Transporter-18—which launched Thursday from Vandenberg—had one: getting power to compute in orbit. Three of its payloads are each testing a different piece of the ODC puzzle. - Cowboy Space’s Reason-1 will attempt to beam solar power to Earth via laser—a test run for the optical links its future data centers will need. - Google’s Project Suncatcher will run AI chips on traditional solar power to see how they hold up in orbit. - Star Catcher’s Protostar will try to beam power between two spacecraft, with orbital data centers among its customers. “We passed the point of saying, ‘Will there be people doing AI computing in space?'” Cowboy Space COO and Chief Legal Officer Joseph Yaffe told Payload. “We’re focused on building the infrastructure for that.” cowboy like me: Cowboy Space began as Aetherflux—a power-beaming startup—before rebranding in May to focus on orbital data centers and rockets. Reason-1 is the stepping stone that brings the two efforts together. - Cowboy hopes to attempt to beam as soon as late October, sending solar power via infrared laser to a 10–20 m spot at a ground test facility and aiming to deliver 30–100 W. Cowboy calls it the first commercial kilowatt-class laser in space designed to deliver energy to Earth. - The same laser technology will form the backbone of the data link on Reason-2, which is slated to fly H200 GPUs in the first half of 2027—this time beaming data instead of power. - Longer term, Cowboy is building its own rocket, whose upper stage doubles as a 1 MW data center, targeted to launch in December 2028. “We’re an orbital energy infrastructure company that’s delivering power, computing power, and the ability to connect all of those things through laser infrared technology,” Yaffe said. Hot N Cold: While Cowboy is testing the laser, Google is testing out chips. Its Project Suncatcher MVP—built with Planet Labs—was announced last year as a research “moonshot” to run AI in orbit. The fridge-sized satellite carries four Trillium TPUs—roughly one server’s worth of compute—using about 1kW of solar to run Gemini queries in short bursts. On Thursday, Google also released an updated, peer-reviewed version of its Suncatcher paper in the energy research journal Joule, sketching the company’s long-term vision: - The constellation: Satellites that could eventually hold a data-center rack’s worth of compute, roughly 50–100 kW each, flying in tight, laser-linked clusters. One illustrative example packs 81 satellites within a 1 km radius. - Radiation: In ground tests, the TPUs survived a radiation dose equivalent to five years in orbit. Radiation still caused occasional silent errors—about one per three million queries—which is manageable for answering questions but may be a problem for training models. - Heat: The paper calls thermal management a major challenge. MVP’s chips will have to power down every 15 to 20 minutes to avoid overheating. Google says its two follow-up satellites in 2027 will run continuously. If launch costs fall to $200/kg, Google estimates the cost of launching a kilowatt of solar power to orbit would be about $810 per year, comparable to what US data centers spend on electricity. Its learning-curve analysis suggests that price is possible by the mid-2030s, if Starship flies about 180 times a year. Pocketful of Sunshine: The final piece is power. Star Catcher’s Protostar will be the company’s first end-to-end in-space demo. - Protostar will deploy a cubesat and beam measurable power to its off-the-shelf solar panels—aiming to validate commercial power-beaming operations. - Orbital computing companies Starcloud and Aethero are among Star Catcher’s publicized customers. As Yaffe put it, the “if” of AI compute in space may be settled. The next few weeks will give a glimpse into how far along the “how” is.

artigo.texto: China, already dominating the global lithium-ion battery market, plans to expand this position to solid-state batteries, too. The government in Beijing will seek to cut solid-state battery costs, boost their performance, and begin commercial production by 2030. "Over the next five years, the new-type battery industry is at a critical window for technological upgrading, and we must seize the strategic opportunities presented by technological and industrial innovation," China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology said in a news release, as cited by the South China Morning Post. The five-year plan for solid-state batteries comes amid a global race in that segment, as researchers and businesses in other parts of the world try to circumvent or challenge China's existing dominance in lithium-ion battery tech, and diversify away from lithium-ion technology as well. As of last year, China's solid-state battery market was worth some $42.5 million, the Global Times reported in a news piece on the battery plan. This should grow to $384.8 million by 2030 as a result of government encouragement, with an annual compound growth rate at an impressive 44.4%, compared to a global average CAGR projected for batteries of 37.5%. Related: U.S. Threatens Diesel Export Ban Unless Europe Releases Stockpiles Bringing costs down seems to be priority number-one for solid-state battery developers—an issue that battery tech shares with lithium-ion technology. Focus areas also include developing new electrode materials, new electrolytes—a vulnerability for solid-state batteries right now—and other new materials to use in solid-state batteries. The plan covers technologies including sodium batteries and flow batteries, two potential challengers to lithium-ion technology that have yet to become as popular as the dominant battery technology. Lithium-ion batteries are dominant on the EV market and all other markets for products that use batteries, as much thanks to their performance as to the absence of real rivals. Lithium-ion batteries are expensive, they can be a fire hazard, and they rely on some costly materials, including lithium itself. By comparison, researchers see solid-state batteries as a viable alternative that can be cheaper and more reliable, with higher energy density than lithium-ion batteries, faster charging times, a longer life, and, importantly, the possibility of extended ranges for electric vehicles. But first, they need to solve the problem with solid-state battery failures, which has plagued research in the area for years.

artigo.texto: Big Tech Will Spend $735 Billion on Data Centers. This Boring Electrical Contractor Collects the Checks. Hyperscalers are going all-in on artificial intelligence (AI). Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Meta Platforms are expected to spend a combined $735 billion on data centers this year, and this may be just the beginning. PwC estimates global investment in AI infrastructure could reach a staggering $31.6 trillion by 2050. All that computing power needs electricity, cooling, and a company with the expertise to deliver it. As hyperscalers race to build AI infrastructure, the biggest constraints are shifting from chips to power access and skilled labor. That puts Quanta Services (NYSE: PWR) in an enviable position to collect the checks. Here's what investors need to know. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Quanta Services is perfectly positioned to facilitate the data center build-out Besides chips, hyperscalers need energy. That requires high-voltage electrical, mechanical, and grid interconnection engineering, which is Quanta Services' specialty. The company provides engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) services, with a particular focus on electric power, renewable energy, underground utility, and other energy infrastructure. One of the biggest factors that sets Quanta apart is its skilled labor force of 85,000 employees, which the company spends $250 million per year training. Developing a skilled trade workforce, including electricians, lineworkers, plumbers, and engineers, takes years, giving Quanta a robust competitive advantage. The infrastructure company's revenue and backlog are surging Quanta focuses on data center build-out outside chips, and its "balance of plant" approach aims to capture 80% of total facility capital expenditure, excluding chips. This includes high-volatility electrical and grid interconnection, cooling infrastructure, site development, and off-site prefabrication and integration. Quanta has made this possible by acquiring specialized platforms such as Cupertino Electric, Dynamic Systems, Phalcon, and Enerfab. Quanta is seeing robust growth as data center spending rises. In the first half of 2026, Quanta earned $17.4 billion in revenue, a 34% increase from the same period last year. Meanwhile, net income surged 80% to $672 million. It finished the second quarter with a record backlog of $53 billion, with 60% of this expected to convert into revenue within the next 12 months.

artigo.texto: News Mercedes-Benz Secures Deal To Advance Solid-State Battery Technology Mercedes-Benz has strengthened its decade-long partnership with ProLogium to gain priority access to its fourth-generation solid-state battery cells, marking a significant advancement in EV technology. Solid-state batteries offer higher energy density, faster charging, and increased safety compared to traditional lithium-ion cells. Mercedes-Benz is partnering with ProLogium to test these Gen4 lithium ceramic batteries, aiming to integrate the technology into its next-generation electric vehicles within the coming year. “At Mercedes-Benz, we are committed to shaping the future of electric mobility,” said Jörg Burzer, Board of Management member. “Our partnership with ProLogium helps us advance next-generation battery technology. By combining ProLogium’s solid-state expertise with our development capabilities, we are reaching a milestone in evolving our future electric vehicle fleet.” ProLogium currently operates a significant battery manufacturing facility in Taiwan and is planning a new site in Dunkirk, France, with a projected capacity of up to 44 GWh. This facility is expected to facilitate the supply of cells to European customers, including Mercedes-Benz. Beyond its collaboration with ProLogium, Mercedes-Benz is actively diversifying its solid-state battery initiatives by testing lithium-metal battery cells from the American firm Factorial Energy. In a notable development last year, a Mercedes-Benz EQS equipped with a Factorial solid-state battery pack successfully achieved a range of 748.8 miles (1,205 km) on a single charge. artigo.texto: (The Center Square) – Wisconsin voters continue to believe the costs of data centers outweigh the benefits and also said data centers were the least desirable of five development options and that state tax incentives reward companies that don’t pay their fair share in a new poll of registered voters in the state. The poll showed 54% of voters believe state incentives reward companies that don’t pay their fair share while 45% believe that the economic benefits of state incentives for business are worth the cost. When it comes to data centers specifically, however, 74% of Wisconsin voters said that the costs of data centers outweigh the benefits, down from 78% who said the same last month in the Marquette Law School Poll. The Marquette Poll was conducted Sept. 16-23, interviewing 843 Wisconsin registered voters, with margin of error of +/-4.3 percentage points. For likely voters, the sample size is 692 with a margin of error of +/-4.8 percentage points. The September poll expanded what it asked about data centers and development in September, with just 9% of voters saying data centers were the most desirable of large-scale developments they would like to see in their area with none of the five (44%), a semiconductor fabrication plant (33%), an e-commerce fulfillment center (27%), an automobile manufacturing plant (24%) and a steel or aluminum mill (14%) all more desirable. Respondents could choose more than one option on what they would like to see. The poll showed 49% of registered voters felt that new manufacturing and commerce developments were very important for jobs while 43% said they were somewhat important while 61% felt that unfairness favoring the wealthy was a larger problem than over-regulation.

artigo.texto: Solar Firms Build BESS Capacity for Next Growth Phase: Interview Solarworld has commissioned a 3.6 GWh BESS manufacturing facility at Roorkee, Uttarakhand October 1, 2026 Follow Mercom India on WhatsApp for exclusive updates on clean energy news and insights As energy storage becomes increasingly important to renewable energy integration, solar companies are positioning themselves for the next phase of growth by building battery energy storage system (BESS) manufacturing capabilities. In an exclusive interview with Mercom India, Kartik Teltia, Managing Director at Solarworld Energy Solutions, discussed the growing role of energy storage, the dominance of TOPCon solar module technology, and the need for upstream manufacturing capabilities. What is Solarworld’s current solar module manufacturing capacity, and what are the company’s expansion plans for solar cell and module production? Our ALMM-listed module manufacturing facility in Roorkee, Uttarakhand, has a capacity of 1.55 GW and uses N-Type TOPCon technology. This gives us a strong base to serve both our own EPC pipeline and the wider market as India scales solar manufacturing. We have entered into a joint venture with Rays Power Infra to set up a 2.4 GW solar cell manufacturing facility in Narmadapuram, Madhya Pradesh, with commercial production targeted for June 2027. Once operational, this will allow us to supply modules with domestically manufactured cells rather than relying on imports. Which solar module technologies is Solarworld prioritizing? How do you expect the TOPCon, HJT, and larger wafer format technologies to evolve in India? At Solarworld, our modules are built on N-Type TOPCon, currently the technology of choice across the industry. Recent industry data shows TOPCon accounted for close to 40 GW of the roughly 44 GW of new module capacity India added in the first half of this year. In contrast, HJT capacity was added for the first time at a much smaller scale, at around 1 GW. I expect that gap to persist for the next few years. TOPCon has reached a point where the supply chain, equipment, and cost curve are all mature, whereas HJT still carries higher capital costs and a thinner domestic ecosystem. On wafer formats, the industry has largely settled on the larger M10R and G12R formats, which we also use, since they improve output per module and reduce balance-of-system costs for developers. HJT will likely find its place in premium or space-constrained applications rather than replacing TOPCon at utility scale in the near term. Our own investment plans, including the upcoming cell facility, are built around this TOPCon-led trajectory. Project developers often raise concerns about module reliability, including micro-cracks and long-term degradation. What manufacturing and quality-control measures does Solarworld use to address these concerns? At Solarworld, we build reliability into the manufacturing process itself, rather than checking for it only at the end of the line. Our facility uses automated production processes, reducing manual handling and inconsistent thermal exposure that can contribute to micro-cracks and soldering-related defects in solar modules. Every module we manufacture goes through extended reliability testing and compliance checks against the requirements of the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), and the ALMM before it leaves our Roorkee facility. This layered testing approach is designed to identify defects, whether cosmetic or structural, well before a module reaches a project site. Our experience with large-scale EPC projects also shapes how we manufacture and test our modules. Energy storage is becoming increasingly important for grid stability. Solarworld has commissioned an automated 3.6 GW BESS manufacturing line. What is the engineering architecture of this facility, and how is the company positioning its storage solutions in the market? Energy storage is becoming a critical part of the renewable energy ecosystem. India’s storage requirement is projected to grow several times over by the early 2030s as renewable capacity scales and grid stability needs increase. We see BESS manufacturing as a natural extension of our solar manufacturing base and existing utility relationships. We have commissioned a fully automated 3.6 GWh BESS manufacturing facility at Roorkee, built with KUKA robotics across the production line to ensure consistency at scale. The facility is designed around a liquid-cooled architecture for both our commercial and industrial units and larger containerized systems, as thermal management is critical to battery life and safety at grid scale. India is rapidly expanding domestic solar manufacturing, but upstream segments such as wafers and ingots are heavily import-dependent. How should the industry prepare for the possibility of ALMM requirements extending further upstream? MNRE has extended the ALMM framework to cells from June 2026, and further upstream to ingots and wafers under a new List III from June 2028, with conditions requiring at least three independent manufacturers with a combined manufacturing capacity of 15 GW before the list can be issued. Wafers and ingots are capital-intensive and still almost entirely import-dependent in India, so the runway before 2028 needs to be used effectively. At Solarworld, we will evaluate wafer and ingot integration as the domestic ecosystem matures. The industry must prioritize building a domestic wafer and ingot supply base with meaningful operating scale rather than relying solely on announced capacity. artigo.texto: Google launches Project Suncatcher, a step towards AI data centers in space Google just put a refrigerator-sized satellite into space, part of a research project the company hopes can pave the way for orbiting AI data centers powered by the sun. The prototype satellite has four specialty chips in it called Tensor Processing Units, or TPUs, that Google designed for machine learning and has already deployed in data centers on Earth. The chips will run a version of the company's Gemma AI model for 15 minutes at a time due to heat management constraints, using the open weight model to answer simple queries. In a blog post, Google said the mission will gauge how the TPUs handle "the physical stress of spaceflight and the radiation and thermal extremes of space." Use of AI has grown sharply over the last few years, fueling demand for data centers. At Google's annual developer summit in May, CEO Sundar Pichai said demand for AI services exceeds supply and he expects capital expenditures this year to be $180 billion to $190 billion — more than six times as large as in 2022 — as the company builds computing infrastructure and develops chips. At a time when opposition to the proliferation of power-hungry data centers on Earth is growing, Google is one of a handful of companies advancing plans to put them in orbit where there is virtually unlimited free energy and no protesters. "The sun puts out almost all of the power in our solar system. All of the other power sources that humanity has tapped into are just a tiny fraction of a percent," said Travis Beals, senior director and lead of Project Suncatcher. "So in some sense, this project is about tapping into the best way to use solar power to run AI compute." The satellite will be in a sun-synchronous orbit where its solar panels will almost never be in the shade. That eliminates the need for carrying heavy batteries or backup power on the spacecraft. Last November, a venture-backed startup called Starcloud launched a spacecraft that carried an Nvidia H100 chip on board and demonstrated a version of Google's Gemini AI from space. Elon Musk's SpaceX is also working on space data centers, and has said it expects to start deploying "orbital AI compute satellites" as early as 2028. Google developed the experimental satellite in partnership with the aerospace and satellite imagery company Planet. It eventually envisions clusters of satellites orbiting together to form space-based data centers. Each satellite will carry dozens of TPU chips and communicate with the others — and Earth — via lasers. Next year, the company plans to put two more satellites into orbit to test their connection. The satellite launched today is a prototype that Beals called "a very minimal test" to make sure the chips can run in space. A SpaceX rocket carried it into orbit, and Planet will get it up and running. Beal said Google will then fire up and test the TPUs. The goal is for the mission to be operational for a year. Brandon Lucia, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at Carnegie Mellon University, said the idea sounds "very sci-fi," but much of the technology has been proven at a research level. Still, there are huge challenges. Heat is a big one. Computer chips get hot, and on Earth the heat can be dissipated with wind or water. That's not possible in the vacuum of space. "In a satellite in particular, using more power to do the computations means dumping more heat into the confined environment inside of the satellite," Lucia said. In its blog post, Google called cooling the chips "a crucial research challenge," and outlined some of the approaches it's working on, including using a combination of pipes and radiators to wick heat away from the chips. Beal said the radiators are one of the heaviest components on the current mission — a drawback because heavier objects are more expensive to launch — and his team is working on ways to cool chips more efficiently. Lucia points out that there are also major questions about upkeep. When a chip malfunctions in a terrestrial data center, or something goes on the fritz, a technician can walk in and fix it. That's harder when the data center is circling hundreds of miles above Earth. "Those all have their cost and complexity amplified by a factor of 10, maybe a factor of 100. And so there has to be a big payoff," Lucia said. And there are environmental questions, too. While space data centers would run on solar power, the rockets that launch them run off of carbon-based fuels. And eventually they will re-enter earth's atmosphere, potentially adding pollution as they burn up. Elon Musk has said that space is the "only way to scale" data centers to meet future demand for AI. But the economics are still a question mark. Launches are costly, repairs are difficult, and communication by laser across hundreds of miles and through Earth's atmosphere is slower. And it will take constellations of many satellites to equal the computing capacity of a terrestrial data center. Beals said he and his small team think about these questions a lot. "It doesn't help a lot if this is technically possible, if it's always going to be too expensive to be practical," he said. He added that it is difficult to know when space-based data centers will be economically viable. "I don't see this being something where it's cheaper to do this in the next five years. I think it will take longer than that," he said. And he doesn't think that space data centers will replace terrestrial data centers any time soon. "I think that there are going to be use cases that make more sense to do on Earth and use cases that make more sense to do in space," Beals said. "In the really-long run, perhaps the set of things you do in space gets larger and larger until that's where most of the compute is happening. But I think for a long time you'll have both coexisting." The whole project, he said, is a "moonshot." "It's going to take a long time," he said. "It's not going

artigo.texto: GMP grows battery storage program aimed at preventing outages COLCHESTER, Vt. (WCAX) - Green Mountain Power is working to make sure customers’ lights never go out through what it calls a “virtual power plant.” GMP’s shared battery storage system takes energy from the grid and stores it away to be used later. Then, when there’s a severe storm or another extreme weather event that knocks out power, people who have the batteries in their home are able to keep their lights on. This energy stored in the batteries flows back into the grid during peak periods when demand is high. GMP says it’s now Vermont’s biggest energy source, made up of clean energy. “Energy storage is seamless and simple backup power. So it connects into your home; a lot of our customers tell us they don’t even know they have an outage because it’s so seamless, and so they can last for days and days with this energy storage,” said Kristin Carlson of Green Mountain Power. The system is growing; GMP says it has approximately 5,600 customers, up from around 5,000 in July. The batteries cost about $55 a month, or $5,500 outright. Copyright 2026 WCAX. artigo.texto: The Pegasus long endurance drone, developed by Li-S Energy, V-TOL Aerospace and Halocell Energy, completes a successful series of test flights over Queensland Key Highlights: - The EATP Pegasus long endurance drone completed several successful test flights in Queensland, culminating in an endurance flight of almost 2 hours covering more than 75 kilometres, on a single Li-S Energy battery pack. - The endurance flight met expected flight performance and landed safely with battery capacity to spare. - On a same cell weight basis, the Li-S Energy cells delivered 80% more range and flight time than would have been achieved by an equivalent high-performance professional lithium polymer UAV battery pack # - The Pegasus drone comprises V-TOL Aerospace's airframe, Li-S Energy's lithium sulfur battery system, and Halocell Energy's perovskite solar array. - Designed to accommodate two Li-S Energy battery packs, in due course Pegasus is expected to deliver flight durations of 5-8 hours, and 250 kilometres, ideal for long endurance mapping, surveillance, and agricultural, utilities and environmental monitoring missions. - Demand for drones is growing exponentially across commercial and defence markets, with proposed US and Australian government investment in drone and counter-drone technologies now exceeding A$100 billion[1]. - Following this success, the collaboration partners intend to assess further commercial development, targeting future platform sales. - See a one-minute video of the flight here: https://lis.plus/EATP BRISBANE, Australia , Sept. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Li-S Energy Limited (ASX: LIS) ("Li-S Energy", "LIS" or "the Company") is pleased to announce that Pegasus, the long endurance drone developed under the Emerging Aviation Technology Partnership (EATP) programme, has completed a series of successful test flights in Queensland, culminating in endurance flight of almost 2 hours, powered by a single Li-S Energy lithium sulfur battery pack. The twin motor, five-metre wingspan Pegasus was designed and built from the ground up through the collaboration of three innovative Australian companies. It combines an airframe and power systems designed and developed by V-TOL Aerospace (V-TOL), the 382 Wh lithium sulfur battery packs and battery management system designed and built by Li-S Energy, and a perovskite solar cell array fabricated by Halocell Energy (Halocell). As announced in June 2024, the project is supported by a grant of just over $1.35 million from the Commonwealth Government under the EATP programme, matched by the collaboration partners. The collaboration is targeting the development of a family of long endurance surveillance drones powered by Li-S Energy batteries. This flight marks the culmination of the EATP project and the successful completion of its practical development and flight test work. Milestone flight testing The flight test programme comprised several flights, culminating in an endurance flight of almost 2 hours on a single Li-S Energy battery pack. The aircraft met its expected flight performance throughout and landed safely with battery capacity to spare. The Li-S Energy battery system enabled sustained cruise flight of more than 75 kilometres, with the Company's battery management system integrated with V-TOL's power management system controlling the battery power for the twin motors and control systems, while being capable of simultaneously managing the feed-in from the solar array. The Pegasus was designed to accommodate two Li-S Energy battery packs, and with the latest improvements to Halocell's solar array performance beyond those fitted to the current airframe, we expect the platform to be capable of flight missions of five to eight hours and 250 kilometres, ideal for long endurance mapping and surveillance, and for agricultural, utilities and environmental monitoring missions. The flight data will now be analysed by the partners to characterise platform performance and inform the assessment of the platform's commercial potential. Toward commercial development Demand for long endurance uncrewed aircraft continues to grow rapidly across commercial and defence markets, and both endurance and sovereign supply are decisive competitive strengths. With their integrated technologies now proven in flight, the collaboration partners intend to capitalise on this market potential. Li-S Energy filed two patent applications to protect innovative developments during the project relating to the battery management system and battery pack design. Quotes Dr Lee Finniear, Chief Executive Officer and Managing Director of Li-S Energy, said: "With the exponential growth of drones and uncrewed systems in both commercial and military applications, flight endurance and sovereign capability are critical to Australia's future in this sector. Today, with our partners, we have shown what Australian innovation and collaboration is capable of. The EATP Pegasus drone is the result of two years of work by the teams from V-TOL Aerospace, Halocell and Li-S Energy, proving that Australia has the sovereign capability and the unique technology to be leaders in this field." Mark Xavier, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of V-TOL Aerospace, said: "The Pegasus flew exactly as our team designed it to. Our airframe and power systems performed faultlessly throughout the flight, and pairing them with Li-S Energy's new lightweight pouch cell battery system gives the platform an endurance advantage operators will immediately recognise. I am proud of what our engineers have delivered, and our focus now turns to the pathway from successful trials to commercial platform sales." Paul Moonie, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Halocell Energy, said: "Seeing our ultra-lightweight perovskite cells take to the air on the Pegasus is a proud moment for the Halocell Energy team, whose skill in fabricating flexible solar modules for such a demanding application has been outstanding. artigo.texto: No Brasil, um maço de cigarros carrega 83% de tributos. Um casaco de pele, 81%. Já as baterias que armazenam energia limpa e garantem a confiabilidade do sistema elétrico pagam 84%. Tributamos como supérfluo, ou como vício, um equipamento que se tornou infraestrutura essencial no mundo inteiro e que, no Brasil, poderia ajudar a reduzir a conta de luz. A distorção ganha urgência às vésperas das eleições. Com eventos climáticos extremos e mais frequentes, decisões sobre o setor elétrico dizem respeito à segurança energética e à competitividade da indústria nacional. O Brasil reúne condições únicas para liderar essa transformação: um dos melhores recursos solares do mundo e uma matriz elétrica predominantemente renovável. A energia solar já é a segunda maior fonte da matriz, fruto de uma década que mobilizou mais de R$ 320 bilhões em investimentos. Mas o sistema não foi projetado para essa velocidade. Cortes de geração renovável, inversões de fluxo nas redes e pressões tarifárias mostram que desperdiçamos energia limpa e barata enquanto o consumidor paga uma conta de luz que sobe acima da inflação. É exatamente esse o problema que as baterias ajudam a resolver. Elas armazenam energia nos momentos de maior geração e a devolvem quando o sistema mais precisa, aumentando a confiabilidade, reduzindo desperdícios e custos sistêmicos e diminuindo a dependência de combustíveis fósseis nos horários de pico. Segundo a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), o armazenamento pode atrair mais de R$ 200 bilhões em investimentos na próxima década. O que trava esse potencial é, em boa medida, a tributação. Corrigi-la não é conceder subsídio: é dar às baterias tratamento isonômico em relação às demais tecnologias do setor elétrico. Enquanto essa distorção persistir, a sociedade seguirá exposta a riscos operacionais e custos desnecessários. O próximo governo também precisará evitar retrocessos. A inclusão recorrente de “jabutis” em projetos de lei para privilegiar combustíveis fósseis aumenta a conta dos consumidores e indica ao mercado uma direção na contramão do mundo. Cada política pública deve ser guiada pela eficiência e pelo interesse coletivo. A transição energética precisa ser política de Estado, com planejamento, estabilidade regulatória e visão de longo prazo. Aos candidatos deste ano, fica uma pergunta: por que o Brasil ainda cobra mais imposto da bateria do que do cigarro? Quem tiver a melhor resposta estará mais preparado para decidir o futuro energético do País.

artigo.texto: Lao Cai se prepara para participar do mercado de créditos de carbono florestal. Na tarde de 29 de setembro, o Sr. Phan Trung Bá, Vice-Presidente do Comitê Popular Provincial, presidiu uma reunião para discutir o desenvolvimento de serviços de sequestro e armazenamento de carbono, a redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa e a exploração eficaz do potencial e das vantagens florestais, preparando assim as condições necessárias para que Lao Cai participe do mercado de créditos de carbono florestal. Estiveram presentes na reunião líderes dos Departamentos de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente, Finanças, Indústria e Comércio, Construção, Ciência e Tecnologia; do Subdepartamento de Proteção Florestal e do Fundo Provincial de Proteção Florestal e Ambiental. Segundo um relatório do Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente, na implementação do Decreto Governamental nº 180/2026/ND-CP sobre serviços de sequestro e armazenamento de carbono florestal, a província de Lao Cai está gradualmente concluindo seu banco de dados e preparando as condições necessárias para o desenvolvimento de projetos de carbono florestal. Até o momento, a província concluiu o levantamento do estado das florestas e das reservas de carbono florestal em 48 municípios e distritos da região norte. Os resultados indicam uma reserva total de carbono de 14,33 milhões de toneladas. O Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente finalizou o esboço e o orçamento para o levantamento do estado das florestas para o período de 2026-2027 em 51 comunas e distritos da região sul, servindo como base para a construção de linhas de referência para projetos de carbono na província. Além de investigar e avaliar o potencial, a província está preparando as condições necessárias em termos de mecanismos, projetos e recursos para desenvolver créditos de carbono florestal. O Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente prestou consultoria sobre o desenvolvimento de conteúdo relacionado à gestão e ao uso de créditos de carbono; elaborou o documento do projeto "Transformando os Resultados da Redução de Emissões e a Gestão Florestal Sustentável no Vietnã, Província de Lao Cai", financiado pelo Fundo Verde para o Clima (GCF). Simultaneamente, está desenvolvendo o plano técnico e o orçamento para o projeto de créditos de carbono em florestas de propriedade de toda a população. Você também pode gostar Segundo o Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente, os projetos de desenvolvimento de carbono florestal são uma área nova, sendo implementados pela primeira vez na província. O processo de implementação ainda requer aprimoramento em diversas áreas, principalmente no que diz respeito aos requisitos técnicos, padrões econômico -técnicos, sistemas de medição, relatórios, avaliação e verificação dos resultados da redução de emissões. Na reunião, os delegados concentraram-se na discussão da investigação e desenvolvimento de uma base de dados florestal e de carbono; métodos de medição, monitorização e digitalização de dados; recursos para implementação; e as condições necessárias para a implementação do projeto de crédito de carbono florestal na província. Ao concluir a reunião, o Sr. Phan Trung Bá, Vice-Presidente do Comitê Popular Provincial, enfatizou que o desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono florestal está passando da fase de pesquisa para a implementação concreta, com demandas cada vez maiores em relação a dados, base legal, recursos e capacidade de implementação. Portanto, o Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente precisa assessorar proativamente e preparar dados de entrada suficientes sobre florestas, como base para a integração com o sistema geral de dados e para servir à gestão e ao desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono. O camarada solicitou ao Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente que continue investigando e atualizando o estado atual das florestas em 51 comunas e distritos; e, ao mesmo tempo, revise e delimite especificamente as áreas florestais, especialmente naquelas onde a entidade gestora não foi claramente identificada. Com isso, o objetivo é completar gradualmente o banco de dados florestal e preparar as condições para o desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono na província. Você também pode gostar Em relação aos recursos para implementação, o camarada Phan Trung Bá solicitou ao Departamento de Finanças que revisasse e assessorasse sobre a alocação de verbas para atividades de proteção florestal, levantamentos do estado das florestas e implementação de projetos de carbono florestal. Quanto ao orçamento proposto, ele enfatizou que se trata apenas de uma estimativa inicial, servindo de base para o desenvolvimento de um plano e orçamento detalhados. O uso dos recursos deve ser calculado com base em normas estabelecidas, conteúdo e etapas reais de implementação, garantindo a conformidade com as normas e a eficácia. O vice-presidente do Comitê Popular Provincial também enfatizou que a gestão e a exploração de informações e dados sobre carbono florestal devem ser realizadas com rigor. Organizações e empresas que necessitem realizar levantamentos e avaliações de recursos florestais para projetos de carbono devem ser orientadas de acordo com as normas, prevenindo o risco de exploração indevida de levantamentos e avaliações para fins de exploração, troca ou transferência de informações e dados sobre recursos de carbono. Além disso, o Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente, em coordenação com o Departamento de Ciência e Tecnologia, está pesquisando soluções tecnológicas e equipamentos para apoiar a investigação, medição e coleta de dados sobre florestas; e preparando informações para integrar e digitalizar gradualmente os dados florestais da província. O vice-presidente do Comitê Popular Provincial, Phan Trung Bá, solicitou que os departamentos e agências continuem a coordenar pesquisas e a fornecer consultoria sobre a avaliação da capacidade de absorção de carbono das florestas; proponham soluções para melhorar a qualidade e o valor das flor

artigo.texto: Czech Republic and Italy Propose Easing the European Carbon Market Prague and Rome present a joint package to the European Council aimed at adjusting the carbon market, free allocations and methane obligations to reduce industrial energy costs. Andrej BabiÅ¡, the Czech prime minister, and Giorgia Meloni, president of the Italian Council of Ministers, presented a joint package of proposals intended for the European Council meeting of October 15 and 16, 2026, in Brussels. The document, titled "Energy costs and European industrial competitiveness," was published on September 30, 2026, by the Office of the Czech Government, a day after a bilateral meeting at the Strakova akademie in Prague. It aims to ease the energy costs borne by European industry through adjustments to the carbon market and to fossil fuel supply rules. An alternative to a general suspension of the carbon market According to Prague and Rome, a general suspension of the European emissions trading market would not have sufficient support among member states. The package therefore proposes targeted adjustments to the Market Stability Reserve, the mechanism that regulates the supply of allowances auctioned according to predefined rules. The two governments are requesting the ability to reduce or suspend withdrawals from this reserve and, if necessary, to organize an exceptional release of allowances. The volume concerned would correspond to a flow withdrawn from auctions, distinct from the reserve's total stock. Free allocations and the role of electricity The text also calls for greater flexibility in the allocation of free emission allowances, which protect certain industrial activities against the risk of production relocating to jurisdictions with weaker carbon constraints. Both countries are seeking a revision of the performance benchmarks used to calculate these allocations, as well as a pause in their reduction for sectors already covered by the carbon border adjustment mechanism. For electricity, the package envisions a temporary adjustment of the carbon obligations imposed on fossil-fuel plants that set the market's marginal price. Prague and Rome are also requesting greater recognition of the transitional role of gas and of nuclear power within the European taxonomy of sustainable investments. Certain nuclear and gas-related activities are already included, under conditions, as investments considered sustainable. The package does not specify the additional criteria that would be applied to broaden this recognition. Methane obligations and a new carbon market for buildings On methane, the initiative seeks the temporary suspension of obligations relating to fossil fuel imports. Current European regulation requires importers to demonstrate the equivalence of the monitoring, reporting and verification measures applied to the production of crude oil, natural gas and coal, with a different treatment for pre-existing contracts. The package finally calls for a reassessment of the launch of the new emissions trading system covering buildings, road transport and other sectors, separate from the existing carbon market and whose obligations fall on fuel suppliers. The two governments propose a postponement conditional on its effects on the energy crisis, along with coordinated monitoring of financial positions in this market, without establishing the existence of any manipulation. The publication of this package confirms the two governments' common position, without constituting an adoption of the measures by the European Union.

artigo.texto: No dia 29 de setembro, a Academia Vietnamita de Ciências Florestais, por meio do Centro Vietnamita de Certificação de Gestão Florestal (VFCC), em colaboração com a Forest Trends, organizou um workshop de consulta sobre "Soluções Baseadas na Natureza (SbN) para a Restauração Florestal Após a Extração Mineral e Oportunidades de Participação no Futuro Mercado de Carbono". Restauração florestal após mineração: abrindo oportunidades para participar do mercado de carbono. (Chinhphu.vn) - De acordo com especialistas, a aplicação de soluções NbS não só ajuda a regenerar a vegetação nativa e a restaurar ecossistemas danificados pela mineração, como também abre grandes oportunidades para que empresas e localidades participem do mercado de carbono no futuro. Durante o workshop, especialistas argumentaram que, embora muitas commodities que representam risco de desmatamento, como madeira, café, borracha, soja e óleo de palma, estejam sujeitas a requisitos de controle cada vez mais rigorosos, as atividades de mineração, apesar de seu impacto significativo nas florestas, ainda não foram inseridas em uma estrutura de governança proporcional. O Dr. To Xuan Phuc, especialista da Forest Trends, observou que o impacto da mineração na vegetação e nos ecossistemas florestais está se tornando cada vez mais evidente, mas os minerais raramente são reconhecidos como uma "mercadoria com risco de desmatamento". Isso cria uma lacuna nas políticas públicas, já que a cadeia de suprimentos de minerais ainda não atende aos requisitos equivalentes em relação à responsabilidade pela proteção e restauração florestal. Essa ausência cria uma lacuna significativa em termos legais e políticos. Enquanto os produtos de madeira e café passam por rigorosos processos de due diligence para verificar sua origem não desmatada antes de entrarem em mercados exigentes, a cadeia de suprimentos de minerais carece de obrigações comparáveis em relação à proteção e restauração florestal. Segundo especialistas, as atividades de mineração podem levar à perda de vegetação, perturbar a estrutura do solo, fragmentar habitats, aumentar o risco de deslizamentos de terra e poluir fontes de água. Análises de sensoriamento remoto também mostram um declínio na cobertura vegetal em muitas áreas de mineração, enquanto a infraestrutura que serve à mineração pode aumentar a pressão sobre as florestas próximas. No Vietnã, foram emitidas regulamentações sobre a conversão de terras florestais e os depósitos para restauração ambiental, mas sua implementação ainda é limitada. A restauração pós-florestamento em algumas áreas não restaurou completamente as funções ecológicas da floresta e não está intimamente ligada aos padrões de manejo florestal sustentável. Integrar a restauração florestal na governança da mineração. Dr. Tran Lam Dong , Vice-Diretor da Academia Vietnamita de Ciências Florestais. Conclusão: É hora de as agências reguladoras mudarem sua mentalidade e considerarem o controle do impacto da indústria de mineração nas florestas como parte integrante da estratégia nacional de proteção florestal e resposta às mudanças climáticas. Especialistas propõem considerar os minerais como um fator de controle de risco para o desmatamento, estabelecer padrões obrigatórios de responsabilização e avaliações de impacto florestal para projetos de licenciamento de mineração; fortalecer os mecanismos de coordenação intersetorial e conectar estreitamente as agências de gestão de recursos minerais e as agências de gestão florestal ao longo de todo o ciclo de vida do projeto de mineração, desde o planejamento e licenciamento até o fechamento da mina e a restauração ambiental. Uma das abordagens discutidas no workshop foi a aplicação de Soluções Baseadas na Natureza (SbN) para restaurar áreas florestais impactadas pela mineração. O professor Vu Tan Phuong, diretor do Centro de Certificação de Gestão Florestal do Vietnã (VFCC), afirmou que a aplicação de soluções de NbS não só ajuda a regenerar a vegetação nativa e a restaurar ecossistemas danificados pela mineração, como também abre grandes oportunidades para que empresas e localidades participem do mercado de carbono no futuro. Segundo o Professor Vu Tan Phuong, as áreas onde as operações de mineração são restauradas, se devidamente reflorestadas e restauradas ecologicamente de acordo com os padrões de Soluções Baseadas na Natureza (SbN), gerarão um sequestro significativo de carbono. Esse aumento nos estoques de carbono pode ser medido, relatado e verificado (MRV) para ser convertido em créditos de carbono florestal de alta qualidade. Isso oferece um benefício duplo: apoia as empresas no cumprimento de suas responsabilidades sociais e ambientais, ao mesmo tempo que gera financiamento adicional com a venda de créditos de carbono nos mercados nacional e internacional, criando um incentivo econômico intrínseco para o reflorestamento pós-mineração. artigo.texto: One of the first power purchase agreements for space-based solar is being announced today, and it’s with a data center. Virtus Solis Technologies, a Michigan-based startup working to put solar panels into space, signed a 20-year PPA with startup Brae Systems, which hopes to use the electricity — beamed back to Earth from satellites — to power the data centers it plans to build, not on land but underwater. Per the agreement, Virtus Solis will provide 100 megawatts of 24/7 orbital solar power, amounting to over 875,000 megawatt-hours annually; Brae has the option to increase the agreement to 250 MW within three years from initial commercial operations. Unlike a PPA for a typical solar project, power delivery is still years away — if it comes at all. John Bucknell, Virtus Solis founder and CEO, told Latitude Media he expects first power to happen around 2030, roughly when Brae Systems plans to launch its first megawatt-scale underwater data center. A lot needs to happen, including actually proving out the technology, in the interim. “There are technical and financial milestones associated with both sides,” Bucknell said. “We agree to deliver power in the future… and they agree to purchase [it]. But obviously, we need to do our fiduciary duty along the way, and so do they.” For Virtus Solis, the milestones include putting a 100-kilowatt pilot plant into orbit within the next 24 months and securing project financing for its first 100 MW power plant, among other things. But — as was true when Commonwealth Fusion Systems signed its first PPA with Dominion Energy in late 2024 — a PPA for a technology that hasn’t yet been proven at commercial scale is a symbolic as much as a financial agreement. In this case, it demonstrates that the market’s interest in space-based solar is becoming very real, as data centers’ need for power extends to encouraging even the most nascent technologies. Momentum has also come by way of Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which earlier this year filed with the FCC for permission to deploy an orbital data center “constellation.” The SpaceX concept, however, would have both the energy source and the compute located in space, with data sent back to Earth via optical links. Virtus Solis, meanwhile, takes a more “traditional” approach to space-based solar, Bucknell said. It aims to put solar cells in orbit, “where the sun always shines,” convert the energy into radio waves, and beam it back to Earth, where antennas would then receive them and convert them back into electricity once again. “We operate in radio frequency physics as opposed to photovoltaic physics,” Bucknell said. “The power plants just happen to have an element in orbit and an element on the ground.” The advantage of this approach is that solar power can be harvested at its maximum intensity 24/7, unencumbered by the cycle of night and day or by weather. It’s an idea that has existed for several decades, albeit in a niche corner of the energy and tech worlds, but has always been too expensive to become a reality. In fact, what is believed to be the first PPA for space-based solar was actually signed in 2009 between PG&E and startup Solaren, for 200 MW of capacity to be delivered starting in 2016. The contract was mutually cancelled in 2015, after Solaren failed to secure financing for its technology. Bucknell says the prices of solar cells, electronics, and commercial space launches have since collapsed, making the idea more viable today than it was a decade ago. Next steps For the Brae Systems PPA, Virtus Solis’ plan is to launch its satellites on commercial heavy-lift rockets, such as the ones SpaceX operates, and assemble them in orbit into arrays of up to two kilometers across. Once in orbit, the arrays will beam radio waves down to a receiver station in Illinois, where the data center developer — clearly not shy about technological experimentation — plans to submerge its first data centers in the cooling ponds of a retiring coal-fired power plant. The radio waves would then be converted back into electricity and used to power the data center behind the meter. The plan’s success hinges on many factors. So far, Virtus Solis has not announced any funding raises and has operated mostly in stealth “for the last number of years,” Bucknell said, financing its operations through a mix of venture capital and government funding. The latter includes a roughly $2-million ARPA-E award won in January 2025 to develop the power electronics needed to make its wireless power transfer more efficient. The company plans to show the results of the work it has done for this award in a public demonstration scheduled for March 2027. Bucknell hopes that the demo will show that more than 50% of the electricity sent through its wireless link comes out as usable electricity on the other end; previous demos only managed about 4%. But for this project, it would have to also find project financing, which can be tricky for the most cutting-edge technologies — though a PPA certainly helps. And while it’s true the price of rocket launches has decreased since 2009, it’s certainly not cheap to get things into orbit. A commercial launch with SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket costs $74 million. “All by ourselves, just this first power plant would be hundreds of launches of the Falcon series, and I think 18 launches of the Starship series,” Bucknell said. The prices of commercial launches with SpaceX’s Starship rockets, the most advanced model that has so far only done text flights, aren’t public at the moment. Plus, while submerged data centers exist, most notably in China, they’re not in wide use yet, and Brae has yet to announce a successful deployment. Ultimately, the company aims to deploy its data centers in the deep sea, “where it’s nice and cold,” to replace the need for expensive cooling systems, according to Bucknell. But that would require using undersea cables to connect to Virtus Solis’ ground power plant, which come with a high price of their own. None

artigo.texto: The Clackamas County Board of County Commissioners will hold two public hearings to consider adopting a temporary moratorium on data center development in unincorporated Clackamas County. The hearings give community members a chance to share their opinions on the potential moratorium and provide concerns and other feedback about data centers. Public hearing dates: Wednesday, Oct. 21, 6 p.m. Board Meeting Room, 4th floor Clackamas County Public Services Building 2051 Kaen Road Oregon City, OR Thursday, Oct. 22, 10 a.m. Board Meeting Room, 4th floor Clackamas County Public Services Building 2051 Kaen Road Oregon City, OR Can't attend in person or virtually? You can submit written testimony to bcc@clackamas.us, and it will be included in the record. What to expect County staff will provide information about the criteria for establishing a moratorium. The staff presentation will focus on those criteria. Staff will not propose changes to county code related to data centers during these hearings. If the Board adopts a moratorium, public input received during the hearings could help inform the Board's consideration of future code changes. About data centers Data centers are facilities that house computer systems and related equipment used to store, process, and manage digital information. The growth of artificial intelligence and cloud computing is contributing to increased data center development nationwide. Data centers can involve considerations related to land use, energy, water, infrastructure, noise, and other factors. The National Association of Counties (NACo) has developed an informational resource for county officials that provides an overview of data center development and topics counties may consider as they evaluate local regulations. Learn more: NACo Informational Primer and County Considerations: Data Centers

artigo.texto: Kern supervisors approve new solar, battery storage near California City BAKERSFIELD, Calif. (KGET) – The Kern County Board of Supervisors have approved a new solar project for the county. The Board approved the request to build a solar facility called the Galaxy Solar PV and Storage Project, which developers say will bring millions of dollars to the county. With the Board's new approval, Terra-Gen, the solar development company, can take the next step forward in constructing the solar facility, which will generate 600 megawatts of electricity and four gigawatt-hours of battery energy storage. Craig Murphy, director of the Kern County Planning & Natural Resources Department, told the Board of Supervisors on Tuesday, Sept. 29, that the project is proposed to be built on 184 parcels – about 3,519 acres – of land in California City. He said the project would be built and live on the southern side of Highway 58, approximately 2,900 feet east of Highway 14, straddling both the north and south sides of Silver Queen Road. County documents show that project's site is on privately owned land in unincorporated areas of southeastern Kern County. Sam Sours, Terra-Gen's vice president of solar development, told the Board on Tuesday afternoon that the Galaxy Solar project is estimating about $16.1 million in property taxes during its first full year of operation. He said the project is expected to generate about $120 million in property tax contributions over the facility's 35-year lifespan. Sours added that the project would help the state meet its goal of 60% of electric retail sales by 2030. He said the project will employ about 350 people – 650 workers during peak times of construction – and that the facility's employees will be hired through a local union labor, adding that the worker's agreement has already been signed. With the project's approval representatives from Terra-Gen said that Joshua Trees in the vicinity of the project will be moved wholly and rerooted in a tree sanctuary in Los Angeles County. artigo.texto: Battery energy storage is rapidly becoming an essential part of the energy transition. Yet, while technology itself has developed significantly, the financing of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) projects is still evolving, particularly in markets where storage is relatively new. In my experience, one of the main challenges is not necessarily the maturity of the technology itself, but the level of understanding of what a BESS project really involves from a financing perspective. As the European BESS market scales, the next challenge is increasingly important: enabling these assets to access bank financing and project finance structures. A bank is not simply financing a battery. It is financing an asset expected to generate revenues and perform reliably for many years. Therefore, bankability needs to be considered much earlier than financial close. Bankability should start at the design stage One of my strongest recommendations to developers is to start discussing financing requirements with lenders while the project is still being designed. Too often, financing is considered after the technology has been selected and the main supply contracts are already substantially negotiated. By then, changing certain contractual or technical conditions can be difficult and expensive. The project should begin with a robust financial model and a clear understanding of the expected return on investment and revenue structure. At this stage, developers should already be engaging not only with potential lenders, but also with financial and technical advisers and key technology partners. Understanding what lenders will require can influence technology selection, contractual structures, guarantees, operating strategy and even project design. In other words, bankability should be designed into the project rather than tested at the end of it. Revenue certainty remains fundamental A technically excellent BESS project without a credible revenue model will remain difficult to finance. This is one of the major differences between storage markets today. There is already considerable experience in more mature European storage markets, particularly in Great Britain, Poland, Belgium and Italy, where capacity mechanisms or dedicated storage procurement schemes provide BESS projects with access to contracted revenue streams. Italy's MACSE, for example, represents a particularly interesting development as a mechanism specifically designed to procure electricity storage capacity. Other markets, including Spain, are now developing their own capacity mechanisms and moving towards a framework in which storage can increasingly access long-term contracted revenues. Where this type of framework is not available, developers need to build credible alternatives. Depending on the market, these may include tolling or swap agreements (including revenue-floor structures), PPAs or other offtake arrangements designed to reduce merchant exposure and provide greater revenue certainty. Batteries have the advantage of being able to access multiple revenue streams, but flexibility should not be confused with certainty. From a lender's perspective, the question is not simply how many markets a battery can participate in, but how predictable those revenues are throughout the financing period. There is also an important connection between revenue and technology: the operating profile assumed by the financial model must remain compatible with the technical capabilities and warranty conditions of the BESS. The bankability of the supplier matters too Technology selection is obviously important, but lenders look beyond technical specifications. They need confidence in the company standing behind the technology. Supplier financial strength, manufacturing capability, track record, supply-chain resilience and the ability to provide long-term technical support all become part of the risk assessment. The same applies to the complete system architecture. Batteries, PCS, EMS and other critical components need to comply with applicable technical requirements, certifications and grid codes. Traceability of materials and components, quality control, manufacturing procedures and regulatory project documentation are increasingly relevant parts of technical due diligence. For an asset expected to operate for 15 or 20 years, the question is therefore not simply whether the technology performs today. The lender also needs confidence that the supplier and service structure can support that performance over time. Ultimately, bankability becomes contractual This is perhaps one of the areas that is sometimes underestimated. When lenders and their advisers analyse a BESS project, many technical and financial assumptions eventually need to be translated into contractual protections. Payment milestones, Advance Payment Bonds, Performance Bonds, Warranty Bonds, letters of credit and their corresponding wording can all be subject to review. The lender will want to understand what protects the investment from the first payment through delivery, commissioning and long-term operation. This extends to delivery obligations, transfer of title and risk, delay liquidated damages, performance liquidated damages, acceptance procedures, commissioning requirements, warranties, liability limits and available remedies. The objective is not to eliminate every project risk; that would be impossible, but to understand who carries each risk and what happens if the underlying assumptions are not achieved. Performance guarantees must match the financial model Degradation is a good example of where technical, commercial and financial assumptions meet. A financial model may assume a certain available capacity or energy throughput over 10, 15 or 20 years. The lender therefore needs confidence that these assumptions are technically realistic and appropriately supported. Performance warranties should consequently be assessed alongside expected cycling, depth of discharge, C-rate, temperature

artigo.texto: Volkswagen Group, PowerCo and China's Gotion have agreed plans for three battery joint ventures in Spain, Slovakia and Morocco, involving combined estimated investment of approximately €3.22bn ($3.65bn). Gotion is expected to invest about €1.59bn, while PowerCo – Volkswagen's battery manufacturing subsidiary – will contribute approximately €1.62bn. The ventures are planned to produce lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells and cathode materials in Valencia, Šurany and Kenitra. Volkswagen Group technology management board member and PowerCo supervisory board chairman Thomas Schmall said: "This marks a major breakthrough for both companies and brings us one step closer to the forefront of electric mobility. "Volkswagen is the first European automotive manufacturer to cover the entire battery value chain, from development and cathode materials through to production." In Valencia, PowerCo's under-construction gigafactory is expected to transfer into a joint venture producing LFP cells, with an annual capacity of 29.1GWh. PowerCo will hold 51% and Gotion 49%, making the venture a controlled PowerCo subsidiary. Gotion is expected to invest about €1.1bn for its stake. The Valencia facility is intended to serve as a European production hub for Volkswagen's LFP-based Unified Cells. Gotion's planned cell factory in Šurany will also transfer into a joint venture. The facility will have an annual capacity of 8.4GWh and produce LFP cells for electric vehicles and energy storage systems. Gotion will own 51%, with PowerCo holding 49%. In Kenitra, the companies plan to establish a facility producing 100,000t of LFP cathode material annually. Gotion will retain a 51% stake, while PowerCo will own 49%. The project is intended to diversify supply sources for key cathode active materials. PowerCo is expected to contribute approximately €470m to the Šurany and Kenitra projects by 2030 for its 49% stake in each project. The agreement extends a partnership that began in 2020 and covers joint procurement and sales activities in Europe. The transactions remain subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions, including approval from Gotion shareholders and governmental approvals in China and overseas. Gotion said implementation would take place in phases. Volkswagen Group, through its subsidiary Volkswagen (China) Investment, has also entered definitive agreements to sell a 5.3% equity stake in Gotion. The company said its voting rights, board representation, nomination rights and position as a strategic investor would remain unchanged after completion.

artigo.texto: Companies sign MOU to explore collaboration on deployable structures, spacecraft integration and scalable architectures for in-orbit Artificial Intelligence and edge computing LAS VEGAS , Sept. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Sophia Space and Redwire Corporation (NYSE: RDW), a global leader in aerospace and defense technology solutions, today announced they have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to advance the development and deployment of scalable computing infrastructure in orbit, combining Sophia Space's modular orbital compute architecture with Redwire's extensive technology solutions in deployable space systems, solar power generation and distribution, heat management and rejection, spacecraft integration, avionics, and systems engineering. Under the MOU, the companies will explore collaboration across near-term demonstration missions and longer-term orbital data center architectures. Sophia Space is developing a new class of computing infrastructure designed specifically for the space environment. Its modular TILE architecture integrates high-performance computing, solar power and passive radiative thermal management into scalable systems designed for Artificial Intelligence (AI) inference, data processing and other compute-intensive workloads in orbit. By combining Sophia Space's compute architecture with Redwire's space infrastructure and engineering capabilities, the companies aim to address one of the central challenges facing the emerging orbital computing market: moving from individual technology demonstrations toward the repeatable, scalable infrastructure needed for the global build-out of orbital data centers. "We're past the point of asking whether high-performance computing belongs in orbit," said Rob DeMillo, CEO and Cofounder of Sophia Space. "The question now is how quickly we can scale it. Redwire brings the deployment and systems expertise that can help us move from individual missions to persistent computing infrastructure in orbit. That is the transition we're building toward now." "The demand for global computing is scaling exponentially, and the advancement of orbital data centers represents an exciting paradigm shift where space infrastructure can scale critical capacity beyond the constraints of terrestrial infrastructure," said Al Tadros, Chief Technology Officer, Redwire Space. "As a leading space infrastructure provider, Redwire is translating the maturation of the orbital data center market into exciting opportunities to build next-generation architectures that could unlock significant economic value. Sophia Space and Redwire intend to jointly pursue select U.S. government and commercial opportunities, including potential programs involving DARPA, the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL), the Space Development Agency (SDA) and the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO). Areas of potential collaboration include concept development, joint proposals, internal research and development activities, customer engagement, and international market opportunities. --- About Sophia Space Inc. Sophia Space is building the future of orbital computing and in-space data centers. Its modular TILE technology enables passive computing alongside in-situ data processing, AI acceleration, and edge computing for satellites, defense systems, and commercial space stations, dramatically reducing latency and delivering actionable insights where and when they are needed. Learn more at www.sophia.space About Redwire Redwire Corporation (NYSE: RDW) is an integrated space and defense tech company focused on advanced technologies. We are building the future of aerospace infrastructure, autonomous systems, and multi-domain operations leveraging digital engineering and AI automation. Redwire's approximately 1,400 employees located throughout North America and Europe are committed to delivering innovative space and airborne platforms transforming the future of multi-domain operations. For more information, please visit RDW.com. artigo.texto: The companies behind the proposed Marshall Springs battery energy storage system (BESS) and solar project agreed to largely halt site development last Thursday, Sept. 24, after agreeing to the terms of a temporary injunction filed against them by Gillespie County. Marshall Springs Storage, LLC; Marshall Springs Solar, LLC; and AMPYR Energy USA, LLC agreed to the injunction as a compromise to avoid a contested hearing. The agreement does not constitute an admission by the companies or waive either side’s claims or defenses in the case. The agreement comes after AMPYR’s lawyers attempted to get the county’s temporary injunction order thrown out by the state district court earlier this summer. In August, the court ruled against AMPYR’s dismissal bid. Now that the two sides have agreed, a hearing over the temporary injunction that was set for Tuesday, Sept. 29, has been canceled. The county’s lawsuit over the BESS and solar farm project is scheduled for trial in June 2027. Per the terms of the temporary injunction, the defendants have agreed to pause the following actions until the conclusion of the trial: - tree or brush clearing - grading, digging or drilling - stockpiling materials or equipment such as panels, batteries and containers - building roads, pads, structures or utility lines - altering creeks or drainage - installing wells or septic systems - bringing crews or equipment onto the site to prepare for any of that The companies are still permitted to perform certain tasks on the property. They may construct and maintain a single access road from Texas Highway 16 to the property, use the site for agricultural purposes, including grazing, haying and maintaining livestock water, perform routine maintenance and survey the property. The agreed order also states that the property lies wholly or partly within an area of special flood hazard regulated by the county’s Flood Damage Prevention Ordinance. The order says a development permit is required before development occurs in that area and that no such permit has been issued for the property. The parties have also been ordered to mediate. They must agree on a mediator by Oct. 9 and conduct mediation by Oct. 31. The two sides will meet for trial in the 216th Judicial District Court of Gillespie County at 9 a.m. June 7, 2027. Background Back in March, the county filed a lawsuit against three companies that are behind a BESS site and solar project that is proposed on more than 1,100 acres near Texas 16 North and Clear Springs Road, north of Fredericksburg. Marshall Springs Storage, LLC; Marshall Springs Solar, LLC; and AMPYR Energy USA, LLC are listed as the defendants in the case. The county has argued that a large-scale lithium-ion battery storage facility poses a significant threat to the safety of local residents because of its potential for fire and environmental damage. According to the National Fire Protection Association, lithium-ion batteries can catch fire or explode if damaged, improperly charged or improperly stored. The Fredericksburg Fire Department has said it cannot properly respond to a fire caused by a lithium-ion battery malfunction. The county also argues the project’s location is inappropriate because it sits in an area devastated by the 2025 Crabapple Fire, which burned nearly 10,000 acres. It contends a battery fire could quickly grow out of control and threaten nearby watersheds through pollution.
