artigo.texto: Meta (NASDAQ:META) cut its taxes by $3.9 billion in 2025 with research tax credits, up from $2 billion in 2024 and $700 million in 2023, according to the company's securities filings. A New York Times investigation published Sept. 30 reported that Meta classifies its AI data centers as "pilot models" for tax purposes — the term federal tax rules use for test versions of a product built to resolve open questions during development. The Times cited four people familiar with Meta's operations. Meta uses that label to claim a federal research tax credit on the Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) chips inside the data centers, a practice the Times dates to late 2024. Meta did not immediately respond to Moneywise's request for comment. A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change Meta's second-quarter guidance calls for $130 billion to $145 billion in spending this year on buildings and equipment, much of it to build out AI computing power. "AI is accelerating our core business today," CEO Mark Zuckerberg said in the same release. No other publicly traded company gets more out of the credit, according to a Times review of securities filings. How Meta's research tax credit strategy reportedly works The credit dates to 1981, when lawmakers worried Japan was pulling ahead in technology, according to the Times. Most companies claim it mainly on what they pay researchers and engineers. Supplies can count too. IRS guidance says they have to be used in "qualified research," meaning experiments to solve a technical unknown. Meta treats its chips as supplies in that kind of research, according to the Times. The IRS has pushed back before when companies tried to claim the credit on off-the-shelf equipment, the Times reported. Andre Shevchuck, who leads the research tax credit practice at California-based advisory firm BPM, told the Times the approach is "kind of wild and out there." "Meta is claiming billions of dollars in tax benefits that its own accountants are telling investors are at risk of being overturned by the IRS," Lisa De Simone, who teaches accounting at the University of Texas and previously worked as a tax adviser at EY, told the Times. Former Rep. James Shannon, D-Massachusetts, sponsored the credit in 1981. He told the Times it was meant to support "people power, knowledge, information." When he heard a tech company was claiming it for AI data centers, Shannon said, "This has gone way, way beyond what anybody could have imagined." Meta spokesperson Andy Stone said the company has put $200 billion into research and development over the past five years, $57 billion of it last year. "Like other companies that invest at this scale, we use the tax incentives Congress established decades ago to encourage this type of domestic investment," Stone said in a statement to the Times. How much the research tax credit costs taxpayers Congress' Joint Committee on Taxation projects the research credit will cost the government $32.1 billion in corporate tax revenue in fiscal year 2025. By the Times' math, Meta's share tops 10%. JCT expects that cost to climb every year, to $41.3 billion by fiscal 2029. Over five years, the total comes to $183.2 billion — more than any other corporate tax break except a lower tax rate on U.S. companies' overseas profits. Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) claimed $1.05 billion in research credits for its 2025 fiscal year. Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) claimed about $2.09 billion in federal research credits in 2025. Meta's $3.9 billion beats the two combined. It's also 15 times the $260 million in research tax credits that Merck (NYSE:MRK) claimed in 2025. Merck makes the cancer drug Keytruda. Shevchuck told the Times the approach might work "if you had a data center that you're building out to cure cancer." EY — Meta's auditor and one of the firms that advised it on the credit — has taken the chip strategy to other companies, according to the Times. Meta is separately set to receive $3.3 billion in state and local tax breaks for its Hyperion data center in Louisiana. Meta's IRS fights and $18.74B in uncertain tax benefits Meta and the IRS are also in U.S. Tax Court over an earlier research credit claim. The agency wants back about $355 million in credits that Meta tied to $4.1 billion in Zuckerberg's stock compensation from 2012 and 2013, according to Bloomberg Tax. Meta argues Zuckerberg personally wrote code and oversaw Facebook's technology in 2005, when it granted the options. The IRS points to the option contract, which says the options weren't payment for anything Zuckerberg did before 2008. In a separate case over how Meta priced deals with its own foreign subsidiaries, the IRS says the company shifted profits to the Cayman Islands. The agency is seeking nearly $16 billion, including penalties, according to the Times. Meta is fighting the case in Tax Court, its annual filing shows. Meta's gross unrecognized tax benefits — tax savings it has claimed but hasn't counted toward its profits because they might not hold up — reached $18.74 billion as of June 30. That's up 45% from $12.91 billion two years earlier. Meta says those benefits are primarily tied to "uncertainties with our research tax credits" and its foreign-subsidiary deals. Meta's June 2024 filing listed the foreign-subsidiary issue first. Three months later, research credits had moved to the top. Stone called the figure "a snapshot in time." What Meta's tax fight means for shareholders If you own an S&P 500 index fund, you own a piece of Meta. Meta has been warning shareholders of the risk, and those $18.74 billion in benefits are excluded from the profits it reports. If its positions hold up, Meta says $12.73 billion of that would flow back into earnings. Often, even when the IRS objects, massive companies like Meta can negotiate settlements that let them keep part of the savings and come out ahead to the delight of shareholders. artigo.texto: Most investors understand that you typically have to pay a premium price to buy good growth stocks. But shares of electric vehicle (EV) maker Tesla (TSLA -0.20%) are taking the premise to an extreme. The stock's currently priced at 200 times this year's projected earnings of $1.75 per share, and over 160 times next year's expected earnings of $2.16 per share. That's expensive by any standard, including in the technology sector. The valuation (sort of) makes sense, though, when you understand what Tesla is in the process of becoming. Soon, it will no longer be an EV company that also makes and markets solar panels and energy-storage batteries. Instead, the plan is for it to be a robotics and robotaxi outfit that also manufactures electric vehicles. Investors are pricing the stock based on this hoped-for future rather than what the business is doing in the present. Here's what they need to know. Comparing and contrasting Although the company is winding down its solar roof tile business, it still makes and markets its own solar panels, as well as the energy storage equipment that makes these panels practical power sources. Moreover, EVs remain Tesla's biggest business -- accounting for $20.5 billion of its $28.2 billion in Q2 revenue -- and Tesla is still the second-biggest name in the global EV market, right behind China's BYD. Moreover, last quarter's year-over-year top-line growth of 26% suggests the company still has a little bit of magic left. Its stock's price, however, has left the organization's fiscal results in the rear-view mirror. NASDAQ: TSLA Key Data Points Shares aren't expensive simply because Tesla is struggling to turn its revenues into profits, to be clear. The stock's also expensive by revenue standards, trading at 13 times trailing-12-month sales versus the S&P 500's trailing price-to-sales ratio of 3.7. For further comparison, the S&P 500 is currently trading at a trailing price-to-earnings ratio of 23.5 and a forward P/E of just under 20. Based on these numbers, Tesla trades at valuations between 4 and 10 times those of the average publicly traded company. It's not like we've never seen something like this before, though. Sometimes, a company eventually grows into such steep valuations. Think Amazon, for example. The market's pricing in growth that hasn't even started yet Getting straight to the point, investors are pricing in a large amount of the future growth they expect from Tesla, as opposed to pricing the stock based on the business's current results. And there are two key components to this highly anticipated future. One of them is robotaxis. Tesla's robotaxi ride-hailing venture, which at this early stage still relies largely on its Model Y vehicles, is up and running in a handful of markets. Its purpose-built Cybercab, however, represents the next generation of this venture's tech. Although the company has only rolled out a small fleet of Cybercabs in one market so far-- Austin, Texas -- it's reportedly planning to launch Cybercab-supported robotaxi services in a dozen states before the end of this year. Although the development of these autonomous taxis has been agonizingly slow, once they're ready for wider-spread commercialization, the deployment is apt to happen fast. This will plug Tesla into a robotaxi market that Goldman Sachs expects to grow from nearly nothing now to $415 billion globally by 2035, with $48 billion of that being generated within the United States alone. The other factor pumping up Tesla stock's premium valuation is arguably even more exciting. That's Tesla's entry into the AI-enabled humanoid robotics space. CEO Elon Musk suggested early this year that the company would be commercially selling its humanoid Optimus robots at scale by the end of 2027, and he hasn't said anything since to suggest that the timeline will have to be pushed back. The commercial debut of these robots could be game-changing for the company -- not to mention the world -- in light of Musk's assessment that "Optimus will be not just Tesla's biggest product ever, but probably the biggest product ever." Although that remains to be seen, Barclays believes the market for humanoid work robots will grow to $200 billion annually by 2035. While even Musk concedes his company is facing stiff robotics competition from China, just capturing a healthy fraction of this potential business could be a boon for Tesla and its shareholders. The growth Tesla needs from robots and robotaxis So how much optimism about the robotics and robotaxi businesses are investors pricing in here? It's difficult to say for sure. But we can come up with a rough idea. As it stands right now, Tesla is on pace to do on the order of $106 billion worth of EV, solar panel, and battery-storage business this year, en route to a top line of over $120 billion next year. How much more revenue would the company need to generate with robotaxis and Optimus to make its current $1.4 trillion market cap make sense? Even allowing for the type of premium valuation that many technology stocks achieve, Tesla would need a top line on the order of $300 billion to $400 billion for its current stock price to reflect a valuation in line with its peers. That's about 3 times its current sales, and most of that growth will need to come from robots and robotaxis rather than EVs and solar, as both of those businesses are now running into competitive headwinds. Or if you want to look at the matter through the lens of earnings, Tesla's earnings per share would arguably need to quintuple -- at a minimum -- to justify the stock's current price. That would put its annual bottom line in the ballpark of $10 per share (or hopefully more) to bring the stock to a valuation that's closer to that of a typical technology company. It's likely that to deliver that type of earnings growth will take improving contributions from all of the businesses it's going to be in for the foreseeable future. The battery system was supplied to Indian Energy and forms part of the Viejas Enterprise Microgrid, where it is integrated with a 15 MW solar array. Invinity said the system has met or exceeded its contracted performance parameters and is providing near-continuous, on-demand electricity for operations at the resort. Battery Integrated With 15 MW Solar Array The Viejas Enterprise Microgrid is supported by the California Energy Commission and is described as California's largest tribal microgrid. Invinity's 10 MWh system provides long-duration energy storage alongside the project's solar generation, allowing electricity to be stored and supplied when required. The company said reaching more than 1 GWh of cumulative energy delivery provides additional operating data from a commercial deployment of its vanadium flow battery technology. Invinity Focuses on Long-Duration Energy Storage Invinity Energy Systems manufactures vanadium flow batteries for utility, commercial and industrial energy storage applications. The company operates from the UK and Canada and supplies customers internationally. Its Endurium vanadium flow battery technology is designed for long-duration, high-throughput applications and has an expected operating life of 30 years or more.

artigo.texto: LG Electronics apresenta soluções “Chip-to-Chiller” para resfriamento de data centers de IA na Data Center World Asia 2026 AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 29 de setembro de 2026 Empresa destaca infraestrutura integrada para fábricas de IA e portfólio completo de soluções de resfriamento para data centers de IA Resumo da notícia - A LG Electronics apresenta suas soluções de resfriamento “Chip-to-Chiller” na Data Center World Asia 2026, ao mesmo tempo em que demonstra sua abordagem “One LG” para infraestrutura de fábricas de IA, em conjunto com a LG CNS e a LG Energy Solution. - O portfólio da LG inclui soluções hidrônicas pré-fabricadas, chillers centrífugos refrigerados a ar, Unidades de Distribuição de Líquido Refrigerante (CDUs) qualificadas pela NVIDIA, resfriamento por imersão, Fan Wall Units (FWUs) e o Data Center Cooling Management (DCCM), apoiando uma implementação mais rápida, operação confiável e expansão eficiente da infraestrutura de data centers de IA. - As soluções modulares de resfriamento da LG são projetadas para reduzir o tempo de construção no local, diminuir o investimento inicial e apoiar os operadores de data centers na expansão eficiente de seus ambientes de servidores de IA. - A LG Energy Solution apresenta soluções de baterias otimizadas para data centers de IA, incluindo Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), Battery Backup Unit (BBU) e Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS). - A LG CNS apresenta o “Prefabricated Modular Data Center”, com módulos padronizados e pré-fabricados de GPUs, servidores e energia. SÃO PAULO, 29 de setembro de 2026 /PRNewswire/ — A LG Electronics (LG) apresenta suas soluções de resfriamento “Chip-to-Chiller” para servidores de Inteligência Artificial (IA) na Data Center World Asia 2026 (DCWA 2026), realizada de 29 a 30 de setembro no Marina Bay Sands Expo & Convention Center, em Singapura. A exposição destaca a abordagem integrada da LG para atender às crescentes demandas de gerenciamento térmico e energia do setor de data centers de IA. Uma parceira de ponta a ponta para infraestrutura de fábricas de IA com o “One LG” Participando da DCWA pelo segundo ano consecutivo, a LG demonstra suas capacidades como parceira de ponta a ponta para infraestrutura de fábricas de IA em um espaço de exposição com mais de três vezes o tamanho de seu estande de 2025. A empresa apresenta uma solução integrada de infraestrutura baseada na estratégia “One LG”, que reúne as tecnologias de climatização/HVAC da LG com a expertise da LG CNS em projeto, construção e operação (DBO) de data centers e os equipamentos de energia da LG Energy Solution. A LG Energy Solution apresenta soluções de baterias desenvolvidas para apoiar o fornecimento confiável de energia para data centers de IA incluindo Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), Battery Backup Unit (BBU) e Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS). Implementação acelerada com soluções modulares pré-fabricadas As soluções hidrônicas pré-fabricadas e os chillers centrífugos refrigerados a ar da LG contribuem para uma implementação e expansão mais rápidas da infraestrutura de data centers de IA. A solução hidrônica incorpora equipamentos de resfriamento, equipamentos de energia e sistemas de controle em um único módulo pré-fabricado, reduzindo o trabalho de engenharia no local e encurtando o tempo de implementação. O chiller centrífugo refrigerado a ar da LG incorpora um compressor centrífugo com mancal magnético sem óleo, que minimiza as perdas por atrito mecânico e melhora a eficiência energética. Além disso, o chiller utiliza a tecnologia free-cooling por refrigerante da empresa, que aproveita as baixas temperaturas externas para reduzir a carga sobre o compressor e ajudar a diminuir o consumo de energia do data center. Tecnologias especializadas de resfriamento para servidores de IA de alta densidade A exposição também apresenta as mais recentes soluções de resfriamento líquido da LG para servidores de IA, incluindo suas avançadas Unidades de Distribuição de Líquido Refrigerante (CDUs). Uma CDU é um componente essencial de um sistema de resfriamento líquido direto para o chip (DTC), que fornece e circula o líquido refrigerante para placas frias (cold plates), instaladas diretamente sobre CPUs e GPUs para absorver seu calor. As CDUs de 1 megawatt (MW), 2,6 megawatts (MW) e 600 quilowatts (kW) da LG concluíram a qualificação de infraestrutura da NVIDIA neste ano, atendendo a critérios técnicos que abrangem desempenho de resfriamento, capacidades de failover e confiabilidade do sistema. Além disso, a CDU de 2,6 megawatts (MW) da LG foi qualificada como NVIDIA DSX Ready CDU, atendendo aos requisitos aplicáveis do projeto de referência NVIDIA DSX para soluções de resfriamento líquido da AI Factory Platform. Na DCWA 2026, a LG demonstra uma solução de resfriamento por imersão que remove o calor de forma eficiente ao submergir os servidores em um fluido de resfriamento não condutivo. Paralelamente, a empresa apresenta sua Fan Wall Unit (FWU), uma solução de resfriamento a ar que incorpora ventiladores EC de alta eficiência e serpentinas ovais de baixa perda de pressão para fornecer um fluxo de ar energeticamente eficiente e estável aos racks de servidores. Soluções integradas de gerenciamento e energia A LG apresenta seu Data Center Cooling Management (DCCM), que permite o gerenciamento integrado dos principais equipamentos de resfriamento, incluindo CDUs, FWUs e chillers. Utilizando tecnologia de IA, o DCCM pode prever a carga de resfriamento e otimizar os sistemas de resfriamento para possibilitar uma operação mais eficiente do data center. Como parte da oferta “One LG”, a LG CNS e a LG Energy Solution também apresentam suas soluções para data centers na DCWA deste ano. artigo.texto: As more data centers are being proposed across the country, local residents often have unanswered questions about the effects they may have on their communities. Now, a bipartisan duo in Congress wants to pull back the curtain. Utah Sen. John Curtis is teaming up with Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester to force increased transparency from data centers surrounding potential costs and the environmental effects of massive projects. The pair of bills are aimed toward giving local communities more control over projects being approved in their area as well as offering resources to learn more about their impacts. “Americans are rightly skeptical when a large company tells them not to worry about the impacts of a new data center in their community,” Curtis said in a statement. “The answer to that distrust is transparency. Communities deserve independent, reliable information about what these projects mean for their power bills, water, infrastructure, and local economy. These bills give local leaders the facts and expertise they need to ask tough questions and make informed decisions — without Washington or industry making those decisions for them.” The first bill introduced by Curtis, the Data Center Community Empowerment Act, would establish a program within the Department of Energy to provide technical assistance to local governments on the potential energy, water, infrastructure and economic impacts of proposed projects. The program would provide independent analysis if a community requests a review, and it would prohibit the DOE from unilaterally recommending whether a project should be approved or rejected. Curtis acknowledged that data centers can bring investment and economic opportunities to communities, but he argued the projects can also impose unfamiliar demands on local infrastructure. As a result, the Utah senator says local officials should have access to information before approving such projects. The second bill, dubbed the Data Center Transparency Act, would focus more on implementing federal requirements for environmental and energy reports. Under the proposal, the Environmental Protection Agency and the Energy Information Administration would be required to collect data on the environmental impact as well as the energy and water consumption of data centers. Specifically, it would require the EPA to collect and update data every three months related to the environmental impacts of water consumption, utility costs, potential pollutants and greenhouse gases caused by data centers. The EIA would need to collect and update that data every six months, and it would focus more on the energy consumption of data centers, grid build-out, and the impact on household energy bills. “The development of data centers is rapidly increasing across the country, and there are legitimate concerns about how these projects could raise utility bills, harm our environment, or impact public health,” Blunt Rochester said in a statement. “I am proud to work with Sen Curtis ... to ensure communities have a say in how these projects affect their quality of life. These bills are a necessary step toward creating a safer, more inclusive, and more informed process.” It’s not yet clear how quickly, if at all, the bills could be considered. The Senate is out on recess until Nov. 9, and lawmakers will have a busy legislative calendar when they return. Still, the issue of data centers has become a major issue for lawmakers over the last few months, so it’s likely lawmakers will continue the pressure to address concerns in the next Congress.

artigo.texto: Volkswagen AG VWAGY is strengthening its position in the European electric vehicle (EV) battery market through a partnership with China-based Gotion High-Tech. The companies plan to expand regional production of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries and cathode materials, supporting Volkswagen's strategy to establish a competitive and more secure European battery supply chain. LFP batteries offer competitive costs, long service life and strong durability, making them increasingly important for affordable EVs in the volume segment. Their share of the European battery market is expected to increase from around 10% currently to 40-60% by 2030. Volkswagen Expands LFP Production With Gotion Under the agreement, Gotion will invest around €1.1 billion (about $1.25 billion) for a 49% stake in the Valencia site, with PowerCo retaining a 51% majority. The Valencia plant is expected to become a European production hub for LFP battery cells and Unified Cells. PowerCo is expected to contribute around €470 million in total by 2030 to acquire a 49% stake in the Šurany cell factory in Slovakia and a new cathode-material facility in Kenitra, Morocco. Gotion will hold the 51% majority in both. The deal remains subject to regulatory approvals and Gotion shareholder approval. VWAGY Strengthens European Battery Supply Security The agreement builds on a partnership between Volkswagen and Gotion that dates back to 2020. Gotion already supplies cells to Volkswagen and works with its battery arm, PowerCo, as a strategic partner. Volkswagen is currently Gotion's largest single shareholder, holding about 24%. Separately, it has agreed to sell a 5.3% stake, while keeping its board representation and voting rights, pending regulatory clearances. The joint ventures are expected to strengthen regional battery production, reduce supply-chain concentration and improve access to key cathode materials. The agreement marks a major breakthrough for both companies and brings them closer to the forefront of electric mobility. artigo.texto: Concerns are rising in Africa about the potential water use by data centers. A recent petition by a collection of civil society groups to the South African Human Rights Commission highlighted concerns over the lack of awareness of water consumption in a country that already hosts 60 data centers and is struggling with climate-change-induced drought. Large data centers can consume up to 5 million gallons per day; a recent study modelling water use in African data centers found that ChatGPT-4 used up to 60 liters of water â or a standard washing machine cycle â to produce a 10-page paper. While water usage by data centers is a global problem, Africa is particularly vulnerable to the effects of climate change. âYou are introducing sites which are resource intensive enough to be in many ways comparable to extractive industries,â Michael Marchant, head of investigations at civil society group Open Secrets, which was among the petitioners, told Semafor. âWe see the risk of data centers, especially hyperscale, falling through the cracks.â

artigo.texto: EU ETS: deadline to surrender emissions allowances draws near Oct, 01, 2026 Posted by Gabriel Malheiros Week 202640 The nights are drawing in, there’s an autumnal chill in the air and shipping companies are preparing to surrender emissions allowances. The deadline to surrender allowances for the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) is fast approaching and it is important for parties to act now to avoid penalties for non-compliance. EU ETS surrender deadline is just days away Emissions trading schemes, most significantly the EU ETS, set a cap-and-trade system requiring companies from the maritime sector and other industries, to surrender European Union Allowances (EUAs) to offset their annual emissions. The EU ETS requires EUAs to be submitted by 30 September. An annual obligation for maritime companies since 2024, this year, shipping companies must surrender EUAs to cover 70% of reported emissions from 2025. Starting next year, EUAs will need to be surrendered to cover 100% of reported emissions. Don’t leave yourself open to liability: The 30 September deadline is only for the EU ETS. The equivalent UK legislation doesn’t require allowances to be surrendered until 30 April with special measures covering 2026 and 2027 emissions so no surrender is required until 2028. Looking at EU, responsible shipping companies The “shipping company” is responsible for surrendering the right numbers of EUAs. In cases where a ship manager has signed a mandate taking on the responsibility for the “shipping company,” they will have assumed responsibility for EU ETS obligations. Such managers must ensure that sufficient EUAs are transferred into their holding accounts in good time to surrender to the EU. The administrative process for receipt and then surrendering allowances is not always instantaneous, and any delay in procurement or transfer could leave managers exposed. Any managers carrying an EU ETS mandate should already know where their EUAs are coming from or, preferably, have any required EUAs in hand. Otherwise, urgent action will be needed to meet the 30 September deadline. Absent allowances The industry has become more accustomed to EU ETS, the rhythm of the reporting cycle and agreeing clauses in charters, MOAs and ship management agreements. This, however, has led some into complacency with delays in EUAs being transferred from charterers to managers/owners – often despite specific language in the relevant charterparty. While the deadline was a distant thought parties were willing to give one another leeway but, now that it approaches, attitudes are hardening. Although the registered shipping company will almost invariably have some contractual right of recovery against the charterer or the owner, in the case of ship managers, it also remains the entity liable under the EU ETS. The consequences of failing to surrender EUAs on time are severe. A penalty of €100 per allowance, adjusted for inflation, is levied and the shipping company must still surrender the EUAs next year. Persistent defaults can even result in an expulsion order effectively barring the vessel from entering European ports. Shipping companies must ensure that the requisite EUAs are surrendered by the deadline, even if that means purchasing allowances at their own cost and pursuing reimbursement separately. artigo.texto: Kozlowski and Savela discuss data centers, mining at forum Incumbent Liish Kozlowski and challenger Shawn Savela addressed the Hermantown data center, downtown Duluth and mining DULUTH, Minn. (Northern News Now) - District 8B incumbent Liish Kozlowski and Republican candidate Shawn Savela took the stage Tuesday for a candidate forum hosted by the Duluth News Tribune and Duluth Area Chamber of Commerce, the second of a two-day series of forums. The candidates addressed the proposed Hermantown data center, downtown Duluth, and the economy and mining. Savela said the Hermantown data center project is “a blueprint for how to do things wrong.” He said public officials signing non-disclosure agreements have caused chaos and mistrust for the project. Kozlowski called for more research. “We’re asking for a pause; we’re asking for a comprehensive regulatory framework to look at air, noise, groundwater,” Kozlowski said. Savela said increasing county jails and services would help clean up the streets and increase public safety. “Fund our jails and make them bigger so that we can take people in who are violent offenders, people that need to get off the street,” Savela said. Kozlowski said they want to see Duluth residents receive basic necessities to afford to live. “Basic needs, thrivable wage, access to childcare, good education, housing, all of it to live your best life,” Kozlowski said. Savela spoke about his desire to see copper-nickel mining in Minnesota. “We need these resources, copper and nickel. We need it for your phones, we need it for your cars, we need it for everything,” Savela said. Kozlowski said they are against copper-nickel mining. “We are now in what the international climate community has identified as a water bankruptcy,” Kozlowski said. Kozlowski also brought up the need for the top 1% to be taxed at a higher rate, while Savela called for more republican representation in the state. The two-day forum series also included debates between Sen. Grant Hauschild and challenger Andrea Zupancich, Rep. Pete Johnson and Allan Kehr, and Rep. Natalie Zeleznikar and Aaron Schweiger. artigo.texto: Georgetown council votes to draft ordinance banning data centers Council members raise concerns over water, land and infrastructure GEORGETOWN, Ky. (WKYT) - The Georgetown City Council voted Tuesday night unanimously to ask legal counsel to prepare an ordinance banning data centers. The ordinance would also define what a hyperscale data center is. The action comes as council members shared their concerns about the possibility of a data center in Georgetown. Council members said they also want to be cautious of the impact a ban could have. “I think most of us are talking about the mega ones is what the issue and just making sure that were not trying to take out somebody who has a small one that needs for processing for the facility,” said Mayor Burney Jenkins. Councilmember Karen Tingle-Sames said that the city can’t support a data center. “If you look at the things as we know about data centers as of today, the city of Georgetown can’t handle a data center. We don’t have the water for it, we don’t have the land for it, we don’t have the infrastructure for it,” she said. Jenkins said he also wants to be prepared if a total ban faces legal challenges. The ordinance to completely ban data centers would also need approval from the Planning and Zoning Commission. The Scott County Fiscal Court extended its data center moratorium last week. artigo.texto: Nigeria has moved to its next implementation stage for its carbon market framework by establishing specific criteria to determine which carbon projects the government will approve. The National Council on Climate Change (NCCC) held a National Stakeholder Review and Validation Workshop on the draft Host Country Approval Criteria for Nigeria’s Carbon Market Operations in Abuja. NCCC Director-General Omotenioye Majekodunmi told the workshop that Nigeria had secured approval for the carbon market framework. The task now facing stakeholders is establishing approval criteria that protect national interests while giving credible investors and project developers certainty, she added. University of Nigeria, Nsukka Vice-Chancellor Simon Uchenna Ortuanya, represented by university Professor Nnaemeka Chukwuone, said the approval criteria would provide guidance on the eligibility, screening, and assessment of carbon market projects, describing their development as guided by sound research. The workshop marks a further step in a process that began nearly a year earlier, following President Bola Tinubu’s approval of the National Carbon Market Framework in late October 2025 ahead of COP30 in Belém, Brazil. Tinubu signed off on the framework’s full implementation in January 2026, with oversight resting with the NCCC, chaired by the President and supported by a dedicated carbon market office. Financial projections and international compliance The government has projected the framework could unlock between $2.5 billion and $3 billion annually in carbon finance over the next decade, positioning carbon trading as a significant driver of non-oil revenue. The framework spans forestry, energy, and agriculture, aligning Nigeria’s carbon market activities with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, which governs international cooperation on emissions trading and carbon credits between countries. Read also: Stakeholders advocate domestic financing for Nigeria’s carbon market The host country approval criteria under review are a practical mechanism to determine which offset or reduction projects the government will formally authorise to sell credits internationally. Getting this stage right is designed to prevent problems that have undermined voluntary carbon markets elsewhere, such as projects of questionable integrity, double-counting of credits, and weak enforcement that erodes investor confidence. Whether Nigeria’s final approval criteria succeed in attracting projected investment while avoiding international credibility pitfalls will determine how much of that projected $2.5 billion to $3 billion actually materialises.

artigo.texto: Li Gao, the vice minister of ecology and environment, hopes to see a first group of financial institutions trading on China’s national carbon market by the end of the year. At the moment, market participants are mainly heavily emitting firms required to surrender enough carbon allowances to cover their emissions. So far, institutions such as banks have only been able to provide associated financial services to those traders. If financial institutions begin buying and selling carbon allowances directly, what will it mean for the market? What challenges might lie ahead? Dialogue Earth spoke to the experts and compared it to how things work in Europe. Why add financial institutions to the carbon market? Many of the experts said financial institutions are being brought in to add liquidity to the market, to help companies manage carbon assets, and to improve the accuracy of carbon-pricing signals. The major emitters the carbon market is made up of are obliged to cancel enough carbon allowances to cover their emissions, usually once a year. They’re not doing so to make money but to balance their carbon books. Their trades therefore cluster around the compliance deadline, or in line with internal accounting periods. This means buyers and sellers are often looking to trade at different times. “ Institutions can help companies come up with ways to put the cost of carbon into the cost of the end product. For example, special long-term carbon price contracts or locking in long-term costs, so long-term carbon prices are included in contracts. Chen Zhibin, senior manager for carbon markets and pricing, Adelphi He Qing is carbon finance director for Guotai Haitong, one of the first securities companies to be granted a carbon trading licence. He told Dialogue Earth that financial institutions’ most important role will be to provide extra liquidity by acting as a buffer between supply and demand. “Once there’s more liquidity, we’re likely to see price fluctuations ease,” he said. More liquidity will also help price-discovery mechanisms, so prices better reflect supply and demand. He Qing said the carbon price isn’t just reflective of companies’ compliance costs – it also informs their investments in cutting emissions. “Price discovery will help companies decide, for example, whether or not to buy new technology and to calculate the return on investment once the purchase is made,” he said. Alongside making for a more efficient market, financial institutions can also help companies participate on that market – particularly smaller business which might lack the necessary expertise. Qin Yan, chief analyst for carbon markets consultancy ClearBlue Markets, said that on mature markets like the European Union’s, financial institutions play an important role by providing market access and agency services. She explained that many companies don’t have dedicated teams tracking carbon prices, and some can’t make the trades they need themselves. For example, a company might need 1,522 tonnes of carbon allowances when carbon is traded in units of 1,000 tonnes. A financial institution could split trades up to meet those specific needs. Chen Zhibin is senior manager for carbon markets and pricing at Adelphi, a think-tank headquartered in Berlin, and a member of the secretariat of the International Carbon Action Partnership. He says financial institutions can act as “market-makers”, providing supply and demand when needed and so reducing irrational behaviour. “Investment institutions will always want to sell what they’ve bought, so they help lubricate the market,” he said. Some companies hold on to carbon allowances because they lack the skills to trade them or fear they may need them in the future, he elaborates. This reduces liquidity on the market. But a financial institution, trading for profit on the market, needs to be making ongoing trades and will serve as middleman between different companies. How will it work? Experts told Dialogue Earth they expect financial institutions to invest on their own account and also provide services on behalf of clients. He Qing said the first ones working on the carbon market are very likely to be banks and securities traders using their own funds. Alongside that profit-driven trading, they could also make trades on behalf of clients. For example, if a company expects to need carbon allowances in a future compliance period, the financial institution could buy and hold those, with the trade completing when the allowances are needed. This avoids the company having to pay higher prices in concentrated trading around the compliance deadline. On the European market, financial institutions provide a wider range of risk-management tools. Companies can use futures contracts to manage carbon costs, explains Qin Yan. An industrial firm could, for example, buy futures contracts across the course of a year, rather than purchase all its carbon allowances at once at year’s end. Banks can also design structured products combining spot and futures purchases to help companies spread risk. Chen Zhibin says financial institutions could help companies push carbon costs into supply chains. For example, long-term contracts in the steel and shipping sectors could include carbon prices as part of their costing, allowing companies to better manage their carbon spending. “Institutions can help companies come up with ways to put the cost of carbon into the cost of the end product. For example, special long-term carbon price contracts or locking in long-term costs, so long-term carbon prices are included in contracts,” he said. What changes will financial institutions bring? The experts say the financial institutions will not only bring more trading, but also changes to how the market operates. artigo.texto: A restauração florestal após a exploração mineral abre oportunidades no mercado de carbono. A extração mineral contribui significativamente para o desenvolvimento econômico, mas também exerce pressão sobre os recursos florestais, a terra e os ecossistemas. Com a demanda por minerais para impulsionar a transição energética projetada para continuar aumentando acentuadamente, o controle do desmatamento e a restauração de ecossistemas após a mineração estão se tornando uma necessidade urgente. Especialistas acreditam que, se feita corretamente, a restauração florestal pós-mineração não só ajudará a restaurar as funções ecológicas, como também abrirá oportunidades para gerar financiamento adicional a partir de projetos de carbono. Na manhã de 29 de setembro, em Hanói, o Centro de Certificação de Florestas Sustentáveis da Academia Vietnamita de Ciências Florestais, em colaboração com a organização Forest Trends, realizou um workshop de consulta sobre "Soluções baseadas na natureza para a restauração florestal após a exploração mineral e oportunidades de participação no futuro mercado de carbono". Segundo To Xuan Phuc, Diretor do Programa de Política Florestal, Comércio e Finanças da Forest Trends, a mineração é a quarta maior causa de desmatamento no mundo, sendo responsável por aproximadamente 7% do desmatamento em regiões tropicais. Ao mesmo tempo, a demanda por minerais poderá quintuplicar até 2050 devido ao desenvolvimento de tecnologias de transição energética, como painéis solares, energia eólica, veículos elétricos e sistemas de armazenamento de energia. Isso exige um equilíbrio entre o desenvolvimento econômico e a proteção das florestas e dos ecossistemas. Sem um controle adequado desde as fases de planejamento, licenciamento e operação, o impacto sobre as florestas pode persistir mesmo após o fechamento da mina. No Vietnã, segundo o Sr. Vu Tan Phuong, Diretor do Escritório de Certificação de Gestão Florestal do Vietnã (VFCO), o país possui mais de 5.000 áreas de mineração com cerca de 60 tipos de minerais, incluindo bauxita, apatita, titânio, carvão, elementos de terras raras e granito. A exploração mineral (excluindo petróleo e gás) contribui com cerca de 4 a 5% do PIB anualmente, impulsionando o desenvolvimento econômico local. No entanto, a mineração a céu aberto pode fragmentar a paisagem, destruir a vegetação florestal, perturbar as camadas do solo, poluir as fontes de água e degradar a qualidade do solo. Esses impactos dificultam a restauração da floresta após a exploração madeireira, especialmente em áreas de rejeitos. Você também pode gostar Segundo o Sr. Vu Tan Phuong, a mineração a céu aberto de carvão, apatita e bauxita tem um forte impacto na cobertura vegetal, na topografia e nas camadas do solo. As condições do solo e do local nas áreas de rejeitos de carvão e apatita representam muitos desafios para a restauração florestal. Portanto, a restauração não pode se limitar ao simples plantio de árvores para arborizar a área, mas precisa ser realizada de forma contínua, formando gradualmente um ecossistema florestal estável. As soluções baseadas na natureza devem ser escolhidas de acordo com as condições específicas de cada área após a mineração. A restauração deve ser baseada nas características do local para determinar as espécies de árvores apropriadas, a densidade e os métodos de intervenção. Para depósitos de rejeitos de carvão e apatita, o objetivo principal é restaurar a função ambiental, estabilizar o solo, limitar a erosão e estabelecer gradualmente um ecossistema florestal, gerando simultaneamente benefícios de carbono. Em áreas com condições mais favoráveis após a extração de bauxita, a regeneração florestal pode ser orientada para objetivos econômicos, combinada com a geração de créditos de carbono. Essa abordagem contribui para a restauração da terra e da paisagem, além de criar valor econômico adicional a partir da área florestal após a mineração. No entanto, para traduzir esse potencial em resultados tangíveis, especialistas acreditam ser necessário abordar as lacunas na gestão da extração mineral e da conversão florestal. De acordo com o Dr. Nguyen Thanh Long, membro da equipe de pesquisa apoiada pelo projeto "Apoio Técnico para Atividades no Vietnã com o Apoio do Programa de Governança Florestal, de Mercado e Climática (FGMC)", as lacunas existem desde as fases de planejamento e licenciamento. O planejamento de recursos minerais e o planejamento florestal são desenvolvidos dentro de sistemas de gestão diferentes, o que pode levar a sobreposições entre áreas com potencial mineral e áreas florestais. Outra questão é a avaliação do impacto ambiental de projetos de mineração. Os relatórios precisam considerar de forma mais completa os impactos cumulativos, a fragmentação de habitats, a perda de biodiversidade e os efeitos de instalações auxiliares, como depósitos de rejeitos, rotas de transporte e plantas de processamento. Além disso, a gestão pós-licenciamento precisa ser fortalecida. O monitoramento dos limites da mineração, a expansão dos depósitos de rejeitos, a restauração ambiental e o reflorestamento após a mineração não foram implementados de forma sincronizada em todos os setores, o que dificulta a inspeção, a supervisão e a determinação da responsabilidade pelas áreas florestais após o encerramento do projeto. O Dr. Nguyen Thanh Long sugeriu que os critérios de proteção florestal sejam integrados desde a fase de planejamento da exploração mineral; que a qualidade das avaliações de impacto ambiental para projetos que se sobrepõem ou são adjacentes a áreas florestais seja aprimorada; que o monitoramento pós-licenciamento seja fortalecido; e que a coordenação entre as agências de gestão mineral, fundiária e florestal seja reforçada. artigo.texto: The Director General/Chief Executive Officer of National Council on Climate Change, Mrs. Omotenioye Majekodunmi has stated explicitly that Nigeria’s carbon projects must deliver genuine mitigation outcomes as we’ve already taken important steps to establish the architecture. Majekodunmi spoke at the Stakeholders’ Review/Validation Workshop on the draft Host Country Approval Criteria for Nigeria’s Carbon Market Operations, organized by National Council on Climate Change in Abuja. She also explained that the task before the participants is to establish Host Country Approval Criteria that would protect the national interests, while providing the certainty that that credible investors and project developers need. According to Majekodunmi, the heart of this process is a simple principle: Nigeria must participate in carbon markets on terms that are credible, transparent, equitable and beneficial to Nigerian people, especially in the area of strong national oversight. “If we get this right, carbon markets can help finance clean energy, sustainable agriculture, nature -based solutions, improved waste management and methane reduction, while creating green jobs, and supporting Nigeria’s wider economic transformation,” she added. Also,the Vice Chancellor, University of Nigeria, Nsukka, Prof.Simon Uchenna Ortuanya expressed optimism that the country has taken a concrete step to institutionalize the governance of the carbon market by approving its framework,building partnerships between government and research institutions in developing evidence-based policies. Prof. Ortuanya also explained that the approval represents an important step towards establishing a structured system for carbon market operations, adding, the next critical task is to ensure that the framework is supported by clear, practical and transparent Host Country Approval criteria. Similarly ,the VC maintained that these criteria will provide guidance on the eligibility, screening and assessment of carbon market projects as a well-governed carbon market can help mobilise the resources required to support these objectives. He declared: Our investment in research institutions, policy development and stakeholder engagement is an investment in Nigeria’s capacity to respond effectively to climate change while pursuing sustainable economic development. “The global carbon market presents important opportunities for countries seeking to mobilise climate finance, support greenhouse gas emission reductions and removals, and accelerate the transition to a low-carbon economy,” Ortuanya added. He emphasized, for Nigeria, these opportunities are particularly significant, and it has become imperative for our country to pursue economic growth, industrial development, and energy access and poverty reduction while responding to the challenges of climate change. Ortuanya further noted that they will clarify institutional responsibilities,approval procedures, measurement, reporting and verification requirements, environmental and social safeguards, alignment with Nigeria’s Nationally Determined Contribution. “At the University of Nigeria, we recognise that effective public policy should be informed by credible research, sound evidence and meaningful engagement with the people and institutions responsible for implementation.” He therefore commended the National Council on Climate Change and the Resource and Environmental Policy Research, Environment for Development (REPRC-EfD Nigeria), for bringing together stakeholders to strengthening the implementation of Nigeria’s carbon market framework.

artigo.texto: Brasil deve dobrar capacidade de data centers até 2030, diz Kanamaru Em entrevista, Senior advisor do BCG relaciona expansão da infraestrutura ao ReData, à soberania digital e demanda por processamento no País. O Brasil deve duplicar sua capacidade instalada de data centers até 2030, na avaliação de Márcio Kanamaru, senior advisor do Boston Consulting Group (BCG) para telecomunicações, mídia e tecnologia (TMT). Em entrevista ao Tele.Síntese, ele associou a expansão aos investimentos em infraestrutura digital e às políticas voltadas ao setor, entre elas o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (ReData). “Então o Brasil deve, até 2030, duplicar a sua capacidade em data center”, afirmou Kanamaru. Segundo ele, grandes projetos de investimento em andamento no País estão relacionados à construção dessa infraestrutura. O executivo também relacionou o cenário à aprovação do ReData e a outros estímulos tributários. Para ele, essas medidas deverão acelerar investimentos e projetos de data centers no mercado brasileiro. Acompanhe a entrevista: Soberania passa pela infraestrutura instalada no Brasil A disponibilidade de capacidade computacional no território nacional também aparece, na avaliação de Kanamaru, como parte da discussão sobre soberania digital. Ele citou empresas interessadas em manter no País dados de clientes e parceiros e o treinamento de modelos. “É importante a gente ter uma capacidade instalada aqui de data centers para que isso possa ser feito”, afirmou. Para Kanamaru, porém, a instalação de data centers não encerra a discussão. Ele defendeu que as políticas públicas considerem uma cadeia tecnológica mais ampla, chegando à capacidade nacional relacionada aos semicondutores. “O Brasil tem que buscar, através dessas políticas públicas, a construção de uma soberania mais verticalizada”, disse. Como horizonte para os próximos anos, ele cita “inclusive a construção e desenho de semicondutores no país”. Futurecom terá casos de uso com retorno sobre investimento Kanamaru também antecipou alguns dos temas que estarão em discussão na Futurecom 2026. A 31ª edição terá cinco eixos: inteligência artificial e economia de dados; infraestrutura digital; regulação e soberania; indústrias digitais; e uma arena dedicada a entretenimento e esportes. Na área de IA, a mudança apontada pelo executivo é a passagem da discussão sobre possibilidades da tecnologia para aplicações empresariais já implementadas. “Nas últimas edições a gente estava falando muito sobre perspectivas, oportunidades que a IA poderia propiciar. Nós veremos aqui casos de uso já materializados, com retorno sobre investimento”, afirmou. Segundo Kanamaru, a programação deverá apresentar business cases já construídos pelas empresas. Ele também destacou a evolução dos modelos generativos em áreas como ciência, matemática, física e saúde, além do avanço dos modelos abertos. Empresas poderão desenvolver modelos próprios baseados em open source, tema que também deverá aparecer nos debates do evento. BCG discutirá agentes e integração com redes orbitais O BCG participará de dois painéis na Futurecom, nos dias 6 e 7 de outubro. O primeiro tratará da utilização de agentes de IA no Brasil, com foco nos casos de uso e em como essas aplicações estão sendo implementadas. No segundo, o debate avançará sobre a integração das redes terrestres com redes orbitais. Kanamaru citou o uso dessas redes para ampliar a conectividade em áreas de difícil atendimento e em situações de missão crítica, onde a disponibilidade de infraestrutura por cabo, fibra ou redes móveis é mais limitada. Segundo ele, a discussão contará com a Anatel e outros participantes do ecossistema e abordará a integração entre diferentes infraestruturas de conectividade.

artigo.texto: Google aims to answer questions on Pine Island Data Center project (ABC 6 News) — Pine Island residents are still pushing back against the prospect of a Google-based data center project. Google and partner companies attempted to address some of the main concerns expressed to the residents. One of the main concerns surrounded Google’s water use, with residents expressing worries about discharge and usage. Presenters at the webinar attempted to assure that the center would not overuse water at a more-than-necessary level. “Overall, the water strategy is focused on safe and sustainable construction process, reducing ongoing demand and relying on public infrastructure in a planned and regulated way,” Dave Meadows of Kimley-Horn said. “ Some residents were skeptical about the center’s plan, wondering if they will commit to their goal of limiting water usage. “My biggest concern is the water,” resident Lee Ondler said. “They won’t tell you how they’re going to dispose of it.” Another major concern for residents surrounded the rural land that would be repurposed for the center. “What makes me worry about the idea is it’s taking up farmland,” resident Calob Darci said. The webinar presenters spent time focused on the water conversation, as it is a common concern among communities in the early stages of data center development. “People care deeply, deeply about the quality of water in this state,” said John Wade of Rochester Area Economic Development, Inc. Construction is currently halted on this project as it navigates a temporary restraining order and court proceedings. Other data centers The city of Harmony is continuing progress on the creation of a new ordinance related to data centers. The ordinance draft will now go to the Planning and Zoning Commission on Oct. 14. They will determine whether it will go to the council for approval. In Hancock County, the board discussed a resolution that could have put a moratorium on data centers for six months. However, the motion died from the board’s desire to study the public health effects and concerns, along with building an ordinance to create guidelines for prospective companies.

artigo.texto: Guest columnist: Data centers benefit ratepayers, homeowners Published 10:44 pm Thursday, October 1, 2026 The data center battle is about more than money, but one thing is clear: There are potentially massive financial benefits to individuals both as ratepayers and homeowners. Getting real-life data on the modern hyperscale data center has required a bit of “wait and see.” Supply and demand indicators are not always immediate; economic revenue projections need to be verified, and reports of whether data centers make electricity and property taxes more affordable need to bear out. New data are promising. Economic principles suggest data centers should mean rate cuts for the average ratepayer. Adding a massive, steady demand to an electric grid spreads fixed infrastructure costs over a great volume of energy consumption should drive per-unit prices down for everyone. New data from California, Indiana, and Georgia show that data center development is directly responsible for rate cuts. California’s Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E) has cut rates four times over the past two years, decreasing rates for customers by 11%. In Indiana, Indiana Michigan Power (I&M) recently proposed a 5% reduction, annually saving the average homeowner roughly $100, tied with a three year freeze on residential rates, and directly crediting them to new revenue from Amazon and Microsoft data centers. An agreement with OpenAI has led Georgia Power to announce household power bills will be cut by $180 annually starting in 2029. It is often difficult to find a signal through all the noise in electricity bills — federal and state policies have a massive impact on rates, ranging from monopoly arrangements to environmental regulations — but these are clear cases of cause and effect. Data centers have been a convenient boogeyman as rates have risen across the country, but there has been little correlation between rising rates and data center development. Aside from the effects on electricity rates, there’s been much hype around how much data center construction can affect local taxes. In Loudoun County, Virginia — ground zero for the data center boom — local property tax rates have dropped by 40%, resulting in a tax cut of almost $6,000 per household. Loudoun County is the single richest county in the United States, and it is home to the largest number of data centers of any locality in the country, so using this figure to project what this would mean for Kentucky is difficult. However, recently a study produced by Commonwealth Economics Partners for NetChoice, a trade association, projected a typical hyperscale data center over a 12-year period would generate between $227 million and $232 million in state tax revenue and up to $435 million in local taxes, a massive portion of which would go directly toward funding local public schools. There are also knock-on effects: around 3,000 temporary construction jobs annually and 200 permanent operational roles with an average salary of $105,000. This means a 400 MW data center would generate local property tax revenue equal to roughly $1,800 per household per year in a county like Muhlenberg, $1,250 in Pike, $900 in McCracken, and $670 in Boone. Local leaders can decide if that shows up as a tax cut for residents as it did in Virginia or, as Gov. Andy Beshear has suggested he prefers, a handout to interest groups. The data center battle is about more than money, but one thing is clear: There are potentially massive financial benefits to individuals both as ratepayers and homeowners. artigo.texto: Insight and analysis on the data center space from industry thought leaders. The Hidden Failure Domain in N+1 Data Center Cooling N+1 capacity can hide shared-control dependencies, turning many units into a single failure domain. Learn how to design for degraded operation and commission real resilience. Data centers continuously convert electrical power into heat. Cooling, therefore, has to keep running. Many plants look resilient on paper: redundant pumps, computer room air handlers (CRAHs), coolant distribution units (CDUs), and power feeds. Yet those assets can still depend on a single controller, network path, or sensor. That shared layer can turn an N+1 design into one large failure domain. What Can One Fault Take Down? A failure domain is the part of a system that one fault can take down. Four pumps arranged as three duty and one standby look straightforward. If a motor fails and only that pump is lost, the domain is one unit. The spare starts and the flow continues. Now, assume that all four pumps receive lead-lag selection, staging, and run commands from one controller. If that controller fails and the pumps have no local fallback, a single control fault can stop all four. The machines are mechanically redundant. They are not operationally independent. The same pattern appears with CRAHs, chillers, and CDUs. Several units may share a supervisory controller, a network switch, a control power source, a gateway, or a critical process signal. The useful question is not only how many units are installed; it is how much of the cooling plant a single failure can disable. N+1 on Paper, One Control System in Practice N+1 is easy to see on a mechanical schedule. If three pumps are required for design flow, install a fourth. If one cooling unit can drop out and the rest can carry the load, the plant appears robust. The equipment count does not show every dependency. Redundant assets may still rely on the same plant controller, switch, control power supply, or remote sensor. In a fault, the common layer decides whether the spare equipment can actually run. Centralized controls have a job. Plant-level logic can rotate lead equipment, optimize pressure setpoints, and coordinate chillers and pumps. The risk appears when the optimization layer also becomes essential to basic circulation. A supervisory controller may choose which pumps should run. Should the loss of that controller also remove the ability of healthy pumps to move water? A building management system (BMS) may issue schedules and resets. Should the loss of BMS communication stop local cooling? That behavior should be designed, not discovered during an incident. The issue is growing with liquid cooling. CDUs, variable-speed pumps, control valves, sensors, and leak detection add control and communication layers. Mechanical redundancy can fail due to dependencies that are never shown on the piping drawing. Designing for Degraded Operation Not every control failure should produce the same response. Some conditions should trigger specific starts or stops. Others justify continued operation in a conservative fallback state. For critical cooling, losing supervisory control does not have to mean losing cooling. Local controllers, such as programmable logic controllers (PLCs) in pump panels or unit controllers in CRAHs, can retain sufficient autonomy to maintain basic operation when higher-level communication is unavailable. That may mean holding a local pressure setpoint, reverting to a predefined pump speed, using locally available temperature signals, or allowing manual control until supervisory functions return. Efficiency, optimization, and remote visibility may drop. That is still different from a plant-wide stop. This is not an argument for duplicating every PLC, sensor, and network path, which adds cost and complexity. It is an argument for listing shared dependencies and defining, in advance, what should happen when each one disappears. Test the Failure Domain, Not Just the Spare Unit Commissioning is where installed redundancy and demonstrated redundancy part ways. A conventional functional test stops the lead pump and confirms that the standby starts. That demonstrates that the spare machine functions and the normal changeover sequence works. It does not prove what happens if the mechanism that commands that sequence fails. Functional testing should remove the shared layer. What happens when the supervisory network is disconnected, or when a plant controller restarts? What happens when a remote differential-pressure signal becomes invalid, or when control power is lost to one panel? The goal is to confirm that the actual failure domains align with the design intent. A system can have two of everything and still have only one path to a critical decision. If that path has never been taken away during commissioning, the resilience on the drawings has not been proven in operation. Redundancy that Survives Its Dependencies N+1 remains a useful capacity principle. It is not a complete description of cooling resilience. A stronger review question is: What is the largest failure domain in this architecture? That question exposes common controllers, shared networks, single sensors, and other ties between otherwise redundant assets. The review question leads to two more: What continues to operate when that shared dependency is lost? Has that behavior been tested? A redundant cooling plant needs spare capacity. That spare capacity must also remain usable when the controls, communications, and signals that coordinate it fail to behave as expected.

artigo.texto: DE PERE, Wis. — De Pere, Wis., and Milwaukee are moving toward one-year moratoriums on large-scale data center development, as Wisconsin communities consider how to address potential impacts on land use, utilities and local infrastructure. Planning bodies in both communities approved proposed moratoriums Monday night. Both measures still need final approval from their respective common councils. De Pere Mayor James Boyd said the moratorium would give the city time to review its local rules. “The City of De Pere doesn’t have any of them in the works. We don’t have the land for it, most likely. That said, you just never know,” Boyd said. “The moratorium gives you a chance to pause and get your code up to date regarding the hyper-scale centers.” Boyd said local officials are seeking more direction as data center proposals become a larger issue across Wisconsin. “What’s most likely going to happen is you’re going to see legislation at the state and federal level that will give us guidance,” Boyd said. “That’s really what we’re hoping for. I don’t know of any municipality that cherishes this moment where they’re handling this by themselves.” The issue has drawn attention from residents concerned about how large developments could change the landscape. Lauren French lives in Denmark, Wis., and drives through rural Brown County to her downtown De Pere business: Idolscape. “Driving here, there’s so much open space,” she said. “I don’t want that leveled. I don’t want to look and see this big, huge building and big, huge parking lot, and it’s just another concrete thing. We don’t need that.” Concerns about data center development also extend to utility costs and infrastructure needs. Tom Content, executive director of the Citizens Utility Board of Wisconsin, said part of the organization’s work is making sure data centers pay their own way for needed infrastructure. “Communities want to be ready,” Content said. “If a data center comes, they want to be ready to make sure the community impacts are talked about. The energy costs are talked about. The water issues are addressed, and the community needs are part of the conversation.” Boyd said the scale of large data centers became clearer to him after seeing one of them near Port Washington, Wis. “I didn’t really realize the size and scope of it until you drive down 43 and go toward Milwaukee and back,” Boyd said. “Then you really get a handle on what you’re looking at. The magnitude. The size. And the usage those things need to survive.”

artigo.texto: Next Upcoming Canary Live Bay Area By Canary Media On a sunny September day in New York City, I followed a throng of people off the subway and into Queens’ Flushing Meadows Corona Park. The crowds were there for the U.S. Open tennis tournament, but I wasn’t — I’d come to see a novel experiment to wean the city’s iconic food carts off dirty generators. Street vendors in NYC and around the world use fossil-fueled generators that contribute to climate change, can sicken workers, and are just plain noisy. Batteries are a silent, emissions-free alternative, but they represent an upfront cost and introduce logistical challenges around when and where to charge. So Brooklyn-based startup PopWheels is testing a model that doesn’t require vendors to buy their own batteries, allowing them to instead access swappable batteries throughout the day at nearby charging cabinets. In July, the firm launched a six-month pilot in the Flushing Meadows Corona Park area, installing two black-and-yellow cabinets where the 10 participating vendors can exchange their dead batteries for fresh ones. Right now, the vendors can access these batteries for free, thanks to $46,000 in grant funding from the City Parks Foundation and another $30,900 from the nonprofit Resilient Cities Catalyst. But PopWheels’ vision is that vendors would eventually pay a monthly subscription fee to use the battery-swapping infrastructure, plus a fee to buy or lease the inverter that houses the batteries in the food cart itself. The firm aims to make the setup price-competitive with the cost of buying and fueling a generator. “We understand that this only works if we meet not just our green needs but also the economic needs and the logistic needs of these vendors,” said Ben Rosenn, PopWheels’ director of deployments. “They’re not going to want to switch if it’s more expensive.” Scaling the battery-swapping model is not far-fetched. The company already runs a similar program for New York’s delivery workers, charging them between $65 and $95 a month to access batteries for their e-bikes from over 45 cabinets scattered across the city. “We know that this technology is safe, and it has been used before,” said Isabelle Thomas, policy adviser for living streets and public spaces at the NYC Mayor’s Office of Climate and Environmental Justice, a partner on the PopWheels pilot. “It’s just that it hasn’t necessarily been used in this way” for food vendors. And get this: The batteries used for the e-bikes are the same exact ones that are used for the food carts, meaning that delivery workers and street vendors could eventually take advantage of the same infrastructure. PopWheels has also identified another neat symbiosis in its food-cart pilot, paying some of the delivery workers who already rely on the service to shuttle batteries to street vendors that are farther away from the charging cabinets. William Arevalo, the owner of the food cart I toured, said that his batteries have worked well so far and that he’d be willing to pay for a subscription to keep using the service. It would likely cost far less than the roughly $500 to $600 a month he pays to fuel his generator, which also requires regular maintenance and repairs. Finances aside, the generator’s noise sometimes makes it hard for customers and workers to hear each other, Arevalo said, and he’s acutely aware of the smoke’s insidious effects. “Little by little, there can be damage to the lungs,” he said. “I have a lot of friends who have this problem.” Though the electrical equipment in Arevalo’s cart now runs on batteries, the grill still uses propane gas. And, within eyeshot of his battery-powered food cart, which fries up empanadas and other savory dishes, Arevalo operates an ice cream truck that still relies on a diesel-fueled generator. PopWheels’ batteries are not capable of providing enough power for that operation. “To be honest, right now the technology can’t serve ice cream trucks,” said Rosenn. “I don’t think it’s feasible, and you would have to be constantly swapping it.” Electrifying super-energy-intensive vendors would likely require a substantially different battery type and cabinet fleet, according to PopWheels. PopWheels’ model isn’t the only option for electrifying food carts. Vendors can purchase their own batteries and charge them up at home or in the commissaries and depots where they park overnight. Arevalo said a friend with a food truck in Brooklyn did that after receiving lots of noise and pollution complaints, switching his generator for a battery he charges at a depot. But it’s not a given that vendors have access to a space with the electric infrastructure needed to safely charge. “Every commissary really is different, and some of them have the capacity for there to be charging happening there,” Thomas said. “But then there are others that would need electrical upgrades or don’t have enough outlets.” Batteries also tend to cost more upfront than generators, and vendors must be able to afford a system big enough to get them through the entire day. The nonprofit Street Vendor Project — a partner on the PopWheels effort in Queens — ran a pilot a couple of years ago in which it provided NYC vendors with batteries they were responsible for charging themselves. Given the rules around cart footprints, the organization offered batteries that were around the same physical size as generators, but that capacity was sufficient for fewer vendors than expected, said Andrew Conca-Cheng, programs manager at the Street Vendor Project. artigo.texto: Portos Porto Central estuda hub de data centers com até 5 GW de capacidade Projeto em Presidente Kennedy (ES) prevê aproveitamento de energia, água, áreas disponíveis e conexão por cabos submarinos de telecomunicações O Porto Central, em Presidente Kennedy (ES), estuda a implantação de um hub de data centers voltado a empresas brasileiras e estrangeiras. O projeto aproveita a infraestrutura prevista para o complexo portuário, incluindo oferta de energia, água, áreas disponíveis e conexão por cabos submarinos de telecomunicações. A proposta ainda está em fase de concepção e estruturação. As próximas etapas incluem a definição do modelo de empreendimento, o dimensionamento da infraestrutura necessária e dos insumos, como energia e água, além da prospecção de empresas interessadas em utilizar os futuros data centers. Segundo Fabrício Cardoso Freitas, CEO da Macro Investimentos e membro do Conselho de Administração do Porto Central, o empreendimento já conta com um dos principais ativos necessários para esse tipo de operação: capacidade energética. O complexo desenvolveu e licenciou 5 gigawatts (GW) de capacidade, além de prever estrutura para fornecimento de gás natural liquefeito (GNL). A disponibilidade de energia é considerada um dos fatores centrais para a implantação de data centers, que demandam fornecimento contínuo para manter a operação da infraestrutura de processamento e armazenamento de dados. Além da energia, o projeto poderá utilizar áreas do complexo portuário, disponibilidade de água e a infraestrutura logística do Porto Central, que também prevê possibilidade de conexão ferroviária. Outro diferencial em estudo é a conexão internacional por cabos submarinos de telecomunicações. O Porto Central já possui autorização para receber um cabo, e as tratativas para viabilizar a instalação estão em andamento. A proposta é que a estrutura permita receber, processar e distribuir dados tanto para o mercado brasileiro quanto para outros países, criando uma nova frente de negócios associada à infraestrutura portuária.

artigo.texto: Applied Digital holds town hall on AI data center campus in Brookwood BROOKWOOD, Ala. (WBRC) -Brookwood’s Mayor Joe Barger said a planned $3.2 billion AI data center campus is essentially a done deal, with the city council needing only to vote on a resolution backing the Tuscaloosa County Economic Development Authority, which approved the project last week. Applied Digital wants to build the data center campus on about 160 acres, with more than a million square feet of facilities. Company cites power infrastructure During a town hall hosted Thursday by Applied Digital, the company said Brookwood’s power infrastructure is a big reason it picked the site. The company is promising thousands of construction jobs and just over 100 full-time jobs, along with hundreds of millions of dollars for schools and community benefits over time, according to the company. “We love that people care deeply about Brookwood and the surrounding area and want to have good conversation. We are very responsible. We take pride in the work that we do, and we’re here tonight to explain how we do things and what that looks like and how we’ll be able to work with the community and also make sure we can address all the various environmental concerns and other concerns that are out there,” Nick Phillips, Applied Digital Executive Vice President of External Affairs said. Phillips said retention ponds and other measures will protect the environment. Some neighbors are still pushing back against the project, but at least one said she feels better about it after the meeting. “I feel much better, much more pleased and cautiously optimistic,” said Samantha Carter, a Brookwood native. Mayor addresses community concerns “I have zero concerns. And I would do nothing to harm this community or any citizens. I live here. My family lives here. Friends and family mean more to me than any dollar that you could bring to our community, and I would never jeopardize our community for the sake of a dollar,” said Mayor Joe Barger of Brookwood. Barger expects a vote on the resolution in the coming days. WBRC will keep you updated. Get news alerts in the Apple App Store and Google Play Store or subscribe to our email newsletter here.
