Amazon is making a significant new commitment to data center infrastructure as the AI revolution drives unprecedented demand for computing power. The company's latest announcement comes as tech giants race to build the backbone that will power tomorrow's artificial intelligence applications, with Amazon positioning itself as a key player in what it calls 'the race our nation can't afford to lose.' Amazon just threw down the gauntlet in the AI infrastructure wars. The company's latest announcement positions its data center expansion as nothing less than a national imperative, framing the buildout in terms of America's competitive edge in artificial intelligence. The timing couldn't be more strategic. As OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google burn through computing resources training increasingly powerful AI models, the companies that control the underlying infrastructure hold the keys to the kingdom. Amazon's AWS already commands roughly 30% of the global cloud market, but the AI boom has created entirely new categories of demand. 'This is the race our nation can't afford to lose,' Amazon's announcement declares, echoing the rhetoric that's become common as tech executives lobby for favorable infrastructure policies. The company is betting that positioning itself as essential to American technological leadership will smooth the path for rapid expansion. The community investment angle represents a savvy political move. As data centers face increasing scrutiny over their environmental impact and strain on local power grids, Amazon is getting ahead of potential opposition by emphasizing local benefits. The strategy mirrors approaches by Meta and Microsoft, who've similarly coupled infrastructure announcements with community commitments. Behind the patriotic messaging lies hard business reality. Amazon Web Services generated $90.8 billion in revenue last year, with operating margins that make it Amazon's most profitable division. Every new data center represents not just increased capacity but a competitive moat against rivals like Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud. The AI infrastructure race has fundamentally changed the economics of data center construction. Traditional cloud workloads required general-purpose computing power, but AI training and inference demand specialized chips like Nvidia's H100 GPUs, which cost upwards of $30,000 each and require entirely different cooling and power systems. Amazon's emphasis on national competitiveness also reflects growing concerns about China's AI capabilities. As the Biden administration restricts chip exports to China and pushes for domestic semiconductor manufacturing, tech companies are finding that wrapping business expansion in national security language opens doors in Washington. The community investment component suggests Amazon has learned from past battles over data center construction. Local opposition has delayed or derailed projects in Virginia, Ireland, and elsewhere, often centered on concerns about power consumption and environmental impact. By front-loading community benefits, Amazon hopes to build local support before opposition can organize. What remains unclear is the scale of Amazon's commitment. The company has been characteristically vague about specific investment amounts or timelines, preferring to let the announcement generate buzz while keeping competitors guessing about its actual plans. Amazon's latest data center push represents more than infrastructure expansion - it's a calculated bet that positioning itself as essential to American AI leadership will unlock both regulatory support and competitive advantage. As the AI arms race intensifies, the companies that control the computing infrastructure will increasingly find themselves at the center of national technology policy. For Amazon, that's exactly where it wants to be.

artigo.texto: Texas has become the epicenter of the nation’s data center growth with the conspicuous buildings popping up next to neighborhoods and on farmland throughout the state. Though the sight of them has drawn considerable public backlash, few people can say they’ve physically walked through the doors of a data center and into the cloud. Only a handful of staff work there. The gates are locked to all but construction crews and those with security clearances. The doors to the massive, windowless warehouse-style structures with their own power grids are tightly guarded. Media requests for a look behind the curtain had gone unfulfilled — until now. In the Texas Research Park on the far Northwest Side of San Antonio, several large industrial buildings in various stages of completion have been built along what’s become a data center corridor. On Omicron Drive, a high-security palisade fence, its sharp black teeth curved outward, wraps around 22 acres of land acquired by data center developer CyrusOne. Through a swing gate with crossing arms on either side, the San Antonio Report and other members of the press entered the premises recently for a first-ever media tour of the facility. Invited to the site by the company and its political affairs representatives, the tour began in the lobby of a gray and white building that houses the data center and offices. Uniformed security officers sitting behind glass checked IDs and handed out red visitor badges only after electronic confidentiality forms were signed. During introductions, a spokeswoman told reporters and a podcaster that all conversations during the media tour should be considered “off the record” and only exterior photos of the center were permitted. Data centers are critical infrastructure — storing and processing a growing amount of digital data on behalf of clients, from government entities, financial services firms and health care systems to streaming services and social media. So as the media tour made its way down long stretches of brightly lit corridors, empty of most anything but the galvanized steel duct work and fiber overhead, the secured double doors to actual data halls were opened only enough for a quick peek. No one was allowed in. No pictures. To protect client confidentiality and the company’s proprietary information, a spokeswoman declined to identify the customers using the data halls. ‘Do it responsibly’ Asked why CyrusOne, the nation’s seventh-largest data center company by capacity, is pulling back the curtain now, Katy Hancock said it is a reflection of their pride in the facilities and how it operates, and to dispel myths and misinformation. “We build digital infrastructure, and we do it responsibly, and we want to let people know about it,” Hancock said. Founded in 2000, the Dallas-based CyrusOne operates enterprise-class, carrier-neutral data center properties, according to its website, providing data storage and processing for more than 925 customers. It owns or has planned more than 100 data centers throughout Europe, the Far East and the United States, including 15 in Austin, Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston and San Antonio. In addition to its Omicron sites, another is under construction far west of San Antonio, just past Castroville in Medina County. That facility sprawls across 250 acres of former ranch and farmland along Highway 90 West, adjacent to a Microsoft data center also under construction. It is expected to be completed in June. Welcome mat Recently, in addition to inviting the small group of handpicked journalists, CyrusOne has led tours for elected officials like council members Ric Galvan (D6) and Phyllis Viagran (D3), plus local leaders and industry folks. The spokeswoman said the company has previously laid out the welcome mat at another San Antonio facility for its residential neighbors, arranging it through the homeowners association. Such site visits are intended to make data centers seem less mysterious, she said, and perhaps less onerous given the questions about how they operate. A wave of litigation challenging the secrecy behind development and the use of water and power in recent years has followed the unprecedented growth of data centers. Bowing to public pressure, state and local governments have called for audits, investigations and moratoriums. Community acceptance has become the industry’s greatest challenge, according to a report by the commercial real estate firm, JLL. “Transparency and early engagement with communities around electricity, water and noise, as well as benefits, including jobs, investment and tax revenue are essential,” the report states. Chillers and generators After breakfast tacos and a presentation, CyrusOne’s senior director of operations, Robert Orms, led a tour of the SAT 5 data center facility at the Omicron site. The campus includes two operating facilities and two under construction. Another three are planned for a nearby parcel of land on Omicron Drive. The company’s first data centers in San Antonio, SATs 1-4, are located in Westover Hills off State Highway 151. Opening secure doors with his badge, Orms explained the 87,500-square-foot data center’s power requirements and the closed-loop cooling system it uses, and how the fire suppression system works, one using water and the other air. Though well-lit for the tour, the center’s spaces are generally kept dark for energy efficiency, he said. The only noise during the tour came in the form of a loud whirr from the data halls only when the doorways were opened. Up a set of stairs, Orms led us to a second-level control room where several staff members keep track of the power and cooling systems by watching a wall of monitors. We met one member of the staff who was a U.S. Navy veteran and another who started in the data center after working as an HVAC technician, both common career paths in the data center industry. artigo.texto: Sept. 30 (UPI) -- Democrats in the U.S. Senate on Wednesday blocked a bill that would have made states consider adopting ways to make data center developers pay for water and energy costs, calling the legislation "toothless." The Ratepayer Protection Act, which was led by Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, would not force states to adopt these standards. Democrats said they sought legislation to mandate that developers cover the costs, The Hill reported. The act, which would set a federal standard on the issue, passed the House by a vote of 417-3 earlier this month. The procedural vote Wednesday was 57-43, short of the 60 votes needed to break a filibuster. Data centers, which use huge amounts of energy, are increasingly unpopular among voters, an NBC News poll earlier this month said. By nearly 6 to 1, voters said they'd be less likely to vote for a candidate who supports building a data center in their community, the poll said. Some Democratic senators, including Sens. Jon Ossoff of Georgia, Raphael Warnock of Georgia, Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire and Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota, joined Republicans to vote for the bill. However, Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said that the act was "optional" for states and "a fraud." "It does not require any protections at all," Schumer said Tuesday. "While Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, Republicans are offering a toothless messaging bill. We need real action on data centers." Husted said Tuesday that the act could be a "bipartisan win." "I heard they said they wanted lower electricity prices," he said of Democrats. "All they have to do is not block it, vote for it, and it will be on the president's desk." Former Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, who is running against Husted, has criticized him as "the point man to bring these data centers to Ohio" when Husted was Ohio's lieutenant governor.

artigo.texto: Em 21 de maio de 2026, o Governo emitiu o Decreto nº 180/2026/ND-CP que regulamenta os serviços de sequestro e armazenamento de carbono florestal, estipulando os procedimentos e a autoridade para o desenvolvimento, avaliação e aprovação de projetos de carbono florestal, a confirmação dos resultados de redução de emissões e a utilização dos fundos obtidos com créditos de carbono florestal. O camarada Phan Trung Bá presidiu a reunião. O processo de criação, emissão de créditos e verificação dos resultados de redução de emissões inclui o registro, a avaliação e a aprovação do projeto; a implementação do projeto e a emissão de créditos de carbono florestal; a verificação dos resultados de redução de emissões; e somente então as transações podem ocorrer. Os créditos só podem ser negociados por meio de contratos comerciais ou bolsas de carbono centralizadas; o volume total de exportação é limitado a um máximo de 50% dos créditos gerados para garantir a segurança nacional de emissões. Na implementação das novas regulamentações, o Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente emitiu um documento para implementar o Decreto nº 180/2026/ND-CP aos departamentos, agências e Comitês Populares de comunas e distritos. A província concluiu o levantamento do estado atual das florestas e das reservas de carbono florestal em 48 comunas e distritos na parte norte da província de Lao Cai para o período de 2024-2025. Os resultados determinaram que as reservas totais de carbono atingiram 14,33 milhões de toneladas. Segundo o Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente, o projeto de carbono florestal é uma área completamente nova, sendo implementado pela primeira vez na província; e nenhuma província em todo o país concluiu ainda a construção e recebeu a aprovação das autoridades competentes para um projeto de carbono florestal, conforme estipulado no Decreto nº 180/2026/ND-CP. Os documentos legais pertinentes foram emitidos apenas em 2026 e continuam sendo utilizados como guia para a implementação. Além disso, atualmente, o Vietnã não possui nenhuma organização reconhecida por ter capacidade suficiente para desempenhar a função de avaliar e verificar os resultados da redução de emissões e os créditos de carbono florestal de acordo com os padrões nacionais. Delegados presentes na reunião No próximo período, a província realizará um levantamento do estado das florestas para o período de 2026-2027 em 51 comunas e distritos na antiga área da província de Yen Bai, após aprovação do Comitê Popular Provincial; e, simultaneamente, implementará o "Projeto de Carbono em Áreas Florestais de Propriedade Pública na Província de Lao Cai ", após aprovação da política, do plano técnico e da estimativa orçamentária. Durante a reunião, os delegados discutiram as dificuldades e os obstáculos e propuseram soluções para a implementação do Decreto nº 180/2026/ND-CP. Em seu discurso na reunião, o Sr. Phan Trung Bá, Vice-Presidente do Comitê Popular Provincial, solicitou aos departamentos e agências competentes que continuem revisando e concluindo as tarefas sob sua jurisdição; atualizem proativamente as regulamentações e diretrizes sobre o mercado de carbono; e coordenem com agências especializadas, unidades de consultoria e especialistas para resolver dificuldades técnicas e jurídicas. Dessa forma, a província visa explorar gradualmente o potencial de absorção e armazenamento de carbono das florestas de maneira eficaz, criando as bases para que Lao Cai esteja preparada para participar do mercado de créditos de carbono florestal, contribuindo para a redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa e para o aumento do valor econômico das florestas. artigo.texto: Exide Tops ₹5,200 Crore in EV Battery Bet as Bengaluru Plant Goes Live Key Takeaways - Exide Industries has committed ₹5,202.23 crore to EESL as of 29 September 2026, a cumulative figure equivalent to nearly 30% of the parent's FY26 annual revenue, all directed into a subsidiary yet to generate meaningful commercial revenue. - Phase I of EESL's 6 GWh Bengaluru gigafactory was commissioned on 23 September 2026, making it one of the only operational domestic lithium-ion cell manufacturing facilities in India, where total commissioned PLI-ACC capacity stood at just 1.4 GWh out of a 50 GWh target as of October 2025. - First revenue from LFP cells is targeted for Q3 FY27, with break-even projected at late FY27 or early FY28 only if utilisation exceeds 40-50% of Phase I capacity, a threshold that remains unproven at this stage. - EESL's loss after tax widened from ₹209.12 crore in FY25 to ₹248.16 crore in FY26, a pattern consistent with the depreciation and interest burden of heavy capital expenditure overwhelming nascent revenue during a ramp-up phase. - Zero PLI-ACC incentives have been disbursed to any beneficiary as of September 2026, meaning the investment economics that underpin EESL's case rest on government payments that have not yet materialised, representing the single most consequential structural risk to watch over the next four to six quarters. Exide Industries has now committed ₹5,202.23 crore to a single battery subsidiary, closed the latest ₹99.99 crore tranche of that commitment just yesterday, and switched on the plant it has been funding less than a week ago. That is a landmark figure for the Indian energy storage sector, and the timing is what makes it worth reading closely. Exide Energy Solutions Limited (EESL) has crossed a threshold. It is no longer a construction project on a balance sheet; it is an operating facility chasing its first commercial revenues. To reach this point, the parent has poured in more than five thousand crore rupees, and the next phase, where revenue arrives from Q3 FY27 and break-even hinges on how fast the plant fills up, is where an ambition of this size either proves out or strains. Here is what the ₹5,200 crore commitment actually tells you about Exide’s strategic direction, what the commissioning of Phase I means in practical terms, and the specific variables that will decide whether this concentrated bet was correctly sized. Exide closes ₹100 crore rights issue in EESL as cumulative bet crosses ₹5,200 crore The mechanics of the latest transaction are straightforward. Exide subscribed to a fresh rights issue of equity in EESL, its wholly owned cell manufacturing arm, on a cash consideration basis at arm’s length. No ownership percentage changed; Exide already held 100% of the subsidiary and still does. Here is what the tranche involved: - 2,85,71,428 equity shares allotted - Face value of ₹10 per share, issued at a premium of ₹25 per share - Total raised: ₹99.99 crore - Allotment completed on 29 September 2026 This tranche did not arrive in isolation. In January 2026, Exide’s board approved up to ₹1,400 crore in additional infusions to keep the project moving, and management has executed that approval across multiple tranches through the year. Yesterday’s rights issue is simply the latest instalment in a steady, deliberate drip of capital. Add it all up and the number lands with real weight. ₹5,202.23 crore invested in EESL as of 29 September 2026 That figure only becomes fully legible against the parent’s own scale. Standalone Exide Industries reported revenue of roughly ₹17,269 crore in FY26. So the cumulative commitment to EESL now equals close to 30% of the parent’s annual turnover, all directed into a subsidiary whose net worth stood at ₹3,991.06 crore as of 31 March 2026 and which has yet to generate meaningful revenue. For anyone tracking Exide’s balance sheet and capital allocation, the message is unambiguous. This is not a paper reorganisation or an accounting entry. It is a genuine cash commitment at commercial terms, and both the size of the total and the pace at which it has grown deserve scrutiny. When big ASX news breaks, our subscribers know first Phase I of Exide’s 6 GWh Bengaluru gigafactory enters commercial operations The capital has been buying something concrete, and six days before the latest tranche, that something switched on. EESL commissioned Phase I of its lithium-ion cell manufacturing facility on 23 September 2026 at the Hi-Tech Defense and Aerospace Park in Devanahalli, Bengaluru. Phase I carries a 6 GWh design capacity built on two chemistries, a configuration that hedges the plant against shifts in demand across different end-markets. The commercial sequencing follows demand readiness. Initial revenue will come from LFP cells serving three-wheelers, telecom, and battery energy storage systems (BESS), stationary units that store power for later use. NMC cells for two-wheelers follow once that line ramps. Global BESS demand is one of the key demand drivers underpinning the LFP line at Devanahalli, with grid-scale stationary storage contracts offering longer-term, higher-volume offtake compared to the more cyclical two-wheeler segment. A few facts anchor the facility: - Total design capacity of 12 GWh across two phases, with Phase II timing dependent on demand signals - Phase I capital expenditure estimated at approximately ₹6,000 crore through FY28 - Cell manufacturing technology underpinned by a technical collaboration with SVOLT The six-day gap between commissioning the plant and injecting fresh capital was not coincidental. Exide is funding the ramp-up phase, the stretch that converts a commissioned facility into a revenue-generating one. That distinction matters for how you read the risk. Until last week, EESL carried construction risk, the danger that a plant might not get built on time or on budget. artigo.texto: As elétricas que podem lucrar com o medida tributária Redata, segundo o Safra O presidente Luis Inácio Lula da Silva aprovou, neste mês, o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center, mais conhecido como Redata. A medida envolve incentivos fiscais para centros de processamento de dados no Brasil. Com o Redata, o Safra enxerga uma oportunidade para as companhias do setor elétrico. O relatório do banco cita a estimativa que a demanda de eletricidade dos data centers deve crescer 15% ao ano até 2030, dado da Agência Internacional de Energia – IEA. Além disso, o Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia (PDE 2035), elaborado pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), projeta que o Brasil pode alcançar 20 GW de capacidade instalada de data centers até 2035. O Safra ainda diz que esse número pode ser ainda maior com o Redata. Nesse contexto, o banco acredita que sete companhias do setor elétrico podem se beneficiar desse cenário. As ações que podem se beneficiar com o Redata O Safra utiliza a experiência dos Estados Unidos como referência. Por isso, eles enxergam um potencial para um aumento de 2,7% na demanda, caso a participação dos data centers passe de 5% para 8% da demanda total de energia. Esse cenário beneficiaria distribuidoras como ENEL, CPFL (CPFE3), Light (LIGT3), Equatorial (EQTL3) e Energisa (ENGI3). Além disso, o banco cita a alta de preços de energia em regiões dos EUA, que aumentaram aproximadamente 30% entre 2020 e 2025 tanto por uma maior demanda dos data centers, quanto possivelmente por condições climáticas e custos de combustíveis. Nesse contexto, maiores pagamentos por capacidade podem beneficiar Axia (AXIA3) e Copel (CPLE3), segundo os analistas. *Sob supervisão de Renan Dantas

artigo.texto: Nigeria has moved to its next implementation stage for its carbon market framework by establishing specific criteria to determine which carbon projects the government will approve. The National Council on Climate Change (NCCC) held a National Stakeholder Review and Validation Workshop on the draft Host Country Approval Criteria for Nigeria’s Carbon Market Operations in Abuja. NCCC Director-General Omotenioye Majekodunmi told the workshop that Nigeria had secured approval for the carbon market framework. The task now facing stakeholders is establishing approval criteria that protect national interests while giving credible investors and project developers certainty, she added. University of Nigeria, Nsukka Vice-Chancellor Simon Uchenna Ortuanya, represented by university Professor Nnaemeka Chukwuone, said the approval criteria would provide guidance on the eligibility, screening, and assessment of carbon market projects, describing their development as guided by sound research. The workshop marks a further step in a process that began nearly a year earlier, following President Bola Tinubu’s approval of the National Carbon Market Framework in late October 2025 ahead of COP30 in Belém, Brazil. Tinubu signed off on the framework’s full implementation in January 2026, with oversight resting with the NCCC, chaired by the President and supported by a dedicated carbon market office. Financial projections and international compliance The government has projected the framework could unlock between $2.5 billion and $3 billion annually in carbon finance over the next decade, positioning carbon trading as a significant driver of non-oil revenue. The framework spans forestry, energy, and agriculture, aligning Nigeria’s carbon market activities with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, which governs international cooperation on emissions trading and carbon credits between countries. Read also: Stakeholders advocate domestic financing for Nigeria’s carbon market The host country approval criteria under review are a practical mechanism to determine which offset or reduction projects the government will formally authorise to sell credits internationally. Getting this stage right is designed to prevent problems that have undermined voluntary carbon markets elsewhere, such as projects of questionable integrity, double-counting of credits, and weak enforcement that erodes investor confidence. Whether Nigeria’s final approval criteria succeed in attracting projected investment while avoiding international credibility pitfalls will determine how much of that projected $2.5 billion to $3 billion actually materialises.

artigo.texto: Nordic independent power producer (IPP) Alight has acquired a portfolio of 40 utility-scale solar PV projects in southern Sweden from Swedish developer Soltech Energy Solutions, with a combined planned solar capacity of around 2GW. The projects are located across Sweden’s SE3 and SE4 electricity price areas and include options for co-located battery energy storage systems (BESS) at most sites. The acquisition increases Alight’s solar PV and energy storage development pipeline in the Nordic region to more than 5GW. A portfolio with secured land, permits in progress and room for battery storage lets us reach ready-to-build faster than if we developed new projects from scratch,” said Warren Campbell, CEO at Alight. Alight will take responsibility for the continued development of the projects, including permitting and grid connection work, with the portfolio to be advanced towards ready-to-build status. The company said the projects will be developed primarily for long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs). Under its PPA model, Alight develops, builds, owns and operates the solar parks, selling generated electricity to commercial and industrial customers at fixed, long-term prices. “We have spent several years building this portfolio and taking the projects from early development to today’s level of maturity. The projects are now entering a phase where a long-term investor is better placed to take them towards investment decision and construction. We look forward to continuing our good collaboration with Alight for many years to come,” says Christoffer Caesar, CEO of Soltech Energy Solutions. The acquisition expands Alight’s existing utility-scale solar development activities in the Nordic region. Last year, Alight’s Annelie Westén wrote for PV Tech Premium on the Nordic solar growth (subscription required), including Finland’s expanding utility-scale market, PPAs and solar-plus-storage, but warned that grid congestion and permitting delays could constrain further expansion. The IPP recently inaugurated the 215MWp Lidsø Solar Park in Lolland, Denmark, which it described as one of the largest solar parks in the Nordic region. The company also recently inaugurated the 101MWp Eurajoki Solar Park in Finland with automotive supplier Autoliv.

artigo.texto: Governor Spanberger’s Energy Plan Highlights Need to Rein in Data Centers Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger on Thursday released a comprehensive energy policy roadmap that features options prioritizing transitions to cleaner energy—while forecasting data centers will likely eat up a massive chunk of the Commonwealth’s energy needs and capacity in the coming years. The proposal thankfully includes positive priorities like establishing a state-based renewable energy marketplace and prioritizing public health when building out our energy infrastructure—but also lays bare the sobering fact that data centers and their energy use must be reined in if Virginia hopes to have a sustainable energy future. Projections forecast that the power needed to accommodate anticipated data center growth would eclipse residential use in Virginia in the coming years. Data centers are harming Virginians and our communities. They’re threatening the state’s water supply and helping send power bills ever higher. Even the companies behind them are pumping the brakes on associated technologies over safety concerns. The transition to clean energy is important for the health of Virginia’s rivers and the Chesapeake Bay. About a third of the nitrogen pollution that ends up in the Bay starts as air pollution from power plants and other sources. Data centers are making the clean energy transition harder by straining the grid and stretching thin Virginia’s already limited energy supplies. There is no realistic clean, sustainable energy future for Virginia without strong guardrails for data centers to ensure they’re transparent throughout their lifecycles, offset their water use, and fuel their operations with clean energy. Chesapeake Bay Foundation Virginia Policy Manager Jay Ford issued the following statement: “Governor Spanberger and her team should be commended for laying out an energy roadmap that promotes public health and Virginia’s transition to clean energy. This plan prioritizes the health and economic well-being of Virginians and represents a model for how state energy planning should be done. “However, this plan also makes clear that unchecked data center growth is swiftly pushing Virginia toward an unsustainable set of choices for our energy future. All scenarios in the proposal involve significant reliance on fossil fuels to meet ever-skyrocketing anticipated power demands for data centers. “Virginians should not have to sacrifice their health and well-being to make the wealthiest companies in human history even more profitable. “This plan makes clear that lawmakers need to build on the governor’s strong Data Center Accountability Framework and act aggressively in the coming 2027 legislative session to rein in these out-of-control energy and water guzzlers.”

artigo.texto: Medford council, planning commission to discuss data centers Published 4:26 pm Tuesday, September 29, 2026 Medford man launches online petition urging city officials to prohibit the facilities, which have been a subject of extensive environmental concerns A Medford man is urging residents to tune in for a planned discussion of data centers by Medford city officials on Wednesday night. The joint study session, which will include Medford City Council and the city’s Planning Commission, is set for 6 p.m. Sept. 30 in the Medford Police Department’s Prescott Room. The agenda for the meeting — residents can attend in person or via Zoom — is posted to the city website. Discussion of data centers comes amid ongoing conversations around the state and nation as community leaders grapple with how to navigate a growing number of the facilities. While data centers provide technology for artificial intelligence, data storage and other online services, concerns range from heavy electricity usage, large consumption of water for equipment cooling purposes and environmental impacts. Land use considerations range from the amount and cost of available land to demands on water, sewer, transportation and stormwater infrastructure. Large facilities may require 50 to 150 acres. City and county municipalities tout economic development, with the facilities projected to create millions in tax revenues and thousands of jobs. Medford city officials report no existing applications have been submitted and no decisions will be made during the study session. Online petition Medford resident Matthew Damigos expressed concern that consideration of data centers by city officials could mean proposed data centers could soon be under consideration. Damigos has launched an online petition on Change.Org titled, “Prevent the construction of an AI data center in Medford, Oregon.” Damigos told the Rogue Valley Times he was “deeply concerned about the potential implications for our city and our way of life” if a data center should be constructed, and he said he felt the topic warranted a community conversation “and not just a discussion between the council and planning commission.” Damigos expressed concern about the council’s “willingness to take citizen input,” pointing to a recent back-and-forth involving changes to downtown Main Street, where traffic pattern changes were made and then changed again. Damigos said he hoped citizens would weigh in on the topic of data centers. “Public comment is absolutely necessary regarding an AI data center. AI data centers simply have shown negative effects on communities, and (there are) long-term effects that are unknown,” he told the Times. “This is not a political matter. This is a public health matter, and the Medford and nearby communities in Jackson County should be heard,” Damigos said. Damigos said notice of the study session posted Friday did not allow for enough time for residents to plan to attend. “I just think it’s odd to announce they’re having this discussion and then, ‘Oh, by the way, you have only two business days for the public to even see it.’ Everything the city of Medford does is quite questionable in my opinion. This is an important issue for our community,” he said. “I was concerned they were entertaining the discussion, and I wanted to make sure people were aware because not everyone is going to go to the city of Medford website to see that this discussion is happening.” Currently, Medford Land Development Code Section 10.337 allows data centers in all commercial zones as well as the Light Industrial zone. They are not permitted in the General or Heavy Industrial zones, and the city has no special design or location standards established for data centers. Council and planning commission members will discuss whether to make changes to city land-use regulations pbefore any future proposals for data centers. State and national date center headlines Following concerns raised by a large coalition of environmental, farm and social advocacy groups, and the urging of a moratorium of data centers, Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek earlier this month ordered a pause on data centers on state lands, effective through July 2027. A report this week by the Oregon Capital Chronicle detailed plans for a data center proposed on 100 acres of BLM land near Hermiston — the project would be the first on federal public land in Oregon and one of a dozen proposed in six western states. Reach reporter Buffy Pollock at 458-488-2029 or buffy.pollock@rv-times.com. Follow her on Twitter @orwritergal.

artigo.texto: da Agência iNFRA O ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico) propôs à ANEEL (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) que o encargo para custear a contratação de baterias seja reduzido para as fontes que entregam mais potência na ponta de carga – janela em que a geração solar cai e o consumo aumenta, exigindo resposta rápida do sistema. A proposta introduz um novo conceito, batizado de “ICP-JC”, que mede a contribuição de cada usina para adequar a potência no período mais crítico do dia, entre 18h e 22h. Segundo o ONS, o indicador deveria ser usado para graduar o rateio do encargo entre os geradores. O ONS disse que essa metodologia para verificar a contribuição de potência de cada fonte já está em desenvolvimento para subsidiar o montante a ser contratado no leilão de baterias, em dezembro. Para isso, solicitou à ANEEL que incorpore a variável de potência verificada em um intervalo de tempo à consulta pública em andamento. A sugestão foi apresentada em reunião com o gabinete do diretor Gentil Nogueira, no último dia 14, e disponibilizada na terça-feira (29). O operador frisou que a definição sobre o critério de rateio deve ser conhecido pelos agentes antes do leilão.

artigo.texto: Data centers are at the center of a Baltimore County Council race, as candidates disagree about whether the county’s moratorium, which expires in December of 2027, goes far enough. They also are accusing each other of using data centers as a political football. Council District 5 extends from Timonium north to the Pennsylvania line. The race is one of the county’s most intriguing contests, pitting a well-financed Republican councilman with name recognition against a Democrat who is running with help from public campaign financing, and a third candidate, an independent, who is leaning into affordability issues. Before campaign sign waving during morning rush hour at the busy intersection of Padonia and York Roads in Timonium, Democrat Shawn McIntosh criticized Republican Councilman Nino Mangione for pushing to extend the moratorium, which unanimously passed the council last month. She said the hyper-scale data centers should be banned until the industry finds ways to deal with their water and energy consumption. McIntosh said, “Hyper-scale data centers are really dangerous to our environment, and there are ways to do it better, but they're not using them. I believe that banning them will force the industry to adopt the better technologies.” But Mangione said the moratorium gives the county time to gather facts. “We know that there are enormous projects, and there's potentially enormous financial upside,” Mangione said. “We've heard a lot about that, but we also know there are very serious potential consequences.” McIntosh questioned Mangione’s motives behind having a moratorium rather than a ban. McIntosh said, “We already know the impact of current data centers, so just ban them until we know they're not going to harm the environment, we know they're not going to harm our county or our state.” Mangione said McIntosh is not looking for answers. “She screams,” Mangione said. “She’s screaming and yelling because she thinks it’s a political advantage. It’s nothing more but political opportunism.” Cory Shaffer, an unaffiliated candidate, said the county council’s data center moratorium “is just a way to kick the can down the road to a non-election year so we can continue with the politics as usual when the microscope is not on people quite as much.” Shaffer said he supports a ban because he fears back room deals will be made that shuts out the community. “I’m not totally against data centers, it’s just the way it’s been done has shown me that we can’t trust the people that are doing it,” Shaffer said. While Mangione is a sitting councilman, he is not running for reelection. He was appointed to the council earlier this year to finish the term of Wade Kach, who resigned for health reasons. Before that, Mangione was in the Maryland House of Delegates.

artigo.texto: Battery storage (BESS) financing in the Netherlands In the Netherlands, several reports were published in 2026 predicting growth of battery energy storage systems (BESS) located in the Netherlands in terms of both Dutch GWh capacity and Dutch market share in Europe. For lenders, investors and developers, this expansion presents opportunities. However, financing, regulatory and business-case challenges require careful navigation. In this blog, we highlight some key developments and considerations for the financing of BESS projects. The Dutch BESS market The Netherlands is fast developing into a more attractive jurisdiction for BESS projects. Whereas other countries took an early lead in BESS project development, the Dutch market was behind the curve due to limitations in supporting legal infrastructure for BESS development, grid capacity and connection issues, high grid fees and limited bankability of the business case. However, this has changed as a result of various initiatives yielding results starting from 2025. In various market reports published in 2026, the Dutch BESS market is predicted to grow into a major European BESS jurisdiction. Opportunities for BESS in the Netherlands - Dutch government priorities for BESS In the Dutch state budget for 2027, published on 15 September 2026, the Dutch government announced further support for energy storage, in the form of enhanced tax advantages for companies investing in innovative energy storage systems. In the updated National Energy System Plan, also published on 15 September 2026, the Dutch government acknowledged the need for risk-sharing to facilitate the scale-up of energy infrastructure and storage.From 2027, the Netherlands must establish goals for non-fossil flexibility to stabilise the electricity grid pursuant to the EU Electricity Regulation, on the basis of assessments determining how much clean flexibility electricity systems require and identifying existing barriers. Although the outcomes of the Dutch assessment and the Dutch goals are not yet known, these may encourage BESS projects further. These developments follow earlier initiatives that have mitigated and supported the business case for Dutch BESS projects. - The Dutch grid operator reduced grid rates The Dutch grid operator TenneT published a position paper on BESS in 2024 to clarify its position regarding the application of large batteries (>70MW) by market parties to the grid, which served as guidance to the market and public authorities. TenneT also started offering new flexible contract forms with lower transport rates for batteries and other flexible capacity: TenneT now offers time-based transmission rights for high-voltage grids and transmission rights of at least 85% availability. By leveraging time-based rights, flexible grid users like batteries can achieve significant discounts. - Improved bankability for debt and equity funding The willingness of debt and equity investors and financiers to fund BESS projects in the Netherlands has traditionally been undermined by uncertainty around cash flows and floor prices of BESS projects. These days, the Dutch government’s subsidies mitigate the floor price risk and the measures taken by TenneT help reduce the cost and risk elements, improving the cash flows in relation to BESS projects. The new developments described above may improve the bankability of BESS projects further.The bankability of a BESS project could require both debt and equity funding, with alternative lenders and investors providing a mix of both. The Netherlands is known for its flexible legal framework in respect of corporate and finance laws. This effectively provides access to corporate and project-based debt and equity funding solutions, allowing capital flows into and within the Netherlands. BESS projects in the Netherlands have been financed through corporate financings or project financings. Other forms of BESS financing – already applied internationally and depending on the BESS project involved – could also include innovative forms of securitisation, green bonds, possibly in combination with corporate or project financing. Legal expertise of the Stibbe team We are a multidisciplinary team of professionals who are top-ranked practitioners in projects, energy, administrative law, corporate law and debt finance, with expertise in BESS projects. The Stibbe team has market-leading expertise in the Benelux in respect of the full development and financing life-cycle of utility-scale BESS projects, from advising on site acquisition, zoning & permitting, energy regulatory matters, procurement structure and supplier contracts, to FDI, competition, corporate and project financing expertise. We have been involved in various roles (as developers’, equity investors’ and lenders’ counsel) in many of the utility-scale projects to have achieved financial close in the Benelux to date. Through our experience in working with investors, lenders, developers, contractors and other key players in these areas, we have an excellent understanding of the objectives and challenges facing this fast-developing critical segment of the energy industry. If you have any questions, please contact Marieke Driessen or Ellen Vintges from Stibbe’s Financial Markets team.

artigo.texto: A startup wants to build a massive nuclear-powered data center on public land in Utah A startup whose founder has vowed to "make nuclear great again" is planning to place hundreds of reactors on federal land in Utah, according to documents reviewed by NPR. Valar Atomics is planning what it calls "Project Beehive" on over 9,000 acres of land held under the Bureau of Land Management near Price, Utah. The facility would include data centers and some 456 small nuclear reactors, along with a facility to produce nuclear fuel and others for storing nuclear waste, according to a proposal from the company to federal regulators. In aggregate, the reactors would produce around 9.6 gigawatts of power for the data centers and even more thermal heat for other industrial applications. Currently, the entire state of Utah produces only around 4 gigawatts of electricity on average (though its peak capacity in summer can reach around 10 gigawatts). The project's timeline calls for nonnuclear construction to begin as soon as the end of this year, with the first reactors coming online sometime in 2028. Loading... Valar has also sought the use of around 650 acres of state land as part of the same project, according to state records. The Salt Lake Tribune first reported on the project's use of state land last week, but not the much larger proposed use of federal lands. The project has raised alarm among local activists, who are already facing a slew of data center proposals in the state. "It's concerning to see that the Trump administration, with the support of the state of Utah, is pushing this forward on significant acreage of public lands," said Neal Clark, wildlands director at the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, a Utah-based nonprofit that seeks to protect public lands. "The coalition of people who are concerned about these things completely transcends political lines," added Lexi Tuddenham, the executive director of the Healthy Environment Alliance of Utah, which has tracked nuclear-related industries in the state. Tuddenham said that at the moment her primary goal is to raise awareness. "The biggest thing we can do right now is to let people know about it." In a written statement, the Bureau of Land Management's Utah office confirmed it had received an application from the company. "We are currently reviewing the application for completeness," it told NPR in an email. As the application moves through the required National Environmental Policy Act process, "we will make sure the public has meaningful opportunities to provide input," it added. Valar did not immediately respond to NPR's request for comment. In an interview with NPR in July, Valar CEO Isaiah Taylor said his company was committed to safety and community engagement. "We're doing it responsibly and accountably to this community," he said of a smaller test reactor that the company was operating in a neighboring county. Small reactors, big plan Project Beehive reveals the scale of the ambitions held by a new generation of companies planning a comeback for nuclear power. The companies are backed by the Trump administration, which has enacted a slew of regulatory reforms over the past year and a half to make their "small modular reactors" easier to test and build. Valar has been both closely involved with those reforms and a beneficiary of them. Taylor was in the room when President Trump signed a series of executive orders last year designed to accelerate the development of nuclear power, and his company was accepted into the Department of Energy's Reactor Pilot Program in August 2025. This past February, the U.S. military flew Valar's test reactor from California to Utah aboard a C-17 transport aircraft. The reactor, known as Ward 250, received rapid approval this year after the Department of Energy conducted a quiet overhaul of its internal safety and security regulations for nuclear reactors. It achieved criticality by reaching a self-sustaining nuclear reaction in June, in a tentlike structure in the Utah desert about 30 miles from the site of Project Beehive. At a press event on July 1, the company marked another milestone when it used Ward 250 to produce electricity. Taylor powered up the test reactor and used a simple thermoelectric system to run a single Nvidia microchip. "Ladies and gentlemen, Valar Atomics just became the first startup in history to make nuclear electricity right here," he told the crowd. The scale of Project Beehive vastly outstrips that July demonstration. Since the turn of the century, the U.S. has switched on just three new nuclear power plants, producing a total of around 3.4 gigawatts of electricity. Those reactors are far larger than the small modular reactors that Valar plans to use, and each costs many billions of dollars to build. Valar and other companies are hoping to upend the nuclear business model because small reactors can be mass-produced and placed in series, like a set of nuclear batteries. Valar's 25-megawatt electric units could be installed one at a time, allowing Project Beehive to be built in phases over a number of years. That in turn would reduce the cost and allow the site to enter operation relatively quickly. According to a document reviewed by NPR, the full site could be completed by 2032. Tuddenham said she thinks the use of federal lands for such a project is unprecedented. "In this case, I think it's bigger than the local community," she said. "If we have facilities like this on public land for waste storage, for massive nuclear development, for data centers, that's going to have tremendous implications for how public lands are used." NPR's Shannon Bond contributed to this report. Contact Geoff Brumfiel on Signal at gbrumfiel.13

artigo.texto: Geraldo Campos Jr., Lais Carregosa e Marisa Wanzeller, da Agência iNFRA O MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) publicou na terça-feira (29) uma portaria com o cronograma de leilões de geração até 2029, incluindo a possibilidade de baterias e usinas hidrelétricas reversíveis disputarem os LRCAPs (Leilões de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência) com fontes fósseis. Enquanto os agentes renováveis comemoraram, as termelétricas manifestaram contrariedade com o modelo e avaliaram que será necessário corrigir a portaria. Em 2026, o governo separou os leilões, deixando as baterias fora do primeiro LRCAP de potência. Para um agente do segmento renovável, a nova portaria mostra que o governo já poderia ter feito o mesmo desenho neste ano e permitido que as fontes disputassem sob o critério de modicidade tarifária. Mas, para o presidente da Abraget (Associação Brasileira de Geradoras Termelétricas), Xisto Vieira, a unificação dos produtos de baterias e térmicas em um mesmo certame seria um “erro técnico grosseiro”. Embora tenha elogiado a confirmação de leilões anuais de reserva de capacidade, Xisto avaliou a portaria como “genérica” e disse que ela foi elaborada para atender a uma exigência do TCU (Tribunal de Contas da União). “Não está explícito que vai competir junto, a meu ver. É uma abstração técnica do nível de colocar para jogarem juntos um jogador de futebol contra um jogador de tênis de mesa. É altamente contestável colocar no mesmo leilão para competir junto bateria e térmica”, disse Xisto à Agência iNFRA. “Tenho certeza que a portaria vai ser corrigida porque não é possível um erro desse calibre.” Na visão da Abraget, as principais dificuldades seriam o fato de que as baterias químicas “não resolvem o problema de estabilidade de tensão e de frequência” e têm “limitação forte de corrente de curto-circuito”, afirmou Xisto Vieira. Ele defendeu que os sistemas de armazenamento químico sejam usados preferencialmente na baixa tensão, junto à GD (Geração Distribuída) e que a única fonte que poderia competir com térmicas seriam hidrelétricas com reservatórios. “O resto todo seria intermitente.” Um agente aponta que baterias e hidrelétricas não podem disputar a mesma demanda que as termelétricas, porque ambas possuem limitações na potência que podem entregar ao sistema. Esse executivo não descarta, porém, a possibilidade de as fontes estarem em um mesmo processo licitatório, mas em produtos diferentes. “Isso demandará da EPE [Empresa de Pesquisa Energética] um trabalho antes do leilão para saber bem qual é o portfólio que ela precisa para atender aos critérios de segurança do sistema”, disse. Planejamento O diretor-executivo da Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia), Fabio Lima, chama atenção para o fato de que a portaria coloca a realização dos leilões anuais, no segundo semestre de cada ano, condicionada à avaliação técnica quanto à necessidade sistêmica apresentada conjuntamente pela EPE (Empresa de Pesquisa Energética) e pelo ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico) até 30 de abril de cada ano. Assim, segundo ele, quando a portaria diz que o leilão poderá considerar todas aquelas soluções, dependerá do que a análise do planejamento setorial indicar. “Teremos que ver ano a ano quais as necessidades e quais os atributos que podem atender aquilo que o sistema precisa. Há uma discricionariedade na portaria”, afirmou Lima. A advogada Ana Karina Souza, sócia da área de Infraestrutura e Energia do Machado Meyer, ressalta que a portaria é mais genérica e não deixa clara a intenção de fazer um certame para todas as fontes. “Ela [a portaria] fala que essas fontes podem ser consideradas no leilão, então não dá para cravar uma conclusão de que o leilão vai ser para, necessariamente, todas essas fontes competirem entre si em um único certame”, disse. Marcello Cabral, diretor de Novos Negócios da Abeeólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica), pondera que o cronograma ainda não estabeleceu que as baterias, hidrelétricas e térmicas disputarão em um único produto – mesmo que dentro do mesmo certame. “Na minha visão, a contratação deve ser organizada conforme as necessidades do sistema, com produtos ou requisitos que reconheçam duração do fornecimento, velocidade de resposta e flexibilidade operativa”, ressaltou. Para o setor de renováveis, aponta o executivo, é fundamental valorizar soluções que evitem “inflexibilidade adicional” e que contribuam para reduzir os cortes de geração obrigatórios de fontes eólica e solar. Competição Na avaliação de Fabio Lima, da Absae, as baterias serão competitivas especialmente para desenhos de necessidade de potência com despachos menores. “Para o atendimento por 4h, seja da ordem de contratação de gigawatts ou não, o armazenamento em baterias é muito barato e muito eficiente. Acima de 6h, ainda não tem uma eficiência econômica tão boa. Aí já começa a ir para o hidráulico e para as térmicas.” Fabio Lima destacou que os leilões de reserva de capacidade “neutros” do ponto de vista tecnológico já vêm sendo adotados em vários países do mundo, a exemplo da Inglaterra, e que as baterias têm provado o potencial de ajuda na oferta de potência. “O que acontece nestes casos é que há redução na participação de usinas a gás no horário de ponta, o que naturalmente reduz a receita de alguns agentes e gera críticas”, disse à Agência iNFRA. Previsibilidade Já a presidente da Abrage (Associação Brasileira das Empresas Geradoras de Energia Elétrica), Marisete Pereira, afirma que a inclusão das reversíveis é uma “sinalização muito positiva”, já que a fonte proporciona armazenamento de longo prazo. Além disso, ela destaca que o fato de o MME divulgar o calendário permite que os agentes planejem os seus investimentos e projetos, mobilizando a cadeia produtiva. “Um calendário de leilões não é apenas uma agenda do setor elétrico. artigo.texto: The construction industry accounted for around half of the non-farm job growth in Wisconsin over the last year, as a few high-profile data center projects moved forward in the state. Wisconsin added 10,500 construction jobs from August 2025 to August 2026, more than half of the 19,400 total non-farm jobs added over that period, according to data from the state Department of Workforce Development. The industry accounted for 156,500 jobs as of August, the most recent month with available data. That growth has come in a year in which Microsoft completed the first phase of its data center campus in Mount Pleasant, while construction continued on other campuses in Port Washington and Beaver Dam. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. Scott Hodek, an economist at the Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development, said there’s a variety of factors contributing to the sector’s growth statewide and the agency did not have the “specificity of data” to break out construction jobs tied to data centers. Hodek said there was demand coming out of the COVID-19 pandemic, and — as inflation has remained high — more companies are deciding to move forward with building projects in hopes of beating future cost increases. “We’re seeing a lot of growth in construction in general, and that’s all across the board,” he said. “Honestly, that’s generally a good sign when you’re still seeing construction, even though materials and labor costs are up.” Data center development is widely unpopular with the public in Wisconsin. In a Marquette Law School Poll of Wisconsin residents released in August, 67 percent of respondents said they would like to ban data center development for at least a year. For voters questioned for the poll, data centers were a bigger issue than abortion policy, public schools and crime in their communities. Despite pushback from the public, the industry has been growing fast in the state. Especially in southeast Wisconsin — home to two of the three major data center projects under construction in the state — business and labor leaders say data centers are driving growth in both the construction and manufacturing industries, though manufacturing job growth has been weaker statewide. Union construction industry views data centers as ‘decade-long runway’ for growth Chris Mambu Rasch is the executive director of Building Advantage, a labor management association for the union construction industry in southeast Wisconsin. He said both data center campuses being developed in southeast Wisconsin “are essentially 100 percent union construction” projects. The Microsoft development in Mount Pleasant completed its first phase earlier this year. Mambu Rasch said the phase had around 3,000 union construction workers at peak construction, while roughly 10,000 workers cycled through the site over a two-year period. He said phase two is expected to “see similar numbers” and is already “pretty heavy” into construction, with one union sending 600 workers to that project alone. In Port Washington, he said there are between 2,500 and 2,800 union construction workers at the data center site. He said he expects “well over 4,000” union jobs on that project during peak construction. “Data centers have created an extraordinary amount of work related to the projects in Mount Pleasant and in Port Washington,” he said. Meanwhile, social media giant Meta, the company behind the data center being developed in Beaver Dam, has said its project would support “approximately 1,000 construction jobs.” Mambu Rasch said he believes there’s a “decade-long runway” where union construction could see strong growth tied to data centers. He said Microsoft plans to build 15 more in Mount Pleasant, while the Port Washington project is in the first phase of development. He said data center developers are interested in other sites in Wisconsin. “This is sustained, long-term employment,” Mambu Rasch said. “We have the utmost confidence that this work is going to be there for the next decade, and that shows because our contractors are bringing on a record number of apprentices.” Data centers help spur construction of power facilities Aside from building data centers themselves, the projects are also spurring construction of new power plants and electric infrastructure to help meet an expected spike in power demands. Mambu Rasch said union workers generally build Wisconsin’s power infrastructure, from natural gas power plants to solar and wind farms. “The energy infrastructure buildout to supply the energy for the data centers is certainly having a positive impact on our industry,” he said. A recent draft report from state regulators found peak electricity demand in Wisconsin could increase by more than 40 percent by 2032, with more than 70 percent of that increase tied to data centers. The Port Washington and Mount Pleasant data centers are in We Energies’ service territory. WEC Energy Group, the parent company of We Energies and Wisconsin Public Service, has received approval from state utility regulators to develop seven solar farms, five battery storage projects, two wind projects, two natural gas power plants, a natural gas storage facility and a 33-mile natural gas pipeline project, according to a September presentation to investors. “The new power generation facilities we are building are creating jobs, supporting local businesses and strengthening the electric grid for our customers,” said Brendan Conway, a spokesperson for WEC Energy Group. “More than 3,000 people will be employed during construction as we make critical investments in a reliable and resilient energy future.” The company has other planned construction projects awaiting regulatory approval, including seven solar projects and a pair of natural gas plants in Kenosha and Walworth counties, the presentation shows. “With We Energies

artigo.texto: da Agência iNFRA O Copergs (Comitê de Planejamento Energético do Rio Grande do Sul) defendeu que a regulamentação do Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter) permita o uso de gás natural em projetos de data centers no estado como fonte para “soluções eficientes de geração dedicada, potência firme, flexibilidade operativa e segurança de suprimento”. Em manifestação institucional enviada ao presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva nesta terça-feira (29), o comitê, vinculado à Sema (Secretaria do Meio Ambiente e Infraestrutura), afirma que a elegibilidade dos projetos deve ser definida por critérios de desempenho, como eficiência energética e hídrica, intensidade de emissões, confiabilidade, rastreabilidade dos combustíveis e trajetória de descarbonização. O Copergs argumenta que “a exclusão prévia do gás natural reduziria as alternativas de engenharia disponíveis e poderia impedir que os estados transformem vantagens concretas de energia e conectividade em investimento produtivo” e afirma que conectividade e energia precisam avançar de forma integrada. Segundo o documento, data centers operam de forma contínua e exigem estabilidade, redundância e potência firme, condições que não seriam garantidas apenas por contratos de energia renovável ou por baterias. “Contratos de energia renovável são fundamentais para reduzir emissões e assegurar lastro comercial, mas não garantem, isoladamente, que a potência estará fisicamente disponível no local e no instante da necessidade. Sistemas de alimentação ininterrupta e baterias respondem por milissegundos, minutos ou poucas horas. Contingências prolongadas, restrições de rede e recomposição do sistema exigem recursos controláveis de maior duração.” O comitê destaca que a matriz gaúcha tem elevada participação de fontes renováveis, mas sustenta que isso não elimina a necessidade de recursos despacháveis. Nesse contexto, o gás natural é apontado como alternativa para reserva, ponta, acompanhamento de carga ou operação contínua, conforme os critérios técnicos e ambientais de cada projeto. Para o Copergs, excluir previamente o gás natural do Redata poderia reduzir a capacidade do Rio Grande do Sul de transformar conectividade internacional e infraestrutura energética em desenvolvimento econômico. “O gás natural não substitui a vocação renovável local. Ele assegura que ela possa sustentar cargas digitais críticas sem comprometer confiabilidade, resiliência e competitividade. Excluí-lo previamente do Redata significaria reduzir a capacidade de converter infraestrutura energética e conectividade internacional em desenvolvimento econômico”, afirma o posicionamento.

artigo.texto: 29 de set, 2026 A descarbonização da economia brasileira pode ser não apenas uma resposta às mudanças climáticas, mas também uma estratégia para reduzir custos e aumentar a competitividade das empresas. “Usar formas de energia mais limpa, renovável, já é uma estratégia de negócio,” Grazielle Parenti, vice-presidente de Sustentabilidade da Vale, disse em um debate promovido pelo Brazil Journal durante a Climate Week, em Nova York. A executiva destacou ainda que o Brasil tem alternativas próprias para a transição, como a biomassa, e que grandes empresas precisam trabalhar em conjunto com fornecedores e outras companhias para desenvolver tecnologias em escala. Já Paulo Skaf Filho, CEO da ComBio, empresa de energia térmica renovável para a indústria, lembrou que o custo de capital influencia muito nos projetos de transição energética. “Não é um problema de tecnologia, é um problema de capital e de demanda.” Como os projetos de transição são intensivos em capital e exigem investimentos altos e compromissos de longo prazo, disse Skaf Filho, a incerteza sobre o custo de capital e a falta de previsibilidade regulatória podem dificultar a tomada de decisão das empresas. Roberto Waack, presidente do Comitê de Sustentabilidade da MBRF, chamou atenção para outro desafio: adaptar as metodologias internacionais de mensuração de carbono à realidade brasileira. “Nós estamos num ambiente tropical e a maior parte das metodologias de mensuração de carbono não capturam as características da agricultura e dos ecossistemas brasileiros.” Waack também defendeu o reconhecimento econômico do capital natural brasileiro e afirmou que o mercado de carbono será um dos temas centrais para a transição no país. Para os três executivos, a agenda de descarbonização avançará apenas se o Brasil conseguir transformar soluções que miram uma economia de baixo carbono em negócios.

artigo.texto: Lynus AG, a subsidiary of Enerfin AG, starts manufacturing large-scale battery storage systems in Dillingen an der Donau, Bavaria. With the Lynus BESS Cube 2.0, the company produces a modular storage system with a usable battery capacity of around 800 kWh. The system is scaled by cascading, can be integrated into energy projects on both the DC and AC sides, and can also be used as a gray current storage system. Lynus has developed the BESS Cube 2.0 specifically for the requirements of the German market and can flexibly adapt the configuration to project-specific grid connection conditions. The storage system is supplemented by an energy management system (EMS), also developed by Lynus, as well as the multi-market marketing of electricity and storage flexibility. Lynus thus offers hardware, control and marketing as an integrated, European overall solution. The machine learning-based multi-use EMS is already in use in more than 1,500 plants in Germany and Switzerland. Developed for the requirements of the German market One focus in the development of the BESS Cube 2.0 was on flexible integration into PV systems. This is especially true for co-location projects in which existing photovoltaic parks are subsequently expanded to include battery storage systems. Here, storage systems must fit into existing plant layouts and grid connection concepts. With a footprint of just over 5 m2 and a weight of around 7.5 tons per cube, the system is compactly designed and thus facilitates transport and positioning on existing plant areas. Another basis for development was the different technical grid connection conditions in Germany: Depending on the grid operator, voltage level and existing infrastructure, the requirements for a storage project can differ considerably. “EPC companies and operators are regularly faced with the challenge of adapting storage systems to the specific grid and plant situation on site. Since we develop and manufacture the BESS Cube 2.0 ourselves in Germany, we can react quickly to project-specific requirements and significantly accelerate adjustments,” says Paul Hauser, CEO of Lynus. DC and AC coupling for new and existing systems In new photovoltaic systems, the BESS Cube 2.0 can be connected directly to the DC side via MPPT modules. This saves additional AC components such as inverters and reduces conversion losses. AC coupling, on the other hand, is particularly suitable for retrofitting existing systems. LFP technology, liquid cooling and multi-stage safety concept Technologically, the BESS Cube 2.0 relies on lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells. The battery cells are designed for more than 8,000 full cycles with 80 percent residual capacity. The rack system achieves DC round-trip efficiency (RTE) of at least 94 percent at 0.5 C. The storage system is available with the voltage levels 400 volts, 690 volts and 800 volts. The charging and discharging capacity is up to 500 kW, depending on the version. An integrated liquid cooling and heating system keeps the battery cells within as homogeneous a temperature range as possible, thus supporting performance and service life. The multi-level safety concept includes smoke, gas and temperature sensors, an automatic aerosol extinguishing system and mechanical pressure relief.

artigo.texto: CATL Leading global battery maker, launched first-gen sodium-ion battery in 2021 A new life cycle assessment from China, drawing on factory data, has concluded that layered-oxide sodium-ion battery packs carry a lower production footprint than lithium iron phosphate packs, even as recent European research points the other way for cells. The findings, reported by ESS News, indicate that making a one kilowatt-hour sodium-ion pack in China emits 56.8 kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent, which is 24.9 percent below the 75.5 kilograms attributed to an LFP pack. The researchers gathered inventory data directly from Chinese battery manufacturers operating at gigawatt-hour scale. For both chemistries, the assessment attributes the bulk of emissions to the electricity used in manufacturing, a pattern the authors link to China's coal-heavy grid. They suggest sodium-ion's footprint could decline further through process optimization and cleaner power supplies, while LFP producers would need to pursue raw-material substitution and reduce material intensity. The study's authors note that earlier work, including research by Peters and colleagues in 2016 and by Guo and colleagues in 2023, placed sodium-ion's footprint slightly above that of lithium-ion, a result they attribute to reliance on lab-scale data and default European databases. A 2025 study by researchers at Fraunhofer and RWTH Aachen University, also built on primary factory data, reached the opposite conclusion. That work put cradle-to-gate emissions for layered-oxide sodium-ion cells at 75 to 87 kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent per kilowatt-hour, compared with 59 to 70 kilograms for LFP cells. Because the European study measured cells rather than packs, the two sets of figures are not directly comparable. Both assessments stop at the factory gate, so neither incorporates cycle life, meaning they compare manufacturing impacts rather than emissions per unit of lifetime energy delivered. Both also cover only layered-oxide cathodes. HiNa Battery, for instance, uses layered oxides, while Hithium's 785 Ah storage cell relies on a sodium iron pyrophosphate cathode. The Chinese researchers additionally modeled a scenario in which broader sodium-ion adoption avoids 147 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2035. Using a cradle-to-gate boundary spanning raw materials through manufacturing, they determined that the total environmental impact of sodium-ion packs is 27.3 percent lower than that of LFP packs. The scientists set out their findings in a paper titled Comparative life cycle assessment and carbon footprint of sodium-ion and Lithium Iron phosphate batteries, recently published in Environmental Impact Assessment Review. artigo.texto: Governo fará 3 leilões incluindo baterias de 2027 a 2029 Ministério de Minas e Energia projeta 11 certames para o setor elétrico nos próximos 3 anos O MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) publicou nesta 4ª feira (30.set.2026) o cronograma de leilões do setor de energia elétrica para o triênio 2027-2029. Serão ao menos 11 certames nos próximos 3 anos, dos quais 3 vão permitir soluções de armazenamento de energia, as chamadas baterias. O calendário também inclui outras modalidades inéditas para os leilões do setor, como usinas reversíveis nas disputas de Reserva de Capacidade e inclusão de usinas térmicas com resíduos, além de diretrizes para certames de energia nova e existente. Leia a íntegra da portaria do MME com o cronograma (PDF – 189 kB). No 1º semestre de cada ano, serão realizados leilões para contratação de Reserva de Capacidade de centrais hidrelétricas de até 50 MW. O cronograma também estabelece, em 2027 e 2029, leilões para assegurar suprimento de Sistemas Isolados –instalações ou redes de distribuição que não têm conexão com a rede elétrica principal do país. A maior parte está nos Estados de Rondônia, Acre, Amazonas, Roraima, Amapá e Pará. Nessas disputas, o atendimento será condicionado ao planejamento de expansão feito pela EPE (Empresa de Pesquisa Energética) ou ao direcionamento estratégico de substituição de geração térmica com combustível fóssil por fontes renováveis. Com essa regra, o governo assegura que a realização de novos leilões só ocorra quando houver necessidade real de carga ou quando houver uma diretriz para descarbonizar a matriz dessas regiões, substituindo fontes poluentes por soluções limpas. Já os LRCap (Leilões de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência), que contratam potência elétrica disponível para assegurar a segurança do abastecimento de energia do país, dependerão de estudo técnico conjunto da EPE e do ONS (Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico) sobre a necessidade sistêmica. Os dados devem ser encaminhados ao MME até 30 de abril de cada ano. Assim como nos Sistemas Isolados, a inclusão desses leilões no calendário do MME funciona como uma previsão, mas a sua efetivação prática depende de aprovação prévia. À princípio, haverá um LRCap por ano até 2029, sempre no 2º semestre. Se os estudos do ONS e da EPE demonstrarem que o sistema elétrico precisa de reforço de potência de reserva para garantir a segurança do abastecimento na época da respectiva disputa, o leilão será confirmado. Caso contrário, o certame pode não ser realizado naquele ano. A medida busca evitar contratações desnecessárias e questionamentos como os do último leilão de reserva, de março deste ano, quando foram contratados cerca de 20 GW a R$ 515 bilhões. Ao longo do 1º semestre, as contratações foram amplamente criticadas, inclusiva no Congresso, e resultaram em processos na Justiça Federal, TCU (Tribunal de Contas da União) e no Cade (Conselho Administrativo de Defesa Econômica). Os resultados acabaram sendo mantidos pelo Judiciário e pela Corte de Contas. Leia o cronograma de leilões do setor elétrico para 2027, 2028 e 2029: 2027 - 1º Semestre: – Leilão para Contratação de Reserva de Capacidade de centrais hidrelétricas de até 50 MW (megawatt); – Leilão para Suprimento aos Sistemas Isolados. - 2º Semestre: – Leilão para Contratação de Reserva de Capacidade, na forma de potência, podendo considerar, entre outras, soluções de armazenamento de energia em baterias eletroquímicas, sistemas de armazenamento hidráulico, usinas hidrelétricas e usinas termelétricas, inclusive aquelas movidas a biometano, biogás, biocombustíveis e resíduos; – Leilões de Compra de Energia Elétrica Proveniente de Novos Empreendimentos de Geração e de Empreendimentos de Geração Existentes. 2028 - 1º Semestre: – Leilão para Contratação de Reserva de Capacidade de centrais hidrelétricas de até 50 MW. - 2º Semestre: – Leilão para Contratação de Reserva de Capacidade, na forma de potência,podendo considerar, entre outras, soluções de armazenamento de energia em baterias eletroquímicas, sistemas de armazenamento hidráulico, usinas hidrelétricas e usinas termelétricas, inclusive aquelas movidas a biometano, biogás, biocombustíveis e resíduos; – Leilões de Compra de Energia Elétrica Proveniente de Novos Empreendimentos e de Empreendimentos Existentes. 2029 - 1º Semestre – Leilão para Contratação de Reserva de Capacidade de centrais hidrelétricas de até 50 MW. - 2º Semestre: – Leilão para Contratação de Reserva de Capacidade, na forma de potência, podendo considerar, entre outras, soluções de armazenamento de energia em baterias eletroquímicas, sistemas de armazenamento hidráulico, usinas hidrelétricas e usinas termelétricas, inclusive aquelas movidas a biometano, biogás, biocombustíveis e resíduos. – Leilões de Compra de Energia Elétrica Proveniente de Novos Empreendimentos de Geração e de Empreendimentos de Geração Existentes; – Leilão para Suprimento aos Sistemas Isolados.
