artigo.texto: KP Group Unveils KP 3.0 with 10 GWh Battery Manufacturing Goal KP Group to develop cell manufacturing and BESS assembly capabilities while targeting 10 GW each in IPP capacity and third-party EPC execution by FY32. October 01, 2026. By News Bureau KP Group has unveiled KP 3.0 at its Investor Day and announced revised commitments for FY32. The Group is targeting 10 GW of IPP (Independent Power Producer) through KPI Green Energy, 10 GW of third-party EPC execution, excluding related-party projects and 10 GWh of integrated battery manufacturing capability spanning cell production and Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) assembly. KP Group’s renewable energy portfolio including operational and under construction projects is on track and is expected to achieve the goal of 10 GW in next few quarters. KP Group’s total portfolio stands at 9.21 GW. This progress has prompted the KP Group to set higher ambitions and a more focused roadmap for its next phase. The new targets cover three distinct businesses: power assets the Group will own, renewable projects it will execute for external customers and storage systems and cells it plans to manufacture. KP 3.0 marks the induction of a group team of highly experienced professionals in leadership roles across renewable energy, emerging renewable opportunities, international business, green hydrogen, investor relations and governance. This team will also strengthen engineering and manufacturing execution as KP Group scales its businesses. KP Group is expanding into several emerging clean-energy segments. Sundrops Energia serves as the Group’s dedicated Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) platform, with activities spanning BESS IPP, group captive and C&I projects, as well as assembly and cell manufacturing. The Group is also developing a floating solar platform, including the 110 MW AC/142 MW DC Kadana Dam project in Gujarat. In energy trading, KP Group has obtained CERC and GERC licences and is developing capabilities across power exchanges and bilateral markets. In addition, the Group is building capabilities in green hydrogen and green ammonia, covering hydrogen production, mobility, logistics and utilisation. Its Matar facility currently operates a 1 MW electrolysis-based green hydrogen plant with an output of 432 kg per day. As on Q1 FY27, KP Group’s reported renewable energy portfolio stood at more than 9.2 GW across solar, wind and hybrid. Its operating platform includes approximately 12,104 acres of land footprint, 5.10 GW of power evacuation capacity, 400,500 MTPA of manufacturing capacity, a 6.4 GW EPC portfolio and a 2.8 GW IPP portfolio. In the renewable energy sector, KP Group's rapidly expanding footprint now extends across Gujarat, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh. Furthermore, international opportunities presented span Botswana, Zambia and Tanzania in Africa, as well as Saudi Arabia in the GCC. In Botswana, the Group is pursuing a proposed 5 GW renewable power and associated infrastructure development, with an initial phase planned at 500 MW. In the manufacturing sector the group continues to secure diverse order from pan India. The Group’s revised targets are supported by a clearer business structure and an emphasis on disciplined execution and governance as the next generation assumes wider responsibilities. Dr. Faruk G. Patel, Founder and Chairman, KP Group, said, “Looking our orderbook to grow nearly to 10GW. It shows commitment of our people and the trust of our customers, partners and investors. We have always delivered and will be delivering what we commit. Hence at KP 3.0 we are updating our commitment: to expand owned renewable generation, deliver more projects for customers and build battery manufacturing capability in India. Known for our faster execution, we are committed to achieving these new targets ahead of schedule as well. I am proud to see the next generation take on greater responsibility alongside our experienced professional team. As our ambitions grow, we will remain guided by the principle on which this Group was built: what we commit, we deliver.” please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: China, already dominating the global lithium-ion battery market, plans to expand this position to solid-state batteries, too. The government in Beijing will seek to cut solid-state battery costs, boost their performance, and begin commercial production by 2030. “Over the next five years, the new-type battery industry is at a critical window for technological upgrading, and we must seize the strategic opportunities presented by technological and industrial innovation,” China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology said in a news release, as cited by the South China Morning Post. The five-year plan for solid-state batteries comes amid a global race in that segment, as researchers and businesses in other parts of the world try to circumvent or challenge China’s existing dominance in lithium-ion battery tech, and diversify away from lithium-ion technology as well. As of last year, China’s solid-state battery market was worth some $42.5 million, the Global Times reported in a news piece on the battery plan. This should grow to $384.8 million by 2030 as a result of government encouragement, with an annual compound growth rate at an impressive 44.4%, compared to a global average CAGR projected for batteries of 37.5%. Related: U.S. Threatens Diesel Export Ban Unless Europe Releases Stockpiles Bringing costs down seems to be priority number-one for solid-state battery developers—an issue that battery tech shares with lithium-ion technology. Focus areas also include developing new electrode materials, new electrolytes—a vulnerability for solid-state batteries right now—and other new materials to use in solid-state batteries. The plan covers technologies including sodium batteries and flow batteries, two potential challengers to lithium-ion technology that have yet to become as popular as the dominant battery technology. Lithium-ion batteries are dominant on the EV market and all other markets for products that use batteries, as much thanks to their performance as to the absence of real rivals. Lithium-ion batteries are expensive, they can be a fire hazard, and they rely on some costly materials, including lithium itself. By comparison, researchers see solid-state batteries as a viable alternative that can be cheaper and more reliable, with higher energy density than lithium-ion batteries, faster charging times, a longer life, and, importantly, the possibility of extended ranges for electric vehicles. But first, they need to solve the problem with solid-state battery failures, which has plagued research in the area for years. Some recent advances have been made in that respect by researchers in the lab, while automakers eye solid-state batteries as the next big hit. Indeed, China’s own BYD recently said it planned to start the mass manufacturing of solid-state batteries for its electric vehicles by 2030. The company, which is a major player on the EV market globally, will not drop lithium-ion technology in favor of solid-state but would rather use both in its future models. China is the world’s biggest market for electric vehicles and a top player in battery storage as well. Just like EVs and solar panels, these energy transition-linked industries have enjoyed years of generous subsidies that have allowed them to grow without any consideration of overcapacity and its consequences. Now, China is having to tackle battery overcapacity—in lithium-ion technology. The news about the solid-state battery plan, however, suggests it can also expand in battery technology while dealing with overcapacity in lithium-ion technology, both for EVs and for battery storage. The plan for solid-state batteries also reflects demand trends, which have been moving upwards, thanks to energy transition policies in key markets and, most recently, to the fast expansion of the data center industry, which is being encouraged, and sometimes ordered, to generate as much of its own electricity as possible—while saving the planet by using fewer hydrocarbons. artigo.texto: Macurco Introduces 10-Year Hydrogen Detector for BESS and Data Center Applications UL 2075-Listed HD-6 offers early fault detection with minimal maintenance SIOUX FALLS, S.D., September 29, 2026 (Newswire.com) - Macurco Inc., a DwyerOmega brand and a leader in fixed gas detection solutions, announces the launch of the new HD-6 Hydrogen Gas Detector, designed specifically for continuous hydrogen monitoring in Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) applications and other critical environments where hydrogen detection is essential. Hydrogen detection in BESS applications is vital for safety and monitoring normal equipment operation. When a battery begins to malfunction, it can emit hydrogen gas, which may create explosive and dangerous conditions. Early detection can help identify fault events, prevent further equipment damage, and keep personnel informed of potentially hazardous environments. The new HD-6 provides reliable, continuous hydrogen monitoring and early warning to help protect personnel, equipment, and facilities. The detector features two configurable alarm levels with relay activation, allowing facilities to automate responses such as activating fans, valves, louvers, horns, and strobes. Standard features also include local audible alarms, bright visual indicators, and analog communication for seamless integration with Building Management Systems (BMS). The HD-6 is UL Listed to UL 2075 and CAN/ULC 588 and is CE marked. These listings and the CE marking reflect rigorous electrical safety, performance, and gas detection requirements, demonstrating the detector's electrical integrity, accurate response to hydrogen gas, and reliable operation. CE marking supports the HD-6's availability in the European market. The detector is engineered for long-term performance with a robust, low-maintenance design ideal for demanding applications, including data centers, BESS facilities, and industrial hydrogen monitoring "The Macurco HD-6 is an iteration and upgrade of our current flagship hydrogen detector, the GD-6," said Jonathon DeKam, Macurco Line Product Manager for DwyerOmega. "The new HD-6 includes many significant upgrades - minimal maintenance, resistance to silicone poisoning, additional alarm setpoints, and a generous 10-year lifespan. Macurco developed the HD-6 to address ongoing customer requests for a hydrogen detector that is more robust, more reliable, and lasts longer in the field. "With a UL 2075 listing for hydrogen gas detection, customers can be confident in relying on the HD-6 to monitor their data centers, BESS facilities, or any application where hydrogen detection is imperative. artigo.texto: CHEYENNE — City officials are considering leasing a portion of Belvoir Ranch for a proposed 140-megawatt solar project and battery storage facility. Representatives from Hanwha Renewables, a Korean utility-scale solar and energy storage developer, presented a preliminary proposal, called Project Wrangler, to members of the Cheyenne City Council at a work session Friday. The company is seeking to lease approximately 3,300 acres of the 18,800-acre ranch while it conducts environmental, engineering and other feasibility studies. The project is expected to eventually occupy 1,200 to 1,400 acres. Councilman Tom Segrave said the city has been exploring ways to generate additional revenue from portions of Belvoir Ranch that aren’t reserved for the city’s planned landfill and water development. “(Hanwha has) been working with the city and me, specifically, on a proposed solar development on the Belvoir Ranch,” Segrave said. “This has been a council goal for, I don’t know, four or five years. … We have areas that we’ve been leasing for grazing, and we’ve been looking for opportunities to increase the revenue off of those lands that are not set aside for the original purposes.” Tyler Nokleby, Hanwha project developer, said the company isn’t looking to gain formal project approval yet. Instead, he wants to enter an option-to-lease agreement that would allow it to conduct necessary studies. “We’re not asking for a permit, we’re not asking to annex,” Nokleby said. “We are hoping to engage with the city, to be the land owner in this process, so that we can kick off everything.” The agreement would last up to four years, although Nokleby said the company hopes to complete its studies within two. During that period, Hanwha would conduct environmental and wildlife studies, geotechnical work, topographical surveys and other assessments. Existing uses of the land, including grazing, would not be affected, Nokleby said. Lida Jauregui-Rivera, Hanwha project engineer, said the solar panels would be around 4 to 5 feet above the ground, but the final design is subject to change based on study results. The battery storage facility would be located near the project’s substation and would occupy around five acres of large, container-like battery units, Jauregui-Rivera said. Hanwha is considering connecting the project to Black Hills Energy’s West Cheyenne substation, which is located a mile from the proposed project area. Council members questioned how the facility would withstand severe weather conditions like hail, and Jauregui-Rivera said the company would consider thicker-glass solar panels and tracking systems that would automatically reposition panels during hailstorms. She estimated crews could inspect the facility and return it to operational condition within four to eight hours after a significant storm, if panels become damaged. The proposed agreement also includes a $50,000 one-time payment to the city for future development at Belvoir Ranch. Payment would occur within 30 days of signing the option-to-lease. “If the project falls through, that $50,000 is the city’s to keep,” Nokleby said. “So that’s kind of a no-strings-attached payment there, as well — a good-faith payment, we’ll say.” Additionally, if the project falls through after the four-year agreement period, Nokleby said the city would also receive $912,160 in option payments, which includes the $50,000. But the larger financial benefit would come if the project becomes operational. Nokleby said projected lease revenue could range from $30 million to $60 million, depending on the project’s final size and how long the lease remains in effect. The currently proposed lease has a 30-year operating term with four potential five-year extensions. While Hanwha is the proposed developer of the project, Nokleby said it would not own or operate the solar farm long term. Southern Power, which owns South Cheyenne Solar, could potentially become the owner. Hanwha developed the 150 megawatt South Cheyenne Solar project off South Greeley Highway in unincorporated Laramie County under its former name, Qcells Development. Black Hills Energy is also interested in purchasing the electricity, he said, but neither arrangement has been finalized. Because the land is widely known for its wildlife inhabitants, Nokleby said the proposed agreement also includes protections similar to those used at South Cheyenne Solar, including dividing the solar facility into separately fenced sections to preserve wildlife migration corridors. “We did not get into the sustainable energy industry to destroy the environment,” Nokleby said. “These projects are obviously very large and impactful, so we do everything we can to mitigate those impacts.” Nokleby further clarified that signing the option agreement is not a guarantee that the project will be constructed. “Not every lease or option-to-lease turns into a project,” Nokleby said. “If we run our studies and they come back with a very rare type of butterfly that only lives in this one specific spot on Earth, we’re not in the business of putting solar over that. … We won’t be cutting corners. We’re not asking for rubber stamps on any approvals.” The developer’s option-to-lease agreement is planned to be introduced at the City Council meeting for consideration Oct. 12.

artigo.texto: Porto Central pode receber investimento em data centers Porto estuda estrutura para receber data centers, com oferta de energia e conexão por cabos submarinos O Porto Central, em Presidente Kennedy, desenvolve um projeto para implantar um hub de data centers voltado a empresas do Brasil e do exterior. A iniciativa pretende aproveitar a oferta de energia do Espírito Santo e a infraestrutura do complexo portuário para criar uma nova frente de desenvolvimento econômico. Segundo Fabrício Cardoso Freitas, CEO da Macro Investimentos e membro do Conselho de Administração, o empreendimento poderá contar com energia, água, áreas disponíveis e a estrutura logística do porto, incluindo a possibilidade de conexão ferroviária. Freitas afirmou que o Porto Central já desenvolveu e licenciou 5 gigawatts (GW) de capacidade e destacou a segurança de fornecimento associada ao terminal de Gás Natural Liquefeito (GNL). Para ele, essas condições podem atender à crescente demanda mundial por infraestrutura de processamento de dados. Outro ponto em estudo é a chegada de cabos submarinos de telecomunicações. O porto já possui autorização para receber um cabo, e as tratativas avançam. A proposta é receber, processar e distribuir dados para o mercado brasileiro e também para o exterior. O projeto ainda está em fase de concepção e estruturação. A próxima etapa será definir o modelo do empreendimento, dimensionar infraestrutura e insumos, como energia e água, e prospectar empresas que possam utilizar os futuros data centers.

artigo.texto: Os Leilões de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência por meio de Sistemas de Armazenamento de 2026 (LRCAP Armazenamento) serão os primeiros certames de reserva de capacidade voltados exclusivamente a sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias no Brasil. Até aqui, o país contratava potência de reserva majoritariamente de grandes hidrelétricas e termelétricas. Na prática, os novos leilões buscam contribuir para suprir o déficit de potência do sistema, especialmente nos horários de pico, e ampliar sua flexibilidade operativa. As baterias poderão absorver excedentes de geração e devolvê-los à rede quando necessário, sob comando do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS). O desenho adotado prevê dois certames. O Leilão de Armazenamento Nacional será realizado primeiro, em 2 de dezembro, seguido pelo Leilão de Armazenamento Aberto, em 4 de dezembro. A divisão busca conciliar dois objetivos: contratar potência e, ao mesmo tempo, fomentar uma cadeia nacional de baterias. O desafio é que ainda não se sabe quanto a indústria brasileira consegue entregar no curto prazo. Por outro lado, sem essa exigência, a indústria local, ainda incipiente, teria de competir com equipamentos importados provenientes de cadeias já consolidadas. A solução adotada foi realizar primeiro o leilão nacional, com a contratação de volume compatível com a capacidade da indústria local. O leilão aberto completará a necessidade do sistema, descontada a capacidade contratada no primeiro certame. Um mesmo projeto vencedor no primeiro leilão não poderá disputar o segundo. Para os empreendedores, porém, um dos principais desafios está na estrutura contratual necessária para cumprir as obrigações assumidas no Contrato de Potência de Reserva de Capacidade (CRCAP). A Portaria nº 136/2026 já determina que o CRCAP preveja penalidades ao empreendedor por indisponibilidade e pelo descumprimento do despacho centralizado, conforme definido pelo ONS, além da extinção do contrato em caso de não atendimento aos requisitos mínimos de nacionalização. Embora responda por essas obrigações, o empreendedor depende de terceiros para cumpri-las. Por isso, será necessário alinhar os diferentes contratos envolvidos na viabilização do CRCAP, como os de fornecimento, execução das obras e operação durante os 15 anos de vigência. O ponto central é garantir que os riscos sejam adequadamente alocados entre esses instrumentos. E essa estruturação precisa ocorrer antes da apresentação do lance, porque o preço ofertado depende das responsabilidades assumidas e das garantias efetivamente obtidas pelo empreendedor. Um risco que não possa ser transferido ou mitigado contratualmente precisa, em última análise, ser considerado na formação do preço. Outro ponto de atenção está na habilitação dos projetos. O cadastramento na Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) foi encerrado em 31 de julho, mas o simples registro não significa que os empreendimentos estejam aptos a participar dos leilões. Os projetos cadastrados passarão pelas etapas de análise e habilitação técnica na EPE. Somente depois será conhecida a quantidade de empreendimentos e, consequentemente, a potência efetivamente apta a participar das fases subsequentes dos certames. Entre os projetos com maior risco estão aqueles concentrados em pontos da rede sem capacidade de escoamento suficiente para todos os interessados e os que não atingirem a capacidade de recarga. No Leilão de Armazenamento Nacional, há ainda os projetos que declararam conteúdo local sem fornecedor credenciado: eles podem vencer o certame e, posteriormente, não conseguir assinar o contrato. A quantidade de projetos cadastrados também indica que a disputa pode ser elevada. Foram 6.091 projetos, somando quase 297 GW de potência. Mesmo que apenas uma parcela chegue à fase de lances, a relação entre oferta e demanda tende a ser alta. A experiência internacional aponta na mesma direção. Na Itália, cujo leilão de 2025 tem parâmetros semelhantes aos dos certames brasileiros, com contratos de 15 anos e entrega em 2028, as ofertas superaram a demanda e o preço médio ficou abaixo do esperado. Esse cenário exige cautela. Uma competição agressiva pode levar a lances muito baixos e a projetos com margem insuficiente para absorver riscos como atrasos, variação cambial ou penalidades contratuais. O desafio, portanto, começa antes do lance e não termina com o resultado do leilão. Para os empreendedores, será necessário estruturar previamente contratos, responsabilidades e garantias que sustentem o preço ofertado e, uma vez contratados, assegurar o cumprimento das obrigações assumidas durante os 15 anos de vigência do CRCAP. Ana Luisa Dala Déa é advogada da área de desenvolvimento de projetos e contratos complexos do Toledo Marchetti Advogados.

artigo.texto: A second Alachua City Commission meeting confused residents Monday after the meeting was abruptly cancelled because three commission members, including Mayor Walter Welch, weren’t present. Vice Mayor Jennifer Ringersen and Commissioner Shirley Green Brown were also absent, while commissioners Jacob Fletcher and Jackson Youmas attended. The city’s ordinance doesn’t allow business to be conducted at commission meetings without at least three commissioners present. The no-shows come just two weeks after a Sept. 14 city commission meeting in which Welch abruptly killed Fletcher’s motion to revisit a moratorium, or pause, on data center development. The pause was proposed by Ringersen earlier that night, and Fletcher was unable to get specifics from the rest of the commission. He moved for the board to further hash them out at Monday’s meeting. However, when Fletcher reminded Welch a few minutes later that he had to second the motion to delay the vote to Monday’s meeting, Welch replied with, “It died.” Welch’s response garnered reactions from residents and Fletcher because the mayor doesn’t have the power to deny a motion before it’s seconded and voted on. During an interview Sept. 15, Commissioner Jacob Fletcher said many Alachua residents have called moratoriums “a good step to figuring out the next step.” The Sept. 14 data center discussion resembled one step in a long process requiring community participation, he said. “I think there [are] more conversations to be had,” Fletcher said. “A moratorium, again, is only a Band-Aid.” He said the next step will require the commission to listen to Alachua residents and ensure the city’s regulations align with their concerns. Following the Sept. 14 meeting, attendees expressed confusion over whether the data center moratorium would be further discussed at Monday’s meeting. It was on the agenda leading up to the meeting. Zoe King, a transit maintenance manager for Gainesville’s Regional Transit System, stayed over an hour after the meeting’s cancellation Monday to speak with Fletcher, Youmas and fellow residents. More than 70 people attended the meeting, and King said most had come to comment on data centers. “We were told that the draft for the moratorium would be presented today to the commissioners,” King said. Following its cancelation, the meeting was rescheduled to Oct. 5, when the commission plans to discuss and vote on the meeting’s agenda items. The city’s budget, a data center moratorium and a contract between the city and Duke Energy were among items on the agenda. “This is becoming a game,” she said. To King, it feels like every time an important topic is scheduled to be discussed, something pushes it back. It’s caused residents to lose faith in the city, she added. On Sept. 8, a planning and zoning board committee meeting, during which data centers were set to be discussed, was canceled for the same reason: a lack of board attendance. Fletcher and Youmas met with citizens outside Alachua City Hall on Monday to discuss the meeting's cancellation, its rescheduling and to catch up with supporters. Deborah Bagley, a 60-year-old Alachua resident, questioned the qualifications of some of Alachua’s public officials, including Matthew Webster, who was appointed to the planning and zoning board in August. Webster is the son-in-law of Virginia Johns, a former planning and zoning board member whose term expired a month before Webster assumed the role, according to Bagley and a Facebook post by Our Alachua Water. “[Webster] has monetary gain, so they knew that he would vote yes on things related to development,” said Bagley, adding that Webster’s construction company, Sterling Builders Group, would benefit from more development. A special planning and zoning board meeting is scheduled for Oct. 6 at 6 p.m., where the board is scheduled to discuss permits, site plan proposals and the city’s comprehensive plan. Contact Christian Haas at chaas@alligator.org. Follow him on X @ChristianH58745. Christian is an environmental reporter with The Alligator, and studies journalism at the University of Florida. He is a fourth-year student who prefers to spend his free time trying new and random things, cooking, reading, watching TV, or hiking.

artigo.texto: Spring Hill, Tennessee is blazing a new trail in battery technology, as Ultium Cells LLC â a joint venture between General Motors and LG Energy Solution â just announced plans to produce lithium manganese rich (LMR) prismatic battery cells at its plant just outside Nashville. This is expected to make Ultium Cells the first manufacturer globally to commercially produce this next-generation technology, positioning GM at the forefront of bringing the technology to market in future electric vehicles. LMR prismatic battery cells mark a major step forward for GMâs future EVs. The technology is designed to offer energy density 33% greater than lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry â todayâs leading, low-cost battery technology â but at a comparable cost. Establishing LMR prismatic cell production at Ultium Cells in Spring Hill is a key step in our strategy to match the right battery technology to customer needs and strengthen our leadership in domestic battery manufacturing and innovation. High-nickel batteries will continue to give customers the highest range in our portfolio, while adding LMR positions us to leapfrog today's more affordable chemistries and deliver lower costs with better performance. This flexibility allows us to scale efficiently, reach more customers, and support our long-term EV strategy and profitability journey. Adding LMR to the Ultium Cells portfolio also demonstrates the flexibility of its manufacturing capabilities. Ultium Cells will be able to produce battery cells in multiple chemistries and form factors, helping tailor battery technology to the needs of different vehicles and applications. Beyond flexing manufacturing might, bringing this new battery cell to market first is a milestone moment for keeping America competitive globally in EV and battery technology leadership. Construction and facility upgrades at Ultium Cells Spring Hill will begin later this year and are expected to be completed in 2028. This expansion is projected to create 500 new jobs, in addition to the facilityâs total current workforce of 1,200 employees.

artigo.texto: Green T-shirts with “No Data Centers” written in big block letters have become a common sight at Clinton City Hall. For weeks, the grassroots group Clintonians Against Data Centers has bird-dogged city council meetings as the industrial community on the Mississippi River tries to write a data center ordinance. Developer QTS is eyeing Clinton for a $10-billion data center campus. Opponents are demanding city leaders address their concerns about water use, air pollution and noise. “We are not against technology, innovation or progress,” Christine Voss said as she testified to the Clinton City Council in August. “We are for transparency, accountability and protecting what matters to our community: Our land, our water, our voice, our future. No data centers. Let the people decide.” Clinton isn’t unique. Data center development is expanding rapidly across the state thanks to Iowa’s cheap land and energy. Now, communities are trying to figure out what they can do when faced with proposed hyperscale projects. The data center debate isn't entirely new This is not completely uncharted territory for the state. “The amount of land that is required for data centers is pretty similar to wind energy," said Mae McDonough, an instructor at the University of Iowa’s Tippie College of Business. "Certain industrial uses, certain types of factories have similar considerations, as far as water and energy use." But McDonough said data centers have some distinct differences. Linn County Planning and Development Director Charlie Nichols agrees. “I do think data centers are different from other heavy manufacturing uses. I don't think that they are more destructive or more negative than other heavy manufacturing uses,” Nichols said. “They're essentially very large computers that need access to all this infrastructure. I think the concerns that communities and residents are having are really around the use of infrastructure.” Nichols said counties are more likely than cities to field requests from developers, which is another thing that sets data centers apart from typical manufacturers. “Industries like to locate in cities, where they have access to transportation networks, employer base, employee bases, things like that,” he said. “Data centers don't have to locate in cities; they have to locate near a high transmission line and digital infrastructure, and that's in the counties.” What can local government do if a data center comes knocking? It’s up to local governments to decide how to navigate data center development. They currently have limited options. Neither cities nor counties have the authority to ban data centers the way some opponents would like. “You can't use zoning code as an overall ban on data centers or any other type of industry,” Nichols said. What local government can do is write zoning rules to set specific standards for data centers. If they feel pressed for time, they can put a moratorium, or a pause, in place while they research what to include in the ordinance. Ten counties in Iowa have data center ordinances already in place. More than 40 counties are in the drafting process. As city attorney for Clinton, Patrick O’Connell helped create the initial draft ordinance for the city. He introduced it to the city's planning commission in July. “This is 16 pages long. It's very difficult to wrestle with this issue because for each of the 10 years or so that these data centers have been built, new and emerging problems have been found,” O'Connell said. The growth of hyperscale data centers poses new questions around water consumption, power usage and noise pollution. To combat that, ordinances can require data centers to do water studies, pay for their own power or be set back a certain distance from residential areas. Ordinances can be very specific. For example, if a data center needs more power than the grid can provide, an ordinance can dictate what kind of power the data center can bring onsite. Clintonians Against Data Centers are trying to prohibit QTS Data Centers from bringing diesel generators as backups. But since a lot of these questions are new, communities are struggling to find the research they need to draft specific requirements, like which water cooling systems are most efficient or what level of constant vibrations affects nearby residents? Jennifer Terry, who leads the University of Iowa's Hubbell Environmental Law Initiative, worked with McDonough to build a data center decision toolkit. Their team interviewed Iowans across the state in hopes of providing them with resources. “What we’re hearing from communities is they wish they had more credible, reliable information about long-term jobs, long-term impacts and usage of water and energy,” Terry said. Water is an especially tricky subject. An ordinance might require data centers to have “efficient” water use. But Johnson County Urban and Regional Planner Joe Wilensky told the Iowa Chapter of the American Planning Association in a virtual webinar that efficiency might not be as protective a word as some people think. “Efficiency does not mean they’re not drawing large amounts of power and water — just that they’re efficient with its use,” Wilensky said. “So you can have a huge draw and they can still be very efficient, according to industry standards. Efficiency does not mean low amounts.” It's hard for communities to know how much water they can afford to give a data center. The Iowa Department of Natural Resources (DNR) is responsible for water-use permitting. But Nichols said the DNR doesn't have much up-to-date information on how much water the state has, which is an issue for data centers and beyond. “There’s questions about how much water can a community or an area sustainably give to industrial uses, not just data centers,” Nichols said. artigo.texto: Gov. Abigail Spanberger dropped a few hints Tuesday about what will be in the energy plan she’s releasing on Thursday. She said she backs more on-site electricity generation for data centers so they’re not pulling power from the grid. She also said her energy plan will lay out multiple options for Virginia to meet its power needs in the years ahead. “What are the gives and takes?” Spanberger asked. “What are you sacrificing? What are you getting from the different energy mix choices? And so we modeled out and actually pushed out a variety of different examples where we show these different types of plants have various different localized pollutant risks with these types of energy generation. We have this amount of CO2 emissions. And what is the ultimate cost to the user? So that really anyone who chooses to read a 100-page report on Virginia’s energy plan has a good sense of what all the options are. “And importantly, I think as you’ll see when we release it, there’s not one single right path because there’s something you give up with every choice that you make. When you forego one option, you’re giving something up even when you’re gaining something. And so, making sure that people have a clear understanding of the push and pull as we create the right energy mix into the future is something that very intentionally will be including in the plan we’re going to be releasing later this week.” She said one goal of the energy plan is “making sure that people have a clear understanding of the push and pull as we create the right energy mix into the future.” Spanberger’s hints about the energy plan came at an event in Danville sponsored by Cardinal News and the Institute for Advanced Learning and Research where the governor was invited to speak about economic development and then took questions from the audience. I served as moderator to read those audience questions. (Cardinal sponsored a similar event during then-Gov. Glenn Youngkin’s first year in office; the event was held in Bristol.) Those remarks came in the context of a question about data centers and their energy requirements. While data centers have become pariahs in many localities, political and business leaders in Danville and Pittsylvania County have embraced a large-scale data center coming to the Southern Virginia Megasite at Berry Hill. The developer, Stack Infrastructure, has signed a performance agreement that calls for creating 2,500 permanent jobs over the next 20 years at the site. The Stack project prompted several questions from the audience about how Virginia can guarantee that localities that want data centers can still host them — and about on-site power generation. The governor said her chief of staff had spoken recently with Stack representatives to make sure that the project is a go; she also noted that the company had spoken favorably of her recent executive order — and related legislative proposals — on data centers. “This is a project that, importantly,” she said, “is a project that is wanted by the local community. And when I’m looking at how it is that we handle data center investment, or frankly, any type of investment into the future, it is a question of what do communities want.” She was asked specifically about whether data centers could use natural gas to generate power on site. She enthusiastically backed on-site power — “It’s incredibly important that we have on-site generation” — but did not specifically address natural gas, something that environmental groups oppose. “This is a place where I’ll go back to the word that I mentioned before, innovation,” she said. “Here is a lot of work being done as it relates to fuel cell, other types of noncombustion natural gas types of energy generation, where we can really ensure that we are meeting long-term the Virginia Clean Economy Act goals into the future, and also ensuring that we’re adding greater stability and reliability to the grid by having a behind-the-meter work, the bring-your-own generation.” She also mentioned the prospect of small nuclear reactors and fusion technology, the latter of which is being developed by Commonwealth Fusion Technology in Chesterfield County. “There are, on the path outside of Richmond, the potential, there are deals in place with data centers to develop small modular reactors,” the governor said. Her staff later said Spanberger was referring to previously announced plans by Amazon to work with Dominion Energy on a small nuclear reactor at Dominion’s North Anna nuclear station in Louisa County. (Disclosure: Dominion is one of our donors but donors have no say in news decisions; see our policy.) Separately, Appalachian Power has announced plans to explore a small nuclear reactor at its Joshua Falls substation in Campbell County. Last year, the Goochland County Board of Supervisors voted to adopt a Technology Overlay District designed to attract data centers; it specifically allows small modular reactors. Among other things the governor said Tuesday at the Danville event: She acknowledged ‘solar fatigue’ in some rural counties One questioner told the governor that Pittsylvania County, and other rural counties, “have complete solar fatigue” by the number of solar facilities in those communities. artigo.texto: Jesup advances data center regulations despite pushback from packed crowd SAVANNAH, Ga. (WTOC) - Following hours of fierce public debate inside a packed Cracker Williams Recreation Center, Jesup city officials voted Tuesday night to advance proposed regulations governing data centers. In a 4-2 vote, commissioners approved the first reading of an ordinance that formally defines data centers and permits them as a “conditional use” in light industrial zoning districts. Because Tuesday’s vote was only a preliminary step, the measure must pass additional readings before taking final effect. Dozens of residents lined up at the microphone to voice concern, urging leaders to enact a complete moratorium rather than moving ahead with regulations. Opponents argued a temporary freeze on new applications would allow the city adequate time to study potential impacts on local water resources and the power grid. “My concern is that commissioners are talking about — we need the ordinance because if the moratorium doesn’t go through, then we’re not protected,” said Jesup resident Erin Wallace. “But then the others are saying they don’t want the ordinance because the moratorium will give us time to make the ordinance stronger. It just seems disingenuous to me that we don’t do both.” City officials have not yet announced the date for the ordinance’s second reading. Copyright 2026 WTOC. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Even as a group of Aurora residents opposes the Trident Data Center near Green Valley Ranch, city officials are looking at a second data center proposal for a plot of land next to The Aurora Highlands. A search for data centers in the city’s development portal results in four application listings, one for the Trident Data Center, a second for a data center near The Aurora Highlands, a third without any documentation attached yet and a fourth for a data center project on a site that already has a data center. Recommended Stories The Aerotropolis Logistics Center, proposed by company Aerotropolis Industrial Development, would be about 3 miles south of Denver International Airport. The proposed site plan calls for about 500 acres of new data centers “to provide the necessary infrastructure to support digital services, businesses, and technologies that people and organizations rely on every day,” according to documents in the city’s development portal. The 1 million-square-foot site is proposed to go just east of The Aurora Highlands master-planned community, south of 48th Avenue, north of 26th Avenue, east of Aerotropolis Parkway and west of Monaghan Road. There is no available information about water or electricity needs for the site online and the listed developer did not respond to The Denver Gazette’s inquiries. Also in Aurora’s development portal is an application listed as a site plan for a 1.5 million-square-foot data center campus. There are no attached documents and the application date is listed as Oct. 12, 2026. On Monday, the Aurora City Council faced a chamber with many residents opposed to the Trident Data Center proposal from Vantage Data Centers, which would go next to Green Valley Ranch if approved. Both Trident and Aerotropolis Logistics Center are in industrial zone districts, where data centers are permitted. The city attorney also noted that, if an application meets zoning standards, Aurora could face potential liability if administrative officials denied it. Broadly speaking, supporters have argued that data centers bring jobs and investment to local communities as well as new tax revenues. They have also insisted that cultivating and growing data centers in America has positive repercussions for national security. Meanwhile, a political split is emerging in how cities and counties deal with data centers: The Colorado counties that recently approved data center construction are conservative-leaning, while cities calling for or imposing moratoriums lean progressive. Plans for the new Trident center, which is proposed to sit at the northwest corner of the intersection of E-470 and East 48th Avenue, have already been through two formal city reviews and a third is underway, an Aurora spokesperson told The Denver Gazette. If built, the data center would be two stories and 1.5 million square feet on 108 acres of land, according to public documents submitted by Vantage through the city’s development portal. The Aurora City Council has also been in the process of considering regulations on future data centers, including setbacks and evaporative cooling bans, but those regulations would only apply to future data center proposals.

artigo.texto: Dixon City Council approves 45-day ban for data center development Dixon's City Council unanimously voted Wednesday night to impose a 45-day moratorium on data center developments, allowing city staff to evaluate their potential impacts on the community. "It's a national conversation right now about data centers and battery storage," said Vice Mayor Jim Ernest. The special meeting comes in response to recent council discussions about Dixon's regulations and its ability to manage this type of development. City officials said they need to prioritize evaluating potential strains on local infrastructure and environmental impacts associated with these facilities. "I'm not for or against it at this point, but I think it's very obvious our citizens want to know what's going on," Ernest said. "They don't want to be surprised by a project moving into town without them knowing." During the meeting, a member of the public asked, "What the hell is a data center for?" The moratorium gives city staff time to investigate the potential effects of data centers, including their impact on water, air, noise, and the local tax base. "There are things that could happen with our water, our air, our tax base, noise. A lot of things," Ernest said. "The transparency, I think, is what we're looking for." Dixon High School seniors Nick Albertazzi and Christian Morelos attended the meeting as part of a school assignment and expressed their support for the moratorium. "Data centers have a lot of downside, such as material consumption, water usage which could be a concern," Albertazzi said. Morelos added, "Put the pause so they can actually talk over it, think about it more clearly, than just rushing through something. Because if you rush it and you don't get the votes or talk to the people before building something, then the residents of Dixon are not gonna like it." The moratorium could be extended twice, for up to two years at a time, with a four-fifths council vote required for each extension. "Get ahead of this to get a planning process in place, so when one does come, which I'm sure it will, we're ready for it," Ernest said. Dixon also pointed to a statewide increase in the development of data centers and battery energy storage systems, known as BESS facilities. Dixon joins other cities in addressing the rapid growth of data centers. Earlier this month, the city of Riverbank approved a 45-day moratorium on data centers. Last week, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed seven bills into law to strengthen California's approach to data centers. The Dixon City Council would also have the authority to extend the moratorium, twice for up to two years, if needed. artigo.texto: Q3 Executive Roundtable Recap For Data Center Frontier’s Q3 2026 Executive Roundtable, three industry leaders examined a question increasingly central to the AI infrastructure buildout: What happens when data centers are asked to become larger, denser and faster at the same time? Across three discussions, a consistent theme emerged. AI is not simply increasing the amount of infrastructure required to support the modern data center. It is exposing assumptions that were easier to tolerate at lower densities, expanding the boundaries of what operators must consider mission-critical, and making the interaction between systems increasingly important to overall resilience. That begins with density. As the value and power concentrated in individual racks rises, traditional approaches to redundancy, monitoring and risk mitigation can leave less room for error. Resilience can no longer be measured simply by installed capacity or the presence of backup equipment. Operators increasingly need to understand how electrical, thermal and control systems behave together under dynamic AI workloads — and how quickly the facility can respond and recover when something goes wrong. The same shift is broadening the definition of critical infrastructure. Power generation, UPS systems and network connectivity remain fundamental, but energy storage, liquid cooling, leak detection, controls, monitoring and the interfaces connecting them are becoming part of the same reliability equation. A component can perform exactly as designed while the larger system still fails if coordination, communications or control logic break down. And all of this is happening while the market is demanding faster deployment. Standardization, modular construction, factory integration and earlier modeling can legitimately compress project schedules. But the Q3 panelists drew a clear distinction between eliminating unnecessary time and eliminating rigor. As infrastructure becomes more tightly coupled, commissioning, integrated systems testing, operational visibility and system-level validation may need to become more thorough precisely because projects are moving faster. Taken together, the Q3 discussion points toward a broader change in how AI data center resilience must be understood. The challenge is no longer simply designing enough redundancy, specifying reliable equipment or reaching first power quickly. It is building an increasingly complex infrastructure system whose components, controls and operators can perform together — under load, under stress and at the speed the AI market now demands. Here's the full question-and-answer session, organized by topic: - Roundtable: AI Infrastructure Under Pressure - Roundtable: Redefining Critical Infrastructure - Roundtable: Speed Without Compromise Here are links to the individual Q&A summaries for each of our panelists: - Chrissy Olsen, Vice President of Critical Power Solutions, MPI Energy - David Shepard, Global Head of Data Center Business, Chemelex-Raychem - Pierre-Adrien Bel, Product Manager, EMEA, Rehlko The conversation is moderated by Data Center Frontier Editor in Chief Matt Vincent. Thanks to all of our executive participants for sharing their time and insights! About the Author Matt Vincent Matt Vincent is Editor in Chief of Data Center Frontier, where he leads editorial strategy and coverage focused on the infrastructure powering cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and the digital economy. A veteran B2B technology journalist with more than two decades of experience, Vincent specializes in the intersection of data centers, power, cooling, and emerging AI-era infrastructure. Since assuming the EIC role in 2023, he has helped guide Data Center Frontier’s coverage of the industry’s transition into the gigawatt-scale AI era, with a focus on hyperscale development, behind-the-meter power strategies, liquid cooling architectures, and the evolving energy demands of high-density compute, while working closely with the Digital Infrastructure Group at Endeavor Business Media to expand the brand’s analytical and multimedia footprint. Vincent also hosts The Data Center Frontier Show podcast, where he interviews industry leaders across hyperscale, colocation, utilities, and the data center supply chain to examine the technologies and business models reshaping digital infrastructure. Since its inception he serves as Head of Content for the Data Center Frontier Trends Summit. Before becoming Editor in Chief, he served in multiple senior editorial roles across Endeavor Business Media’s digital infrastructure portfolio, with coverage spanning data centers and hyperscale infrastructure, structured cabling and networking, telecom and datacom, IP physical security, and wireless and Pro AV markets. He began his career in 2005 within PennWell’s Advanced Technology Division and later held senior editorial positions supporting brands such as Cabling Installation & Maintenance, Lightwave Online, Broadband Technology Report, and Smart Buildings Technology. Vincent is a frequent moderator, interviewer, and keynote speaker at industry events including the HPC Forum, where he delivers forward-looking analysis on how AI and high-performance computing are reshaping digital infrastructure. He graduated with honors from Indiana University Bloomington with a B.A. in English Literature and Creative Writing and lives in southern New Hampshire with his family, remaining an active musician in his spare time.

artigo.texto: Data centers in Alaska: Fairbanks leaders weigh in on controversial issue FAIRBANKS, Alaska (KTUU/KTVF) - Candidates running for seats on the Fairbanks North Star Borough Assembly have weighed in on whether they support the building of data centers in the borough. The issue garnered attention earlier this year, when the U.S. Department of Defense announced potential data centers housing artificial intelligence servers to be constructed near three installations in Alaska, including Eielson Air Force Base. On Aug. 27, the Assembly voted 6-1 in favor of adopting a set of legislative priorities for 2027 which includes a moratorium on commercial data centers on municipal or state-owned lands in Alaska, pending the creation of standards for addressing community concerns. Alexis Howell, who is running for the open Assembly seat D, agreed with the idea of a moratorium in the borough. “There is a lot of interest and excitement in this idea that we’re going to move these data centers forward, that they’re going to create jobs. I think they might do that for a month or two while they’re being built,” she said. Arguing that the borough’s grid is currently struggling, Howell said, “I would hate to see us dump a data center on top of that.” “I think that at the end of the day, a lot more analysis needs to go into that. A lot more processes should be in place before a data center just gets built,” she said. Her opponent Miguel Ramirez said there should be a study on these centers’ environmental impact before they are built. “I think we should, you know, do a study where we can all agree and see the, work with the environmental folks and find out where the goods are, where the pros are, where the cons are, if it’s good, if it’s not, but I can’t really say ‘yay’ or ‘nay’ because I think there need to be more studies done,” he explained. Nick LaJiness, running for reelection to seat E, didn’t mince words on his opinion on data centers. “I don’t think that data centers are good for any community, to be honest with you,” LaJinness said. Shelly Shupe, meanwhile, who is running for the same seat, divided public opinion on data centers into three groups: those who are concerned about environmental impacts from data centers, those who support them, and those who are not discounting them but need more information. “I’m somewhere in between the ‘I’m worried about what it might bring’ and ‘I don’t want to discount it’ groups,” she said. Scott Crass, who is running to retain seat H on the Assembly, defended his vote in favor of the moratorium. “I think that’s important that we understand the potential impacts that come from these large data centers,” Crass said. “Energy costs in our community have skyrocketed. They’re incredibly high, some of the highest in the nation, and grappling with that while thinking about a project that would consume more energy than our entire town is absolutely terrifying at first blush.” Adding that a data center which supplied its own power might be a different conversation, Crass discussed the advantages to data centers of Fairbanks’ cold climate. “That moratorium would allow us to find some time to figure out if our community is ready to accommodate those sorts of large-scale projects,” he said. Joshua Leaders, who hopes to unseat Crass from seat H, said he likes the idea of data centers as long as their presence benefits the community. “We need to take a serious look at the impact on the infrastructure, the power grid, the water and how that’s affected, and we need to see if that benefit outweighs the cost,” Leaders explained, adding that he supports a temporary moratorium while data is collected. artigo.texto: As battery energy storage systems move into larger and denser configurations, fire and explosion risk has become one of the industry’s most closely scrutinized engineering challenges. At Wärtsilä Energy Storage, Mishaal SyedNaveed has focused his work on that challenge. That combination of utility experience, product engineering, testing, and standards work has made SyedNaveed a finalist for POWER’s 2026 Rising Star Award. SyedNaveed is product manager for fire protection at Wärtsilä Energy Storage, where he focuses on product development, compliance, verification, and risk assessment for the company’s GridSolve battery energy storage system portfolio. A licensed Professional Engineer in fire protection, he has experience in risk engineering, design, loss prevention, and code consulting across the energy industry. His work at Wärtsilä has centered on translating battery fire and explosion hazards into engineering requirements, test programs, and product design. According to his Rising Star nomination, SyedNaveed played a central technical role in the company’s 2025 fire safety testing for the 5-MWh GridSolve Quantum3 system, including UL 9540A unit-level testing, large-scale fire testing, and testing of Wärtsilä’s Active Ignition Mitigation System, or AIMS. The large-scale fire test intentionally ignited a fire and allowed it to burn for more than 22 hours. Wärtsilä reported that the event remained contained within the initiating unit and did not propagate to adjacent units, without suppression or intervention. AIMS testing evaluated a different hazard: the accumulation of flammable gases during a thermal event. The system is designed to ignite those gases early, before they can produce an uncontrolled deflagration. According to the nomination, CSA Group witnessed the tests for third-party verification. SyedNaveed also supported large-scale and full-system testing of Wärtsilä’s GridSolve Quantum2 platform. Testing included U.S.-based AIMS validation under worst-case gas-release scenarios, as well as large-scale fire testing that showed no unit-to-unit propagation. Wärtsilä said those results have also helped inform evolving industry guidance, including future editions of NFPA 855. His work extends beyond Wärtsilä’s own products. SyedNaveed participates in CSA and UL technical committees related to energy storage and works with customers, authorities having jurisdiction, fire protection engineers, insurers, and first responders. Wärtsilä credits his ability to translate test data into design guidance and permitting support with reducing project risk and improving permitting outcomes. Before joining Wärtsilä, SyedNaveed worked as a fire protection engineer at Dominion Energy, where he served as subject matter expert for more than 64 MWh of installed and 284 MWh of planned energy storage projects. He holds a master’s degree in Energy Systems Engineering from Northeastern University and a bachelor’s degree in Fire Protection Engineering from the University of Maryland, College Park. —POWER

artigo.texto: Subestações nos estados do Rio Grande do Sul, Rondônia, Bahia, Ceará e Pernambuco têm restrições para conexão de baterias, segundo nota técnica (.pdf) divulgada na quarta-feira (30/9) pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) e a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE). O objetivo do documento é identificar a capacidade remanescente para conexão de baterias nas redes do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN) dados os leilões de baterias, que ocorrem em 2 e 4 de dezembro. A previsão das entidades é que os disjuntores dessas subestações vão ter as capacidades superadas com a adição de baterias e que não vai ser possível substituir os equipamentos até a entrada em operação dos empreendimentos que serão contratados nos leilões deste ano. Os leilões de reserva de capacidade (LRCAPs) de baterias vão negociar contratos com previsão de entrada em operação a partir de agosto de 2028. As restrições nas redes indicam que parte dos 6.091 projetos cadastrados na EPE devem ficar de fora dos certames. Mesmo assim, a Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae) considera que o número de projetos habilitados continuará muito acima da quantidade a ser contratada. Os projetos cadastrados para a concorrência totalizam 296,8 GW de potência, sendo 71,1% deste total no Nordeste; 18,8% no Sudeste; 5,1% no Sul; 3,4% no Centro-Oeste; e 1,6% no Norte. A Absae estima que há uma margem de conexão no SIN de cerca de 56 GW. Já o déficit de potência previsto entre 2028 e 2030 é de 4,5 a 10 GW, ainda abaixo dos cerca de 13,7 GW de margem agregada dos barramentos bonificados. “A nota do ONS é uma boa notícia para o leilão (…) Com tantos projetos cadastrados, a disputa deve ser decidida por preço, o que favorece o consumidor”, afirmou o diretor-executivo da Absae, Fabio Lima. Dos 129 barramentos bonificados, 93 têm margem reconhecida. Esses projetos estão concentrados no Nordeste, principalmente na Bahia, no Piauí e no Ceará, e no norte de Minas Gerais, regiões que reúnem os maiores blocos de capacidade, de até cerca de 3,7 GW. A habilitação para participação nos leilões será divulgada em 17 de novembro.

artigo.texto: Das ‘baterias de água’ às novas soluções de armazenamento de energia Em artigo à CNN Infra, Fernanda Genova Martins, da CTG, afirma que o leilão de baterias dará mais flexibilidade ao sistema elétrico, mas será apenas parte da solução Antes das baterias de lítio, o Brasil já contava com armazenamento de energia em larga escala. Por décadas, os reservatórios das usinas hidrelétricas funcionaram como “baterias de água”: deslocaram a disponibilidade hídrica entre períodos chuvosos e secos e ofereceram flexibilidade para atender às variações sazonais da demanda. Essa capacidade foi um diferencial estratégico da matriz elétrica brasileira. O país construiu um sistema renovável, integrado e capaz de aproveitar a complementaridade entre regiões. Mas essa característica já não responde sozinha à complexidade da operação. A expansão hidrelétrica ocorreu com maior participação de empreendimentos a fio d’água, com menor capacidade de regularização, enquanto a geração eólica e solar avançou rapidamente. Em 2025, as fontes renováveis responderam por 86,8% da oferta interna de eletricidade. Eólica e solar, somadas, já representam 26,4%, ante 10,9% em 2020, segundo a EPE (Empresa de Pesquisa Energética). Esses resultados ampliam a necessidade de recursos capazes de oferecer flexibilidade, potência, controle e deslocamento temporal de energia. Mais renováveis exigem novas formas de flexibilidade Solar e eólica apresentam perfis variáveis de geração: a produção solar se altera ao longo do dia, enquanto a eólica depende dos ventos. Em determinados momentos, restrições elétricas, energéticas ou operativas exigem reduzir parte da produção renovável porque o sistema não consegue absorvê-la ou transportá-la. Em 2025, o corte de geração eólica e solar (curtailment) chegou a 20,6%, mais que o dobro de 2024, com prejuízo estimado acima de R$ 6 bilhões, segundo a Volt Robotics. O desafio é ajustar oferta e demanda, armazenando o excedente e disponibilizando energia quando ela gera mais valor ao sistema. Essa flexibilidade pode vir de baterias, reservatórios, usinas reversíveis, transmissão, resposta da demanda e gestão inteligente da geração distribuída. As usinas hidrelétricas reversíveis merecem atenção especial. Ao combinar armazenamento em grande escala e maior duração com resposta às necessidades de potência e flexibilidade, elas podem aproveitar a experiência hidrelétrica do Brasil e complementar as baterias em serviços de maior duração. O debate deve incluir soluções capazes de sustentar a expansão renovável nas próximas décadas. Já as baterias ganharam protagonismo pela rapidez de implantação, capacidade de resposta e queda de custos. Em 2025, foram instalados 108 GW de novos sistemas no mundo, avanço de 40%, segundo a Agência Internacional de Energia. Já não é uma tecnologia experimental. No Brasil, o ambiente econômico e regulatório precisa direcioná-la aos pontos e serviços em que o benefício para o sistema seja maior. Leilão será um teste para o desenho do mercado Os primeiros leilões no Brasil voltados ao armazenamento em baterias, previstos para dezembro, marcam a passagem dos projetos-piloto para uma nova escala. O desenho prevê contratos de 15 anos, início do fornecimento em 2028 e entrega de energia por pelo menos quatro horas. O interesse foi imediato: a EPE recebeu 6.091 projetos, que somam 296.807 MW. O número é expressivo, mas o cadastro não equivale a projeto habilitado, investimento contratado ou necessidade do sistema. Avaliação técnica, capacidade de conexão e volume demandado ainda funcionarão como filtros. Essa diferença entre intenção e execução é central. Para atrair capital de longo prazo, o marco regulatório deverá oferecer previsibilidade sobre remuneração, alocação de riscos, medição do desempenho e tratamento das limitações da rede. Será preciso, ainda, evitar que a competição pelo menor preço produza ativos incapazes de sustentar o desempenho por 15 anos. Baterias perdem capacidade com o tempo, e conexão, software, manutenção e destinação final fazem parte da conta. Escala depende de uma combinação de soluções O primeiro leilão é voltado a baterias com ciclos de quatro horas de duração. Esse produto pode contribuir para o deslocamento intradiário de energia, a gestão de rampas e a resposta rápida a necessidades operativas. Sua contribuição, contudo, deve ser avaliada com outros recursos de flexibilidade, porque nenhuma tecnologia de armazenamento atende isoladamente a todos os requisitos do sistema elétrico brasileiro, por isso a importância da diversificação e complementariedade. Nesse contexto, as usinas hidrelétricas reversíveis podem ocupar posição estratégica. Esses empreendimentos utilizam energia para bombear água a um reservatório superior e voltam a gerar quando o sistema requer energia, potência ou outros serviços de flexibilidade. O Brasil reúne experiência hidrelétrica e condições naturais favoráveis; sua inserção dependerá de inventários, licenciamento, conexão e mecanismos de remuneração compatíveis com os serviços prestados. As tecnologias devem ser comparadas conforme o serviço requerido. Duração, tempo de resposta, localização, disponibilidade, prazo de implantação, conexão, impacto ambiental, usos múltiplos do reservatório e custo total são atributos relevantes. Conforme a necessidade, a alternativa poderá ser bateria, usina reversível, transmissão, participação da demanda ou uma combinação desses recursos. Projetos-piloto ajudam a converter hipóteses em evidências. Em janeiro, a CTG Brasil inaugurou, na Usina Hidrelétrica Ilha Solteira (SP), o FlexBess, laboratório que combina geração solar e baterias para avaliar desempenho, segurança e modelos de operação. A experiência reforça que armazenar energia exige inteligência operacional, qualificação técnica e regras que reconheçam o valor entregue ao sistema. artigo.texto: Despite the measure passing with overwhelming bipartisan support in the House, it was beyond clear that Senate Democrats would vote against the Ratepayer Protection Act. On Wednesday, all but four of them—Sens. Jon Ossoff (D-GA), Raphael Warnock (D-GA), Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), and Maggie Hassan (D-NH)—did just that. The bill, sponsored by Sen. Jon Husted (R-OH), directs state utility regulators to consider a standard whereby data centers pay for the full incremental costs of infrastructure needed to serve them. It did not secure the 60 votes required to advance to the Senate floor, failing in a 57-32 vote. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer was vocal about his plans to oppose the legislation in the days leading up to the vote, with Senate Democratic leadership broadly framing it as a bailout for Husted. The Republican incumbent from Ohio faces a tough re-election campaign. Husted’s opponent, former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, has plenty of ammunition, and he hasn’t been afraid to use it. Brown notably capitalized on Husted’s past comments supporting data centers, which the Republican made during his tenure as Ohio’s lieutenant governor. At the time, Husted characterized himself as the “point man” for data center development in Ohio. Husted has been trailing Brown in the polls, with the most recent one putting Husted three points behind the Democrat trying to unseat him. Although Brown has raised more money than Husted, outside Republican PACs have an enormous spending advantage in the race. Recent figures indicate those PACs have spent $68 million more than their Democratic counterparts on boosting their respective candidates. “The Ratepayer Protection Act was such a no brainer that some of the most conservative and the most liberal representatives all agreed it was good policy,” Husted wrote in a post on X. “Senate Democrats are the only ones who refused to take yes for an answer.” Given what the bill actually does, it appears that Senate Democrats—save for the fantastic four—made a logical calculation in killing the Ratepayer Protection Act. As noted above, it only requires states to consider ratepayer protection, without mandating any actual safeguards around paying for data center energy use. “At a time when Americans are calling out for real guardrails on AI, Senate Republicans are trying to secure an ineffectual participation trophy before they skip town,” Schumer said on the Senate floor. “Instead of trying to score cheap political points with hollow proposals, Senate Republicans need to work with us to take meaningful action that will actually contain these existential risks.” Today on TAP This story first appeared in our free Today on TAP newsletter, a weekday email featuring commentary on the daily news from Prospect reporters. The congressional bill is behind even some of America’s most conservative states. In Alabama, which has long relied on a formula-based ratemaking process that does not provide for formal rate case proceedings, legislators have directed their public utility commission to adopt a large-load tariff for data center customers. In April, Gov. Kay Ivey (R) enacted legislation mandating the Alabama Public Service Commission to ensure that any contracts between Alabama’s investor-owned utilities and their data center customers are consistent with the public interest. The ensuing process is well under way; the law took effect today. In Husted’s home state, the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio (PUCO) ordered the investor-owned utility AEP Ohio to implement a tariff targeting high-demand customers like data centers in July 2025. Meanwhile, the Ohio legislature passed legislation to codify PUCO’s decision in August 2025, requiring the state’s other investor-owned utilities to adopt cost allocation frameworks for data centers. Dozens of other states have proposed or approved data center–specific large-load tariffs. For their part, Democrats in both chambers of Congress have proposed a range of legislation to shield ratepayers from bearing the brunt of the data center build-out, and rein in excess utility profits. Some of that legislation has seen bipartisan support, such as the pair of bills introduced by Sens. John Curtis (R-UT) and Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE). The first bill is designed to provide the public with adequate information about data center projects being built in their backyards, which as the Prospect reported today, has been a major point of contention in communities pushing back against these developments. It seeks to establish a Department of Energy program providing communities with technical expertise on the costs and benefits of proposed projects. The second bill would impose federal reporting requirements, namely an environmental impact assessment, for hyperscale data centers. If Husted and other Republicans are serious about protecting ratepayers, they certainly have more than one legislative option to choose from. But siding with Democrats? The GOP may not want to risk inviting the optics that come with that, especially considering how such a transgression would likely anger Donald Trump. Yet the president has hit a record-low approval rating, and some vulnerable Republicans have already been distancing themselves from his administration. Is backing legislation that actually protects ratepayers a risk Republicans are willing to take?

artigo.texto: Jackson County leaders seek public input on data centers, battery storage KANSAS CITY, Mo. (KCTV) - Jackson County leaders called a meeting Thursday at 5:30 p.m. at the South Independence Branch Library to gather resident input on data centers and battery storage facilities. County legislators will be on site to hear from residents on the topics. Resident raises concerns Charlie Morris spent decades as an engineer and is a fifth-generation farmer in northeast Jackson County. A battery storage facility proposed near his land caught his attention. “I thought I was retired until this happened,” Morris said. Morris said that in June, he and others worked with the county to put a moratorium in place on battery energy storage systems and data centers. “We basically got with the county and got them to put a moratorium and put the brakes on trying to stop BESS and data centers because there are really no rules,” Morris said. County outlines goal of meeting Sean Smith is leading the discussions along with Legislator Venessa Huskey. “So the idea is to go out into the community and say, okay, we’ve listed what we think are your concerns. Did we get them all?” Smith said. Smith said the goal is not to keep the new technologies away, but to provide guidance on best practices. “We’ve heard folks and are trying to address their concerns. And we’re trying to do that at some point where we don’t hinder good economic development. So that’s the kind of balancing act,” Smith said. Smith said the effort is meant to help provide a blueprint for other communities that receive requests from private companies to move in. “These are the things that are kind of our gold standard,” Smith said. Smith said the county does not yet know what those standards are, but officials are ready to hear from residents like Morris. “I would encourage anyone concerned with it to show up at the meeting or show up at any meeting,” Morris said. artigo.texto: UL Solutions Launches Certification for Direct-to-Chip Liquid Cooling Equipment Used in AI Data Centers Certification evaluates liquid cooling subassemblies for safety, performance, leak integrity and interoperability, helping support reliable AI infrastructure. - AI chips generate intense heat, making effective cooling essential to data center performance and reliability. - The certification provides a consistent way to assess critical cooling components before deployment in AI data centers. - Certification can help manufacturers demonstrate product readiness and help data center customers make informed purchasing and integration decisions. This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260929465054/en/ UL Solutions today launched a certification program for liquid cooling subassemblies that target powerful chips directly, providing more effective cooling in AI data centers and other high-density computing systems. AI computers use chips that produce a large amount of heat. If that heat is not removed, equipment may slow down, shut off or become damaged, but traditional air cooling, such as fans or chilled air, may not be enough for today’s most powerful computing systems. With direct-to-chip liquid cooling, coolant flows through a cold plate that is attached to the chip. The coolant absorbs heat from the chip and carries it away, much like water flowing through a radiator. “As AI data centers handle more powerful computing, they depend on even more advanced cooling systems to operate safely and reliably,” said AI and other high-performance computing systems are increasing energy use and heat in data centers. Global data center electricity use is expected to more than double between 2024 and 2030. Cooling can account for up to 40% of a data center’s energy use. Liquid cooling can improve heat control, but it also brings risks. Leaks, corrosion, contamination or parts that do not work well together can affect system safety, performance and reliability. Connecting parts from different suppliers can also be a challenge. Parts may fit together but require different coolants, pressure levels or operating conditions. Industry observers have identified integration problems and limited standards as barriers to wider use of liquid cooling. The UL Solutions certification program covers eligible liquid-filled parts and subassemblies that move coolant through information and communication technology equipment. These may include: - Cold plates, which absorb heat directly from computer chips - Manifolds, which send coolant to servers and equipment racks - Quick disconnects, which allow equipment to be serviced without draining the full cooling system UL Solutions uses UL 4501, the Outline of Investigation for Safety, Performance and Interoperability of Liquid-Filled Components and Assemblies Used in Liquid Cooling Systems, to evaluate eligible liquid cooling subassemblies. The evaluation covers coolant compatibility, pressure and leak integrity, durability, liquid flow, interoperability, production controls and installation requirements. Evaluating these parts before adding them to a complete cooling system can help identify problems earlier and reduce the need for repeated testing. Independent certification demonstrates that an eligible product meets applicable requirements. This helps manufacturers support their product claims and helps data center customers make informed buying and integration decisions. “AI infrastructure must scale without sacrificing safety or reliability,” said UL Solutions can also evaluate other data center cooling equipment under applicable UL Standards. This equipment includes coolant distribution units, self-contained liquid-filled systems, liquid-cooled busways, cables, connectors, power whips, gaskets, O-rings and hoses. Requirements depend on each product’s design, function and intended use. Learn more about UL Solutions services that support data center development and operations. About UL Solutions A global leader in applied safety science, UL Solutions (NYSE: ULS) transforms safety, security and sustainability challenges into opportunities for customers in more than 110 countries. UL Solutions delivers testing, inspection and certification services, advisory offerings and software solutions that support our customers’ product innovation and business growth. The UL Mark serves as a recognized symbol of trust in our customers’ products and reflects an unwavering commitment to advancing our safety mission. We help our customers innovate, launch new products and services, navigate global markets and complex supply chains, and grow sustainably and responsibly into the future. Our science is your advantage. Learn more about UL Solutions.
