artigo.texto: The Aurora City Council on Monday faced a chamber packed with residents opposed to a data center that is proposed to go up next to their neighborhoods, even as the city attorney reiterated that the site is an industrial zone district where data centers are permitted. The city attorney also noted that, if an application meets zoning standards, Aurora could face potential liability if administrative officials denied it. Recommended Stories The council heard from about 40 Aurora and Denver residents who are upset about the plans for Trident Data Center, which would go up near Green Valley Ranch if approved. Before the public comment period began, City Attorney Pete Schulte asked everyone attending who opposed the Trident Data Center to stand up. Almost everyone in the room did so. When Schulte asked if anyone in the room supported the data center, nobody stood. Broadly speaking, supporters have argued that data centers bring jobs and investment to local communities as well as new tax revenues. They have also insisted that cultivating and growing data centers in America has positive repercussions for national security. Meanwhile, a political split is emerging in how cities and counties deal with data centers: The Colorado counties that recently approved data center construction are conservative-leaning, while cities calling for or imposing moratoriums lean progressive. Plans for the new data center, which is proposed to sit at the northwest corner of the intersection of E-470 and East 48th Avenue, have already been through two formal city reviews and a third is underway, an Aurora spokesperson told The Denver Gazette. Vantage Data Centers submitted the application for Trident to the city on Aug. 25, 2025. If built, the data center would be two stories and 1.5 million square feet on 108 acres of land, according to public documents submitted by Vantage through the city’s development portal. Residents said they feel “totally blindsided” by the proposal. The Aurora residents opposed to the data center claimed that, until early September, they had not heard a word about the plan from the city or Oakwood Homes, the real estate developer for the community. The property where Trident is proposed is in an industrial zone district, where data centers are a permitted use and can be approved administratively as long as no major adjustments are requested, a city spokesperson said. Residents from both Aurora and Denver spoke at the meeting, with those in Denver saying they are close to the data center’s location but have no say in its location. Bre Kennedy, 16, told council members that the data center plan is “ridiculous,” asking councilmembers to raise their hands if they would want to live next to a data center. None of the councilmembers did. “You don’t want this near your neighborhood, so why is it OK for it to be near others’?” Kennedy said. “When you’re writing new regulations, please think about the people who are actually going to have to live next to these facilities.” “We the residents of The Reserve and the groups impacted by this were never informed,” added Dan Bergander, who has lived at The Reserve 55+ community since 2021. In fact, Aurora officials were not required to notify area residents of the plans for a data center because of the land’s zoning, according to Schulte, the city attorney. When applications go to the city for use of land that’s zoned for that use, it goes to administrative approval. “If the council had to approve every project that had to go through, our meetings would be two days long,” Schulte said. “That’s why we have zoning laws.” If an application meets the zoning standards, the city is subject to potential liability if administrative officials deny it, he said. Development and zoning information is public record, Schulte added. “We’re not in the game of hiding the ball,” he said. “Everything we do is open, on our website and can be searched. I encourage any homeowner with parcels of land by their neighborhood to figure out what the land is zoned for.”

artigo.texto: Jackson City Hall meeting called to educate residents on data centers "What we did not hear was the actual benefit, because there is none," said a Jackson Resident Jackson City Hall was filled Wednesday night as residents attended a special meeting to discuss data centers. It's a topic that has sparked intense debate in recent months and led city council members to impose a moratorium on their development. Councilman Vernon Hartley stressed the importance of educating the public about data centers. "We can't have our head in the sand concerning data centers," Hartley said. "We need to understand it. There is a huge data center being built on the northern border of the city of Jackson." Former IT entrepreneur Gerrad Gibert, invited by Councilman Kenneth Stokes, gave an overview of data centers, explaining their purpose and how they are already a part of daily life. "Gain a better understanding of what these sorts of obscure, windowless buildings are and what's in them and how they affect our lives," Gibert said. Gibert, who was involved in building Mississippi's first commercial data center in the 1980s, said data centers are integral to modern life and should not be feared. "I think Jackson can benefit quite a bit from a data center investment," Gibert said. "Jackson is poised well for it. Every business around uses IT systems that are typically housed in data centers." Despite the presentation, some residents, including Natalie Speaks, voiced dissatisfaction with the meeting, saying it lacked opportunities for public input. "People think when you're anti-data center that means you're anti-advancement, and that's not the case," Speaks said. She added that the presentation failed to address the benefits of data centers for the community. "We just heard a presentation about what data centers are and how you build them, [about] venture technologies and what he's done," Speaks said. "But what we did not hear was the actual benefit, because there is none." While city leaders viewed the meeting as a way to inform the public, some attendees left feeling puzzled and unfulfilled, underscoring the ongoing debate over data center developments in Jackson.

artigo.texto: EU ETS: prazo para entrega de licenças de emissão termina para armadoras out, 01, 2026 Postado porGabriel Malheiros Semana202640 As empresas de navegação sujeitas ao Sistema de Comércio de Emissões da União Europeia (EU ETS) tinham até 30 de setembro para entregar as licenças necessárias para cobrir parte das emissões de gases de efeito estufa reportadas em 2025. O descumprimento pode resultar em multas e outras sanções. O EU ETS funciona pelo sistema de limite e comércio de emissões (cap-and-trade) e exige que empresas do setor marítimo, assim como companhias de outras atividades abrangidas pelo mecanismo, entreguem European Union Allowances (EUAs) correspondentes às emissões sob sua responsabilidade. Em 2026, as companhias de navegação precisam entregar EUAs suficientes para cobrir 70% das emissões reportadas em 2025. A obrigação vem sendo implementada de forma gradual desde a inclusão do transporte marítimo no sistema: no ano passado, a cobertura exigida era de 40% das emissões de 2024. A partir de 2027, as empresas terão de entregar licenças equivalentes a 100% das emissões reportadas no ano anterior. O prazo de 30 de setembro é específico do EU ETS. No Reino Unido, a legislação equivalente estabelece 30 de abril como data para entrega das licenças, com regras especiais para as emissões de 2026 e 2027, que adiam a primeira obrigação de entrega para 2028. Responsabilidade recai sobre a empresa de navegação Pelas regras do EU ETS, cabe à empresa de navegação responsável garantir a entrega da quantidade correta de EUAs. Nos casos em que um gestor de navios tenha recebido formalmente, por meio de mandato, a responsabilidade pelas obrigações da companhia perante o EU ETS, passa a ser dele também a responsabilidade pelo cumprimento dessas exigências. Esses gestores precisam assegurar que haja EUAs suficientes em suas contas dentro do prazo. O recebimento e a posterior entrega das licenças envolvem procedimentos administrativos que nem sempre são imediatos, o que torna atrasos na compra ou transferência das permissões um risco relevante. Para os gestores que assumiram formalmente as obrigações do EU ETS, portanto, a origem das licenças necessárias já deveria estar definida antes do encerramento do prazo. Atrasos na transferência de EUAs elevam risco À medida que o setor se acostumou ao EU ETS, também avançaram os procedimentos de reporte e a inclusão de cláusulas específicas em contratos de afretamento, compra e venda de navios e gestão de embarcações. Ainda assim, segundo a Reed Smith, começaram a surgir casos em que as EUAs não foram transferidas pelos afretadores aos gestores ou proprietários dentro do prazo esperado, mesmo quando os contratos estabeleciam expressamente essa obrigação. Enquanto o prazo ainda estava distante, as partes tendiam a aceitar algum atraso. Com a proximidade — e agora o encerramento — da data-limite, o risco contratual aumentou. Mesmo quando a companhia registrada possui o direito contratual de cobrar posteriormente do afretador ou do proprietário os custos das licenças, ela continua sendo a responsável perante o EU ETS caso tenha assumido formalmente essa obrigação. Multa pode chegar a €100 por licença não entregue As consequências do descumprimento podem ser significativas. A falta de entrega das EUAs dentro do prazo sujeita a empresa a uma multa de €100 por licença não entregue, valor sujeito a atualização pela inflação. O pagamento da penalidade não elimina a obrigação: a companhia ainda terá de entregar posteriormente as licenças correspondentes às emissões. Casos persistentes de descumprimento podem resultar em medidas ainda mais severas, incluindo uma ordem que, na prática, impeça o navio de entrar em portos da União Europeia. Por isso, as empresas responsáveis pelo EU ETS precisam garantir a entrega da quantidade necessária de EUAs, mesmo que, para cumprir a obrigação, tenham de comprar as licenças com recursos próprios e buscar posteriormente o reembolso da parte contratualmente responsável. Com a ampliação gradual do EU ETS no transporte marítimo, o custo do carbono ganha peso crescente nas operações das armadoras. A partir do próximo ciclo, a exigência passará a abranger 100% das emissões reportadas, aumentando a importância do planejamento financeiro, da gestão contratual e da transferência de licenças entre armadores, afretadores e gestores de navios. artigo.texto: The vivo X Fold6 is finally going global, three months after its original launch in China. vivo's latest foldable combines two 120Hz LTPO displays, a huge battery and a 200MP ZEISS camera system in a surprisingly slim body. The global launch is confirmed , but vivo has not announced international pricing yet. In China, the X Fold6 starts at RMB 7,999, which is around $1,120 before taxes and local pricing differences. Two 120Hz LTPO displays The X Fold6 uses an 8.02-inch 2K+ LTPO AMOLED inner screen with a 2,504 x 2,312 resolution. The cover display measures 6.51 inches and offers 2,528 x 1,120 resolution. Both panels support an adaptive 1-120Hz refresh rate and can reach up to 5,000 nits of local peak brightness. This is one area where vivo clearly wants the X Fold6 to feel like a premium flagship, rather than just another foldable with a large screen. 200MP ZEISS camera The rear camera setup is built around a 200MP main sensor with OIS and ZEISS T* coating. It is joined by a 50MP 3x periscope telephoto and a 50MP ultra-wide camera. The phone also supports 4K 60fps Dolby Vision recording and up to 100x ZEISS HyperZoom. For me, the camera system is one of the strongest parts of the X Fold6. A 200MP main sensor combined with a proper periscope camera gives vivo plenty of hardware to work with. 6,900mAh battery in a slim foldable Inside is a 6,900mAh BlueVolt battery, with 80W wired and 40W wireless charging. The battery uses fifth-generation silicon-anode technology and a third-generation semi-solid-state design. vivo also claims the X Fold6 can deliver up to 9.37 hours of multitasking in Origin Workbench testing. The phone runs OriginOS 7 Fold based on Android 17 globally, with features such as Multi-Split Screen, AI Cross-App Drag, AI Meeting Assistant and AI File Manager. Slim, but built for real use The X Fold6 is just 4.4mm thick when unfolded in Prism Black and weighs 228 grams. It also carries IP58, IP59, IPX8 and IPX9 protection, depending on the market specification. That combination is what makes the X Fold6 interesting to me. vivo is not relying on one big feature. It is trying to make the whole foldable experience better, from the screens and cameras to battery life and multitasking. Now the big question is simple: how much will the X Fold6 cost in Europe? vivo says pricing and availability will be announced separately for each market.

artigo.texto: Abbott says data center permits frozen until power, water concerns addressed HEMPHILL, Texas (KTRE) - Two AI data centers, AmpZ and Hyper Data Grid, are targeting Angelina County, but state permits for the facilities remain on hold. Governor Greg Abbott placed a moratorium on new data centers statewide earlier this month to assess their strain on local resources. During a stop in Hemphill, Abbott drew a hard line on electricity. “They must provide their own power as opposed to taking power off the Texas power grid,” Abbott said. Utility costs and firm purchase agreements Abbott said new facilities must prove they will drive down utility costs for neighboring residents. “Firm purchase agreements for buying a certain amount of electricity. Knowing full well they will not all the time buy that electricity, and that additional supply on the marketplace will then drive down the cost of electricity rates,” Abbott said. Abbott also said cities and counties need more control over where these facilities build, a power local leaders currently lack. Local control over land use Without tax abatement agreements, county leaders have no say on land use. That prompted both Angelina County commissioners and the Lufkin City Council to lobby state lawmakers for regulatory oversight. “And the reason we’re doing this - if we can’t get an abatement, if there’s not going to be an abatement, then there are zero control that we have over these data centers,” said Keith Wright, Angelina County judge. Abbott said he supports giving communities that authority. “Local communities should have the authority and the independence to make their own decision about whether they do or do not want data centers,” Abbott said. Abbott said the state Legislature and the Texas Water Development Board are drafting new rules to prevent data centers from draining local water supplies. The Texas Legislature’s next regular session begins Jan. 12, 2027. Copyright 2026 KTRE. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Por Conrad Fonseca, Head de Energia da Tractebel Brasil, Chile e Canadá. A publicação da Portaria Normativa MME nº 136, de 1º de junho de 2026, consolida as diretrizes e a sistemática do primeiro leilão brasileiro dedicado à contratação de potência elétrica a partir de novos sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias. Mais do que uma inovação regulatória, a medida transforma o BESS em instrumento formal de planejamento da segurança do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), justamente quando o Brasil vive sua maior expansão solar e eólica da história, mas ainda desperdiça parcela relevante da geração renovável potencial por limitações de flexibilidade, transmissão e operação. O primeiro certame, previsto para 2 de dezembro de 2026, será o LRCAP de 2026 – Armazenamento Nacional, restrito a sistemas que atendam a requisitos mínimos de nacionalização, conforme critérios de credenciamento no Sistema CFI do BNDES. O segundo, previsto para 4 de dezembro de 2026, será o LRCAP de 2026 – Armazenamento, aberto aos demais projetos elegíveis de armazenamento em baterias. Juntos, os dois leilões podem representar um passo relevante na formação de um novo mercado de armazenamento no país, associado à queda de 93% nos custos das baterias nos últimos 15 anos e à necessidade crescente de flexibilidade operativa no sistema elétrico brasileiro. A Portaria MME nº 878, de novembro de 2025, cumpriu o papel de abrir a consulta pública e testar o desenho inicial do certame. A Portaria Normativa MME nº 136/2026, agora, consolida a estrutura final: contratação de disponibilidade de potência em megawatts, a partir de novos sistemas de armazenamento eletroquímico conectados ao SIN, com potência mínima de 30 MW, capacidade de operação contínua por pelo menos quatro horas, eficiência total mínima de 85%, tempo máximo de recarga completa de seis horas e atendimento aos requisitos técnicos de conexão definidos por ONS e EPE, incluindo funcionalidades de grid-forming. Os contratos deverão ter prazo de 15 anos, com início de suprimento em 1º de agosto de 2028. A realização dos leilões se apoia na evolução recente do marco legal e regulatório do setor elétrico, que passou a reconhecer o armazenamento como categoria própria e a abrir espaço para sua contratação como recurso de potência, flexibilidade e segurança sistêmica. Na prática, a Portaria Normativa MME nº 136/2026 aproxima o BESS do centro do planejamento operativo e de expansão do SIN, ao transformá-lo em uma alternativa contratável para atender necessidades sistêmicas específicas. O mercado global de BESS viveu em 2025 seu ano mais transformador. O mundo instalou 247 GWh em novos sistemas de baterias no ano passado, um salto de 35% sobre o ano anterior. A projeção para 2035 é de 7,3 TWh, oito vezes o nível atual. Por que o curtailment tornou o BESS urgente Entre 2023 e 2025, o Brasil cortou 48,7 TWh de geração solar e eólica, o equivalente a dez meses inteiros de produção da usina de Belo Monte, ou 8% do consumo nacional anual. Em 2025, segundo a consultoria Volt Robotics, o curtailment médio foi de 20% da energia renovável potencial, com pico solar de 34,1% no terceiro trimestre, e concentração geográfica no triângulo Minas Gerais-Ceará-Rio Grande do Norte, que sozinho acumulou R$ 2,24 bilhões em perdas. O problema tem três causas que se alimentam mutuamente: gargalo de transmissão Nordeste-Sudeste, atualmente 13,8 GW, com 16,4 GW planejados para 2027; sobreoferta ao meio-dia; e critérios operativos mais conservadores adotados pelo ONS após o apagão de 15 de agosto de 2023, quando tecnologias conectadas por inversores falharam em entregar o desempenho dinâmico esperado. Estima-se que apenas 5% dessas perdas sejam efetivamente ressarcidas aos geradores hoje. Um sistema BESS de 500 MW com quatro horas de autonomia, instalado em um ponto adequado do Nordeste, poderia absorver parte relevante do excedente solar que hoje é cortado entre 10h e 14h e devolvê-lo ao SIN no horário de ponta, quando a demanda ultrapassa 100 GW e os preços tendem a se elevar. Em termos financeiros, cada MWh deslocado do piso para o pico pode capturar parte relevante do spread do PLD (Preço de Liquidação das Diferenças), criando uma fonte adicional de receita que, no agregado, pode contribuir para viabilizar o investimento ao longo do tempo. O curtailment, portanto, não é apenas um desperdício contábil: é um dos sinais de mercado mais claros que o sistema elétrico brasileiro tem produzido em favor do armazenamento. A nova portaria reforça essa lógica ao prever mecanismos de competitividade locacional: projetos conectados em pontos do SIN que proporcionem benefícios sistêmicos adicionais poderão receber bonificação para fins de competição no leilão, conforme estudos da EPE e do ONS. Na prática, o desenho regulatório começa a reconhecer que o valor de uma bateria não depende apenas de sua potência ou duração, mas também do ponto exato em que ela reduz restrições de transmissão, alivia áreas críticas, aumenta a confiabilidade do atendimento e melhora a integração das fontes renováveis variáveis. As cinco aplicações que o BESS pode assumir no SIN A aplicação mais consolidada no Brasil é o chamado peak-shaving, que consiste em usar baterias para aliviar a sobrecarga da rede nos horários de maior consumo. O Brasil pode seguir o exemplo do vizinho Chile, onde a Usina Tamaya BESS, localizada em Tocopilla, na região Antofagasta, no norte do país, armazena a energia excedente gerada pela Usina Solar Tamaya para ser injetada no sistema elétrico nos horários de pico de demanda. A usina, que conta com 152 contêiners de baterias de lítio tem um sistema de 68 MW e capacidade de 418 MWh capaz de abastecer mais de 50 mil residências. A segunda aplicação, a arbitragem energética, explora a diferença de preço entre os horários de sobra e de escassez no sistema. artigo.texto: For much of Gov. Wes Moore’s first term, he worked to “supercharge” the development of data centers, seeing them as just the kind of rocket fuel Maryland needed for its stagnating economy. AI’s endless appetite for computing power had the industry booming in nearby Northern Virginia, the data center capital of the world. And building these server farms held even more appeal after President Donald Trump’s moves to dismantle federal agencies hit Maryland’s tax base. But then data center politics rapidly shifted. Now, Democratic- and Republican-led counties across the state have passed development moratoriums, and Moore is trying to balance the allure of an economic driver that has labor support against opposition from environmentalists and community groups. The space between courting data centers and public demand for regulation has narrowed. With Moore considered a 2028 presidential contender, his decisions today could be viewed in a different light by primary voters in two years. Last week, the governor laid out a new review process for data centers and argued that the state needs to change its approach in response to the industry’s expanding scale. Read More “If you’re not protecting your people from this,” he said, “then I think you’re derelict in your duty.” This tough talk on data centers contrasts with the governor’s previous approach. At points, he has smoothed pathways for large-scale data center projects. He’s also opposed legislation to bolster regulatory reviews of data centers, vetoed a study of their energy and environmental impacts, and warned against the repeal of a 2020 industry tax break that has cost the state tens of millions of dollars in forgone revenues. Moore now seems more open to a data center slowdown. Though he has not called for a statewide moratorium, he said last month that he would “absolutely” sign a pause or ban if lawmakers pass one next year. Moore’s recent action follows other governors across the country who have looked to crack down on data centers in response to a public backlash. New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul and Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott have imposed sweeping development stoppages in their states, while others have looked to tighten regulations on data centers’ use of land, water and energy. Chris Borick, a political scientist at Lehigh University, sees similarities in how Moore and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro — another 2028 contender — have evolved on this issue. Both Democrats followed a timeworn playbook. It’s typical for governors to roll out a red carpet for tech investment, using fiscal incentives and relaxing regulatory barriers for industries that promise community investment and lots of jobs. But Borick said the desire for economic success meant both governors turned “a little bit of a blind eye” to data centers’ downsides. One report by the pro-data center Maryland Tech Council estimated that the industry could deliver $16 million annually in state revenues for every million square feet of new development, while counties stand to gain even more from property taxes and benefits packages. “They were primed to buy into the sales pitch,” Borick said. A ‘bright future’ for data centers In the span of a few years, Moore has gone from pitching Maryland as prime territory for data centers to assailing the boom he invited. When state utility regulators in 2023 denied fast-track reviews for massive, diesel-powered backup generators at Maryland’s first hyperscale data center development — a 2,000-acre campus in Frederick County — Moore promised to rewrite policy to “ensure the industry has a bright future” in Maryland. He pushed a bill the next year to roll back reviews of those controversial generators, legislation that the General Assembly approved unanimously. Moore’s office also lent a hand to a wealthy entrepreneur and campaign donor hoping to build a massive data center at an old coal-fired power plant on the Potomac River. After repeated requests from the developer, the state’s top environmental official sent a letter offering expedited approvals for the project. And while Moore’s order last week instituted a new vetting process for data centers, in 2025 he vetoed legislation to study the industry’s energy and environmental consequences. Lawmakers overrode him months later. As the data center debate heated up, Moore said he wanted to prioritize projects that could check certain boxes: employing local union workers, prioritizing clean power and paying for their own electricity needs. Maryland could court economic opportunity without becoming the next “Data Center Alley,” he maintained. In legislative testimony this year, Moore’s Department of Commerce defended the state’s data center tax exemption and opposed a bill to establish new reporting requirements for data center developers, arguing that the measures would “send a message” to data center companies that the “cost of doing business in Maryland is too high and burdensome.” But in recent weeks, Moore’s rhetoric has shifted. On a podcast last month, he said he would sign a statewide pause or ban on data centers should lawmakers put one on his desk next year. At his executive order signing the following week, the governor said Maryland should repeal its data center tax credit, which lawmakers adopted before his term. Asked in an interview about his administration’s reversal, Moore said the state must constantly “pressure test” its laws and that his administration had found this one to be “outdated.” The governor has attributed his pivot to the Trump administration’s recent rollbacks on data center regulations and to the industry’s expanding scale. The impact of today’s data centers “is different,” he said last week. “As a state, we’ve got to have a different type of posture, because we are seeing how the landscape has changed.” Some don’t see it that way. artigo.texto: SAN DIEGO, Sept. 30, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Beam Global (Nasdaq: BEEM), a leading provider of innovative and sustainable infrastructure solutions for energy storage and security, electrification of mobility, and smart city infrastructure, will share developments in its advanced battery technologies for high-power applications, including AI data centers and electric aviation, during the Company’s presentations at The Battery Show North America, in Detroit, on October 12th through the 15th. Beam Global is developing battery energy storage systems designed to manage the extreme power fluctuations generated by the rapidly increasing workloads of AI data centers. The research focuses on high-speed, multi-timescale control strategies that can reduce peak utility demand and required grid capacity while using less battery capacity than conventional approaches. The Company is also applying its proprietary passive thermal management technology to support frequent, high-rate battery cycling while managing battery temperatures and degradation. Beam Global is evaluating its proprietary solutions to address thermal runaway initiation and propagation in high-power and high-energy lithium-ion battery systems for applications including electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft. Testing includes side and bottom nail penetration, external heating and overcharge to evaluate thermal and electrical behavior during cell failure. At the module level, Beam’s engineering and science teams are evaluating how battery architecture, enclosure design, thermal coupling, liquid-cooled cold plates and Beam’s phase-change composite (PCC™) technology affect cell-to-cell thermal propagation. Electro-thermal modeling is being used alongside physical testing to further characterize failure mechanisms and support the development of next-generation battery systems. "Beam’s core competency and protected IP are centered on our ability to deliver high power bursts under extreme operating conditions using our superior engineering and proprietary thermal management solutions,” said Desmond Wheatley, CEO of Beam Global. "These capabilities are becoming increasingly essential for data centers and electric aviation applications like drones and eVTOLs. We are seeing significant increases in demand for our unique approach to these challenges. The Battery Show North America gives us the ideal opportunity to share the advances we are making to the very audiences who are seeking solutions to these critical challenges.” Beam Global's Chief Battery Scientist, Dr. Said Al-Hallaj, and Donald Gilmore, Director of Energy Storage Systems, will present preliminary findings from two of the Company’s research programs. Research into AI data center power transients will be presented by Donald Gilmore on October 13, followed by Dr. Said Al-Hallaj's presentation on thermal runaway in drone and eVTOL battery systems on October 14. Both presenters will be available at Beam’s Booth 3403 for further discussion. The markets for advanced battery technologies are expanding rapidly. According to MarketsandMarkets, the global data center energy storage systems market is projected to grow from $5.17 billion in 2026 to $10.48 billion by 2032, representing a 12.5% CAGR. The global eVTOL battery market is projected to grow from $6.90 billion in 2025 to $26.26 billion by 2032, representing a 21.0% CAGR, according to Fortune Business Insights. About Beam Global Beam Global is a sustainable technology innovator that develops and manufactures infrastructure products and technologies. The Company operates at the nexus of innovative and reliable energy, transportation and smart city solutions with a focus on sustainable energy infrastructure, rapidly deployed and scalable EV charging solutions, safe energy storage, energy security and intelligent infrastructure. With operations in the U.S., Europe and the Middle East, Beam Global develops, patents, designs, engineers and manufactures unique and advanced technology solutions that power transportation, provide secure sources of electricity, enable smart city services, save time and money, and protect the environment. Beam Global is headquartered in San Diego, CA, with facilities in Yuma, AZ; Broadview, IL; Belgrade and Kraljevo, Serbia; and Abu Dhabi, UAE. Beam Global is listed on Nasdaq under the symbol BEEM. artigo.texto: WEG investirá R$ 840 milhões em geradores para atender data centers A WEG anunciou na segunda-feira (28) um investimento de US$ 165 milhões, cerca de R$ 840 milhões, para ampliar a produção de geradores na América do Norte. O plano mira a procura por energia para operações críticas nos Estados Unidos, especialmente data centers. Segundo o comunicado ao mercado, a expansão ocorrerá em duas etapas. A companhia prevê chegar a uma capacidade global de cerca de 50 geradores por dia em 2030, ante os atuais 10. A meta considera as fábricas no México, nos EUA, no Brasil e na China. O investimento amplia os negócios incorporados com a aquisição da Marathon. A expansão dos centros de dados abre mercado para fabricantes de equipamentos elétricos, além de fornecedores de chips e servidores. Expansão começa pelo México A primeira etapa terá US$ 24 milhões para comprar e adaptar um prédio ao lado do parque industrial de Quma I, em Atotonilco de Tula, no México. A unidade fará a montagem de geradores, com início previsto para o segundo trimestre de 2027. A segunda fase receberá US$ 141 milhões para construir duas instalações industriais. A WEG ainda definirá a localização na América do Norte. O projeto inclui a fabricação de componentes, como eixos, carcaças e enrolamentos elétricos. Energia acompanha expansão da IA Os data centers abrigam equipamentos que processam e armazenam informações. A expansão da inteligência artificial aumenta a necessidade de eletricidade e de infraestrutura capaz de manter essas operações. Em relatório publicado em abril de 2026, a Agência Internacional de Energia (AIE) estimou que o consumo mundial de eletricidade dos centros de dados quase dobrará até 2030. A projeção passa de 485 terawatts-hora em 2025 para 950 terawatts-hora no fim da década, cerca de 3% do consumo global. A agência também identificou restrições no fornecimento de equipamentos elétricos e atrasos na conexão de novos projetos às redes. Nos Estados Unidos, essas dificuldades levam desenvolvedores a buscar geração de energia no próprio local. Para a WEG, o plano anunciado busca atender a esse mercado com mais capacidade industrial. O cronograma distribui a expansão até 2030, quando a companhia prevê concluir a segunda etapa. Fonte: WEG, Agência Internacional de Energia. artigo.texto: WASHINGTON — The Senate on Wednesday rejected separate bills to regulate data centers and limit stock trading by members of Congress. Battleground Republicans were hoping to campaign on the bills, but Democrats blocked both measures, saying they don’t go far enough. The two votes failed on the Senate floor in a final burst of business before senators headed home for the election, now less than five weeks away. Republicans scheduled votes on the two campaign issues, hoping to deliver something for battleground Republicans to campaign on. The Stop Insider Trading Act would prohibit most members of Congress and their spouses from trading stocks. The Ratepayer Protection Act is designed to prevent data centers from driving up local electricity rates. “It would simply promote the adoption of a standard that would require data centers to shoulder the electricity costs associated with their operation and construction,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said of the data center bill. Democrats argued the data center bill lacks teeth and is more about political messaging. On the stock trading bill, they accused Republicans of adding a poison pill in the form of new voter ID requirements, and criticized the measure for not forcing lawmakers to sell stock they already own. “The Republican toothless stock trading bill is as ineffective as a screen door on a submarine,” said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. The spread of data centers has emerged as a potent campaign issue in states such as Ohio. Incumbent Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, sponsored the bill in part to counter relentless attack ads from his opponent, former Sen. Sherrod Brown, focused on Husted’s past support of data centers. “If Democrats block this bill, they will prove beyond a shadow of a doubt that they do not care about affordability,” Husted said on the Senate floor. Despite failing in the Senate, both bills had bipartisan support in the House. The Ratepayer Protection Act won the support of nearly all House Democrats, but in the Senate, just four Democrats backed the legislation.

artigo.texto: Publicidade A Samsung concordou em investir US$ 1 bilhão na Helix Digital Infrastructure, empresa de infraestrutura para inteligência artificial (IA) apoiada por KKR e Nvidia, em mais um aporte na corrida global por data centers, energia e redes capazes de sustentar a demanda por IA. O investimento eleva o capital já assegurado pela Helix para mais de US$ 11 bilhões, a ser usado na estratégia de entregar uma nova geração de data centers, geração de energia e transmissão. A Helix foi criada em junho por um consórcio liderado pela KKR, com investidores-âncora que incluem Nvidia, a Kuwait Investment Authority e a Vistra, empresa de geração e varejo de eletricidade. Leia também: OpenAI segura lançamento de novo modelo de IA após falhas em testes de segurança O CEO e cofundador da Helix, Adam Selipsky, disse que o compromisso da Samsung é um “voto de confiança” na estratégia da companhia para atender a uma demanda sem precedentes de grandes provedoras de nuvem por infraestrutura de IA cada vez mais complexa e em alta velocidade. Gigantes como Microsoft (MSFT34), Amazon (AMZO34), Meta (M1TA34) e Alphabet (GOGL34) vêm gastando centenas de bilhões de dólares para expandir infraestrutura de IA. O gasto de capital das quatro empresas chegou a US$ 410 bilhões no ano passado, quase o triplo do nível de 2022. Estimativas do economista Stijn van Nieuwerburgh, publicadas pela Brookings Institution, projetam US$ 10,3 trilhões em investimentos em data centers e infraestrutura relacionada entre 2025 e 2032. Leia também: AMD compra startup de pioneira da IA por US$ 8,2 bilhões Continua depois da publicidade A Helix afirma que, além do papel da Nvidia em tecnologia e infraestrutura de ponta e da Vistra em energia, pretende aproveitar capacidades da Samsung em tecnologia avançada, construção, armazenamento de energia e refrigeração para desenvolver infraestrutura em escala. A Samsung disse que o aporte ajudará suas afiliadas a avançar de fornecedoras de componentes para funções de maior valor em sistemas e infraestrutura de IA. O movimento também ocorre enquanto empresas sul-coreanas ampliam investimentos para capturar o boom de IA. Samsung Electronics e SK Hynix planejam investir mais de US$ 520 bilhões em um polo de semicondutores no sudoeste do país, como parte de uma iniciativa liderada pelo governo estimada em US$ 2 trilhões para desenvolver capacidades domésticas completas em IA. Analistas da BMI, da Fitch Solutions, apontam que a competição deve se intensificar e que projetos maiores podem pressionar preços. Eles também alertam que a rede elétrica pode não acompanhar o ritmo e que regras recentes de licenciamento exigem padrões de eficiência energética, elevando as dificuldades para garantir energia para instalações de IA, intensivas em consumo. Fonte: Dow Jones Newswires. artigo.texto: SAN ANTONIO – San Antonio leaders are looking at whether data centers should be required to use recycled water instead of drinking water as concerns grow about the potential impact of future artificial intelligence facilities. San Antonio’s District 6 Councilman Ric Galvan filed a council consideration request (CCR) almost a year ago to have city staff look into the impact data centers have on city resources and look at the possibility of requiring data centers to use recycled water. Water is used to cool down the industrial servers that data centers use for extended periods of time. Water is also used to produce power for the facilities. KSAT attempted to speak to Galvan about the recycled water proposal, but his office sent a statement. In it, Galvan said he wants to keep data centers from using any drinking water, and in order for a mandate on recycled water usage by data centers can move forward, San Antonio Water System (SAWS) must adopt a policy first, specifically outlining that that is what data centers must do. Donovan Burton, the senior vice president of water resources and governmental relations for SAWS, said when talking about data centers in the city, there must be a distinction made between existing data centers and future AI data centers and their water consumption. He said 23 of the existing data centers in the city account for a very small amount of the water pulled from the city’s water supply. “The existing data centers are very small (and have a) very, very small footprint. In fact, they’re using about .1% of our potable water supply,” Burton said. He said it is the future AI data centers that could potentially use a lot more water, and added SAWS’ Recycled Water Network could help data centers comply if the recycled water use became an official requirement. “Our Recycle Water Network has been in place for over 20 years,” he said. He explained that it is 130 miles of purple pipeline that specifically carries recycled water that is used and paid for by contracted, non-residential customers. “The recycle water programs, after (water) has been used, we treat it and put it into a purple pipe network that goes around ... a good portion of the entire city,” Burton said. “That network then takes it from three different plants, and we can move water back and forth.” SAWS headquarters, CPS Energy, Toyota, the San Antonio Zoo and the River Walk are among the multiple big entities and attractions that are connected in part or entirely to SAWS’ Recycled Water Network, and you can tell by the designated purple pipes present on or near the respective properties. Burton said if a recycled water use restriction is implemented, data center owners would have to choose to obtain a permit from SAWS and enter into a contract for a specific amount of water to connect to the purple pipeline. But he shared there is another option data centers have that can be a conservative measure. “Some of them are going to a closed loop (water) system, which will end up using a lot less water,” Burton said. An internet search on what a closed loop water system is yielded a general definition, describing how data center use the same water or a cooling liquid through sealed pipes to absorb heat and as it moves along the pipe path it removes heat from servers over and over again without pulling in or using fresh water. Until further notice, Burton said SAWS will continue its forward strategy. “It’s a matter of making sure that that works for all future customers, not just a very few one or two or five data centers or anything else,” he said. In the statement sent to KSAT, Galvan said he asked SAWS leadership to come up with a possible plan to move forward with the water usage restriction for new data centers. The statement went on to say he is interested in hearing from SAWS this week as to whether or not the board has made any movement on the proposal over the summer.

artigo.texto: A primeira cena que vemos ao entrar na sede do território indígena Anacé, em Caucaia, na região metropolitana de Fortaleza (CE), é um caminhão-pipa despejando água em uma cisterna. Com cerca de 16 mil litros, o carro-pipa custa R$ 250 e o abastecimento costuma durar seis meses. É nesse cenário de escassez hídrica que, a apenas três quilômetros dali, 70 hectares de vegetação, o equivalente a cerca de 100 campos de futebol, foram devastados para a construção de um data center de inteligência artificial para servir ao TikTok – em um projeto da Casa dos Ventos, empresa de usinas eólicas, e da Omnia, de tecnologia. A instalação deste data center está sendo ruidosa. O Ministério Público Federal (MPF) e a Defensoria Pública da União (DPU) questionam na Justiça a legalidade do licenciamento ambiental, que foi feito com um relatório simplificado, modalidade prevista para empreendimentos de baixo impacto, e pedem que o data center só opere após elaboração de um Estudo de Impacto Ambiental (EIA/Rima). O caso acende um alerta para o que pode acontecer em Pernambuco e em toda a região Nordeste. No dia 15 de setembro, o presidente Lula sancionou a lei do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), que abre as portas do Brasil para o mercado dos data centers de IA, com uma série de benefícios fiscais. Para ter acesso às vantagens do Redata, a empresa precisa, entre outras exigências, atender a toda a sua demanda de energia elétrica com contratos de suprimento ou autoprodução a partir de “fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão”. 1. PIS/Cofins, IPI e Imposto de Importação ficam suspensos na compra de equipamentos de TI listados pelo governo, como servidores e componentes. A suspensão vira alíquota zero quando o equipamento é incorporado ao patrimônio da empresa e ela cumpre as exigências de sustentabilidade, energia, água e pesquisa. Se não cumprir, paga os tributos com juros e multa. 2. O governo estima que os equipamentos respondem por até 85% do custo de instalação de um data center. A Associação Brasileira das Empresas de Software (ABES) calcula que o regime alcance até um terço do investimento total, porque obra, sistema elétrico e refrigeração ficaram de fora. 3. Com a reforma tributária, PIS/Cofins e IPI só ficam suspensos até 31 de dezembro de 2026. Depois sobra o Imposto de Importação, e só para equipamentos sem produção nacional equivalente. 4. Fabricantes nacionais que fornecem equipamentos a data centers habilitados também podem se beneficiar, porque a lei permite que eles sejam coabilitados. Sócia-fundadora do Instituto Terramar, que vem dando suporte aos indígenas Anacé, Soraya Vanini Tupinambá diz que o Nordeste vai ser a “zona sacrificial” do Brasil para a instalação dessas grandes estruturas de computadores. “O Nordeste concentra a maior produção eólica do Brasil, com destaque para Bahia, Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte, Piauí e Pernambuco. Projetou-se uma produção de energia maior do que a capacidade de transmiti-la para o Sudeste pelas linhas de transmissão e de absorvê-la na própria região”, conta Soraya. A ideia anterior era usar essa energia sobressalente na indústria de hidrogênio verde, lembra a ativista. “Todos os estados criaram marcos legais e assinaram memorandos de entendimento, mas as plantas de hidrogênio verde não avançaram como se esperava. É essa sobreoferta de energia que hoje atrai os data centers, ávidos por água e energia”, avalia. O Semiárido do Nordeste, porém, é uma região de escassez hídrica, onde os recursos já são insuficientes para as necessidades das populações locais. “Atrair um setor que também consome muita água é extremamente desafiador. Nos data centers, há um balanço entre água e energia: se usa muita água, gasta-se menos energia; se usa pouca água, gasta-se muita energia. Os impactos são claros. Mesmo num sistema fechado, há perda de água por evaporação e contaminação pelo uso de fluidos e químicos. Por isso, de tempos em tempos, essa água precisa ser reposta. Não existe sistema fechado sem perdas. Para entender os impactos de um data center, é preciso conhecer a eficiência dele no uso da água e da energia”, explica Soraya. O Instituto Terramar acompanhou de perto a luta dos Anacé contra a instalação do data center em Caucaia. Pouco antes de o MPF e a DPU entrarem na Justiça contra o empreendimento, os indígenas Anacé assinaram um acordo com os empresários, para diminuir os impactos na comunidade. O acordo prevê a construção de itens básicos na comunidade, como uma escola e uma horta, e impede os representantes dos Anacé de darem entrevistas criticando o projeto. Fundador do IP.rec – Instituto de Pesquisa em Direito e Tecnologia do Recife, o advogado André Lucas Fernandes, doutor em direito com foco em IA, diz que o Redata é um erro por primeiro conceder benefícios fiscais para as empresas antes de estabelecer regras para que essa instalação tenha menos impactos sociais e ambientais. Também não há como as comunidades saberem previamente sobre a instalação de um data center na vizinhança. “O Redata não garante essa informação para os moradores. Em Caucaia há uma população indígena no entorno, e o Brasil é signatário da Convenção 169 da OIT, que obriga à consulta livre, prévia e informada. Prévia ela já não foi. E agora houve um acordo com a liderança Anacé para que aceitem o data center em troca de coisas que já eram obrigação do Estado: escola, estrada, água, saúde”, critica André Fernandes. Há basicamente dois tipos de data centers. Os chamados edge (de borda) são instalações pequenas, espalhadas e próximas dos usuários, muitas vezes dentro de prédios nas cidades. Servem para reduzir o tempo de resposta da internet (a latência), em aplicações como streaming, internet das coisas ou cirurgia remota. Os que vêm causando problemas mais sérios são os de hiperescala. São complexos gigantescos, com galpões que podem ocupar áreas equivalentes a dezenas de campos de futebol e consumir centenas de megawatts, como o de Caucaia, projetado para 3

artigo.texto: The Lemmo 3 is the first cargo bike from the respected German e-bike maker. This premium, step-through longtail is a slightly less insane take on Rivian’s Also TM-B, with one major advantage: It’s one of the first electric bikes to feature a semi-solid state battery. This very fancy e-bike is one of the first to go semi-solid state The Lemmo 3 has more range, fewer explosions. The Lemmo 3 has more range, fewer explosions. Semi-solid state batteries are far safer than traditional lithium-ion batteries. Their gel-like composition offers improved energy density, with far less risk of thermal runaway. That translates to improved range and longevity from a more compact battery that’s unlikely to catch fire when left charging overnight in your house or business. The semi-solid state electrolyte even remains stable when punctured in a crash. The Lemmo 3 is fitted with a massive 960Wh battery promising up to 180km (110 miles) of range. And by going with a semi-solid state chemistry, the company claims the battery is 20 percent smaller and lighter while still offering 30 percent longer lifespan. The removable battery can also power your AC appliances (up to 1000W) and USB-C devices (up to 66W) once you arrive at your destination, similar to Cake’s now-defunct Ösa. The Lemmo 3 is being marketed as an eSUV just like the Amflow TL Carbon I reviewed. But this very heavy full suspension cargo bike will feel more comfortable on daily commutes to daycare, work, and stores than weekend single tracks. The bike weighs 39kg (86 pounds) with the 5kg (11 pound) battery installed. Instead of doing something proprietary, Lemmo made its longtail compatible with MIK HD accessories. These include a wide variety of child seats, bags, and boxes that can be mounted on the rear rack. It can handle a 200kg (441lb) total load, with 80kg (176lbs) supported in the rear and 20kg (44lbs) on the front rack. A quick-adjust saddle and handlebar makes the Lemmo 3 easily shareable, supporting riders from 155cm (5 feet 1 inch) to 195cm (6 feet 5 inches). The bike is fitted with wide tires on a 24-inch front wheel paired with a smaller 20-inch wheel in the back. Powering this beast is a rear-hub motor (750W in the US, 500W Canada, 250W for Europe). It can deliver up to 90Nm of torque to get heavy loads rolling or to help surmount hills. Naturally, there’s AI baked in as well. The motor and e-derailleur combine data from a variety of sensors to “feed an adaptive Al model that selects the optimal gear in real time, creating a natural, responsive, and effortless ride.” That sounds expensive to fix when the drivetrain eventually needs servicing. The motor can also be paired with a 3-speed auto-shifting gearbox and belt drive for flatter environments. Other features include fully integrated lighting (with turn signals and brake lights), a 3.5-inch touchscreen, a USB-C port to charge your phone, OTA updates, rear-facing radar to alert you of approaching vehicles, and hydraulic brakes that apply stopping power to both wheels simultaneously when pulling just one brake lever. Security features include embedded frame and battery locks and GPS / LTE tracking. The Lemmo 3 already has a teaser page up on Kickstarter that says “launching soon” for the EU, UK, US, and Canada. You can reserve it now for a refundable deposit of €39.90, which locks you into tax-exclusive pricing of €1,890 (or about $2,155). The company says retail pricing will climb well beyond €3,390 (over $3,800). Lemmo is targeting first deliveries for April 2027.

artigo.texto: Jakarta (ANTARA) - Indonesia is offering carbon market incentive schemes to global business leaders investing in green projects across the archipelago, Coordinating Minister for Food Zulkifli Hasan announced during the 81st UN General Assembly and Climate Week NYC 2026. Addressing more than 20 global corporate executives at the High-Level and CEO Forum on Low-Emission Rice and Sustainable Agriculture in New York, the minister emphasized that carbon pricing mechanisms would allow investors to unlock additional financial value from verifiable emissions reductions in Indonesia. "Indonesia is facing a waste emergency that must be addressed immediately, one of which is through waste-to-energy. Therefore, the government is encouraging green investment in the waste sector as a priority," Zulkifli said in a statement on Tuesday (September 29). Zulkifli outlined three primary sectors open to green investment: sustainable agriculture through low-emission rice cultivation, waste-to-energy processing, and marine conservation through blue carbon development. As chair of the Carbon Economic Value (NEK) Steering Committee, he said Jakarta is streamlining regulatory frameworks and strengthening carbon trading governance to ensure high-credibility carbon assets. A key step came on July 6, 2026, when the Financial Services Authority (OJK) enacted POJK No. 10/2026, mandating that all exchange-traded carbon units be formally registered under the Carbon Unit Registry System (SRUK). OJK data as of August 31, 2026, revealed that 159 service users have registered on the Indonesian Carbon Exchange since its inception on September 26, 2023. Total transaction volume reached 1.98 million tons of CO2 equivalent (tCO2e), with a cumulative value of Rp93.90 billion (approximately US$5.24 million). Government projections indicate that the carbon pricing framework could mobilize up to US$5.80 billion in green investment while reducing greenhouse gas emissions by roughly 570 million tCO2e. Beyond waste management, Indonesia is seeking various international partners to scale up low-emission rice production to strengthen domestic food security while reducing agricultural methane emissions. Zulkifli noted that implementing low-emission rice cultivation on a large scale requires technological support, financing, market certainty, and clear economic benefits for farmers. He added that climate action must translate into concrete, field-level projects that directly benefit farmers and coastal communities. artigo.texto: JETOUR G700 2027: price, 59.45-kWh battery and 260 km range The Chinese-market Zongheng G700, known internationally as the JETOUR G700, has gained a much longer-range version for the 2027 model year. Chery presented the updated SUV on September 29. The lineup includes five versions priced at 329,900–442,900 yuan, with temporary benefit prices of 304,900–422,900 yuan. These figures apply to China and should not be treated as pricing for other markets. JETOUR G700 2027 electric range reaches 260 km CLTC Long-range versions use a 59.45-kWh CATL battery, with up to 260 km of electric range under CLTC or 210 km under WLTC. The earlier G700 specification used a 34.13-kWh battery and was rated at 150 km CLTC, so the maximum electric range has increased by 110 km. The three upper trims also receive Huawei Qiankun ADS 5 with a dual-optical-path 896-line lidar. The cabin retains the 35.4-inch panoramic display, a 15.6-inch central screen and the Snapdragon 8255 platform. 665 kW, three locking functions and air suspension The powertrain is essentially unchanged. The CDM-O plug-in hybrid system with a 2.0-liter turbo engine delivers a claimed 665 kW, or about 904 metric hp, and 1135 Nm. The G700 remains a body-on-frame four-wheel-drive SUV with front and rear differential locks, a central energy-management locking function, air suspension and the GAIA off-road mode management system. artigo.texto: Two Workshops on EU-China ETS Cooperation Successfully Held in Wuhan On 16 September, the EU-funded project ‘EU-China Dialogue and Cooperation on ETS-related Policies and Measures’ organised two public workshops as official side-events during the 2026 China Carbon Market Conference in Wuhan. The workshops were hosted jointly by the European Commission and the Chinese Ministry of Ecology and Environment (MEE). It brought together senior officials, experts, and crucial stakeholders from China, the European Union, Brazil, the World Bank and UNEP, offering the audience engaged in China's national carbon market and observers from other parts of the world the latest policy developments and insightful opinions on the EU, Chinese, Brazilian, and international carbon markets, as well as the priorities of ongoing EU-China ETS cooperation. European Union, 2026 The morning workshop presented the main outcomes of the Joint Research Activity (JRA) on the conception and implementation of allowance auctioning in China's national ETS. Mr. LU Shize, Deputy Director-General of the Department of Climate Change of MEE, received three joint research reports on behalf of MEE from Mette QUINN, Deputy Director for Carbon Markets and Clean Mobility at DG CLIMA, and thanked the EU for its continued support to the joint research. The afternoon session turned to the important role and challenges of cap setting, a fundamental element for the credibility and environmental integrity of any emissions trading system. Following opening remarks by Ms QUINN and Mr LU, Ms QUINN shared the European Union's experience of setting the cap under the EU ETS. A highlight of the afternoon was the formal launch of the Joint Research on cap-setting supported under the EU project. European Union, 2026 Both workshops underscored the value of lessons-learnt from EU ETS on core ETS design elements. By combining international experience with China's specific institutional context, the project's joint research activities aim to provide a solid evidence base to support the inauguration of allowance auctioning and cap setting under China's national carbon market. Learn more about the ETS project https://www.eu-chinaets.org/

artigo.texto: Stryten Energy Completes Acquisition of C&D Trojan, Creating a Leading Battery Manufacturing Platform for Transportation, Industrial, Critical Infrastructure and Military Applications Creates one of North America’s most comprehensive battery manufacturing and energy storage portfolios serving transportation, golf cart, marine, specialty motive, industrial, critical infrastructure, military and government markets Establishes a footprint of 15 U.S. manufacturing plants to support American energy independence, industrial resilience and military readiness Strengthens global presence to better serve customers worldwide through operations in Mexico and China and offices across Europe and AsiaExpands AGM battery manufacturing capacity to meet the growing demand for start-stop and hybrid vehicle applications ALPHARETTA, Ga.–(BUSINESS WIRE)–Stryten Energy LLC (“Stryten” or “Stryten Energy”) today announced the successful completion of its acquisition of C&D Technologies, Inc. and Trojan Battery Company, LLC (“C&D Trojan”), creating one of North America’s most comprehensive battery manufacturing and energy storage companies, with expanded capabilities across transportation, essential power, industrial, military and government markets. The combined company operates 18 battery manufacturing and component facilities across the U.S., Mexico and China and employs approximately 4,800 people worldwide, significantly expanding Stryten’s manufacturing scale, global reach and customer support capabilities. The company will continue to operate under the Stryten Energy name while preserving the C&D Technologies and Trojan Battery product brands. Terms of the transaction were not disclosed. Mike Judd, Chief Executive Officer and President of Stryten Energy, said: Today, we are proud to officially welcome the talented employees of C&D Trojan to the Stryten Energy team. ”Together, we bring decades of manufacturing expertise, innovation and customer commitment as one company. We intend to accelerate investments in domestic battery manufacturing capacity, advanced energy storage technologies and military production capabilities, creating a stronger company with the scale, technology portfolio and manufacturing capabilities to support growing customer demand across transportation, specialty motive, data center, telecommunications, industrial and military applications. As we begin this next chapter together, we move forward as One Company. Powering What’s Possible.” Expanding U.S. Manufacturing Stryten expects to make strategic investments in U.S. battery manufacturing capacity, facility modernization, equipment upgrades and workforce development. These investments are intended to strengthen domestic production capabilities across advanced lead and lithium battery technologies while supporting long-term American manufacturing competitiveness. In addition, the company plans to expand its Absorbent Glass Mat (AGM) battery manufacturing capacity to meet growing demand from automotive aftermarket customers for start-stop and hybrid vehicle applications requiring high-performance batteries. Judd, said: The addition of C&D Trojan significantly expands our ability to serve the automotive aftermarket with advanced AGM battery technology. ”As vehicle electrification continues to evolve, AGM batteries remain a critical technology for start-stop systems, hybrid and advanced electrical loads. By expanding domestic AGM manufacturing capacity, we are strengthening our ability to provide our customers with reliable, high-performance energy storage solutions while reinforcing U.S. battery manufacturing leadership,” Strengthening Military Production Capacity The combination of the companies’ military battery portfolios creates one of the most comprehensive domestic battery platforms supporting U.S. defense, government and national security applications. Planned investments will support the scaling of U.S.-based manufacturing capacity to meet increasing demand for batteries used in land warfare systems, air defense systems, Naval surface/undersea systems, logistics, reserve power systems, nuclear power and other essential infrastructure. The combined platform strengthens the domestic industrial base while supporting secure access to mission-critical battery technologies. Paul Hastings LLP served as legal counsel for Stryten. Jefferies served as financial advisor and Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton and Garrison LLP as legal counsel for C&D Trojan. artigo.texto: Alabama data center law takes effect Oct. 1: Here’s what it means for your power bill BIRMINGHAM, Ala. (WBRC) - Kirsten Allen bought her home in Birmingham’s Oxmoor Valley for quiet streets and long-term equity. Now, a data center and substation are planned near her property and she has broad concerns about what’s ahead. “We got notified through our HOA that Oxmoor Valley was targeted for a data center,” Allen said. “There was a meeting at our community center so we could learn more about the impact it would have. That’s where I got really involved, because I realized a lot of the impact was going to be on our resources and that the residents were going to pay the price, while the data center was getting tax incentives and cheap property.” Those concerns also involve whether the data center will increase her utility bills. “Both Alabama Power and Birmingham Water have said, ‘Oh, there won’t be any rate increases,’” Allen said. “But none of us homeowners have gotten any contracts saying this is a guarantee.” The closest thing Allen may get to that guarantee is a new law that goes into effect Oct. 1, which sets the rules the state must use to decide whether a data center’s contract keeps its costs off other customers’ bills. A WBRC 6 News investigation examined the law, the contracts filed since the commission began reworking its review process and how much of that process the public is allowed to see. The reason it matters to every ratepayer: Traditionally, electric utilities build infrastructure and spread the cost to everyone who uses the grid. “The utility builds all that infrastructure and then it spreads the cost to everyone, and we all pay for that infrastructure through our monthly bills,” said Ari Peskoe, director of Harvard Law School’s Electricity Law Initiative, which studied whether regulators can shield residential customers from data center costs. “Figuring out the right formula to apportion these costs among all different users is always a source of controversy.” What the law requires The law applies to data centers that need 150 megawatts or more of electricity at peak demand in Alabama Power’s service territory. For perspective, that’s about as much electricity as roughly 95,000 average Alabama homes use in a month while running around the clock, based on federal energy data. Those data centers sign large-load contracts with the utility and those contracts must be approved by the state’s utility regulators, the Alabama Public Service Commission (APSC). Under the law, the APSC can approve a data center energy contract if it’s expected to: - Pay the extra costs the utility takes on to serve it: Power generation, transmission lines, fuel and taxes. - Benefit the utility’s other customers, weighing whether the deal could lower costs for other customers, makes Alabama Power’s system more efficient, and benefits the local economy. APSC President Cynthia Almond explained the law isn’t much different than customer protections the commission had already put in place to consider these contracts. “We require that data centers pay their fair share of any incremental costs that are incurred from their project,” Almond explained, noting all additional costs for transmission, energy generation or infrastructure to service this data center must be paid by the company bringing the data center. “The second thing is that, due to the increased revenue from the data center, there be downward pressure on rates for existing customers. That’s you and me.” Other items include billing requirements, minimum contract lengths and some costs to be paid up front, according to Almond. The public versions of the contracts are heavily redacted. The pricing, contract length and minimum billing terms are blacked out. There’s no public hearing and no public vote. The APSC and the Alabama Attorney General’s Office, which represents ratepayers in the proceedings, receive unredacted copies. Alabama Power declined an on-camera interview, but defended the redactions in writing. “Publishing negotiated terms could weaken Alabama Power’s ability to secure strong protections for existing customers in future negotiations, as well as the data center customer’s ability to negotiate elsewhere,” stated company spokesperson Teisha Wallace. When asked what Almond would tell people who are wary of that secrecy, she said “Times are changing. Transparency is important, and we have ways of being more transparent than we used to be able to do, frankly. So, I’m hopeful that we will be able to put anything out in the open, that we’re able to put out in the open.” Energy Alabama, a clean energy nonprofit, believes there’s a way to build data center infrastructure in a way that won’t impact residential ratepayers, but says transparency is key. “Even if everybody is doing the right thing, if you’re not showing your work, no one’s going to believe you,” said Energy Alabama’s executive director, Daniel Tait. While the law goes into effect Oct 1, the APSC still has broad authority to determine how it will review these contracts and how much access the public will have. On July 8, the APSC opened a proceeding asking the public how it should review these contracts. It also extended the review window for data center contracts filed during that proceeding to 45 days, up from the 10-day review that’s been standard since 1996. (If the APSC doesn’t disapprove a contract within the review period, it’s automatically deemed approved.) The commission has proposed a 60-day window going forward. The Alabama Attorney General’s Office, Alabama Power, Energy Alabama and other businesses and residents filed written statements in that proceeding. Three large-load contracts have been filed since the proceeding began in July: - ADC Holdings, LLC - connected to the Nebius AI project in Oxmoor Valley, near Allen’s home has been deemed approved. - Wooster, LLC and APLD BHM-01 LLC (tied to Applied Digital in Tuscaloosa County) are still under review. artigo.texto: Commission Endorses Milwaukee Data Center Moratorium After Fiery Hearing After two hours of testimony, planners unanimously backed a one-year halt on new facilities citywide. A proposed data center moratorium for the City of Milwaukee received its first endorsement Monday, but only after nearly two hours of discussion on the proposal’s legal limits and testimony for and against it. The proposal would prohibit construction of new data centers for up to one year. Ald. Marina Dimitrijevic said AI and data centers have become some of the public’s hottest issues. “That’s what this is all about. Listening to what the people wanted,” said Dimitrijevic. “What’s happening is technology is moving at such a fast speed. We’re in an interesting time to live right now. Government can’t keep up, but we’re being asked to, though, and we need to rise to that occasion.” She framed the proposal as a “pause” and not an end to data center development. The pause, she said, would allow the city to craft zoning regulations to respond to the energy and water use of data centers, as well as their design and noise impacts. “This is not us closing the book,” said Dimitrijevic. The moratorium would be rescinded after one year or after a zoning framework is adopted, whichever comes first. The alderwoman has already introduced a draft framework, but the proposal has yet to move through the public hearing process. Department of City Development Planning Manager Tanya Fonseca said the moratorium is a “stopgap” measure because the current zoning code doesn’t even define what a data center is. The proposal has the support of Mayor Cavalier Johnson and his administration. A number of the individuals who spoke in support of the moratorium, including Stacy Smiter and Mabel Lamb, also showed up to oppose the redevelopment of the vacant Midtown Center Walmart, 5825 W. Hope Ave., into a mixed-use facility with a library, self-storage complex, affordable housing and a 19,000-square-foot data center. Dimitrijevic’s proposed data center zoning regulations, developed before the proposal was revealed, wouldn’t have affected it because it was under 20,000 square feet. Support for a moratorium is far from unanimous. Joel Roberts, a tech entrepreneur who founded Shepherd Traffic and a doctoral student at UW-Milwaukee, said data centers would provide the city tax revenue and that a number of facilities already existed in the city, like the Forest County Potawatomi Community‘s data center at 3135 W. Highland Blvd. “We’re not morons. We’re smart. We can do this,” he said. But the general manager of the Potawatomi data center, Data Holdings CTO Ryan Brooks, said he supports the moratorium. “It is a public data center, not a hyperscaler. It has been here operating in Milwaukee since 2013. We have about 80 customers,” said Brooks. Unlike the billion-dollar “hyperscale” campuses that Microsoft, Oracle and others are building, Brooks said the Potawatomi facility is modest in scale, solar powered and a good neighbor. A pending amendment to the proposal, listed as being offered by Ald. Robert Bauman, would exempt Potawatomi from the moratorium. It previously appeared in the council’s legislative file but is no longer included. Potawatomi did not respond to an earlier request for comment on the proposed exemption. Letters in opposition to the moratorium were submitted by Andrew Davis of the Metropolitan Milwaukee Association of Commerce and Chris Mambu Rasch of Building Advantage. “The city should reject the moratorium and instead act promptly through its existing public-review process to establish clear, predictable and enforceable standards that address community concerns without sacrificing economic growth, job creation and Milwaukee’s regional competitiveness,” wrote Davis in a letter to the council. “Rather than implementing industrywide pauses or reverting to overly restrictive de facto bans, the Common Council should use the special use or conditional use zoning process. A formalized special use review ensures the city can rigorously evaluate legitimate concerns — such as energy grid capacity, noise, sustainability and neighborhood compatibility — without shutting the door on high-value, responsible development,” wrote Mambu Rasch. But many supporters spoke to concerns about unknown impacts. “We need a pause. What we can’t do is approve development when we don’t know what the impact would be,” said Metcalfe Park Community Bridges Deputy Director Melody McCurtis. She said if development was allowed to occur immediately on land already zoned for heavy industrial use, it would disproportionately impact Black and Brown residents because of where that land is located. Ald. Alex Brower said the economy has become a “techno-nightmare” and he’s committed to working to address the resulting issues. After more than an hour of public testimony, acting Commission Chair Allyson Nemec and Commissioner Ranell Washington thanked all of the participants for presenting a wide range of viewpoints. The commission voted unanimously for the moratorium. Commissioners Stephanie Bloomingdale and Catrina Crane were excused from the meeting. The proposal next heads to the Common Council for review. In addition to Dimitrijevic and Brower, the proposal is cosponsored by Sharlen P. Moore, Bauman and Russell W. Stamper, II. artigo.texto: Located in Terang, in the state of Victoria, the project has a capacity of 100 MW/200 MWh, helping to strengthen the stability and resilience of the electricity grid. The commissioning of Terang marks a crucial milestone for FRV Australia, as it becomes the company’s first standalone battery energy storage project, increasing its portfolio of operational assets in Australia to nine and adding dispatchable energy capacity to FRV Australia's predominantly solar generation portfolio. The project was further bolstered by an $7 million grant awarded through the second round of the Victorian Government’s Energy Innovation Fund (EIF), supporting the deployment of new grid-forming inverter technology. This initiative forms part of the Victorian Government’s efforts to achieve its target of 65 percent renewable energy generation by 2030. Canadian Solar served as EPC contractor for the project, with TEC-C delivering the balance-of-plant works. The facility incorporates 48 SolBank 3.0 e battery containers, manufactured by e-Storage, and 38 SMA inverters. The project supported approximately 40 full-time-equivalent roles during the construction and generated business and procurement opportunities for local companies and suppliers. As part of their commitment to the communities in which they operate, FRV Australia supported several social initiatives throughout the development of the project, including sponsorship programmes for the Australian Indigenous Education Foundation (AIEF) and the Terang Mortlake Netball Club. “The commissioning of Terang marks a defining moment for FRV Australia” said Michael Steiner, CEO of FRV Australia. “The project demonstrates our ability to develop and operate utility-scale dispatchable energy infrastructure that supports Australia’s energy transition. It provides critical firming capacity during peak hours while helping to strengthen grid reliability. We are proud to contribute to Victoria’s energy future through a solution that combines sustainability, innovation and benefits for local communities.” Terang forms part of FRV Australia's expanding battery energy storage portfolio in Victoria. The company is developing the 250 MW/500 MWh Gnarwarre Battery Energy Storage System, currently under construction and targeted for completion by the end of 2027. artigo.texto: The 15 MW/60 MWh Albispark battery energy storage system, located in Castelo Branco, is integrated with an existing 34.4 MWp solar plant, making it one of the largest battery energy storage systems currently in operation in Portugal. The project represents an important milestone for both companies. For Prosolia Energy, Albispark is its first international utility-scale battery storage [DF1] hybridisation project, while for Trina Storage it marks the company's first commissioned battery storage installation in Portugal, supporting the country's transition towards a more flexible, renewable-based electricity system. “The successful commissioning of Albispark represents an important milestone for Trina Storage in Portugal” said Gabriele Buccini, Head of Trina Storage Europe at Trinasolar. “As our first operational battery storage project in the country, it demonstrates our ability to deliver integrated utility-scale storage solutions that support Europe's evolving energy landscape. We are proud to partner with Prosolia Energy on this landmark project and look forward to supporting many more storage deployments across Portugal in the coming years.” Under the project, Trina Storage supplied an integrated utility-scale battery energy storage solution, including Elementa battery cabinets, power conversion systems (PCS), medium-voltage skids, power plant controller (PPC) and commissioning services, delivering a complete solution designed to maximise renewable energy utilisation while supporting grid flexibility. As Portugal continues to increase renewable generation, battery energy storage is becoming essential for improving grid stability, increasing renewable utilisation and providing greater operational flexibility. The Albispark project demonstrates how hybrid solar-plus-storage systems can enable renewable energy to be stored and dispatched when demand is highest, helping maximise the value of renewable generation while strengthening grid resilience. “Albispark is an important milestone for Prosolia Energy and demonstrates the value that battery storage brings to the energy transition” added Pedro Pereira da Silva, Country Manager of Prosolia Energy in Portugal. “Together with Trina Storage, we have delivered a project that improves grid flexibility and reinforces the foundations for future hybrid renewable projects in Portugal.” The commissioning of Albispark marks the beginning of Trina Storage's expansion in Portugal. In addition to this project, the company is currently supporting several battery energy storage projects across the Portuguese market[FT2] [CC3], reflecting growing demand for utility-scale storage as the country accelerates renewable energy deployment and grid modernisation. The project also forms part of Portugal's Recovery and Resilience Plan (PRR), supporting the country's efforts to increase grid flexibility and accelerate renewable energy integration.
