artigo.texto: Key takeaway:In the third quarter of 2026, the solid-state battery industry is at a critical stage of transition from “pilot-scale validation” to “the eve of mass production.” National-level special plans have been implemented, and the standards system is being accelerated and improved. On the materials side, sulfide electrolytes are seeing “rising volume and falling prices,” entering a transition period of ton-level volume ramp-up. On the technology side, solid-liquid (semi-solid) batteries are the first to be deployed in scenarios such as commercial vehicles, energy storage, and eVTOL, while pilot lines for all-solid-state batteries are being built intensively. Capital and industry are collaborating deeply, equipment orders continue to be secured, and downstream application scenarios are flourishing in multiple areas. At the same time, however, risks such as insufficient capacity utilization, lagging orders, and interface and manufacturing bottlenecks remain, requiring a rational view of the pace of industrialization. Foreword: Material Price Analysis—Policy Side Hot, Spot Side Cold, Sulfide “Rising Volume, Falling Prices” In Q3 2026, the solid-state battery sector showed a striking divergence: “hot on the policy side, cold on the materials spot side.” On September 28, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and six other departments issued the “15th Five-Year Plan for the Development of the New Battery Industry,” clarifying preliminary large-scale application of all-solid-state batteries by 2030, which drove the battery sector and solid-state battery sector stronger on September 29. However, on the materials spot side, the pricing anchor centered on lithium salts declined unilaterally, and sulfide electrolytes showed a typical pattern of “rising volume, falling prices.” On lithium salts, the average spot price of battery-grade lithium carbonate in Q3 was about RMB 148,000/ton. At the end of the quarter, the quotation on September 29 for battery-grade lithium carbonate was RMB 123,000/ton, with a Q3 cumulative decline of -22.9%. On solid-state-battery-specific materials, sulfide electrolytes were the segment with the most obvious “price collapse” this quarter. From January to August 2026, China’s cumulative output of sulfide electrolytes was 70 tons, up 119.7% year-on-year, already exceeding the full-year 2025 output of 58.29 tons, but only 19.6% of the annual forecast target of 360 tons was completed. In August, capacity utilization was only 5.82%, product prices continued to plummet, and LPSC fell by more than 24% in a single month. Lithium sulfide also ramped up simultaneously: in August, China’s battery-grade lithium sulfide output was 7.79 tons, up 3.6% month-on-month and up 143% year-on-year; the January-August cumulative total was 52.9 tons, already exceeding the global full-year 2025 output of 34 tons. China’s output accounts for about 95% of the world total. It is expected that monthly output in Q4 will rise to 9–10 tons, with full-year output of 85–95 tons. On the supply side, Q3 saw the concentrated landing of “hundred-ton-level” production lines: Tinci Materials’ hundred-ton-level lithium sulfide and solid electrolyte pilot line was completed and put into production in Q3; Shandong Chuanglu’s 150-ton/year solid electrolyte production line completed installation and commissioning; Capchem’s oxide electrolyte will put thousand-ton-level capacity into operation in 2026. However, in the first half of the year, both supply and demand for lithium sulfide and sulfide electrolytes were weak, and price pressure was the main theme of Q3. Anode materials were relatively resistant to decline, and additives were structurally strong. Overall, the solid-state battery materials sector has entered a transition stage from “kilogram-level transactions” to “ton-level transactions,” with the price center moving downward. Q4 needs to verify the quality of ton-level volume ramp-up. I. Solid-State Battery Materials - Electrolytes: Sulfide Upstream Volume Rises but Prices Remain Under Pressure; Oxide Capacity Takes the Lead in Scaling; Halides Accelerate Reserve The sulfide route was the most intensively expanded direction on the materials side in Q3. The high-purity lithium sulfide pilot line of a subsidiary controlled by Semcorp has been completed, with plans to achieve thousand-ton-level mass production of sulfur-halide solid electrolytes in 2026–2027. Tinci Materials’ hundred-ton-level lithium sulfide and solid electrolyte pilot line was completed and entered trial production in Q3, using a self-developed liquid-phase method with costs 30%–40% lower than the mainstream solid-phase method. XTC New Energy’s high-purity lithium sulfide entered trial production. Yahua Group’s lithium sulfide pilot line entered the demonstration and design stage and has been sent to customers for samples. Tianqi Lithium’s 50-ton lithium sulfide pilot project is under construction and is expected to be completed in the second half of the year; most processes for argyrodite-type sulfide electrolyte preparation have been removed from glove boxes. Gotion Holding’s world’s first ten-thousand-ton-level high-purity lithium sulfide line started in Anqing, with plans to complete pilot testing by the end of 2026 and full mass production in 2027, with purity reaching 99.99%. Qinghai Weixiang’s 3,000-ton lithium sulfide project completed filing, with Phase I of 500 tons and Phase II of 2,500 tons, planned for completion in July 2027. Easpring’s sulfide electrolyte has entered small-scale validation with leading solid-state battery customers and has scalable supply capability. Guoci Materials’ sulfide solid electrolyte automated production line was completed, with a strategic focus on sulfides. Langu New Energy’s sulfide and halide solid electrolytes have achieved hundred-ton-level capacity, with the next step planned to expand to thousand-ton or even ten-thousand-ton levels. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred The two candidates to become California’s next governor painted vastly different portraits of the state they want to lead during a televised CNN debate Wednesday night — though they both agreed the state faces tremendous challenges. Democrat Xavier Becerra, leading in polls, cast the state as an economic engine and a critical bulwark against the disastrous economic policies and creeping authoritarianism of the Trump administration, but also a victim of Trump policies, including tariffs and the war in Iran, that have made life less affordable and the nation less safe. Becerra said he would work hard to help struggling Californians — including by cutting red tape on housing and regulating AI to ensure it doesn’t destroy jobs — while his challenger, Republican Steve Hilton, would harm them further by backing President Trump’s agenda at every turn. Hilton, endorsed by Trump, blamed the state’s most entrenched ills on years of Democratic governance, awash in unnecessary state bureaucracy and regulation that have made it wildly unaffordable, and wrongly obsessed with fighting the president instead of bringing down costs and fixing related local issues like homelessness. Hilton said he would help struggling Californians by cutting taxes, cutting the cost of building new housing, eliminating fraud and bringing common sense back to state policy-making. Both candidates came out of the gate on offense, and at times it got intensely personal, particularly on immigration — with Becerra accusing Hilton of welcoming white immigrants into the country while rejecting Latino immigrants, and Hilton accusing Becerra of handing migrant children over to sex and labor traffickers during his time as U.S. Health and Human Services secretary. With ballots soon arriving in voters’ mailboxes and the Nov. 3 midterm election rapidly approaching, the hour-long debate — moderated by CNN anchors Jake Tapper and Dana Bash in Burbank and aired live by the national news network — provided the public with its latest look at two candidates vastly different both in politics and campaign style. Becerra, a former Congress member from Los Angeles, California attorney general and Health secretary under President Biden, surged past a slate of other Democrats to win the June primary after onetime front runner Rep. Eric Swalwell dropped out of the race amid sexual assault allegations. Hilton placed second after Republican voters and others coalesced behind his message to shake up Sacramento — earning him the right to face off against Becerra in November. Hilton, a former British political aide, former Fox News host and Silicon Valley entrepreneur, has been crisscrossing the state looking for votes anywhere he can find them — an uphill battle given registered Democrats outnumber Republicans by a nearly 2-to-1 margin, and opposition to Trump is widespread in the state and growing even among Republican voters. A poll this month by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times found 58% of likely voters surveyed said they support Becerra, compared with 33% who back Hilton — a slight increase to Becerra’s lead compared with an August IGS poll. California voters identified the high cost of living as their top concern, but that was followed closely by opposition to the Trump administration. The same poll found found that 76% of Republican voters in the state approve of the president’s performance, down from 83% last year. Becerra has taken a less visible approach to campaigning, with critics accusing him of intentionally keeping a low profile in an effort to cruise to victory in a state that last elected Republicans to statewide office two decades ago. “I just want to say thank you to CNN for bringing Xavier out of hiding,” Hilton said at the beginning of Wednesday’s face-off. “He’s barely been seen in public since the primary four months ago; it’s very important we have this debate.” During the debate, both candidates seemed prepared to focus on the lack of affordability — namely by blaming the other’s political party for it. But they also discussed artificial intelligence and data centers, immigration policy and, of course, Trump. Tackling gas prices, high cost of living California has some of the highest housing and energy costs in the nation, and affordability tops the list of concerns for likely voters. It also was the first issue the candidates debated. Hilton has made the cost of living a central theme of his campaign, with a plan he calls “Califordable” to cut gas prices and end income taxes on earnings up to $150,000. He blamed California’s high costs on Democrats, who have controlled the Legislature and statewide offices for more than 15 years. Hilton says he can lower costs by slashing onerous state regulations on businesses. Hilton said the “quickest way to get more money in people’s pockets is for the government to take less out” and to reduce regulations to allow more housing to be built — including in “10 new cities” he said he would help build in the state. Becerra has blamed higher prices on Trump’s tariffs and the war against Iran. In response to attacks from the U.S. and Israel, Iran has for months choked off a major oil trade route, sending global gas prices soaring — to a national average of $4.48 per gallon this month. Becerra said Hilton’s plan to end income taxes would amount to a massive tax cut for “billionaires and millionaires” that would take money from schools, healthcare and other critical services. “The math doesn’t add up to what he’s talking about. He’s going to have to take it out of somewhere. It will come out of our schools,” Becerra said. artigo.texto: $200M Indiana Battery Storage Plan Gains County Approval A planned 200-MW battery storage project in deep southwestern Indiana cleared an important local hurdle this month. Vanderburgh County Commissioners approved a request to site the $200 million Elliot Battery Energy Storage System near a Centerpoint Energy utility substation in Scott Township. The project reportedly would store excess wind and solar energy to deploy during periods of peak demand and high prices. The concept of the Elliot BESS was created by German-based RWE’s Americas renewable energy division in 2024. RWE Americas has or is developing more than 13 GW of wind, solar and battery storage capacity in the U.S. “Elliot BESS adds critical capacity to Indiana’s power grid, helping to stabilize electricity supplies and strengthen the state’s overall energy infrastructure,” reads RWE Americas website detailing the project still under development and with no announced timeline. “Through its advanced battery technology, Elliot BESS can discharge stored energy instantly, providing much-needed backup during emergency events such as storms or unexpected outages. By offering rapid-response power and improving the integration of intermittent generation like wind and solar, this project reduces reliance on imported fuels and supports state-of-the-art grid resiliency.” Total U.S. battery storage installed capacity topped 52 GW nationwide this summer and has risen 70% over the past three years, according to federal data. Energy storage systems are valued both for storing renewables and smoothing out intermittencies of solar and wind, but also having versatility to deal with fluctuations in data center loads. The facility is named after nearby Elliot Road in Vanderburgh County. The 41-acre project still requires other regulatory approvals before going into construction. RWE Americas has not named a specific battery supplier for Elliot BESS, but companies such as Samsung and SMA Americas were selected to supply the developer’s Cartwheel and Crowned Heron battery installations under way in Texas. artigo.texto: Gotion will invest 1.1 billion euros to acquire 49 percent of Volkswagen’s battery gigafactory in Sagunto. The move cements a powerful alliance and signals a new era for European battery production. Volkswagen’s battery gigafactory in Sagunto, Valencia, is still under construction. Now, Gotion is putting 1.1 billion euros on the table for a 49 percent stake. The deal was confirmed on September 28, 2026. Both companies say this is part of Volkswagen’s push to build a local battery supply chain in Europe, as reported by Reuters. The agreement still needs regulatory and shareholder approval. If it goes through, Gotion and Volkswagen’s PowerCo will run the plant together. This site is set to become Europe’s main hub for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery production. Europe has depended on Chinese-made LFP battery cells for years. That could change. Volkswagen and Gotion want to build a regional supply chain and cut that reliance. The Sagunto plant will anchor a network of joint ventures. These will stretch from Spain to Slovakia and Morocco. All will focus on LFP cell and cathode material manufacturing. Volkswagen Group’s official press release says the Valencia project is meant for a joint venture, with PowerCo and Gotion sharing management. The partnership goes beyond Valencia. PowerCo will put 470 million euros into new plants in Surany, Slovakia, and Kenitra, Morocco. It will take a 49 percent stake in each. These sites, together with Sagunto, are designed to speed up the rollout of affordable, robust LFP batteries across Europe. The companies call this technology “competitive prices, long life and great robustness.” Anadolu Agency and other industry sources confirm the total investment for these joint ventures in Europe and North Africa is about 1.5 billion euros. PowerCo will keep a 51 percent majority in the Sagunto joint venture. The original investment of over 2.3 billion euros stands. So does the promise of more than 1,500 direct jobs in the first phase. Both companies have publicly promised to keep jobs and investment levels in the region. Joint management will oversee the next steps. El Norte de Castilla reports these commitments have been reaffirmed after the new partnership structure. Volkswagen is also making a financial move. The group has signed binding agreements to sell a 5.3 percent stake in Gotion. The goal is to optimize its shareholder structure and deepen long-term synergies. Volkswagen will still hold a significant stake in Gotion. This should help keep the alliance stable. Industry analysts say the LFP battery market in Europe is set for rapid growth. Market share could jump from about 10 percent now to as much as 40–60 percent by 2030. But Volkswagen admits Europe still lacks real LFP production capacity. This deal aims to close that gap. According to just-auto and other sector analysts, the Sagunto project is expected to help Europe rely less on imported Chinese LFP cells. Spain’s car industry has seen a surge of foreign investment and new competition. A recent report on the changing landscape among carmakers highlights this trend. The Gotion-Volkswagen alliance adds a new chapter. Valencia is now a key player in Europe’s electric future. This deal is not just about money. It is a clear move to secure technology and supply chain strength in a market long dominated by Asia. By building LFP battery production in Spain and expanding into Slovakia and Morocco, Volkswagen and Gotion are not just reacting to demand. They are shaping the next phase of European electromobility. The size of the investment, the job guarantees, and the focus on affordable battery tech all point to a strategy that could change Europe’s place in the global auto supply chain.

artigo.texto: Plataformas Broadcast Soluções de Dados e Conteúdos Soluções de Tecnologia 1 de outubro de 2026, às 15:19 Com a contratação de 410 profissionais nesta quinta-feira, 1º, a BYD alcança a marca de 8,5 mil colaboradores diretos no complexo industrial de Camaçari (BA). A meta da companhia é atingir 10 mil contratações até o fim de 2026. Inaugurada em outubro de 2025, a unidade é a maior fábrica da BYD fora da Ásia. A capacidade inicial de produção é de 150 mil veículos por ano, podendo chegar a 600 mil quando o projeto estiver completo. De acordo com a companhia, a nova rodada de contratações acompanha o avanço das próximas fases industriais do complexo, que até o final do ano deve iniciar as operações das fábricas de soldagem, pintura e estamparia. As vagas preenchidas são compostas majoritariamente por operadores de produção e logística. Os profissionais serão alocados no terceiro turno da produção da fábrica de montagem final e fábrica de soldagem, reforçando o quadro operacional para atender à demanda de veículos da marca no país. Do total de novos colaboradores, mais de 90% são baianos e metade deles moradores de Camaçari. Em nota, a BYD afirmou que as novas contratações refletem a expansão de sua operação no Estado baiano. “A chegada de novos profissionais mostra que a BYD segue avançando na Bahia, combinando expansão industrial, geração de empregos e desenvolvimento regional. É um crescimento que reforça o papel estratégico de Camaçari para a BYD e para o futuro da mobilidade no Brasil”, afirma o vice-presidente sênior da empresa no Brasil, Alexandre Baldy. Com investimentos de R$ 5,5 bilhões e projeção de criação de 20 mil empregos diretos e indiretos, a fábrica da BYD em Camaçari ocupa uma área de 4,65 milhões de metros quadrados. No local, são produzidos o BYD Dolphin Mini, o sedã BYD King e o SUV BYD Song Pro. A companhia afirma que o resultado consolida a BYD como a maior geradora de empregos do setor automotivo no País em 2026, com cerca de quatro vezes mais contratações do que a segunda colocada, segundo dados recentes do Novo Cadastro Geral de Empregados e Desempregados (Caged), divulgados pelo Ministério do Trabalho e Emprego na terça-feira. artigo.texto: Elsewedy Electric has connected a 50 MW / 100 MWh battery energy storage system to Greece’s transmission grid, marking a step toward the national goal of between 5 GW and 7 GW by 2030. The government is also providing support for batteries for small and mid-sized firms, to be integrated with solar panels. In addition, deadlines for BESS investments in coal regions are set to be extended. While its neighbor Bulgaria is at the top of the chart on a global scale in battery energy storage systems, Greece is rushing to become a major player itself. The country has some 600 MW of operating power from the 13 active facilities in the system controlled by Independent Transmission System Operator (IPTO or Admie). The goal is 5 GW to 7 GW by 2030. In 2027, the total would need to reach 1.5 GW. Elsewedy adds 100 MWh to Greece’s battery storage fleet Elsewedy Electric energized a standalone BESS early this month. The project was developed by Elsewedy Energy and EPC and implemented by Elsewedy Electric Power Systems Projects and BMS. The battery facility has 50 MW in capability and a two-hour duration, which translates to 100 MWh in storage capacity. It is the Egypt-based firm’s first BESS in Europe. Elsewedy won government support three years ago at the country’s first auction for standalone energy storage, in the form of a contract for difference (CfD). Connected to the 150 kV network and a new 33/150 kV substation, the facility is located in Oinofyta in the municipality of Tanagra, part of the regional unit of Viotia in Central Greece. The investment was worth EUR 41.9 million. In early 2025, Elsewedy obtained a EUR 18.2 financing package from the National Bank of Greece. It also benefits from a EUR 10 million grant and EUR 5.5 loan, both from the European Union’s Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF). SMEs win subsidies for BESS backup for solar power Expansion is underway in other segments of battery storage as well. The ministry recently published the provisional list of beneficiaries of the support program for small and mid-sized enterprises. The subsidies total EUR 8.15 million. Overall operating power for 209 firms is 28.2 MW, with 49.3 MWh of storage. BESS facilities will support 30.8 MW of photovoltaics altogether. It took almost eleven months since the applications deadline for the first list. The package was intended to cover 333 MW of battery capability with EUR 153 million. More time for projects in coal regions in transition Futhermore, the Ministry of Environment and Energy is prolonging a deadline for the winners of the third auction. The beneficiaries would be able to submit the so-called declarations of readiness to the Independent Power Transmission Operator (IPTO or ADMIE) by mid-December, according to a bill of law, Energypress reported. The procedure is for four-hour BESS projects in the coal regions of Western Macedonia and the Peloponnese. HELLENiQ Renewables and government-controlled Public Power Corp. (PPC) were the biggest winners, with two plants of 25 MW and one 50 MW system, respectively. The rest of the list comprises Amber Energy (18 MW), Plain Solar (7.9 MW), Enercoplan (25 MW), Eunice Group’s Arkadia Storage (10 MW), EDF’s subsidiary Heliothema (10 MW) and Ardassa Energy (18 MW). The three standalone energy storage tenders resulted in contracts for 900 MW overall.

artigo.texto: O Fórum Nacional de Secretários Estaduais de Minas e Energia (FNSME) pediu ao presidente Lula (PT) a abertura de um diálogo institucional com os estados antes da conclusão da regulamentação do Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata) e o reconhecimento do gás natural como alternativa energética potencialmente elegível como fonte de baixa emissão incentivada pela política. O FNSME entende que o Redata deve preservar condições isonômicas entre os estados na atração dos investimentos em data centers. “Uma política pública de alcance nacional deve preservar condições isonômicas de participação entre os estados, evitando que critérios tecnológicos previamente definidos produzam, ainda que indiretamente, concentração regional dos investimentos”, cita o ofício enviado ao presidente da República nesta quarta-feira (30/9). O posicionamento ocorre em meio ao tensionamento, dentro do governo federal, sobre a regulamentação do Redata. A Fazenda, responsável pelo desenho do programa, tem pressionado para que o presidente Lula sancione o decreto regulamentador sem incluir o gás como fonte energética incentivada, mantendo assim a ênfase em fontes renováveis. O grupo de secretários defendeu também que os empreendimentos beneficiários do Redata devem “assumir adequadamente os custos de conexão, potência, infraestrutura e eventuais reforços sistêmicos que decorram de sua implantação”. O objetivo, nesse caso, é evitar a transferência indevida desses custos aos demais consumidores. Diversidade energética não pode ser fator de exclusão O Fórum defende a neutralidade tecnológica na definição das soluções de suprimento energético e a possibilidade de utilização de soluções híbridas envolvendo gás natural, fontes renováveis, armazenamento e outras tecnologias. A entidade alega que o Brasil possui diferentes realidades energéticas, com estados com expressiva disponibilidade de recursos renováveis e outros com reservas de gás natural, além de diferentes níveis de infraestrutura de transmissão e distribuição de energia e distintas condições de conexão ao Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). “Essa diversidade não deve ser transformada em fator de exclusão. O gás natural possui papel relevante na segurança energética brasileira e pode, em determinadas configurações, integrar soluções de suprimento que combinem geração térmica, fontes renováveis, armazenamento, resposta da demanda e outras tecnologias”. Antes de o FNSME fechar posição sobre o assunto, diferentes estados já vinham se mobilizando para pleitear a inclusão do gás como fonte elegível aos incentivos do Redata. Esta semana, o Comitê de Planejamento Energético do Estado do Rio Grande do Sul (Copergs), em conjunto com o governo estadual, já havia enviado ofício ao presidente Lula reforçando o pleito. O Rio Grande do Sul tem atraído investidores interessados em investir em data centers no estado – a principal iniciativa, nesse sentido, é o Projeto da Scala AI City, com capacidade prevista de até 4,8 GW. Com capacidade de suprimento de gás natural limitada pelos gargalos do Gasbol, o estado defende que possui alternativas de diversificação do suprimento – como a conclusão do trecho do gasoduto Uruguaiana-Porto Alegre, que permitiria a chegada do gás de Vaca Muerta, na Argentina, ao mercado gaúcho, além da avaliação de rotas de gás natural liquefeito (GNL) e comprimido (GNC). Na semana passada, aliás, a Edge assinou com o governo do Rio Grande do Sul um memorando de entendimento para a estruturação de um terminal de GNL no estado. Antes dos gaúchos, os governos do Amazonas e Sergipe também já haviam solicitado formalmente a inclusão do gás na regulamentação do Redata.

artigo.texto: JAMES CITY — James City County residents on Tuesday learned more about a proposed battery energy storage system that could transform an abandoned industrial site in the county’s southeastern community of Grove. Pelican Energy Storage LLC has applied for a special use permit that would allow the construction of a battery energy storage facility on parts of a 220-acre industrial waterfront site in Grove. Pelican, a subsidiary of Tenaska based in Omaha, Nebraska, hosted a public informational meeting at the Abram Frink Jr. Community Center. Tenaska spokeswoman Jamie Wagner said the company seeks public engagement early and frequently when approaching a project like this and seek to ensure that they’re a good neighbor. “As with any new project, we understand that members of the Grove community may have questions,” she said. Pelican has touted benefits that would come with the redevelopment of the former BASF Corp. site, but some Grove residents are concerned about industrial redevelopment. The county’s planning commission is slated to consider and hold a public hearing on the special use permit application on Oct. 7. The proposed facility would consist of what Pelican describes as purpose-built battery energy storage system enclosures capable of storing 650 megawatts of energy. The lithium-ion batteries would hold energy that power plants generate and that can be fed back into the power grid when demand is highest. The battery site would connect to Dominion Energy’s 500-kilovolt Surry-Skiffes Creek transmission line, which crosses the property. Pelican officials say James City County and the wider southeastern Virginia community would benefit from the construction of an energy storage facility. Construction would create more than 275 direct and indirect jobs, Pelican estimates. The facility will have no emissions, use no water during operation and provide $90 million in direct revenue to the county, according to company estimates. “We find many communities are open to this type of investment,” Wright said. But some Grove residents feel as though they’re being overlooked as this proposal moves forward. “Why does Grove continually seem to be the part of James City County where things are put, rather than the part of the county that gets invested in?” Joshua Blue, a Grove resident since 2008, asked on Tuesday. He was one of a few dozen residents who attended the meeting. Grove lacks public amenities such as sidewalks in many areas and has no public access to the James River despite being adjacent to it. Redeveloping industry at the BASF site locks in industrial use for decades. “I would much rather see the county seriously explore whether this land could become a public park, natural area, river access or some other permanent community asset,” Blue said. Blue said the county has invested in public access elsewhere and wants the same consideration for Grove, an area populated by many descendants of people displaced in the 20th century to make way for federal military installations. “I’m not categorically opposed to battery storage,” he said. “But I am very concerned about permanently giving up one of Grove’s last opportunities for meaningful public riverfront access without first having a serious conversation about what that land could mean for the people who actually live here.” Once used for the manufacture and burial of synthetic fibers, which led to soil and groundwater contamination, the BASF Corp. site underwent cleanup and in 2021 was declared remediated by the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality, according Grant Weaver, an environmental analyst with Tenaska. Weaver said public waterfront access would not work for the site because of its prior use. Public beach access would be “very difficult given the residual contamination,” he said. Wright said the company nevertheless values the feedback from the community and wants to know their concerns and observations. John McGlennon, chairman of the county’s Board of Supervisors, attended Tuesday’s meeting and said some of the citizens he spoke to expressed genuine concerns about the site’s redevelopment, but that most simply wanted to know more about the proposal. McGlennon said a project like the proposed battery energy storage system would be increasingly important for feeding energy into the electrical grid, but whether this is the right location and project to do that has yet to be determined. Another energy company, Charlottesville-based East Point Energy, in July withdrew a request to bring a major battery storage facility to Chesapeake, saying it wanted “to continue sharing information and answering questions” for residents before proceeding. At the time, proponents emphasized that these type of facilities don’t pose the same risks as data centers. Chesapeake’s planning commission had recommended denial of the project. Ben Swenson, ben.swenson05@gmail.com

artigo.texto: What’s it like living in the shadow of an AI data center? These Vineland residents know. They are some of the first in the Philly area to experience firsthand what it’s like to live near the massive facilities. Some of their neighbors have sold their homes to the data center developers. When Amber Ayrer bought her Vineland home 25 years ago, she envisioned growing old there, enjoying lazy afternoons with the windows open and a view of farmland from her front door. After her adult daughter, Ally, suffered a traumatic brain injury, Amber made the rancher accessible, installing a ramp that aides use to push Ally’s wheelchair outside for her daily walks. The place had all the makings of a forever home, Amber Ayrer said — until a massive AI data center moved in across the street. Now, the 71-year-old looks out her front windows at the hulking DataOne facility, a windowless compound surrounded by walls and metal fences. In recent months, Ayrer said, the 2.4-million-square-foot complex has emitted a near-constant hum. She struggles to sleep, she said, and has suffered from headaches. She turns the TV on to mask the sound. Residents who live farther away have also complained about the noise, including in a recent lawsuit that was thrown out due to procedural issues. In the suit, residents said the Cumberland County Department of Health measured the hum as higher than 50 decibels a mile away in the middle of the night. A sound higher than 50 decibels is equal to a running refrigerator and is 10 times louder than a typical suburban area at night. Ayrer, who was not involved in the lawsuit, said she doesn’t want to move, even as she sees neighbors sell their homes to the data center developers. “In order to get another home, I’d have to get one built” to be accessible, Ayrer said, standing in her entryway. She shrugged, adding, “I need to be here for my daughter.” The noise has quieted, she noted, since around Sept. 22. That’s when the New Jersey DEP ordered the data center to pay a $1 million fine for running 62 gas generators without the required permits. She isn’t sure why the hum stopped, or whether it is related to the fine. » READ MORE: Vineland AI data center hit with a $1 million fine But the sound will eventually return, she assumes, perhaps even louder when the center is fully operational. The Ayrers are some of the first Philly-area residents to live in the shadow of a massive AI data center. Only a handful of homeowners live within eyesight of DataOne’s South Lincoln Avenue complex in Vineland. They used to have more neighbors. But since 2025, DataOne Vineland and LJR Real Estate — which is registered to the address of Northeast Precast, a local company that has partnered with DataOne — have purchased at least five surrounding homes for a combined $3 million, according to online property records. DataOne and Northeast Precast did not respond to requests for comment about the acquisitions. Several former Vineland residents who sold their homes to these companies could not be reached or declined to comment. Asked about residents’ concerns, DataOne spokesperson Naomi Rice shared a previous statement, which said in part that the facility was “transitioning to low-emission, quiet fuel cells.” These generate energy through an electrochemical reaction rather than combustion, pistons, or rotating machinery. Nebius Group, which is operating the center’s internal AI infrastructure, says the fuel cells from Bloom Energy — a company expanding locally — and enhanced sound mitigation will make for a quieter environment than what residents experienced during construction, according to spokesperson Ava Iuliucci. Charles-Antoine Beyney, DataOne’s founder and chief executive officer, previously said the Vineland center would use “breakthrough” technology to reduce its environmental impact. He said the complex would be a good neighbor, promising a vertical farm — which uses technology to grow crops indoors — to help feed Vineland residents in need. “Most of the data centers that are being built today suck, big time,” Beyney said in January. “No freaking way am I going to do what the entire industry is doing … just killing our communities and killing our lungs to make money.” What it looks like near a South Jersey data center The dark exterior of DataOne abuts busy South Lincoln Avenue, towering above homes and farms on the outskirts of Vineland City. In spots, rows of crops extend to the data center’s walls. On a recent day, the data center appeared abuzz with activity, although residents said it was relatively quiet, as cars and yellow school buses drove in and out of its gated-off parking lot. Giant “no trespassing” signs are prominently displayed. While the front portion of the data center appeared complete, cranes farther back reached into the sky. Meanwhile, several large homes across from the entrance — purchased by the data center developers and associates — appeared abandoned, with recycling cans askew in the driveways, indoor and outdoor lights on in the middle of the day, and swing sets sitting empty in the backyards. No one answered the doors. At another home, a woman shook her head, saying she’d lived there forever and would never speak publicly about the development across the street. Who is behind the Vineland data center? Data centers like this one handle the cloud-storage and computing needs of increasingly sophisticated AI tools. DataOne, a French company that manages advanced data centers, is the owner, operator, and builder of the Vineland data center. Its client, Nebius Group, an Amsterdam-based AI-infrastructure company, operates the center’s internal technology, which fuels Microsoft’s AI tools. As demand for these facilities has surged, so has the controversy surrounding them. Across the country, proposed complexes have received fierce pushback from nearby residents concerned about environmental, noise, quality-of-life, and property-value impacts. » READ MORE: Human reporters explai

artigo.texto: Vanderburgh County Commissioners approve $200 million battery storage facility EVANSVILLE, Ind. (WFIE) - Vanderburgh County Commissioners this week approved a series of agreements that clear the way for a new battery energy storage system, or BESS, next to the Elliott Station substation in Scott Township. Project details The developer, Elliot Battery Storage, an affiliate of RWE Clean Energy Development, plans to invest about $200 million in the project. The facility will store roughly 200 megawatts of power. This power could be used to help utilities manage high-demand periods. “So it’s a large station on the far east side of Vanderburgh County... they’re key to peak load... they’re a modern way of dealing with the peak load, and they need to be next to a substation, which this one is,” said Mike Schopmeyer, Vanderburgh County attorney. Zoning approval and neighbor notification The project already passed a Board of Zoning Appeals vote, 5-0. Schopmeyer said people living near the site off East Baseline Road were notified and briefed before that vote. “Everything’s approved now, so the petitioner... can move ahead with the construction. They’ve got to go through a building permit process,” Schopmeyer said. Payments to the county and timeline As part of the deal, the company will pay the county $250,000 for local development projects, plus cover the county’s legal costs for negotiating the agreements. The company must break ground by the end of 2029 or the deal falls apart. The facility is expected to be up and running no later than November 2031. Copyright 2026 WFIE. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: “Ratepayer Protection Act” sets a standard intended to keep data center power costs off ratepayers’ bills. Opponents call the bill “toothless.” clarification: This article has been updated to reflect the 57-43 cloture vote on a motion to proceed HR 9340, which would have allowed the bill to move forward in the Senate. WASHINGTON, D.C. (WTAP) - A bill that passed the U.S. House earlier this month aims to keep the cost of powering data centers off the bills of ratepayers. The Ratepayer Protection Act would set a federal standard that, if considered and adopted by states, would require utilities to design rates so that data centers using 100 megawatts or more recover the full cost of any new generation, transmission or distribution needed to serve them. That includes cases where a data center later ends its contract, so utilities and ratepayers aren’t left holding the bag. Utilities would also have to collect financial assurances required to cover the cost of any upgrades up front. West Virginia Congressman Riley Moore co-sponsored the bill and said he encouraged House leadership to bring it to the floor. “It’s trying to ensure that people’s utility bills are not going to go up, that my citizens and citizens around this country are not footing the bill for data centers that are being built in their area,” Moore said. The bill sets a federal standard but few hard requirements, leaving the details and implementation to the states. State regulators would have a year to begin considering it and two years to make a decision. Moore said that scope is intentional, to avoid federal preemption of state laws, though he said he’d be open to the Senate adding more teeth. Democrats have criticized the bill for only requiring states to “consider” the proposal intended to protect ratepayers. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Shumer (D - NY) on Tuesday said the bill doesn’t go far enough to ensure data centers are held accountable. “Americans are demanding real guard-rails on AI and data centers, but all the Republicans offer is a toothless messaging bill,” Shumer said on the Senate floor. “The bill is a fraud” The House passed the bill Sept. 16. A 57-43 cloture vote on a motion to proceed stalled the bill in the Senate on Sept. 30. The Senate also has its own version of the bill, introduced by Sen. Jon Husted (R - Ohio). A separate bill, the GRID Savings Act, introduced by Sen. Martin Heinrich (D - N.M.) seeks to have federal regulators, rather than the states, set rules for how utilities bill data centers for the cost of connecting to the power grid, preempting the consideration of state regulators. That bill has been referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Moore’s Democratic opponent for his seat in this year’s general election, Morgantown community organizer Ace Parsi, drafted a bill called the “Neighbors, Not Servers Act,” which he says will be the first piece of legislation he introduces a lawmaker if elected. The bill would go further than the Ratepayer Protection Act, requiring local community consent before any data center could receive federal permits or grid interconnection approval, and would override state laws, like West Virginia’s, that currently limit local control over data center siting. Parsi announced the proposal last week. Moore’s office did not respond to a request for comment on it, though a spokesperson reached out afterward to highlight his work on the Ratepayer Protection Act. artigo.texto: A DHL está a expandir a sua rede mundial de logística de baterias, que integra já mais de 20 instalações especializadas. A operação acompanha todo o ciclo de vida destes equipamentos, desde o apoio à produção e transporte até ao diagnóstico, reparação, logística inversa e preparação para reciclagem. A eletrificação dos setores automóvel, industrial e energético está a criar novas cadeias de abastecimento e a aumentar a procura de soluções logísticas especializadas. Para responder a esta transformação, a DHL está a desenvolver uma rede integrada de Centros de Excelência de Veículos Elétricos e Baterias nos principais mercados mundiais. A plataforma reúne competências da DHL Supply Chain, DHL Global Forwarding e DHL Express, combinando logística de produção, transporte, armazenagem, serviços pós-venda e gestão do ciclo de vida das baterias. A rede liga já mais de 20 instalações, estando prevista a abertura de novas localizações. A expansão surge num contexto em que as baterias deixaram de estar associadas apenas aos veículos elétricos. Os mesmos sistemas são cada vez mais utilizados em equipamentos industriais, operações mineiras, infraestruturas de rede elétrica e projetos de armazenamento de energia renovável. Algumas destas unidades ultrapassam as 50 toneladas, exigindo soluções de transporte pesado, equipamentos específicos e um planeamento logístico próprio. A classificação como mercadoria perigosa, as diferenças regulamentares entre mercados e modos de transporte e as exigências de documentação e controlo aduaneiro aumentam igualmente a complexidade das operações. “A logística de baterias é fundamentalmente diferente das cadeias de abastecimento tradicionais”, afirma Francisco Milián, Head of Inbound to Manufacturing da DHL Supply Chain EMEA. Segundo o responsável, os clientes necessitam de capacidades especializadas em todas as fases, desde a logística de entrada e o apoio à produção até ao armazenamento, distribuição, recondicionamento, devolução e reciclagem. As instalações especializadas da DHL combinam áreas de armazenagem preparadas para baterias com serviços técnicos, entre os quais diagnóstico, testes, carregamento, condicionamento, reparação, logística inversa e preparação dos equipamentos para reciclagem. Em Halle, na Alemanha, o operador disponibilizou recentemente 13 mil metros quadrados de espaço de armazém adaptado a este tipo de produto. Na Hungria, está a ser preparada uma nova instalação dedicada à logística de baterias, cuja entrada em funcionamento está prevista para 2027. A DHL está também a construir um hub europeu em Holtum, nos Países Baixos. A infraestrutura contará com 17 mil metros quadrados de armazenagem e serviços especializados para baterias de alta tensão e deverá iniciar atividade no princípio de 2027. A proximidade à operação automóvel já existente permitirá criar um campus integrado, dedicado à mobilidade elétrica e aos sistemas de armazenamento de energia. Muitas destas instalações integram transporte, serviços aduaneiros e operações transfronteiriças, procurando concentrar num único parceiro várias etapas da cadeia de valor. A proposta dirige-se a fabricantes de baterias e automóveis, mas também a empresas de energia, operadores industriais e projetos ligados à exploração de minerais críticos. Eletrificação cria novos corredores logísticos A concentração de uma parte significativa da produção de baterias na Ásia, conjugada com o crescimento da procura na Europa e noutras regiões, está a alterar os fluxos comerciais. Ao mesmo tempo, a instalação de novas gigafábricas gera movimentos de equipamentos produtivos, matérias-primas, produtos químicos, componentes e baterias acabadas. “A transição energética está a criar corredores comerciais e padrões de cadeias de abastecimento inteiramente novos”, sublinha Hendrik Venter, Global CEO da DHL Supply Chain. Para o responsável, as empresas estão a redesenhar as suas operações para apoiar a mobilidade elétrica, o armazenamento de energia e a expansão das fontes renováveis. A logística de baterias ganha ainda uma nova dimensão com o crescimento dos sistemas BESS – Battery Energy Storage Systems – utilizados para armazenar energia e apoiar a estabilidade das redes elétricas. No primeiro semestre de 2026, a DHL entregou mais de 1100 destas unidades em diferentes mercados. Estes projetos podem envolver sistemas de grandes dimensões, transporte multimodal, operações de elevação de cargas pesadas e entregas em locais remotos, além do cumprimento das regras aplicáveis às mercadorias perigosas. A área New Energy é um dos setores de crescimento definidos pelo DHL Group na sua Strategy 2030. O grupo desenvolve soluções logísticas para oito segmentos: energia eólica, solar, veículos elétricos e baterias, sistemas BESS, carregamento de veículos elétricos, infraestruturas de rede, hidrogénio e combustíveis alternativos.

artigo.texto: A ABB anunciou o lançamento do Infinitus, um portfólio de soluções de corrente contínua (CC) projetado para gerenciar as crescentes demandas de energia dos Data Centers de IA. O portfólio acelerará a adoção de arquiteturas CC em Data Centers, melhorando a eficiência energética e reduzindo a área ocupada pela infraestrutura de energia, ao mesmo tempo em que aumenta a capacidade de computação disponível. A ABB espera que outros setores de alto consumo energético façam a mesma transição. A Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA) prevê que a demanda global de eletricidade dos Data Centers mais que dobrará até 2030, e a ABB estima que aproximadamente 25–40% da nova capacidade instalada em 2030 poderá utilizar distribuição CC. Espera-se que os chips de IA de próxima geração consumam 1 MW ou mais por rack, um aumento em relação aos quase 200 kW atuais, exigindo uma mudança para uma arquitetura CC capaz de sustentar o desempenho e, ao mesmo tempo, impulsionar a eficiência energética. Com a distribuição em 800 VCC, a pegada é mais compacta, eliminando etapas redundantes de conversão e reduzindo as perdas de calor dos sistemas convencionais de corrente alternada (CA). Um relatório recente da BCG/ABB calculou que a distribuição CC gera ganhos de eficiência energética superiores a 5% e aumenta o espaço disponível para racks de computação. Para um Data Center de 500 MW, um ganho de eficiência de 5% pode significar 25 MW adicionais de energia para cargas de TI geradoras de receita e mais de US$ 300 milhões em receita adicional potencial por ano. Com ganhos de eficiência de 5% em um campus de data center de 500 MW, a economia de energia ao longo de um ano seria equivalente a abastecer Washington D.C. por quase uma semana inteira. “A ABB é pioneira em tecnologia CC há mais de 25 anos em diversos segmentos. Estamos trabalhando em estreita colaboração com fabricantes de chips, clientes hyperscale, parceiros de fornecimento e entidades do setor para definir os padrões e o ritmo da implementação de arquiteturas CC de alta eficiência. O Infinitus é o primeiro portfólio a fornecer os blocos de construção para qualquer arquitetura de data center — seja CC nativa ou híbrida CA/CC — para alimentar com eficiência os chips de IA de próxima geração. Essa tecnologia trará ganhos de eficiência energética semelhantes a outros setores de alto consumo, como manufatura em larga escala, energias renováveis e operações marítimas”, disse Giampiero Frisio, presidente da área de negócios de Eletrificação da ABB. O Infinitus é o primeiro portfólio integrado source-to-rack de CC do setor. Em seu núcleo está a inovadora tecnologia de transformador de estado sólido Infinitus da ABB, que permite que as instalações operem com uma pegada menor e maior eficiência energética. Como o único grande fornecedor de eletrificação com o primeiro disjuntor de estado sólido totalmente certificado pela IEC do mundo e um UPS estático de média tensão pioneiro no setor em produção, a ABB oferece uma amplitude de tecnologia incomparável no mercado. O portfólio CC Infinitus da ABB inclui cinco blocos de construção principais: – Powertrains de Média Tensão fornecem energia estável e resiliente da rede elétrica ou de geração no local; – Fontes CC e Qualidade de Energia convertem CA em CC, eliminando a conversão do white space; – Distribuição de Energia CC entrega energia de forma segura e confiável, permitindo maior densidade de potência em uma pegada menor; – Proteção de Energia CC fornece proteção para operadores, servidores de IA e hardware contra sobrecorrentes CC; – Otimização de Resfriamento reduz o consumo de energia no grey space e no white space com acionamentos de velocidade variável e motores conectados em CC. A ABB trabalha com os clientes para projetar soluções adaptadas às suas demandas específicas de energia, layout das instalações e matriz energética. Essa abordagem de parceria garante que cada implantação seja otimizada para máxima eficiência e confiabilidade. O portfólio Infinitus complementa os sistemas CA tradicionais com a flexibilidade da CC, apoiando os clientes em todas as arquiteturas de energia e, ao mesmo tempo, permitindo eficiência, confiabilidade e escalabilidade sem precedentes para os data centers da era da IA. Para Data Centers de próxima geração, essa arquitetura integrada permite a entrega de energia de alta densidade e alta eficiência que os futuros chips de IA exigem. Com vários componentes principais produzidos nos próximos 12 meses, espera-se que as primeiras instalações nativas em CC que utilizam o portfólio Infinitus completo sejam instaladas e operacionais em dois a três anos. O lançamento do portfólio amplia o apoio à colaboração contínua da ABB com a Nvidia, anunciada pela primeira vez em outubro de 2025, para desenvolver arquiteturas de energia de 800 VCC para instalações de IA em escala de gigawatts. A ABB traz mais de 25 anos de experiência em CC e mais de 700 patentes abrangendo energias renováveis, geração de energia, armazenamento de energia, motores e inversores de frequência. artigo.texto: Massachusetts awards more than $40 million for energy storage projects The Massachusetts Department of Energy Resources (DOER) has awarded more than $40 million to a group of 36 energy projects across the state, officials from the department announced Sept. 18. Delivered through the DOER’s Advancing Massachusetts Power Energy Storage Grant Program, the funding aims to bolster the Bay State’s grid through distributed energy resources. Specifically, the 36 projects all focus on one or more of three focus areas: Community Resilience, Safety and Education, and Long Duration Energy Storage (LDES). Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey says the projects cover a variety of community infrastructure and local businesses, including affordable housing, schools, community centers, and public works facilities. “This is about lowering energy costs and keeping the lights on when communities need it most,” she says. “These investments will help schools, affordable housing, community centers and other critical facilities stay powered during outages while strengthening our grid for the future. We’re also making sure first responders and local officials have the training and tools they need as more energy storage comes online across Massachusetts.” Bolstering community resilience As extreme weather events continue to rise due to climate factors, and area-wide brownouts and blackouts become commonplace across parts of the U.S., community energy resilience is a top priority. A sizable piece of the $40 million in grant money will go toward these efforts, as Massachusetts aims to install battery storage in schools, as well as affordable housing developments and community centers. Together, the projects will add about 10 MW / 44 MWh of storage across the state. “Communities need reliable power and the confidence that new energy technologies are being deployed safely,” says Massachusetts Lieutenant Gov. Kim Driscoll. “These grants will help cities and towns strengthen critical infrastructure, prepare first responders and local officials, and take advantage of storage technology that can save money and improve resilience.” A safe, educated state for installations Paired energy storage has gone from “nice to have” to “absolute necessity” for the solar project world in record time. Another piece of the Bay State’s new grant money will support first responders, as well as municipal officials, electricians, and other installation contractors. The grant funding, going to sites like the Metropolitan Area Planning Council and the Boston Fire Department, will train officials on battery safety, fire codes, permitting, inspections, and other crucial areas. “Batteries supplied more electricity to the grid in the first eight months of 2026 than in all of 2025 – we’re bringing that momentum to the Massachusetts communities that need it the most,” says Massachusetts Energy and Environmental Affairs Secretary Rebecca Tepper. “We are also excited to be supporting two innovative zinc- and sodium-based storage systems to help us get through major storms, showing that Massachusetts is a great place to deploy and scale the latest tech.” Pushing innovation forward for the Northeast Long-duration energy storage ties into the first priority for Massachusetts with this particular grant fund: community resilience. LDES projects are on the rise in the Northeast at large, and this grant section will support a duo of sites using sodium-iron chloride and zinc-based technologies, officials say. These projects could potentially store electricity for 10 to 20 hours, representatives add. The grants, going to community businesses like the Berkshire East Mountain Resort and Mystic Place Apartments, can also help companies scale and test innovative LDES technologies throughout the state. “This investment recognizes that emerging energy technologies require a coordinated public-safety response,” says Tracy Rogers, director of emergency management for the Franklin Regional Council of Governments in western Massachusetts. “By providing specialized battery energy storage system training to first responders across the region, this grant will build shared knowledge, improve preparedness, and help protect the people who respond when communities need them most.”

artigo.texto: Os bastidores de ser rainha de bateria Para elas, a coroa exige mais do que samba no pé Atualizado Antes do samba-enredo começar, da bateria entrar e das câmeras se voltarem para ela, existe uma história que quase ninguém vê. O carnaval mostra apenas o fragmento mais luminoso da vida de uma rainha de bateria. Por trás dele, há mulheres para quem aquele posto não é vitrine, mas o reconhecimento de um laço construído com a escola, e a realização de um sonho. Tania Bisteka, Patricia Costa e Fabíola Andrade sabem bem o que é isso. Tânia, por exemplo, soube exatamente o que queria desde o dia em que a Mangueira anunciou um concurso para escolher a rainha de bateria em 1999. Não tratou como brincadeira, encarou como se concorresse a um cargo político. Espalhou faixas com o próprio nome pela quadra, abordava os integrantes da bateria para contar sua trajetória com a escola e, a quem estivesse por perto, defendia com convicção que merecia sair vencedora. Na época, o concurso reunia dez candidatas e um júri escolhido pela própria bateria, que avaliaria três entradas de cada uma. Durante o mês entre a inscrição e a disputa, Tânia lutou à sua maneira e sonhou com o que viria. Pôs em prática as ideias para viver o que define como uma festa: “Eu fiz blusas com a minha cara. Eu entrei, fiz uma roupa linda, fiz um biquíni lindo e ganhei. As pessoas desciam o morro para assistir! Só que você imagina, o morro todo lá embaixo gritando, berrando e falando.” A emoção foi grande quando descobriu que o que tanto queria se realizou. E deixa claro que ser rainha não é fácil. Estava o ano todo presente em ensaios, na academia e no boxe. Cuidava da alimentação, mesmo que reconheça que ter nutricionista não era tão acessível quanto hoje. E estava sempre na quadra, sem desculpas, para sambar até o fôlego acabar. Tudo na intenção de melhorar a resistência. Esse era seu preparo. Mas além da preparação em relação a exercícios e alimentação, Tania também se preparou psicologicamente e com a sua fé. A partir da espiritualidade, tomou uma atitude totalmente inusitada antes do desfile para que entrasse na avenida com energia boa. Conta que a Mangueira estava na concentração em um local que existia um valão, onde tirou sua roupa: “Eu fiquei pelada. Convoquei a todos, e quando as pessoas passavam e me viam diziam “meu Deus, a rainha está pelada!” E foi muito louco. Eu estava só com uma canga, eu arranquei a canga e comecei meu ritual.” Nascida no morro da Mangueira, foi muito bem recebida pela bateria. Algumas pessoas a chamam de rainha até hoje e, ao lembrar daquele ano, ela percebe que o processo é diferente para uma rainha cria. "É um trabalho árduo, mas que vale muito a pena. Principalmente quando você é da comunidade, uma rainha pé no chão. Quando eu digo pé no chão, quero dizer uma rainha do povo, né? Quando a rainha é cria da escola, ela é mais cobrada do que quando não é. Porque está ali para mostrar que realmente mereceu estar naquele lugar de rainha." Patrícia Costa, rainha de bateria da Viradouro de 1991 a 1998, também sentiu essa diferença. Ela conta que as pessoas famosas pareciam ter mais abertura para ocupar esse espaço. Quando foi chamada, já fazia balé, jazz e sapateado. O convite veio de forma surpreendente, quando foi prestigiar o mestre Maçal, com quem já havia feito um trabalho, e acabou sambando muito com os passistas. Foi um verdadeiro teste de fogo. Naquele dia, o então presidente da escola viu o movimento e ficou interessado em conhecê-la. No fim, a chamou ao camarote e fez o convite, quando teve que assumir uma postura: "Eu precisei me colocar assim, com muita responsabilidade e auto valorização da minha posição como uma artista do samba, uma artista, uma sambista que sabia o que estava fazendo ali à frente da bateria. Não foi fácil. Assim, fui conquistando a comunidade com a minha presença e dedicação." Patrícia explica que a relação com os mestres de bateria e os ritmistas é essencial. Durante os ensaios, a sintonia vai sendo construída. A partir das frases musicais e dos sons da bateria, surge uma criatividade que forma combinações capazes de ajudar a rainha a se movimentar em harmonia com os ritmistas. Nem tudo, porém, são flores. Sobre os perrengues, ela lembra de um ano em que desfilou com o sapato fechado e arrasou na avenida, mas terminou o desfile carregada no colo pelo namorado. Se sente neta da Águia da Portela, já que o avô foi um dos fundadores da escola. Cresceu ouvindo as histórias e foi ali que o amor pelo samba começou. Durante o desfile, essa paixão mantinha qualquer desconforto longe: “Nunca aconteceu de eu sentir alguma dor durante o desfile. O corpo fica quente, acontece uma troca de energia maravilhosa com o público, uma energia tão boa que não tem muito lugar para sentir dor. Para mim, naquele palco tem uma magia, o show acontece. Sem dor.” Energia essa também que também guia Fabíola Andrade. Foi rainha de bateria da Mocidade Independente de Padre Miguel de 2024 a 2026 e hoje é rainha da escola. Desde criança, já se encantava com a festa, o ritmo e a energia das escolas de samba. Para ela, ser rainha de bateria é fazer parte da história viva do carnaval carioca, levar alegria e garra a uma comunidade inteira. Pensando nas fantasias, diz que é um trabalho artesanal e demorado, feito em equipe com o carnavalesco e estilistas renomados do Carnaval. Segundo ela, os costeiros podem pesar de dez a vinte quilos e o salto alto exige estrutura. Então, garantir que nada saia do lugar é uma verdadeira engenharia. A rainha lembra que já precisou até de uma costura de última hora na fantasia, na concentração, com o coração aos pulos e frio na barriga. Assim como Patrícia, acredita que a adrenalina é um anestésico natural inacreditável, fazendo com que a garra da comunidade e a troca de energia impulsionem toda a animação: "É uma relação de puro amor, cumplicidade e respeito. O mestre de bateria e os ritmistas são o coração da escola, e eu estou ali para ser a energia vibrante daquele ritm

artigo.texto: With the rising tide of data center developments showing no sign of receding, a new Linn County Data Center Advisory Committee will soon be in place to help evaluate possible changes to the county’s existing data center ordinance. Preliminary plans for the committee were discussed during Wednesday’s Linn County Board of Supervisors meeting. The committee was suggested by Supervisor Brandy Z. Meisheid, who said Wednesday it will give local residents a say in how data center decisions are made at the county level. “This process is really something that allows… our constituents to have a voice in how Linn County grows,” Ms. Meisheid said, noting that residents and constituents should “help drive how we make decisions, how we look at these projects.” The move comes as Linn County is three months into an 18-month moratorium on consideration of any new data center proposals in the county’s unincorporated areas. Once formed, the new committee is expected to complete its work before that moratorium expires at the end of December 2027. Linn County Planning and Development director Charlie Nichols outlined the committee’s framework at Wednesday’s meeting. He said the committee will consist of 40 members, including a “substantial portion” representing Linn County cities and regional partners, each chosen by those areas’ governmental bodies. Bordering counties, including Benton County, will also be invited to provide members. Residents of Linn County’s rural areas would then fill the remaining seats through an open application process. Linn County staff will review applications and recommend names, with supervisors making the final choices. Mr. Nichols said the county will seek a geographic balance of committee members, as well as a balance of views and related experience. Applicants will be required to live in Linn County, be 18 or older, and be able to make evening meetings consistently. Each meeting is tentatively set for 6-8 p.m. No formal action was taken on the proposal Wednesday, as the board decided to postpone an official vote until Monday’s work session. Board chair Kirsten Running-Marquardt asked for the delay because the agenda item didn’t tell the public how the committee would be set up. “It’s been three months since the moratorium vote, so I think waiting a couple extra days isn’t going to materially change the process,” Ms. Running-Marquardt said. Ms. Meisheid agreed. “I’d rather do it right than speed it along too quickly,” she said. Once the committee is formally approved, membership applications will be open for about two weeks in October, Mr. Nichols said. Committee members will then be appointed in November, with the first committee meeting in December. The group is expected to meet six to eight times, with all meetings in the evening. Meetings will be open to the public. Potential meeting topics include energy issues, water resources, siting and land use, existing county regulations, and the life cycle and decommissioning of data center facilities – all issues mentioned in the county’s data center moratorium. The committee’s scope will also cover “larger industrial or energy-related development,” not just data centers, Mr. Nichols said. Each meeting will open with a presentation to the full 40-member group, with outside experts as needed. Members will then split into eight groups of five, each with a facilitator taking notes, and report back to the full group – an idea borrowed from the county’s earlier solar moratorium process. Ms. Meisheid said the facilitator model came from the Alburnett School District. She said facilitators are “not to influence… but just to guide conversation” and to manage the “differing views on how we grow.” Materials and notes from each meeting will be uploaded to a dedicated page on the county’s website. “Maximum transparency is what we are going for,” Mr. Nichols said. Before the final meeting, an open house will be held, allowing the public to talk with committee members about the draft recommendations. The committee’s work will then conclude with a set of statements guiding the board on how to update the county’s data center zoning ordinance, which was approved in February after extensive public input. Also Monday, the board will consider a facilitation contract with the East Central Iowa Council of Governments (ECICOG). Ten Linn County staffers, plus Ms. Meisheid, have already agreed to serve as committee facilitators, but under the proposed contract, ECICOG would fill any gaps if staff members can’t attend a meeting. The ECICOG facilitators, which may never be needed, would be paid $225 each per meeting, county officials said. A formal decision to establish the committee, and to approve a contract with ECICOG for backup facilitators, will be made at the board’s meeting Monday, and the application period is set to open Monday as well. “By our residents and constituents (helping to) drive how we make decisions, how we look at these projects, how we look at the growth of Linn County – I think that is the fairest and most transparent way to look at how we how we grow as a community and how we work together beyond just jurisdictional boundaries,” Ms. Meisheid said. “I’m really excited to have the collaboration with our towns, but also to have resident input as well.” To learn more about the committee and the application process, contact Mr. Nichols at (319) 892-5139 or by email at [email protected].

artigo.texto: CFMoto Ibex 450: ela rouba vendas da Himalayan 450 e da Honda NX500? | Teste A CFMoto Ibex 450 chegou ao Brasil para disputar um dos segmentos mais interessantes do mercado de motocicletas. Com motor bicilíndrico de 450 cm³, 44 cv de pot. Crédito: Estadão 30 de setembro de 2026 era a data de abertura do quinto lote de motocicletas da CFMoto, mas a marca cancelou a venda de 700 motocicletas, que seria feita online, por conta de “instabilidades técnicas no servidos do banco de dados”. A promessa de abertura foi feita no último dia 25 de setembro, e as vendas abririam hoje a partir das 12h. Seriam oferecidas unidades da Ibex 450, Ibex 700, CL-C 450 e CL-C 450 Bobber. Ainda não há uma nova data para abertura do quinto lote. Contudo, a reserva continuará sendo feita exclusivamente pela internet, por meio da plataforma da marca. A marca afirmou em nota: “Devido a instabilidades técnicas no nosso servidor de banco de dados, informamos que a abertura de vendas do Lote de Motocicletas, originalmente prevista para hoje (30/09) às 12h00, foi adiada. Tomamos essa decisão de forma preventiva para garantir a estabilidade da plataforma, assegurando que todos tenham as mesmas chances de participação e realize suas reservas com total segurança, sem falhas no processo. Em breve, divulgaremos a nova data e horário de abertura. Agradecemos a compreensão de todos." Inicialmente, a fabricante planejava dedicar o novo lote apenas à Ibex 450. Segundo a CFMoto, a procura pelos outros modelos fez a empresa ampliar a composição da remessa, incluindo novamente as quatro motos que formam atualmente sua linha no País. O lote, quando estiver disponível, será distribuído pelas operações da marca em São Paulo, Campinas, Piracicaba, Rio de Janeiro, Curitiba, Florianópolis, Porto Alegre e Caxias do Sul. LEIA MAIS: - GWM Ora 5: SUV elétrico mais barato do Brasil anda bem, mas dinâmica não combina com o visual - Exclusivo: estas 5 motos da CFMoto podem desembarcar no Brasil em 202 - CFMoto, a ‘BYD das Motos’, fatura mais de R$ 80 milhões em apenas 4 meses no Brasil Os preços atualmente anunciados para a linha são: - CL-C 450: R$ 32.990; - CL-C 450 Bobber: R$ 33.990; - Ibex 450: R$ 35.990; - Ibex 700: R$ 44.990. A Ibex 450 é equipada com motor bicilíndrico de 450,6 cm³ e 44 cv. Já a Ibex 700 utiliza motor de 693 cm³ e 67,9 cv. As quatro motos têm ABS, controle de tração e painel TFT com conectividade Bluetooth. Como reservar uma CFMoto? As reservas começam às 12h de 30 de setembro de 2026. O processo será feito pela plataforma oficial da fabricante. O interessado deverá: - acessar a plataforma de reservas; - escolher a concessionária; - selecionar o modelo; - preencher os dados cadastrais; - concluir o pagamento via Pix. Depois da confirmação, a concessionária escolhida dará continuidade ao processo de compra. A CFMoto mantém o sistema de reservas exclusivamente digital para os lotes. A fabricante afirma que a plataforma foi criada para centralizar as vendas e evitar listas paralelas. CFMoto já vendeu 500 motos em três minutos O novo lote chega depois de uma sequência de remessas esgotadas rapidamente pela CFMoto. No quarto lote, aberto em agosto, 500 motocicletas foram vendidas em três minutos, segundo a fabricante. A maior parte das reservas foi da Ibex 450, e o site registrou 9.347 usuários únicos durante a abertura. O número, porém, precisa ser analisado considerando o tamanho reduzido das remessas. A própria reportagem do Jornal do Carro destacou que a quantidade limitada ajuda a explicar a velocidade do esgotamento. Como comparação, a Honda CG 160 supera 40 mil emplacamentos em um mês. Nos três primeiros lotes, a CFMoto havia colocado pouco mais de 1.700 motocicletas à disposição. O primeiro tinha 700 unidades e acabou em pouco mais de 40 minutos; o segundo, de aproximadamente 500 motos, terminou em menos de cinco minutos; e o terceiro também teve mais de 500 reservas em poucos minutos. artigo.texto: Trending LANSING - Stormwater runoff at the sites of data centers is another environmental challenge facing developers because the runoff contains particulates harmful to the public and the ecosystem, according to Reese Dillard, the Michigan Environmental Council's water policy coordinator. Amidst growing public concerns about possible adverse climate effects of data centers such as high energy use and greenhouse gas emissions, the lesser-known threat in stormwater runoff and waste could be just as dangerous, Dillard said. Data centers are facilities used to store, process and transmit digital information. Construction sites need to "upgrade stormwater infrastructure," she said. She said that due to climate change there is increased precipitation and subsequently more flooding at data centers. Data centers use large amounts of water, most drawing from municipal systems, treated wastewater or directly from surface or groundwater. That water is used to absorb heat generated by the computer servers and equipment, and then cycled into cooling towers where some of it evaporates into the atmosphere. The remaining water is cycled back through to absorb more heat. "The pollutants that may be present in data center wastewater discharges depend upon several factors," according to a July report from the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service. They include the "source and quality of the water being used for cooling, the cooling technology being used, site-specific operations and whether the discharges are from normal operations or from construction and commissioning phases," the report said. Data centers typically use a variety of chemical treatments for their cooling systems. They include, but are not limited to, acids, disinfectants, biocides, corrosion inhibitors and dispersants, according to the report. And data center discharges may include those chemicals during maintenance or center start-up. Discharges are typically released into wetlands or streams, introducing harmful pollutants into the nearby ecosystem, the report said, and they could end up in the water lines if not properly treated. "Wastewater discharges may also contain pollutants that are products of metal pipe corrosion, such as copper, nickel and chromium," the report said. Ingesting these chemicals raises public health concerns as they can cause problems such as severe nausea, vomiting, headaches and dizziness, as well as harm to liver, kidneys, respiratory systems, stomach and intestinal lining, according to the National Library of Medicine.

artigo.texto: Gabe Evans rips Democrats for blocking data center bill Critics say bill ‘has no teeth’ Republican U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans tore into Senate Democrats on Wednesday after most of the party’s lawmakers blocked a measure designed to rein in electricity costs associated with building large new data centers. Opponents have insisted the legislation “has no teeth.” Recommended Stories The Senate failed to advance the Ratepayer Protection Act on a 57-43 procedural vote, falling short of the 60 votes needed to overcome a Democratic filibuster. Four Democrats joined every Republican voting in favor of the legislation. Colorado’s two Democratic U.S. senators, Michael Bennet and John Hickenlooper, voted against moving the legislation forward. Earlier this month, the bill passed the House, where Evans was a prime sponsor, on a nearly unanimous bipartisan vote. Evans accused the opposition party of playing politics, while critics countered that the “toothless” legislation was an attempt to hand a symbolic win to its vulnerable Republican sponsors. Although the bill doesn’t require that data centers “pay their own way,” as some of its Republican backers have claimed, the legislation gives state utility regulators two years to “consider” whether to adopt federal standards that would force new data centers to cover the “full incremental cost” of upgraded electrical generation and transmission infrastructure associated with the facilities. Evans is seeking reelection to a second term in Colorado’s most competitive district against Democratic nominee Manny Rutinel, a former state legislator. Decided by less than 2,500 votes two years ago, the race has already drawn nearly $10 million in outside spending, making it the most expensive toss-up seat in the country so far this cycle. The bill’s Senate sponsor, Republican Jon Husted, is seeking reelection in Ohio, where former U.S. Sen. Sherrod Brown is attempting to unseat him. “Rather than joining the House in putting Americans first, Senate Democrats choose to prioritize political games over a commonsense solution that protects ratepayers across the country,” Evans said in a statement after the Senate killed his bill. Evans said that the Democrats who backed the bill in the House — including the Democratic members of Colorado’s delegation — “understand protecting hardworking families from costs they didn’t create shouldn’t be controversial. The House proved that this wasn’t a partisan issue. Senate Democrats decided to make it one.” Hickenlooper said in an online video that it was Senate Republicans who were standing in the way of making data centers pick up the tab for increased utility costs. “(The) Republicans’ Ratepayer Protection Act has no teeth,” Hickenlooper said in a social media post. “It won’t actually protect families like yours from paying more on your energy bills.” “Families like yours shouldn’t be forced to pay for their new infrastructure needs,” Hickenlooper said in a video. “Republicans say their bill fixes that. It doesn’t.” Hickenlooper added that Republicans blocked a Democratic amendment “with real teeth” that, he said, would have required that “big new power users pay their fair share of costs.” “If big tech wants a data center, Big Tech should pay for it,” Hickenlooper concluded. “Congress needs to get serious and actually protect ratepayers now.” Evans responded to Hickenlooper on X, pointing out that Colorado’s House Democrats supported the bill. “You had the opportunity to join your Colorado colleagues and protect ratepayers,” Evans posted. “Shocker — you chose not to. One thing is for sure: given the choice, you put your partisan political games over the American people every time.” The exchange continued, with Hickenlooper accusing Evans of voting to approve “$70 billion in tax cuts for data centers” and Evans firing back that Hickenlooper had voted to raise costs for American consumers. The Republican-controlled House adjourned earlier this month until after the November election, and the Senate was expected to conclude its business later on Wednesday, without plans to return until after voters have weighed in.
