artigo.texto: O plano de levar data centers de inteligência artificial (IA) para o espaço foi um dos ganchos que atraíram os investidores para o IPO recorde da SpaceX, em junho, quando a companhia captou US$ 75 bilhões, foi avaliada em US$ 1,77 trilhão e registrou a maior abertura de capital de todos os tempos. Agora, a empresa de Elon Musk está ganhando a companhia de um outro peso pesado na jornada para transformar essa ambição em realidade: a Alphabet, holding avaliada em US$ 4,1 trilhões e dona do Google. O embarque oficial dessa parceria rumo ao espaço acontece na quinta-feira, 1º de outubro, quando o foguete Falcon 9 será lançado em órbita da base aérea de Vandenberg, na Califórnia, levando a bordo um satélite e um protótipo movido a energia solar equipado com chips desenvolvidos pelo Google. Esse lançamento marca o primeiro teste em órbita do Projeto Suncatcher, uma iniciativa que o Google tornou pública no fim de 2025. E que, segundo a empresa, busca explorar a possibilidade de o espaço um dia abrigar uma infraestrutura escalável de aprendizado de máquina. “Em órbita baixa, os satélites podem acessar luz solar quase constante, gerando até oito vezes mais energia solar do que na Terra. Eventualmente, será possível interligar múltiplas constelações de satélites, permitindo a gestão de cargas de trabalho de IA maiores enquanto estiverem em órbita”, escreveu a companhia, em comunicado. A SpaceX tem propagado um discurso similar, ao defender o espaço como a melhor alternativa para acompanhar a escala exigida pela IA. No início deste ano, Musk afirmou que esses data centers seriam a maneira mais barata de treinar essa tecnologia e que isso seria realidade em, no máximo, três anos. Alinhada com essa tese, a Alphabet é uma das grandes investidoras por trás da SpaceX, mesmo sob um cenário onde as duas companhias competem no campo da IA. Segundo a rede americana CNBC, sua fatia na empresa de Musk está avaliada em mais de US$ 82 bilhões – a SpaceX vale hoje US$ 2 trilhões. A dona do Google já testou os chips a caminho agora do espaço executando cargas de trabalho de IA na Universidade da Califórnia. Entretanto, a companhia ainda não sabe como eles irão se comportar nas condições desafiadoras em órbita baixa da Terra. No comunicado, a companhia ressaltou que explorar o espaço como um local viável para a computação escalável de IA não acontecerá da noite para o dia. E requer engenharia metódica, começando por comprovar como os equipamentos conseguem lidar com as imprevisibilidades desse ambiente. “Este primeiro lançamento tem como objetivo verificar o que funciona, identificar pontos de falha e aplicar essas descobertas em missões futuras”, escreveu a empresa. Do seu lado, a SpaceX anunciou que planeja construir e lançar seus próprios data centers em órbita. Essas estruturas serão compostas por satélites que a empresa desenvolve internamente, equipados com processadores e painéis solares que devem ser produzidos em parceria com a Tesla, também de Musk. Em meio a esses planos, especialistas do setor mantêm o pé no chão ao afirmar que os data centers espaciais ainda são uma realidade muito distante. Parte deles questiona, inclusive, se esses projetos são viáveis, dado que os lançamentos de foguetes ainda têm capacidade limitada e são caros. Ao mesmo tempo, eles alegam que esses centros de dados exigiriam sistemas de refrigeração capazes de suportar temperaturas extremas, além de proteção contra radiação e de possíveis obstáculos, como os detritos orbitais. Há quem enxergue boas perspectivas, porém, nessa “viagem”. “Os custos dos data centers na Terra estão crescendo, enquanto os custos dos centros de dados no espaço vão cair, e, em algum momento, essas curvas se cruzarão”, disse Matthew Weinzierl, autor do livro Space to Grow, sobre economia espacial, à revista americana Fast Company. “Não sabemos quando, mas os grandes investimentos do Google, da SpaceX e de outras empresas buscam antecipar esse dia”, afirmou Weinzierl, para quem os esforços da dupla são talvez o melhor exemplo de como as forças do mercado podem impulsionar a inovação no espaço.

Decision Could Point to Regulatory Hurdles for Data Centers North Carolina utility regulators this month denied a request by Duke Energy to add a gas-fired combustion turbine unit at a power plant Released Thursday, October 01, 2026 Written by John Egan for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary North Carolina utility regulators this month denied a request by Duke Energy to add a gas-fired combustion turbine unit at a power plant, saying the utility did not provide enough information for the commission to issue a certificate of convenience and necessity. N.C. Regulators Nix Duke Request Duke Energy Corporation has an ambitious capital construction program in North and South Carolina: it wants to spend at least $34 billion to construct roughly 50,300 megawatts (MW) of new generation capacity by 2041. For more on that, see August 24, 2026, article - Duke Energy Files 2026 Carolinas' Resource Plan. All of Duke's proposed Carolina project activity can be viewed in these project reports and plant profiles. Those plans include adding a 255-MW, gas-fired combustion turbine unit at the company's Sherwood H. Smith, Jr., Energy Complex in Hamlet, North Carolina. That proposed generator, which also could burn hydrogen, has an estimated total investment value of about $584 million. Duke plans to begin construction in September 2027, and finish construction by October 2029. But the schedule for that unit addition could be pushed back. On September 18, the North Carolina Utilities Commission (NCUC) voted 2-1 to deny Duke a certificate of public convenience and necessity (CCN) for that planned unit addition. The commission cited a lack of specificity in Duke's application, particularly around planned data centers, and how the utility would implement the White House "Ratepayer Protection Pledge" it signed in March 2026 to protect captive residential and business customers from paying for the cost to serve data centers. "We are disappointed by the North Carolina Utilities Commission's decision regarding the Smith Energy Complex CPCN application and are reviewing the order and assessing potential next steps," Duke Energy spokesperson Bill Norton told Industrial Info Resources in an email. "We believe we have demonstrated that the Smith CT is part of a least-cost path to maintain reliable and affordable service for customers as energy demand continues to grow across North Carolina." The North Carolina regulators flagged other issues as well. For example, how would the plan to add this gas-fired generator, with its attendant carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions, affect Duke's ability to meet state laws that require utilities to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050? Also, the request was filed before the panel ruled on Duke's integrated resource plan (IRP), a decision expected later this year. The NCUC majority pointed out that state law required utilities to pursue the lowest-cost resources to meet customer electric demand. Would investing more than half a billion dollars be the least-cost option, as required by state law? The North Carolina regulators are scheduled to issue their decision on that IRP by the end of this year. The commission's decision to deny a CCN is not the final word. The commission order would allow Duke to re-apply at a future date. By the Numbers - 584: The total investment value (TIV) in millions of US dollars, that Duke plans to invest to add a new generating unit to its Smith Energy Complex. - 255: The generating capacity, in megawatts, of the planned unit addition Duke wants to build. - 24,500: The amount of new generating capacity, in megawatts, that Duke plans to add to its resource base by 2035. - 70: The estimated proportion of Duke's electric load growth to 2035 that will come from data centers, according to regulatory filings. Big Plans to Build Data Centers in the Carolinas Industrial Info Resources is tracking 120 active and proposed data center projects in the Carolinas, currently slated to begin construction between the start of 2026 and the end of 2041. Not all these projects will be built in Duke's service territory. But as the utility is the largest provider of power in both states, serving more than 4.8 million customers, a majority, if not a significant majority, of those proposed projects likely are slated to be built in Duke's service area. The total investment value (TIV) of these 120 data center projects is about US$102 billion. Readers can learn more from a full list of related project reports. Data Center Issue Called Out by One N.C. Commissioner In a concurrent opinion to the September 18 NCUC decision, Commissioner Tommy Tucker wrote, "the proposed facility's significant and 'staggering' costs, as described by the public staff, are certain, while the proposed facility's value and need is overall uncertain due to the insufficiency of the evidence of record." He added, "As noted in the order, the speculative (electric load) growth noted by (Duke Energy) and the public staff includes significant data center growth, and the record does not adequately establish the specific extent to which the proposed facility is intended to serve the anticipated growth in data center customer demand. While the public staff witness panel indicated that the proposed facility was not being built for a particular customer, it is not lost on me that the proposed facility will be built in the same county as a transmission project previously approved by the Commission to support the load needs of a new customer data center campus." The utility "should provide additional evidence regarding the extent to which the Proposed Facility is needed to provide service to data centers, and how much those data centers will contribute to costs," Tucker wrote. artigo.texto: Understanding Thermal Runaway to Build Safer Battery Energy Storage Systems Editor’s Note: The following article is based on the FDNY Plenary Session, “Considerations for promoting the safe utilization of various lithium-ion battery technologies in the advancement of public policy initiatives in today’s world,” presented at ISPCE 2026 in May 2026. Lithium-ion batteries have become so common that they are easy to take for granted. They power phones, laptops, tools, e-bikes, and electric vehicles, and are associated with convenience and portability. That familiarity makes it easy to overlook the amount of energy these batteries store and how quickly that energy can be released when something goes wrong. New York City began seeing a sharp increase in lithium-ion battery fires beginning in early 2021. Investigations showed that these fires were occurring at an alarming rate, particularly in micromobility devices such as e-bikes and e-scooters. Fires involving lithium-ion batteries were growing rapidly, producing severe conditions earlier than expected and contributing to deaths and injuries across the city. Data from the Fire Department of the City of New York (FDNY) later documented 268 lithium-ion battery-related fires in 2023 and 277 in 2024, with 18 deaths in 2023 before prevention efforts began to reduce that number. The severity of these incidents also showed in the types of rescues firefighters were being forced to perform. One of the clearest examples was the increased use of the life-saving rope, a high-risk technique used only in extreme circumstances to lower a firefighter from a floor above to rescue someone trapped at a window. In normal conditions, this is a rarely used tactic. It is the kind of rescue that might happen once a decade. Seeing multiple deployments in a single year showed lithium-ion battery fires were trapping occupants before they could reach an exit more frequently than other fire types. Like micromobility devices, battery energy storage systems (BESS) share the same underlying fire hazards. These systems generally use the same lithium-ion technology, but they can scale that energy storage into larger, more complex installations that support buildings, infrastructure, and power systems. As the scale increases, the importance of managing the hazard increases with it. Conditions that drive battery failure do not change, but the consequences depend more heavily on how the system is designed, installed, used, and controlled. Therefore, safe deployment of BESS depends on how these systems are built to perform, not only during normal operation but also when something goes wrong. Understanding how lithium-ion batteries function, how they fail, and how system design influences those outcomes is essential to evaluating risk and supporting safe installation and operation. Known Hazards Battery-powered products are filling the space between small consumer devices and large stationary systems. Portable power packs, battery‑supported appliances, and plug‑in photovoltaic systems with portable storage all raise similar questions about stored energy, use environment, and safety expectations. As lithium-ion batteries appear in more forms, the safety discussion becomes less about product category and more about how the system stores energy, controls failure, and interacts with its surroundings. The Battery Fundamentals Behind the Risk A lithium-ion battery stores and releases energy by moving lithium ions between two electrodes inside a cell. The basic internal structure includes a cathode, an anode, a separator, and an electrolyte. The cathode is typically made from metal oxide-coated aluminum foil. The anode is usually carbon-coated copper foil. The separator is a very thin plastic layer that keeps the two electrodes apart while still allowing ionic movement. The electrolyte is usually made up of an organic solvent, lithium salts, and additives that support charge transfer. That arrangement allows energy to move efficiently during charging and discharging, which is one reason lithium-ion batteries became so central to modern electrical products. The battery can be recharged many times, can deliver power quickly, and can be built in different shapes for different applications. Pouch cells are common in smartphones and laptops. Prismatic cells are used in some electric vehicles and large-scale battery energy storage systems. Cylindrical cells, including the commonly used 18650 format, are used in power tools, e-mobility devices, and some laptops and vehicles. Thermal Runaway Lithium-ion batteries can fail for many different reasons. While the initiating causes may vary, many serious battery safety incidents involve a phenomenon known as thermal runaway. Thermal runaway occurs when an internal short circuit or other condition destabilizes the cell, causing an uncontrolled charge movement across the separator between the anode and cathode. This uncontrolled flow of electricity creates a lot of heat. As the flow continues, the cell generates heat faster than it can dissipate it. That process accelerates internal decomposition, releases more heat, and pushes the cell further into failure. Once thermal runaway begins, it often spreads to adjacent cells. That chain reaction is known as propagation. This is the point at which lithium-ion batteries become fundamentally different from many other electrical hazards. The battery is not simply overheating from the outside. It is generating heat internally in a self-accelerating way. That process can continue until all affected cells are consumed or until sufficient cooling slows the reaction. In large systems, the difference between a single failing cell and a propagating event is one of the most important risk distinctions to understand. artigo.texto: Green Party comptroller candidate demands transparency on Texas data center spending TYLER, Texas (KLTV) - Shehla Faizi, the Green Party nominee for Texas comptroller, called for more transparency from the comptroller’s office on recent data center construction. “We don’t even have a really concrete data on the benefits of these AI data centers when it comes to job production,” she said. “It’s all shoddy data from here, there and everywhere.” Faizi said Texas should divest from Israeli bonds, redirecting the state’s $280 million investment to Texas. “In Israel, you have free heath care, free higher education. Those are the things that even Texans don’t have,” she explained. “So why are foreign entities getting an advantage over our own people?” She said opposes Texas’ school voucher program, citing data showing most applicants already attended private schools. “I am very against this,” Faizi said. “Why are our tax dollars going into private ownership hands?” Faizi, who is Muslim, addressed anti-Islamic rhetoric at this year’s Texas Republican Convention, saying no officeholder could implement Sharia law on others. “That’s not possible because Sharia, by definition, is a very personal law,” she explained. “The way we pray, the way we fast, everything. It’s on a very personal level. It’s not something you can implement on other people.” Copyright 2026 KLTV. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: BROKEN BOW, Neb.— The Custer County Board of Supervisors met in regular session for just short of two hours on Tuesday morning starting at 9 AM. Toward the end of the meeting, public hearings were held for the possible closure of road 351 outside of Sargent, data center regulations that were passed to the board from the planning commission, and a possible temporary moratorium on battery energy storage systems. Landowners alongside road 351 came before the board to express their support of the closure, saying the road hasn’t been graded since the floods that happened several years ago. They did express an interest in an easement agreement since a party would be land locked with the closure of the road. Ultimately the board decided to give the township its 120 days time to decide if they want to maintain the road. During that time, they will check to see if the county is to have involvement in the easement process or if the private parties handle it themselves. Ahead of the public hearing regarding data center regulations that were put in the hands of the supervisors from the planning commission last week, Zoning Administrator Darci Tibbs made a statement regarding the process. “The purpose of these regulations is to not encourage or attract data centers, but to make sure that if one is proposed in Custer County, we have appropriate standards and safeguards in place to protect the health, safety, and welfare of our citizens, and to protect the ag and rural character of the county,” said Tibbs. Hear the full statement from Tibbs here: No members of the public came forward to make a statement during the public hearing and a resolution will appear for consideration by the board at an upcoming meeting. Tibbs also made a statement expressing the planning commission’s desire for a 12 month moratorium on battery energy storage systems so that ample time could be given to researching them and working toward regulations. Tibbs explained that the systems typically include battery units or containers, inverters, transformers, cooling equipment, electrical controls, monitoring systems, and safety equipment. The facilities can range from small systems serving one property to large commercial or utility scale facilities that can occupy multiple acres and connect to the electrical grid. No members of the public came forward to speak and a resolution that would put the moratorium in place will be on an upcoming agenda. Other items from Tuesday’s meeting: - The Cozad Road and Dunning Road were approved for closure for next year’s Sandhills Open Road Challenge races that happen in Custer County. (August 13 and 14 respectively) - One parcel in the county was delinquent and on the report to the county, attached to two years worth of taxes at $327.11 and a utility assessment of $3,091.06 - It was reported by the treasurer that nine of the 43 distress warrants issued to the Sheriff remain uncollected and have been returned. The initial amount certified, including interest and fees was $52,611.63. The Sheriff’s office collected $36,314.60. Those not returned were for a variety of reasons including no property being found or bankruptcies. The $8,467.15 was approved to be stricken from the tax rolls. - A representative from Oak Creek Engineering came before the board with an amendment request for engineering services on the Anselmo south road project, stating that the quote given for service hours came in low and additional funds were needed. The original quote of $30,400 was eclipsed and the ask was for $15,250 worth of service hour dollars. The amendment passed with supervisors Markham and Kleeb voting no. - Mark Rempe was appointed as the voting member for the East Central 911 Region board, with Chip Blowers as alternate - A motor vehicle tax exemption for Callaway Hospital District was approved for a tax loss of $239.65 - Applications to cross right-of-way were approved for Hamilton Telecommunications for projects outside of Mason City as well as private landowners for culvert work outside of Oconto and on Victoria Springs Road - During public comments, Zelle HR representatives came forward to announce that the person from their company working with the county would be changing and to introduce her

artigo.texto: O Ministério do Planejamento, Orçamento e Gestão (MP) está exigindo que todos os órgãos governamentais apenas contratem serviços de cloud computing que tenham data centers localizados no Brasil. Ou seja, nada de armazenar os dados via nuvem baseada em computadores estrangeiros. A decisão surgiu por meio de um manual de "boas práticas, orientações e vedações". "A nossa expectativa é que os próprios fornecedores tenham o total interesse em resguardar o sigilo das informações quando assim for exigido. Se, eventualmente, houver problemas de judicialização, é importante que isso seja feito na jurisdição brasileira”, comentou o secretário de Tecnologia da Informação da pasta, Cristiano Heckert, segundo o CW. Para reduzir os gastos, o manual também diz para os órgãos do Sistema de Administração dos Recursos de TI (SISP) não contratarem salas-cofre e salas seguras. O documento tem o apoio de Heckert, que comenta que essas orientações devem otimizar os recursos de infraestrutura. Espionagem? Se alocar os dados de servidores em data centers nacionais é um medo de espionagem ou vazamento de informações, é necessário lembrar que a tecnologia de espionagem internacional está bem na frente. artigo.texto: The U.S. data center boom has entered a new, contradictory phase. On the one hand, both data center construction activity and credible forecasts for near-term capacity additions to the electric grid to serve data centers remain robust. The Electric Power Research Institute, for example, said in February that data centers will represent up to 17% of U.S. electricity demand in 2030 and as much as 20% in 2035. On the other hand, data center and utility infrastructure projects face a host of challenges. These include both physical constraints, such as equipment and labor shortages, as well as mounting public opposition driven by concerns about large-scale computing facilities’ impact on water supplies, the cost and reliability of power and natural gas supplies, and the quality of life in host communities. The upshot is that even some data center development projects advanced enough to appear in utility load forecasts with a named hyperscaler attached are not certain to move forward. Near Grand Rapids, Michigan, for example, a Microsoft data center touted by Consumers Energy faces an uncertain future amid local permitting delays. “[Data centers] are running into physical problems that are manifesting as market problems, political problems, regulatory problems and ultimately problems down on the ground." Blake Nixon President and CEO of Geronimo Power Another Microsoft-backed data center in Vineland, New Jersey, was recently hit with a $1 million fine for running dozens of gas-powered generators without the proper permits, and ordered to obtain them within 45 days or shut down. A proposed Google data center that would interconnect in Xcel Energy’s Minnesota territory faces a court-ordered work stoppage to allow time for environmental review. Even projects that sought to circumvent interconnection delays by building off-grid generation have seen setbacks. Last week, Oracle moved to protect itself financially from the delay or cancellation of Project Jupiter, a massive, 2.5-GW data center campus planned for Doña Ana County, New Mexico, after state regulators blocked a gas pipeline proposed to serve it. Data center opposition “has reached a pitch I have never seen before in my 20-plus years in development,” Blake Nixon, president and CEO of Geronimo Power, told Utility Dive in an interview. This spring, officials in Nobles County, Minnesota, shot down a proposal by Geronimo to build a 400 MW “data park” there, despite the company’s efforts at community outreach. Now, Nixon said his team is considering alternative sites in nearby communities. “[Data centers] are running into physical problems that are manifesting as market problems, political problems, regulatory problems and ultimately problems down on the ground,” he said. In May, Goldman Sachs said only 50%-60% of planned data center capacity will come online as expected in the next two years amid delays and cancellations. And while the 36 GW of capacity added to the development pipeline in the first quarter of 2026 sounds impressive, that’s down 19% from the last quarter of 2025 as developers “continue to shift their focus to existing … pipelines in the face of an increasingly challenging development and regulatory environment,” Caitlin Connelly, a senior analyst with Wood Mackenzie, said in a July note. Experts say these developments raise questions about just how much data center load will come online in the near term — injecting unwelcome uncertainty into utility planning cycles that must look years, even decades, into the future. Working around grid constraints with flexibility, BYO capacity It’s increasingly difficult for developers of large-scale data center campuses to find sites with the hundreds of megawatts, let alone gigawatts, of spare grid capacity they expect their projects to need at full build-out. In the PJM Interconnection, real or perceived power scarcity is a major driver of both local opposition and top-down political backlash to the industry. The independent market monitor in July blamed data centers for 38% of charges at the most recent capacity auction. The Democratic governors of Pennsylvania, Virginia and New Jersey have taken action in recent months to push regulators to require data centers to bring more generation and transmission capacity online. These moves are not only in PJM states with Democratic governors. Power scarcity and cost concerns have triggered organized opposition and political backlash to data centers in places developers until recently believed were sympathetic to their cause, like Texas and Utah. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, R, successfully pushed for a sweeping pause on data center grid interconnections that threatens up to 20% of the total U.S. development pipeline, BloombergNEF said earlier this month. Utilities and data centers are responding in several ways. The most straightforward is through “bring your own capacity” arrangements in which computing facilities colocate with new generation or finance local capacity additions. Some of these arrangements are massive: OpenAI agreed earlier this month to take 8 GW of the capacity from a planned 10 GW power generation project in Ohio that includes 9.2-GW gas assets. The facility, which is being pursued by Japan’s SoftBank Group and the U.S. Department of Energy, would be the country’s largest generation source if built. If not, that title would go to Amazon’s proposed 7.7-GW gas-fired power plant in West Texas, which would also be larger than the current titleholder, Washington state’s 6.8-GW Grand Coulee hydroelectric dam. Smaller-scale capacity procurements are also in the works, like Google’s “first-of-its-kind” deal with Voltus for 100 MW of virtual power plant capacity in PJM. Elsewhere, utilities and data centers are pursuing asset-light alternatives using software to find previously untapped headroom on the grid or to ramp down computing loads during periods of peak demand. artigo.texto: Data centers have gained considerable attention in Upstate South Carolina and across the United States. The growing number of these facilities throughout the country supports the modern digital age, specifically the rising demand for artificial intelligence and cloud computing. Despite this growth, many questions remain about how many data centers are in operation or planned. South Carolina has become an increasingly attractive location for data centers due to land availability, low regulatory barriers and economic incentives. However, public opposition to the development of these facilities has grown in recent years. Upstate Business Journal took a closer look at data centers to provide more information on what they are, where we think they are located and what local governments are doing about them. What are data centers? Data centers are facilities that house and operate computer systems, storage devices and network equipment. These facilities are used for the storage, management and processing of significant amounts of data. Types of data centers There are three main types of data centers: - Enterprise Data Centers: Private data centers owned and operated by a business or organization. - Colocation and Service Provider Data Centers: Shared data centers offering leasable space for multiple businesses and organizations. - Hyperscale Data Centers: Massive data centers operated by major technology companies for large-scale data processing, storage and computing. Source: Pew Research Center and International Energy Agency’s Energy and AI Statewide tracking The South Carolina Department of Commerce does not track how many data centers are in the state. Instead, the agency monitors the number of facilities that apply for a sales tax exemption. This tracking method does not provide an accurate list of data centers in South Carolina. Alex Clark, the agency’s deputy director of communications, said not all data centers pursue this certification, and not all certified data centers begin operations in South Carolina. According to SC Commerce, the agency has received one sales tax exemption application since the beginning of 2026 and four applications in the past three years. Estimated data centers in SC The total number of data centers in South Carolina and where they are located remains unclear. Data Center Map, an industry database, estimates there are 48 data centers across 12 markets in South Carolina. Markets in the Upstate with data centers include Spartanburg, Greenville, Anderson, Seneca and Gaffney. National and regional breakdown More than 3,000 data centers are estimated to be in operation in the United States, with more than 1,500 new data centers under development. - South: 1,209 existing and 754 planned data centers - Midwest: 655 existing and 419 planned data centers - West: 807 existing and 277 planned data centers - Northeast: 397 existing and 106 planned data centers Source: Pew Research Center Environmental concerns Common environmental concerns regarding data center development include: - Water and energy consumption - Noise disruption - Air pollution - Large land use Source: Southern Environmental Law Center Energy consumption Powering and cooling the computer systems and equipment within data centers require vast amounts of electricity and water. According to the International Energy Agency, a 100-megawatt data center consumes: - As much electricity annually as 100,000 households. - As much water per day as around 6,500 households (an average of 2 million liters) Source: International Energy Agency’s Energy and AI Fast fact The United States made up the largest share – 45% – of global data center electricity consumption in 2024. Data center energy consumption grew by approximately 12% between 2015 and 2024. Source: International Energy Agency’s Energy and AI Notable local projects Valara Holdings High Performance Compute Center NorthMark Strategies, through its subsidiary Valara Holdings, is constructing a high-performance computing data center southeast of Spartanburg. The $2.8 billion project, announced in April 2025, redevelops the former Kohler manufacturing plant at 4000 S. Pine St. Spartanburg County Council approved economic incentives for the project in 2025. The new data center campus will feature an on-site power plant with 24 permitted natural gas generators and 11 proposed natural gas-fired turbines. An application was submitted in March to the South Carolina Department of Environmental Services for a second synthetic minor air construction permit for the additional turbines. If approved, the data center would have a power generation capacity of more than 450 megawatts. DartPoints Greenville Data Center DartPoints announced plans to invest $125 million into its existing data center in Greenville in November 2025. The enterprise-class data center is located at 78 Global Drive in Greenville’s Global Business Park near the intersection of Interstate 85 and Laurens Road. The expansion adds 88,000 square feet to the Greenville data center and creates 10 new high-tech jobs. The facility’s total capacity will be increased from 2.5 megawatts to 12.5 megawatts to support artificial intelligence, enterprise and edge applications. Data center moratorium Multiple government entities in Upstate South Carolina are considering or have approved a moratorium on approving new data center applications. - Spartanburg County: Spartanburg County Council has approved the first and second readings of a one-year data center moratorium. The third and final reading of the moratorium was expected to be held during County Council’s meeting on Sept. 21. - Anderson County: Anderson County Council gave final approval to a six-month moratorium on data center applications in August. - Greenwood County: Greenwood County Council approved the third and final reading of a one-year moratorium on data center applications in July. - South Carolina: House Bills 5526 and 5286 were introduced in early 202

artigo.texto: Bring on more robots and self-driving cars to help the tech firms make money. Hyperscalers are rushing to build more data centers to run AI workloads — but will the AI industry ever generate enough revenue to pay for that infrastructure? Researchers at Bain and Company have looked into this and concluded that productivity gains from existing AI services are not enough to justify the money being pumped in: AI companies and the hyperscalers that power them will need to create brand new markets for their services. Bain said the “arms race” among hyperscalers is accelerating to the extent that their capital expenditures could reach $780 billion in 2026, a fivefold increase in three years. And, it estimates, annual spending on AI infrastructure could reach $1.5 trillion by 2031. Making the assumption that hyperscalers’ capital expenditure amounts to about 25% of revenue, they would need the AI market to be worth $6 trillion annually. But, said Bain, the current consumer and enterprise AI markets together could be worth up to $1.8 trillion by 2031, leaving a whopping $4.2 trillion still to find from new markets. Bain highlighted four potential areas: the use of AI in search; the development of more autonomous vehicles, including drones; physical AI, including digital twins and robotics; and new product development, for example, breakthroughs in pharmaceuticals.

Proprietary iron & saltwater electrolyte According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Flow Battery Energy Storage market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global flow battery energy storage market is entering a decisive commercial phase as utilities and developers seek long-duration storage solutions that can economically shift renewable generation across four to twelve hours or more. Unlike lithium-ion systems, flow batteries separate power and energy, allowing independent scaling of duration and capacity, which makes them attractive for grid operators facing rising renewable curtailment and peak-shaving needs. As of 2026, deployment remains concentrated in utility-scale projects and selected industrial microgrids, but the pipeline is broadening as vanadium supply chains mature, project bankability improves, and grid interconnection standards become clearer. The market is supported by ambitious decarbonization targets, renewable portfolio standards, and the need for resilient grid infrastructure. However, growth is tempered by vanadium price volatility, competition from lithium-ion and other long-duration technologies, and the complexity of project financing. This report provides a structured analysis of the market from 2026 to 2035, covering demand drivers, supply chain dynamics, pricing logic, competitive positioning, and regional outlooks. It is designed for manufacturers, integrators, utilities, investors, and policymakers seeking a commercially grounded view of where flow battery energy storage is heading and which segments will lead adoption. The baseline scenario for the world flow battery energy storage market through 2035 assumes continued policy support for renewable integration and long-duration storage, steady improvement in vanadium electrolyte supply, and gradual cost reduction as manufacturing scale increases. Under this scenario, the market is projected to grow at a compound annual growth rate of 18.5% from 2026 to 2035, reaching a market index of 520 by 2035 (2025 = 100). Growth is expected to be front-loaded in Asia-Pacific, particularly China, where large-scale vanadium redox flow battery projects are already being deployed for grid balancing and renewable time-shifting. North America and Europe will follow, driven by utility procurement mandates and the need to replace retiring thermal peaking capacity. The baseline assumes no major breakthrough in alternative long-duration technologies that would displace flow batteries in the 4–12 hour duration range, but it also assumes that lithium-ion will continue to dominate shorter-duration applications. Key uncertainties include vanadium price spikes, delays in grid interconnection queues, and the pace of cost declines in competing technologies. The market outlook remains positive, with flow batteries carving out a durable niche in long-duration, high-cycle applications where safety, scalability, and longevity are paramount. Electric utilities and grid operators are the primary adopters of flow battery energy storage, driven by the need to integrate high shares of variable renewable generation and maintain grid reliability. Flow batteries are increasingly chosen for renewable time-shifting, peak shaving, and ancillary services where discharge durations of four to twelve hours are required. Utilities value the independent scalability of power and energy, which allows them to size systems precisely to grid needs, and the long cycle life that matches asset lifetimes. Through 2035, demand will be supported by capacity auctions, clean energy standards, and the retirement of coal and gas peakers. artigo.texto: Bucksport Town Council advances proposed 180-day moratorium on commercial data centers BUCKSPORT, Maine (WABI) - The Bucksport Town Council voted to advance a proposed 180-day moratorium on commercial data centers following a public discussion at its Sept. 24 meeting. Bucksport’s Community and Economic Development Director confirmed to WABI that an interested developer recently toured the former paper mill site. Backers of the moratorium argue the temporary freeze is essential to study energy, water, and environmental impacts before any formal proposal is filed. One councilor cast the sole opposing vote, contending that the town should encourage smaller data centers to rebuild the industrial tax base. The proposed ordinance moves to a second reading and formal public hearing on Oct. 8. Copyright 2026 WABI. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: O edital para a segunda parte da concessão da Floresta Nacional do Bom Futuro, em Porto Velho (RO), foi publicado. A área de quase 40 mil hectares será usada para restaurar áreas degradadas, gerar empregos locais e produzir créditos de carbono, ajudando o Brasil a cumprir sua meta de restaurar 12 milhões de hectares até 2030. O Serviço Florestal Brasileiro (SFB) e o Ministério do Meio Ambiente (MMA) divulgaram as regras para a venda do segundo lote de gestão da Floresta Nacional (Flona) do Bom Futuro, localizada em Porto Velho, no estado de Rondônia. O processo foi preparado com ajuda técnica do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) e tem como objetivo principal recuperar áreas que foram degradadas na região da Amazônia, permitindo que empresas privadas gerenciem o espaço de forma sustentável. O documento do edital mostra que a área disponível é muito grande, ultrapassando 39 mil hectares. Para dar uma noção do tamanho, isso equivale a quase 55 mil campos de futebol. Deste total, cerca de 6,4 mil hectares serão usados especificamente para plantar árvores e restaurar a floresta. As empresas interessadas devem entregar suas propostas na sede da bolsa de valores B3, em São Paulo, entre 10h e 12h do dia 4 de novembro. A abertura das propostas, para ver quem ganhou, está marcada para o dia 18 de novembro. - Área Gigante: São mais de 39 mil hectares, o que é maior que muitas cidades do interior. - Meta Climática: A ação ajuda o Brasil a cumprir a promessa de recuperar 12 milhões de hectares de vegetação até 2030. - Carro de Ouro: A empresa vencedora poderá vender créditos de carbono, o que ajuda a pagar pela restauração. - Empregos Locais: O projeto exige contratação de moradores da região e compra de sementes locais. - Primeiro Caso: O lote anterior foi ganhado pela empresa Re.Green, marcando a primeira concessão de restauração no Brasil. Modelo de concessão e impacto social Este é o segundo leilão para recuperar a floresta neste local. O primeiro lote foi arrematado pela empresa Re.Green em março. Naquela ocasião, foi a primeira vez no Brasil que uma empresa ganhou o direito de cuidar de uma floresta pública principalmente para gerar receita com a venda de créditos de carbono (prova de que a atividade removeu poluição do ar). Agora, com esse segundo lote, o governo espera repetir o sucesso e ampliar a restauração. O contrato da concessão não fala apenas de plantio. Ele exige que parte do dinheiro ganho com o projeto seja investida em pesquisa científica, educação ambiental e proteção da floresta. Além disso, o edital manda que a empresa ajude as comunidades que moram no entorno da reserva, incluindo a população indígena Karitiana. Há regras para garantir que mulheres tenham chances iguais, que povos indígenas sejam incluídos no processo e que a economia local seja fortalecida com a compra de insumos e contratação de mão de obra da região. Desafio nacional de recuperação da vegetação Esta concessão faz parte de um plano maior do Brasil para recuperar a mata nativa. De acordo com os dados divulgados, essa ação contribui diretamente para a meta de restaurar 12 milhões de hectares até o ano de 2030, estabelecida pelo Plano Nacional de Recuperação da Vegetação Nativa (Planaveg). Atualmente, o país já tem 3,4 milhões de hectares em processo de recuperação. Isso representa quase um terço da meta total. O novo lote da Flona do Bom Futuro vem justamente para impulsionar esse número, focando em uma das regiões mais importantes e frágeis da Amazônia.

Partilhar Acordo de 10 anos, estruturado através de um modelo de tolling, que atribui à Statkraft a gestão comercial da utilização das baterias nos mercados de energia e flexibilidade. Abrange os projectos Ełk e Turośń Kościelna, ambos na Polónia, com 200 MW / 800 MWh de capacidade cada. É o maior acordo de BESS do género publicamente comunicado na União Europeia até à data A Greenvolt e a Statkraft, o maior produtor europeu de energia renovável e um dos principais fornecedores de PPAs na Europa, assinaram um acordo de tolling com uma duração de 10 anos, abrangendo 400 MW de capacidade de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) em dois projectos na Polónia. O acordo é, até à data, o maior publicamente comunicado na União Europeia e marca o primeiro contrato de grande escala da Statkraft para BESS no mercado polaco. O acordo abrange dois parques de baterias: o Ełk (200 MW/800 MWh) e Turośń Kościelna (200 MW/800 MWh), localizadas, respetivamente, em Nowa Wieś Ełcka e Turośń Kościelna. A estrutura de um acordo de tolling confere à Statkraft o direito de decidir quando as baterias carregam e descarregam nos mercados de energia e de flexibilidade, proporcionando simultaneamente à Greenvolt uma fonte adicional de receitas previsíveis e de longo prazo, a par das receitas já asseguradas através do Mercado de Capacidade da Polónia. “Este acordo com a Statkraft traz uma sofisticada capacidade de optimização de mercado para estes projectos, permitindo monetizar a flexibilidade das baterias em diferentes mercados de electricidade e desbloquear receitas adicionais”, sublinha Łukasz Zagórski, business origination and market regulation director da Greenvolt Power. “Com a maior transacção de BESS realizada até à data no país, continuamos a desempenhar um papel activo no apoio à transição energética da Polónia. Os dois projectos de BESS complementam o nosso portefólio de activos eólicos e solares de terceiros, a partir do qual podemos oferecer preços competitivos e estáveis a grandes consumidores de energia”, acrescenta Kornel Koronowski, head of origination poland da Statkraft. À medida que o sistema eléctrico da Polónia integra quantidades crescentes de energia renovável, prevê-se que os sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias desempenhem um papel cada vez mais importante. Ao armazenarem o excedente de electricidade renovável e libertá-lo quando a procura é mais elevada, as baterias de grand escala contribuem para equilibrar a oferta e a procura, estabilizar a rede e facilitar a integração de mais energia eólica e solar no mix energético da Polónia.

artigo.texto: TAMPA, Fla. — Tampa Electric says it filed a plan with the Florida Public Service Commission aimed at protecting customers from potential costs tied to future data centers and other large-load electric users. The filing, called a tariff, is required under a data centers law Gov. Ron DeSantis signed in May. DeSantis said the law is meant to protect consumers from having to pay for one of those facilities. Tampa Electric spokesperson Cherie Jacobs said the tariff would require large-load customers, such as data centers, to pay for the electric infrastructure that powers them. Those facilities would also be responsible for some of the cost of maintaining and operating the broader electric system. “We are seeing interest from large-load customers for potential opportunities in the future,” Jacobs said. “Right now, Tampa Electric does not serve any large-load customers, but this plan does pave the way for the future to make sure that our customers remain protected and that reliable service is maintained.” Electricity use has been a recurring topic at meetings about data centers across Tampa Bay. Residents have raised concerns about whether local electric grids can handle the power required by large facilities and whether their own utility bills could increase. According to Tampa Electric, requiring companies to help maintain the overall system could also help lower bills for existing customers. Jacobs said the plan still needs approval from the Public Service Commission, which could happen late this year or early next year. Duke Energy has also submitted a tariff to the Public Service Commission. A Duke spokesperson said the company was the first utility in Florida to present its plan. In a statement, Duke said it does not currently have a large-load client in Florida and was a signer of President Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge. The company also said it requested a rate cut for customers on Sept. 3 that could take effect in 2027.

artigo.texto: TRENTON, Ohio — Trenton voters will decide in November whether to ban new large data centers, as city leaders consider a package of resident benefits that opponents say is intended to influence the vote. The ballot issue would ban new data centers over 25 megawatts if voters approve it. If voters reject the issue, the ban would fail, opening the door for more data centers in the city. Amy Humbert, a Trenton resident and member of Woodsdale and Trenton Environmental Resistance, known as WATER, said she is concerned about a data center planned north of Cincinnati in Trenton. “Seeing this is just destruction of what I moved into Trenton for,” Humbert said. “I’m worried about the noise. I’m worried about pollution.” WATER sued the city of Trenton over the issue, and the case went to the Ohio Supreme Court. The court cleared the way for the issue to go to voters. “We actually have been fighting over a year,” Humbert said. “We have collected enough signatures to get it on the ballot.” The group is also raising concerns about what it says the city is doing to encourage voters to reject the proposed ban. “It just felt like the city was trying to bribe everybody by not putting on taxes and not putting on levies over the next several years to get the citizens to vote down the issue,” Humbert said. At Thursday night’s council meeting, city leaders plan to discuss multiple resolutions tied to resident benefits if the data center ban fails. The proposals include no new tax levies for 10 years, rolling back the property tax and a 30% discount on a membership to the new YMCA being built. City leaders say the proposals are not a bribe. “We’re just trying to give the voters information on what the city has always planned to do with future, current and future economic development fundraising,” said Matthew Mesiskois, finance director for the city of Trenton. Mesiskois said the benefits have been discussed as part of the city’s economic development plans. He said the city needs economic development to remain financially stable. “We don’t have the pool of funding to promise that, hey, we won’t go back and ask if we need to sustain our five part time fire and EMS operations,” Mesiskois said. “We can’t make that promise and be financially solvent without economic development.” Thursday night’s discussion would be the first reading of the benefits resolutions. Council would still need to vote to move them forward. The larger decision will come in November, when voters decide whether to ban large data centers in Trenton.

artigo.texto: A controversial data center — the first of three planned by Google in Chesterfield County — has already racked up a handful of environmental violations, according to a letter sent out by the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality. According to a Sept. 29 letter to Aaron McGarry, the Google official listed on the notice of violation, DEQ staff “received email correspondence indicating unauthorized filling of surface waters … outside the permitted impact areas at the Project Peanut site.” DEQ received seven reports between December 2025 and August 2026 and conducted five inspections during the same period. Many of the violations referenced in the notice stem from the discharge of sediment into local waterways. One reads as follows: “During the March 4, 2026 inspection, DEQ staff observed filling of state waters from the discharge of sediment pollutant. In total, sediment accumulation was observed in approximately 1,356 linear feet of stream channel.” Courtney Bernhardt, director of research at the nonprofit Environmental Integrity Project, adding outside sediment — loose soil generated by construction projects — to waterways may seem like a small issue, but can have major impacts on the ecosystem. “If you smother the bottom of the stream, you’re going to kill all the little critters that live in that stream bed, and that is the base of the food web,” she said. “You’re essentially destroying the aquatic ecosystem from the bottom up.” According to the notice of violation, it appears construction on the 300-acre site caused about a foot of polluted sediment, affecting almost an acre of wetlands not far from the Meadowville Technology Park. Project Peanut’s campus is being built off of Old Bermuda Hundred Road. VPM News emailed DEQ, Chesterfield County and McGarry. DEQ would not make additional comment, a spokesperson for Chesterfield County declined to comment and McGarry did not return requests. Peanut officials have until Oct. 29 to answer DEQ’s notice. Project officials could receive penalties of up to $32,500 per violation per day, according to the notice — as much as $7 million per month in total. Google’s three planned data centers in Chesterfield County have been the source of controversy, with some residents crying foul over a lack of transparency and negative economic impacts. Next month, the county’s board of supervisors is set to consider a car tax cut linked to tax revenue the data centers generate. Bernhardt is also a resident of the county, and has attended many board meetings discussing data centers. She said the board members “repeatedly say they’re happy Google is building data centers. If they really were the best, I wouldn’t expect them to be violating the law. Especially during construction.”

artigo.texto: Trending Communities hosting hyperscale data centers are seeing benefits even while the protests grow. "New recreational spaces, water and wastewater infrastructure, traffic lights, build-outs of local roads and grants for schools were among the pluses for communities hosting them. "Our roads around our data centers are beautiful," said Etta Lockey, director of Commercial Energy Supply, Meta, also known as Facebook, Instagram, What's App and maker of novel hardware such as tech glasses. "Growth can pay for growth," she cited at the 16th annual Marcellus Shale Coalition INSIGHT 2026 in Erie. "My team is responsible for bringing the high voltage and electrons to our data centers in partnership with our utilities and energy development partners," she said. The goal, she said, is "not to shift costs onto the families in the communities where the data centers exist." Meta also has placed a priority on its commitment to the community and ongoing community engagement. "None of this is possible without our communities more than the jobs that data center development can support, we want to be good neighbors and good community partners," she said. This is done through hiring local contractors, boosting local tax revenue, paying for local infrastructure, and adding new energy to the grid, she added. This phenomena is where electrons and molecules are meeting the real economy. The workers, the townships, the utilities, the producers, a consortium of folks that have been powering the U.S. for generations are now having to address national AI dominance and meet demand. To do this right, developers need community partners who are seeing the upside and serving as home to some of the most innovative technology in the world. Meta, she noted, provides millions of dollars in grants year after year to support schools and nonprofits. In fact, Meta has given $94 million supporting over 3,700 grants and communities where it has data centers around the globe. One criteria screened for site selection is the availability of natural gas "We are also investing in partnerships and solutions that reduce the footprint over time," Lockey said. That includes support for U.S.-produced low methane natural gas. At Meta, energy innovation has become as important as software or chip innovation. The evolution of artificial intelligence is changing how thoughts are evolving on infrastructure, pushing innovation at every layer, Lockey said. For those in Appalachia, this presents an enormous opportunity. "We have the resources, we have the expertise and the workforce to help meet that demand," said Jim Welty, president of Marcellus Shale Coalition Meta is a company helping drive a new era of energy demand, he said. Lockey, an attorney by training, continues to lead efforts to secure the affordable, reliable energy needed to support the company's growing data infrastructure, he said.

artigo.texto: Two Workshops on EU-China ETS Cooperation Successfully Held in Wuhan On 16 September, the EU-funded project ‘EU-China Dialogue and Cooperation on ETS-related Policies and Measures’ organised two public workshops as official side-events during the 2026 China Carbon Market Conference in Wuhan. The workshops were hosted jointly by the European Commission and the Chinese Ministry of Ecology and Environment (MEE). It brought together senior officials, experts, and crucial stakeholders from China, the European Union, Brazil, the World Bank and UNEP, offering the audience engaged in China's national carbon market and observers from other parts of the world the latest policy developments and insightful opinions on the EU, Chinese, Brazilian, and international carbon markets, as well as the priorities of ongoing EU-China ETS cooperation. European Union, 2026 The morning workshop presented the main outcomes of the Joint Research Activity (JRA) on the conception and implementation of allowance auctioning in China's national ETS. Mr. LU Shize, Deputy Director-General of the Department of Climate Change of MEE, received three joint research reports on behalf of MEE from Mette QUINN, Deputy Director for Carbon Markets and Clean Mobility at DG CLIMA, and thanked the EU for its continued support to the joint research. The afternoon session turned to the important role and challenges of cap setting, a fundamental element for the credibility and environmental integrity of any emissions trading system. Following opening remarks by Ms QUINN and Mr LU, Ms QUINN shared the European Union's experience of setting the cap under the EU ETS. A highlight of the afternoon was the formal launch of the Joint Research on cap-setting supported under the EU project. European Union, 2026 Both workshops underscored the value of lessons-learnt from EU ETS on core ETS design elements. By combining international experience with China's specific institutional context, the project's joint research activities aim to provide a solid evidence base to support the inauguration of allowance auctioning and cap setting under China's national carbon market. Learn more about the ETS project https://www.eu-chinaets.org/

artigo.texto: ARCHBALD — Data center opponents challenged Tuesday whether changing conceptual plans for a proposed power plant on Eynon Jermyn Road is enough to prove the project meets the borough’s requirements for protecting public health and safety — continuing a months-long standoff between Stop Archbald Data Centers and Essential Energy LLC. “You are here to testify to this borough council that despite the fact that it is a conceptual design, it can be designed, constructed and operated in a safe way?” asked attorney Justin Richards, who represents residents challenging proposed data centers in Archbald. “There is a way that we can do this,” replied KCI Technologies Technical Lead of Power Generation Andrew Markle, testifying on behalf of Essential Energy. “We can do this — I’m not telling you how we’re going to do it — I’m saying that we can do this.” Borough council held its sixth conditional-use hearing to consider Essential Energy’s March 12 application for a 400-megawatt natural gas power plant on Eynon Jermyn Road. About 70 residents clustered throughout the Valley View High School auditorium, occasionally applauding or jeering during the three-hour hearing. There are 51 data centers proposed in Archbald across six projects, though more are likely on the way. Essential Energy is a firm tied to Kriger Construction Inc. of Archbald and its executive leadership — President Jim Marzolino and Vice President Dave Stiles. Other Kriger-linked firms propose the nearly 620,000-square-foot Project Boson data center across the street from Essential Energy, as well as four data centers and three power plants across Bell Mountain in Dickson City. Essential Energy’s plans have been contentious at hearings due to the power plant’s proximity to homes, schools, businesses and a popular borough park. The proposed power plant would nearly border Archbald’s Staback Park; it is opposite the Highlands Archbald residential community on Eynon Jermyn Road; and the Valley View School District’s campuses begin about half a mile away on Columbus Drive. There is also a preschool in the plaza in front of the Highlands, and a developer plans to build assisted living and skilled nursing facilities in the area. The debate over Essential Energy has largely revolved around the conceptual nature of its plans, with opponents pressing for more specific information and invoking Archbald’s zoning criteria for credible evidence, while power plant representatives counter that specifics will come later as the development evolves and navigates the regulatory processes. Markle, who cited his experience overseeing a fleet of 180 natural gas power plants in the United States representing about 5% of the grid, compared Essential Energy to a smaller version of the nearly 1,500-megawatt Lackawanna Energy Center in Jessup, characterizing natural gas power plants as “cookie-cutter” designs with specific protections and design elements tailored to the location and community. ‘Credible evidence’ Richards, of Elliott Greenleaf PC in Wilkes-Barre, opened his cross-examination by asking Markle to provide his Pennsylvania engineering license number; Markle authored the two-part report that was the subject of Tuesday’s hearing and the previous Aug. 18 hearing. “I do not have one,” Markle said, explaining he is a registered professional engineer in the province of Ontario, Canada. W. Casey Deller, a vice president at KCI Technologies in Mechanicsburg, reviewed and sealed the report as a professional engineer in Pennsylvania, Markle said. He later defended it as a standard practice in engineering due to the difficulty of maintaining licensing across individual states and provinces, each of which has its own licensure board. Richards also reiterated his contention that the hearing itself is a legally null because Essential Energy LLC did not exist March 12 when it submitted a zoning permit application in Archbald. The limited liability company organized with the state March 13. Markle said he had no idea about it. The attorney representing Stop Archbald Data Centers members referenced changing site plans and different testimony and reports from various engineers, changing the number of turbines and equipment multiple times. “If multiple different assumptions have been provided to the borough council based on wildly varying equipment, which one is the most accurate?” Richards said, listing multiple engineers who previously testified. It’s the normal progression of a conceptual design, where people examine different ways of approaching the same problem, Markle said. “We’re refining the design as we’re going,” Markle said. artigo.texto: Google put its own artificial intelligence chips into orbit Thursday, launching a refrigerator-sized test satellite designed to answer a question that would have sounded like science fiction a few years ago: Could the data centers powering AI one day run in space? The satellite, which Google nicknamed MVP, lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California at 11:32 a.m. PT aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket as part of SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare mission. It was one of 130 payloads on the flight, which carried everything from cubesats to orbital transfer vehicles. The launch is the first in-orbit test for Project Suncatcher, a research effort Google announced in November 2025. Google is not the first to test AI hardware in space, but MVP is the first step by a major tech company toward building orbital data centers. Inside are four of Google's tensor processing units, or TPUs, the specialized chips the company builds to run AI. Together, they reportedly have about the computing power of one server in a data center. The satellite will answer simple AI queries using Google's Gemini and operate for about a year. It could keep circling Earth for up to six years before gravity pulls it down and it burns up in the atmosphere. IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | How much water do data centers really use? Here's what we learned from public records The pitch for orbital data centers comes down to power. In low Earth orbit, satellites get near-constant sunlight and can generate up to eight times more solar power than panels on the ground, according to Google. That matters as AI's appetite for electricity keeps growing and data centers on the ground run into resistance, as rural communities across the U.S. are fighting to keep AI data centers out of their backyards. Many of those facilities also strain local water supplies, using cooling towers that shed heat by evaporating water. Google framed the mission around a basic question: "Can our AI hardware operate in space?" The first hurdle was getting there. Google says the roughly 10-minute ride to low Earth orbit puts loads of up to 10 times the force of gravity on a spacecraft. Before launch, engineers shook the satellite on all three axes to mimic a rocket's vibrations, and the hardware held. Radiation is the next threat. Solar events and cosmic rays can cause "bit flips," errors that switch a chip's binary code. Starting in February 2025, Google took its chips to UC Davis's Crocker Nuclear Laboratory, where a particle accelerator called a cyclotron blasted them with a radiation dose equal to five years in space. Restarting the chips could usually reset the bit flips. Then there's heat. On Earth, fans, air and water carry heat away from hot chips. In the vacuum of space, heat can only be shed through radiators. Google built a layered system: the chips sit on a motherboard, a putty-like thermal material draws heat into aluminum and copper layers, and a radiator panel projects it into space. IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Trump wants communities to embrace data centers, but opposition is growing Even so, MVP's chips can't run nonstop. Travis Beals, Google's senior director for Project Suncatcher, told the New York Times they can operate for about 15 minutes before shutting down to cool off. "This first launch is about seeing what works, identifying points of failure, and applying those findings to future missions," Beals wrote in Google's announcement. Google has plenty of company. SpaceX, which gave MVP its ride, has filed plans with the Federal Communications Commission for up to 1 million orbital data center satellites, according to Data Center Dynamics, and the idea helped fuel SpaceX's record IPO earlier this year. Startup Starcloud launched an Nvidia H100 GPU into orbit in November 2025 and trained a small AI model there. Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has said gigawatt-scale data centers will be in space within 10 or more years, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has also backed the concept.

artigo.texto: Agenda climática global também foi tema da 144ª reunião, que contou com a participação de representante do Ministério da Fazenda Da Redação (*) Brasília – O status regulatório e as perspectivas econômicas da implementação do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE) para o mercado de carbono foram discutidos, nesta segunda-feira (28), durante a 144ª reunião do Conselho Temático de Meio Ambiente e Sustentabilidade da Confederação Nacional da Indústria (CNI), a Coemas. Na ocasião, o presidente do conselho e vice-presidente da CNI, Marcelo Thomé, informou que a CNI representa o setor industrial no Comitê Técnico Consultivo Permanente (CTCP), da Secretaria Extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono (SEMC), do Mnistério da Fazenda. A Confederação também participa ativamente dos grupos de trabalho dedicados aos aspectos para a implementação do SBCE. “A CNI e diversas associações do setor produtivo também vêm realizando reuniões bilaterais junto às equipes do Ministério da Fazenda para tratar de especificidades de cada subsetor industrial contemplado no SBCE, de modo a contarmos com regulamentações aderentes à realidade da indústria brasileira”, explicou. Relevância da implementação do SBCE A secretária da SEMC, Cristina Fróes de Borja Reis, apresentou um resumo do andamento regulatório do SBCE, agradeceu a parceria contínua com a CNI e ressaltou que a regulamentação do mercado de carbono é imprescindível para a política industrial. Ela também defendeu que as regras devem ser desenhadas observando as capacidades internas e valorizando a resiliência e os avanços em sustentabilidade já alcançados pelo setor produtivo nacional. Cristina apresentou projeções que indicam que o SBCE poderá proporcionar um impacto positivo adicional ao Produto Interno Brasileiro (PIB) de 5,8% até 2040 e de 8,5% até 2050, além de contribuir para uma redução de até 27% nas emissões de gases de efeito estufa até 2050. “Nós estamos atuando fortemente para fomentar o mercado de carbono e estamos numa luta contra o tempo, mas sempre com muita seriedade e robustez técnica para publicar as normas infralegais”, afirmou. A secretária relatou os desdobramentos da consulta pública sobre a portaria de cobertura setorial inicial do mercado regulado, que recebeu quase mil contribuições do setor produtivo e do meio acadêmico, com subsídios para ajustes em segmentos como óleo e gás, resíduos e setor elétrico. Além disso, informou que, ainda em 2026, serão realizadas mais duas consultas públicas de dois decretos regulamentadores: do Programa Brasileiro de Monitoramento, Relato e Verificação (MRV) e o de Credenciamento de Metodologias para a geração de créditos de carbono. O superintendente de Meio Ambiente e Sustentabilidade da CNI, Davi Bomtempo, agradeceu a parceria com a equipe do Ministério da Fazenda e ressaltou que o diálogo com o setor privado foi iniciado ainda na elaboração do projeto de lei e se consolida agora, na etapa de regulamentação do mercado de carbono, por meio do trabalho conjunto em grupos técnicos para compreender as especificidades da indústria nacional. “Estamos juntos com a Secretaria desde a construção do projeto de lei, em permanente diálogo com o setor produtivo. Agora, nesta fase mais complexa de regulamentação do mercado de carbono no Brasil, a equipe segue trabalhando com a indústria brasileira, estudando em conjunto seus processos e formas de regulação”, enfatizou. artigo.texto: CHINA unveiled a new five-year plan for its battery industry on Monday, aiming for the initial large-scale application of all-solid-state batteries by 2030 as the country accelerates the transition of next-generation battery technology from research to commercialization. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, together with six other government agencies, jointly issued the new development plan for the battery industry, outlining the sector’s development priorities over the 15th Five-Year plan (2026–2030) period. The plan comes as China continues to expand its role in the global battery supply chain and seeks to strengthen its leadership in the global energy transition, according to Chinese experts. The country already has strong battery manufacturing capacity, but industry experts said that it still needs to improve basic research and core technologies to maintain long-term competitiveness. To promote the high-quality development of the industry, efforts will be made to accelerate technological innovation, industrial transformation and upgrading, improve the industrial system, enhance the capacity of industrial science and technology services, and raise the quality and level of trade and investment cooperation, according to the document. China will seek steady growth in its new battery industry over the next five years, while making major breakthroughs in advanced electrode materials, new electrolytes and high-end auxiliary materials. It also called for significant progress in new battery systems, with all-solid-state batteries moving toward initial large-scale deployment by 2030. New batteries refer to energy storage and conversion devices built on new mechanisms, materials, structures and manufacturing processes. They include lithium batteries, sodium batteries and flow batteries, which analysts said are becoming key parts of China’s push to develop new industrial sectors, build a new energy system and strengthen its capabilities. China’s battery industry has strong manufacturing capabilities but still needs to strengthen fundamental research, Sun Xiaohong, former secretary-general of the automotive branch of the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Machinery and Electronic Products, told the Global Times on Monday. All-solid-state batteries are one of the plan’s key technological priorities. Compared with conventional lithium-ion batteries, which typically use flammable liquid electrolytes, solid-state batteries use solid electrolytes and are considered safer and potentially capable of offering higher energy density, according to Sun. The plan calls for faster breakthroughs in commercialization technologies, with a focus on improving ionic conductivity, cycle stability and cost efficiency. It also stresses the need to advance key materials and processes, including interface contact technology, high ionic conductivity, long life cycles and engineering pressure system design. China’s solid-state battery market is projected to grow from $42.5 million in 2025 to $384.8 million by 2030, a compound annual growth rate of 44.4 percent, significantly outpacing the global average of 37.5 percent. Meanwhile, substantial research and development investments by domestic manufacturers such as CATL and BYD are accelerating solid-state battery commercialization and deployment, according to media reports. Sun said that solid-state battery technology worldwide is still in the research and testing stage, and has not yet entered large-scale commercial use. He noted that the main challenges remain manufacturing consistency and cost reduction. “Small-scale commercialization is already possible, but large-scale adoption still depends on lowering costs further and improving production processes,” Sun said.

artigo.texto: Insight and analysis on the data center space from industry thought leaders. Zinc Whiskers: The Hidden Contamination Risk Beneath Data Center Floors As AI density and airflow rise, legacy raised-floor and zinc-plated components can shed conductive whiskers that jeopardize equipment reliability. As data centers evolve to support higher-density computing and AI infrastructure, attention naturally goes to power, cooling, and equipment reliability. A less visible issue also deserves attention in that discussion: zinc whiskers. The risk isn’t new, but the operating conditions inside today’s facilities – especially increases in airflow – make it worth revisiting. Zinc whiskers are microscopic, electrically conductive crystalline filaments that can grow from electroplated zinc surfaces. In data centers, the best-documented source is the underside of older raised-floor tiles. However, cable trays, pedestals, stringers, electrical hardware, and other zinc-plated components can also be susceptible. The risk arises when whiskers detach, become airborne, and are carried by the cooling airflow. Once inside equipment, they can settle on circuit boards and other components, potentially creating unintended conductive paths, signal disturbances, and equipment failures. A Risk Hidden in Legacy Infrastructure Whiskers can be difficult to identify without the appropriate inspection techniques, and growth may take months or years to become apparent. The risk is particularly relevant to older facilities and buildings with mixed-vintage infrastructure. Modern raised-floor manufacturing has shifted toward materials and coatings that behave differently from the electroplated zinc historically associated with whisker growth. That means the risk is not uniform across every data center. However, facilities that have been operating for decades or contain legacy infrastructure should not assume the problem is purely theoretical. Routine facility work can increase exposure. Moving floor tiles, running new cabling, reconfiguring equipment, or conducting nearby construction can disturb accumulated whiskers and release them into the environment. AI Infrastructure Changes the Equation The growth of AI infrastructure adds another consideration. High-density GPU clusters move significantly more air than traditional computing infrastructure. Increased airflow through a subfloor plenum can create more opportunities for contaminants to become airborne and travel toward equipment. As data centers become denser and move more air, operators need to look beyond the newest technology and understand the conditions created by the infrastructure already in place. AI deployments also represent a substantially greater equipment investment in many facilities. That makes contamination control an operational consideration, not simply a housekeeping issue. When Cleaning Can Make the Problem Worse Conventional cleaning practices may be counterproductive. Vacuuming without HEPA filtration can aerosolize whiskers and release them back into the environment through the equipment’s exhaust. Sweeping, brushing, or other aggressive mechanical cleaning can disturb susceptible surfaces and shed additional whiskers. Even moving floor tiles can spread contamination. A maintenance activity intended to improve conditions in one area can seed a wider contamination event if the underlying risk is not identified. That makes identification the first step. High-intensity oblique lighting can help reveal whiskers through reflection, allowing facility teams to inspect susceptible surfaces before beginning cleaning or maintenance activities. A More Controlled Response Once contamination is identified, the response should focus on both containment and removal. Work areas may need to be isolated, airflow controlled, and nearby equipment intakes protected to prevent migration into unaffected areas. Cleaning alone may not solve the problem if a component is actively generating whiskers. Source remediation can include replacing affected floor tiles or other components with non-whiskering alternatives. Documentation is also important. Document where contamination is identified, actions taken, and remaining conditions to support future maintenance, remediation, and operational decisions. Zinc whiskers are not a universal threat to every data center, but in facilities with older raised-floor systems, legacy infrastructure, or mixed-vintage environments, they represent a contamination risk worth understanding and managing. As operators invest heavily in AI and higher-density computing, reliability depends not only on the newest technology entering the data center but also on the conditions created by the infrastructure already in place.
