artigo.texto: Principais destaques - TPU em órbita: Google colocou seu primeiro chip de inteligência artificial no espaço para testar computação, energia, resfriamento e resistência à radiação. - 1.800 voos da Starship: estudo do Google estima que seriam necessários cerca de 370 mil toneladas de carga colocadas em órbita para chegar a custos próximos de US$ 200 por quilo até 2035. - Data center orbital: a visão de longo prazo envolve uma constelação de 81 satélites trabalhando em conjunto, mas a frequência de lançamentos necessária ainda está muito distante da realidade atual. O Google está levando sua ideia de colocar infraestrutura de computação em órbita para um teste que parece saído de um filme de ficção científica. Mas, para transformar essa visão em um negócio real, existe um problema bem terrestre: lançar tudo isso ao espaço ainda custa caro demais. O primeiro chip do Google já está no espaço 🚀 O protótipo do Google foi lançado nesta quinta-feira a bordo de um foguete da SpaceX, a partir da Califórnia. Construído pela Planet Labs, o satélite leva uma unidade de processamento Tensor Processing Unit, ou TPU, tecnologia desenvolvida pelo Google para competir no mercado de computação de IA. É um teste importante porque simular o espaço em laboratório tem limites. “Não existe teste que seja completamente tão bom quanto a coisa real”, explicou Travis Beals, executivo do Google responsável pelo Project Suncatcher. E agora o Google terá a oportunidade de descobrir o que acontece quando uma TPU realmente precisa trabalhar em órbita. ☀️ O desafio não é apenas fazer o chip funcionar: O sistema precisa fornecer aproximadamente 1 quilowatt de energia continuamente, controlar a temperatura e manter o processamento funcionando em um ambiente sujeito à radiação espacial. Por enquanto, a TPU será acionada em ciclos de aproximadamente 15 minutos. A estratégia reduz a pressão sobre os sistemas de energia e gerenciamento térmico do satélite. O próximo passo será mais ambicioso. Google e Planet Labs estão preparando uma demonstração para o próximo ano com dois satélites projetados especificamente para cargas de computação mais avançadas. Eles deverão trabalhar juntos usando comunicação a laser. 💡 A ideia deixa de ser “colocar um computador no espaço” e começa a parecer uma infraestrutura de computação distribuída em órbita. E se o data center inteiro fosse para lá? 🌎 É justamente essa visão que está por trás do Project Suncatcher. O Google imagina uma rede de 81 satélites voando em formação próxima, funcionando como uma espécie de data center orbital distribuído. Cada unidade teria capacidade de processamento e, juntas, elas poderiam executar cargas de trabalho de IA em paralelo. Parece futurista. E é. Mas existe uma razão prática para o Google estar estudando isso agora: a demanda por computação está crescendo mais rápido do que a infraestrutura tradicional consegue acompanhar em alguns cenários de IA. O espaço poderia oferecer uma combinação interessante de energia solar abundante e uma infraestrutura que não depende da mesma lógica dos data centers terrestres. O problema é colocar os equipamentos lá em cima. A conta começa nos foguetes 💰 Em sua nova análise revisada por pares, publicada em conexão com a revista Joule, pesquisadores do Google examinaram justamente essa questão. O estudo não pretende ser uma análise de viabilidade econômica completa. Ainda assim, apresenta uma estimativa bastante concreta sobre o que precisaria acontecer com o mercado de lançamentos. O Google parte de uma premissa importante: os custos para colocar carga em órbita precisam continuar caindo. 📉 A aposta é em uma curva de aprendizado: Segundo os pesquisadores, a SpaceX teria conseguido reduzir custos seguindo uma curva de aprendizado de aproximadamente 20% ao ano desde os primeiros lançamentos do Falcon 1. A partir dessa trajetória, o estudo considera plausível chegar a um custo próximo de US$ 200 por quilograma em 2035. É aí que entra a Starship. 370 mil toneladas. 1.800 lançamentos. 😳 Para atingir essa escala de redução de custos, os pesquisadores estimam que a Starship precisaria colocar aproximadamente 370 mil toneladas de carga em órbita. Considerando uma capacidade de cerca de 200 toneladas por missão, isso significaria aproximadamente: Ou seja, cerca de 15 lançamentos por mês, em média, durante uma década. E existe um detalhe que torna a conta ainda mais impressionante. A Starship nunca realizou mais de cinco voos em um único ano. 🚀 O salto de frequência seria gigantesco: Para chegar aos números utilizados pelo estudo, a SpaceX precisaria passar de uma cadência experimental para uma operação de lançamento em escala industrial. Elon Musk já falou em uma possibilidade ainda mais extrema: uma Starship capaz de realizar lançamentos com intervalo de aproximadamente uma hora em 2029. Isso representaria uma transformação radical na frequência de acesso ao espaço. Mas, por enquanto, essa é uma meta projetada para o futuro, não uma capacidade operacional demonstrada. O chip parece estar sobrevivendo à radiação ☢️ Há, porém, uma notícia mais concreta para o Google. Os testes realizados pela empresa indicam que suas TPUs podem ser capazes de sobreviver ao ambiente espacial durante a vida útil planejada dos satélites. O Google precisou repetir parte dos experimentos depois de perceber que a configuração física dos chips oferecia mais proteção contra radiação do que eles teriam em uma aplicação orbital real. Na segunda rodada, os pesquisadores observaram um aumento nos erros da lógica do chip. Mesmo assim, o resultado continuou considerado compatível com grandes cargas de inferência. 🧠 O problema aparece quando a escala aumenta: Travis Beals estima que, para operações típicas de inferência, a taxa de erro poderia ficar em torno de uma ocorrência a cada milhão. Isso pode ser administrável. Mas treinamento de modelos gigantes é outra história. Um processo envolvendo milhares de chips funcionando durante meses aumenta drasticamente as oportu

artigo.texto: O BYD Dolphin Mini de segunda geração está cada vez mais diferente do modelo atual. Revelado na China como Seagull, o hatch ganhou carroceria maior, interior mais sofisticado e novos equipamentos, incluindo banco do motorista com função de massagem. As informações são do site chinês CarNewsChina, que teve acesso aos detalhes da cabine do modelo. O novo Dolphin Mini será 42 cm maior que a primeira geração e terá 4,20 m de comprimento, 1,81 m de largura, 1,57 m de altura e 2,65 m de entre-eixos. Ou seja, ficará apenas 6 cm mais curto que o Dolphin atual. A segunda geração substituirá o carro que é atualmente vendido no Brasil. A cabine também muda bastante. O painel deixa de ter o quadro de instrumentos tradicional à frente do motorista e passa a concentrar as informações em uma tela flutuante maior. Segundo o CarNewsChina, o display tem divisão 3/7: uma parte exibe velocidade, marcha, autonomia, consumo de energia e modos de condução, enquanto a outra fica dedicada a funções de entretenimento, como navegação e música. As imagens reveladas mostram ainda um console central mais amplo e volante de dois raios. Os bancos dianteiros têm ajustes elétricos e o motorista ganha função de massagem. Há também iluminação ambiente com múltiplas cores e saídas de ar-condicionado ajustáveis para os ocupantes traseiros. Outro detalhe são dois compartimentos de armazenamento sob os bancos da segunda fileira. O modelo também mantém os botões magnéticos “mágicos” usados pela BYD em outros veículos. Mais espaço para bagagem A mudança para um motor elétrico instalado no eixo traseiro também libera espaço sob o capô. O novo Dolphin Mini terá um compartimento dianteiro de 94 litros, enquanto o porta-malas poderá chegar a 1.380 litros com os bancos traseiros rebatidos. O conjunto mecânico também sobe de nível. O hatch terá motor elétrico de 95 kW, equivalentes a 127 cv, e duas opções de bateria de 30 kWh e 39,2 kWh. A autonomia declarada varia de 320 a 420 km no ciclo chinês CLTC, enquanto no WLTP os números ficam entre 262 e 344 km. O novo Dolphin Mini também poderá receber carregamento rápido capaz de levar a bateria de 10% a 97% em nove minutos, segundo a publicação. artigo.texto: This article was featured in the Daily Prospect newsletter. Sign up for it here. Lowndes County is rural and impoverished, and its scars are in plain view. Residents have been plagued with a decades-old raw sewage crisis so horrible that a United Nations special representative traveled to Alabama to investigate. After discovering cancer-causing emissions, federal officials fined a plastics plant on U.S. Highway 80, the historic route of the 1965 Selma-to-Montgomery march. Martin Luther King Jr. and Congressman John Lewis led thousands down that road, an action that led to passage of the Voting Rights Act. On the third night of their five-day journey, as they traveled through Lowndes County, the marchers stopped at what is now known as Campsite #3, located on the Gardner farm. Less than a mile from where exhausted civil rights activists rested after hours of marching, one developer is vying to make roughly 800 acres of farmland shovel-ready for a $1.5 billion hyperscale data center facility dubbed “Project Red Clay.” More from Naomi Bethune | James Baratta As Alabama’s plantation and sharecropping economies withered away in the Black Belt, so named for its fertile, dark soil, the region’s local white power brokers turned to another style of racism. They have burdened the residents—60 percent of the men, women, and children who live here are African American—with substandard infrastructure and poorly maintained industrial projects that have produced environmental catastrophes. Many Lowndes County community members fear that Project Red Clay would lead to another such crisis. Cloverleaf Infrastructure, a Houston-based company, is a data center real estate developer. It does not own, operate, build, or even own data centers. Company officials identify parcels of land for future development, often signing options to buy them at a fraction of the purchase price while working to secure power, water, and tax concessions from local governments. Cloverleaf then sells the primed site to a data center developer—as it plans to do with Project Red Clay. The Lowndes Signal first reported in April that Cloverleaf had talked with local leaders and utility providers about the viability of a hyperscale data center project in northern Lowndes County. Later that month, the Alabama legislature passed a bill capping the maximum tax abatement for data centers at 20 years, down from 30. With that legislation going into effect on January 1, 2027, the clock is ticking for Cloverleaf to formally request a 30-year tax abatement before the end of the year. Details of the abatement proposal remain scant, but in Alabama more broadly, these abatements enable developers to avoid most sales and use taxes, as well as property taxes, that would otherwise apply to data center projects. The local body that will decide whether Project Red Clay receives any tax breaks is the Lowndes County Commission. Cloverleaf must also secure regulatory approval for electricity with Alabama Power, which is owned by Southern Company and serves some 1.5 million customers across the southern two-thirds of the state. For water service, the developer must reach an agreement with the Pintlala Water System, a member-owned nonprofit water utility. There’s widespread skepticism about Cloverleaf’s commitments to minimize air, noise, and light pollution, prevent contaminant leaks, and ensure that the local drinking water supply is not disrupted. Rev. Tom Gardner is a Vietnam veteran whose property is right next to the site’s footprint. “I don’t know which way to turn if it comes, but I know I couldn’t live here,” he says. Project Red Clay is at the center of countervailing forces: local activists primed to confront environmental miscues, neighbors familiar with historical injustices, and a web of players who thought they’d find plenty of sellouts. What they found instead were community members more than willing to take them on. IT IS EASY TO SEE WHY Cloverleaf has set its sights on Lowndes County. Not only does Lowndes lack zoning, but the Project Red Clay site is located in an opportunity zone. Opportunity zones provide tax breaks for investors so long as they reinvest untaxed capital gains into local businesses and infrastructure. But this framework, born out of the mid-to-late-20th-century neoliberal push for alternatives to Keynesianism, has been criticized for failing to alleviate poverty in economically disadvantaged communities. Investors secure rewards for putting capital in these communities. However, they aren’t required to invest new capital there or demonstrate that their investments materially improve residents’ quality of life. Congress established the Qualified Opportunity Zone program under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017. The One Big Beautiful Bill made this program permanent, leaving no shortage of incentives for developers to target communities like Lowndes for data center projects. The Lowndes County Economic Development Commission works to attract new investment, preserve and expand existing businesses, and support workforce development in the county. The economic development commission was created by the Lowndes County Commission, local municipalities, utilities, and other businesses. It does not have public meetings and is not a municipal entity. Community members have accused the county’s economic development commission and Cloverleaf of overstating the project’s benefits. According to the developer, Project Red Clay will create 1,000 construction jobs and at least 50 full-time “high-paying” positions, such as data center technicians, network engineers, and IT support staff. Cloverleaf has also suggested that a local workforce is “preferred,” and would be “frequently sourced through local training programs funded by the end user” (meaning the eventual tenant of the data center); the developer has not disclosed the identity of that end user. To sweeten the deal, Cloverleaf has offered up to $10 million for community development

artigo.texto: Mercedes-Benz and ProLogium have entered into a joint testing agreement, including a preliminary technology evaluation of ProLogium’s latest Gen4 Superfluidized All Inorganic Solid State Battery Cell Technology Mercedes-Benz continues to drive solid-state battery technology, and has secured priority access to ProLogium’s latest Gen4 Superfluidized Inorganic Next-Generation Lithium Ceramic Battery (Gen 4 battery) cells. • ProLogium’s Gen4 battery technology highlights an innovative next generation battery technology approach with balanced and promising characteristics, such as high energy density, cell safety and high rate capability. • This testing scheme builds upon the nearly 10-year partnership between the two companies that has included Mercedes-Benz’s investing in ProLogium and joint technical development agreements. TAIPEI, Taiwan – September 24, 2026 – Mercedes-Benz AG and ProLogium Holding Inc. have signed a joint testing agreement, giving Mercedes-Benz priority access to test ProLogium’s latest Gen4 battery cells and further building on the companies’ nearly ten-year partnership in advancing next-generation battery technologies for mobility. Under the agreement, ProLogium’s Gen4 battery technology will undergo extensive electrical, thermal and safety testing at Mercedes-Benz’s dedicated facilities and specialized external testing institutes. The results will help assess the technology’s suitability for potential use in future vehicles. The Gen4 battery platform aims to combine five core advantages: intrinsic safety, high performance, high energy density, scalable manufacturing and competitive cost structure. Its safety architecture integrates a non-flammable inorganic electrolyte, ceramic separator technology and ProLogium’s proprietary active safety mechanism, while supporting fast charging, high power output and good low-temperature performance. Vincent Yang, Founder and CEO of ProLogium, said: Over nearly a decade, our collaboration with Mercedes-Benz has evolved from early cell development and validation to testing our latest Gen4 technology for future vehicle applications. ”For next-generation batteries, true value comes from turning years of innovation into scalable manufacturing and commercially viable products. With Mercedes-Benz’s early investment and support for our European expansion, together with the strong support of the French government and the European Union, we are advancing toward large-scale production in Europe and building a manufacturing footprint to serve global markets.” Jörg Burzer, Member of the Board of Management, Mercedes‑Benz Group AG, Chief Technology Officer, Development & Procurement, said: At Mercedes-Benz, we are committed to shaping the future of electric mobility through technological leadership and innovation. ”Our long-standing partnership with ProLogium is a strong example of how we bring the best expertise together to advance next-generation battery technologies. By combining ProLogium’s pioneering solid-state battery approach with Mercedes-Benz’s deep battery development, testing and integration capabilities, we are taking the next step in exploring advanced battery technologies for future electric vehicles.” Since 2016, the partnership between the two companies has progressed from early hybrid-solid-state GEN 3 which has more than 10 years of commercial references across industries and joint development to potential future vehicle platform planning. Mercedes-Benz became one of ProLogium’s long-term global automotive partners and strategic investors, expanding the relationship beyond product validation. The collaboration has validated multiple lithium ceramic battery formats, including pouch and the first next generation prismatic cells, as well as ProLogium’s Bi-Polar technology. Mercedes-Benz has a Director on the Board of Directors of ProLogium and is fully supportive of ProLogium’s development plans for its Dunkirk plant as well as ProLogium’s further plans to become publicly listed on the NASDAQ in 4Q2026. ProLogium’s Taoke Gigafactory in Taiwan has completed GWh-scale manufacturing validation and supports C-sample production, Demo Car programs and future commercial production. ProLogium’s planned Dunkirk Gigafactory, with a future capacity of up to 44 GWh, is expected to establish localized European manufacturing and supply-chain capacity, replicating the proven production model developed in Taiwan. Once the first phase of this factory is completed, ProLogium will be able to provide commercial cells to European customers at a scale large enough to support electric vehicle platforms on the continent. artigo.texto: 247 – O Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) identificou cerca de 380 pontos físicos da rede de transmissão que podem receber sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, dos quais aproximadamente 85% ainda possuem capacidade remanescente para novas conexões. Os dados constam de nota técnica elaborada pelo ONS em conjunto com a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) e a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE). Os pontos, tecnicamente chamados de barramentos, serão relevantes para os Leilões de Reserva de Capacidade destinados à contratação de baterias. Apenas cerca de 15% dos locais mapeados não apresentam capacidade disponível para receber novas instalações. Minas Gerais concentra os dois barramentos com maior disponibilidade identificados no levantamento. Arinos 2 e Janaúba 3 somam 5,8 gigawatts (GW) de capacidade para conexão de sistemas de armazenamento. O avanço da infraestrutura ocorre enquanto o país prepara os primeiros leilões específicos para armazenamento de energia em baterias. Segundo informação publicada anteriormente pelo Broadcast, Petrobras, Axia, Engie, Taesa e Isa Brasil estão entre as empresas que cadastraram projetos para participar das contratações. Os Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias, conhecidos pela sigla BESS, também poderão contribuir para aproveitar parte da eletricidade atualmente perdida devido aos cortes de geração. Levantamento da Volt Robotics para a Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae) estima que até 88% da energia necessária para recarregar esses sistemas poderá vir dessa geração que hoje deixa de ser aproveitada. Uma referência utilizada na Análise de Impacto Regulatório da Aneel aponta ainda que o custo efetivo dos sistemas BESS fica entre 63% e 83% abaixo do registrado no último Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência. A adoção das baterias também pode reduzir parcelas de encargos cobrados dos consumidores, entre elas despesas relacionadas às restrições de operação do sistema elétrico. O Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia 2035 estima que o Brasil precisará incorporar aproximadamente 7 GW em sistemas de armazenamento ao longo dos próximos dez anos para atender às necessidades de potência do sistema. O dado foi apresentado no Encontro do Armazenamento 2030, promovido pela Absae. Leilões estão marcados para dezembro O Ministério de Minas e Energia publicou em junho a portaria com as regras iniciais para a contratação dos sistemas de baterias, destinados a contribuir para a segurança do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). O calendário prevê dois leilões em dezembro: o primeiro, em 2 de dezembro, terá exigência de conteúdo nacional; o segundo, em 4 de dezembro, será aberto aos demais projetos de armazenamento em baterias. A EPE recebeu o cadastramento de 6.091 projetos para as disputas. artigo.texto: AMD to Acquire World Labs for $8.2B to Advance AI Models and Robotics Analysts say the deal will help AMD inform future chip designs as AI evolves. AMD has struck a deal to purchase AI research lab World Labs in an all-stock transaction valued at about $8.2 billion, the chipmaker announced Monday, Sept. 28. The deal aims to co-design hardware, software, and systems for emerging AI models and applications such as robotics and physical AI. The transaction is expected to close by the end of 2026, subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals. San Francisco-based World Labs develops spatial intelligence “world models” that use text, images, and video to generate and simulate interactive 3D environments, AMD said. AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li, co-founder and CEO of World Labs, will join AMD as executive vice president and chief scientist. Upon closing, World Labs will continue to focus on AI model research, the company said. “Building the compute platforms for the next generation of AI requires a deep understanding of how models are evolving,” said AMD CEO Lisa Su in a statement. “Fei-Fei and the World Labs team bring exceptional research leadership and model expertise. Together, we can use that insight to develop the hardware, software, and systems that will power the next generation of AI and strengthen the open AI ecosystem.” Why the Deal Matters for AMD Matt Kimball, vice president and principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, said the acquisition allows AMD to understand chip requirements better as AI advances. AMD’s purchase doesn’t come out of left field because it had invested in World Labs previously, he noted. “This isn’t about AMD buying a model company. This is about being able to understand the requirements of compute and memory – and the relationship between the two as the next generation of AI emerges,” Kimball told Data Center Knowledge in an interview. “I like the move. To me, it is AMD looking a few years out and capturing those needs today – needs that get baked into low-level architectural decisions and designs.” “This isn’t about AMD buying a model company. This is about being able to understand the requirements of compute and memory – and the relationship between the two as the next generation of AI emerges." – Matt Kimball, vice president and principal analyst, Moor Insights & Strategy Brendan Burke, a research director at Futurum Group, said the purchase puts AMD in a stronger position in the emerging physical AI market, which AMD estimates could reach $200 billion by 2035. “AMD identified a transformative category that has yet to produce a significant commercial impact, and shows the company is using its recent momentum to think long-term about the future of AI,” Burke said. “You can’t hire a more accomplished researcher than Dr. Fei-Fei Li, and access to talent is the biggest advantage in AI training.” Nvidia has already moved into physical AI with its Cosmos world model, along with its Isaac and Omniverse platforms and Project GR00T robotics models, which give it an early lead in the market, Kimball said. Burke said the acquisition gives AMD access to leading researchers in the field of physical intelligence. They could help AMD train useful models and inform the design of AMD’s rack-scale systems for those model architectures, potentially helping AMD gain market share. Burke added that AMD increasingly sees itself as an AI research organization, having invested in internal generative AI training efforts and creating open-source models. Buying World Labs allows AMD to move deeper into the market. Co-designing with World Labs could help AMD “move toward leadership in fields that aren't yet captured by leading labs,” he said. Building World Models World Labs builds world models, not large language models (LLMs). While LLMs focus on the relationship between language, tokens, and information, world models are about environments – geometry, physics, objects, motions, and dynamics, Kimball said. “Think of it as a model for the physical world,” he said. “Any physical AI and robotics require all of this 3D modeling, geometric understanding, physics, etc., to work properly.” For example, in training a robot to place a cup on a table, the model must account for the motions and contact dynamics so that the cup lands flat on the surface rather than half on and half off, he explained. Talent and IP at the Core Overall, World Labs is an acquisition of intellectual property, talent, and insights, Kimball said. The value of the deal extends beyond physical AI and into what comes next, he added. “Fei-Fei is a rock star. You could argue that she is as much of the target as the company is. She and her team bring world-class talent to AMD, and this will enable the company to much more quickly find a competitive footing against Nvidia in this space,” he said.

artigo.texto: Ameren Missouri wants to significantly ramp up power plant construction to meet data center electricity needs, according to a 20-year plan released this week. The new plan significantly increases the company’s reliance on natural gas plants while scaling back the percentage of energy produced by renewable sources like wind and solar. And in a change from previous plans, the company is no longer discussing a goal to reach net-zero carbon emissions. Monopoly utilities publish these plans, called Integrated Resource Plans, every three years as required by Missouri law. This plan is now a case before the Missouri Public Service Commission, which will include pushback from outside parties and public comment submitted to regulators before being finalized. Data center growth There are currently 40 potential large data centers that could be built within Ameren Missouri’s footprint, according to the document, including multiple projects that have signed binding agreements with the company. New data centers represent the majority of the company’s projected growth over the next 20 years, said Ajay Arora, executive vice president, chief growth officer and chief generation development officer for Ameren Missouri. He said those projects could benefit regular consumers. “Economic development is vital to the state,” Arora said. “It helps us modernize our electric grid to ensure reliability for everybody and have that fixed cost be spread over new customers.” To meet that new demand, Ameren is planning to build power plants and renewable energy projects that would generate almost double the amount of electricity it was projecting to build in its 2023 projection. Shifting climate goals In 2020 and 2023, Ameren focused its planning on renewable energy, discussing goals to reach net-zero carbon emissions. Ameren removed that language in the 2026 Integrated Resource Plan, discussing how its plan will decrease carbon emissions, but saying technology like carbon capture would have to advance to achieve net-zero emissions. “We are not changing our net-zero targets right now,” Arora said. “However, we do outline in the plan that new technology would need to mature in order for us to achieve our net-zero goals.” Much of the new power would come from natural gas — in 2023, the Integrated Resource Plan called for two such plants. In 2026, the new plan lists nine plants to be built over the next two decades. Environmental advocates took issue with that new focus on natural gas, including Jenn DeRose, the Sierra Club’s campaign organizing strategist for Beyond Coal in Missouri. “Their own research shows that solar and wind are the cheapest forms of energy to build, and they're still choosing gas,” DeRose said. “I find that very interesting. I also find it very interesting that they cite extreme weather as a reason for building gas. Do you know what causes extreme weather? Climate change. Do you know what contributes to catastrophic climate change? Coal and gas.” Ameren Vice President of Regulatory and Legislative Affairs Rob Dixon said a reliable energy system needs a diversity of energy sources. “It's really important to remember that no single technology type can meet every customer need in every hour under every condition,” Dixon said. Increasing renewables and keeping coal The 2026 Integrated Resource Plan also increases the company’s renewable energy buildout, with new solar plants and battery storage. “They are adding solar, they are adding batteries, and I think that's good,” said James Owen, executive director of Renew Missouri. “I think that makes sense for long-term considerations. But I think the continued reliance on fossil fuels is going to end up costing customers more money than Ameren is currently anticipating.” For the IRP, Ameren calculated the lifetime costs of each source of new energy it is considering building. The company found wind, solar and the kinds of natural gas plants that run consistently were the least expensive per kWh, while nuclear plants and the kind of gas plants that can turn on and off, potentially to supplement renewables, were the most expensive. The new plan also extends the lives of two coal plants. The Sioux Coal plant would close three years later than planned in 2023, while the Labadie plant would keep all four units operational until 2042, when two were originally set to retire in 2035. Arora said that decision was made to save money. “Labadie remains one of the most affordable plants in the country and recognizing the economic conditions for all our customers and how important reliability and affordability is, that's really factored into delaying the retirement of a few of the Labadie units by a few years,” he said. Environmental advocates said there are other costs that come with coal. “Do you know why that plant is so affordable?” DeRose said. “It’s because it doesn't have any modern pollution controls. So it's only affordable for the company. Those health externalities, those are what we have to pay for.” Paying for new plants To actually build power plants or to set new electricity rates, Ameren still has to take each request to the Public Service Commission as a case. While this plan does not change people’s bills, Owen said the cost of the new power plants will trickle down to customers eventually. “Any time they build more generation, it's going to increase rates,” Owen said. “I don't know how they can say that, ‘Oh, this is [only costing] data centers,’ when that's the main thing driving energy consumption right now. It's not that we're having this huge influx of people moving into Missouri. It is not this huge influx of other manufacturing jobs. artigo.texto: Chino residents concerned by city-approved battery storage facility after hazardous La Verne fire Chino residents are preparing to fight back against a newly approved battery storage facility following a hazardous lithium-ion battery fire that forced hundreds to evacuate their homes in La Verne last week. The storage facility, part of the Dirac Energy Storage Project by Aypa, is planned for construction next to the existing Southern California Edison substation across the street from Ayala Park. Though it was previously denied by the city's planning commission in July, it was recently approved by a 4-1 city council vote. It's not expected to be approved by October 6. Residents say they were confused by the sudden reversal. "I thought most of the residents would say no, and I thought they would listen to the residents," said William Custodial. "Maybe I'm wrong." With the new facility located so close to homes and public areas, they're concerned that they could be put in the same danger that La Verne residents were when the lithium-ion batteries being stored at the Metropolitan Water District plant caught fire and caused some explosions, then evacuations. "I hope that what they've done is they've learned from that mistake," said Fabi, a Chino resident who lives across the street from where the facility will be built. The Chino project was approved just a week before the La Verne fire broke out, and now, residents have heightened safety concerns, especially after comments from Shane Chapman, the water district's assistant general manager. "It's a risk management conversation, and given the experience that we're going through here, my own opinion at this point: it's not worth the risk," Chapman said. In comparison, the Chino Diract proejct aims to store 400 megawatts of power storage to the 1 megawatt of battery units being stored in La Verne. In a news release shared on Monday, Chino city officials said that fire safety was a "key part" of the project review. "The project includes battery management, fire detection and proection systems, and required testing related to battery safety and fire spread," the release said, in part. CBS LA reached out to all five Chino City Council members and Mayor Eunice Ulloa for comment on the project, but none responded.

artigo.texto: Replus Engitech To Supply 1.5 GWh BESS Capacity To Indus Towers Over Two Years HEG Advanced Materials subsidiary Replus Engitech will provide 1.5 GWh of Battery Energy Storage System production capacity to Indus Towers over two years for telecom infrastructure, the company announced on September 30, 2026. Mumbai: Replus Engitech Private Limited, a subsidiary of HEG Advanced Materials Limited, has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Indus Towers Limited to explore collaboration on Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) solutions for telecom infrastructure in India. Production Capacity Commitment Under the MoU, Replus Engitech will make available dedicated BESS production capacity of 1.5 GWh over a two-year period. This capacity is intended to support the energy requirements of telecom infrastructure. Technology Expansion Replus plans to expand its portfolio of telecom energy storage solutions to include higher-capacity battery systems. The company will also explore emerging technologies like sodium-ion batteries to enhance reliability, energy efficiency, and lifecycle performance across telecom applications. Strategic Importance Riju Jhunjhunwala, Chairman, Managing Director and CEO, HEG Advanced Materials Limited, said the initiative reflects an opportunity to build a made-in-India energy storage ecosystem for critical infrastructure. He added that Replus is building manufacturing scale, technology capabilities, and an innovation platform to address evolving requirements and contribute to India's energy transition. Future-Ready Solutions Hiren Pravin Shah, Managing Director and CEO, Replus Engitech Private Limited, stated that the initiative aims to build manufacturing scale and technology capabilities for telecom infrastructure. Shah noted the ambition to combine innovation, reliability, and Indian engineering to create future-ready energy storage solutions. Domestic Manufacturing Replus aims to strengthen domestic manufacturing capabilities and advance next-generation battery technologies. This effort supports a resilient indigenous energy storage ecosystem and the evolving requirements of India's telecom sector. artigo.texto: From Opposition to Buy-In: Tactics for Data Center Developers Data center developers are responding to growing community opposition by embracing transparency, funding power infrastructure, and prioritizing locations with supportive residents. Two years ago, a new wave of massive AI data centers dominated the headlines. A year ago, murmurings of discontent began to be heard. As 2026 heads into its final quarter, those murmurings have become a cacophony of opposition. Whether it is local communities complaining about water, power, or noise, or government bodies imposing bans or moratoria on data centers, pushback has caught the public eye. It is no surprise, therefore, that several sessions at the recent Data Center World Power event in Dallas, which ran Sept. 21-23, addressed this issue. Concerns about power availability and potential electricity rate hikes in the local area are among the biggest worries voiced by data center opponents. In some regions, data centers are being blamed for increases in electricity rates. In response, many data center developers are expressing a willingness to fund upgrades needed to support their projects. Some have paid for entire battery energy storage systems (BESS) that benefit both the grid and their data centers. Others are contributing to transmission upgrades or purchasing transformers, substations, and other power electronics infrastructure to avoid passing extra costs on to ratepayers. Some grid planners and utilities are formalizing such arrangements to make them standard practice for new projects. Here are some top tips from Data Center World Power for interacting with community groups. Be Transparent Early: Retire the NDA Playbook Diane Sullivan, chief development officer of Hecate Energy, a Chicago‑based US developer of utility‑scale energy parks, believes that the current backlash against data centers is partly due to past practices. She cited non-disclosure agreements with city officials and developing projects under the radar, getting them largely set up before announcing them. That approach may have worked for smaller projects that exerted relatively little impact on the local grid. However, AI data centers are becoming so large that transparency has become essential. It is in the developer’s long-term interest to engage with the community upfront. “In the past, developers would sometimes obtain permits before informing the public about a data center project, which is a terrible idea,” Sullivan said. “We must become open and be fully transparent about our plans.” Bring Power with You: Co-Develop Power with Utilities and EPCs A data center development of any size requires a plan for both the facility and its power. That might include wind, solar, batteries, geothermal, natural gas, or nuclear. But permitting and system operator approval are unlikely without a clear plan for adding new power resources, typically funded by the developer. Data center developers are urged to partner with power plant developers, EPC (engineering, procurement, and construction) contractors, and utilities to line up a portfolio of options. In many cases, that will entail multiple resources – perhaps solar, gas-fired generation, backup generators, and batteries. “Any project proposal should also include a power generation solution, or you are probably wasting your time,” Sullivan said. Community Support Now Trumps Power Availability Once upon a time, the primary criteria for a good data center site were proximity to a major metro area and fiber availability. Over the past couple of years, power has become the key factor. Now there is another essential element: community support. The project must benefit the local area, and there should be a largely positive attitude towards it. “You could have a perfectly executable project that’s real, it’s commercial, and has well-allocated risk, but the community shows up and doesn’t want you there,” said Dado Slezak, executive vice president of energy capital and strategy at QTS Data Centers. “You could have a perfectly executable project that’s real, it’s commercial, and has well-allocated risk, but the community shows up and doesn’t want you there.” – Dado Slezak, EVP of energy capital and strategy, QTS Data Centers To avoid that outcome, economic benefits should be made tangible to residents. Beyond tax payments, developers can support local schools or help stabilize electricity rates. Slezak cited a QTS project in Iowa where the company reached an agreement with the utility to fix and subsidize community electricity rates for five years. Benefits can also extend beyond economics; some developers invest in water restoration. “There are also different types of jobs that the data center brings,” added Alise Porto, vice president of sustainability and strategic initiatives at Switch. In addition to direct data center roles, construction generates significant employment during development. Some developers are working to translate those jobs into permanent positions via on-site retraining programs. Tour Working Facilities to Debunk Water and Noise Myths Most developers attend community meetings armed with facts and figures on power draw, water consumption, and noise abatement. But opposition can harden to the point where data isn’t persuasive. Slezak suggested that touring people around a comparable facility can make a difference. “I can tell them that you consume less water in a hyperscale campus than a restaurant would, but they often don’t believe me,” he said. “It is sometimes better to show them. I’ve toured groups through a facility and shown them our closed-loop system where there is no water consumption.” Closed-loop designs can significantly reduce process water usage compared to traditional evaporative systems. artigo.texto: As duas maiores margens individuais para conexão de baterias nos leilões de reserva de capacidade de dezembro estão em Minas Gerais: Arinos 2, com 2,96 GW, e Janaúba 3, com 2,92 GW. Em sentido oposto, há pontos com capacidade remanescente zero em estados como Bahia, Alagoas, Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte, São Paulo, Rio Grande do Sul e Santa Catarina. Os cálculos já consideram, quando representam a condição mais restritiva, os montantes reservados na primeira Temporada de Acesso. Os valores se referem aos barramentos, pontos elétricos das subestações aos quais se conectam linhas, transformadores e outros equipamentos. As margens de cada ponto, porém, não podem ser somadas. A capacidade disponível para os leilões é definida simultaneamente em três níveis, por barramento, subárea e área, e um projeto fica sujeito a todos os limites aplicáveis à sua localização. Arinos 2 e Janaúba 3, por exemplo, integram uma área que reúne instalações do norte de Minas Gerais e do oeste da Bahia e está sujeita a um limite agregado de 3,2 GW. Assim, apesar das margens individuais de 2,96 GW e 2,92 GW, a capacidade conjunta dos projetos nessa área não poderá ultrapassar o teto definido para o conjunto das instalações. Os quantitativos constam de nota técnica divulgada em conjunto pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) e pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) em 30 de setembro. O documento foi elaborado pelo ONS com subsídios da EPE. Os limites serão considerados no leilão com exigência de conteúdo nacional, marcado para 2 de dezembro, e segundo certame, previsto para o dia 4. Nos dois casos, o início do suprimento está previsto para 1º de agosto de 2028. A nova nota complementa um primeiro documento elaborado conjuntamente por ONS e EPE e publicado em julho, que definiu a metodologia, as premissas e os critérios para o cálculo da capacidade remanescente. Agora, são apresentados os quantitativos resultantes dos estudos para cada barramento candidato, subárea e área do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). Temporada de Acesso entra no cálculo Na definição das margens, o ONS considerou os consumidores já em operação ou que tinham contratos de uso dos sistemas de transmissão ou distribuição celebrados até o fim do prazo de cadastramento. Também entraram no cálculo os montantes reservados na primeira Temporada de Acesso, quando resultaram em uma condição mais restritiva para a conexão dos sistemas de armazenamento. Ficaram de fora os projetos que solicitaram a devolução das garantias associadas à participação na temporada. Segundo o ONS, o tratamento busca evitar que uma mesma capacidade da rede seja disponibilizada nos dois processos de alocação de acesso. Limites variam dentro das regiões As diferenças também aparecem dentro de uma mesma região. Na Bahia, Igaporã III, em 230 kV, tem margem individual de até 2 GW. A subárea que inclui o próprio barramento, Bom Jesus da Lapa, Bom Jesus da Lapa II, Igaporã II e Pindaí II, entretanto, está limitada a 900 MW. Na região de Barreiras, também na Bahia, Barreiras e Barreiras II, em 230 kV, têm limites individuais de 340 MW cada. A subárea que reúne esses pontos e instalações como Tabocas do Brejo Velho, Rio das Éguas, Rio Formoso II e Rio Grande II tem margem de 50 MW. Em uma área maior, que reúne instalações da Bahia, Piauí e Ceará, o limite agregado é de 3,67 GW. Dentro desse conjunto, há barramentos com margens individuais elevadas, como Futura, na Bahia, com até 2,165 GW, e Queimada Nova II, no Piauí, com até 2,1 GW. A nota também aponta barramentos sem capacidade remanescente. Entre eles estão Paulo Afonso III-A, na Bahia, e Xingó, em Alagoas. Para os dois pontos, o ONS identifica como fator limitante uma sobrecarga na linha de transmissão de 500 kV Sapeaçu-Camaçari II diante da contingência da linha Sapeaçu-Camaçari IV. Há barramentos com margem zero também em outras regiões do país. As razões variam conforme a instalação e incluem restrições de desempenho elétrico, limitações de curto-circuito e falta de disponibilidade física para novas conexões. Nos casos em que não há disponibilidade física no barramento, o documento ressalva que a margem pode ser considerada para projetos conectados à rede de distribuição com impacto em uma subestação de fronteira da Rede Básica. Carregamento das baterias também restringe margens Para chegar aos quantitativos, o ONS avaliou a disponibilidade física das instalações e o desempenho da rede tanto no descarregamento quanto no carregamento dos sistemas de armazenamento. Também foram consideradas limitações de curto-circuito que possam comprometer a entrada dos projetos em operação na data prevista para o início do suprimento. Em diferentes pontos, a capacidade disponível foi limitada por problemas identificados especificamente nos cenários de carregamento das baterias. O estudo também considera empreendimentos conectados às redes de distribuição quando a injeção ou a absorção de potência produz impacto sobre a Rede Básica, as Demais Instalações de Transmissão (DITs) ou as Instalações de Transmissão de Interesse Exclusivo de Centrais de Geração para Conexão Compartilhada (ICGs).

artigo.texto: FRV Australia commissions Terang, its first large-scale battery energy storage project in Australia - Terang is FRV’s first utility-scale Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project delivered in Australia. - Located in Terang, the project has a capacity of 100 MW / 200 MWh, helping to strengthen the stability and resilience of the electricity grid. - The project received AUD 7 million in funding for the installation of new grid-forming inverters through the second round of the Victorian Government’s Energy Innovation Fund (EIF). Fotowatio Renewable Ventures (FRV) Australia, a leading developer of sustainable energy solutions, and part of Jameel Energy and the Canadian infrastructure fund OMERS Infrastructure, has announced the successful commissioning of Terang, its first utility-scale Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project in Australia. Located in Terang, in the state of Victoria, the project has a capacity of 100 MW / 200 MWh, helping to strengthen the stability and resilience of the electricity grid. The commissioning of Terang marks a crucial milestone for FRV Australia, as it becomes the company’s first standalone battery energy storage project, increasing its portfolio of operational assets in Australia to nine and adding dispatchable energy capacity to FRV Australia’s predominantly solar generation portfolio. The project was further bolstered by an AUD 7 million grant awarded through the second round of the Victorian Government’s Energy Innovation Fund (EIF), supporting the deployment of new grid-forming inverter technology. This initiative forms part of the Victorian Government’s efforts to achieve its target of 65% renewable energy generation by 2030. Canadian Solar served as EPC contractor for the project, with TEC-C delivering the balance-of-plant works. The facility incorporates 48 SolBank 3.0 e battery containers, manufactured by e-Storage, and 38 SMA inverters. The project supported approximately 40 full-time-equivalent roles during the construction and generated business and procurement opportunities for local companies and suppliers. As part of their commitment to the communities in which they operate, FRV Australia supported several social initiatives throughout the development of the project, including sponsorship programmes for the Australian Indigenous Education Foundation (AIEF) and the Terang Mortlake Netball Club. “The commissioning of Terang marks a defining moment for FRV Australia. The project demonstrates our ability to develop and operate utility-scale dispatchable energy infrastructure that supports Australia’s energy transition. It provides critical firming capacity during peak hours while helping to strengthen grid reliability. We are proud to contribute to Victoria’s energy future through a solution that combines sustainability, innovation and benefits for local communities.” said Michael Steiner, CEO of FRV Australia. Terang forms part of FRV Australia’s expanding battery energy storage portfolio in Victoria. The company is developing the 250 MW / 500 MWh Gnarwarre Battery Energy Storage System, currently under construction and targeted for completion by the end of 2027. In addition, FRV Australia also has a pipeline of stand-alone BESS and solar-BESS hybrid projects under development in New South Wales, Victoria and Queensland.

artigo.texto: PowerCo Advances St Thomas Gigafactory with EllisDon Appointment and Phased Development Approach - EllisDon appointed as general contractor as construction advances, with on-site workforce ramping toward ~1,300 at peak - Project progressing through a phased, demand-aligned build, with production ramp-up to scale over time - Major Canadian investment supporting jobs, suppliers, and long-term economic growth across the region ST. THOMAS, ONTARIO – September 24, 2026 – PowerCo Canada today announced it has selected leading Canadian construction firm EllisDon Corporation as general contractor for its St. Thomas gigafactory, marking a key milestone as the project advances into its next phase of construction. The appointment enables work on-site to continue building on steady progress since groundbreaking in 2025. Construction is now moving into core infrastructure and structural phases that will support future production. Joel Karlsberg, Chief Procurement Officer, PowerCo Canada, said: Today’s announcement is an important step forward for St. Thomas, “Partnering with EllisDon allows us to keep construction moving while ensuring we retain the flexibility to scale the facility in line with market demand and long-term industry evolution.” Initial works are focused on the first phase of development, including core building structures and site-wide infrastructure needed to support future production. Construction includes the production-building shell, mechanical, electrical and plumbing installations, energy and utility systems, and supporting site services. Approximately 60 EllisDon workers are currently on site, expected to ramp up to roughly 1,300 workers at peak, alongside additional personnel supporting parallel project activities. Max Mantha, President, Construction, EllisDon, said: The PowerCo facility represents a transformative investment in Canada’s industrial future, and EllisDon is proud to play a role in its delivery, “As a Canadian-headquartered, employee-owned company, we are committed to building the infrastructure that will help support Canada’s growing electric vehicle and battery manufacturing sector. This project will create opportunities for skilled tradespeople, local businesses, and communities across southwestern Ontario, and we look forward to working with PowerCo and our partners on this landmark development.” In parallel, PowerCo is aligning the project’s timeline and product strategy with evolving market demand, technological advancements, and the Volkswagen Group’s long-term strategy. St. Thomas is now expected to begin operations in 2029 to accommodate next-generation battery technology, while retaining the flexibility to scale over time as market conditions evolve. Karlsberg, said: The St. Thomas gigafactory remains a cornerstone of our North American strategy, “We are continuing to build now while determining how and when the facility scales over time. This is about getting the pacing right—not stepping back—to protect our long-term investment, support regional jobs, and position Canada, Ontario, and St. Thomas to benefit in a dynamic and evolving market.” READ the latest Batteries News shaping the battery market PowerCo Advances St Thomas Gigafactory with EllisDon Appointment and Phased Development Approach, source

artigo.texto: As fabricantes de baterias Moura e WEG, além da Associação Brasileira da Indústria de Máquinas e Equipamentos (Abimaq), defenderam que a exigência de conteúdo nacional no leilão de reserva de capacidade de baterias alcance também equipamentos incorporados aos sistemas ao longo dos 15 anos de contrato, inclusive em substituições e ampliações destinadas a compensar a degradação dos ativos. As propostas foram apresentadas nas consultas públicas da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) sobre os dois leilões de baterias previstos para dezembro. A exigência de nacionalização é específica do certame do dia 2 de dezembro, quando há exigência de conteúdo nacional. Outros pontos, como a aferição da eficiência dos sistemas e as penalidades previstas nos contratos, foram discutidos nas duas consultas. Pela minuta do edital do leilão nacional, o empreendedor deverá comprovar junto ao Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) o atendimento aos requisitos de nacionalização e conteúdo local aplicáveis aos sistemas de armazenamento. WEG e Abimaq propuseram deixar expresso que a obrigação continuará válida durante todo o período de suprimento, de 1º de agosto de 2028 a 31 de julho de 2043. Assim, equipamentos, módulos, sistemas ou componentes incorporados posteriormente para ampliação, substituição, recomposição ou manutenção da capacidade contratada também teriam de atender às mesmas exigências previstas para a implantação inicial. As entidades argumentam que a operação por 15 anos poderá exigir novos equipamentos em razão da degradação das baterias e que a ausência de uma regra específica para essas substituições pode permitir tratamento diferente para componentes instalados posteriormente. “A ausência de previsão expressa para a aplicação dos requisitos de conteúdo local às futuras aumentações poderá criar uma assimetria regulatória”, afirmam as contribuições. A Moura apresentou proposta semelhante. A empresa pediu que a exigência também seja aplicada a substituições e ampliações feitas durante o período de suprimento, por degradação, reinvestimento, defeito ou falha de equipamentos. Eficiência das baterias A forma de medir a eficiência total dos sistemas, ou round-trip efficiency (RTE), também recebeu propostas de alteração. As diretrizes estabelecem eficiência mínima de 85%, enquanto a minuta contratual prevê apuração mensal de ressarcimento quando o desempenho ficar abaixo desse patamar. A Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (Absae) propôs que os efeitos financeiros sejam apurados anualmente, mantendo a medição mensal para acompanhamento. Segundo a entidade, o resultado mensal pode ser influenciado pelo perfil de despacho, temperatura, consumo auxiliar, tempo em espera e quantidade de ciclos realizados no período. A Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica (Apine) também sugeriu apuração anual. A entidade argumentou que meses com poucos ciclos ou longos períodos sem despacho podem não refletir adequadamente o desempenho do sistema e pediu que o cálculo considere os consumos necessários para manter a bateria disponível, como climatização, proteção e controle. A Associação Brasileira dos Investidores em Autoprodução de Energia (Abiape) propôs uma janela móvel de 12 meses e uma regra específica para períodos com baixa quantidade de dados. A Huawei também sugeriu apuração financeira anual, com acompanhamento mensal, e propôs uma referência de eficiência de 87% nos primeiros 36 meses de suprimento e de 85% a partir do 37º mês. A Sungrow apresentou outra metodologia. A empresa sugeriu aferir uma RTE de referência por meio de um ciclo padronizado de carga e descarga, com parâmetros definidos para potência, estado de carga, temperatura e consumos auxiliares. O resultado serviria de referência para a apuração econômica mensal. Penalidades do leilão As regras para indisponibilidade e descumprimento dos despachos do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) também foram alvo de contribuições. Apine e Abiape pediram que um mesmo evento operacional não resulte em penalidades cumulativas. A Apine também propôs que as sanções sejam calculadas sobre a potência contratada, e não sobre a potência total instalada, caso o empreendimento tenha capacidade adicional. A Absae questionou a previsão pela qual o resultado parcial de um teste de disponibilidade solicitado pelo ONS pode produzir efeitos sobre todas as horas do mês. A associação sugeriu limitar a penalidade ao período em que a indisponibilidade estiver comprovada e permitir novo teste após a correção do problema. A entidade também pediu tratamento específico para situações em que o atendimento ao despacho seja afetado pelo estado de carga da bateria decorrente de comandos do ONS ou de outras condições operativas impostas ao sistema. Em outro ponto, a Absae questionou a possibilidade de uma mesma indisponibilidade provocar redução da receita fixa e, ao mesmo tempo, outras penalidades por falha de desempenho. A associação propôs retirar a redução adicional da receita ou impedir a acumulação de efeitos financeiros sobre o mesmo evento. A Câmara de Comercialização de Energia Elétrica (CCEE) também sugeriu ajustes nas fórmulas de penalidade. Para a Câmara, a injeção de potência acima do montante determinado pelo ONS também deve ser considerada descumprimento do despacho, por poder reduzir a energia disponível para atendimento posterior. A CCEE propôs ainda que, quando o despacho em tempo real for reduzido por indisponibilidade da própria bateria, a penalidade considere o valor originalmente programado. Quando a alteração decorrer apenas de comando do ONS, sem responsabilidade do agente, deve ser considerado o montante efetivamente determinado em tempo real.

artigo.texto: WASHINGTON — Senate Democrats blocked legislation Wednesday aimed at protecting consumers from paying higher prices when new data centers are built in their communities. The vote was 57-43, short of the 60 needed to break a filibuster. The Ratepayer Protection Act, which passed the House by a vote of 417-3 two weeks ago, would set a federal standard on the issue. It would also instruct state public utility commissions to find ways to make developers of data centers that use huge amounts of energy cover their own costs of water and electricity to consumers. The Senate version is led by appointed Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, who’s locked in a competitive battle as he seeks his first full Senate term. He is facing heat at home from Democratic rival Sherrod Brown, a former senator who has branded him “the face of data centers” for promoting developments when he was lieutenant governor. “I heard they said they wanted lower electricity prices,” Husted said of Democrats on Tuesday. “All they have to do is not block it, vote for it, and it will be on the president’s desk, and we will have a bipartisan win.” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the bill would be merely “optional” for states and wouldn’t achieve much beyond partisan messaging for Republicans. “Plain and simple, the Ratepayer Protection Act is a fraud,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday. “It does not require any protections at all. While Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, Republicans are offering a toothless messaging bill. We need real action on data centers.” Schumer said Republicans should instead take up bills by Sens. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., and Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., that would go further in imposing cost-related rules on data centers. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., rejected Democratic arguments that the bill is simply a Republican political move to protect Husted’s re-election bid. He noted that nearly every House Democrat voted for the measure. Hakeem Jeffries voted for it over there. This is a bill that could go to the president and become law. Evidently, a lot of Democrats in the House of Representatives thought it was important to be for and thought that it did exactly what the bill says it does.” An NBC News poll this month found that data centers are unpopular: By nearly 6-to-1, voters said they’d be less likely to vote for a candidate who supports building a data center in their community. The survey found that voters trust Democrats over Republicans by a margin of 12 percentage points to deal with data centers. Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who is retiring, said Husted was “right to get the message out” on data center costs. But when he was asked whether the bill would achieve much beyond that, Tillis said, “No.” “I think the best way to deal with this is ... down in North Carolina, most utilities are managed through public utility commissions,” Tillis said. “They’re managed through local and state decision-making. That’s where it should be.”

artigo.texto: [DigitalToday reporter Choi Jae-won (최재원)] German electric bicycle company Lemmo (LEMMO) unveiled the Lemmo 3 (LEMMO 3), a new cargo e-bike equipped with a semi-solid-state battery. It is one of the early e-bikes to adopt a semi-solid-state battery, highlighting longer range and higher safety than existing products. IT outlet The Verge reported on Oct. 1 (local time) that the Lemmo 3 uses a 960Wh semi-solid-state battery and can travel up to 180 km on a single charge. Lemmo said, "Compared with conventional liquid-electrolyte-based lithium-ion batteries, we reduced size and weight by 20 percent and increased lifespan by 30 percent." It uses a gel-type electrolyte to lower the risk of thermal runaway and boost stability even if cells are damaged in a crash. The battery can be detached and used as an auxiliary power source. With an optional V2L inverter connected, it can supply power to home appliances with output of up to 1,000W, and USB-C devices can be charged at up to 66W. The Lemmo 3 is a longtail cargo e-bike and weighs 39 kg including the battery. Total payload capacity is 200 kg. It can carry up to 80 kg on the rear rack and up to 20 kg on the front rack. It supports the MIK HD standard, allowing various accessories such as child seats, bags and cargo boxes to be mounted. The rear hub motor is offered by region with specifications of 750W in the United States, 500W in Canada and 250W in Europe, with maximum torque of 90Nm. It also applies an adaptive AI shifting function that selects an appropriate gear in real time based on sensor information. Buyers can also choose a combination of a three-speed automatic transmission and a belt drive system. It also supports rear radar, turn signals and brake lights, a 3.5-inch touchscreen, GPS and LTE tracking, and OTA updates. Lemmo is preparing the launch through Kickstarter, with an early reservation price of 1,890 euros (about 2.89 million won) excluding tax. The first delivery target is April 2027.

artigo.texto: RABAT (MOROCCO) (ITALPRESS) – Morocco is becoming increasingly integrated into new European industrial supply chains. The joint venture announced in Kenitra between Gotion High-Tech and PowerCo—a Volkswagen Group company—marks a new step in the Kingdom’s integration into the strategic supply chain for electric mobility batteries. According to the Moroccan news site Le360, the new plant involves an investment of approximately €480 million and will produce LFP (lithium iron phosphate) cathode materials, with a capacity reaching up to 100,000 tonnes per year. Most significant is the intended destination of this output: Kenitra will be linked to other industrial projects developed by Gotion and Volkswagen in Spain and Slovakia, effectively creating a production chain that spans both shores of the Mediterranean. The project illustrates the growing industrial complementarity between Morocco and the European Union; alongside traditional automotive manufacturing, the country is increasingly producing batteries, advanced materials, and technologies linked to transport decarbonization. The Kingdom’s geographical location, the competitiveness of its industrial platform, its infrastructure, and its growing reliance on renewable energy all boost its appeal at a time when Europe is aiming to diversify and build greater resilience into its supply chains. With this Gotion-Volkswagen investment, Kenitra is establishing itself not merely as an automotive hub, but as a key new Euro-Mediterranean node in the battery industry. – photo Pexels.com – (ITALPRESS).

artigo.texto: Data Center Insights: David Shepard, Chemelex-Raychem The Data Center Frontier Executive Roundtable features insights from industry executives with lengthy experience in the data center industry. Here’s a look at the Q3 2026 insights from David Shepard, Global Head of Data Center Business, Chemelex-Raychem. David Shepard is Global Head of Data Center Business at Chemelex-Raychem, a company with 44 offices in 28 countries. In this role, he is responsible for building and leading the company's data center business worldwide. Prior to his current position, David served as Vice President of Sales for Chilldyne, where he built global partnerships, drove the sales pipeline to nearly $200 million, and helped orchestrate the company's acquisition by Daikin Corporation. During more than 30 years in the technology industry, David has worked across all aspects of IT, from field engineering to the C-suite, with a focus on data center sales and operations, cloud services and IaaS, enterprise software, managed services, outsourcing, multi-vendor support, and professional services sales and operations. Reducing cost and complexity through the strategic use of technology has been a central theme throughout David's career. As an entrepreneur, he has worked in startup and turnaround environments, building and operating data centers and multi-cloud environments, optimizing workloads, developing secure cloud IaaS and PaaS solutions, conducting IT performance audits, and designing business continuity programs. He has also delivered disaster recovery solutions to help organizations meet critical business continuity requirements. David has extensive experience building sales organizations across global markets, including the Americas, Asia-Pacific, and EMEA, and has successfully brought technology solutions to market worldwide. Throughout his career, he has carried a sales quota, led services and sales organizations, rebuilt businesses, and established successful global partnerships. A U.S. Air Force veteran, David is also actively involved in supporting veteran-focused causes and initiatives. Data Center Frontier: What is AI infrastructure exposing that the data center industry could get away with overlooking at lower densities — and which traditional design or redundancy assumptions now need to be reconsidered? David Shepard, Chemelex-Raychem: The deployment and rapid adoption of AI infrastructure is beginning to expose a few areas of risk that were previously not top of mind with operators. Holding aside the “new normal” of extended supply chain issues, deploying IT infrastructure that is, say, 10 times more dense and 10 times more expensive puts a lot of pressure on operators to mitigate this new level of risk and protect these now far more expensive assets. As a for instance, we do leak detection in the white space. Leak detection SOP 5 years ago was ropes or point sensors on the floor, or under the raised floor. With AI infrastructures, those individual racks run between $2-7M per rack. That means traditional leak detection is simply not good enough, and “in rack, in CDU, in server” has become necessary. Data Center Frontier: As data centers become larger, denser and more power-constrained, where is the definition of “critical infrastructure” expanding — and are the interfaces between power, storage, cooling, controls and other systems becoming the real reliability risk? David Shepard, Chemelex-Raychem: “Critical infrastructure” – once simply power and connectivity – now must be thought of more holistically, and must now include adjacent technology like leak detection, freeze protection and Data Center Infrastructure Monitoring (DCIM). Data Center Frontier: With time-to-power compressing development schedules, where can operators safely accelerate deployment — and where do commissioning, testing and operational visibility need to become more rigorous rather than less? David Shepard, Chemelex-Raychem: Deployments on a smaller scale, where possible, enable the operators to gain real world operational competence. When done that way, the scale up is more easily managed, though it is always a challenge. And managing it is far more rigorous. Practically speaking, think of it like this: Operator A is a large colocation provider. The million square feet under management today are handled by expert staff who know the gear and the process. The operator wants to deploy AI infrastructure in a secure, well-run environment and introduce risk (density/cost, water/plumbing, etc…) into a massively risk-averse environment. Starting up a smaller version of the final deployment, building competency and comfort around the new infrastructure, will pay dividends. artigo.texto: Sumitomo Electric Industries Longest operating history, major projects According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Vanadium Redox Flow Battery market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global Vanadium Redox Flow Battery (VRFB) market is transitioning from demonstration projects to commercial deployment, driven by the structural need for long-duration energy storage (LDES) that exceeds the economic and technical limits of lithium-ion batteries. VRFBs offer decoupled power and energy scaling, inherent safety, and exceptional cycle life, making them suitable for utility-scale renewable firming and grid services. However, high upfront capital costs and dependence on vanadium electrolyte supply remain challenges. The market is consolidating around vertically integrated providers that control stack, electrolyte, and power conversion. Growth is closely tied to renewable energy penetration targets and explicit LDES procurement mechanisms. This report provides a comprehensive analysis of the market from 2026 to 2035, covering demand drivers, supply chain dynamics, competitive landscape, and regional outlooks. It is an essential resource for battery manufacturers, utilities, investors, and policymakers seeking to understand the trajectory of this emerging energy storage technology. The baseline scenario for the Vanadium Redox Flow Battery market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates robust growth, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 15.2%, reaching a market index of 450 by 2035 (2025=100). This outlook is underpinned by the increasing deployment of renewable energy sources, which require long-duration storage to manage intermittency and ensure grid stability. As lithium-ion batteries face constraints in cost-effectiveness for durations beyond 4-6 hours, VRFBs are poised to capture a significant share of the LDES market. Key drivers include supportive government policies, declining vanadium electrolyte costs through leasing models, and technological advancements that enhance system efficiency and reduce footprint. However, the market faces restraints such as high initial capital expenditure, competition from alternative LDES technologies, and supply chain bottlenecks for high-purity vanadium. The baseline assumes steady policy support and continued cost reductions, but sensitivity to vanadium price volatility and project financing conditions remains high. By 2035, VRFBs are expected to be a mainstream option for 8+ hour storage applications, with cumulative deployments exceeding 20 GWh globally. Electric utilities and grid operators are the primary adopters of VRFBs, driven by the need to firm renewable energy generation and provide ancillary services. As renewable penetration exceeds 30-40% in many regions, the limitations of lithium-ion for durations beyond 4-6 hours become apparent. VRFBs enable utilities to shift solar energy to evening peaks, manage transmission congestion, and provide frequency regulation. Demand-side indicators include renewable capacity targets, grid modernization budgets, and capacity payment mechanisms for 8+ hour storage. Through 2035, utilities will increasingly procure VRFBs for large-scale projects, often through competitive tenders. The trend is toward larger project sizes, with average durations increasing from 4 hours to 8-10 hours. Utilities value the 20-year lifespan and low degradation, which align with long-term infrastructure planning. However, adoption depends on regulatory frameworks that recognize the value of long-duration storage. In markets with clear LDES procurement mandates, such as California and parts of Europe, VRFB deployments are accelerating. Utilities are also exploring ownership models, including build-own-operate and power purchase agreements, to manage capital costs. Current trend: Rapid growth as utilities seek to integrate renewables and defer grid upgrades.. Major trends: Increasing project sizes from 10 MWh to 100+ MWh, Shift from pilot projects to commercial-scale deployments, Integration with renewable energy projects for firming, Growing use of capacity payment mechanisms for LDES, and Standardization of grid codes for long-duration storage. Representative participants: Sumitomo Electric Industries, Rongke Power, VRB Energy, Invinity Energy Systems, and Stryten Energy. Commercial and industrial users are adopting VRFBs for behind-the-meter applications to manage demand charges, enhance resilience, and integrate onsite renewable generation. Unlike utilities, C&I customers are more sensitive to upfront costs, which has slowed adoption. However, as electricity tariffs become more complex and resilience becomes critical, the value proposition strengthens. VRFBs are particularly attractive for facilities with high daily cycling requirements, such as data centers, manufacturing plants, and cold storage. Demand-side indicators include electricity price volatility, demand charge levels, and frequency of outages. Through 2035, cost reductions and innovative financing models, such as energy-as-a-service, will drive growth. The trend is toward hybrid systems combining VRFBs with solar PV to maximize self-consumption and reduce carbon footprint. C&I customers also value the safety of VRFBs, which can be installed indoors without fire suppression systems. However, competition from lithium-ion for shorter durations remains intense. VRFB adoption in C&I will be concentrated in regions with high demand charges and strong resilience incentives, such as parts of the US, Europe, and Australia. Current trend: Moderate growth driven by demand-charge management and resilience needs.. artigo.texto: Biggest US Grid’s Data-Center Plan Accepted With 5-Month Pause (Bloomberg) -- US energy regulators accepted but suspended a plan by the country’s biggest electric grid to accelerate the addition of new power supply in a region struggling to meet demand from data centers. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission said Tuesday that it would accept the filing of grid operator PJM Interconnection LLC’s plan to procure new capacity but would suspend it until Feb. 28 and establish a paper hearing on unresolved issues. The regulator also encouraged PJM to submit a new filing that answers the issues it raised, which could shorten the delay. A PJM spokesperson didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment outside normal working hours. The artificial intelligence boom is driving the fastest growth in power demand in decades for PJM, which is home to the biggest US concentration of digital warehouses. The regulator agreed PJM needs more generation quickly and approved many parts of the operator’s plan, but said cost allocation, collateral and exit-rule issues need to be fixed before it can proceed. “This Commission will not be forced into accepting a deeply flawed, 11th-hour procurement mechanism with billion-dollar implications for consumers,” Commission Chairperson Laura Swett said in the order. “We are prepared to promptly act on a subsequent proposal that addresses the concerns raised in this order and meets the standards of the Federal Power Act. The region’s reliability hangs in the balance.” PJM’s struggle to keep up with demand growth prompted the Trump administration to call for changes. The FERC, in particular, in recent months has been pushing for reforms. State governors, utilities and investors have also criticized PJM’s response to the AI boom. In an effort to address those concerns, PJM plans to hold a one-time auction to cover a 6.8-gigawatt shortfall. In an earlier auction this year, it failed to attract sufficient commitments to satisfy power demand on peak-usage days. Early this year, the Trump administration pushed for a one-time auction with 15-year instead of annual contracts. PJM’s proposal is contentious because other consumers would bear the costs in the event of data center failures, according to Monitoring Analytics, the grid’s independent watchdog. “Existing customers should not be left paying costs attributable to new demand,” Commissioner Lindsay See said in the order. ©2026 Bloomberg L.P.
