artigo.texto: Investimentos reforçam aposta da companhia em negócios ligados à expansão da infraestrutura de energia A WEG (WEGE3) não esperava o ritmo que os data centers imprimiriam ao negócio de geradores. “Não imaginávamos que teria esse boom”, afirmou Alberto Kuba, CEO da companhia, em entrevista para a edição 2026 do prêmio Maiores e Melhores, da Revista EXAME. Segundo o executivo, a demanda pelo equipamento ganhou força com a expansão dos data centers, que precisam de grupos geradores para garantir o fornecimento de energia em caso de interrupções. E a reação da companhia a esse movimento vem aparecendo cada vez mais nos investimentos.Na última sexta-feira, 25, a multinacional que fabrica equipamentos elétricos anunciou a ampliação da fábrica de baterias em Santa Catarina e, três dias depois, na segunda, 28, divulgou um investimento de US$ 165 milhões, cerca de R$ 869 milhões, para aumentar a produção de geradores na América do Norte. Os dois movimentos colocam a WEG em uma frente que combina geração, armazenamento e infraestrutura elétrica — e que ganhou força com o avanço dos data centers e a necessidade de redes mais robustas. Para o BTG Pactual (do mesmo grupo controlador da EXAME), Ativa Investimentos e Citi, os movimentos colocam a WEG em segmentos que podem sustentar o crescimento da companhia nos próximos anos, embora os efeitos dos novos investimentos sobre os resultados devam aparecer de forma gradual. No caso da iniciativa para ampliar a capacidade de produção de geradores na América do Norte, o projeto será dividido em duas fases e foi anunciado com foco na crescente demanda por soluções de geração de energia para aplicações críticas nos Estados Unidos, especialmente para atender à expansão dos data centers. A primeira fase receberá US$ 24 milhões para a aquisição e adequação de um prédio industrial próximo ao atual Parque Industrial Quma I, em Atotonilco de Tula, no México. A unidade será destinada à montagem de geradores e tem início de operação previsto para o segundo trimestre de 2027. Na segunda etapa, a WEG pretende investir US$ 141 milhões na construção de duas novas instalações industriais, em local ainda a ser definido na América do Norte. A estrutura terá produção verticalizada, incluindo a fabricação de lâminas, bobinas de baixa e média tensão, eixos e carcaças. Com a conclusão da segunda fase, prevista para 2030, a capacidade global da WEG para fabricar geradores deverá passar das atuais 10 unidades por dia para cerca de 50. A produção será distribuída entre as fábricas da companhia no México, EUA, Brasil e China. O movimento amplia uma operação que já vem se beneficiando da expansão dos data centers. “O negócio de alternadores, sob a marca Marathon, tem apresentado um forte desempenho, apoiado pela robusta demanda por energia de reserva por parte dos data centers”, escreveu o BTG em relatório nesta terça-feira, 29. Para o banco, o novo investimento aumenta a capacidade da WEG de atender a uma demanda que tende a exigir cada vez mais equipamentos para garantir o fornecimento de energia. O BTG considera o anúncio positivo e afirma que a expansão cria uma plataforma para o crescimento do negócio de geração de energia da companhia na América do Norte no médio prazo. O banco, porém, ressalta que o investimento não deve trazer uma contribuição relevante para o lucro imediatamente. Mas ressalta que “embora os gastos de capital iniciais impliquem uma contribuição limitada para os lucros no curto prazo, a adição de capacidade deve proporcionar uma plataforma para um maior crescimento dos negócios de geração de energia da WEG na América do Norte no médio prazo”, afirmou. “A WEG realizará seu Investor Day nesta semana, onde esperamos mais detalhes sobre sua estratégia para aproveitar as oportunidades de crescimento no mercado norte-americano”, acrescentou o banco sobre o evento que ocorre nesta sexta-feira, 2. BESS vira outra frente de crescimento O investimento em geradores veio três dias depois de outro anúncio relacionado à infraestrutura de energia. Na sexta-feira, 25, a WEG ampliou o projeto de sua fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, os BESS, em Itajaí, no litoral norte catarinense. O investimento previsto para a unidade passou de R$ 280 milhões para R$ 330 milhões, enquanto a capacidade anual de produção foi dobrada, de 2 para 4 gigawatts-hora (GWh). O início das operações está previsto para o segundo semestre de 2027. A expansão ocorre às vésperas do primeiro leilão de armazenamento de energia do país, previsto para dezembro de 2026. A expectativa é de crescimento da demanda por baterias para integrar fontes renováveis, como solar e eólica, ao sistema elétrico. Na avaliação da Ativa Investimentos, há aí uma oportunidade para a WEG. “Como temos discutido, as iniciativas de BESS e o crescimento de data centers são os principais gatilhos para destravar valor para a companhia”, disse o analista da casa, Lucas Dias. O Citi também coloca os dois anúncios dentro de uma mesma tese. Para o banco, geradores para data centers e sistemas de armazenamento aumentam a exposição da WEG a dois segmentos ligados à expansão da infraestrutura energética. No caso dos geradores, o Citi destaca que a capacidade global da companhia deverá passar de 10 para 50 unidades por dia após a conclusão do projeto em 2030. Já no BESS, chama atenção para a velocidade da expansão: em sete meses, a WEG dobrou a capacidade planejada da fábrica e aumentou o investimento em R$ 50 milhões. “Essa rápida expansão destaca a confiança no mercado emergente de armazenamento de energia do Brasil e fortalece ainda mais o posicionamento da WEG em um segmento-chave da cadeia de valor da transição energética. O início das operações está previsto para o segundo semestre de 2027”, afirmou o Citi. WEG vê oportunidade além dos geradores A própria companhia vê os data centers como uma oportunidade que vai muito além dos geradores. artigo.texto: Mercedes-Benz is taking another step toward next-generation electric vehicle batteries after signing a joint testing agreement with ProLogium Holding Inc. The agreement gives Mercedes-Benz priority access to ProLogium’s latest Gen4 battery cells for extensive testing as the automaker evaluates advanced battery technology for future EV applications. The partnership builds on nearly a decade of cooperation between Mercedes-Benz and ProLogium, which has included battery development, validation and testing of multiple cell formats and technologies. Under the new agreement, ProLogium’s Gen4 battery technology will undergo electrical, thermal and safety testing at Mercedes-Benz facilities as well as specialized independent testing institutes. The testing is expected to provide Mercedes-Benz with data needed to determine whether the new battery technology could eventually be integrated into future electric vehicles. ProLogium Gen4 Battery Targets Higher Energy Density and Faster Charging ProLogium’s Gen4 battery platform is designed around five key objectives: intrinsic safety, high performance, increased energy density, scalable production and a competitive cost structure. The battery architecture uses a non-flammable inorganic electrolyte and ceramic separator technology. ProLogium also incorporates its proprietary active safety mechanism, which is intended to improve the overall safety characteristics of the cells. Alongside safety improvements, the Gen4 technology is being developed to deliver fast charging, high power output and improved performance in low-temperature conditions. These characteristics could be particularly important as automakers continue working to reduce charging times while increasing EV range and performance. ProLogium says its approach is designed to move advanced battery technology beyond laboratory development and toward large-scale commercial production. “Over nearly a decade, our collaboration with Mercedes-Benz has evolved from early cell development and validation to testing our latest Gen4 technology for future vehicle applications,” said Vincent Yang, founder and CEO of ProLogium. Yang added that the company is focused on turning years of battery development into scalable manufacturing and commercially viable products, with its European expansion supported by Mercedes-Benz as well as the French government and European Union. Mercedes-Benz and ProLogium Have Worked Together Since 2016 The relationship between the two companies dates back to 2016. Since then, their collaboration has expanded from early hybrid-solid-state Gen3 battery development and joint validation toward potential applications in future vehicle platforms. Mercedes-Benz has become a long-term global automotive partner and strategic investor in ProLogium. The German automaker has also supported the development and validation of several lithium ceramic battery formats, including pouch cells, next-generation prismatic cells and ProLogium’s Bi-Polar technology. Jörg Burzer, member of the Board of Management of Mercedes-Benz Group AG and chief technology officer for development and procurement, said the partnership combines ProLogium’s solid-state battery technology with Mercedes-Benz’s expertise in battery development, testing and vehicle integration. The latest testing agreement therefore represents another stage in a partnership that has increasingly focused on technologies that could be used in future electric vehicles. ProLogium Expands Battery Manufacturing in Europe Large-scale manufacturing is a key part of ProLogium’s strategy. The company’s Taoke Gigafactory in Taiwan has completed GWh-scale manufacturing validation and supports C-sample production, demonstration vehicle programs and future commercial production. In Europe, ProLogium is developing a planned gigafactory in Dunkirk, France. The facility is expected to eventually have production capacity of up to 44 GWh, providing localized battery manufacturing and supply-chain capabilities for European customers. The Dunkirk facility is intended to replicate the production model established in Taiwan. Once its first phase is completed, ProLogium expects to have the capacity to supply commercial battery cells to European automakers at a scale suitable for electric vehicle platforms. Mercedes-Benz is also represented on ProLogium’s Board of Directors and has expressed support for the company’s Dunkirk development plans. ProLogium is additionally planning a potential NASDAQ listing in the fourth quarter of 2026. What the Gen4 Battery Could Mean for Future Mercedes EVs The latest agreement does not confirm that ProLogium’s Gen4 cells will be used in a production Mercedes-Benz EV. The technology must first complete Mercedes-Benz’s electrical, thermal and safety evaluation before its suitability for future vehicle applications can be determined. However, the testing highlights the growing importance of advanced battery technology as Mercedes-Benz continues developing its next generation of electric vehicles. If ProLogium’s Gen4 cells meet the automaker’s requirements, the combination of high energy density, fast charging, high power output, low-temperature performance and safety-focused cell architecture could make the technology a candidate for future EV platforms. For ProLogium, the agreement also represents an important step in moving its solid-state battery technology closer to automotive-scale commercialization, particularly as the company prepares to expand production in Europe.

artigo.texto: O aumento da demanda por eletricidade aumentou à medida que a atividade dos Data Centers se expandiu e essa tendência deve continuar nos próximos três a cinco anos. O relatório “IA encontra a rede elétrica: moldando o cenário energético dos Data Centers”, da Capgemini, examina o rápido crescimento das operações de Data Center e destaca como a Inteligência Artificial (IA), a IA Generativa e os agentes de IA podem criar valor nas operações da rede e no desempenho do sistema. Realizada com executivos de energia em 21 países, a pesquisa indica que mais de 60% dos executivos do setor elétrico esperam que a IA desbloqueie ganhos significativos em eficiência e operações. No entanto, apenas 45% das concessionárias usam a IA para otimização da rede, o que revela uma oportunidade significativa para escalar operações digitais e impulsionadas por IA para acompanhar a demanda crescente. Além disso, apenas 16% das empresas elétricas usam atualmente Agentes de IA para otimização e confiabilidade da rede, no entanto, 58% planejam implementá-los nos próximos dois anos. O estudo aponta que as empresas do setor elétrico que aliarem uma modelagem disciplinada da demanda a uma entrega mais rápida e flexível, sustentada por operações impulsionadas por IA e por talentos preparados para o futuro, estarão mais bem posicionadas para liderar a próxima fase de expansão dos data centers e oferecer confiabilidade, resiliência, viabilidade econômica e sustentabilidade na velocidade da era da IA. “O sucesso dependerá da capacidade de alinhar investimentos em infraestrutura, fornecimento de energia e operações habilitadas por IA para gerenciar tanto a escala quanto a volatilidade da demanda, equilibrando confiabilidade, custo e sustentabilidade” conclui Claire Gauthier, VP global de Energia e Utilities da Capgemini. Sobre o estudo A pesquisa examina como o rápido crescimento das operações de Data Centers, especialmente as cargas de trabalho impulsionadas por IA, tem remodelado a demanda por eletricidade e desafiando as organizações do setor energético. Foram pesquisados 612 executivos seniores de eletricidade de nível de diretor e acima que estão trabalhando ativamente com data centers, 175 executivos seniores de organizações proprietárias e operadoras de data centers e cinta com insights de quase 20 executivos seniores do setor nas principais organizações globais. A pesquisa foi realizada em 21 países na América do Norte, Europa, APAC e América Latina, incluindo o Brasil. Sobre a Capgemini A Capgemini é uma parceira global de transformação de negócios e tecnologia impulsionada por Inteligência Artificial, que gera valor tangível no mercado. Imaginamos o futuro das organizações e o tornamos realidade por meio de IA, tecnologia e pessoas. Com nossa sólida trajetória de quase 60 anos, somos um grupo responsável e diverso com 420 mil profissionais, em mais de 50 países. Oferecemos serviços e soluções de ponta a ponta que contam com nossa profunda expertise setorial e um robusto ecossistema de parceiros, elevando nossas capacidades em estratégia, tecnologia, design, engenharia e operações de negócios. O Grupo reportou em 2025 receitas globais de 22,5 bilhões de euros. Serviço www.capgemini.com/br-pt

artigo.texto: VW-backed Gotion claims solid state battery breakthrough, aims for 150 USD/kWh & 400 Wh/kg At the 2026 World Manufacturing Convention in Hefei, Volkswagen-backed battery maker Gotion announced breakthroughs in producing its solid-state batteries (SSBs). It also published commercialisation benchmarks and is aiming for an energy density of 400 Wh/kg and pricing of 150 USD/kWh. Baby steps towards mass production CarNewsChina previously reported that Gotion locked in on a 2GWh SSB production line design in March 2026. The firm says it has continued work to ready its Jinshi (Gold Rock) SSB cells for real-world commercialisation, including safety testing. Gotion says its SSB cells have endured “extreme testing scenarios”, including puncture and high-temperature evaluations. It claims the new cells produced neither smoke nor flames, proving that safety and energy density can coexist in SSB cells. Potential pricing and specs The battery maker has also disclosed its financial aims for its new cells, with the ultimate goal of bringing SSBs into the “one-yuan era”, referring to the benchmark of 1 yuan/Wh. This is equivalent to 150 USD/kWh, more than double the current average price of LFP cells in China. Gotion has also renewed its energy-density claims, saying the new cell will reach 400 Wh/kg. The firm is using a sulfide-based solid electrolyte in its Jinshi cells and previously claimed an energy density of 350 Wh/kg. More on Gotion Founded in 2006 in Hefei, Gotion High-Tech is China’s fifth-largest battery maker with 20 manufacturing bases worldwide. It is also closely aligned with Volkswagen, its largest shareholder. According to China EV DataTracker, Gotion achieved 4.61 GWh of battery installations in August 2026, trailing behind similar second-tier suppliers like EVE Energy and CALB. It has slipped to fifth place, and SSBs may be an opportunity to leapfrog competitors. The race for SSBs is heating up, with a plethora of Chinese battery makers and automotive brands announcing plans for trial production and vehicle tests in 2027. BYD has made headlines with its upcoming Yangwang flagship sedan, which may become the first SSB-equipped car to hit the market. Source: libattery.net

artigo.texto: Os bastidores de ser rainha de bateria Para elas, a coroa exige mais do que samba no pé Atualizado Antes do samba-enredo começar, da bateria entrar e das câmeras se voltarem para ela, existe uma história que quase ninguém vê. O carnaval mostra apenas o fragmento mais luminoso da vida de uma rainha de bateria. Por trás dele, há mulheres para quem aquele posto não é vitrine, mas o reconhecimento de um laço construído com a escola, e a realização de um sonho. Tania Bisteka, Patricia Costa e Fabíola Andrade sabem bem o que é isso. Tânia, por exemplo, soube exatamente o que queria desde o dia em que a Mangueira anunciou um concurso para escolher a rainha de bateria em 1999. Não tratou como brincadeira, encarou como se concorresse a um cargo político. Espalhou faixas com o próprio nome pela quadra, abordava os integrantes da bateria para contar sua trajetória com a escola e, a quem estivesse por perto, defendia com convicção que merecia sair vencedora. Na época, o concurso reunia dez candidatas e um júri escolhido pela própria bateria, que avaliaria três entradas de cada uma. Durante o mês entre a inscrição e a disputa, Tânia lutou à sua maneira e sonhou com o que viria. Pôs em prática as ideias para viver o que define como uma festa: “Eu fiz blusas com a minha cara. Eu entrei, fiz uma roupa linda, fiz um biquíni lindo e ganhei. As pessoas desciam o morro para assistir! Só que você imagina, o morro todo lá embaixo gritando, berrando e falando.” A emoção foi grande quando descobriu que o que tanto queria se realizou. E deixa claro que ser rainha não é fácil. Estava o ano todo presente em ensaios, na academia e no boxe. Cuidava da alimentação, mesmo que reconheça que ter nutricionista não era tão acessível quanto hoje. E estava sempre na quadra, sem desculpas, para sambar até o fôlego acabar. Tudo na intenção de melhorar a resistência. Esse era seu preparo. Mas além da preparação em relação a exercícios e alimentação, Tania também se preparou psicologicamente e com a sua fé. A partir da espiritualidade, tomou uma atitude totalmente inusitada antes do desfile para que entrasse na avenida com energia boa. Conta que a Mangueira estava na concentração em um local que existia um valão, onde tirou sua roupa: “Eu fiquei pelada. Convoquei a todos, e quando as pessoas passavam e me viam diziam “meu Deus, a rainha está pelada!” E foi muito louco. Eu estava só com uma canga, eu arranquei a canga e comecei meu ritual.” Nascida no morro da Mangueira, foi muito bem recebida pela bateria. Algumas pessoas a chamam de rainha até hoje e, ao lembrar daquele ano, ela percebe que o processo é diferente para uma rainha cria. "É um trabalho árduo, mas que vale muito a pena. Principalmente quando você é da comunidade, uma rainha pé no chão. Quando eu digo pé no chão, quero dizer uma rainha do povo, né? Quando a rainha é cria da escola, ela é mais cobrada do que quando não é. Porque está ali para mostrar que realmente mereceu estar naquele lugar de rainha." Patrícia Costa, rainha de bateria da Viradouro de 1991 a 1998, também sentiu essa diferença. Ela conta que as pessoas famosas pareciam ter mais abertura para ocupar esse espaço. Quando foi chamada, já fazia balé, jazz e sapateado. O convite veio de forma surpreendente, quando foi prestigiar o mestre Maçal, com quem já havia feito um trabalho, e acabou sambando muito com os passistas. Foi um verdadeiro teste de fogo. Naquele dia, o então presidente da escola viu o movimento e ficou interessado em conhecê-la. No fim, a chamou ao camarote e fez o convite, quando teve que assumir uma postura: "Eu precisei me colocar assim, com muita responsabilidade e auto valorização da minha posição como uma artista do samba, uma artista, uma sambista que sabia o que estava fazendo ali à frente da bateria. Não foi fácil. Assim, fui conquistando a comunidade com a minha presença e dedicação." Patrícia explica que a relação com os mestres de bateria e os ritmistas é essencial. Durante os ensaios, a sintonia vai sendo construída. A partir das frases musicais e dos sons da bateria, surge uma criatividade que forma combinações capazes de ajudar a rainha a se movimentar em harmonia com os ritmistas. Nem tudo, porém, são flores. Sobre os perrengues, ela lembra de um ano em que desfilou com o sapato fechado e arrasou na avenida, mas terminou o desfile carregada no colo pelo namorado. Se sente neta da Águia da Portela, já que o avô foi um dos fundadores da escola. Cresceu ouvindo as histórias e foi ali que o amor pelo samba começou. Durante o desfile, essa paixão mantinha qualquer desconforto longe: “Nunca aconteceu de eu sentir alguma dor durante o desfile. O corpo fica quente, acontece uma troca de energia maravilhosa com o público, uma energia tão boa que não tem muito lugar para sentir dor. Para mim, naquele palco tem uma magia, o show acontece. Sem dor.” Energia essa também que também guia Fabíola Andrade. Foi rainha de bateria da Mocidade Independente de Padre Miguel de 2024 a 2026 e hoje é rainha da escola. Desde criança, já se encantava com a festa, o ritmo e a energia das escolas de samba. Para ela, ser rainha de bateria é fazer parte da história viva do carnaval carioca, levar alegria e garra a uma comunidade inteira. Pensando nas fantasias, diz que é um trabalho artesanal e demorado, feito em equipe com o carnavalesco e estilistas renomados do Carnaval. Segundo ela, os costeiros podem pesar de dez a vinte quilos e o salto alto exige estrutura. Então, garantir que nada saia do lugar é uma verdadeira engenharia. A rainha lembra que já precisou até de uma costura de última hora na fantasia, na concentração, com o coração aos pulos e frio na barriga. Assim como Patrícia, acredita que a adrenalina é um anestésico natural inacreditável, fazendo com que a garra da comunidade e a troca de energia impulsionem toda a animação: "É uma relação de puro amor, cumplicidade e respeito. O mestre de bateria e os ritmistas são o coração da escola, e eu estou ali para ser a energia vibrante daquele ritm

artigo.texto: Foi aprovado, nesta terça-feira (29), na Câmara de Maringá, um conjunto com Projetos de Lei (PL) para que o município crie uma empresa pública responsável por implantar e operar o data center previsto pela Prefeitura. A proposta é de autoria do executivo. Ao todo, foram 20 votos registrados: 13 favoráveis e seis contrários. Votaram a favor os vereadores Akemi Nishimori (PSD), Angelo Salgueiro (PODE), Bravin Junior (PP), Diogo Altamir da Lotérica (PSDB), Flávio Mantovani (PSD), Guilherme Machado (PL), Jeremias (PL), Luiz Neto (AGIR), Maninho (Republicanos), Mário Hossokawa (PP), Odair Fogueteiro (PP), Uilian da Farmácia (União) e William Gentil (PP), totalizando 13 votos. Votaram contra Daniel Malvezzi (NOVO), Italo Maroneze (PDT), Lemuel do Salvando Vidas (PDT), Mário Verri (PT), Professor Pacífico (NOVO) e Professora Ana Lúcia (PDT), somando seis votos. A proposta O Projeto de Lei nº 18.401/2026 autoriza a criação da Maringá Data e Tecnologia S.A., empresa pública constituída como sociedade anônima de capital fechado e com capital integralmente pertencente ao Município. A companhia terá como finalidade a implantação, operação e exploração de um data center, apresentado no projeto como empreendimento-âncora da futura Zona de Processamento de Exportação (ZPE) de Maringá. Um dos projetos que acompanha a proposta, o PL nº 18.398/2026, autoriza a abertura de um crédito adicional especial de R$10 milhões no orçamento de 2026. O recurso será destinado à constituição e estruturação da nova empresa. Além desse valor inicial, o projeto que cria a empresa prevê que o Município poderá fazer aportes de até R$20 milhões ao longo de quatro anos. Com a aprovação nas duas discussões, o projeto segue para sanção do executivo.

artigo.texto: By — Kevin Freking, Associated Press Kevin Freking, Associated Press By — Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press By — Didi Tang, Associated Press Didi Tang, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-data-center-bill-falls-short-as-senate-holds-final-votes-before-the-midterms Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Data center bill falls short as Senate holds final votes before the midterms Politics Updated on Sep 30, 2026 8:02 PM EDT — Published on Sep 30, 2026 3:45 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — A bill that attempts to address voter worries about data centers and their impact on energy costs failed to advance in the Senate on Wednesday, falling victim to an election-year clash on how best to address a growing concern. Watch the Senate floor in the video player above. Before leaving Washington to campaign, Senate Republicans reserved one of the chamber's final votes for a bill they hoped would underscore efforts to address the impact data centers have on voters' monthly energy bills. The bill needed 60 votes to advance, but fell short, 57-43. WATCH: How data centers became a major issue in the midterms The bill is a modest one. It requires utility regulators to consider adopting a federal standard that charges large power customers a rate that covers the cost of the system upgrades needed to serve them. Democrats say it amounts to a suggestion and that more is needed. Republicans say the bill sends a message to regulators to act. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The bill's sponsor, Sen. Jon Husted, a Republican from Ohio, is in a tough reelection battle and has been labeled in campaign ads as the "face of data centers" by his Democratic challenger, former Sen. Sherrod Brown. "You all know this is the only game in town," Husted told reporters in advocating for his bill. "This bill passing is the only way to get a chance to prove to the American people before the midterm elections whose side you're on." Senate Democrats say the bill isn't tough enough The measure passed the House by a vote of 417-3. It needed support from at least seven Democratic senators to proceed to a final vote, but that didn't happen given the criticism from within their ranks that it doesn't go far enough and knowing that passage could give Husted's reelection prospects a lift. "The bill is a fraud, plain and simple," Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said. Democrats have offered competing proposals. Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. sponsored legislation that would direct the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to issue rules for large electricity customers that requires them to pay for necessary grid upgrades. "They want it optional, which means zero. We want it mandatory," Schumer said. Republicans are looking to position Democrats as obstructionists who are blocking progress on key voter concerns. Husted's bill is one example. Another would be the bill from Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., that would bar members of Congress from purchasing individual stocks. The issue is a popular one with candidates running for office this election cycle, but also includes voter identification requirements that Democrats have called a poison pill. Thune teed up both bills for procedural votes and both failed to meet the 60-vote threshold for advancing. "Both pieces of legislation strike at the very heart of issues that the American people care deeply about, passionately about, and we'll see if the Democrats are willing to take yes for an answer," Thune said. Data centers have become a top campaign issue The House and Senate are both expected to be out of session for all of October. The House left in mid-September, canceling nearly two weeks of votes as Republicans were anxious to get on the campaign trail in a bid to keep their majority in the next Congress. President Donald Trump has embraced the building of more data centers, but there is growing wariness from voters. About 6 in 10 Americans support limiting the number of new data centers that can be built, including most Democrats and Republicans. And a majority of Americans are "extremely" or "very" concerned about the impact of data centers on electricity prices or the water supply in the communities where they are built. In Ohio, a data center hot spot with closely contested races for governor and U.S. Senate, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned in a recent memo that Husted is vulnerable to losing his seat because of the centers. Husted helped promote Ohio as a destination for data centers while serving as lieutenant governor. The Ohio race is seen as vital to determining control of the Senate, helping explain why the data center bill has generated so much scrutiny and is so hotly contested despite the overwhelming vote it received in the House. Speaking on the Senate floor before the vote, Husted said that the bill requires states to at least confront the issue of data centers paying their own way for their power and the grid improvements needed to serve them. He said the bill could hardly get broader support than it did in the House, but by blocking the bill in the Senate, Democrats would be showing they don't care about the issue of affordability. "Let's hold data centers accountable and let's stop blocking a path to affordability," Husted said. artigo.texto: EU chooses secrecy over transparency on data centers’ environmental cost The EU faced a choice: reveal the environmental cost of data centers or protect the industry’s secrets. A year-long battle for answers across all 27 member states shows how European authorities chose commercial secrecy – and how a first-of-its-kind legal challenge could change that. European officials faced a political choice over their proposed sustainability rating system for data centers: make consumption figures public or protect the industry’s commercial secrets. A study they commissioned made that choice explicit. They chose secrecy. A year-long investigation by Solomon and its partners found that the proposed system would keep crucial energy and water consumption figures from public view while relying on incomplete and flawed data. Unveiled by the European Commission this month and described in media coverage as potentially the most comprehensive of its kind in the world, the proposal promises “transparent information about the actual use of resources (energy, water)” by data centers. These facilities underpin Europe’s massive digital expansion and contribute to its growing environmental footprint. Yet the rating system would show how efficiently individual facilities use energy and water, while keeping their total consumption and carbon emissions confidential. For communities living near data centers, those totals answer a basic question: How much electricity and water are the facilities around them using? As Europe expands the infrastructure powering artificial intelligence (AI), the answers would help residents assess what that growth means for local supplies. Led by Lighthouse Reports, journalists filed formal records requests with authorities in all 27 EU member states and the Commission. We requested basic information on data centers’ energy use, water consumption and sustainability performance, along with correspondence about the implementation of the reporting system. Hundreds of exchanges, appeals and challenges to refusals uncovered missing reports, seemingly impossible efficiency readings and European officials encouraging submissions even when they contained little or no data. Our investigation – conducted with Mediapart (France), El Confidencial (Spain), Il Manifesto (Italy) and Trouw (the Netherlands) – also examined how industry demands shaped the information the public will be allowed to see. And it revealed how difficult it is to obtain consumption figures that operators are required to report. The secrecy is built into EU rules. Data centers with an installed information technology capacity of at least 500 kilowatts must report their energy and water consumption. But the rules treat individual facilities’ submissions as commercially confidential, shielding them from public disclosure to protect companies’ business interests. Those are the consumption figures we spent a year trying to obtain across the EU. Some governments called them commercial secrets. Others said they were held in Brussels. The Commission, which runs the European database, also refused to release them. Two countries provided partial data that could not be linked to specific facilities. France supplied a spreadsheet but shuffled values between rows, leaving reporters unable to reliably connect a data center’s electricity use with its water consumption. The findings underpin a first-of-its-kind legal challenge launched this week by our reporting consortium under the Aarhus Convention, a binding international treaty protecting access to environmental information. We argue that EU rules treating individual data centers’ environmental information as commercially confidential violate the treaty – both in their wording and in how authorities apply them to deny public access. At stake is the public’s ability to understand – and have a say in – one of the defining environmental developments of our time: the enormous and accelerating build-out of data centers powering the AI boom, and its impact in their communities. “There is a clear public interest in understanding the material impact that infrastructure of this scale may have, including its total water and electricity consumption,” said Nicolás González Casares, a Spanish Socialist Member of the European Parliament (MEP) who works on energy policy and the environmental impact of AI. He added, “Protecting commercially sensitive information when necessary is one thing; systematically preventing the public from understanding this environmental impact is quite another.” In response to our findings, the Commission defended the system, saying it had significantly improved transparency and that its confidentiality rules complied with EU law and the Aarhus Convention. A “fairly useless” system? Data centers are warehouses packed with computers and cooling systems that power everything from everyday online services to AI systems. They are vital to the development of the AI industry. They are also extremely energy-intensive, requiring vast amounts of electricity and, depending on how they are cooled, water. In Ireland, data centers consumed nearly as much electricity as all the country’s homes combined in 2025 — accounting for 23 percent of recorded electricity consumption, compared with 28 percent for households. A decade earlier, data centers’ share was just 5 percent, according to the country’s statistics authority. The EU aims to triple its data center capacity over the next five to seven years. That expansion comes amid a global backlash against data centers over their demands on electricity and water supplies. In parts of the United States, households are already paying higher electricity bills partly because of data centers’ growing demand for power. “Every new data center stakes a claim on something a community needs, from the water we drink to the energy that heats our homes,” said Cori Crider, executive director of the Future of Tech Institute. “A smart plan for European compute

artigo.texto: North Carolina energy company holds open house for proposed battery energy system TOPEKA, Kan. (WIBW) - A North Carolina-based energy company, Deriva Energy, held its third open house on Sept. 30th for a proposed 20-acre battery energy storage system (BESS) in Tecumseh. A BESS houses technology that charges energy from the grid and then discharges it back to the grid. A storage container for megawatts. “Anything that stores energy is just like a double-A battery. This is just a really big double-A battery,” Patrick Smith, Senior Director at Deriva Energy, said. The 270-megawatt facility is being proposed just south of the decommissioned Tecumseh Energy coal plant. “This is an area that already has the infrastructure to accept a project,” Smith said. “It’s already got a switching station, so it’s kind of been identified as an area of need, and there is enough land to fit the project on.” While the project wouldn’t be operational until 2030, Deriva said there’s already a need across the country. “They provide a lot of support to the grid because they can charge and discharge on command. They provide a lot of stability as the grid goes through ups and downs throughout the day,” Smith said. “The grid needs more capacity by 2027. That’s when they’re projected to need capacity.” Since this is a giant battery, area fire departments are already being looped in. “It’s really important to get them involved early on to make sure they understand the equipment that’s gonna be on site and that they understand we’re coordinating to make sure we’re, you know, kind of in lock step,” Smith said. With Wednesday being the third open house, they’re already hearing a lot of feedback. “A lot of curiosity, a lot of great questions, so the community wants to know who we are, they want to know more about battery,” Smith said. “Absolutely, yes, a lot of information. Very candid answers to our questions,” Vicki Arnett, Climate Committee member for the League of Women Voters, said. “You know, we’re in support of strengthening the grid, you know, for the public good.” Deriva’s sharing what it wants people to know. “It’s a stand-alone storage system. It’s not associated or similar to a data center in any way,” Smith said. “This is a resource for the grid to use.” The BESS is still early on in the proposal project, and the anticipated capital investment is expected to be around $350 million. artigo.texto: Princeton NuEnergy and SK Battery America Expand Collaboration on US Closed-Loop Battery Recycling COMMERCE, Ga., Sept. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Princeton NuEnergy Inc. (PNE) today announced its ongoing collaboration with SK Battery America (SKBA) to advance the development of a closed-loop recycling pathway for battery manufacturing scrap generated at SKBA’s facilities in Commerce, Georgia. Under the planned collaboration, PNE will receive battery manufacturing scrap from SKBA. The company is exploring a recycling facility near the manufacturing site to develop a streamlined system for battery materials recycling. Designed to process battery manufacturing scrap, the facility would recover and rejuvenate cathode active material for potential return to battery manufacturing, helping support a more integrated domestic battery supply chain. PNE recently announced that it has been selected by the U.S. Department of Energy to enter award negotiations for up to $50 million in support of a proposed $110 million project to develop a Cathode-to-Cathode® rejuvenation facility in the United States. Unlike conventional recycling methods that break battery materials down into their constituent elements, PNE’s direct recycling process is designed to preserve and rejuvenate the engineered structure of cathode materials. The collaboration reflects PNE and SKBA’s shared interest in improving material circularity, recovering value from battery manufacturing scrap, and strengthening domestic supply chain for critical battery materials. A localized recycling pathway also reduces reliance on imported inputs while supporting U.S. energy security and industrial competitiveness. PNE and SKBA are continuing discussions regarding the technical and commercial framework for the collaboration. Chao Yan, Co-Founder and CEO of PNE, said: Our business collaboration with SK Battery America reflects growing interest in direct recycling solutions for U.S. battery manufacturing, “By leveraging PNE’s Cathode-to-Cathode® process, we aim to support a more localized and circular domestic battery materials supply chain.” READ the latest Batteries News shaping the battery market Princeton NuEnergy and SK Battery America Expand Collaboration on US Closed-Loop Battery Recycling, source

artigo.texto: The Glendale City Council recently considered a 160-acre land annexation for Project Eagle, located west of the northwest corner of Litchfield Road and Olive Avenue — approximately 1 mile north of Luke Air Force Base. The proposed land use for the property includes three data centers, totaling 1.1 million square feet, and a gas generation plant. Amid the discussion, multiple speakers voiced their thoughts on the proposed annexation. “This project has been before so many different boards and each time it has passed — it has the Luke Air Force Base approval, otherwise the board of supervisors would’ve said no,” Surprise resident Lisa Everett said. “The people who are concerned about this, I hear them and I understand their concerns — but if not this project, what would they accept? “Change is hard and it’s different — but the reality is the sky is not falling.” “I’m not opposed to economic development — my concern is that the proposed protections for the nearby neighborhoods are simply not adequate for a development of this size,” said Troy Mortensen, a Waddell resident who said he lives 2,000 feet from the project site. “The proposed PAD relies primarily on 75-foot setbacks, 6-foot-high walls and limited landscaping as a transition for this massive industrial campus. “Growth and neighborhood protection are not mutually exclusive — we can have both.” As the purpose of the public hearing was to give the public an opportunity to provide feedback, the City Council did not make any final decision with regard to the land annexation. Senior Planner Sydney Tirella explained that the adoption of the annexation application and rezoning is expected to return to the dais on Oct. 27 for further consideration. According to Tirella, the project is organized in phases, with the data centers and turbines being constructed in phases one and two. Phase three will include an APS substation in the northeastern corner of the site. The proposed access points for the project site include Hatcher Road to the west and Olive Avenue to the south. Tirella said that in its future phases, the site will also include access to the north via the extension of the 143rd Avenue alignment to Peoria Avenue. As it stands, the Maricopa County jurisdiction zoning for the 160-acre land package is IND-3, for heavy industrial with an approved military compatibility permit — which would become M-2 once the annexation is complete. To accommodate the proposed data centers and gas generation plant, the city would need to rezone the property to Planned Area Development (PAD). The property sits within Luke Air Force Base’s noise contours and is designated for Luke-compatible land use under Glendale’s General Plan. Following the staff presentation and public comment section, Councilmember Leandro Baldenegro asked whether the taller walls, berms, trees and other protections Mortenson noted in his argument could be added. Project attorney Edwin “Ed” Bull clarified that the proposal did include some of the protections, including a block wall at least 8 feet high along portions of the site, as well as “landscaping where it’s appropriate.” “Maybe not to the degree they’re requesting them — but what was deemed appropriate setbacks, appropriate walls, appropriate landscaping, other screening mechanisms and so on is all part of what’s included in the County approval, and as part of what’s being brought forward in your design review analysis,” Bull said. Additionally, Mayor Jerry Weiers asked Bull to clarify whether Luke Air Force Base had any issues with the project. Bull explained that the base issued a letter that lists certain conditions of approval that his client, the applicant, agreed to. Vice Mayor Ray Malnar also asked about the distance between the project and land available for future residential development — noting that “there’s a pretty big distance between the property and the next available property that can be developed for residential.” The attorney confirmed and explained that statutory, General Plan and zoning limitations exist to regulate what development can exist around the project site. Councilmember Lupe Conchas asked whether similar developments combining large-scale data centers and on-site power generation have been successfully developed elsewhere in the country. Bull described the configuration as an “evolving trend,” but said he could not cite a completed example during the meeting and would provide additional information when the project returns to council.

artigo.texto: Vendas da BYD cresceram pelo quinto mês seguido puxadas por exportações Na comparação com setembro de 2025, houve alta de 17%, chegando a 463.561 unidades no mês passado As vendas globais da BYD subiram pelo quinto mês consecutivo em setembro, impulsionadas por fortes exportações, que vêm se tornando cada vez mais um pilar fundamental para compensar a demanda doméstica persistentemente fraca. As vendas de veículos aumentaram 17% em relação ao mesmo período do ano anterior, chegando a 463.561 unidades no mês passado, uma desaceleração em relação ao aumento de 17,8% registrado em agosto. As exportações de carros e picapes dispararam 153,9%, atingindo 179.877 unidades, de acordo com cálculos da Reuters com base nos dados divulgados pela BYD nesta quinta-feira (1°). A fabricante chinesa de veículos elétricos vendeu 3.131.576 unidades nos primeiros nove meses de 2026, incluindo 1.337.831 exportadas. A BYD enfrenta uma concorrência cada vez mais acirrada no mercado interno, onde a rival Geely lançou um sistema de recarga mais rápido. A BYD espera que as exportações ultrapassem 2,5 milhões de veículos em 2027, segundo corretoras de ações.

artigo.texto: The revision of Europe’s carbon market has become a proxy for a much bigger argument about the future of European industry. This week, Italy and the Czech Republic insisted on calling for softer carbon-market rules to reduce energy costs. Yet, other governments, companies and investors continue to stress the value of a stable carbon price for long-term investment in Europe’s industrial future. The debate is no longer neatly split between “industry” and “climate”, though. Some of the sharpest disagreements now run within the same sectors, between companies and even between businesses and the associations that represent them. The debate is ultimately about how to reconcile competitiveness with decarbonisation. One carbon price, different strategies The EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) puts a price on emissions from power stations, heavy industry, aviation and shipping. Companies need a permit for every tonne of carbon they emit, while the total number of permits falls over time. Emissions in the sectors it covers have fallen by around half since 2005. The next phase is harder. Cutting emissions from steel, cement or chemicals often means replacing core production equipment, securing much more clean electricity or building new infrastructure. Companies do not all enter this phase from the same starting point. But those starting points are not simply imposed on them. Some businesses invested early in cleaner technologies, changed their business models and started developing markets for clean products. Others have continued to invest around existing high-emission assets, or postponed hard decisions about how their businesses will compete in a lower-carbon economy. Governments have also made choices. Countries that expanded renewables, strengthened grids or invested in infrastructure have changed the options available to their industries. Those choices now shape positions on the ETS. A company that has invested in cleaner production has an interest in a predictable carbon price that preserves the value of that investment. A company whose current assets face higher costs may place greater weight on short-term relief. Similarly, among the European countries most vocal against the ETS are those most exposed to high fossil fuel prices, such as Italy, despite the ETS being part of the solution to reducing that dependence. Competitiveness is also about renewal Europe faces real immediate pressures: high energy costs, weak demand in some sectors and strong international competition. Policymakers therefore worry about production or investment moving abroad. But the difficulties facing Europe’s energy-intensive industries did not begin with today’s carbon price. The European Commission describes two decades of persistent competitive pressure, declining production and rising import dependence in sectors such as steel, chemicals and aluminium. European steel production is now far below pre-financial-crisis levels, while the chemicals sector has also suffered plant closures and lost capacity in recent years. Those changes what “protecting industry” means. Europe is unlikely to build a durable competitive advantage around a hope for cheap fossil fuels: it imports most of them and remains highly exposed to global price shocks. A business model that depends on permanently cheaper gas than Europe can access is therefore a difficult foundation for long-term competitiveness. Modernising production, expanding clean power and improving energy efficiency are therefore not simply climate objectives. For many industrial activities, they are part of the economic case for keeping production, investment and jobs in Europe. The carbon market has a particular role in that renewal. By making emissions more expensive, it improves the relative economics of cleaner production. It also raises public revenues that can be reinvested in the transition and gives companies a clearer basis for long-term investment decisions. But a carbon price cannot build a grid connection, create demand for green steel or make electricity affordable. Much of that responsibility sits with Member States. National governments shape power systems, infrastructure, permitting and the use of carbon-market revenues. The success of the ETS therefore also depends on governments doing their part to create the conditions in which companies can invest – instead of simply blaming Brussels. A new bargain around the carbon market The European Commission’s July proposal reforming the ETS reflects these pressures. It would keep the basic carbon-market system but give industry more flexibility after 2030, including a slower withdrawal of free permits for industries covered by Europe’s new carbon border charge. At the same time, it would create a new €100 billion EU fund for cleaner industrial investment, direct more carbon-market revenues towards industrial transformation and link continued free permits more closely to companies investing in Europe. Framing the review as “ETS: yes or no?” misses the point. The real argument is about the bargain around it: how much protection companies receive, what they do in return, how predictable the carbon signal remains, and whether Europe turns the money and incentives created by carbon pricing into industrial renewal. The answers to these questions reflect competing views on how to keep European industry competitive: by cushioning existing business models for longer, by accelerating investment in new ones, or - as many companies will have to do - by managing both at the same time. The ETS review is bringing those choices into the open. But something is clear: the decision is not just about the price of carbon today, it is about which industrial model Europe makes viable for tomorrow.

artigo.texto: Uma nova frente de negócios: créditos de carbono Elétricas ampliam a venda de créditos de carbono e miram nova demanda com avanço do mercado regulado Atualizado Com o desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono nacional, as empresas do setor de energia passaram a enxergar a comercialização de créditos de carbono como uma extensão de seus negócios. Foi uma evolução natural do setor, uma vez que as fontes renováveis respondem por cerca de 85% da matriz elétrica brasileira e que as reduções de emissões de carbono podem dar origem a créditos. Embora essa frente de negócios não seja relevante em termos de faturamento, integra a sustentabilidade das operações. Trata-se de um negócio complementar, cuja relevância pode aumentar com o mercado regulado de carbono, o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE), em implementação. Na Auren Energia, a estratégia ganhou uma área dedicada em 2022 e foi integrada à comercialização. A companhia já vendeu oito milhões de créditos a clientes de mais de 20 países, a maioria deles empresas que precisam neutralizar suas emissões. Ela também mantém o Carbonless, comércio eletrônico para pequenas empresas e pessoas físicas que queiram zerar sua pegada de carbono. Eduardo Diniz, diretor de comercialização, diz que a estratégia da Auren é se tornar um “one-stop-shop” para clientes de energia, de forma que estes possam comprar tanto o fornecimento de energia quanto os créditos para zerar ou compensar as emissões. No momento, a empresa desenvolve um projeto que prevê a restauração de até 2.795 hectares e o plantio de até 5,6 milhões de árvores na bacia do rio Tietê — projetos do tipo geram créditos mais valorizados. Já a Axia Energia comercializou mais de 12 milhões de créditos entre 2013 e 2026. A companhia vê a experiência como credencial para o SBCE, que estabelecerá limites de emissão para agentes regulados e permitirá a negociação de ativos para o cumprimento das metas. A expectativa das empresas é que créditos hoje negociados no mercado voluntário possam, desde que atendam a critérios previstos na regulamentação, ganhar espaço também nesse sistema. “Queremos alcançar empresas que estão começando a jornada de sustentabilidade e empresas maiores com alta demanda de crédito”, diz Cecília Essinger, gerente-executiva de produtos estruturados e ativos ambientais da Axia. Segundo ela, créditos originados em energia renovável são negociados no mercado por cerca de US$ 1 a US$ 3. A Engie atua no mercado de carbono desde 2004. A empresa tem 14 projetos de energia eólica, solar, hidrelétrica e biomassa que geram créditos pela redução de emissões de gases de efeito estufa (GEE). Antes registrados no Mecanismo de Desenvolvimento Limpo (MDL), esses projetos estão sendo adaptados às regras do Acordo de Paris. Nos empreendimentos controlados integralmente pela Engie, as reduções de emissões somaram cerca de 6,5 milhões de toneladas de CO2 e até 2020, sendo que 5,3 milhões de créditos já foram usados para compensar emissões e, por isso, saíram de circulação. A empresa também mantém a plataforma Descarbonize, que ajuda clientes a medir e administrar suas emissões e a comprar créditos para compensá-las. Já na EDP, o Parque Eólico Monte Verde, no Rio Grande do Norte, tornou-se em 2025 o primeiro projeto do grupo no mundo certificado para emitir créditos, evitando a emissão de 533 mil toneladas de CO2 por ano. Como o mercado voluntário de créditos de carbono só se sustenta se houver credibilidade e confiança de que os projetos contribuíram para a redução ou remoção das emissões, as empresas têm buscado verificadoras independentes como Verra e Gold Standard, mecanismos vinculados à ONU e o Global Carbon Council. Nem toda redução de emissões entrega o mesmo resultado climático. Daniela Mota, head de meio ambiente e sustentabilidade do escritório Felsberg Advogados, diz que tecnologia, data de geração, metodologia e certificação influenciam qualidade e preço dos créditos. Entre os riscos estão a falta de adicionalidade — quando a redução ocorreria mesmo sem o projeto —, a dupla contagem e benefícios que não se confirmam. “É muito ruim, do ponto de vista reputacional, ter um projeto de carbono que não entrega aquilo que estava prometendo”, afirma. Enquanto alguns monetizam emissões evitadas e projetos de restauração florestal, uma nova fronteira está nas tecnologias de captura, transporte, utilização e armazenamento de CO2, conhecidas pelas siglas CCS e CCUS. O Decreto nº 13.095/2026, publicado em agosto, reconhece o CCS como atividade de redução ou remoção de GEE, que poderá ser considerada no SBCE. A Petrobras informa ter armazenado 86 milhões de toneladas de CO2 em sistemas de CCUS do pré-sal entre 2008 e 2025, sendo 18 milhões no ano passado. Já o piloto Cabiúnas-São Tomé deverá capturar até 100 mil toneladas anuais por três anos a partir de 2028 e armazená-las em reservatório salino profundo no norte fluminense. A licença ambiental integrada foi emitida em agosto. Apesar da escala, a estatal não tem projeto para gerar créditos destinados à venda; suas compras ou compromissos de aquisição são, a princípio, para uso próprio.

artigo.texto: Data Center Private Power: Who Regulates Behind-the-Meter Generation? Key Highlights - Behind-the-meter generation does not necessarily mean going off grid: most privately powered data centers will still depend on public transmission, standby capacity, emergency imports or other reliability services. - As utility timelines stretch and large-load tariffs become more demanding, data center operators are increasingly evaluating dedicated generation as a way to gain greater control over capacity, deployment schedules and expansion. - Private power shifts more of the reliability stack onto the data center itself, including fuel security, operating reserves, black start, voltage and frequency control, maintenance and response to sudden load changes. - FERC, PJM and state utility regulators are now defining how co-located and self-supplied data centers should be treated, including the critical question of whether grid obligations should reflect a facility’s normal net demand or the larger load the system may need to support during an outage. - Cases involving Amazon–Talen, Ohio and Michigan point toward an emerging hybrid-grid model in which data centers can supply more of their own power while remaining financially and operationally accountable for the public system they continue to rely on. For years, data center power followed a familiar development model: secure utility capacity, negotiate the interconnection, build the substation, and bring the facility online. That model is becoming harder to rely on. As utility timelines lengthen, available capacity tightens, and regulators push large customers to shoulder more of the infrastructure costs created by their demand, data center operators are increasingly pursuing power they can build, finance, control, or contract for themselves. The technology and configurations vary. A campus may pair its load with dedicated gas generation, batteries, fuel cells, renewables, or a co-located power plant. It may operate behind the meter, contract with an independent generator, or design an electrical system capable of islanding during grid disruptions. The objective is largely the same: gain greater control over capacity and deployment timelines than the conventional utility-service process can currently provide. But private generation does not necessarily create a private electricity system. Even a data center that supplies most or all of its own primary power may still depend on the public grid for transmission access, emergency imports, reserve capacity, voltage and frequency support, black-start capability, surplus-power exports, or future expansion. Those connections carry costs and obligations that do not disappear simply because the electrons normally feeding the servers originate on or beside the campus. That is moving the regulatory debate beyond whether a utility can serve a new data center load. The emerging question is what happens when a large customer supplies much of its own electricity while retaining access to the wider system. Utilities and grid operators contend that customers relying on public-system reliability must pay an appropriate share of the infrastructure and standby capability required to support them. Data center operators, meanwhile, need to know whether investments in dedicated generation will be treated as genuine self-supply or remain subject to many of the costs and constraints of conventional utility service. Hyperscale AI has accelerated the issue because of the size and speed of its power requirements, but the implications extend across the data center industry. Any operator facing constrained utility capacity, uncertain construction schedules, new large-load tariffs, or the need for greater energy resilience now confronts some version of the same question: When a data center supplies its own power but remains connected to the grid, what does it owe the grid — and who gets to decide? The answer crosses multiple jurisdictions. State utility commissions govern retail service and utility territories; regional transmission organizations and independent system operators oversee interconnection and grid reliability; the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission regulates interstate transmission and wholesale power markets; and state and local agencies govern the permitting and operation of the generation assets themselves. The rules emerging from those overlapping authorities will help determine whether behind-the-meter power becomes a practical new path to data center capacity — or simply another form of grid-connected development carrying a different set of costs, responsibilities, and constraints. GPC Infrastructure’s Connor Stone discusses how grid constraints are pushing data center developers toward behind-the-meter generation — and how those assets could ultimately interact with the wider electric system. The Break From the Utility Model The electric grid evolved from localized generating systems into an interconnected network designed to share reserves, balance supply and demand, and spread the cost of long-lived infrastructure across a broad customer base. That evolution also established the utility model under which most customers — including large industrial users — buy power from a regulated provider responsible for planning and delivering the infrastructure needed to serve them. Data centers largely developed within that framework. A developer selected a site, the utility studied the load, the parties negotiated service and interconnection, and the utility built or upgraded the substations, transmission and distribution infrastructure required to bring the facility online. That model becomes more difficult when a single project requires hundreds of megawatts, expects to ramp quickly, and cannot wait years for transmission planning, permitting, equipment procurement and construction. artigo.texto: Interest in building hyperscale data centers in Arlington is minimal, but the city could see smaller facilities either through new construction or repurposing of existing infrastructure. Arlington City Council members were presented Tuesday with a report detailing the types of data centers that could operate in Arlington and the factors that guide where developers build the supercomputer hubs. The city’s unified development code does not currently outline how data centers would be permitted or which zoning districts the hubs would be categorized in, according to city documents. As a result, Arlington staffers may bring forward amendments to the city’s development code for the council’s consideration. According to city documents, the amendments would introduce standards on location, design and operations of data centers that protect nearby properties and neighborhoods while also accommodating economic development. Amendments involving data centers would also include regulations on lot sizing, building setbacks from homes, noise, water use and water discharge restrictions — including closed-loop system requirements. In this week’s meeting, Mayor Jim Ross said Arlington has not received much interest from companies to build or operate data centers. “We really don’t have any way to specifically guide them through the process, if they come up here, and make sure that they’re a good fit for us,” Ross said. Should the city receive interest from developers, stand-alone data centers would be interpreted by the city’s development code as a “high-impact use,” planning and development services director Gincy Thoppil told council members. “We might be at a point where somebody comes to us and we won’t have the right answers right away,” when developers look to build or operate data centers that do not require their own building, Thoppil explained. The hubs with the most compatible infrastructure to operate in Arlington are edge data centers: relatively small and decentralized facilities that are located close to end users, devices or systems to locally process data and support applications requiring rapid response, according to city documents. These data centers are designed to reduce delays in processing. Edge data centers support mobile and media customers or users. Unlike hyperscale or large facilities, edge data centers require less power, ranging between 100 kilowatts to 1 megawatt. A megawatt unit is enough to power about 250 homes during ERCOT’s peak hours. The smaller centers are also estimated to use between 1 to 2 acres of land if operating in their own building. The centers are likely already located at cell tower sites as equipment boxes rather than singular buildings. Enterprise facilities, another type of data center, have a high chance of coming to Arlington, according to city documents. They typically require between 5 to 10 acres and are primarily used by a single consumer or company for their own business use. That includes Arlington’s D.R. Horton data center located off Interstate 30. Arlington has a very low likelihood of seeing hyperscale data centers due to the city’s lack of land for industrial uses, city documents state. The city is about 95% built out, according to the Fort Worth Report’s previous coverage. The city’s existing warehouses or industrial buildings could be repurposed for data centers smaller in size. Hyperscale data centers are those owned and operated by large companies, such as Meta and Google. The facilities are designed to process major loads of data, including artificial intelligence, automation and storage, among other types of computing. While not expected in Arlington, hyperscale data centers already operate or are in the planning phase in other parts of North Texas, such as the current facilities operated by Meta in north Fort Worth and Google in Red Oak. High-performance computing data centers also have low odds of setting up shop in Arlington but are more likely to be considered. The technology consists of clusters of powerful processors that work in parallel to process massive data sets and solve complex problems, according to IBM. These types of centers have high cooling needs and can require between 5 to more than 50 megawatts of power, city documents show. UT Arlington’s supercomputer research hub in Fort Worth is considered a high-performance computing facility. The last of the data center types detailed in the city’s report are co-located facilities. The infrastructure is designed to house computing equipment shared by multiple tenants. Their probability of developing in Arlington is considered moderate, requiring between 15 to 20 acres of land. Nicole Lopez is the environment reporter for the Fort Worth Report. Contact her at nicole.lopez@fortworthreport.org. The Report’s environment coverage is supported by the Marilyn Brachman Hoffman Foundation. artigo.texto: Trump firma pacto voluntário de segurança com CEOs de IA e defende expansão de data centers O presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, afirmou nesta terça-feira (29) que executivos do setor de tecnologia concordaram em estabelecer padrões voluntários para a inteligência artificial e reiterou seu apoio à rápida expansão dos data centers, em meio a crescentes preocupações com a segurança da IA e com a crescente presença do setor nas comunidades. Trump fez essas declarações após se reunir com executivos do setor de tecnologia na Casa Branca. As empresas concordaram em trabalhar com “auditores independentes” para avaliar se os sistemas de IA estão funcionando conforme pretendido por seus desenvolvedores, de acordo com uma cópia do acordo publicada por Trump em sua rede social. As empresas também afirmaram que trabalharão para garantir que suas ferramentas de IA não “invadam ou acessem sistemas técnicos de maneiras indesejadas”. O governo enfrenta um escrutínio cada vez maior sobre os riscos apresentados pela IA avançada, depois que a OpenAI e a Anthropic relataram que seus agentes de IA haviam se rebelado e invadido os sistemas de outras empresas. Os data centers, que fornecem o poder de computação para treinar e executar modelos de IA, têm gerado oposição em comunidades por todo o país devido a preocupações com a demanda por eletricidade, custos de serviços públicos e outros impactos locais. A reação negativa representa um desafio político para os republicanos às vésperas das eleições de meio de mandato dos EUA, em 3 de novembro. “É quase como uma constituição, de certa forma”, disse Trump, referindo-se ao acordo entre as empresas. “E as pessoas mais importantes do mundo assinaram isso, e eu assinei como presidente. E isso realmente é uma forma de proteção.” O que começou como um almoço a portas fechadas com executivos do setor de tecnologia ganhou visibilidade pública quando Trump se juntou ao presidente da Câmara, Mike Johnson, e a um grupo de CEOs na entrada da Casa Branca, uma área raramente usada pelo presidente para falar com jornalistas. Ele respondeu a perguntas dos repórteres por cerca de 30 minutos sobre segurança da IA e outros temas, com os CEOs posicionados atrás dele. A cena incomum ocorreu em um momento em que a pressão sobre o governo para lidar com os riscos e a rápida disseminação da IA tem aumentado, e ressaltou a aliança que Trump cultivou com líderes do setor de tecnologia. Entre os executivos presentes na reunião estavam Greg Brockman, da OpenAI; Dario Amodei, da Anthropic; Mark Zuckerberg, da Meta; Sundar Pichai, do Google; e Jensen Huang, da Nvidia. Zuckerberg, chamado à frente do grupo de executivos bilionários por Trump para falar, disse que as empresas concordaram em desenvolver “controles internos robustos” para seus sistemas de IA. Trump afirmou que está considerando criar um conselho de 10 pessoas para fiscalizar a segurança das ferramentas de IA. Ele não especificou possíveis membros desse grupo. Acrescentou ainda que em breve nomearia um novo responsável para liderar as políticas da Casa Branca em matéria de IA. Aposta dobrada em data centers Questionado se estava preocupado com a possibilidade de seu apoio aos data centers prejudicar os republicanos em novembro, Trump disse que as empresas de tecnologia trabalhariam para deixar as comunidades “felizes” com a construção dos data centers. “Essas empresas grandes, poderosas, muito ricas e muito inteligentes vão fazer contribuições enormes para as comunidades”, disse Trump mais tarde aos repórteres reunidos na entrada da Casa Branca, cercado pelos executivos das empresas. Mas as empresas têm sido criticadas por não fazerem o suficiente para tornar a IA mais segura. Uma pesquisa nacional Reuters/Ipsos, realizada de 17 a 20 de setembro, mostra que cerca de 73% dos entrevistados temem que as empresas de IA não tenham feito o suficiente para impedir que a IA cause danos graves à sociedade, e 55% das pessoas afirmaram que seria bom desacelerar o desenvolvimento da IA. Executivos e investidores de empresas de IA estavam entre os maiores doadores individuais em 2025 para o MAGA Inc., um comitê de ação política alinhado ao presidente. Brockman, da OpenAI, e sua esposa, Anna Brockman, doaram juntos US$25 milhões ao comitê em 2025, de acordo com registros da Comissão Eleitoral Federal. Trump se reuniu com os CEOs no mesmo dia em que seus assessores anunciaram uma nova ferramenta de IA que, segundo eles, facilitará o uso dos serviços governamentais pelo público. Executivos do Vale do Silício participaram de um evento de lançamento da nova ferramenta, incluindo Dina Powell McCormick, da Meta, e Shaun Maguire, sócio da Sequoia Capital. O cofundador da Airbnb, Joe Gebbia, liderou o projeto da nova ferramenta. As empresas do Vale do Silício Google, SpaceX, Meta e 8VC foram listadas no programa do evento de lançamento como patrocinadoras. Trump, no evento de lançamento, afirmou que a ferramenta de IA não poderia, “em teoria, ser hackeada” por agentes mal-intencionados. Ele não apresentou evidências. Trump, nesta terça-feira, também instruiu as agências governamentais a usarem as palavras “superinteligência” em vez de “inteligência artificial” ao se referirem à tecnologia.

artigo.texto: WKYT Investigates: Kentucky Power says data centers could lower electric bills in eastern Kentucky Some Kentucky communities have passed moratoriums on data centers over utility bill concerns, but Kentucky Power says the opposite could be true ASHLAND, Ky. (WKYT) - Several Kentucky communities have passed moratoriums temporarily halting approval and construction of data centers, giving elected officials more time to understand how data centers work and what protections are needed. Some residents fear data centers will drive up their utility bills. “The energy of those data centers increases our electric bill as citizens,” said Nicole Merz, who lives in Nicholasville. However, Kentucky Power says data centers could actually lower electric bills for eastern Kentuckians. Coal decline has driven up costs Eastern Kentucky has faced decades of challenges, many driven by the decline of the coal industry. “Those challenges have sort of come to knock on the door of Kentucky Power and its customers,” said Amanda Clark, director of economic and business development for Kentucky Power. Kentucky has lost more than 19,000 coal-related jobs since 2009, and the number keeps falling. “Rates keep going up because we’re losing load and we’re losing customers,” Clark said. “As we add load and as we add customers, those rates get stabilized.” Large project could offset costs Kentucky Power says data centers are part of the solution. Bitcoin mining company TeraWulf announced plans to build a hyperscale data center in Kentucky Power’s service territory in Ashland. It will eventually need more than one gigawatt of electricity. “That equates to essentially all the other customers that we have in Kentucky Power service territory,” Clark said. “That’s a very large piece of those fixed costs. If you have one customer who’s paying 50% of the fixed costs of everything else, logic tells you that helps relieve rate pressures.” Without data centers, Clark said stabilizing Kentucky Power’s rates would require 175,000 new residential customers. “We have 162,000 right now,” Clark said. “So I need 175,000 new homes across our service territory. I need about 800 Hobby Lobbies and TJ Maxx stores. So in terms of how do we get there quicker, this is the path.” Sister company plans rate cuts in Indiana and Michigan In July, Kentucky Power’s sister company, Indiana Michigan Power, laid out a plan to lower rates for residential customers based on large load growth there. “What this looks like is we are lowering the base rate for our customers,” said Stephanny Smith, director of communications and engagements for Indiana Michigan Power. “If our customers look at their monthly bill, that base rate is one of the largest line items on their monthly bill. So we’re lowering that by five percent.” Smith said the move is only possible because data centers are covering a large share of fixed costs. Kentucky Power points to tariff protections Kentucky Power says it is protecting existing customers through its large load tariff, a framework large customers like data centers must follow before coming to the state. “We put those protections in place in tariff,” Clark said. “There’s no special contract. There’s no special rate for these customers. It is their fair share and then some. Any infrastructure upgrades, they’re paying for up front. If they decide to leave, they’re paying for that too.” Asked about critics who question whether Kentucky Power benefits financially from data centers coming into the state, Clark responded. “For us, yes, it’s load. Yes, it’s revenue,” Clark said. “That revenue directly affects every customer that we have. If we don’t do anything to affect that, those rates keep going up.” Public Service Commission points to executive order WKYT requested an interview with the Kentucky Public Service Commission for this story, but they were unavailable. In response to our request, the Kentucky Energy and Environment Cabinet sent us a statement. They pointed to Gov. Andy Beshear’s executive order protecting ratepayers, which requires the Public Service Commission to prohibit utility companies from increasing rates to recover costs caused by the development or operations of a data center. Read the full statement below: Last month, Gov. Beshear announced an executive order that protects ratepayers by requiring the Public Service Commission to prohibit utility companies from increasing rates to recover costs caused by the development or operations of a data center. The executive order also requires data center developers to submit an energy plan to the Energy and Environment Cabinet (EEC) showing how they will protect Kentucky families and businesses by not raising electric bills. The Public Service Commission reviews the rates and contracts that utilities use when serving large customers like data centers. These rates and contracts can include protections for ratepayers by: - Requiring data centers to pay their share of the costs associated with their electricity use. - Allowing the utility to reduce or temporarily stop the data center’s power during certain situations. - Requiring the data center to pay a deposit for expensive upgrades to the electric system. In addition to those ratepayer protections, Gov. Beshear’s executive order also directs EEC to deny any permitting applications where a data center would negatively impact air quality, water use, water quality, water supply, federal jurisdictional wetlands or natural resources, requires any data center project developer to pay their fair share of taxes, and requires developers to engage in a transparent dialogue with the communities they are seeking to join – ultimately leaving the final decisions up to local communities once all other requirements are met.
